(p-264) Sūrat al-A'rāf

﷽

﴿Alif. Lām. Mīm. Ṣād.﴾ ﴿A Book sent down to you, so let there be no tightness in your breast because of it, that you may warn by it, and as a reminder for the believers.﴾ ﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and do not follow other than Him as protectors. Little do you remember.﴾ [al-A'rāf: 3] ﴿How many a town We have destroyed; Our punishment came upon it by night, or while they were taking their midday rest.﴾ [al-A'rāf: 4] ﴿So their plea, when Our punishment came upon them, was only that they said, "Indeed, we were wrongdoers."﴾ [al-A'rāf: 5] ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers.﴾ [al-A'rāf: 6] ﴿Then We will relate to them with knowledge, for We were not absent.﴾ [al-A'rāf: 7] ﴿And the weighing that Day is the truth. Those whose scales are heavy, they are the successful.﴾ [al-A'rāf: 8] ﴿And those whose scales are light, they are the ones who have lost themselves, because they used to wrong Our signs.﴾ [al-A'rāf: 9] ﴿And We have certainly established you on the earth and made for you therein means of livelihood. Little do you give thanks.﴾ [al-A'rāf: 10] ﴿And We certainly created you, then gave you form, then said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," and they prostrated, except Iblīs; he was not among those who prostrated.﴾ [al-A'rāf: 11] ﴿He said, "What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?" He said, "I am better than him. You created me from fire and created him from clay."﴾ [al-A'rāf: 12] ﴿He said, "Then descend from it; it is not for you to be arrogant therein. So go out; indeed, you are among the humiliated."﴾ [al-A'rāf: 13] ﴿He said, "Reprieve me until the Day they are resurrected."﴾ [al-A'rāf: 14] ﴿He said, "Indeed, you are among those reprieved."﴾ [al-A'rāf: 15] ﴿He said, "Because You have led me astray, I will surely sit in ambush for them on Your straight path.﴾ [al-A'rāf: 16] ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them and behind them, and from their right and from their left, and You will not find most of them grateful."﴾ [al-A'rāf: 17] ﴿He said, "Go out from it, reviled and expelled. Whoever follows you among them, I will surely fill Hell with all of you."﴾ [al-A'rāf: 18] ﴿And, O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden, and eat from wherever you wish, but do not approach this tree, or you will be among the wrongdoers.﴾ [al-A'rāf: 19] ﴿Then Satan whispered to them to reveal to them what was concealed from them of their private parts, and said, "Your Lord has only forbidden you this tree, lest you become angels or become of the eternal."﴾ [al-A'rāf: 20] ﴿And he swore to them, "Indeed, I am to you among the sincere advisers."﴾ [al-A'rāf: 21] ﴿So he brought them down by deception. And when they tasted the tree, their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to fasten over themselves from the leaves of the Garden. And their Lord called to them, "Did I not forbid you from that tree and tell you that Satan is to you a clear enemy?"﴾ [al-A'rāf: 22] ﴿They said, "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers."﴾ [al-A'rāf: 23] ﴿He said, "Descend, some of you being enemies to others. And for you on the earth is a dwelling place and enjoyment for a time."﴾ [al-A'rāf: 24] ﴿He said, "Therein you will live, and therein you will die, and from it you will be brought forth."﴾ [al-A'rāf: 25] ﴿O children of Adam, We have certainly sent down to you clothing to cover your private parts and as adornment; but the clothing of righteousness, that is best. That is from the signs of Allah, that they may remember.﴾ [al-A'rāf: 26] ﴿O children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you as he removed your parents from the Garden, stripping them of their clothing to show them their private parts. Indeed, he sees you, he and his soldiers, from where you do not see them. Indeed, We have made the devils allies to those who do not believe.﴾ [al-A'rāf: 27]

Kam (كَمَ) is a simple noun, not compound, made up of the particle of comparison (kāf al-tashbīh) and the interrogative mā, whose alif is dropped because a preposition has entered upon it, and it becomes sukūn. It is like their saying lima (لِمَ), a combination that does not separate. It is compounded in the same way as in ka-ayyin (كَأيِّنٍ) with ayy. It comes as an interrogative and as a informative (khabariyyah), and the informative use occurs frequently in the Qur'an. Its specification (tamyīz) in the Qur'an comes only in the genitive with min. Its rulings in both of its kinds are mentioned in the books of grammar.

Al-qaylūlah: sleep at midday, and it is al-qā'ilah. This is what al-Layth said. Al-Azharī said: it is resting at midday when the heat is intense and there is no sleep. Al-Farrā' said: one says yaqīlu qaylūlatan, qaylan, qā'ilatan, and maqīlan, meaning he rested in the middle of the day.

Al-'aysh: life. 'Āsha ya'īshu 'aysh-an, ma'āsh-an, 'īshatan, ma'īshatan, ma'īshan. Ru'bah said:
"To you I complain of the hardship of livelihood, and of the struggle of days that have plucked my feathers."

Ghawā yaghwī ghayyan and ghawāyah: his affair became corrupt for him, and he himself became corrupt within himself. From this comes ghawā al-faṣīl: the young camel drank too much of its mother's milk until its insides were corrupted and it came close to perishing. It was said its origin is destruction, and from it is His saying: ﴿So they will meet error﴾ [Maryam: 59].

Al-shamā'il: (p-265) the plural of shimāl, which is a broken plural; its plural in the paucity form is ashmul. The poet said:
"He comes to her from the right and from the left."
Shimāl is applied to the left hand and to its side. Al-shamā'il is also the plural of shamāl, which is the wind. Al-shamā'il also means character traits; one says: he has good character (ḥasan al-shamā'il).

Dha'ama-hu: he blamed him; yadhha'uhu dha'man with the hamza silenced, and it is permissible to change the hamza into an alif. The poet said:
"I kept company with you when my eye had a veil over it, but when it cleared, I cut off my soul, blaming it."
In the proverb: "The beautiful woman will never lack blame." It was said: you wanted to disparage him, so you praised him. Al-Layth said: dha'amtahu means you belittled him. Ibn Qutaybah and Ibn al-Anbārī said: dha'ama and dhamma (both mean) to blame.

Daḥara: he banished him, removed him and expelled him, daḥūran. The poet said:
"I drove the sons of al-Ḥaṣīb away to Qudayd, though they had been people of pride and boasting."

Waswasa: he spoke a hidden speech repeating it. Al-waswās is the sound of ornaments, the whisper being likened to it. It is an intransitive verb that does not take an object, like wawalat and wa'wa'a. Ibn al-A'rābī said: rajulun muwaswis (with kasra on the waw), and one does not say muwaswas with fatḥa. Others said: one says muwaswas lahu and muwaswas ilayhi. Ru'bah said, describing a hunter:
"He whispered, calling sincerely upon the Lord of the daybreak; when the game drew near, he drew near the snare."
He means: when he sensed the game and wanted to shoot it, he whispered within himself whether he would miss or hit. Al-Azharī said: waswasa and warwara have the same meaning.

Naṣaḥa: he exerted effort in clarifying good. It is the opposite of ghashsha (to deceive), and it is transitive by itself and with the lām: naṣaḥtu Zaydan and naṣaḥtu li-Zaydin. It is unlikely that it takes one object directly and another with a preposition. Its origin is naṣaḥtu li-Zaydin al-thawb, meaning "I sewed the garment for Zayd," from their saying, contrary to those who went that way.

Dhāqa al-shay'a yadhūquhu dhawqan: he touched it with his tongue or mouth, and it is also applied to eating. Ṭafiqa, with kasra or fatḥa on the fā', and it is said ṭabbaqa with the bā', and it means akhadha; it is among the verbs of approximation (af'āl al-muqāraba).

Khaṣafa al-na'l: he placed one leather over another leather and joined the two with a strap. Al-khaṣf is stitching.

Al-rīsh is well known and belongs to birds; it is used in meanings that will be mentioned in the explanation of the compounds. They derived from it: rāshahu yarīshuhu. It was said al-rīsh is the verbal noun of rāsha.

Al-naz'a: removal and pulling with force.

﴿Alif. Lām. Mīm. Ṣād.﴾ ﴿A Book sent down to you, so let there be no tightness in your breast because of it, that you may warn by it, and as a reminder for the believers.﴾

This sūrah is entirely Meccan, according to Ibn 'Abbās, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, 'Ikrimah, 'Aṭā', Jābir ibn Zayd, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and others. Muqātil said: except His saying ﴿Ask them about the town﴾ [al-A'rāf: 163] up to His saying ﴿from their backs their offspring﴾ [al-A'rāf: 172], for that is Medinan. This was also related from Ibn 'Abbās. (p-266) It was also said: up to His saying ﴿when We lifted the mountain﴾ [al-A'rāf: 171].

The connection of this sūrah with what precedes it is that when He, exalted is He, mentioned His saying ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed, so follow it﴾ [al-An'ām: 155], and digressed from it to what follows, and up to His saying at the end of the sūrah ﴿And He it is who made you successors on the earth﴾ [al-An'ām: 165], and mentioned their being tested in what He gave them, and that cannot happen except through the legal obligations (al-takālīf al-shar'iyyah), He mentioned what the obligations depend upon, which is the Divine Book, and the command to follow it, as He commanded in His saying ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed, so follow it﴾ [al-An'ām: 155].

The discussion of these disjointed letters (al-ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭa'ah) at the beginning of the sūrah has been presented at the beginning of al-Baqarah, and what people conjectured about them was mentioned, and no evidence has been established for any of their explanations that specifies what they said. Here they added, because of the ṣād, that its meaning is: "I am Allah, the Knowing and the Distinguisher." This was related by Abū al-Ḍuḥā from Ibn 'Abbās, or: "al-Muṣawwir" (the Fashioner). This was said by al-Suddī. Or: "Allah, the King, the Helper." This was said by some. Or: "I am Allah, the One to whom is the return (al-maṣīr ilayya)," related by al-Māwardī. Or: "al-Maṣīr" is a book, so the yā' and the rā' were dropped by tarkhīm (apocope, a shortening of a word by dropping its final letters), and "al-Maṣ" was used to refer to al-Maṣīr. This was said by al-Tibrīzī. It was also said about it: "I am Allah, the Truthful." And it was said: its meaning is ﴿Did We not expand your breast?﴾ [al-Sharḥ: 1]. This was said by al-Kirmānī, who said: he suffices with part of the speech. These sayings about the disjointed letters, were it not that the exegetes filled their books with them, generation after generation, we would have turned away from mentioning them entirely, for mentioning them points to what should not be mentioned of the interpretations of the Bāṭiniyyah (esoteric sects) and the people of riddles and symbols.

His prohibiting that there be in his breast a tightness from it, i.e., from its cause, because of what it contains of the burdens of the message and conveying it to those who did not believe in a Book, nor believed in the validity of a message, and the imposition of its rulings upon people. These are difficult matters, and their meanings are burdensome for him. He attributed the prohibition to the tightness, and its meaning is prohibiting the addressee from exposing himself to tightness. This was more eloquent than prohibiting the addressee himself, because in it is the implication that if tightness were something prohibited, We would have prohibited it from you; so you, desist from it by not exposing yourself to it. Also, in it is an exaltation of His Prophet ﷺ, that He would not forbid him, for then the construction would be "do not be tight from it." For what Allah, exalted is He, sent down to him is fitting that he should be gladdened by it and his breast expanded by it, because of the specification of him with it, and the honor, in that He qualified him for the sending down of His Book upon him and made him an envoy between Him and His creation. Because of these benefits He turned away from forbidding him, and forbade the tightness.

Tightness here was explained as doubt, and this is an unsettled explanation. Doubt was called tightness because the doubter has a constricted breast, just as the one who is certain has an expanded breast. If this is authentically related from Ibn 'Abbās, then it is one of the matters in which the address is directed to him verbally, while it is meant for his community in meaning; that is, let them not doubt that it is from Allah.

Al-Ḥasan said: tightness here means constriction, i.e., let your breast not be constricted from conveying what you were sent with, out of fear that you may not fulfill its right. Al-Farrā' said: its meaning is: let your breast not be constricted by their denying you, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Perhaps you would destroy yourself with grief over their traces if they do not believe in this discourse﴾ [al-Kahf: 6]. It was also said: tightness here means fear, i.e., do not fear them even if they deny you and conspire against you. They said: it is possible that the address is to him and to his community. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "minhu" refers to the Book. It was also said it refers to the conveying which is implied by the meaning, and it was said it refers to the denial which is indicated by the meaning, and it was said it refers to the sending down, and it was said it refers to the warning. Ibn 'Aṭiyyah said: all this specification has no basis, for the wording is general to all the aspects that are a cause of the Book and for which it was sent, and that covers conveying, warning, the opposition of the polytheists, the denial of the deniers, and other things.

And ﴿so let there be no tightness in your breast because of it﴾ is an interjection (i'tirāḍ) in the middle of the speech (i'tirāḍ: a phrase inserted between parts of a sentence that are closely connected). For this reason some people said that there is in it a transposition (taqdīm wa-ta'khīr).

And (*li-tundhira*) is related to *unzila* (was sent down). End of quote. Likewise al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari said that the *lam* is related to His words: ﴿It has been sent down﴾ [al-A'raf: 3]. Before them, al-Farra' said the same. It follows from their view that His words ﴿so let there be no constraint in your breast﴾ would be an *i'tiraḍ* (interjected clause) between the governing element (*'amil*) and what it governs (*ma'mul*). Ibn al-Anbari said: the implied sense is, "so let there be no constraint in your breast about it, in order that you warn with it," and he thus made it related to what is related to *fi sadrika* (in your breast). Sahib al-Nazm (Ibn Fari') also linked it in this way. On this view, the clause is not an interjection. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa' both allowed the two readings. However, al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, to what does His words *li-tundhira* relate? I answer: to *unzila*, meaning it was sent down to you for your warning with it; or to the prohibition, [p. 267] because when he does not fear them, he warns them. For this reason, when he is certain that it is from God, certainty encourages him to warn, since the possessor of certainty is bold and relies on His protection." End of quote.

His statement "or to the prohibition" apparently means it relates to the prohibition, which is related to His words *fa-la yakun* (let there not be). The relation of a prepositional phrase and the action of a temporal adverb within it (*ta'alluq al-majrur wa-l-'amal fi al-zarf*) is disputed. The basis of the dispute is whether the defective verb *kana* (to be) signifies an event (*hadath*) or not. Whoever says it signifies an event allows it, and whoever says it does not signify an event does not allow it.

Al-Farra' and others parsed ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. Sad.﴾ as a subject (*mubtada'*) with ﴿a Book﴾ as its predicate (*khabar*). Some also parsed ﴿a Book﴾ as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "this is a Book." The word *dhikra* (reminder) is the verbal noun of *dhakara* with a light *kaf*. They allowed it to be in the nominative case, coordinated with *kitab*, or as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "and it is a reminder." It may be in the accusative as a verbal noun, by implying a verb coordinated with *li-tundhira*, meaning "and you remember a reminder." Or it may be accusative on the basis of the position of *li-tundhira*, since its position is accusative. In that case it is coordinated with the meaning, as the circumstantial clause (*hal*) is coordinated with the position of the prepositional phrase in His words: ﴿He calls Us for his side, or sitting, or standing﴾ [Yunus: 12]. It would then be an accusative of purpose (*maf'ul min ajlih*), as when you say: "I came to you for kindness and out of longing for you." The genitive case is based on the position of the particle *an* (to), the *li-tundhira* which combines with it and the verb to form a verbal noun, meaning: "for your warning with it and reminder." Some people said it is coordinated with the pronoun in *bihi* (with it), and this is a Kufan view. The alternation between the accusative and genitive is based on meaning. *Tadhkir* is the verbal noun of the intensive *dhakkara*.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: souls are of two kinds. One is ignorant, drowned in pursuing bodily pleasures. The other is noble, illuminated by divine lights, perceiving spiritual events. Prophets and messengers were sent to the first kind for warning and intimidation, since they were drowned in the sea of heedlessness and the sleep of ignorance and needed one to awaken and alert them. For the second kind they were sent for reminder and alertness, because these souls, by the nature of their original essences, sense an attraction to the world of holiness and a connection to the eternal presence. Yet sometimes the veils of the sensible world overcome them, and a kind of distraction occurs. When they hear the call of the prophets and the spirits of God's messengers connect with them, they remember their origin, perceive their source, and long for what they attained there of spirit, rest, and fragrance. Thus it is established that He, the Exalted, sent down the Book to His Messenger so that it would be a warning for one group and a reminder for another. This is a philosophical discourse outside the words of those who follow the Shari'ah. Such is the speech of this man; may God protect us from it.

Dhāqa al-shay'a yadhūquhu dhawqan: he touched it with his tongue or mouth, and it is also applied to eating. Ṭafiqa, with kasra or fatḥa on the fā', and it is said ṭabbaqa with the bā', and it means akhadha; it is among the verbs of approximation (af'āl al-muqāraba).

Khaṣafa al-na'l: he placed one leather over another leather and joined the two with a strap. Al-khaṣf is stitching.

Al-rīsh is well known and belongs to birds; it is used in meanings that will be mentioned in the explanation of the compounds. They derived from it: rāshahu yarīshuhu. It was said al-rīsh is the verbal noun of rāsha.

Al-naz'a: removal and pulling with force.

﴿Alif. Lām. Mīm. Ṣād.﴾ ﴿A Book sent down to you, so let there be no tightness in your breast because of it, that you may warn by it, and as a reminder for the believers.﴾

This sūrah is entirely Meccan, according to Ibn 'Abbās, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, 'Ikrimah, 'Aṭā', Jābir ibn Zayd, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and others. Muqātil said: except His saying ﴿Ask them about the town﴾ [al-A'rāf: 163] up to His saying ﴿from their backs their offspring﴾ [al-A'rāf: 172], for that is Medinan. This was also related from Ibn 'Abbās. (p-266) It was also said: up to His saying ﴿when We lifted the mountain﴾ [al-A'rāf: 171].

The connection of this sūrah with what precedes it is that when He, exalted is He, mentioned His saying ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed, so follow it﴾ [al-An'ām: 155], and digressed from it to what follows, and up to His saying at the end of the sūrah ﴿And He it is who made you successors on the earth﴾ [al-An'ām: 165], and mentioned their being tested in what He gave them, and that cannot happen except through the legal obligations (al-takālīf al-shar'iyyah), He mentioned what the obligations depend upon, which is the Divine Book, and the command to follow it, as He commanded in His saying ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed, so follow it﴾ [al-An'ām: 155].

The discussion of these disjointed letters (al-ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭa'ah) at the beginning of the sūrah has been presented at the beginning of al-Baqarah, and what people conjectured about them was mentioned, and no evidence has been established for any of their explanations that specifies what they said. Here they added, because of the ṣād, that its meaning is: "I am Allah, the Knowing and the Distinguisher." This was related by Abū al-Ḍuḥā from Ibn 'Abbās, or: "al-Muṣawwir" (the Fashioner). This was said by al-Suddī. Or: "Allah, the King, the Helper." This was said by some. Or: "I am Allah, the One to whom is the return (al-maṣīr ilayya)," related by al-Māwardī. Or: "al-Maṣīr" is a book, so the yā' and the rā' were dropped by tarkhīm (apocope, a shortening of a word by dropping its final letters), and "al-Maṣ" was used to refer to al-Maṣīr. This was said by al-Tibrīzī. It was also said about it: "I am Allah, the Truthful." And it was said: its meaning is ﴿Did We not expand your breast?﴾ [al-Sharḥ: 1]. This was said by al-Kirmānī, who said: he suffices with part of the speech. These sayings about the disjointed letters, were it not that the exegetes filled their books with them, generation after generation, we would have turned away from mentioning them entirely, for mentioning them points to what should not be mentioned of the interpretations of the Bāṭiniyyah (esoteric sects) and the people of riddles and symbols.

His prohibiting that there be in his breast a tightness from it, i.e., from its cause, because of what it contains of the burdens of the message and conveying it to those who did not believe in a Book, nor believed in the validity of a message, and the imposition of its rulings upon people. These are difficult matters, and their meanings are burdensome for him. He attributed the prohibition to the tightness, and its meaning is prohibiting the addressee from exposing himself to tightness. This was more eloquent than prohibiting the addressee himself, because in it is the implication that if tightness were something prohibited, We would have prohibited it from you; so you, desist from it by not exposing yourself to it. Also, in it is an exaltation of His Prophet ﷺ, that He would not forbid him, for then the construction would be "do not be tight from it." For what Allah, exalted is He, sent down to him is fitting that he should be gladdened by it and his breast expanded by it, because of the specification of him with it, and the honor, in that He qualified him for the sending down of His Book upon him and made him an envoy between Him and His creation. Because of these benefits He turned away from forbidding him, and forbade the tightness.

Tightness here was explained as doubt, and this is an unsettled explanation. Doubt was called tightness because the doubter has a constricted breast, just as the one who is certain has an expanded breast. If this is authentically related from Ibn 'Abbās, then it is one of the matters in which the address is directed to him verbally, while it is meant for his community in meaning; that is, let them not doubt that it is from Allah.

Al-Ḥasan said: tightness here means constriction, i.e., let your breast not be constricted from conveying what you were sent with, out of fear that you may not fulfill its right. Al-Farrā' said: its meaning is: let your breast not be constricted by their denying you, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Perhaps you would destroy yourself with grief over their traces if they do not believe in this discourse﴾ [al-Kahf: 6]. It was also said: tightness here means fear, i.e., do not fear them even if they deny you and conspire against you. They said: it is possible that the address is to him and to his community. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in "minhu" refers to the Book. It was also said it refers to the conveying which is implied by the meaning, and it was said it refers to the denial which is indicated by the meaning, and it was said it refers to the sending down, and it was said it refers to the warning. Ibn 'Aṭiyyah said: all this specification has no basis, for the wording is general to all the aspects that are a cause of the Book and for which it was sent, and that covers conveying, warning, the opposition of the polytheists, the denial of the deniers, and other things.

And ﴿so let there be no tightness in your breast because of it﴾ is an interjection (i'tirāḍ) in the middle of the speech (i'tirāḍ: a phrase inserted between parts of a sentence that are closely connected). For this reason some people said that there is in it a transposition (taqdīm wa-ta'khīr).

And (*li-tundhira*) is related to *unzila* (was sent down). End of quote. Likewise al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari said that the *lam* is related to His words: ﴿It has been sent down﴾ [al-A'raf: 3]. Before them, al-Farra' said the same. It follows from their view that His words ﴿so let there be no constraint in your breast﴾ would be an *i'tiraḍ* (interjected clause) between the governing element (*'amil*) and what it governs (*ma'mul*). Ibn al-Anbari said: the implied sense is, "so let there be no constraint in your breast about it, in order that you warn with it," and he thus made it related to what is related to *fi sadrika* (in your breast). Sahib al-Nazm (Ibn Fari') also linked it in this way. On this view, the clause is not an interjection. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa' both allowed the two readings. However, al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, to what does His words *li-tundhira* relate? I answer: to *unzila*, meaning it was sent down to you for your warning with it; or to the prohibition, [p. 267] because when he does not fear them, he warns them. For this reason, when he is certain that it is from God, certainty encourages him to warn, since the possessor of certainty is bold and relies on His protection." End of quote.

His statement "or to the prohibition" apparently means it relates to the prohibition, which is related to His words *fa-la yakun* (let there not be). The relation of a prepositional phrase and the action of a temporal adverb within it (*ta'alluq al-majrur wa-l-'amal fi al-zarf*) is disputed. The basis of the dispute is whether the defective verb *kana* (to be) signifies an event (*hadath*) or not. Whoever says it signifies an event allows it, and whoever says it does not signify an event does not allow it.

Al-Farra' and others parsed ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim. Sad.﴾ as a subject (*mubtada'*) with ﴿a Book﴾ as its predicate (*khabar*). Some also parsed ﴿a Book﴾ as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "this is a Book." The word *dhikra* (reminder) is the verbal noun of *dhakara* with a light *kaf*. They allowed it to be in the nominative case, coordinated with *kitab*, or as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "and it is a reminder." It may be in the accusative as a verbal noun, by implying a verb coordinated with *li-tundhira*, meaning "and you remember a reminder." Or it may be accusative on the basis of the position of *li-tundhira*, since its position is accusative. In that case it is coordinated with the meaning, as the circumstantial clause (*hal*) is coordinated with the position of the prepositional phrase in His words: ﴿He calls Us for his side, or sitting, or standing﴾ [Yunus: 12]. It would then be an accusative of purpose (*maf'ul min ajlih*), as when you say: "I came to you for kindness and out of longing for you." The genitive case is based on the position of the particle *an* (to), the *li-tundhira* which combines with it and the verb to form a verbal noun, meaning: "for your warning with it and reminder." Some people said it is coordinated with the pronoun in *bihi* (with it), and this is a Kufan view. The alternation between the accusative and genitive is based on meaning. *Tadhkir* is the verbal noun of the intensive *dhakkara*.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: souls are of two kinds. One is ignorant, drowned in pursuing bodily pleasures. The other is noble, illuminated by divine lights, perceiving spiritual events. Prophets and messengers were sent to the first kind for warning and intimidation, since they were drowned in the sea of heedlessness and the sleep of ignorance and needed one to awaken and alert them. For the second kind they were sent for reminder and alertness, because these souls, by the nature of their original essences, sense an attraction to the world of holiness and a connection to the eternal presence. Yet sometimes the veils of the sensible world overcome them, and a kind of distraction occurs. When they hear the call of the prophets and the spirits of God's messengers connect with them, they remember their origin, perceive their source, and long for what they attained there of spirit, rest, and fragrance. Thus it is established that He, the Exalted, sent down the Book to His Messenger so that it would be a warning for one group and a reminder for another. This is a philosophical discourse outside the words of those who follow the Shari'ah. Such is the speech of this man; may God protect us from it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 3:

﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and do not follow other than Him as protectors. Little do you take heed.﴾ When the Exalted mentioned that this Book was sent down to the Messenger, He commanded the community to follow it. "What has been sent down to you" includes the Qur'an and the Sunnah, based on His saying: ﴿Nor does he speak from desire. It is not but a revelation revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 3-4]. He also forbade them from seeking protectors other than Allah, such as idols, monks, soothsayers, rabbis, fire, stars, and other things.

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿other than Him﴾ refers to "your Lord." It has also been said that it refers to "what" (i.e., what was sent down), and it has been said that it refers to the Book. The meaning is: do not turn away from it toward the abrogated scriptures. It has also been said that by "protectors" is meant the devils, the devils of jinn and mankind, who are the ones who drive people to worship idols, to follow desires and innovations, and who lead them astray from the religion of Allah.

Al-Jahdari read: "ibtaghu" (seek), from al-ibtigha'. Mujahid and Malik ibn Dinar read: "wa la tabtaghu" (and do not seek), also from al-ibtigha'. The apparent reading is that the address is to all people.

Al-Tabari, and he related it, said the implied sense is: "Say: follow," so the word "say" was omitted, because of the preceding warning which indicates it. ﴿Little﴾ is in the accusative as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, and "ma" is redundant, meaning: they take heed a little, i.e., in that they abandon the religion of Allah and follow other than it.

Al-Hawfi permitted that it be an attribute of an omitted verbal noun whose governing verb is "wa la tattabi'u" (and do not follow), meaning: a little following. Ibn 'Atiyyah related from al-Farisi that "ma" is a relative pronoun joined to the verb and is verbal-nominal (masdariyya). He ended there. Others completed this analysis by making "qalilan" in the accusative as an attribute of an omitted adverb of time, meaning: a little time, "we remind you," informing that they do not claim remembrance; it only occurs to them in a short time. And "ma tadhakkarun" is in the nominative position as a subject, with the adverbial phrase before it in the position of the predicate. He who held that "ma" is a negation was far from the mark.

Hafs and the two brothers (al-Akhawan) read ﴿tadhakkarun﴾ with a single "ta" and a lightened "dhal." Ibn 'Amir read "yatadhakkarun" with "ya" and "ta" and a lightened "dhal." The rest of the seven read with the "ta" of address and a doubled "dhal." Abu al-Darda', Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn 'Amir in one narration read with two "ta"s. Mujahid read with "ya" and a doubled "dhal."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 4:

﴿How many a town We have destroyed! Our punishment came upon it by night, or while they were resting at noon.﴾

Here "kam" (how many) is informative (khabariyyah, a quantifier meaning "many"). The implied meaning is: "And many of the towns We destroyed." The pronoun in "ahlaknaha" (We destroyed it) refers back to the meaning of "kam," and "kam" is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'). "Ahlaknaha" is a clause in the position of the predicate (khabar). Some have allowed that it is in the accusative position, with a verb implied that is explained by "ahlaknaha," the estimated meaning being: "And how many a town We destroyed."

In the verse there must be an implied word, a genitive modifier (mudaf) before "aw hum qa'ilun" (or while they were resting). Some estimate it as "how many of the people of a town," and others estimate it as "We destroyed its people." It is better to estimate it at "fajaahaa," meaning "fajaa'a ahlaha" (its people came upon it), with the phrase being a circumstantial clause (hal) of the people of the town, as per the indication of "aw hum qa'ilun." This is because the towns can be destroyed by sinking into the earth, by collapse, and other means, so there is no necessity to delete the modifier before "fajaahaa."

Ibn Abi Abla recited "wa kam min qaryatin ahlaknaha fajaahaa," so the modifier is estimated as "wa kam min ahli qaryatin" (and how many of the people of a town). It is necessary to estimate a deleted descriptive adjective for "qaryah" (town), meaning "min qaryatin 'asiyah" (from a disobedient town). The arrival of the punishment is followed by the occurrence of the destruction, which cannot be conceived; therefore there must be a figurative usage, either in the verb, meaning that "ahlaknaha" is taken to mean "We intended to destroy it" or "We decreed its destruction," or the two meanings differ, meaning "We destroyed it through abandonment and lack of success, then Our punishment came upon it after that." Or the figurative usage may be in the particle "fa" (then), meaning it is used in the sense of "wa" (and), which is weak, or it is used only to indicate the order of the statement, as if He informed about many towns that He destroyed them, then said: "so there came upon them the punishment."

Al-Farra' said: the destruction is the arrival of the punishment, and the arrival of the punishment is the destruction. Since the two are inseparable, it does not matter which is mentioned first in rank, just as you say, "He insulted me, so he did wrong, and he did wrong, so he insulted me," because wrongdoing and insult are one thing.

It has also been said that "fa" is not for sequence but for explanation, like the saying, "He performed ablution, so he washed such-and-such, then such-and-such." "Bayatan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial (hal) and is a verbal noun, meaning "fajaahaa ba'suna" (Our punishment came upon it) while they were spending the night or while they were resting. Here "aw" (or) is for enumeration (tanwi'), meaning that it came at one time at night, like the people of Lut, and at another time at midday rest, like the people of Shu'ayb. This is an unfolding (nashr) of what was folded (laff) in "fajaahaa." The arrival of punishment was specified for these two times because they are times of quiet, ease and rest, so the arrival of punishment in them is more severe and more painful, and because the arrival occurs while the destroyed are heedless, so it is like arrival suddenly.

His saying, "aw hum qa'ilun" (or they were resting at midday), is a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal). Our companions (the Basran grammarians) stated that when the conjunction "wa" (and) enters upon a circumstantial clause, the circumstantial "wa" cannot enter upon it, so it is not permitted to say, "Zayd came walking while he was riding."

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "One does not say, 'Zayd came, he is a horseman,' without a 'wa,'" then what about the saying of the Exalted: "aw hum qa'ilun"? I say: some grammarians estimated the "wa" as deleted, but al-Zajjaj rejected this and said: If you say, "Zayd came to me on foot, or he is a horseman," or "Zayd came to me, he is a horseman," there is no need for a "wa" in it, because the pronoun has returned to the first noun. The correct view is that when it is coordinated with a circumstantial phrase before it, the "wa" is deleted to avoid the heaviness of two coordinating particles together, because the circumstantial "wa" is the coordinating "wa" borrowed for connection. So your saying, "Zayd came walking, or he is a horseman," is an eloquent sentence that conforms to its rule, but "Zayd came to me, he is a horseman" is faulty. End of quote.

As for "some grammarians" whom al-Zamakhshari accused, it is al-Farra'. As for al-Zajjaj's statement regarding the two examples, that there is no need for a "wa" because the pronoun has returned to the first noun, it contains ambiguity. Its determination is that it is not permissible for the "wa" to enter the first example, but it is permissible for it to enter the second example. So the absence of the need is not on the same footing, because in the first it is due to the impermissibility of the entry, while in the second it is due to frequent entry, not its impermissibility. As for al-Zamakhshari's statement, "and the correct view is that..." to the end, his reasoning is not correct, because the circumstantial "wa" is not a coordinating particle, so its mention would not entail two coordinating particles together. For if it were coordinating, it would necessarily follow that what precedes the "wa" is a circumstantial phrase, so that a circumstantial clause is coordinated upon a circumstantial phrase. Therefore its occurrence in a place where it cannot be a circumstantial phrase is evidence that it is not a coordinating "wa," and no meaning of a coordinating "wa" is intended in it. You say, "Zayd came while the sun was rising," so "Zayd came" is not a circumstantial phrase upon which a circumstantial clause could be coordinated. Rather, this "wa" is in every case different from the coordinating "wa." It is a type of "wa" among its types, as it also comes for the oath, and it is not for coordination in it, when you say, "By God, he will surely go out." As for his saying, "so it is faulty," it is not faulty. That is because he based it on the principle that if the nominal clause contains a pronoun referring to the circumstantial noun, then deleting the "wa" from it is anomalous. He followed al-Farra' in this, but it is not anomalous. Rather, its occurrence in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech, both prose and verse, is frequent, and it is more numerous than the sand of Bireen and the wild cattle of Filastin. We have mentioned the frequency of this in the commentary on al-Tashil. Al-Zamakhshari himself returned from this view to the view of the majority.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 5:

﴿So their claim was not, when Our punishment came upon them, except that they said, "Indeed we were wrongdoers."﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Their claim (daʿwaahum) was their supplication (tadarruʿuhum), except their acknowledgment of association (ishrak)." It was also said: "Their claim" means "their supplication" (duʿaaʾuhum). Al-Khalil said: "It means they say, 'O Allah, include us among the good supplications of the Muslims,' and from this comes the phrase, 'So that claim of theirs never ceased.'" It was also said: it means "their pretension" (iddiʿaaʾuhum), i.e., they put forward excuses which would improve their situation and establish their argument in their own opinion. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: The verse may also mean: "Their claims which they had in the state of disbelief did not end except in admission," and from this is the saying of the poet:

"Qays witnessed, yet its support for Qutayba was nothing but biting its fingers with its thumbs."

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is also permissible to read it as: "Their appeal for help was nothing except this their saying," because there is no one to seek help from besides Allah, from their saying "daʿwaahum bil-kaʿb" (they cried out for help with the ankle-bone). They said: "Daʿwaahum" is the subject of "kaana" (the predicate being) "illa an qaaluu," and they permitted the reverse. The first is what the statements of the later scholars require, that it is not permissible except this: that "daʿwaahum" is the noun (ism) and "illa an qaaluu" is the predicate (khabar), because when there is no verbal indicator nor semantic indicator clarifying the agent from the object, it is obligatory to place the agent first and delay the object, as in: "Musa struck ʿIsa." Kaana and its sisters are, in their function, analogous to a verb that transitively takes one object, so just as this is obligatory in that case, it is obligatory in the analogue, which is kaana and "daʿwaahum." And "illa an qaaluu" shows no verbal indicator in either of them that distinguishes the noun from the predicate, nor any semantic one, so it is necessary that the preceding element be the noun and the following element the predicate.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 6–7:

﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers.﴾ (p-270) That is: We will question the nations to whom messengers were sent about their deeds and about what the messengers conveyed to them, in accordance with His saying: ﴿And on the Day He calls them and says, "What was your response to the messengers?"﴾ [al-Qasas: 65]. And the messengers will be questioned about what their nations responded to them, as in His saying: ﴿On the Day when Allah will gather the messengers and say, "What was your response?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 109]. The questioning of the nations is a reproach and rebuke that is followed by punishment for the disbelievers and the disobedient, while the questioning of the messengers is a comforting that is followed by reward and honour for the prophets. The questioning has come both negated and affirmed according to the occasions, or according to the modes, such as the questioning of rebuke and the questioning of comfort. Questioning for pure information is negated of Allah, Exalted, since He encompasses everything in knowledge. It has been said that those to whom messengers were sent are the prophets and the messengers are the angels, but this is far-fetched.

﴿So We will surely relate to them with knowledge, and We were not absent.﴾ That is: We will recount to them their deeds story by story, ﴿with knowledge﴾ from Us concerning that and awareness of it, ﴿and We were not absent﴾ from anything of it. Rather, Our knowledge encompasses all their deeds, outward and inward. This is among the greatest of reproach and rebuke, since they will acknowledge the wrong they did, their prophets will bear witness against them, and Allah will relate to them their deeds. Wahb said: It will be said to one of them, "Do you remember the day you did such and such? Do you remember the time you said such and such?" until it reaches the last of what he did and said in his worldly life. In His saying ﴿with knowledge﴾ there is evidence for affirming this attribute of Allah, Exalted, and a refutation of the view of one who says that Allah has no knowledge.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 6–7:

﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers.﴾ (p-270) That is: We will question the nations to whom messengers were sent about their deeds and about what the messengers conveyed to them, in accordance with His saying: ﴿And on the Day He calls them and says, "What was your response to the messengers?"﴾ [al-Qasas: 65]. And the messengers will be questioned about what their nations responded to them, as in His saying: ﴿On the Day when Allah will gather the messengers and say, "What was your response?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 109]. The weighing on that Day is the truth. As for those whose scales are heavy, they are the successful. And as for those whose scales are light, they are the ones who have lost their souls because they wronged Our signs. ﴿Al-Aʿraf 7:8–9﴾

They differed over whether there is, in reality, a weighing and a balance (mizan), or whether this is an expression for the manifestation of perfect justice, the fair judgment, and the precise reckoning. The Mu'tazila (a theological school that denied the literal balance) held that the balance does not exist, and before them Mujahid, al-Dahhak, al-A'mash and others held this view. They took "heaviness" to mean the abundance of good deeds and "lightness" to mean their scarcity. But the majority of the Muslim community held the first view, that the balance is real, with a pillar, two pans and a pointer. This is what the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and the Sunna indicates. The creatures will look at it to strengthen the proof, to show fairness, and to cut off excuses, just as Allah asks them about their deeds and they acknowledge them with their tongues, while their hands and feet bear witness against them, and the prophets, the angels and the witnesses bear witness against them. As for heaviness and lightness, they are attributes of bodies. It has been reported that what is weighed is the scrolls on which the deeds are recorded, and Allah Most High then causes heaviness and lightness in them. What has been reported about its form, its length and its conditions has not been soundly transmitted. The word "mawazin" (scales) is plural in view of the things weighed, while the balance (mizan) is singular. This is the view of the majority. Al-Hasan said: "For every person on the Day of Resurrection there is a separate balance." Good deeds are sometimes referred to as "mawazin," and in that case there is an ellipsis of a noun, meaning: "whoever's pan of scales is heavy," that is, "whoever's weighed items are heavy," so "mawazin" is the plural of "mawzun" (weighed item), not the plural of "mizan." Likewise: "whoever's good deeds' pan is light." The word "al-wazn" (the weighing) is the subject, and its predicate is the adverbial phrase of time. The estimated meaning is: "the weighing will be occurring [p. 271] on the day when We question them and recount to them," and that is the Day of Resurrection. "Al-haqq" (the truth) is an attribute of the weighed items. It is also permissible for "yawmaʾidhin" (on that day) to be an adverb of time governed by "al-wazn" (the weighing), and "al-haqq" to be the predicate. "Bi-ayatina" (with Our signs) is connected to "yazlimun" (they wrong), because it includes the meaning of "yukadhdhibun" (they deny), or because it has the meaning of "yajhadun" (they reject), and "jahada" takes the preposition "bi," as in ﴿and they rejected them﴾ (al-Naml 27:14). The apparent meaning is that this division applies to believers, those who obeyed and those who disobeyed, and to disbelievers, whose deeds are weighed. Some people said: no scale is set up for them and they are not reckoned, based on His saying: ﴿And We will turn to the deeds they did and make them scattered dust﴾ (al-Furqan 25:23). They said that only the deeds of the believer, whether obedient or disobedient, are weighed.

The weighing on that Day is the truth. As for those whose scales are heavy, they are the successful. And as for those whose scales are light, they are the ones who have lost their souls because they wronged Our signs. ﴿Al-Aʿraf 7:8–9﴾

They differed over whether there is, in reality, a weighing and a balance (mizan), or whether this is an expression for the manifestation of perfect justice, the fair judgment, and the precise reckoning. The Mu'tazila (a theological school that denied the literal balance) held that the balance does not exist, and before them Mujahid, al-Dahhak, al-A'mash and others held this view. They took "heaviness" to mean the abundance of good deeds and "lightness" to mean their scarcity. But the majority of the Muslim community held the first view, that the balance is real, with a pillar, two pans and a pointer. This is what the apparent meaning of the Qur'an and the Sunna indicates. The creatures will look at it to strengthen the proof, to show fairness, and to cut off excuses, just as Allah asks them about their deeds and they acknowledge them with their tongues, while their hands and feet bear witness against them, and the prophets, the angels and the witnesses bear witness against them. As for heaviness and lightness, they are attributes of bodies. It has been reported that what is weighed is the scrolls on which the deeds are recorded, and Allah Most High then causes heaviness and lightness in them. What has been reported about its form, its length and its conditions has not been soundly transmitted. The word "mawazin" (scales) is plural in view of the things weighed, while the balance (mizan) is singular. This is the view of the majority. Al-Hasan said: "For every person on the Day of Resurrection there is a separate balance." Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 10:

﴿And We had certainly established you upon the earth and made for you therein means of livelihood. Little are you grateful.﴾ The meaning of ﴿We established you﴾ (makkannakum) has already been explained in His saying at the beginning of al-An'am: ﴿We established them upon the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 6]. The address returns to those who were addressed by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 3]. What lies between them is presented as a matter of reflection (i'tibar) and awakening, by mentioning what their affair came to in this world and what it will lead to in the Hereafter.

Al-ma'ayish is the plural of ma'ishah (livelihood), and its pattern may be either mafi'ala or maf'ula, with the ayn vowelled with kasra or damma. This is what Sibawayh stated. Al-Farra' said: ma'ishah with a fatha on the ayn of the word. Al-ma'ishah is that by which one lives, such as food, drink and other things by which one attains that. Originally it is a verbal noun (masdar) that has been treated as the instruments (of living). It has also been said that there is an elided modifier, the sense being: "means (asbab) of livelihoods," such as farming, harvesting, trade and what goes in that direction, and it is called ma'ayish because it is a means to that by which one lives. It has also been said that al-ma'ayish are the aspects of benefits, which are either what God brings into being from the outset, such as fruits, or what He brings about through acquisition from the enemy; both require gratitude.

The majority read ﻣَﻌﺎﻳِﺶَ (ma'ayish) with a yā', and this is the analogical reading, because the yā' in the singular is original, not an added letter, and an added letter is only hamzated, as in ﺻَﺤﺎﺋِﻒُ (sahaif) from ﺻَﺤِﻴﻔَﺔٌ (sahifah). Al-A'raj, Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-A'mash, and Kharijah on the authority of Nafi', and Ibn 'Amir in one transmission, read ﻣَﻌﺎﺋِﺶَ (ma'a'ish) with a hamza. This is not analogical, but they transmitted it, and they are trustworthy, so its acceptance is obligatory; this hamza is anomalous, just as it is anomalous in manayir, the plural of manarah, whose original form is manawrah, and in masa'ib, the plural of musibah, whose original form is musawbah; the analogical forms would be manawir and masawib. They have also said masawib in accordance with the original, just as they said maqawim as the plural of maqamah and ma'awin as the plural of ma'unah. Al-Zajjaj said: all the grammarians of Basra claim that its hamza is an error, and I know of no justification for it except the analogy with sahifah and sahaif, and this reading should not be relied upon. Al-Mazini said: the origin of taking this reading is from Nafi', and he did not know what Arabic was, and the sound speech of the Arabs regarding such things is (otherwise). End of quote. We are not bound by the opinions of the grammarians of Basra. Al-Farra' said: the Arabs have perhaps hamzated this and similar forms, imagining that it is fa'ila, so they liken mufi'lah to fa'ilah. End of quote. This is a report from al-Farra' from the Arabs that they sometimes hamzate this and similar forms, and it was transmitted by the trustworthy transmitters of the reading, Ibn 'Amir, who is a pure Arab, and who took the Qur'an from 'Uthman before the appearance of solecism; al-A'raj, who is among the great Successor reciters; Zayd ibn 'Ali, who is of such eloquence and knowledge of standing that few can approach him in this; al-A'mash, who is of such precision, mastery, memorisation and trustworthiness; and Nafi', who recited to seventy of the Successors, and they are of such eloquence, precision and trustworthiness that their standing is not unknown. Therefore the acceptance of what they transmitted to us is obligatory, and there is no regard for the disagreement of the grammarians of Basra in such a matter. As for al-Mazini's statement that the origin of taking this reading is from Nafi', it is not correct, because it was transmitted from Ibn 'Amir, from al-A'raj, from Zayd ibn 'Ali, and from al-A'mash. As for his statement that Nafi' did not know what Arabic was, it is a testimony of negation; and even if we supposed that he did not know what Arabic was, meaning this discipline by which one attains speaking the language of the Arabs, it would not necessarily follow, since he was eloquent, speaking Arabic, transmitting the reading from the eloquent Arabs. Many of these grammarians slander the reciters, and that is not permissible for them.

The parsing of ﴿qalilan ma tashkurun﴾ (little are you grateful) is like the parsing of ﴿qalilan ma tadhakkarun﴾ [al-A'raf: 3].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 11:

﴿And We certainly created you, then We fashioned you, then We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," and they prostrated, except Iblis; he was not among those who prostrated.﴾

When what indicates the division of the responsible beings (al-mukallafun) into the obedient and the disobedient had preceded, for the obedient one carries out what Allah has commanded and avoids what He has forbidden, while the disobedient one does the opposite, [the verse] began to draw attention to the fact that this division occurred at the very first beginning of Allah's command to the angels to prostrate: whoever complied complied, and whoever refused refused. It also [draws attention to the fact] that the Exalted commanded Adam and forbade him, and then it relates his account, which will come. So it first draws attention to the place of reflection (i'tibar), namely the bringing of a thing from pure non-existence (al-'adam al-sirf) into existence, and the fashioning of it in this strange form, which is capable of the wonders of the Maker.

The apparent meaning is that the address is general to all the children of Adam, and it would be [in the sense] of His saying, "thumma qulna" (then We said) [as follows]: "thumma" may be in the sense of "wa" (and), so it does not indicate sequence, and the sequence would be between the creating and the fashioning. Or "thumma" in "thumma qulna" is for sequence in the reporting, not in time; and this is the easiest interpretation of the verse. Among them is one who took "thumma" to indicate sequence in time, and they differed regarding the addressee. It was said that what is meant is Adam, and this is from the use of the plural for the singular. It was said that what is meant is his offspring. According to the first view, the address in both clauses is to Adam, because the Arabs address a single great person with the address of the plural. It was said that the address in the first is to Adam and in the second to his progeny, so a interval occurs between them, and the third "thumma" is for the sequence of the reporting. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. It was also said: "We created you" refers to Adam, and "then We fashioned you" refers to his sons, meaning in his loins at the taking of the covenant; "then We said" – then the sequence falls in its proper place. According to the second view, that the address is to the children of Adam, it was said: the address is on its apparent basis, even though the place of creating and fashioning differs. al-Harith narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "We created you in the back of Adam; then We fashioned you in the wombs." Ibn Jubayr said from him: "We created you in the loins of men; then We fashioned you in the wombs of women." This was also said by 'Ikrimah, Qatadah, al-Dahhak and al-A'mash. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: "We created you as drops (nutfan) in the loins of men and the breastbones of women; then We fashioned you when the drops came together in the wombs." Ma'mar ibn Rashid, relating from some of the people of knowledge, said: "We created you in the bellies of your mothers, and fashioned you therein after the creating, splitting the hearing and the sight." "Thumma" in "thumma qulna" according to these views is for sequence in the reporting. It was also said that the address is to the children of Adam, but with the omission of a modifier; the estimate: "We certainly created your spirits (arwahakum), then We fashioned your bodies (ajsamakum)." This was related by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la in al-Mu'tamad, and "thumma" in "thumma qulna" is for sequence in the reporting. It was said, the estimate: "We certainly created your father, then We fashioned your father, then We said" – so "thumma" in this view is for temporal sequence and interval in its original use. It was also said that it is a shift in address (talwin al-khitab): he addresses the present person while meaning another, so the address is to the children of Adam while Adam is meant, like His saying: ﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾ [al-Baqarah: 49]; ﴿So the thunderbolt seized you while you were looking﴾ [al-Baqarah: 55]; ﴿And when you killed a soul﴾ [al-Baqarah: 72]. The address is to those among the Children of Israel who were present with the Messenger, while their ancestors are meant. From this is the saying of the poet:

When Tamim boasts one day of its bow, and of what it has established of its virtues,
Then you at Dhu Qar—your swords inclined the pillars of those who pawned the bow of Hajib.

This event belonged to their fathers. The explanation of ﴿We said to the angels: prostrate to Adam, so they prostrated, except Iblis﴾ has already passed in Surah al-Baqarah, so it suffices without repeating it. His saying: ﴿he was not among those who prostrated﴾ is a clause having no place in i'rab, confirming the meaning of what the exception removed from the negation of Iblis's prostration, like His saying: ﴿He refused and was arrogant﴾ [al-Baqarah: 34] after His saying "except Iblis" in al-Baqarah.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 7, verses 12–13:**

﴿He said: "What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?"﴾ The apparent meaning is that *la* (لا) is superfluous, serving to emphasize and confirm, as in His words *li-'allā yaʿlama* (لِئَلّا يَعْلَمَ), meaning "so that he may know." It is as if it were said: "So that the knowledge of the People of the Book may be confirmed." The sense is: "What prevented you from prostrating in earnest and binding yourself to it when I commanded you?" The superfluity of *la* is indicated by His words, exalted is He: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating?﴾ [Sad: 75]. Its omission here is evidence that it is superfluous in ﴿*allā tasjud*﴾ (ألّا تَسْجُدَ). The meaning is that He rebuked him and reproached him for refusing to prostrate, although Exalted is He knows what prevented him from prostrating. *Mā* (ما) is interrogative, indicating reproach, as we have said. The grammarians cited, as evidence for the superfluity of *la*, the verse of the poet:

*Afa-ʿanka lā barqun ka-anna wamīḍahu*
*ghābun yuqassimuhu ḍiramun muthqabu*

Is it from you (that the flash comes), not a lightning whose glimmer seems like a thicket, divided by a piercing blaze?

And the verse of another:

*Abā jūduhu lā al-bukhla wa-staʿjalat bihi*
*naʿam min fatan lā yamnaʿu al-jūʿa qātiluh*

His generosity refused, not stinginess, and it was hastened by him, yes, from a youth whose slayer does not hold back hunger.

I say: There is no proof in the first verse, since it is possible that *la* in it is not superfluous, because it may be a conjunction with the conjoined term omitted. The estimated sense is: "Is it from you, and not from other than you?" As for the second verse, al-Zajjaj said: *lā* is an object (*mafʿūlah*), and *al-bukhl* (البخل) is a substitute (*badal*) for it. Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said: the reported reading is *lā al-bukhli* (لا البخلِ) with the *lām* in the genitive, making it a construct with *al-bukhl*, since *lā* may be pronounced without being for stinginess. End of quotation. I have offered another analysis of it, which is that *al-bukhl* is in the accusative as an object of purpose (*mafʿūl min ajlihi*), and *lā* is an object.

Some people said: the *la* in *allā tasjud* is not superfluous, and they differed. It was said: a omitted element is estimated, with which the meaning is correct, namely: "What prevented you, so that you were compelled not to prostrate?" It was also said: His words *mā manaʿaka* (ما مَنَعَكَ, "what prevented you") bear a meaning with which negation is correct, so the meaning of *mā manaʿaka* is "who commanded you" and "who told you not to prostrate."

* *

﴿He said: "I am better than him. You created me from fire and created him from clay."﴾ This is not a response that corresponds exactly to the question, but it contains the answer, since its meaning is: "My superiority over him prevented me, because my element is nobler than his element." This implies, in his view, that fire is better than clay. If that is so, then one who is created from the more excellent does not prostrate to the less excellent. They said: That is because fire is a luminous, elevated, subtle, light, hot, dry body, adjacent to and in contact with the substances of the heavens, while clay is dark, dense, heavy, cold, dry, and far from the proximity of the heavens. Fire has a strong effect and action, while clay has only receptivity and being acted upon, and action is nobler than being acted upon. Fire is suited to innate heat, which is the substance of life, while clay, by its coldness and dryness, is suited to death. Once this is established, what is created from the more excellent is more excellent, so the more excellent is not commanded to serve the less excellent. Do you not see that if Malik and Abu Hanifa were commanded to serve someone below them in knowledge, that would be ugly in reason? Then they said: Iblis erred in that he preferred fire over clay, when both are at one level in that both are created inanimate matter (*jamād makhlūq*), and clay is more excellent than fire in several respects. The first of these: the essence of clay includes gravity, calm, dignity, deliberation, forbearance, modesty, and patience. That is what drew Adam, peace be upon him, after the happiness that preceded for him, to repentance, humility, and supplication, so it bestowed upon him forgiveness, election, and guidance. The essence of fire includes lightness, frivolity, sharpness, elevation, and agitation. That is what drew Iblis, after the wretchedness that preceded for him, to arrogance and persistence, so it bestowed upon him ruin, curse, and punishment. This was said by al-Qaffal. Then they mentioned ten aspects by which the superiority of dust over fire becomes apparent. Then they said: That the matter of one is more excellent does not indicate that its form is more excellent, since excellence is a gift from God, Exalted is He. Do you not see that He, Exalted is He, brings the disbeliever out of the believer and the believer out of the disbeliever, and that a believing Abyssinian is better than an unbelieving Qurashi? And when the premise is not accepted, the conclusion does not follow. The premises (in Iblis's argument) are: Iblis is of fire-origin in substance, and everything of fire-origin is more excellent than everything of dust-origin, so Iblis is more excellent than the one of dust-origin. The second premise is disputed, so the conclusion does not follow.

Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, and Ibn Sirin said: The first to apply analogy (*qiyās*) was Iblis. Ibn ʿAbbas said: He erred, and whoever measures religion by his opinion, God joins him with Iblis. They also said: The sun and the moon were worshipped only through analogies. Some scholars said: His analogy was wrong, and his knowledge failed him that the spirit which was breathed into Adam is not from clay. Those who deny analogy used this story as evidence for its invalidity, but there is no proof in it, since it is an analogy in the presence of an explicit text, so it is invalid, and it does not prove the invalidity of analogy where there is no text. He (the one who denies analogy) also used His words ﴿*idh amartuka*﴾ (إذْ أمَرْتُكَ, "when I commanded you") as evidence that the bare form of command indicates obligation and indicates immediacy, since Iblis was rebuked for refusing to prostrate at once. Had it not indicated obligation or immediacy, he would not have deserved blame at once or at all.

﴿He said: "Then descend from it, for it is not for you to be arrogant therein. So get out; indeed, you are of the debased."﴾ Since his refusal to prostrate was due to his seeing his own nobility above Adam, God countered him with "descend," which implies coming down from a height to a lower place. The pronoun in *minhā* (مِنها, "from it") has no previously mentioned antecedent to which it refers. It was said that it refers to the Garden, and Iblis was among its inhabitants. Ibn ʿAbbas said: They were in the Garden of ʿAdn, not the Garden of Eternity, and Adam was created from the Garden of ʿAdn. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: He was first sent down and expelled from the Garden and went into the heaven, because the reports are consistent that he deceived Adam and Eve from outside the Garden, and then he was commanded at last to descend from the heaven along with Adam, Eve, and the serpent. All of this is according to the wording of the story, and God knows best. End of quotation. It was also said that it refers to the heaven. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Descend from it" means: from the heaven, which is the place of the obedient and humble angels, to the earth, which is the abode of the disobedient and arrogant among the two weighty ones (jinn and humans). It was said that it refers to the earth, as though he had dominion over it; He commanded him to descend from it to the islands of the seas, where his authority lies, so that he would not enter the earth except like a thief, fearing in it until he leaves it. This needs sound transmission. It was said that it refers to his former form in which he was, because he boasted that he was from fire, so his form was disfigured with darkness and the loss of its brightness. This was said by Abu Rawq. It was said that it refers to the city in which he was; this was mentioned by al-Kirmani, and it needs sound transmission. It was said that it refers to the station and the noble rank in which he was, from the place of election and nearness to the place of expulsion and punishment.

The meaning of *fa-mā yakūnu laka* (فَما يَكُونُ لَكَ) is: "it is not valid for you," or "it is not complete," or "it is not fitting." Rather, arrogance is forbidden in every place. It was said that it is with an omitted conjoined term indicated by the meaning, the estimate being: "therein or elsewhere." It was also said that the meaning is: "It is not for the arrogant to be therein." He repeated the sense of descent in His words "get out," since descent from it is going out, but He informed him of his lowliness and humiliation. This is a requital for his arrogance, countered with the opposite of what he was characterized by, namely lowliness, which is the opposite of arrogance. *Takabbur* (التَّكَبُّر) is a *tafaʿʿul* form from *kibr* (greatness), because he was created great and magnificent, but he himself undertook pride. From the words of ʿUmar: "Whoever is arrogant and transgresses his limit, God will cast him down to the earth."
