That is what drew Iblis, after the wretchedness that preceded for him, to arrogance and persistence, so it bestowed upon him ruin, curse, and punishment. This was said by al-Qaffal. Then they mentioned ten aspects by which the superiority of dust over fire becomes apparent. Then they said: That the matter of one is more excellent does not indicate that its form is more excellent, since excellence is a gift from God, Exalted is He. Do you not see that He, Exalted is He, brings the disbeliever out of the believer and the believer out of the disbeliever, and that a believing Abyssinian is better than an unbelieving Qurashi? And when the premise is not accepted, the conclusion does not follow. The premises (in Iblis's argument) are: Iblis is of fire-origin in substance, and everything of fire-origin is more excellent than everything of dust-origin, so Iblis is more excellent than the one of dust-origin. The second premise is disputed, so the conclusion does not follow.

Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, and Ibn Sirin said: The first to apply analogy (*qiyās*) was Iblis. Ibn ʿAbbas said: He erred, and whoever measures religion by his opinion, God joins him with Iblis. They also said: The sun and the moon were worshipped only through analogies. Some scholars said: His analogy was wrong, and his knowledge failed him that the spirit which was breathed into Adam is not from clay. Those who deny analogy used this story as evidence for its invalidity, but there is no proof in it, since it is an analogy in the presence of an explicit text, so it is invalid, and it does not prove the invalidity of analogy where there is no text. He (the one who denies analogy) also used His words ﴿*idh amartuka*﴾ (إذْ أمَرْتُكَ, "when I commanded you") as evidence that the bare form of command indicates obligation and indicates immediacy, since Iblis was rebuked for refusing to prostrate at once. Had it not indicated obligation or immediacy, he would not have deserved blame at once or at all.

﴿He said: "Then descend from it, for it is not for you to be arrogant therein. So get out; indeed, you are of the debased."﴾ Since his refusal to prostrate was due to his seeing his own nobility above Adam, God countered him with "descend," which implies coming down from a height to a lower place. The pronoun in *minhā* (مِنها, "from it") has no previously mentioned antecedent to which it refers. It was said that it refers to the Garden, and Iblis was among its inhabitants. Ibn ʿAbbas said: They were in the Garden of ʿAdn, not the Garden of Eternity, and Adam was created from the Garden of ʿAdn. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: He was first sent down and expelled from the Garden and went into the heaven, because the reports are consistent that he deceived Adam and Eve from outside the Garden, and then he was commanded at last to descend from the heaven along with Adam, Eve, and the serpent. All of this is according to the wording of the story, and God knows best. End of quotation. It was also said that it refers to the heaven. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Descend from it" means: from the heaven, which is the place of the obedient and humble angels, to the earth, which is the abode of the disobedient and arrogant among the two weighty ones (jinn and humans). It was said that it refers to the earth, as though he had dominion over it; He commanded him to descend from it to the islands of the seas, where his authority lies, so that he would not enter the earth except like a thief, fearing in it until he leaves it. This needs sound transmission. It was said that it refers to his former form in which he was, because he boasted that he was from fire, so his form was disfigured with darkness and the loss of its brightness. This was said by Abu Rawq. It was said that it refers to the city in which he was; this was mentioned by al-Kirmani, and it needs sound transmission. It was said that it refers to the station and the noble rank in which he was, from the place of election and nearness to the place of expulsion and punishment.

The meaning of *fa-mā yakūnu laka* (فَما يَكُونُ لَكَ) is: "it is not valid for you," or "it is not complete," or "it is not fitting." Rather, arrogance is forbidden in every place. It was said that it is with an omitted conjoined term indicated by the meaning, the estimate being: "therein or elsewhere." It was also said that the meaning is: "It is not for the arrogant to be therein." He repeated the sense of descent in His words "get out," since descent from it is going out, but He informed him of his lowliness and humiliation. This is a requital for his arrogance, countered with the opposite of what he was characterized by, namely lowliness, which is the opposite of arrogance. *Takabbur* (التَّكَبُّر) is a *tafaʿʿul* form from *kibr* (greatness), because he was created great and magnificent, but he himself undertook pride. From the words of ʿUmar: "Whoever is arrogant and transgresses his limit, God will cast him down to the earth."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 7, verses 14–16:**

﴿He said: "Respite me until the day they are resurrected."﴾ ﴿He said: "Indeed, you are among those given respite."﴾ This indicates his acknowledgment of the Resurrection and his knowledge that Adam would have offspring and progeny who would populate the earth and then die. Among them, some would be given respite, and his request for respite would be so that he could lead them astray and whisper to them. The pronoun in *yubʿathūn* ("they are resurrected") refers to what the meaning indicates, since there is nothing in the wording to which it refers. The wisdom in granting his respite, even though it is a cause of misguidance and trial, is that in it there is a test for the servants through their opposing him and obeying Him, and what follows from that: the magnification of reward for opposing him and the perpetuation of punishment for obeying him. God, Exalted is He, answered him: "Indeed, you are among those given respite," i.e., among those delayed. He did not mention here an endpoint for the respite. In al-Hijr and in Sad it was mentioned in an indefinite form, with His saying: ﴿until the day of the appointed time﴾ [Sad 38:81]. Its explanation will come in al-Hijr, God willing. The meaning of "among those given respite" is among the group whose lifespans were greatly prolonged until their appointed terms came, each at its different time. So that group is included in the respite, even if they were not alive throughout the whole span of time. It has also been said that "among those given respite" refers to a large group, like the people of Jonah.

﴿He said: "Because You have led me astray, I will surely sit in ambush for them on Your straight path."﴾ The apparent reading is that the *bāʾ* (in *fa-bimā*) is for swearing an oath, and *mā* is a verbal-masdar (*maṣdariyya*) particle. For this reason the verse is followed by *la-aqʿudanna* ("I will surely sit"). Al-Zamakhshari said: "He swore by the leading astray, because it was a responsibility from among the best of God's actions, since it was an exposure to eternal happiness, so it was fitting that He swear by it." End of quote. It has also been said that the *bāʾ* indicates cause, i.e., "because of your leading me astray." Ibn ʿAtiyya explained it as meaning recompense, saying: "Just as you say: 'So because of your honoring me, O Zayd, I will honor you.'" He said: "This is more fitting to the narrative." Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: with what is the *bāʾ* connected? Its connection to *la-aqʿudanna* is blocked by the oath-*lām*; you do not say, 'By God, with Zayd I will surely strike.'" I say: It is connected to the omitted verb of swearing, its estimated form being: ﴿So because You have led me astray﴾, "I swear by God ﴿that I will surely sit﴾," i.e., because of your leading me astray, I swear. End of quote. What he mentioned, that the *lām* blocks the connection of the *bāʾ* to *la-aqʿudanna*, is not an agreed-upon ruling; rather, there is disagreement about it. It has also been said that *mā* is interrogative, as if he asked about the cause by which He led him astray, saying: "With what did you lead me astray?" Then he began swearing, saying: "I will surely sit for them." This is weak, because it requires the retention of the *alif* in the interrogative *mā*, which is anomalous, or a poetic necessity, like their saying *ʿammā tasʾal* ("about what do you ask"), and this is anomalous. The poetic necessity is like the line:

*ʿalā mā qāma yashtumunī laʾīm*
*"Over what, that the base man rose to revile me."*

The meaning of *aghwaytanī* ("You led me astray") is: You misguided me. This is said by Ibn ʿAbbas and most of the scholars. Or: You cursed me. This is said by al-Hasan. Or: You destroyed me. This is said by Ibn al-Anbari. Or: You frustrated me. This is said by some. It has also been said: You made me a deviator. It has been said: You made me one who is misguided, because of my arrogance toward prostrating to one who is better than me. It has been said: You placed me in *ghayy*, which is punishment. It has been said: You decreed upon me the blameworthy acts. It has been said: You introduced into me the disease of arrogance. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Because of your leading me astray, I will surely sit for them," which is His imposing upon him what caused him to fall into *ghayy*, just as the angels remained steadfast although they were superior to him and to Adam in essence and in rank. And from al-Asamm: "You commanded me to prostrate, so my pride led me to disobey You." The meaning: because of my falling into *ghayy*, I will strive hard to mislead them, until they become corrupt because of me, just as I became corrupt because of them. End of quote. He and al-Asamm interpreted it according to the doctrine of the Muʿtazila (Mu'tazila, a rationalist school) in denying that misguidance is ascribed to God in its literal sense, which is leading astray. Likewise, whoever interpreted *aghwaytanī* as meaning "you found me in *ghayy*" is fleeing from that. His saying concerning the angels, that they are superior to Adam in essence and rank, is the doctrine of the Muʿtazila. Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi said: "May God fight the Qadariyya (the proponents of free will). Iblis knows God better than they do," meaning that he knew that God guides and leads astray. A man from among the great jurists, who was accused of *qadar* (the doctrine of human power), came and sat with Tawus in the Sacred Mosque. Tawus said to him: "Either you stand up, or you will be made to stand." So the man stood up. It was said to him: "Do you say that this man is a jurist?" He said: "Iblis is more knowledgeable than him." Iblis said: "My Lord, because You have led me astray," and this man says: "I lead myself astray." Al-Zamakhshari made this story one of the lies of the Mujbira (the determinists), and mentioned it, then said words that are ugly, which can be found in his book. He expressed sitting (*quʿūd*) as meaning steadfastness in a place, and the one who is steadfast in it. They said: *ṣirāṭaka* ("Your path") is in the accusative because *ʿalā* ("upon") has been dropped. This was said by al-Zajjaj, who compared it to the Arabic saying *ḍaraba Zayd al-ẓahr wa-l-baṭn* ("Zayd struck the back and the belly"), meaning upon the back and the belly. The dropping of a prepositional particle is not regular in a case like this. One cannot say *qaʿadtu al-khashaba* ("I sat the plank"), meaning *qaʿadtu ʿalā al-khashaba* ("I sat upon the plank"). They said: i.e., upon the place-adverb, as the poet said in it:

*kamā ʿasala al-ṭarīqa al-thaʿlab*
*"As the fox ran along the road."*

This explanation is also weak, because *ṣirāṭaka* is a specific place-adverb, and likewise *al-ṭarīq* ("the road"), so the verb does not reach it except through *fī* ("in"). What comes contrary to this is anomalous or a poetic necessity, and on the basis of poetic necessity they recited the line above. As for what Abu al-Husayn ibn al-Tarawa held, that *al-ṣirāṭ* and *al-ṭarīq* are an indefinite place-adverb, not a specific one, the grammarians refuted him. The better view is that *la-aqʿudanna* be taken to include the meaning of what transitively takes its object directly, so *al-ṣirāṭ* is in the accusative as a direct object. The estimated meaning is: "I will surely hold fast by my sitting to Your straight path." This path is the religion of Islam, and it is what leads to Paradise. The report from Ibn Masʿud and ʿAwn ibn ʿAbd Allah, that it is the road to Mecca specifically, at the well-known ascent called the Ascent of Satan, where he misguides people from the pilgrimage, is weak. The meaning of his sitting is that he stands in their way on the path of Islam, just as an enemy stands in the road to cut it off for travelers. And in a hadith: "Indeed, Satan sat for the son of Adam on his paths; he forbade him from Islam, and said: 'Will you abandon the religion of your fathers?' So he disobeyed him and embraced Islam. He forbade him from emigration, and said: 'Will you leave your family and your land?' So he disobeyed him and emigrated. He forbade him from jihad, and said: 'You will be killed and leave your child behind.' So he disobeyed him and struggled, and for him is Paradise."

*kamā ʿasala al-ṭarīqa al-thaʿlab*
*"As the fox ran along the road."*

This explanation is also weak, because *ṣirāṭaka* is a specific place-adverb, and likewise *al-ṭarīq* ("the road"), so the verb does not reach it except through *fī* ("in"). What comes contrary to this is anomalous or a poetic necessity, and on the basis of poetic necessity they recited the line above. As for what Abu al-Husayn ibn al-Tarawa held, that *al-ṣirāṭ* and *al-ṭarīq* are an indefinite place-adverb, not a specific one, the grammarians refuted him. The better view is that *la-aqʿudanna* be taken to include the meaning of what transitively takes its object directly, so *al-ṣirāṭ* is in the accusative as a direct object. The estimated meaning is: "I will surely hold fast by my sitting to Your straight path." This path is the religion of Islam, and it is what leads to Paradise. The report from Ibn Masʿud and ʿAwn ibn ʿAbd Allah, that it is the road to Mecca specifically, at the well-known ascent called the Ascent of Satan, where he misguides people from the pilgrimage, is weak. The meaning of his sitting is that he stands in their way on the path of Islam, just as an enemy stands in the road to cut it off for travelers. And in a hadith: "Indeed, Satan sat for the son of Adam on his paths; he forbade him from Islam, and said: 'Will you abandon the religion of your fathers?' So he disobeyed him and embraced Islam. He forbade him from emigration, and said: 'Will you leave your family and your land?' So he disobeyed him and emigrated. He forbade him from jihad, and said: 'You will be killed and leave your child behind.' So he disobeyed him and struggled, and for him is Paradise."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 17–18:

﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them and from behind them, and from their right and from their left. And You will not find most of them grateful.﴾ The apparent meaning is that his coming to them from these four directions is a metaphor for his whispering to them, his seducing them, and his earnest effort to misguide them in every way possible. Since the enemy usually attacks from these directions, they were mentioned, not because he literally comes from all four directions.

Ibn Abbas said: "From before them" means the Hereafter: "I will cast doubt on them about it, and that there is no resurrection." "From behind them" means this world: "I will make them desire it and I will adorn it for them." It is also related from him, and from al-Nakha'i and al-Hakam ibn Utbah, that the opposite is meant. Also from him: "From their right" means the truth, and "from their left" means falsehood. And also from him: "From their right" means the good deeds, and "from their left" means the bad deeds.

Mujahid said: "The first two are where they are helped, and the other two are where they are not helped." Abu Salih said: "The first two are the truth and falsehood, and the other two are the Hereafter and this world." It was said: "The first two are the expansion of hope and forgetting the appointed time, and the other two are in what is easy and in what is difficult." It was said: "The first two concern what remains of their lifetimes, so they do not obey, and what has passed of them, so they do not regret any disobedience. The other two concern what their right hands possess, so they do not spend it on what is good, and before their poverty, so they do not refrain from what is forbidden."

Abu Abd Allah al-Razi, relating from those he named, the "ḥukamā' al-Islām" (philosophers of Islam), said: "From before them is the imaginative faculty (al-quwwa al-khayaliyya), which gathers the like of sensible things and their forms, and it is placed in the front part of the brain. From behind them is the estimative faculty (al-quwwa al-wahmiyya), which judges non-sensible things by judgments appropriate to sensible things, and it is placed in the rear part of the brain. From their right is the faculty of desire (quwwat al-shahwa), and it is placed in the right side of the heart. From their left is the faculty of anger (quwwat al-ghadab), and it is placed in the left side of the heart. These four faculties are what produce states that cause the removal of spiritual happiness. The external devils, as long as they do not perceive anything of these four faculties, cannot cast whispering. This is the reason for specifying these four directions, and this is the verified explanation." End of quotation. But this is far from the paths of Arabic usage and of those who speak in terms of the law.

He said: "According to this, there was no need to mention above and below, because these two directions are not the seat of any of the faculties that corrupt the interests of spiritual happiness." End of quotation.

Ibn Abbas said: "He did not say 'from above them,' because God's mercy descends upon them from above. And he did not say 'from below them,' because coming from below involves a kind of alienation."

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: how is it said 'from before them' and 'from behind them' with the preposition of origin (min), while 'from their right and from their left' is with the preposition of passing beyond (ʿan)?" I say: the object of the verb is an adverbial place (al-maf'ūl fīhi), and the verb is transferred to it as it is transferred to the direct object. Just as the prepositions of transfer differ in this, they differ in that. It is a language that is received, not analogized, and one only investigates the correctness of its placement. When we heard them say: jalasa ʿan yamīnihi (he sat away from his right side) and ʿalā yamīnihi (he sat on his right side), and ʿan shimālihi and ʿalā shimālihi, we said: the meaning of ʿalā yamīnihi is that it is possible from the direction of the right, the one who is elevated enabling the one on whom he is elevated. The meaning of ʿan yamīnihi is that he sat distant from the companion on the right, deviating from him and not adjacent to him. Then it became common until it was used for the distant and for other than the distant, as we mentioned in the case of fiʿāl and similar forms of the direct object, such as their saying: ramaytu ʿan al-qaws, ʿalā al-qaws, and min al-qaws (I shot from the bow, on the bow, and from the bow), because the arrow moves away from it, rises above it when placed on its belly for shooting, and the shooting begins from it. Likewise they said: jalasa bayna yadayhi and khalfahu, meaning "in," because they are both adverbs of the verb, and min bayni yadayhi and min khalfihi, because the action occurs in part of the two directions, as you say: I came to him in the night, meaning part of the night. End of quotation. This is a statement with no harm in it.

I say: The reason that "before them" and "behind them" are specified with the preposition of origin, which is more suitable for coming, is that these are the directions from which the enemy most often comes, so he attains his opportunity. "Before them" was placed before "behind them," because it is the direction that indicates the enemy's advance and his bravery in confronting his opponent without fear of him, whereas "behind" is from a direction of treachery and deceit, and the opponent's ignorance of the one who ambushes him, seeking his lapse and heedlessness.

(p-277) "Right" and "left" are specified with the preposition that indicates passing beyond, because they are not the most common directions from which the enemy comes. His coming passes beyond them to the direction that is more common in that. "Right" was placed before "left," because it is the stronger direction in meeting the enemy, and with the right hand comes striking and repelling. So the opponent who comes from its direction is more valiant and braver, since he comes from the direction that is stronger in repelling. The left is a direction that does not have the strength and repelling power of the right.

Ibn Abbas said: "Grateful" means monotheists. It is also related from him and from others: "believers," because the son of Adam does not give thanks for God's blessing except by believing. Muqatil said: "grateful for Your blessing." Al-Hasan said: "steadfast in Your obedience, and none will thank You except a few of them."

This negated sentence may be understood as included in the content of the oath, coordinated with its answer. It may also be understood as a new statement that is not sworn to: he reported that his effort and his coming to them from all directions he will do. Was this report from him made by way of conjecture, based on His saying: ﴿And Iblis had indeed confirmed his assumption about them﴾ [Saba': 20], or by way of certain knowledge? There are two opinions. The way of knowledge is either his seeing it in the Preserved Tablet, or his deducing it from His saying: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ [Saba': 13], or from the angels through God's informing them, or from their saying: ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?﴾ [al-Baqara: 30], or from the seduction of Adam, when his descendants are weaker than he. Or the faculties of the son of Adam may be nineteen faculties: five outward senses and five inward ones, plus desire and anger, and seven prior ones, namely the attractive, the retentive, the digestive, the expulsive, the ejective, the growing, and the generative. All of them call toward the world of the body and toward bodily pleasures. Reason is one faculty that calls to the worship of God, and that is at the beginning of creation, when reason is then weak. Six opinions.

﴿He said: Go forth from it, reproached and expelled.﴾ The majority hold that the pronoun refers to the Garden, and the disagreement about it is like the disagreement over ﴿Then descend from it﴾ [al-A'raf: 13]. These are three commands: a command to descend in an unrestricted way; a command to go forth, informing that he is one of humiliation; and a command to go forth restricted by blame and expulsion. Qatadah said: "madhʾūman" means cursed. Al-Kalbi said: "blamed." Mujahid said: "banished." It was said: "detested." "Madhḥūran" means distanced from God's mercy, or from good, or from the Garden, or from success, or from the special ones among the believers. These sayings are close in meaning.

Al-Zuhri, Abu Ja'far, and al-A'mash read madhūman with a damma on the dhāl without hamza. This reading may bear two possibilities. The first, and it is the more apparent, is that it comes from dhaʾama, with the hamza, and he eased the hamza, deleted it, and placed its vowel on the dhāl. The second is that it comes from dhāma without hamza, yadhīmu, like bāʿa yabīʿu, and he changed the waw into a yā', as they said of makīl: makūl. "Madḥūran" is in the accusative as a second circumstantial qualifier according to those who allow that, or a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in madhʾūman, or an adjective of the word madhʾūman.

﴿Whoever follows you among them, I will surely fill Hell with all of you together.﴾ The majority read "la-man" with a fatha on the lām. The apparent reading is that it is the lām that introduces an oath, and "man" is a conditional in the position of a nominative as the subject. The conditional's answer is omitted, indicated by the answer of the omitted oath that comes before the lām introducing the oath. It is also permissible that the lām is the lām of the beginning (lām al-ibtidāʾ), and man is a relative pronoun. "La-amlaʾanna" is the answer of an omitted oath after "man tabiʿaka," and that omitted oath and its answer are in the position of the predicate of the relative "man." Al-Jahdari and ʿIṣma from Abu Bakr (p-278) from ʿAsim read "li-man tabiʿaka minhum" with a kasra on the lām. They differed in its explanation. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: the meaning is "for the sake of those who follow you among them, I will surely fill." End of quotation. The apparent sense of this estimate is that the lām is connected to "la-amlaʾanna." This is impossible according to the majority's view that what follows the lām of the oath does not govern what precedes it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "with the meaning: for those who follow you among them is the threat, which is His saying: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with all of you together,﴾ with 'la-amlaʾanna' in the place of the beginning, and 'li-man tabiʿaka' as its predicate." End of quotation. If he means the apparent sense of his words, it is an error according to the Basran school, because "la-amlaʾanna" is a clause that is the answer of an omitted oath. From the standpoint of it being a clause alone, it cannot be a beginning. From the standpoint of it being the answer of the oath, it is also impossible, because in that case it has no place in the grammatical structure. From the standpoint of it being a beginning, it has a place in the grammatical structure, but a clause cannot have a place in that way, nor can it be in a place of nominative that is entered upon by a governing element that does not enter it. That cannot be conceived.

Abu al-Fadl ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Razi said: the lām is connected to the reproach (al-dhamm) and the expulsion (al-dahr), and the meaning is: go forth with these two qualities for the sake of your followers. This is mentioned in the book al-Lawāmiḥ on the irregular readings. The meaning of "minkum" is: from you and from those who follow you. The address to the second person prevailed over the third person, as when you say: "You and your brothers, I honor you (all)."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 19–21:

﴿And, O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden, and eat from wherever you wish, but do not approach this tree, or you will be among the wrongdoers.﴾ That is: "And We said, O Adam." The tafsir (explanation) of this verse has already been given in al-Baqarah. However, here it is "fa-kula min haythu shi'tuma" (eat from wherever you wish), whereas in al-Baqarah it is: ﴿And eat from it in abundance wherever you wish﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:35]. They said: this came in one of its possible senses, which is that the second [phrase] follows the first, and "raghadan" (in abundance) was omitted here for brevity and mentioned there, because that [surah] is Madani and this one is Makki, so the meaning was fulfilled there by the wording.

﴿Then Satan whispered to them to reveal to them what was hidden from them of their private parts, and said: "Your Lord has forbidden you from this tree only lest you become angels or become among the immortals."﴾ That is: he did the whispering on their account. As for His saying "fa-waswasa" (he whispered) "ilayhi" (to him), its meaning is that he cast the whispering to him. Al-Hasan said: his whispering reached them in the Garden while he was on the earth, by the power which Allah created in him. Ibn Atiyyah said: this is a weak view, which the wording of the Qur'an refutes. It has also been said that he was in the heaven and they used to come out to him. It has been said that he was at the gate of the Garden while they were inside it. It has been said that he used to enter to them through the mouth of the serpent. Al-Kirmani said: he inspired them. Ibn al-Qushayri said: he presented to them enticing thoughts. These two views contradict the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, because its apparent meaning indicates speech, dialogue and an oath. The apparent meaning is that the "lam" is the lam of purpose (kay), meaning that he intended to reveal their private parts, thereby lowering their rank, and to grieve them by exposing what ought to be concealed, and that they would not avoid the prohibition of Allah, so that he and they would be equal in disobedience: he was commanded to prostrate and refused, and they were forbidden and did not desist. Others said that it is the lam of consequence, because he had no knowledge of this specific punishment so that he would intend it. Al-Zamakhshari said: in this is evidence that uncovering the nakedness is among the grave matters, and that it has always been repugnant in human nature and detestable to the intellects. End. This is in accordance with his Mu'tazili doctrine that reason makes things ugly and beautiful. The apparent meaning is that what is intended is the signified meaning of "sawatihima" (their private parts) themselves, which are the front and the rear. (p-279) It has been said: they did not see them before eating from the tree, and when they ate, they became visible to them. It has also been said: each one did not see the private parts of the other. Qatadah said: he referred by "their private parts" to their whole bodies, and mentioned "sau'ah" (the private part) because it is the most shameful part that appears of the children of Adam. The majority read "wuwiriya" (was concealed). ʿAbdullah [ibn Mas'ud] read "uwiriya", replacing the waw with a hamzah, which is a permissible substitution. Ibn Wathhab read "ma wuriya" with a damma on the waw and no waw after it, on the pattern of "kusiya". Mujahid and al-Hasan read "min sawwatihima" in the singular, with the hamzah eased by changing it into a waw and assimilating the waw into it. Al-Hasan also read, as did Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' and Shaybah ibn Nassah: "min sawwatihima", with the hamzah eased and the waw doubled. It is also recited: "min sawatihima" with a single waw and the hamzah omitted; its explanation is that he dropped it and placed its vowel on the waw. Whoever reads with the plural has used the plural in place of the dual, out of dislike of two similar things coming together. Whoever reads with the singular has used it in place of the dual. It is possible that the plural is in its original sense, taking into account that each nakedness is the rear and the front, and that makes four, so it is plural. "Illa an takuna malakayni" (only lest you become two angels) is an exceptive construction, with the object of purpose omitted: that is, "Your Lord has forbidden you for nothing except out of dislike that you become two angels." The Kufans would supply "illa an takuna" (only lest you become), and the omission of the noun, which is "karahah" (dislike), is better than omitting the particle, which is "la" (not). ﴿Then when they tasted the tree, their private parts became apparent to them﴾ [al-A'raf 7:22]. That is: they found its taste while eating from it, as Allah the Exalted said, ﴿so they ate from it﴾, and the garments of the Garden fell away from them, so their nakedness became apparent to them. It has been mentioned before that prior to this they did not see it on themselves, nor did either of them see it on the other. Ibn Abbas, Qatadah, and Ibn Jubayr said: there was a nail-like covering on them, and when they ate, it peeled away from them and their private parts became visible. What remained on their fingers was an amount by which they would remember the disobedience and so renew their regret. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: there was a light upon them which covered the nakedness of each of them, and by eating that light was removed. It has been said: there was a light upon them which diminished, and something solidified from it on the nails of the hands and feet as a reminder to them, so that they and their descendants after them would seek forgiveness at every time, as happened to Uways al-Qarani when Allah removed the leprosy from him except for a small spot that He left, so that he would remember His blessings and be thankful. This view is far from the indication of the wording and contradicts the view of the majority. Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 19–21:

﴿And, O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden, and eat from wherever you wish, but do not approach this tree, or you will be among the wrongdoers.﴾ That is: "And We said, O Adam." The tafsir (explanation) of this verse has already been given in al-Baqarah. However, here it is "fa-kula min haythu shi'tuma" (eat from wherever you wish), whereas in al-Baqarah it is: ﴿And eat from it in abundance wherever you wish﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:35]. They said: this came in one of its possible senses, which is that the second [phrase] follows the first, and "raghadan" (in abundance) was omitted here for brevity and mentioned there, because that [surah] is Madani and this one is Makki, so the meaning was fulfilled there by the wording.

﴿Then Satan whispered to them to reveal to them what was hidden from them of their private parts, and said: "Your Lord has forbidden you from this tree only lest you become angels or become among the immortals."﴾ That is: he did the whispering on their account. As for His saying "fa-waswasa" (he whispered) "ilayhi" (to him), its meaning is that he cast the whispering to him. Al-Hasan said: his whispering reached them in the Garden while he was on the earth, by the power which Allah created in him. Ibn Atiyyah said: this is a weak view, which the wording of the Qur'an refutes. It has also been said that he was in the heaven and they used to come out to him. It has been said that he was at the gate of the Garden while they were inside it. It has been said that he used to enter to them through the mouth of the serpent. Al-Kirmani said: he inspired them. Ibn al-Qushayri said: he presented to them enticing thoughts. These two views contradict the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, because its apparent meaning indicates speech, dialogue and an oath. The apparent meaning is that the "lam" is the lam of purpose (kay), meaning that he intended to reveal their private parts, thereby lowering their rank, and to grieve them by exposing what ought to be concealed, and that they would not avoid the prohibition of Allah, so that he and they would be equal in disobedience: he was commanded to prostrate and refused, and they were forbidden and did not desist. Others said that it is the lam of consequence, because he had no knowledge of this specific punishment so that he would intend it. Al-Zamakhshari said: in this is evidence that uncovering the nakedness is among the grave matters, and that it has always been repugnant in human nature and detestable to the intellects. End. This is in accordance with his Mu'tazili doctrine that reason makes things ugly and beautiful. The apparent meaning is that what is intended is the signified meaning of "sawatihima" (their private parts) themselves, which are the front and the rear.
