That is among the signs of God, that they may remember.﴾ The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that when He mentioned the story of Adam, in which there is the covering of the private parts, and He made for him a place of settlement and provision on earth, He mentioned what He bestowed upon his descendants and the blessings He granted them: the clothing that covers the private parts and the adornment by which their settling on earth and their enjoyment of what He has given them become possible. Mujahid said: this verse and the three after it were revealed concerning those among the Arabs who would go naked while circling the House. Al-Naqqash mentioned that this was the custom of Thaqif, Khuza'ah, the Banu 'Amir ibn Sa'sa'ah, the Banu Mudlij, and al-Harith and 'Amir, the two sons of 'Abd Manat, both their women and their men.

As for "We have sent down" (أنزلنا): it was said that it is in its literal sense of descent from high to low. So He sent down with Adam and Eve some clothing as an example for others, and then their descendants expanded in crafting, deriving from that example. Or He sent down from the sky the origin of everything at their descent. Or He sent down iron with him, and from it he made the tools of crafts. Or He sent down an angel who taught Adam weaving. These are four opinions. It was also said: the sending down is a metaphor, by naming the cause for its effect, so He sent down the rain, which is the cause of what the clothing is prepared from. Or it means "created," like His saying: ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ [al-Zumar: 6]. Or it means "decreed." Al-Zamakhshari said: He made what is on earth as sent down from the sky, because it was decreed and written there. From the same usage is: ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ [al-Zumar: 6]. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "We have sent down" may be intended to mean gradually: since He sent down the rain, from which comes everything that is worn, the expression "We have sent down" was used about the clothing. This is like the saying of a poet describing rain:

*It came in the two rains from its clouds, like the humps of camels in its rain-pools.*

That is, with the rain. It may also be that He intends "We created," and the expression came with "We sent down," like His saying: ﴿And We sent down iron﴾ [al-Hadid: 25], and His saying: ﴿And He sent down for you of the livestock﴾ [al-Zumar: 6]. Furthermore, God's creation and His acts are from a height of rank and station. End.

The word al-libas (اللباس, clothing) encompasses everything that is worn and covers. Al-Rish (الريش) is an expression for abundance of provision, comfort of life, the availability of clothing, and enjoyment. Most of the lexicographers hold that al-rish is what covers of clothing or livelihood. Some people said: it means women. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, and Mujahid said: it means wealth. Ibn Zayd said: it means beauty. Al-Zamakhshari said: the clothing of adornment is borrowed from the feathers (ريش) of a bird, because it is its clothing and its adornment. That is, He sent down for you two garments: a garment that covers your private parts, and a garment that adorns you, because adornment is a valid purpose, as He said: ﴿That you may ride them and as adornment﴾ [al-Nahl: 8], and ﴿And for you in them is beauty﴾ [al-Nahl: 6]. End.

The coordination of "al-rish" with "libasan" (clothing) implies a difference, and that it is a separate category from clothing, not a part of it. Uthman, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Sulami, 'Ali ibn al-Husayn and his son Zayd, Abu Raja', Zirr ibn Hubaysh, 'Asim in one narration, and Abu 'Amr in one narration read "wa-riyashan" (رياشا). It was said: they are two verbal nouns with one meaning: "God feathered him" (راشه الله يريشه ريشا ورياشا) means He bestowed favor upon him. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is the plural of rish, like shu'ab and shi'ab. Al-Zajjaj said: they both mean clothing. Al-Farra' said: they both mean what covers of garments and wealth, as one says libs and libas. Ma'bad al-Juhani said: al-riyash means livelihood. Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-rish means eating and drinking, and al-riyash means acquired wealth. It was also said: al-rish is what is inward, and al-riyash is what is outward.

Al-Sahibani (Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr? — here: the two companions) and al-Kisa'i read ﴿wa-libasa al-taqwa﴾ (ولباس التقوى) in the accusative, coordinating it with the accusative noun before it. The rest of the Seven read it in the nominative (p-283), and it was said that it is nominative by the omission of an understood subject: "and it is the clothing of piety." So said al-Zajjaj. ﴿That is best﴾: according to this, "that" is the subject and "best" is the predicate. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "wa-libas" be a subject whose predicate is omitted, its estimate being: "and the clothing of piety is the covering of your nakedness." This is not correct. The apparent view is that it is a second subject, and "best" (خير) is its predicate, and the sentence is the predicate of "the clothing of piety," with the linking element being the demonstrative pronoun (اسم الإشارة). It is one of the five linking devices agreed upon in linking a sentence that is the predicate of a subject when it is not the subject itself. It was also said: "that" is a substitute (بدل) for "clothing," and it was said: an appositive (عطف بيان), and it was said: an adjective, and the predicate of "wa-libas" is "best." Al-Hawfi said: I see that "that" should not be an adjective for "the clothing of piety," because demonstrative nouns are more definite than what has "al-" and what is attached to "al-," and the course of the adjective is that it be equal to the noun it modifies or less definite than it. If anyone has previously said this, it is an error. Al-Hawfi also permitted that "that" be a separator (فصل) with no place in the grammatical structure, and "best" be the predicate of His saying: ﴿and the clothing of piety﴾, so that the demonstrative is made a separator like the pronoun. I know of no one who said this. As for his saying: "If anyone has previously said this, it is an error," Ibn 'Atiyya has mentioned it and said: it is the most noble of the views; Abu 'Ali mentioned it in al-Hujjah. End. Abu al-Baqa' also permitted it. What al-Hawfi mentioned is the correct one according to the most well-known views on the order of definite nouns.

Abdullah and Ubayy read: "wa-libasu al-taqwa khayr" (ولباس التقوى خير), with "that" omitted, so it is subject and predicate. The apparent meaning is to take it as literal clothing. Ibn Zayd said: it is the covering of the private parts. This involves repetition, since He has already said: "clothing that covers your private parts." Zayd ibn 'Ali said: it is the coat of mail, the helmet, and the arm-guards, because one protects oneself with them in war. It was also said: wool and wearing coarse clothing. It was reported: "Be rough (in dress) and eat coarse food." It was also said: what protects from heat and cold. Uthman ibn 'Ata' said: it is the clothing of the pious in the Hereafter. It was also said: the clothing of piety is figurative. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is righteous deeds, and he also said: chastity. Uthman ibn 'Affan and Ibn 'Abbas also said: good bearing in the face. Ma'bad al-Juhani said: modesty. Al-Hasan said: scrupulousness and good bearing. 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr said: fear of God. Ibn Jurayj said: faith. It was also said: what appears of tranquility and humility. Yahya ibn Yahya said: submissiveness. The best view is to make it general: everything by which the lawful protection is achieved is from the clothing of piety.

The reference in His saying "that" (ذلك) to "from the signs of God" points to what preceded: the sending down of clothing, the feathers, and the clothing of piety. The meaning is: from the signs of God that point to His bounty and His mercy toward His servants. It was also said: from the requirements of the signs of God. It was also said: the reference is to "the clothing of piety," that is, it is a sign in lessons, a sign and indicator from God that He is pleased with him and has mercy on him, "that they may remember" these blessings, and thus thank God for them.

﴿O children of Adam, do not let Satan tempt you as he removed your parents from the Garden, stripping them of their clothing to show them their private parts.﴾ That is: "let him not seduce you and prevail over you." This is a prohibition directed at Satan, but its meaning is a prohibition to them against themselves from listening to him and obeying his command, just as they say "I will not see you here," meaning: do not remain where he can see you. The phrase "as" (كما) is in the position of an accusative: "a temptation like the temptation of removing your parents." It is also possible that the meaning is: "let him not expel you from the religion through his temptation, with an expulsion like his expulsion of your parents." Yahya and Ibrahim read (لا يفتننكم) with a dammah on the yaa', from afτana (أفتن). Zayd ibn 'Ali read: "la yaftinkum" without the emphatic nun. The apparent view is that "their clothing" (لباسهما) is the clothing they had in the Garden. Mujahid said it is the clothing of piety. "Their private parts" (سوآتهما) is what distresses them of disobedience. "Stripping" (ينزع) is a circumstantial clause (حال) from the pronoun in "removed" (أخرج) or from "your parents," because the sentence contains the pronoun of Satan and the pronoun of the two parents. If "yanza'" were a substitute for "nazi'an," it would be determined to be the first, because in that case, if the second were permitted, it would be a descriptive term applied to something other than its referent, so the pronoun would have to be made explicit, and this is according to the view of the Basrans. "Stripping" is the narration of an event that had already happened, because the stripping of the clothing from them occurred before the expulsion. The stripping was attributed to Satan because he was the cause of it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 23–27 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Indeed, he sees you, he and his tribe, from where you do not see them.﴾ That is, indeed Satan, who is Iblis, sees you, he and his soldiers, his kind and his offspring, from the direction from which you cannot see them. They are subtle bodies (ajsam latifa), and their existence is known from this Shari'a, just as the existence of the angels is also known from this Shari'a. It is not objectionable that there are very subtle bodies that we do not see. Do you not see that air is a subtle body that we do not perceive, while the decisive rational proof has established its existence? Their appearance in dense bodies is also established, and the sighting of them by the children of Adam in those bodies is likewise established. Such is the Satan whom Abu Hurayra saw when he began guarding the zakat dates, and the 'ifrit whom the Messenger (ﷺ) saw, and of whom he said: "Had it not been for the supplication of my brother Sulayman, I would have tied him to one of the pillars of the mosque." Such also is the account of Khalid ibn al-Walid when he was sent to demolish Dhu al-Khalasa, and the account of Sawad ibn Qarib with his jinn companion (ra'iyy). Yet their appearance in forms is rare, just as the angels appear in forms, as in the account of Jibril and the account of the angel who came to the blind man, the bald man and the leper. This is a matter that is widely attested in the Shari'a, so it cannot be rejected; I mean their appearing at times in dense forms.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "In it is clear evidence that the jinn cannot be seen and do not appear to mankind, and that their manifesting themselves is not within their capacity, and that the claim of those who assert that they are seen is falsehood and nonsense." End of quotation. But there is no evidence in the verse for what he mentioned, because God, exalted is He, affirmed that they see us from a direction in which we do not see them, which is the direction in which they exist according to the original nature of their creation as subtle bodies. Had He intended the negation of our seeing them in general, He would not have restricted it to this aspect. The construction would have been: "Indeed he sees you, he and his tribe, and you do not see them." Moreover, even if we supposed that the verse contains an indication, it would be from the general term specified by the widely transmitted prophetic report (al-'amm al-makhsus, a general expression restricted by a specific one), so they would be visible in some forms to some people at some times.

In the book al-Tahrir it is said that a group of philosophers (hukama') denied the repeated appearance of jinn and devils and their taking on any form they wish. The saying ﴿Indeed, he sees you﴾ is a justification for the prohibition and a warning against his temptation, for he is like a deceptive enemy who plots against you and ambushes you from where you do not perceive. In the hadith: "Indeed, Satan flows through the son of Adam like blood" is an indication that he never leaves him and watches for his heedless moments so as to gain power over him. The apparent reading is that the pronoun in (innahu) refers to Satan. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The pronoun in (innahu) is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n, the dummy pronoun referring to the situation), and the hadith is ended." There is no necessity for this.

(wa-qabiluhu) is coordinated with the pronoun hidden in (yarakum). It may also be a subject whose predicate is omitted, or coordinated with the position of the noun of (inna), according to the view of those who permit that. Al-Yazidi read (wa-qabilahu) with a fatha on the lam, coordinated with the noun of (inna), if the pronoun refers to Satan, with (qabilahu) being a direct object accompanying (maf'ul ma'ahu, object of accompaniment), meaning together with his kind. It was also read anomalously as ﴿min haythu la tarawnahu﴾ with the pronoun in the singular, which may refer to Satan, and (qabiluhu) would then be treated as if it were a demonstrative noun, so it would be like the verse of poetry:

*In it are lines of black and white, / as if on the skin is the spotting of leprosy.*

That is, that was the case. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to Satan alone because he is their head and chief, and they follow him, and he is the one singled out by the prohibition at the outset.

﴿Indeed, We have made the devils allies of those who do not believe﴾. That is, We made the devils their helpers and supporters in falsehood. Al-Zajjaj said: "We gave them power over them, so that they increase them in their error, and they follow them in that, and thus they became their allies." It was also said: "We made them companions to them." Al-Zahrawi reported that (ja'ala, made) here means (wasafa, described), and this is a Mu'tazili tendency. Al-Zamakhshari said: "We left them between them and between them, we did not restrain them from them, until they took them as allies and obeyed them in what they embellished for them of disbelief and sins. This is another warning, more forceful than the first," end of quotation. And this follows the path of the Mu'tazila.

﴿When they commit an indecency, they say, "We found our fathers doing it, and Allah commanded us to do it."﴾ That is: when they commit what is grossly sinful, they make excuses. The implied meaning is: when they were asked for proof of their committing it, they said, "Our fathers used to do it, so we follow them, and Allah commanded us to do it." They used to say, "If Allah disliked what we do, He would have diverted us from it." The first statement includes imitation (taqlid) of their fathers, and taqlid is invalid, since it is not a path to knowledge. The second statement is a fabrication against Allah the Exalted.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Although the wording is general, the indecency (fahisha) here is in fact the exposing of the private parts during circumambulation (tawaf). It is narrated from al-Zuhri that he said, 'These verses were revealed concerning that,' and Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said the same." End of quotation. Zayd ibn Aslam and al-Suddi also said this. Al-Hasan, 'Ata' and al-Zajjaj said: the indecency here is shirk (polytheism). It was also said that it refers to the baheera, the sa'iba, the wasila and the ham (animals dedicated by pagan custom). It was also said that it refers to the major sins.

The apparent meaning of ﴿when they commit an indecency﴾ is that it is a new statement about these disbelievers, regarding what they used to say when they committed indecencies. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "﴿When they commit﴾ and what follows is included in the relative clause of ﴿those who do not believe﴾, so that the rebuke falls on the attribute of a people who have been made examples for the believers, since their act resembled the act of those they were compared to." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is related from al-Hasan that Allah sent Muhammad (ﷺ) to the Arabs, and they were Qadariyya (those who deny divine decree) and Mujbira (those who affirm compulsion), attributing their sins to Allah the Exalted. Confirmation of this is the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿When they commit an indecency﴾." End of his quotation from al-Hasan. It is likely that this is not authentically from al-Hasan. Note al-Zamakhshari's subtle insertion in his words, "and they are Qadariyya." Ahl al-Sunna (the People of the Sunna) make the Mu'tazila the Qadariyya, but he reversed this against them and made them the Qadariyya, so that the censure directed at the Qadariyya falls on them. This attribution, from the standpoint of Arabic, is more fitting to one who affirms qadar (divine decree) than to one who denies it. The statement of Ahl al-Sunna that the Mu'tazila are Qadariyya means that they deny qadar and claim that the matter is newly determined. This is similar to what some say of Dawud al-Zahiri, that he was al-Qiyasi, meaning one who denies qiyas (analogical reasoning).

﴿Say: Indeed Allah does not command indecency﴾, that is, the committing of indecency. Taqlid was not mentioned because its invalidity is evident to everyone, since it necessitates adopting contradictory things. Allah the Exalted refuted their claim that Allah commanded it, since the only means of knowing that is revelation through the messengers and prophets, and that did not occur. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Because committing an abomination is impossible for Him, there being no motive for it and the presence of a deterrent, how then would He command its doing?"

﴿Do you say about Allah what you do not know?﴾ This is a denial of their attributing the abomination to Him, and a testimony that their matter rests on extreme ignorance. End of quotation. This is in line with the Mu'tazila. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "He rebuked them for their lying and for their claims about what they have no knowledge of and no transmission for. Rather, it is an assertion and a fabrication."

(p-286) ﴿Say, "My Lord has commanded justice. And set your faces [toward Him] at every place of prostration, and call upon Him, sincere to Him in religion. As He originated you, [to Him] you will return."﴾ ﴿A group He has guided, and a group upon whom error has been decreed. Indeed, they have taken the devils as allies instead of Allah, and they think they are guided.﴾ ﴿O children of Adam, take your adornment at every place of prayer, and eat and drink, but do not be excessive. Indeed, He does not like those who are excessive.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 31] ﴿Say, "Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision?" Say, "They are for those who believed in the worldly life, purely [for them] on the Day of Resurrection. Thus We detail the verses for a people who know."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 32] ﴿Say, "My Lord has only forbidden immoralities, what is apparent of them and what is concealed, and sin, and oppression without right, and that you associate with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority, and that you say about Allah what you do not know."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 33] ﴿And for every nation is a term. So when their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour, nor can they advance it.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 34] ﴿O children of Adam, if messengers from among you come to you relating My verses, then whoever fears Allah and makes reform, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 35] ﴿But those who denied Our verses and were arrogant toward them, those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 36] ﴿So who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah or denies His verses? Those will receive their portion from the Decree, until when Our messengers come to them to take their souls, they will say, "Where is that which you used to invoke besides Allah?" They will say, "They have strayed from us," and they will testify against themselves that they were disbelievers.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 37] ﴿[Allah] will say, "Enter into nations that have passed away before you, of jinn and mankind, into the Fire." Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister, until when they have all overtaken one another therein, the last of them will say of the first of them, "Our Lord, these have misled us, so give them a double punishment of the Fire." He will say, "For each is double, but you do not know."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 38] ﴿And the first of them will say to the last of them, "You had no superiority over us, so taste the punishment for what you used to earn."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 39] ﴿Indeed, those who denied Our verses and were arrogant toward them, the gates of heaven will not be opened for them, nor will they enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle. And thus do We recompense the criminals.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 40] ﴿For them from Hell is a bed, and above them are coverings. And thus do We recompense the wrongdoers.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 41] ﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds, We do not burden any soul except [according to] its capacity. Those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 42] ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts; rivers will flow beneath them. And they will say, "Praise be to Allah, who guided us to this. We would not have been guided had Allah not guided us. The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth." And they will be called, "This is Paradise; you have been given it as an inheritance for what you used to do."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 43] ﴿And the companions of Paradise will call to the companions of the Fire, "We have found true what our Lord promised us; have you found true what your Lord promised?" They will say, "Yes." Then a caller will announce among them, "The curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 44] ﴿Those who turn [others] away from the way of Allah and seek to make it crooked, and they, in the Hereafter, are disbelievers.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 45] ﴿And between them is a partition, and on the heights are men who recognize each by his mark. And they call out to the companions of Paradise, "Peace be upon you," they not having entered it, while they hope [to enter].﴾ [Al-A'raf: 46] ﴿And when their sights are turned toward the companions of the Fire, they say, "Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 47] ﴿And the companions of the heights will call out to men whom they recognize by their marks, saying, "Your gathering and what you used to be arrogant about have not availed you."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 48] ﴿"Are these the ones you swore Allah would not reach with mercy?" [It will be said to them], "Enter Paradise; no fear will be upon you, nor will you grieve."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 49] ﴿And the companions of the Fire will call to the companions of Paradise, "Pour upon us some water or of what Allah has provided you." They will say, "Indeed, Allah has forbidden them to the disbelievers."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 50] ﴿Those who took their religion as amusement and diversion and whom the worldly life deceived. So today We will forget them as they forgot the meeting of this Day of theirs, and as they used to deny Our verses.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 51] ﴿And We had certainly brought them a Book which We detailed with knowledge, as guidance and mercy for a people who believe.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 52] ﴿Do they await except its outcome? On the Day its outcome comes, those who had forgotten it before will say, "The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth. So do we have any intercessors to intercede for us, or could we be returned so that we might do other than what we used to do?" They have certainly lost themselves, and what they used to fabricate has gone astray from them.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 53] ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days; then He established Himself above the Throne. He covers the night with the day, which pursues it swiftly; and [He created] the sun, the moon, and the stars, subjected by His command. Unquestionably, to Him belong creation and command. Blessed is Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 54]

Bada'a al-shay': he originated it and invented it. Al-jamal: the well-known animal; its plurals are jimal and ajmul, and it is not called jamal until it reaches four years of age. Al-jamal also means the rope of a ship, and its dialect forms appear in compounds. Sam al-khiyat: its hole; the sin of sam may be pronounced with a damma, a fatha, or a kasra. Every hole in a nose, an ear, or otherwise, the Arabs call sam. Al-khiyat: al-makhit, and they are two instruments, like izar and mi'zar, liḥaf and milḥaf, and qina' and miqna'. Al-ghill: resentment and hidden enmity in the soul; its plural is ghilal, and from it comes al-ghulul, taking in concealment. Na'am: a particle that serves as affirmation of a pure positive statement, or of what a question contains. Kasra on its ayn is a dialect of Quraysh, and replacing its ayn with a ha' is a dialect. Its occurrence as an answer following a negation intended for confirmation is rare. Al-a'raf: plural of 'urf, which is the elevated part of the ground. The poet said:

"Every thick one whose flesh is firm, like a mountain rising over the a'raf."

Al-Shammakh said:

"So they remained among a'raf, opposing, as if they were spears set by the wind's direction."

From it comes 'urf al-faras (the mane of a horse) and 'urf al-dik (the comb of a rooster), because of their height. Al-sitta: a known rank of number. Its original form was sidsa; they changed the sin to a ta', the change became fixed, then they assimilated the dal into the ta' after changing the dal to ta', and the assimilation became fixed. Its diminutives are sudays and sudaysa. Al-hath: hastening. I hathathtu fulanan fa-ahtha'a (I urged so-and-so, and he hastened). This was said by al-Layth, who added: he is hathith and mahthuth.

﴿Say, "My Lord has commanded justice."﴾ Ibn Abbas said: al-qist here is "There is no god but Allah," because all causes of good arise from it. Ata and al-Suddi said: it is justice, and what appears in speech to be good and correct. It was also said: it is truthfulness and right.

﴿And set your faces [toward Him] at every place of prostration, and call upon Him, sincere to Him in religion.﴾ "Wa-aqimu" (and establish) is coordinated with what the verbal noun al-qist resolves into, meaning: "that you be just and establish [your faces]." Just as the verbal noun can be resolved into "an" with a past verb, as in: "I marveled at Zayd's standing and leaving," meaning "that he stood and left"; and into "an" with a present verb, as in the poet's line: "Wearing a cloak and my eye being cooled," meaning: "that I wear a cloak and my eye be cooled." Likewise, it can be resolved into li-an with an imperative verb. Do you not see that "an" is connected to the imperative verb, as in "I wrote to him, 'an qum' (that you stand)," just as it is connected to the past and present verbs? This differs from the masdariyya "ma," for it is not connected to the imperative verb; and it differs from "kay" when it is not a particle but is masdariyya, for it is connected only to the present verb. Since this analysis was problematic, al-Zamakhshari made "wa-aqimu" depend on a supposed "qul" (say), saying: "aqimu." So it is possible that his statement "wa-qul aqimu" means "aqimu" is the object of the spoken verb, and it is possible that his statement "wa-aqimu" is coordinated with "amara rabbi bil-qist," so it is the object of the "qul" pronounced first. He assumed it so as to show that it is coordinated with it. According to our own analysis, it is in the predicate of the object of "amara." It was also said: "wa-aqimu" is coordinated with a deleted "amara," whose assumed form is "fa-aqbilu wa-aqimu" (so turn and establish). Ibn Abbas, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Qutayba, who chose it, said: the meaning is that when prayer is present, pray in every mosque, and let none of you say, "I pray in my mosque." Mujahid, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is to face wherever you are in prayer toward the Ka'ba. Al-Rabi' said: make your prostration purely for Allah, not for other than Him. It was also said: its meaning is to intend the mosque at the time of every prayer, as a command to congregate. Al-Mawardi mentioned this. It was also said: its meaning is that if there is a mosque near you, establish the congregation there and do not go past it to another. Al-Tibrizi mentioned this. It was also said: it is a command to bring the intention to Allah in every prayer and to direct oneself toward Him, as you say, "I turned my face..." [Al-An'am: 79], the verse. Al-Rabi' also said this. It was also said: its meaning is the permission to pray in every place on earth; that is, wherever you are, it is a mosque for you, and at it prayer is obligatory for you, and the setting of your faces toward Allah is in it. In a hadith: "The earth has been made a mosque for me, so whichever man is reached by prayer, let him pray wherever he is." Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, intend His worship, facing toward Him upright, not turning away from Him to anything else, at every mosque, at the time of every prostration, and in every place where there is prostration, which is prayer. "And call upon Him, sincere to Him in religion." It was said: the supplication is on its original basis, commanded together with sincerity, because the supplication of one who does not make religion purely for Allah is not answered. It was also said: its meaning is "worship," and it was said: "Say: there is no god but Allah."

As He originated you, so you will return. ﴿كما بدأكم تعودون﴾

A group He guided, and a group upon whom error was justly decreed. ﴿فريقا هدى وفريقا حق عليهم الضلالة﴾

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and Qatadah said: it is an announcement of the Resurrection (ba'th). That is, just as He brought you into existence and originated you, so He will restore you after death. Al-Zamakhshari (d. 538 AH), the Mu'tazili commentator, mentioned only this opinion. He said: "As He originated you at first, He will restore you. He argued against them in their denial of the return by means of the origination of creation, and the meaning is: He will restore you and then recompense you for your deeds, so devote your worship to Him alone." End of quote. This is also the view of al-Zajjaj, who said: "As He gave you life in this world, He will give you life in the Hereafter, and your resurrection is no harder than the initial creation of you. This is an argument against them in their denial of resurrection." End of quote.

Ibn 'Abbas also said, and so did Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, Abu al-'Aliyah, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, Mujahid again, and al-Farra' (and its meaning is narrated from the Messenger), that it is an announcement that whoever is destined in this world to be among the people of wretchedness and disbelief will be among their people in the Hereafter, and likewise whoever is destined in this world to have felicity and faith will be among their people in the Hereafter. Nothing of what He, may He be exalted, has decreed and arranged is changed.

This meaning is supported by the reading of Ubayy: "you will return as two groups, a group He guided and a group upon whom error was justly decreed." On this meaning, stopping at ﴿تعودون﴾ is not good (ghayr hasan), because فريقا (fariqan, "a group") is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal), and وفريقا (wa-fariqan) is conjoined to it. The clause of هدى (hada, "He guided") and the clause of حق (haqqa, "was decreed") are in the position of a description (sifah) of what precedes them, and the pronoun has been omitted from the descriptive clause, that is, "He guided them." Abu al-Baqa' permitted that فريقا be the object of هدى, and وفريقا the object of an implied أضل (adalla, "He led astray"), with the two verbal clauses being circumstantial (hal), and هدى being understood with an implied قد (qad), that is: "you will return, having indeed guided a group and led astray a group." On the first meaning, stopping at ﴿تعودون﴾ is good, فريقا is the object of هدى, and وفريقا is in the accusative by an implied verb which is explained by the statement ﴿حق عليهم الضلالة﴾.

Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿فريقا هدى﴾ refers to those who submitted (aslamu), that is, He granted them success in faith. ﴿وفريقا حق عليهم الضلالة﴾, that is, the word of error (kalimat al-dalalah) was decreed for them, and God, exalted is He, knew that they would go astray and not be guided. The accusative of His statement ﴿وفريقا﴾ is governed by a verb which is explained by what follows it, as if it were said: "and He forsook a group upon whom error was justly decreed." End of quote. These are interpretations according to the doctrine of the Mu'tazila (i'tizal, the Mu'tazili school), and it has been said: the meaning is "you will return with no helper for you and no one to assist you," in support of His statement: ﴿ولقد جئتمونا فرادى﴾ "And you have certainly come to Us alone" (al-An'am 6:94).

Al-Hasan said: "As He created you from dust, He will return you to dust." It has also been said: its meaning is "As He created you naked, you will be resurrected naked." As for ﴿حق عليهم الضلالة﴾, that is, it was justly decreed for them from God, or the punishment of error was justly decreed for them. Some scholars estimated it this way.

The attribution of guidance to God is stated, but its opposite, "and a group He led astray," is not stated. This is because the context (masaq) is a context of prohibition against being seduced by Satan, and of informing that the devils are allies of those who do not believe, and that God does not command immorality but commands justice and the establishment of prayer. So this context called for not attributing error to Him, the Exalted, even though He is the Guide, and the agent of error is (the people themselves). Accordingly, He turned to His statement ﴿حق عليهم الضلالة﴾.

﴿إنهم اتخذوا الشياطين أولياء من دون الله ويحسبون أنهم مهتدون﴾ "Indeed, they took the devils as allies instead of God, and they think they are guided." That is, indeed the erring group ﴿اتخذوا الشياطين أولياء﴾ "took the devils as allies," meaning helpers and supporters, whom they turn to and by whom they seek victory, like the saying of some of them: "Exalt Hubal, exalt Hubal." The apparent meaning is that the devils are literal devils, who assist them in their disbelief, and the erring ones take them as allies by submitting to their whisperings. It has been said: the devils are their rabbis and their elders. Al-Tabari said: this verse is evidence against the view of those who claim that God does not punish anyone for a sin he commits or an error he believes in, unless he commits it knowingly, aware of the correct position. End of quote. The point of evidence is His statement ﴿ويحسبون﴾ "and they think," and the mahsabah (ḥusbān, "supposing, thinking") is conjecture (zann), not knowledge (ʿilm).

Al-'Abbas ibn al-Fadl, Sahl ibn Shu'ayb, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read: أنهم اتخذوا (annahumu ittakhadhu, with a fatḥah on the hamzah), which makes it a causal explanation (ta'lil) for the decree of error upon them. The reverse (the causal explanation of the taking of allies) is also possible in meaning. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, they made them allies by obeying them in what they commanded them. This is evidence that the knowledge of God, exalted is He, has no effect on their error, and that they are the ones who go astray by their own choice and by their taking the devils as allies instead of God, exalted is He. End of quote. This is in the way of the Mu'tazila.

(p-286) ﴿Say, "My Lord has commanded justice. And set your faces [toward Him] at every place of prostration, and call upon Him, sincere to Him in religion. As He originated you, [to Him] you will return."﴾ ﴿A group He has guided, and a group upon whom error has been decreed. Indeed, they have taken the devils as allies instead of Allah, and they think they are guided.﴾ ﴿O children of Adam, take your adornment at every place of prayer, and eat and drink, but do not be excessive. Indeed, He does not like those who are excessive.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 31] ﴿Say, "Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision?" Say, "They are for those who believed in the worldly life, purely [for them] on the Day of Resurrection. Thus We detail the verses for a people who know."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 32] ﴿Say, "My Lord has only forbidden immoralities, what is apparent of them and what is concealed, and sin, and oppression without right, and that you associate with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority, and that you say about Allah what you do not know."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 33] ﴿And for every nation is a term. So when their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour, nor can they advance it.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 34] ﴿O children of Adam, if messengers from among you come to you relating My verses, then whoever fears Allah and makes reform, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 35] ﴿But those who denied Our verses and were arrogant toward them, those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 36] ﴿So who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah or denies His verses? Those will receive their portion from the Decree, until when Our messengers come to them to take their souls, they will say, "Where is that which you used to invoke besides Allah?" They will say, "They have strayed from us," and they will testify against themselves that they were disbelievers.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 37] ﴿[Allah] will say, "Enter into nations that have passed away before you, of jinn and mankind, into the Fire." Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister, until when they have all overtaken one another therein, the last of them will say of the first of them, "Our Lord, these have misled us, so give them a double punishment of the Fire." He will say, "For each is double, but you do not know."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 38] ﴿And the first of them will say to the last of them, "You had no superiority over us, so taste the punishment for what you used to earn."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 39] ﴿Indeed, those who denied Our verses and were arrogant toward them, the gates of heaven will not be opened for them, nor will they enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle. And thus do We recompense the criminals.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 40] ﴿For them from Hell is a bed, and above them are coverings. And thus do We recompense the wrongdoers.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 41] ﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds, We do not burden any soul except [according to] its capacity. Those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 42] ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts; rivers will flow beneath them. And they will say, "Praise be to Allah, who guided us to this. We would not have been guided had Allah not guided us. The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth." And they will be called, "This is Paradise; you have been given it as an inheritance for what you used to do."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 43] ﴿And the companions of Paradise will call to the companions of the Fire, "We have found true what our Lord promised us; have you found true what your Lord promised?" They will say, "Yes." Then a caller will announce among them, "The curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 44] ﴿Those who turn [others] away from the way of Allah and seek to make it crooked, and they, in the Hereafter, are disbelievers.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 45] ﴿And between them is a partition, and on the heights are men who recognize each by his mark. And they call out to the companions of Paradise, "Peace be upon you," they not having entered it, while they hope [to enter].﴾ [Al-A'raf: 46] ﴿And when their sights are turned toward the companions of the Fire, they say, "Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 47] ﴿And the companions of the heights will call out to men whom they recognize by their marks, saying, "Your gathering and what you used to be arrogant about have not availed you."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 48] ﴿"Are these the ones you swore Allah would not reach with mercy?" [It will be said to them], "Enter Paradise; no fear will be upon you, nor will you grieve."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 49] ﴿And the companions of the Fire will call to the companions of Paradise, "Pour upon us some water or of what Allah has provided you." They will say, "Indeed, Allah has forbidden them to the disbelievers."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 50] ﴿Those who took their religion as amusement and diversion and whom the worldly life deceived. So today We will forget them as they forgot the meeting of this Day of theirs, and as they used to deny Our verses.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 51] ﴿And We had certainly brought them a Book which We detailed with knowledge, as guidance and mercy for a people who believe.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 52] ﴿Do they await except its outcome? On the Day its outcome comes, those who had forgotten it before will say, "The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth. So do we have any intercessors to intercede for us, or could we be returned so that we might do other than what we used to do?" They have certainly lost themselves, and what they used to fabricate has gone astray from them.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 53] ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days; then He established Himself above the Throne. He covers the night with the day, which pursues it swiftly; and [He created] the sun, the moon, and the stars, subjected by His command. Unquestionably, to Him belong creation and command. Blessed is Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 54]

Bada'a al-shay': he originated it and invented it. Al-jamal: the well-known animal; its plurals are jimal and ajmul, and it is not called jamal until it reaches four years of age. Al-jamal also means the rope of a ship, and its dialect forms appear in compounds. Sam al-khiyat: its hole; the sin of sam may be pronounced with a damma, a fatha, or a kasra. Every hole in a nose, an ear, or otherwise, the Arabs call sam. Al-khiyat: al-makhit, and they are two instruments, like izar and mi'zar, liḥaf and milḥaf, and qina' and miqna'. Al-ghill: resentment and hidden enmity in the soul; its plural is ghilal, and from it comes al-ghulul, taking in concealment. Na'am: a particle that serves as affirmation of a pure positive statement, or of what a question contains. Kasra on its ayn is a dialect of Quraysh, and replacing its ayn with a ha' is a dialect. Its occurrence as an answer following a negation intended for confirmation is rare. Al-a'raf: plural of 'urf, which is the elevated part of the ground. The poet said:

"Every thick one whose flesh is firm, like a mountain rising over the a'raf."

Al-Shammakh said:

"So they remained among a'raf, opposing, as if they were spears set by the wind's direction."

From it comes 'urf al-faras (the mane of a horse) and 'urf al-dik (the comb of a rooster), because of their height. Al-sitta: a known rank of number. Its original form was sidsa; they changed the sin to a ta', the change became fixed, then they assimilated the dal into the ta' after changing the dal to ta', and the assimilation became fixed. Its diminutives are sudays and sudaysa. Al-hath: hastening. I hathathtu fulanan fa-ahtha'a (I urged so-and-so, and he hastened). This was said by al-Layth, who added: he is hathith and mahthuth.

﴿Say, "My Lord has commanded justice."﴾ Ibn Abbas said: al-qist here is "There is no god but Allah," because all causes of good arise from it. Ata and al-Suddi said: it is justice, and what appears in speech to be good and correct. It was also said: it is truthfulness and right.

﴿And set your faces [toward Him] at every place of prostration, and call upon Him, sincere to Him in religion.﴾ "Wa-aqimu" (and establish) is coordinated with what the verbal noun al-qist resolves into, meaning: "that you be just and establish [your faces]." Just as the verbal noun can be resolved into "an" with a past verb, as in: "I marveled at Zayd's standing and leaving," meaning "that he stood and left"; and into "an" with a present verb, as in the poet's line: "Wearing a cloak and my eye being cooled," meaning: "that I wear a cloak and my eye be cooled." Likewise, it can be resolved into li-an with an imperative verb. Do you not see that "an" is connected to the imperative verb, as in "I wrote to him, 'an qum' (that you stand)," just as it is connected to the past and present verbs? This differs from the masdariyya "ma," for it is not connected to the imperative verb; and it differs from "kay" when it is not a particle but is masdariyya, for it is connected only to the present verb. Since this analysis was problematic, al-Zamakhshari made "wa-aqimu" depend on a supposed "qul" (say), saying: "aqimu." So it is possible that his statement "wa-qul aqimu" means "aqimu" is the object of the spoken verb, and it is possible that his statement "wa-aqimu" is coordinated with "amara rabbi bil-qist," so it is the object of the "qul" pronounced first. He assumed it so as to show that it is coordinated with it. According to our own analysis, it is in the predicate of the object of "amara." It was also said: "wa-aqimu" is coordinated with a deleted "amara," whose assumed form is "fa-aqbilu wa-aqimu" (so turn and establish). ﴿O children of Adam, take your adornment at every place of worship, and eat and drink, but do not be wasteful. Indeed, He does not love the wasteful.﴾ The people of the Jahiliyya (pre-Islamic era) used to circumambulate the House naked. During the days of their pilgrimage they would not eat fat, and they would take nothing from food except the bare minimum, out of glorification of their pilgrimage. So this verse was revealed. It is also said that one of them would circumambulate naked and leave his clothes behind the mosque. If he circumambulated while wearing them, he would be struck and they would be torn from him, because they said: "We do not worship Allah in garments in which we have sinned." It is also said that this was done as an omen, so that they would be stripped of sins just as they were stripped of clothes.

The word zina (adornment) is a noun of the form fi'la from the verb tazayyun (to adorn oneself). It is the name of what one beautifies oneself with, such as garments and other things, as in His words: ﴿and the earth adorned itself﴾, meaning with plants. The adornment commanded to be taken here is that which covers the private parts ('awra) during prayer. This is the view of Mujahid, al-Suddi and al-Zajjaj. Tawus said: "The wrap (shamla) is part of the adornment." Mujahid said: "Whatever covers your private parts, even a cloak ('aba'a), is adornment." It is also said that it is what covers the private parts during circumambulation.

In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Urwa, the Arabs used to circumambulate naked except for the Hums, who were the Quraysh, unless the Hums gave them garments. Men would give garments to men, and women to women. In other narrations (outside Muslim): whoever did not have a friend in Makkah to lend him a garment would circumambulate naked, or in his own clothes and then discard them, and no one would touch them. This is called al-luqa' (the discarded). Some of them said:

"Enough sorrow is my returning to it, as if it were a discarded garment before the circumambulators, forbidden to touch."

A woman would recite while circumambulating naked:

"Today some of it or all of it appears, and what appears of it, I will not make lawful."

When Allah sent His Messenger (ﷺ) and revealed to him: ﴿O children of Adam, take your adornment at every place of worship﴾, the Messenger's crier proclaimed: "Let no polytheist perform the pilgrimage to the House after this year, and let no one circumambulate the House naked." This proclamation took place in Makkah in the ninth year (AH).

﴿Say: "My Lord has only forbidden indecencies, whether apparent or hidden, sin, unjust transgression, associating with Allah what He has not sent down authority for, and saying about Allah what you do not know."﴾ Al-Kalbi said: When the Muslims wore clothes and circumambulated the House, the polytheists reproached them for this and said, "They have made the sacred things lawful," so this was revealed. The interpretation of ﴿indecencies, whether apparent or hidden﴾ has already been given at the end of *al-An'am*, but further views are added here. One of them: ﴿what is apparent of them﴾ is a man's circumambulation by day while naked, and ﴿what is hidden﴾ is a woman's circumambulation by night while naked. This is said by al-Tibrizi. Mujahid said: ﴿what is apparent﴾ is the circumambulation of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance) while naked, and ﴿what is hidden﴾ is fornication. It was also said: ﴿what is apparent﴾ is injustice, and ﴿what is hidden﴾ is theft. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid, in one narration, said: ﴿what is apparent﴾ is what the Jahiliyyah used to do of marrying the wives of their fathers, combining two sisters, and marrying a woman together with her paternal aunt or maternal aunt, and ﴿what is hidden﴾ is fornication. ﴿Sin﴾ is general, encompassing the sayings and actions that bring about sin. This is the view of the majority (*jumhur*). It was also said that it refers to minor sins. It was said that it refers to wine, but this view is not sound here, because the surah is Meccan, and wine was not forbidden except in Medina after Uhud. A group of the Companions drank it on the day of Uhud and died as martyrs while it was still in their bellies. As for calling wine "sin," it is said that this comes from the words of a poet:

*"I drank sin until my reason slipped."*

This is a fabricated and invented line. Even if it is authentic, it is by elision of a modifier, meaning "the cause of sin." The saying of Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan, that ﴿sin﴾ is wine, does not prove that it is one of its names, since that would be the use of the effect to denote the cause. Abu al-Abbas (al-Mubarrad) denied that "sin" is one of the names of wine. Al-Fadl said: "Sin is wine," and recited:

*"The Messenger of Allah forbade us to draw near to vileness, and to drink the sin that brings burden."*

Al-Asma'i also recited:

*"I went on grieving, bewildered in mind after them, as though I had drunk sin or been touched by madness."*

He said: "Wine is sometimes called sin," and recited:

*"I drank sin until my reason slipped."*

Ibn Abbas and al-Farra' said: "Transgression (*baghy*) is overbearing." Al-Hasan said: "It is intoxication from every drink." Tha'lab said: "It is a man speaking against another man without right, unless he is avenging himself with right." It was also said that it is injustice and arrogance, as stated by al-Zamakhshari, who said: "They singled it out for mention, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He forbids indecency, what is wrong, and transgression﴾ [al-Nahl: 90]." Ibn Atiyya said: "Transgression (*baghy*) is aggression and exceeding the limit, whether initiated or in retaliation. His words ﴿without right﴾ are an added clarification, and there is no conceivable transgression with right, since what is with right is not called transgression." The interpretation of ﴿what He has not sent down authority for﴾ has been given in *al-An'am*. Al-Zamakhshari said that it contains mockery, because it is not possible that He would send down proof permitting associating with Him others of whom you have no knowledge, such as the forbidding of the *bahair* (slit-eared she-camels) and other things. Ibn Abbas said: He meant by this that the angels are the daughters of Allah. It was also said that their saying is that He forbade them foods, garments, and drinks during the state of ihram (pilgrim consecration) of their own accord.

﴿For every community there is a term. So when their term comes, they cannot delay it by an hour, nor can they advance it.﴾ This is a warning to the people of Mecca of punishment descending at a known term with Allah, as it descended upon the nations. That is, there is a fixed term for the coming of punishment when they oppose the command of their Lord, and so you, O community, are likewise. (p-293) It was also said: the term here is the term of this world. The meaning is that for all the nations there is a term, that is, they advance to what they have already done of deeds. It was also said: the term is the span of life, and the meaning is that for each member of the community there is a lifespan that ends his remaining in this world, and when he dies he will know what he had of right or wrong. Ibn Atiyya said: "*Ummah* is any group or company, a word used for many people." Others said: "*Ummah* is a group, whether few or many, and it may also be applied to one individual, as in His saying about Qus ibn Sa'ida: 'He will be raised on the Day of Resurrection as a community alone.'" The term is singular because it is a generic noun, or because the deeds of the people of each era are close to one another, or because the meaning is: for each individual of a community. Al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin read *fa-idha ja'a ajalahum* in the plural (*ājālahum*). He said *sa'ah* (an hour) because it is the least of times in people's usage: the one hurrying his companion says "in an hour," meaning in the shortest and nearest time. This is said by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn Atiyya said: "It is a word by which is meant the smallest portion of time, and the intended meaning is the totality of its parts." End of quote. A negated imperfect verb with *la* that comes after *idha* in the apparent sense may be linked with the particle of response *fa* (the *fa* of the conditional answer), and it may be left unlinked with it. One should hold that between the *fa* and the verb there is an elided subject, so the clause becomes nominal, and a nominal clause that comes as the answer to *idha* must have *fa* or *idha al-fuja'iyyah* (the sudden *idha*). Some said: *fa* has entered upon *idha* wherever it occurs except in Yunus, because it links a clause to a clause between which there is connection and sequence, so the place called for *fa*. What is in Yunus will come in its place, Allah willing. End of quote. Al-Hawfi said: "*wa-la yastaqdimun*" is conjoined to "*la yasta'khirun*." End of quote. This is impossible, because *idha* is conditional, and what follows it is necessarily future, and nothing follows the coming of the term in the future except something future. That is conceivable regarding the negation of delay, but not regarding the negation of advancing, because advancing precedes the coming of the term in the future. This would be like saying: "If you stand up in the future, your standing will not have preceded in the past," and it is known that if he stands up in the future, his standing will not have preceded in the past. This resembles the saying of Zuhayr:

*"It became clear to me that I will not overtake what has passed, nor will I precede anything when it is coming."*

It is known that when a thing is coming toward one, one does not precede it. What the verse is to be understood as is that His saying ﴿nor can they advance it﴾ is severed from the answer, as a resumed statement of information. That is, they cannot advance the term, meaning they cannot precede it, and the meaning of the verse becomes that they neither precede the term nor delay from it.

﴿Children of Adam, if messengers come to you from among you, relating to you My signs, then whoever is mindful of Allah and makes amends, there is no fear for them, nor will they grieve. And those who deny Our signs and act arrogantly toward them, those are the companions of the Fire, in which they will abide forever.﴾ This address is to the children of Adam. It was said: it is at the beginning. It was said: it is intended for the time of the revelation. It came in the form of the future in order to strengthen the indication of the validity of prophethood for Muhammad (ﷺ). The *in* in *immā* is for emphasis. Ibn Atiyya said: "If it is not so, then it does not permit the heavy *nun* (the energetic *nun*)." End of quote. Some grammarians permit that. The answer of the condition is ﴿whoever is mindful of Allah﴾, and *man* may be conditional, with its answer ﴿there is no fear﴾, so this conditional clause would be independent in its answer as to the first condition, in terms of wording. It may also be that *man* is relative, so this clause and the one after it, from His saying ﴿those who denied﴾, together constitute the answer of the condition. It seems that He intended by the speech the division, and the two parts were made the answer of the condition: meaning, "if messengers come to you," then those who are mindful have no fear, and those who deny are the companions of the Fire. So the fruit of the coming of the messengers and its benefit is this. His saying ﴿whoever is mindful of Allah and makes amends﴾ implies the precedence of faith, since mindfulness and amendment arise from it. And His saying ﴿those who denied﴾ is in contrast, and denial is the emergence of wretchedness, since nothing arises from it except persistence in wrongdoing and corruption. He said: rather, amendment is by arrogance, because the amendment of deeds is a result of mindfulness, while arrogance is a result of denial, which is self-magnification. They would not then follow the messengers in what they brought, nor take as an example what they were commanded, because whoever denies a thing distances himself from following it. Ibn Atiyya said: "These are two states that cover everyone who turns away from the message of the Messenger: either he denies according to his belief that he has denied, or he is arrogant and so denies, even if he is not firmly set in his belief on denial. This is like: disbelief is obstinacy." End of quote. The two sentences contain an elision of a connecting pronoun, and its estimate is: "whoever is mindful and makes amends from among you," and "those who denied from among you." The interpretation of ﴿there is no fear﴾ and ﴿those are the companions of the Fire﴾ has been given, both sentences. Ubayy and al-A'raj read *immā ta'tiyannakum* with the *ta'* (feminine), in accordance with the feminine form of the collective noun, and *yaqussūn* is taken according to the sense, since if it were taken according to the wording it would be *taqussu*.

﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah or denies His signs? Those will receive their portion of the Book.﴾ When He mentioned the deniers, He mentioned one who is in a worse state than them, namely one who fabricates lies against Allah, and He also mentioned one who denies His signs. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, and Mujahid said: their portion is what was written for them of happiness and wretchedness, but this interpretation does not suit the sentence that follows. Al-Hasan said: what was written for them of punishment. Al-Rabi', Muhammad ibn Ka'b, and Ibn Zayd said: what had preceded for them in the Mother of the Book (*Umm al-Kitab*). Ibn Abbas also said, and Mujahid also, and Qatadah: what the guardian angels (*al-hafazah*) recorded in the people's records of good and evil, so it will be said: "This is your portion of that," which is disbelief and sins. Al-Hakam and Abu Salih said: what was written for them of provisions, lifespans, good and evil in this world. Al-Dahhak said: what was written for them of reward and punishment. Ibn Abbas also said, and al-Dahhak also, and Mujahid: what was written for them of disbelief and sins. Al-Hasan also said: what was written for them of misguidance and guidance. Ibn Abbas also said: what was written for them of deeds. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak said: "from the Book" means the Qur'an, and their share in it is the blackening of their faces on the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: what He required of preserving their covenants when they pay the *jizyah* (poll tax). Al-Hasan, al-Suddi, and Abu Salih said: from what is fixed in the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*). It has been established in the Sharia that their share in it is punishment and wrath. What appears to be the case is that what was written for them in this world of provision and term and other things will reach them in it, and for this reason the limit that follows is marked with *hatta* (until). Al-Zamakhshari followed this meaning and said: that is, what He wrote for them of provisions and deeds.

﴿Until, when Our messengers come to them to take their souls, they say, "Where is that which you used to call upon besides Allah?" They say, "They have left us," and they will testify against themselves that they had been disbelievers.﴾ The discussion of *hatta idha* has preceded at the beginning of *al-An'am*. It occurred in the *Tahrir* that *hatta* here is not a limit but an inceptive (*ibtida'*) particle and a preposition (*jarr*), and the clause after it is in the position of a genitive. This is a mistake. Rather its meaning here is the limit. The disagreement about it when it is an inceptive particle is whether it is a preposition, with the clause after it in the position of the genitive and connected to what precedes it as prepositions are connected, or whether it is not a preposition and is not connected to what precedes it in the manner of prepositions in terms of meaning, not in terms of grammatical analysis (*i'rab*). There are two views: the first belongs to Ibn Duristawayh and al-Zajjaj, and the second to the majority (*jumhur*). When it is an inceptive particle, it is for the limit. Do you not see it in the words of the poet:

*"I traveled with them until their mounts grew weary, and even the thoroughbreds were not led by reins."*

And the words of another:

*"The slain did not cease to spill their blood in the Tigris, until the water of the Tigris became tinged with red."*

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 33–39 (part 2 of 2):

It indicates the limit (ghayah), because the meaning is that He extended their resolve in travel until the mounts and the horses became exhausted, and the blood flowed into changing the water of the Tigris. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is the *hatta* after which speech is begun." End of quote. Al-Hawfi said: "*Hatta* is a limit (ghayah) connected to *yanaluhum* (their portion shall reach them). His statement may intend the syntactic connection (ta'alluq sina'i) or the semantic connection (ta'alluq ma'nawi). The meaning is: their portion from what was written for them will reach them until the messengers of death come to them, seize their souls, and ask them a question of rebuke and affirmation: 'Where are the things you worshipped besides Allah?' They answer that they have strayed from us and taken a path other than ours, or that they went astray from us, were destroyed and vanished. The messengers are the Angel of Death and his helpers, and *yatawaffawnahum* is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). *Aynama* is written joined, though its analogical writing would be separated, because *ma* is a relative pronoun, as in ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is coming﴾ [al-An'am: 134], the implied meaning being: 'Where are the gods you used to worship?' It was also said that *tad'un* means you call upon them, i.e., you seek their help for the fulfilment of your needs." What we have mentioned, that this dialogue between the angels and these people takes place at the time of death, and that *tawaffi* means the seizing of souls, is the view of the commentators. A group among them, including al-Hasan, said: "The messengers are the angels of punishment on the Day of Resurrection, the dialogue takes place on that day, and the meaning of ﴿yatawaffawnahum﴾ is that they count them in full as they drive them toward Hell, and taking their share. On this view it occurs in the Hereafter, since if it were in this world the limit would not be realised, because the taking of the share would have ceased long before it by many periods." *Wa-shahidu* (and they bear witness) may be a separate clause after *qalu* (they said), in which case it is part of the answer to the question. It may also be a new report from Allah, the Exalted, about their confession against themselves of disbelief. There is no contradiction between this and His statement ﴿By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23], because this may come from different groups or at different times. Their answer does not correspond verbally, since the question was about a place and the answer was given with a verb; but it corresponds in meaning, since the implied question is: 'What did your gods besides Allah do with you?' ﴿They said: They have strayed from us﴾.

﴿He said: Enter among nations that passed away before you, of jinn and humankind, into the Fire.﴾ That is, Allah says to them, meaning the disbelievers of the Arabs, who are the ones who fabricate lies and deny the signs, and that is on the Day of Resurrection. He used the past tense to affirm that it will certainly occur. This statement is spoken through the angels. *Fi umam* apparently relates to *udkhulu* (enter), and the meaning is: among the company of nations. It may also relate to an implied verb, so that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause. ﴿Who passed away before you﴾ means they preceded you in the life of this world, or they preceded you, i.e., their entering the Fire came before yours. He mentioned the jinn first because they are the origin of seduction and misguidance. This shows that disobedient jinn also enter the Fire. *Fi al-nar* relates to *khalat* (passed away), on the basis that the meaning is that their entering had already occurred; or it relates to an implied word, serving as a description of *umam*, meaning: among nations earlier in time, existing among the jinn and humankind, existing in the Fire; or it relates to *udkhulu* on the assumption that *fi* means *ma'a* (with), which some commentators have said. Then the meaning of *fi* differs: the first *fi* indicates accompaniment, and the second indicates place. When the meaning of the particle differs, both words may depend on a single verb, and in that case *udkhulu* has transitively governed the locative object introduced by *fi*, which is the basic use, although in another place it has governed it directly without the mediation of *fi*, as in ﴿Enter the gates of Hell﴾ [al-Zumar: 72]. It is also permissible for *fi* to remain on its locative meaning, and *fi al-nar* likewise, both depending on the word *udkhulu*, on the basis that *fi al-nar* is a badal al-ishtimal (inclusive apposition, a substitute that includes the thing substituted for) like His statement ﴿Killed were the people of the trench﴾ [al-Buruj: 4–5], ﴿the fire﴾. It is also permissible for a verb to govern two prepositions with a single meaning, by way of substitution.

﴿Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister.﴾ *Kullama* indicates repetition, and this does not apply to the first nation. The later one curses the earlier one, or some of the nation that enters curses some of it. *Ukhtaha* (its sister) means in religion. The meaning is: every time a nation of Jews, Christians, idol-worshippers, and other disbelievers enters. Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Ukhtaha* is the one that went astray by following it." End of quote. The meaning is that the people of the Fire curse one another, oppose one another, and disbelieve in one another, as is mentioned in other verses.

﴿Until, when they have all overtaken one another therein, the last of them will say of the first of them: Our Lord, these misled us, so give them a double punishment of the Fire.﴾ [p. 296] *Hatta* is a limit for what precedes it. The meaning is that they enter in groups, one after another, cursing one another, until they finish overtaking and catching up with one another in the Fire and gathering there. The original of *iddarakū* is *tadarakū*; the *ta'* was assimilated into the *dal* (idgham, merging of two identical consonants), and a hamzat al-wasl (connecting hamza, a hamza used at the start of a word when the initial consonant is unvocalised) was brought in. Ibn Atiyya said: "Abu Amr read *adda­rakū* with a cut hamza (qat' alif al-wasl)." Abu al-Fath said: "This is problematic, and it is not permissible to cut it spontaneously. That occurs only anomalously in poetic necessity, also with nouns. However, he paused as one expressing disapproval, then began and cut it." Mujahid read with a cut alif, sukūn on the *dal*, and fatha on the *ra'*, meaning that some of them overtook others. Humayd read *udrikū* with a damma on the hamza and kasra on the *ra'*, meaning: they were made to enter into its overtaking. Makki said of Mujahid's reading that it is *iddarakū* with a shadda on the open *dal* and fatha on the *ra'*, and said: its original is *idtarakū* on the pattern *ifta'alū*. Ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash read *tadarakū*, and this is transmitted from Abu Amr. End of quote. Abu al-Baqa' said: "It is read *idda­rakū* with one unvocalised alif and the *dal* after it shadda, and this is a combination of two unvocalised letters, which is permitted in a separated word as it is in a joined word. Some have said there are twelve readings, with the alif written and the ‘ayn unvocalised." End of quote. By his statement "as it is in a joined word," he means examples like *al-dallin*, *janin*, and *ukhrahum*. The "last of them" is the last nation in time, which found established misguidances in use by the first nation that instituted them, invented them, and took the path of error from the beginning. Or "the last of them" means in rank and station, and these are the followers and the lowly, and "the first of them" means in rank and station, and these are the leaders who were followed. Or "the last of them" means in entering the Fire, and these are the followers, and "the first of them" means in entering, and these are the leaders. These are opinions; the last of them is attributed to Muqatil. Ibn Abbas said: "The last nation to the first nation." Here *ukhrā* means *ākhira* (last), the feminine of *ākhar* (other). The opposite of *awwal* (first) has no feminine form, and *ākhar* means "other," as in His statement ﴿the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164]. The *lam* in *li-ulahum* is the lam of cause, meaning for the sake of their first ones, because their address is with Allah, not with them. ﴿Misled us﴾: they established misguidance for us, or made us stray and compelled us to it, giving a double punishment beyond our punishment, since they are disbelievers and the causes of our disbelief.

﴿He said: For each there is double, but you do not know.﴾ That is, for each of the later and the earlier there is punishment; for the first there is a multiplied increased punishment without end, because the punishment is everlasting, so every pain is followed by another. The majority read with the *ta'* as address to the questioners, meaning: you do not know what each group has of punishment, or you do not know the measures and forms of punishment. It was said that it may also be address to the people of this world, meaning: but O people of the world, you do not know the measure of that. Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal from Asim read with the *ya'*, so it may be a report about the nation, and the pronoun in *la ya'lamūn* (they do not know) refers to the last nation, which asked that the punishment be doubled for its first ones. It may also be a report about both groups, meaning: each group does not know the measure of what has been prepared for it of punishment, or the measure of what has been prepared for the other group of punishment. It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud that the doubling here means snakes and serpents. This sentence is a rejection of those questioners and a denial of what they asked for.

﴿The first of them said to the last of them: You had no superiority over us, so taste the punishment for what you used to earn.﴾ That is, the group that was followed said to the group that followed. The *lam* in *li-ukhrāhum* is the lam of communication, as in "I told you: do such and such," because the address is with the last of them, unlike the *lam* in *li-ulāhum*, which, as we mentioned, is the lam of cause, because the address there is with Allah the Exalted. The meaning is: you have no superiority over us, and you did not refrain when the messengers and warners came to you; rather you remained in your disbelief and abandoned reflection, so our state and your state became equal. Al-Zamakhshari said: "That is, it has been established that you have no superiority over us, and that we are equal in deserving double punishment." Mujahid said: the meaning of ﴿min fadl﴾ (superiority) is "of lightening," in reference to Allah's statement ﴿for each there is double﴾; the first said to the last: "You were not granted hope that your punishment is lighter than ours, nor were you favoured with relief." End of quote. The *fa* in *fa-ma* (so no): al-Zamakhshari said: "They attached this statement to the saying of Allah, the Exalted, to the lowly ones ﴿for each there is double﴾." What appears to be the meaning is the negation that they were given superiority over the lowly ones in this world, through their following them and agreeing with them in disbelief. That is, your following us and your not following us are the same, because in this world you were too insignificant in our eyes for you to have any superiority over us through following us; rather you disbelieved by your own choice, not because we compelled you to it by force. And His statement *fa-mā* is coordinated with an omitted clause after the saying, indicated by what preceded in the speech. The estimate is: the first said to the last: "What is your calling upon Allah, claiming that we misled you, and your asking what you asked? You had no superiority over us through your misguidance." And His statement ﴿So taste the punishment﴾ is part of the words of the first, addressed to the last, for the sake of avenging themselves on them. The tasting of punishment is for what they earned of sins, not because of your claim that we misled you. It was also said: ﴿So taste﴾ is an address from Allah to all of them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) on Surah 7, verses 33–39 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Say: "My Lord has only forbidden indecencies, whether apparent or hidden, sin, unjust transgression, associating with Allah what He has not sent down authority for, and saying about Allah what you do not know."﴾ Al-Kalbi said: When the Muslims wore clothes and circumambulated the House, the polytheists reproached them for this and said, "They have made the sacred things lawful," so this was revealed. The interpretation of ﴿indecencies, whether apparent or hidden﴾ has already been given at the end of *al-An'am*, but further views are added here. One of them: ﴿what is apparent of them﴾ is a man's circumambulation by day while naked, and ﴿what is hidden﴾ is a woman's circumambulation by night while naked. This is said by al-Tibrizi. Mujahid said: ﴿what is apparent﴾ is the circumambulation of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance) while naked, and ﴿what is hidden﴾ is fornication. It was also said: ﴿what is apparent﴾ is injustice, and ﴿what is hidden﴾ is theft. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid, in one narration, said: ﴿what is apparent﴾ is what the Jahiliyyah used to do of marrying the wives of their fathers, combining two sisters, and marrying a woman together with her paternal aunt or maternal aunt, and ﴿what is hidden﴾ is fornication. ﴿Sin﴾ is general, encompassing the sayings and actions that bring about sin. This is the view of the majority (*jumhur*). It was also said that it refers to minor sins. It was said that it refers to wine, but this view is not sound here, because the surah is Meccan, and wine was not forbidden except in Medina after Uhud. A group of the Companions drank it on the day of Uhud and died as martyrs while it was still in their bellies. As for calling wine "sin," it is said that this comes from the words of a poet:

*"I drank sin until my reason slipped."*

This is a fabricated and invented line. Even if it is authentic, it is by elision of a modifier, meaning "the cause of sin." The saying of Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan, that ﴿sin﴾ is wine, does not prove that it is one of its names, since that would be the use of the effect to denote the cause. Abu al-Abbas (al-Mubarrad) denied that "sin" is one of the names of wine. Al-Fadl said: "Sin is wine," and recited:

*"The Messenger of Allah forbade us to draw near to vileness, and to drink the sin that brings burden."*

Al-Asma'i also recited:

*"I went on grieving, bewildered in mind after them, as though I had drunk sin or been touched by madness."*

He said: "Wine is sometimes called sin," and recited:

*"I drank sin until my reason slipped."*

Ibn Abbas and al-Farra' said: "Transgression (*baghy*) is overbearing." Al-Hasan said: "It is intoxication from every drink." Tha'lab said: "It is a man speaking against another man without right, unless he is avenging himself with right." It was also said that it is injustice and arrogance, as stated by al-Zamakhshari, who said: "They singled it out for mention, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He forbids indecency, what is wrong, and transgression﴾ [al-Nahl: 90]." Ibn Atiyya said: "Transgression (*baghy*) is aggression and exceeding the limit, whether initiated or in retaliation. His words ﴿without right﴾ are an added clarification, and there is no conceivable transgression with right, since what is with right is not called transgression." The interpretation of ﴿what He has not sent down authority for﴾ has been given in *al-An'am*. Al-Zamakhshari said that it contains mockery, because it is not possible that He would send down proof permitting associating with Him others of whom you have no knowledge, such as the forbidding of the *bahair* (slit-eared she-camels) and other things. Ibn Abbas said: He meant by this that the angels are the daughters of Allah. It was also said that their saying is that He forbade them foods, garments, and drinks during the state of ihram (pilgrim consecration) of their own accord.

﴿For every community there is a term. So when their term comes, they cannot delay it by an hour, nor can they advance it.﴾ This is a warning to the people of Mecca of punishment descending at a known term with Allah, as it descended upon the nations. That is, there is a fixed term for the coming of punishment when they oppose the command of their Lord, and so you, O community, are likewise. (p-293) It was also said: the term here is the term of this world. The meaning is that for all the nations there is a term, that is, they advance to what they have already done of deeds.
