Those whose good deeds and bad deeds are equal have a deficient rank, and such honour does not befit them." It was answered that it is possible that ﴿and they will be called﴾ is an address to specific groups, so it does not follow that the people of Paradise are like this. As for the second objection, [God] placed them there not for honour, but because it is like an intermediate station between Paradise and the Fire. And as for ﴿that peace be upon you﴾, it is possible that "an" (أنْ) is explanatory and a lightened form of the heavy particle. And ﴿they had not entered it﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object, meaning: he called them while they were in this state, i.e., the people of Paradise, ﴿and they were hoping﴾ is a declarative clause with no place in grammatical analysis (i'rab), meaning: they called out to the people of Paradise while not having entered it, and then he informed that they were hoping to enter it. This is the meaning given by Abu al-Baqa'. It was also said: the meaning is that the companions of al-A'raf called out to the companions of Paradise with peace, while they had entered Paradise, and the people of al-A'raf had not entered it. Thus ﴿they had not entered it﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of "they called out" referring only to the people of al-A'raf. This is the interpretation of Ibn Mas'ud, Qatada, al-Suddi, and others. Ibn Mas'ud said: "By God, God did not place that hope in their hearts except for a good that He intended for them." This is the most apparent and the most fitting to the context of the verse. Ibn Mas'ud also said: "The companions of al-A'raf only hoped because the light that was in their hands was not extinguished when the light of the hypocrites was extinguished." It was also said: ﴿and they were hoping﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the subject of ﴿they had entered it﴾, and the meaning is: they did not enter it in a state of hoping for it, rather they were in a state of despair and fear, but God's pardon encompassed them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the place (i'rab) of His words ﴿they had not entered it and they were hoping﴾? I say: it has no place, because it is a resumed sentence (isti'naf), as if a questioner asked about the companions of al-A'raf, and it was said to him: ﴿they had not entered it and they were hoping﴾, meaning that their entry into Paradise was delayed behind the entry of the people of Paradise, so they had not entered it because they were being held back, and they were hoping, not despairing." And it is permissible that it has a place by being a qualifying clause (sifah). End of quote. This is a weak explanation for separating the described from its descriptive clause with the clause ﴿and they called out﴾, which is not a parenthetical clause (i'tiraD).

Ibn al-Nahwi read ﴿and they are hoping﴾ (وهم طامِعُونَ). Iyad ibn Laqit read ﴿and they are discontented﴾ (وهم ساخِطُونَ). Al-A'mash read ﴿and when their sights are turned﴾ (وإذا قُلِّبَتْ أبْصارُهم). The pronoun in "their sights" refers to the men of al-A'raf, who greet the people of Paradise, and when they look at the people of the Fire, they call upon God to be delivered from it. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and a group. Abu Mijlaz said: the pronoun refers to the people of Paradise, and they had not yet entered it. In His words ﴿they are turned﴾ there is evidence that most of their states is looking towards the companions of Paradise, and that their looking at the companions of the Fire is due to their sights being turned towards them. So the turning is not from their side; rather they are carried along into it, and it is done to them, because that place of overlooking is frightening to hear of, let alone to see, let alone to be involved in it. The meaning is that when they are made to turn their sights and see what they are suffering from the punishment, they seek refuge with their Lord from being made to be with them. The word ﴿our Lord﴾ indicates the description of Him, the Exalted, as the one who reforms them and is their master, while they are servants. So by calling upon Him with this, they seek His mercy and appeal to His generosity.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 40–47 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Indeed, those who denied Our signs and were arrogant toward them, the gates of heaven will not be opened for them.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿will not be opened﴾ for their deeds, nor for their supplications, nor for anything they intend by it the obedience of Allah, the Exalted. That is, no righteous deed ascends for them, so that the gates of heaven would be opened for it. This is drawn from His saying: ﴿To Him ascend the good word, and the righteous deed raises it﴾ [Fatir: 10], and from His saying: ﴿Indeed, the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyun﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 18]. As-Suddi and others said: ﴿will not be opened﴾ for their spirits. They mentioned, concerning the ascent of the spirits to heaven and the permission granted to the spirit of the believer and the rejection of the spirit of the disbeliever, reports (ahadith), and that occurs at the time of their death. It was also said: the meaning is that ﴿the gates of heaven will not be opened for them﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, so that they may enter through them into Paradise. That is, they will not be permitted to ascend to heaven. It was also said: blessing will not descend upon them, and they will not be given relief. Abu ʿAmr recited ﴿will not be opened﴾ with the feminine ta' and without tashdid (the doubling of the letter), al-Akhawan (the two brothers, Hamza and al-Kisai) recited it with the ya' and without tashdid, and the rest of the seven readers recited it with the ta' at the beginning and with tashdid. Abu Haywa and Abu al-Barahsam recited it with the thaʾ at the beginning, open (fatha), and with tashdid.

﴿And they will not enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle.﴾ This is a negation conditioned upon something impossible. Al-wulud (passing into) means penetrating into a thing. He mentioned the camel because it is the largest animal that deals with humans in bulk, so it can only pass through a wide opening, as the poet said: "The camel has grown large without intellect," and he said: "The body of camels and the dreams of sparrows." He mentioned ﴿the eye of the needle﴾ because it is used as a proverb for a narrow passage; it is said: "Narrower than the eye of a needle" (khart al-ibra). It was also said that a guide is called kharrit because of his guidance through narrow places, by analogy with the hole of the needle (ikhrat al-ibra). The meaning is that they will never enter Paradise. Ibn ʿAbbas was recited, according to what Shahr ibn Hawshab narrated from him, along with Mujahid, Ibn Yaʿmur, Abu Mijlaz, ash-Shaʿbi, Malik ibn ash-Shikhkhir, Abu Rajaʾ, Abu Razin, Ibn Muhaysin, and Aban from ʿAsim, as al-Jummal (الجُمَّلُ) with a damma on the jim and a fatha on the mim with tashdid. It was interpreted as the thick rope (al-qals al-ghalidh), which is the ship's cable: ropes are gathered and twisted and become one rope. It was also said that it is the thick rope made of hemp. It was also said that it is the rope by which one climbs up palm trees. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, though it probably is not authentic, that Allah is too beautiful in comparison than to be likened to a camel, meaning that it is not appropriate, whereas a rope is appropriate for the thread that passes through the eye of a needle. From al-Kisai: the one who transmitted al-Jummal from Ibn ʿAbbas was non-Arab, so he doubled the jim because of his non-Arabic pronunciation. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: this is weak, because of the large number of Ibn ʿAbbas's companions who recited it in the aforementioned reading. (End of quote.) And also because of the large number of readers other than Ibn ʿAbbas who recited it that way. Ibn ʿAbbas also recited, according to a report from Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Qatada, and Salim al-Aftas, with a damma on the jim and a fatha on the mim, without tashdid. Ibn ʿAbbas, according to a report from ʿAta', al-Dahhak, and al-Jahdari, recited with a damma on both the jim and the mim, without tashdid. ʿIkrima and Ibn Jubayr, in one report, recited with a damma on the jim and a sukun on the mim: al-Jumul (الجُمْلُ). Al-Mutawakkil and Abu al-Jawza' recited with a fatha on the jim and a sukun on the mim. Their meaning in these readings is the thick rope, which is the ship's cable. The reading of the majority is ﴿al-jamal (الجَمَلُ)﴾ with a fatha on both the jim and the mim, which is more fitting, because the eye of the needle is used as a proverb for narrowness, and the camel, this well-known animal, is used as a proverb for the largeness of its body, as we mentioned. Ibn Masʿud was asked about the camel, and he said: "It is the mate of the she-camel." This was a way of rebuking the questioner and preventing him from trying to derive another meaning for it. ʿAbd Allah, Qatada, Abu Razin, Ibn Musarrif, and Talha recited the sin of ﴿sam (سَمِّ)﴾ with a damma. Abu ʿImran al-Hawfi, Abu Nahik, and al-Asmaʿi from Nafiʿ recited it with a kasra as "simm (سِمِّ)." ʿAbd Allah, Abu Razin, and Abu Mijlaz (p. 298) recited "al-mikhyat (المِخْيَطُ)" with a kasra on the mim, a sukun on the kha', and a fatha on the ya'. Talha recited it with a fatha on the mim.

﴿Thus do We recompense the criminals﴾: that is, like that recompense, We recompense the people of crimes. Az-Zamakhshari said: this is to indicate that criminality (al-ijram) is the causal means that leads to punishment, and that everyone who commits crimes is punished. Then Allah repeated it, saying: ﴿Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, because every criminal is a wrongdoer to himself. (End of quote.) In this there is a hint of Mu'tazilite doctrine (the Mu'tazila being a theological school that emphasized human free will and divine justice).

﴿For them from Hell will be a bed, and above them will be coverings. Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers.﴾ This is a metaphor for the fire that surrounds them from every side, as He said to them: ﴿Above them are layers of fire, and beneath them are layers﴾ [az-Zumar: 16]. Al-ghawashi is the plural of ghashiya. Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Qurazi, and Ibn Zayd said: they are coverings (al-lufuf, blankets). ʿIkrima said: the smoke covers them from above. Az-Zajjaj said: a covering of fire. ad-Dahhak said: al-mihad means beds, and al-ghawashi means coverings. The tanwin in ﴿ghawashin (غَواشٍ)﴾ is either the tanwin of inflection (sarf) or the tanwin of substitution (ʿiwad), there are two opinions; and the tanwin of substitution in place of the ya' or the vowel, there are two opinions. All of this is established in the science of grammar (ʿilm al-nahw). It was also read as "ghawashun (غَواشٌ)" with a damma, like the reading of ʿAbd Allah: ﴿and His are the ships raised high﴾.

﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds — We do not charge a soul except [with] its capacity; those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.﴾ When He informed of the threat against the disbelievers, He informed of the promise to the believers. The predicate of ﴿those who﴾ is either the clause ﴿We do not charge a soul﴾ and what is among them, or the clause that begins with ﴿those﴾ and what follows it. The clause ﴿We do not charge﴾ would then be an interjection between the subject and the predicate. Its benefit is that, when He mentioned ﴿and did righteous deeds﴾, He pointed out that this deed is within their capacity and not beyond their power. It also serves as a reminder to the disbelievers that Paradise, despite its vast extent, is reached through easy deeds without hardship. Al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Tayyib said: He does not charge anyone with the expenses of wives except what he finds and is able to do, not what is beyond his reach; and the affirmation of capacity before the act is not indicated, and its parallel is ﴿Allah does not charge a soul except with what He has given it﴾ [at-Talaq: 7]. (End of quote.) The context does not require what he mentioned. Az-Zamakhshari said: it is a clause interjected between the subject and the predicate to encourage acquiring what no describer can fully describe of the eternal bliss, together with the great, which is by what is of the wide, meaning wide latitude, not narrow, in faith and righteous deed. (End of quote.) In this there is a hint of Mu'tazilite doctrine. Al-Aʿmash recited it as: ﴿lā tukallafu nafsun (لا تُكَلَّفُ نَفْسٌ)﴾, "no soul is charged."

﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts, [and] rivers will flow beneath them.﴾ That is, We will remove in Paradise whatever rancor their breasts harbored of hatreds. It was also said: the removal of resentment in Paradise means that none of them envies another regarding the differences in their ranks. Al-Hasan said: the resentment of the Jahiliyya (the pre-Islamic period). Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah said: the desires and innovations. It is narrated from ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face: "By Allah, it was revealed about us, the people of Badr." And from him: "I truly hope that I, ʿUthman, Talha, and az-Zubayr are among those about whom it was said, ﴿and We will remove﴾ (the verse)." What appears is that the removal of resentment is a metaphor for their creation in the Hereafter with hearts sound and purified, loving one another and affectionate, as He said: ﴿brothers, upon couches facing one another﴾. And ﴿flowing﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal). This was said by al-Hawfi, who said: the governing element in it is "We will remove." Abu al-Baqa' said: it is a circumstantial clause, and the governing element in it is the meaning of the annexation (idafa). Both of these opinions are not correct, because "flowing" is not one of the attributes of the agent, which is the pronoun of "We will remove," nor an attribute of the object, which is "what is in their breasts." Also, the meaning of annexation does not govern unless it is an annexation in which the annexed noun can govern when stripped of the annexation, in the nominative or accusative case for what follows it. The apparent view is that it is a new predicate describing their state.

﴿And they will say: "Praise be to Allah, who has guided us to this. And we would not have been [able to] be guided had Allah not guided us."﴾ That is, He granted us success in attaining this bliss which we have reached through faith and righteous deeds, since it is a great blessing for which praising Him and extolling Him, the Exalted, is obligatory. It was also said: the guidance here means direction to the path of Paradise and their dwellings within it. In a hadith: "Indeed, one of them is more guided to his dwelling in Paradise than to his dwelling in this world." It was also said: the reference of "this" is to the righteous deed of which this is the reward. It was said: to the faith by which they became worthy of this everlasting bliss. Az-Zamakhshari said: that is, He granted us success in what necessitates this great triumph, which is faith and righteous deed. (End of quote.) In the wording "obligatory" and "righteous deed" there is a hint of Mu'tazilite doctrine. Abu ʿAbd Allah ar-Razi said regarding the meaning of "guided us" (hadana Allah): He gave us the capacity and added to it the firm motive, and made both together for the attainment of that virtue. The Mu'tazila said: the praise was only offered for the fact that He, the Exalted, created reason, placed the proofs, and removed the obstacles. (End of quote.) In Sahih Muslim: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, a caller will call out: 'Indeed, for you is that you will live and never die; indeed, for you is that you will be healthy and never fall ill; indeed, for you is that you will be young and never grow old; indeed, for you is that you will enjoy bliss and never be miserable.' Therefore they say: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has guided us to this.﴾"

﴿And we would not have been [able to] be guided had Allah not guided us.﴾ That is: our own selves would not by themselves have produced guidance had Allah not guided us. This clause clarifies that Allah is the creator of guidance in them, and that if they were left to themselves, no guidance would have come from them. Az-Zamakhshari said: it would not have been proper for us to be guided had it not been for Allah's guidance and granting of success. Abu al-Baqa' said: the waw is for the circumstantial clause, and it may be an independent new clause. (End of quote.) The second is more apparent. Ibn ʿAmir recited "ma kunna (مَا كُنَّا)" without the waw, and it is so in the mushafs of the people of Syria. According to this reading it is a clause explaining the first. Whoever permits the circumstantial clause with the waw should permit it without the waw. What the principles of Arabic grammar require is that the answer to "law la" (had it not been) is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it, meaning: had Allah not guided us, we would not have been guided, or we would have gone astray; for "law la" is for conditionality, and in that it is like the particles of the conditional. Some people have interpreted His saying ﴿law la an ra'a burhana rabbihi (had he not seen the proof of his Lord)﴾ as having an answer that precedes it, which is His saying: "and he was inclined toward her." This will come, Allah willing. This is according to the position of the majority of the Basran grammarians in prohibiting the placement of the answer of the conditional before it.

﴿Indeed, the messengers of our Lord came with the truth.﴾ That is, with the promised [reality] that we were promised in the world. They judged that this is a true judgment, and a seeing with the senses; whereas in the world they judged it through reasoning. Al-Kirmani said: what was promised occurred as the promise had announced. Az-Zamakhshari said: so it was for us a kindness and a reminder toward guidance, so we were guided. They say that out of joy and delight at what they have attained, and out of pleasure in speaking it, not as a form of drawing near to God or an act of worship, as you see: whoever is granted good in the world speaks with something like that and cannot restrain himself from saying it for joy, not for the sake of drawing near to God.

(p. 299)

**[p. 300]** ﴿And they will be called out: "This is the Garden, which you have been made to inherit for what you used to do."﴾ It is possible that the call comes from God, which is more pleasing to their hearts and more elevating to their rank. It is also possible that it comes from the angels. It is further possible that the word *an* here is the light form (*mukhaffafa*) of the heavy *inna*, meaning "that": "they will be called out, [to the effect that] 'This is the Garden'," with its subject being the pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-sha'n*), which is omitted when the particle is lightened. It is also possible that *an* is explanatory (*mufassira*), since its condition is met: there is a clause before it with the sense of speech, and a clause after it, as if it were said: "This is the Garden."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: ﴿Tilkum﴾ is a demonstrative pointing to something absent. It may be because they had been promised it in this world, so the pointing is to "that" (*tilka*), i.e., "this" (*hadhihi*) Garden, and the word "this" has been omitted. Or it may be [pointing] to it before they entered it, or after entering it while they are gathered in one place within it, each being absent from his own dwelling. End of quote.

In *al-Taḥrīr* it is said: "*Tilkum* is a demonstrative pointing to something absent. He said *tilkum* here because they had been promised it in the world, and for the sake of that promise the address came with the word of covenant." And the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Abu Bakr, when asking about 'Aisha, "How is she, *tīkum*?", referring to the earlier covenant. End of quote.

As for *al-Janna* (the Garden), they permitted it to be the predicate of *tilkum*, with ﴿uwritum-ūhā﴾ ("you have been made to inherit it") as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), like His saying: ﴿So those are their houses, empty﴾ [al-Naml 27:52]. Abu al-Baqa said: it is a circumstantial clause from *al-Janna*, and the governing element in it is the meaning of pointing contained in *tilka*; it is not permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause from *tilka*, because of the separation between them by the predicate, and because the subject does not govern a circumstantial clause. End of quote. Regarding what governs the circumstantial clause in a construction like "Zayd is standing," there is disagreement among the grammarians. It is also possible that it is a qualifier (*na't*) or an apposition (*badal*), with ﴿uwritum-ūhā﴾ as the predicate.

Ibn 'Amir... rather, the two grammarians (al-Kisa'i and Hamza) and Hisham assimilated the *thā'* into the *tā'* (in ﴿uwritum-ūhā﴾), while the rest of the Seven pronounced it clearly. The meaning of ﴿uwritum-ūhā﴾ is: it has been made for you like an inheritance. He who went to the view that the meaning is "you have been made to inherit it from your fathers," because it would have been their dwellings had they believed, but they were deprived of it through their disbelief, is far off the mark. Its remoteness lies in the fact that this would apply to all believers, and not all of their fathers were disbelievers.

The *bā'* in ﴿bimā﴾ ("for what") indicates figurative causation. Deeds are a sign from God and an indication of the strength of hope. Entry into the Garden is only by the mere mercy of God, while the degrees within it correspond to the deeds. The word ﴿uwritum-ūhā﴾ points to the divisions of rank, but that is not obligatory upon God, exalted is He. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿uwritum-ūhā﴾ "bimā kuntum ta'malūn" means: by reason of your deeds, not by grace, as the Mu'tazilite (nullifiers) say. End of quote. This is the doctrine of the Mu'tazila. In Sahih Muslim: "No one will enter the Garden by his deed." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Not even I, unless God covers me with His mercy and grace."

﴿The people of the Garden will call out to the people of the Fire, "We have found what our Lord promised us to be true. Have you found what your Lord promised to be true?" They will say, "Yes."﴾ He used the past tense for the future to express the certainty of its occurrence. This call contains rebuke, reproach and a demand for acknowledgment of the outcome of both groups, and an increase in the grief of the people of the Fire by making them hear it, since they were brought within earshot of them, and by God creating in the people of the Fire the ability to perceive that call in their ears. Al-Zamakhshari said: They said this to them out of satisfaction with their own state, gloating over the people of the Fire, and increasing their distress, and so that its relating would be a warning (*lutf*) to whoever hears it. Similarly, the words of the caller (*mu'adhdhin*) among them: "The curse of God is upon the wrongdoers." He is an angel whom God commands, and he calls out among them, making both the people of the Garden and the people of the Fire hear. End of quote.

In the report of the people of the Garden he said ﴿mā wa'adanā﴾ ("what He promised us") with the object mentioned, while in the report about the people of the Fire he said *mā wa'ada* without mentioning the object of *wa'ada*, because the people of the Garden were rejoicing in the realization of their promise, so they mentioned what God had promised them, attributed to themselves. When they asked the people of the Garden, they did not mention the object of *wa'ada* with the second-person address, so they did not say "what your Lord promised you," so that it would include every promise, both the punishment of the people of the Fire and the bliss of the people of the Garden. Their reply "Yes" is a confirmation of everything God promised to happen in the Hereafter to both categories. This is also an acknowledgment by them of the realization of the promise to the believers, so that they would feel grief over what they missed of its bliss, since the bliss of the people of the Garden is something that humiliates them and increases their torment.

It is possible that the omitted object of the address is indicated by what precedes it, and its full form is: ﴿fa-hal wajadtum mā wa'ada rabbukum﴾ ("Have you found what your Lord promised?"). Ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash and al-Kisa'i read *na'im* ("yes") with a kasra on the 'ayn (*ni'm*). It is possible that [the particle] is explanatory, and it is possible that it is the masdar-form lightened from *anna* (heavy). When the lightened particle is followed by a verb that is active and not a supplication, *qad* is placed between them in the best usage, as in His saying: ﴿an qad wajadnā﴾ ("indeed we have found").

**[p. 301]** ﴿Then a caller will call out between them, "The curse of God is upon the wrongdoers, those who bar from the way of God and seek to make it crooked, and who disbelieve in the Hereafter."﴾ That is: a proclaimer will announce. It was said he is Israfil, the bearer of the Trumpet. It was said he is Gabriel, making both groups hear, to cause joy and distress. It was said he is another specific angel. Tawus entered upon Hisham ibn 'Abd al-Malik, who said to him: "Beware the Day of the Call." He said: "And what is the Day of the Call?" He said: "The Day of ﴿Then a caller will call out﴾" to the end of the verse. Hisham fainted. Tawus said: "This is the terror of the description; how then will be the terror of direct witnessing?"

*Bayna-hum* ("between them") may be governed by *adhdhana* ("called out"), or it may be a qualifier of *mu'adhdhin* ("caller"), in which case its governing element is omitted. Al-Akhawan (Hamza and al-Kisa'i), Ibn 'Amir and al-Bazzi read *anna la'nata* with the heavy *anna* and the accusative *la'nata*. 'Isma from al-A'mash read *inna* with a kasra on the hamza, the heavy form, and the accusative *la'nata*, understood as the verb "to say" (*idmār al-qawl*) or treating *adhdhana* in the position of *qāla* ("he said"). The rest of the Seven read *an* with a fatha on the hamza, lightened nun, and *la'natu* in the nominative as the subject, with *an* being the lightened form of the heavy particle or explanatory.

﴿Those who bar from the way of God and seek to make it crooked﴾ has had its explanation given before for similar words. This descriptive relative clause is a report of their earlier words, and the meaning is: those who used to bar from the way of God, because at the time of the call they were not characterized by this description. What is meant by "wrongdoers" is the disbelievers. What refutes the view of one who said it is general, covering both the disbeliever and the sinner, is His saying at the end, ﴿and who disbelieve in the Hereafter﴾, because the sinner is not a disbeliever in the Hereafter, but a believer who affirms it.

﴿And between them is a veil.﴾ That is, between the two groups, since they are the ones being spoken about, and this is the apparent meaning. It was said: between the Garden and the Fire. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya began with this view. The veil was explained as being what is meant by His saying: ﴿so a wall was set up between them with a gate﴾ [al-Hadid 57:13], and this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. What strengthens that it is between the two groups is the word *bayna-hum*, since it is the pronoun for rational beings. Also, setting up a wall does not contradict what lies between the Garden and the Fire, even though the Garden is in the heaven, and the Fire is at the lowest of the low.

﴿And upon the A'raf (heights) will be men who recognize each by his mark.﴾ That is: and upon the heights of the veil, which is the wall set up, will be men who recognize each of the two groups of the Garden and the Fire by their mark, which God has made distinctive for them, such as whiteness of faces and blackness of faces, or by other signs, or by the mark that God inspires them to know. The *A'raf* is a hill between the Garden and the Fire. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: it is a barrier between the Garden and the Fire. It was also said: it is Uhud, placed as an image between the Garden and the Fire, as reported in a hadith, and in another: "Uhud is upon one of the pillars of the Garden." It was said: they are the upper parts of the wall that was set up between the Garden and the Fire. This was said by al-Zamakhshari.

The *rijal* ("men") are a people whose good deeds and bad deeds are equal. They stand there for as long as God wills, their good deeds not having brought them to enter the Garden, nor their bad deeds to enter the Fire. It is reported in the Musnad of Ibn Abi Khaythama from Jabir, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), a hadith in which: "It was said: O Messenger of God, who are those whose good and bad deeds are equal?" He said: "They are the companions of the A'raf; they did not enter it, while they were hoping [to enter]." This was also said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Hudhayfa and Abu Hurayra. Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman also said: they are a people whose minor sins held them back, until they were the last of the people. It was also said: they are warriors who fought without the permission of their parents and were slain in battle. This is reported from the Messenger [of God] that they were held back from the Garden by the disobedience of their parents, but God freed them from the Fire because they were killed in His cause. It was said: they are people whose fathers were pleased with them but not their mothers, or the reverse. It was said: they are the children of fornication. It was said: the children of polytheists. It was said: those who were in captivity and did not change their religion. It was said: scholars who doubted about their provisions. Al-Zamakhshari said: they are men from among the Muslims, the last of them to enter the Garden because of the shortcomings of their deeds, as if they were the *Murji'a* (those who defer the matter) to God's command, held back between the Garden and the Fire until God permits them to enter the Garden. End of quote.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: What is necessarily implied by the verse is that upon the heights of that wall, or upon elevated places above the two groups, wherever God wills, there are men from the people of the Garden whose entry is delayed, and what is described of consideration between the two groups happens to them, and they recognize each by his mark, which is the whiteness and beauty of faces among the people of the Garden, and the blackness and ugliness among the people of the Fire. End of quote.

The previous opinions need clear evidence for their specification. The best of them is the first, because of the hadith of Jabir and because of the interpretation of a group of the Companions. These opinions are based on the view that the A'raf is between the Garden and the Fire. In the poetry of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

*And others upon the A'raf have hoped
for a Garden encircled by pomegranates and greenery.*

Some said it is the Sirat (the bridge), and it was said: a place upon the Sirat. Some said: it is a mountain in the middle of the Garden, or its highest part. These differed in explaining *rijal*. Abu Mijlaz said: they are angels in the forms of male men, and they were called men because of His saying: ﴿And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾ [al-An'am 6:9]. Mujahid and al-Hasan said: they are the virtuous believers and their scholars. It was said: they are the martyrs. This was said by al-Kirmani, and al-Nahhas chose it, saying: this is the best of what has been said about it. It was said: Hamza, al-'Abbas, 'Ali and Ja'far al-Tayyar, and this was reported from Ibn 'Abbas. It was said: they are the prophets.

﴿And they will call out to the people of the Garden, "Peace be upon you," they have not entered it, though they are hoping [to enter].﴾ ﴿And when their sight is turned toward the people of the Fire, they will say, "Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people."﴾ The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in *wa-nādaw* ("they will call out") through the end of the verse refers to the men who are upon the A'raf. On this basis, those pronouns cannot refer to the prophets, nor to anything of what was explained as their being upon a mountain in the middle of the Garden or its upper part. And it is most remote to interpret them otherwise, so that any of those opinions could be correct, that they were seated on those elevated places to witness the states of the two groups, so that joy would reach them by those states. Then, when the two groups settle, they will be moved to their places that were prepared for them in the Garden. Thus the meaning of ﴿they have not entered it﴾ is: they have not entered their dwellings prepared for them in it. The meaning of ﴿and they are hoping﴾ is: they are certain of what God has prepared for them of nearness. The word *ṭama'* ("hope") has come with the meaning of certainty. He said: ﴿And the one from whom I hope that He will forgive me my sin on the Day of Judgment﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:82]. And Abraham's (peace be upon him) hope was certainty. The poet said:

*And indeed I hope that God is capable,
by the goodness of my certainty, my certainty.*

And as for the view of those who say that al-A'raf is a mountain between Paradise and the Fire, al-Qadi and al-Jubba'i criticised it and said: "It is corrupt, because His words ﴿by what you used to do﴾ indicate that everyone who enters Paradise must deserve to enter it, and that rules out the claim that there are groups who deserve neither Paradise nor the Fire and then enter Paradise purely by grace, not by desert. Moreover, their being among the people of al-A'raf indicates that they are distinguished from all the people of the Resurrection, for placing them on high, elevated places above the people of Paradise and the Fire is a great honour that befits only the noble. Those whose good deeds and bad deeds are equal have a deficient rank, and such honour does not befit them." It was answered that it is possible that ﴿and they will be called﴾ is an address to specific groups, so it does not follow that the people of Paradise are like this. As for the second objection, [God] placed them there not for honour, but because it is like an intermediate station between Paradise and the Fire. And as for ﴿that peace be upon you﴾, it is possible that "an" (أنْ) is explanatory and a lightened form of the heavy particle. And ﴿they had not entered it﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object, meaning: he called them while they were in this state, i.e., the people of Paradise, ﴿and they were hoping﴾ is a declarative clause with no place in grammatical analysis (i'rab), meaning: they called out to the people of Paradise while not having entered it, and then he informed that they were hoping to enter it. This is the meaning given by Abu al-Baqa'. It was also said: the meaning is that the companions of al-A'raf called out to the companions of Paradise with peace, while they had entered Paradise, and the people of al-A'raf had not entered it. Thus ﴿they had not entered it﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of "they called out" referring only to the people of al-A'raf. This is the interpretation of Ibn Mas'ud, Qatada, al-Suddi, and others. Ibn Mas'ud said: "By God, God did not place that hope in their hearts except for a good that He intended for them." This is the most apparent and the most fitting to the context of the verse. Ibn Mas'ud also said: "The companions of al-A'raf only hoped because the light that was in their hands was not extinguished when the light of the hypocrites was extinguished." It was also said: ﴿and they were hoping﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the subject of ﴿they had entered it﴾, and the meaning is: they did not enter it in a state of hoping for it, rather they were in a state of despair and fear, but God's pardon encompassed them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the place (i'rab) of His words ﴿they had not entered it and they were hoping﴾? I say: it has no place, because it is a resumed sentence (isti'naf), as if a questioner asked about the companions of al-A'raf, and it was said to him: ﴿they had not entered it and they were hoping﴾, meaning that their entry into Paradise was delayed behind the entry of the people of Paradise, so they had not entered it because they were being held back, and they were hoping, not despairing." And it is permissible that it has a place by being a qualifying clause (sifah). End of quote. This is a weak explanation for separating the described from its descriptive clause with the clause ﴿and they called out﴾, which is not a parenthetical clause (i'tiraD).

Ibn al-Nahwi read ﴿and they are hoping﴾ (وهم طامِعُونَ). Iyad ibn Laqit read ﴿and they are discontented﴾ (وهم ساخِطُونَ). Al-A'mash read ﴿and when their sights are turned﴾ (وإذا قُلِّبَتْ أبْصارُهم). The pronoun in "their sights" refers to the men of al-A'raf, who greet the people of Paradise, and when they look at the people of the Fire, they call upon God to be delivered from it. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and a group. Abu Mijlaz said: the pronoun refers to the people of Paradise, and they had not yet entered it. In His words ﴿they are turned﴾ there is evidence that most of their states is looking towards the companions of Paradise, and that their looking at the companions of the Fire is due to their sights being turned towards them. So the turning is not from their side; rather they are carried along into it, and it is done to them, because that place of overlooking is frightening to hear of, let alone to see, let alone to be involved in it. The meaning is that when they are made to turn their sights and see what they are suffering from the punishment, they seek refuge with their Lord from being made to be with them. The word ﴿our Lord﴾ indicates the description of Him, the Exalted, as the one who reforms them and is their master, while they are servants. So by calling upon Him with this, they seek His mercy and appeal to His generosity.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 40–47 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Indeed, those who denied Our signs and were arrogant toward them, the gates of heaven will not be opened for them.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿will not be opened﴾ for their deeds, nor for their supplications, nor for anything they intend by it the obedience of Allah, the Exalted. That is, no righteous deed ascends for them, so that the gates of heaven would be opened for it. This is drawn from His saying: ﴿To Him ascend the good word, and the righteous deed raises it﴾ [Fatir: 10], and from His saying: ﴿Indeed, the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyun﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 18]. As-Suddi and others said: ﴿will not be opened﴾ for their spirits. They mentioned, concerning the ascent of the spirits to heaven and the permission granted to the spirit of the believer and the rejection of the spirit of the disbeliever, reports (ahadith), and that occurs at the time of their death. It was also said: the meaning is that ﴿the gates of heaven will not be opened for them﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, so that they may enter through them into Paradise. That is, they will not be permitted to ascend to heaven. It was also said: blessing will not descend upon them, and they will not be given relief. Abu ʿAmr recited ﴿will not be opened﴾ with the feminine ta' and without tashdid (the doubling of the letter), al-Akhawan (the two brothers, Hamza and al-Kisai) recited it with the ya' and without tashdid, and the rest of the seven readers recited it with the ta' at the beginning and with tashdid. Abu Haywa and Abu al-Barahsam recited it with the thaʾ at the beginning, open (fatha), and with tashdid.

﴿And they will not enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle.﴾ This is a negation conditioned upon something impossible. Al-wulud (passing into) means penetrating into a thing. He mentioned the camel because it is the largest animal that deals with humans in bulk, so it can only pass through a wide opening, as the poet said: "The camel has grown large without intellect," and he said: "The body of camels and the dreams of sparrows." He mentioned ﴿the eye of the needle﴾ because it is used as a proverb for a narrow passage; it is said: "Narrower than the eye of a needle" (khart al-ibra). It was also said that a guide is called kharrit because of his guidance through narrow places, by analogy with the hole of the needle (ikhrat al-ibra). The meaning is that they will never enter Paradise. Ibn ʿAbbas was recited, according to what Shahr ibn Hawshab narrated from him, along with Mujahid, Ibn Yaʿmur, Abu Mijlaz, ash-Shaʿbi, Malik ibn ash-Shikhkhir, Abu Rajaʾ, Abu Razin, Ibn Muhaysin, and Aban from ʿAsim, as al-Jummal (الجُمَّلُ) with a damma on the jim and a fatha on the mim with tashdid. It was interpreted as the thick rope (al-qals al-ghalidh), which is the ship's cable: ropes are gathered and twisted and become one rope. It was also said that it is the thick rope made of hemp. It was also said that it is the rope by which one climbs up palm trees. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, though it probably is not authentic, that Allah is too beautiful in comparison than to be likened to a camel, meaning that it is not appropriate, whereas a rope is appropriate for the thread that passes through the eye of a needle. From al-Kisai: the one who transmitted al-Jummal from Ibn ʿAbbas was non-Arab, so he doubled the jim because of his non-Arabic pronunciation. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: this is weak, because of the large number of Ibn ʿAbbas's companions who recited it in the aforementioned reading. (End of quote.) And also because of the large number of readers other than Ibn ʿAbbas who recited it that way. Ibn ʿAbbas also recited, according to a report from Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Qatada, and Salim al-Aftas, with a damma on the jim and a fatha on the mim, without tashdid. Ibn ʿAbbas, according to a report from ʿAta', al-Dahhak, and al-Jahdari, recited with a damma on both the jim and the mim, without tashdid. ʿIkrima and Ibn Jubayr, in one report, recited with a damma on the jim and a sukun on the mim: al-Jumul (الجُمْلُ). Al-Mutawakkil and Abu al-Jawza' recited with a fatha on the jim and a sukun on the mim. Their meaning in these readings is the thick rope, which is the ship's cable. The reading of the majority is ﴿al-jamal (الجَمَلُ)﴾ with a fatha on both the jim and the mim, which is more fitting, because the eye of the needle is used as a proverb for narrowness, and the camel, this well-known animal, is used as a proverb for the largeness of its body, as we mentioned. Ibn Masʿud was asked about the camel, and he said: "It is the mate of the she-camel." This was a way of rebuking the questioner and preventing him from trying to derive another meaning for it. ʿAbd Allah, Qatada, Abu Razin, Ibn Musarrif, and Talha recited the sin of ﴿sam (سَمِّ)﴾ with a damma. Abu ʿImran al-Hawfi, Abu Nahik, and al-Asmaʿi from Nafiʿ recited it with a kasra as "simm (سِمِّ)." ʿAbd Allah, Abu Razin, and Abu Mijlaz (p. 298) recited "al-mikhyat (المِخْيَطُ)" with a kasra on the mim, a sukun on the kha', and a fatha on the ya'. Talha recited it with a fatha on the mim.

﴿Thus do We recompense the criminals﴾: that is, like that recompense, We recompense the people of crimes. Az-Zamakhshari said: this is to indicate that criminality (al-ijram) is the causal means that leads to punishment, and that everyone who commits crimes is punished. Then Allah repeated it, saying: ﴿Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, because every criminal is a wrongdoer to himself. (End of quote.) In this there is a hint of Mu'tazilite doctrine (the Mu'tazila being a theological school that emphasized human free will and divine justice).

﴿For them from Hell will be a bed, and above them will be coverings. Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers.﴾ This is a metaphor for the fire that surrounds them from every side, as He said to them: ﴿Above them are layers of fire, and beneath them are layers﴾ [az-Zumar: 16]. Al-ghawashi is the plural of ghashiya. Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Qurazi, and Ibn Zayd said: they are coverings (al-lufuf, blankets). ʿIkrima said: the smoke covers them from above. Az-Zajjaj said: a covering of fire. ad-Dahhak said: al-mihad means beds, and al-ghawashi means coverings. The tanwin in ﴿ghawashin (غَواشٍ)﴾ is either the tanwin of inflection (sarf) or the tanwin of substitution (ʿiwad), there are two opinions; and the tanwin of substitution in place of the ya' or the vowel, there are two opinions. All of this is established in the science of grammar (ʿilm al-nahw). It was also read as "ghawashun (غَواشٌ)" with a damma, like the reading of ʿAbd Allah: ﴿and His are the ships raised high﴾.

﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds — We do not charge a soul except [with] its capacity; those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.﴾ When He informed of the threat against the disbelievers, He informed of the promise to the believers. The predicate of ﴿those who﴾ is either the clause ﴿We do not charge a soul﴾ and what is among them, or the clause that begins with ﴿those﴾ and what follows it. The clause ﴿We do not charge﴾ would then be an interjection between the subject and the predicate. Its benefit is that, when He mentioned ﴿and did righteous deeds﴾, He pointed out that this deed is within their capacity and not beyond their power. It also serves as a reminder to the disbelievers that Paradise, despite its vast extent, is reached through easy deeds without hardship. Al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Tayyib said: He does not charge anyone with the expenses of wives except what he finds and is able to do, not what is beyond his reach; and the affirmation of capacity before the act is not indicated, and its parallel is ﴿Allah does not charge a soul except with what He has given it﴾ [at-Talaq: 7]. (End of quote.) The context does not require what he mentioned. Az-Zamakhshari said: it is a clause interjected between the subject and the predicate to encourage acquiring what no describer can fully describe of the eternal bliss, together with the great, which is by what is of the wide, meaning wide latitude, not narrow, in faith and righteous deed. (End of quote.) In this there is a hint of Mu'tazilite doctrine. Al-Aʿmash recited it as: ﴿lā tukallafu nafsun (لا تُكَلَّفُ نَفْسٌ)﴾, "no soul is charged."

﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts, [and] rivers will flow beneath them.﴾ That is, We will remove in Paradise whatever rancor their breasts harbored of hatreds. It was also said: the removal of resentment in Paradise means that none of them envies another regarding the differences in their ranks. Al-Hasan said: the resentment of the Jahiliyya (the pre-Islamic period). Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah said: the desires and innovations. It is narrated from ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face: "By Allah, it was revealed about us, the people of Badr." And from him: "I truly hope that I, ʿUthman, Talha, and az-Zubayr are among those about whom it was said, ﴿and We will remove﴾ (the verse)." What appears is that the removal of resentment is a metaphor for their creation in the Hereafter with hearts sound and purified, loving one another and affectionate, as He said: ﴿brothers, upon couches facing one another﴾. And ﴿flowing﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal). This was said by al-Hawfi, who said: the governing element in it is "We will remove." Abu al-Baqa' said: it is a circumstantial clause, and the governing element in it is the meaning of the annexation (idafa). Both of these opinions are not correct, because "flowing" is not one of the attributes of the agent, which is the pronoun of "We will remove," nor an attribute of the object, which is "what is in their breasts." Also, the meaning of annexation does not govern unless it is an annexation in which the annexed noun can govern when stripped of the annexation, in the nominative or accusative case for what follows it. The apparent view is that it is a new predicate describing their state.

﴿And they will say: "Praise be to Allah, who has guided us to this. And we would not have been [able to] be guided had Allah not guided us."﴾ That is, He granted us success in attaining this bliss which we have reached through faith and righteous deeds, since it is a great blessing for which praising Him and extolling Him, the Exalted, is obligatory. It was also said: the guidance here means direction to the path of Paradise and their dwellings within it. In a hadith: "Indeed, one of them is more guided to his dwelling in Paradise than to his dwelling in this world." It was also said: the reference of "this" is to the righteous deed of which this is the reward. It was said: to the faith by which they became worthy of this everlasting bliss. Az-Zamakhshari said: that is, He granted us success in what necessitates this great triumph, which is faith and righteous deed. (End of quote.) In the wording "obligatory" and "righteous deed" there is a hint of Mu'tazilite doctrine. Abu ʿAbd Allah ar-Razi said regarding the meaning of "guided us" (hadana Allah): He gave us the capacity and added to it the firm motive, and made both together for the attainment of that virtue. The Mu'tazila said: the praise was only offered for the fact that He, the Exalted, created reason, placed the proofs, and removed the obstacles. (End of quote.) In Sahih Muslim: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, a caller will call out: 'Indeed, for you is that you will live and never die; indeed, for you is that you will be healthy and never fall ill; indeed, for you is that you will be young and never grow old; indeed, for you is that you will enjoy bliss and never be miserable.' Therefore they say: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who has guided us to this.﴾"

﴿And we would not have been [able to] be guided had Allah not guided us.﴾ That is: our own selves would not by themselves have produced guidance had Allah not guided us. This clause clarifies that Allah is the creator of guidance in them, and that if they were left to themselves, no guidance would have come from them. Az-Zamakhshari said: it would not have been proper for us to be guided had it not been for Allah's guidance and granting of success. Abu al-Baqa' said: the waw is for the circumstantial clause, and it may be an independent new clause. (End of quote.) The second is more apparent. Ibn ʿAmir recited "ma kunna (مَا كُنَّا)" without the waw, and it is so in the mushafs of the people of Syria. According to this reading it is a clause explaining the first. Whoever permits the circumstantial clause with the waw should permit it without the waw. What the principles of Arabic grammar require is that the answer to "law la" (had it not been) is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it, meaning: had Allah not guided us, we would not have been guided, or we would have gone astray; for "law la" is for conditionality, and in that it is like the particles of the conditional. Some people have interpreted His saying ﴿law la an ra'a burhana rabbihi (had he not seen the proof of his Lord)﴾ as having an answer that precedes it, which is His saying: "and he was inclined toward her." This will come, Allah willing. This is according to the position of the majority of the Basran grammarians in prohibiting the placement of the answer of the conditional before it.

﴿Indeed, the messengers of our Lord came with the truth.﴾ That is, with the promised [reality] that we were promised in the world. They judged that this is a true judgment, and a seeing with the senses; whereas in the world they judged it through reasoning. Al-Kirmani said: what was promised occurred as the promise had announced. Az-Zamakhshari said: so it was for us a kindness and a reminder toward guidance, so we were guided. They say that out of joy and delight at what they have attained, and out of pleasure in speaking it, not as a form of drawing near to God or an act of worship, as you see: whoever is granted good in the world speaks with something like that and cannot restrain himself from saying it for joy, not for the sake of drawing near to God.

(p. 299)

**[p. 300]** ﴿And they will be called out: "This is the Garden, which you have been made to inherit for what you used to do."﴾ It is possible that the call comes from God, which is more pleasing to their hearts and more elevating to their rank. It is also possible that it comes from the angels. It is further possible that the word *an* here is the light form (*mukhaffafa*) of the heavy *inna*, meaning "that": "they will be called out, [to the effect that] 'This is the Garden'," with its subject being the pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-sha'n*), which is omitted when the particle is lightened. It is also possible that *an* is explanatory (*mufassira*), since its condition is met: there is a clause before it with the sense of speech, and a clause after it, as if it were said: "This is the Garden."

Ibn 'Atiyya said: ﴿Tilkum﴾ is a demonstrative pointing to something absent. It may be because they had been promised it in this world, so the pointing is to "that" (*tilka*), i.e., "this" (*hadhihi*) Garden, and the word "this" has been omitted. Or it may be [pointing] to it before they entered it, or after entering it while they are gathered in one place within it, each being absent from his own dwelling. End of quote.

In *al-Taḥrīr* it is said: "*Tilkum* is a demonstrative pointing to something absent. He said *tilkum* here because they had been promised it in the world, and for the sake of that promise the address came with the word of covenant." And the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Abu Bakr, when asking about 'Aisha, "How is she, *tīkum*?", referring to the earlier covenant. End of quote.

As for *al-Janna* (the Garden), they permitted it to be the predicate of *tilkum*, with ﴿uwritum-ūhā﴾ ("you have been made to inherit it") as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), like His saying: ﴿So those are their houses, empty﴾ [al-Naml 27:52]. Abu al-Baqa said: it is a circumstantial clause from *al-Janna*, and the governing element in it is the meaning of pointing contained in *tilka*; it is not permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause from *tilka*, because of the separation between them by the predicate, and because the subject does not govern a circumstantial clause. End of quote. Regarding what governs the circumstantial clause in a construction like "Zayd is standing," there is disagreement among the grammarians. It is also possible that it is a qualifier (*na't*) or an apposition (*badal*), with ﴿uwritum-ūhā﴾ as the predicate.

Ibn 'Amir... rather, the two grammarians (al-Kisa'i and Hamza) and Hisham assimilated the *thā'* into the *tā'* (in ﴿uwritum-ūhā﴾), while the rest of the Seven pronounced it clearly. The meaning of ﴿uwritum-ūhā﴾ is: it has been made for you like an inheritance. He who went to the view that the meaning is "you have been made to inherit it from your fathers," because it would have been their dwellings had they believed, but they were deprived of it through their disbelief, is far off the mark. Its remoteness lies in the fact that this would apply to all believers, and not all of their fathers were disbelievers.

The *bā'* in ﴿bimā﴾ ("for what") indicates figurative causation. Deeds are a sign from God and an indication of the strength of hope. Entry into the Garden is only by the mere mercy of God, while the degrees within it correspond to the deeds. The word ﴿uwritum-ūhā﴾ points to the divisions of rank, but that is not obligatory upon God, exalted is He. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿uwritum-ūhā﴾ "bimā kuntum ta'malūn" means: by reason of your deeds, not by grace, as the Mu'tazilite (nullifiers) say. End of quote. This is the doctrine of the Mu'tazila. In Sahih Muslim: "No one will enter the Garden by his deed." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Not even I, unless God covers me with His mercy and grace."

﴿The people of the Garden will call out to the people of the Fire, "We have found what our Lord promised us to be true. Have you found what your Lord promised to be true?" They will say, "Yes."﴾ He used the past tense for the future to express the certainty of its occurrence. This call contains rebuke, reproach and a demand for acknowledgment of the outcome of both groups, and an increase in the grief of the people of the Fire by making them hear it, since they were brought within earshot of them, and by God creating in the people of the Fire the ability to perceive that call in their ears. Al-Zamakhshari said: They said this to them out of satisfaction with their own state, gloating over the people of the Fire, and increasing their distress, and so that its relating would be a warning (*lutf*) to whoever hears it. Similarly, the words of the caller (*mu'adhdhin*) among them: "The curse of God is upon the wrongdoers." He is an angel whom God commands, and he calls out among them, making both the people of the Garden and the people of the Fire hear. End of quote.

In the report of the people of the Garden he said ﴿mā wa'adanā﴾ ("what He promised us") with the object mentioned, while in the report about the people of the Fire he said *mā wa'ada* without mentioning the object of *wa'ada*, because the people of the Garden were rejoicing in the realization of their promise, so they mentioned what God had promised them, attributed to themselves. When they asked the people of the Garden, they did not mention the object of *wa'ada* with the second-person address, so they did not say "what your Lord promised you," so that it would include every promise, both the punishment of the people of the Fire and the bliss of the people of the Garden. Their reply "Yes" is a confirmation of everything God promised to happen in the Hereafter to both categories. This is also an acknowledgment by them of the realization of the promise to the believers, so that they would feel grief over what they missed of its bliss, since the bliss of the people of the Garden is something that humiliates them and increases their torment.

It is possible that the omitted object of the address is indicated by what precedes it, and its full form is: ﴿fa-hal wajadtum mā wa'ada rabbukum﴾ ("Have you found what your Lord promised?"). Ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash and al-Kisa'i read *na'im* ("yes") with a kasra on the 'ayn (*ni'm*). It is possible that [the particle] is explanatory, and it is possible that it is the masdar-form lightened from *anna* (heavy). When the lightened particle is followed by a verb that is active and not a supplication, *qad* is placed between them in the best usage, as in His saying: ﴿an qad wajadnā﴾ ("indeed we have found").

**[p. 301]** ﴿Then a caller will call out between them, "The curse of God is upon the wrongdoers, those who bar from the way of God and seek to make it crooked, and who disbelieve in the Hereafter."﴾ That is: a proclaimer will announce. It was said he is Israfil, the bearer of the Trumpet. It was said he is Gabriel, making both groups hear, to cause joy and distress. It was said he is another specific angel. Tawus entered upon Hisham ibn 'Abd al-Malik, who said to him: "Beware the Day of the Call." He said: "And what is the Day of the Call?" He said: "The Day of ﴿Then a caller will call out﴾" to the end of the verse. Hisham fainted. Tawus said: "This is the terror of the description; how then will be the terror of direct witnessing?"

*Bayna-hum* ("between them") may be governed by *adhdhana* ("called out"), or it may be a qualifier of *mu'adhdhin* ("caller"), in which case its governing element is omitted. Al-Akhawan (Hamza and al-Kisa'i), Ibn 'Amir and al-Bazzi read *anna la'nata* with the heavy *anna* and the accusative *la'nata*. 'Isma from al-A'mash read *inna* with a kasra on the hamza, the heavy form, and the accusative *la'nata*, understood as the verb "to say" (*idmār al-qawl*) or treating *adhdhana* in the position of *qāla* ("he said"). The rest of the Seven read *an* with a fatha on the hamza, lightened nun, and *la'natu* in the nominative as the subject, with *an* being the lightened form of the heavy particle or explanatory.

﴿Those who bar from the way of God and seek to make it crooked﴾ has had its explanation given before for similar words. This descriptive relative clause is a report of their earlier words, and the meaning is: those who used to bar from the way of God, because at the time of the call they were not characterized by this description. What is meant by "wrongdoers" is the disbelievers. What refutes the view of one who said it is general, covering both the disbeliever and the sinner, is His saying at the end, ﴿and who disbelieve in the Hereafter﴾, because the sinner is not a disbeliever in the Hereafter, but a believer who affirms it.

﴿And between them is a veil.﴾ That is, between the two groups, since they are the ones being spoken about, and this is the apparent meaning. It was said: between the Garden and the Fire. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya began with this view. The veil was explained as being what is meant by His saying: ﴿so a wall was set up between them with a gate﴾ [al-Hadid 57:13], and this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. What strengthens that it is between the two groups is the word *bayna-hum*, since it is the pronoun for rational beings. Also, setting up a wall does not contradict what lies between the Garden and the Fire, even though the Garden is in the heaven, and the Fire is at the lowest of the low.

﴿And upon the A'raf (heights) will be men who recognize each by his mark.﴾ That is: and upon the heights of the veil, which is the wall set up, will be men who recognize each of the two groups of the Garden and the Fire by their mark, which God has made distinctive for them, such as whiteness of faces and blackness of faces, or by other signs, or by the mark that God inspires them to know. The *A'raf* is a hill between the Garden and the Fire. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid said: it is a barrier between the Garden and the Fire. It was also said: it is Uhud, placed as an image between the Garden and the Fire, as reported in a hadith, and in another: "Uhud is upon one of the pillars of the Garden." It was said: they are the upper parts of the wall that was set up between the Garden and the Fire. This was said by al-Zamakhshari.

The *rijal* ("men") are a people whose good deeds and bad deeds are equal. They stand there for as long as God wills, their good deeds not having brought them to enter the Garden, nor their bad deeds to enter the Fire. It is reported in the Musnad of Ibn Abi Khaythama from Jabir, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), a hadith in which: "It was said: O Messenger of God, who are those whose good and bad deeds are equal?" He said: "They are the companions of the A'raf; they did not enter it, while they were hoping [to enter]." This was also said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Hudhayfa and Abu Hurayra. Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman also said: they are a people whose minor sins held them back, until they were the last of the people. It was also said: they are warriors who fought without the permission of their parents and were slain in battle. This is reported from the Messenger [of God] that they were held back from the Garden by the disobedience of their parents, but God freed them from the Fire because they were killed in His cause. It was said: they are people whose fathers were pleased with them but not their mothers, or the reverse. It was said: they are the children of fornication. It was said: the children of polytheists. It was said: those who were in captivity and did not change their religion. It was said: scholars who doubted about their provisions. Al-Zamakhshari said: they are men from among the Muslims, the last of them to enter the Garden because of the shortcomings of their deeds, as if they were the *Murji'a* (those who defer the matter) to God's command, held back between the Garden and the Fire until God permits them to enter the Garden. End of quote.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: What is necessarily implied by the verse is that upon the heights of that wall, or upon elevated places above the two groups, wherever God wills, there are men from the people of the Garden whose entry is delayed, and what is described of consideration between the two groups happens to them, and they recognize each by his mark, which is the whiteness and beauty of faces among the people of the Garden, and the blackness and ugliness among the people of the Fire. End of quote.

The previous opinions need clear evidence for their specification. The best of them is the first, because of the hadith of Jabir and because of the interpretation of a group of the Companions. These opinions are based on the view that the A'raf is between the Garden and the Fire. In the poetry of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

*And others upon the A'raf have hoped
for a Garden encircled by pomegranates and greenery.*

Some said it is the Sirat (the bridge), and it was said: a place upon the Sirat. Some said: it is a mountain in the middle of the Garden, or its highest part. These differed in explaining *rijal*. Abu Mijlaz said: they are angels in the forms of male men, and they were called men because of His saying: ﴿And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾ [al-An'am 6:9]. Mujahid and al-Hasan said: they are the virtuous believers and their scholars. It was said: they are the martyrs. This was said by al-Kirmani, and al-Nahhas chose it, saying: this is the best of what has been said about it. It was said: Hamza, al-'Abbas, 'Ali and Ja'far al-Tayyar, and this was reported from Ibn 'Abbas. It was said: they are the prophets.

﴿And they will call out to the people of the Garden, "Peace be upon you," they have not entered it, though they are hoping [to enter].﴾ ﴿And when their sight is turned toward the people of the Fire, they will say, "Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people."﴾ The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in *wa-nādaw* ("they will call out") through the end of the verse refers to the men who are upon the A'raf. On this basis, those pronouns cannot refer to the prophets, nor to anything of what was explained as their being upon a mountain in the middle of the Garden or its upper part. And it is most remote to interpret them otherwise, so that any of those opinions could be correct, that they were seated on those elevated places to witness the states of the two groups, so that joy would reach them by those states. Then, when the two groups settle, they will be moved to their places that were prepared for them in the Garden. Thus the meaning of ﴿they have not entered it﴾ is: they have not entered their dwellings prepared for them in it. The meaning of ﴿and they are hoping﴾ is: they are certain of what God has prepared for them of nearness. The word *ṭama'* ("hope") has come with the meaning of certainty. He said: ﴿And the one from whom I hope that He will forgive me my sin on the Day of Judgment﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:82]. And Abraham's (peace be upon him) hope was certainty. The poet said:

*And indeed I hope that God is capable,
by the goodness of my certainty, my certainty.*

And as for the view of those who say that al-A'raf is a mountain between Paradise and the Fire, al-Qadi and al-Jubba'i criticised it and said: "It is corrupt, because His words ﴿by what you used to do﴾ indicate that everyone who enters Paradise must deserve to enter it, and that rules out the claim that there are groups who deserve neither Paradise nor the Fire and then enter Paradise purely by grace, not by desert. Moreover, their being among the people of al-A'raf indicates that they are distinguished from all the people of the Resurrection, for placing them on high, elevated places above the people of Paradise and the Fire is a great honour that befits only the noble. Those whose good deeds and bad deeds are equal have a deficient rank, and such honour does not befit them." It was answered that it is possible that ﴿and they will be called﴾ is an address to specific groups, so it does not follow that the people of Paradise are like this. As for the second objection, [God] placed them there not for honour, but because it is like an intermediate station between Paradise and the Fire. And as for ﴿that peace be upon you﴾, it is possible that "an" (أنْ) is explanatory and a lightened form of the heavy particle. And ﴿they had not entered it﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object, meaning: he called them while they were in this state, i.e., the people of Paradise, ﴿and they were hoping﴾ is a declarative clause with no place in grammatical analysis (i'rab), meaning: they called out to the people of Paradise while not having entered it, and then he informed that they were hoping to enter it. This is the meaning given by Abu al-Baqa'. It was also said: the meaning is that the companions of al-A'raf called out to the companions of Paradise with peace, while they had entered Paradise, and the people of al-A'raf had not entered it. Thus ﴿they had not entered it﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of "they called out" referring only to the people of al-A'raf. This is the interpretation of Ibn Mas'ud, Qatada, al-Suddi, and others. Ibn Mas'ud said: "By God, God did not place that hope in their hearts except for a good that He intended for them." This is the most apparent and the most fitting to the context of the verse. Ibn Mas'ud also said: "The companions of al-A'raf only hoped because the light that was in their hands was not extinguished when the light of the hypocrites was extinguished." It was also said: ﴿and they were hoping﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the subject of ﴿they had entered it﴾, and the meaning is: they did not enter it in a state of hoping for it, rather they were in a state of despair and fear, but God's pardon encompassed them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the place (i'rab) of His words ﴿they had not entered it and they were hoping﴾? I say: it has no place, because it is a resumed sentence (isti'naf), as if a questioner asked about the companions of al-A'raf, and it was said to him: ﴿they had not entered it and they were hoping﴾, meaning that their entry into Paradise was delayed behind the entry of the people of Paradise, so they had not entered it because they were being held back, and they were hoping, not despairing." And it is permissible that it has a place by being a qualifying clause (sifah). End of quote. This is a weak explanation for separating the described from its descriptive clause with the clause ﴿and they called out﴾, which is not a parenthetical clause (i'tiraD).

Ibn al-Nahwi read ﴿and they are hoping﴾ (وهم طامِعُونَ). Iyad ibn Laqit read ﴿and they are discontented﴾ (وهم ساخِطُونَ). Al-A'mash read ﴿and when their sights are turned﴾ (وإذا قُلِّبَتْ أبْصارُهم). The pronoun in "their sights" refers to the men of al-A'raf, who greet the people of Paradise, and when they look at the people of the Fire, they call upon God to be delivered from it. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and a group. Abu Mijlaz said: the pronoun refers to the people of Paradise, and they had not yet entered it. In His words ﴿they are turned﴾ there is evidence that most of their states is looking towards the companions of Paradise, and that their looking at the companions of the Fire is due to their sights being turned towards them. So the turning is not from their side; rather they are carried along into it, and it is done to them, because that place of overlooking is frightening to hear of, let alone to see, let alone to be involved in it. The meaning is that when they are made to turn their sights and see what they are suffering from the punishment, they seek refuge with their Lord from being made to be with them. The word ﴿our Lord﴾ indicates the description of Him, the Exalted, as the one who reforms them and is their master, while they are servants. So by calling upon Him with this, they seek His mercy and appeal to His generosity.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 40–47 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Indeed, those who denied Our signs and were arrogant toward them, the gates of heaven will not be opened for them.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿will not be opened﴾ for their deeds, nor for their supplications, nor for anything they intend by it the obedience of Allah, the Exalted. That is, no righteous deed ascends for them, so that the gates of heaven would be opened for it. This is drawn from His saying: ﴿To Him ascend the good word, and the righteous deed raises it﴾ [Fatir: 10], and from His saying: ﴿Indeed, the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyun﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 18]. As-Suddi and others said: ﴿will not be opened﴾ for their spirits. They mentioned, concerning the ascent of the spirits to heaven and the permission granted to the spirit of the believer and the rejection of the spirit of the disbeliever, reports (ahadith), and that occurs at the time of their death. It was also said: the meaning is that ﴿the gates of heaven will not be opened for them﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, so that they may enter through them into Paradise. That is, they will not be permitted to ascend to heaven. It was also said: blessing will not descend upon them, and they will not be given relief. Abu ʿAmr recited ﴿will not be opened﴾ with the feminine ta' and without tashdid (the doubling of the letter), al-Akhawan (the two brothers, Hamza and al-Kisai) recited it with the ya' and without tashdid, and the rest of the seven readers recited it with the ta' at the beginning and with tashdid. Abu Haywa and Abu al-Barahsam recited it with the thaʾ at the beginning, open (fatha), and with tashdid.

﴿And they will not enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle.﴾ This is a negation conditioned upon something impossible. Al-wulud (passing into) means penetrating into a thing. He mentioned the camel because it is the largest animal that deals with humans in bulk, so it can only pass through a wide opening, as the poet said: "The camel has grown large without intellect," and he said: "The body of camels and the dreams of sparrows." He mentioned ﴿the eye of the needle﴾ because it is used as a proverb for a narrow passage; it is said: "Narrower than the eye of a needle" (khart al-ibra). It was also said that a guide is called kharrit because of his guidance through narrow places, by analogy with the hole of the needle (ikhrat al-ibra). The meaning is that they will never enter Paradise. Ibn ʿAbbas was recited, according to what Shahr ibn Hawshab narrated from him, along with Mujahid, Ibn Yaʿmur, Abu Mijlaz, ash-Shaʿbi, Malik ibn ash-Shikhkhir, Abu Rajaʾ, Abu Razin, Ibn Muhaysin, and Aban from ʿAsim, as al-Jummal (الجُمَّلُ) with a damma on the jim and a fatha on the mim with tashdid. It was interpreted as the thick rope (al-qals al-ghalidh), which is the ship's cable: ropes are gathered and twisted and become one rope. It was also said that it is the thick rope made of hemp. It was also said that it is the rope by which one climbs up palm trees. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, though it probably is not authentic, that Allah is too beautiful in comparison than to be likened to a camel, meaning that it is not appropriate, whereas a rope is appropriate for the thread that passes through the eye of a needle. From al-Kisai: the one who transmitted al-Jummal from Ibn ʿAbbas was non-Arab, so he doubled the jim because of his non-Arabic pronunciation. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: this is weak, because of the large number of Ibn ʿAbbas's companions who recited it in the aforementioned reading. (End of quote.) And also because of the large number of readers other than Ibn ʿAbbas who recited it that way. Ibn ʿAbbas also recited, according to a report from Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Qatada, and Salim al-Aftas, with a damma on the jim and a fatha on the mim, without tashdid. Ibn ʿAbbas, according to a report from ʿAta', al-Dahhak, and al-Jahdari, recited with a damma on both the jim and the mim, without tashdid. ʿIkrima and Ibn Jubayr, in one report, recited with a damma on the jim and a sukun on the mim: al-Jumul (الجُمْلُ). Al-Mutawakkil and Abu al-Jawza' recited with a fatha on the jim and a sukun on the mim. Their meaning in these readings is the thick rope, which is the ship's cable. The reading of the majority is ﴿al-jamal (الجَمَلُ)﴾ with a fatha on both the jim and the mim, which is more fitting, because the eye of the needle is used as a proverb for narrowness, and the camel, this well-known animal, is used as a proverb for the largeness of its body, as we mentioned. Ibn Masʿud was asked about the camel, and he said: "It is the mate of the she-camel." This was a way of rebuking the questioner and preventing him from trying to derive another meaning for it. ʿAbd Allah, Qatada, Abu Razin, Ibn Musarrif, and Talha recited the sin of ﴿sam (سَمِّ)﴾ with a damma. Abu ʿImran al-Hawfi, Abu Nahik, and al-Asmaʿi from Nafiʿ recited it with a kasra as "simm (سِمِّ)." ʿAbd Allah, Abu Razin, and Abu Mijlaz (p. 298) recited "al-mikhyat (المِخْيَطُ)" with a kasra on the mim, a sukun on the kha', and a fatha on the ya'. Talha recited it with a fatha on the mim.

﴿Thus do We recompense the criminals﴾: that is, like that recompense, We recompense the people of crimes. Az-Zamakhshari said: this is to indicate that criminality (al-ijram) is the causal means that leads to punishment, and that everyone who commits crimes is punished. Then Allah repeated it, saying: ﴿Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, because every criminal is a wrongdoer to himself. (End of quote.) In this there is a hint of Mu'tazilite doctrine (the Mu'tazila being a theological school that emphasized human free will and divine justice).

﴿For them from Hell will be a bed, and above them will be coverings. Thus do We recompense the wrongdoers.﴾ This is a metaphor for the fire that surrounds them from every side, as He said to them: ﴿Above them are layers of fire, and beneath them are layers﴾ [az-Zumar: 16]. Al-ghawashi is the plural of ghashiya. Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Qurazi, and Ibn Zayd said: they are coverings (al-lufuf, blankets). ʿIkrima said: the smoke covers them from above. Az-Zajjaj said: a covering of fire. ad-Dahhak said: al-mihad means beds, and al-ghawashi means coverings. The tanwin in ﴿ghawashin (غَواشٍ)﴾ is either the tanwin of inflection (sarf) or the tanwin of substitution (ʿiwad), there are two opinions; and the tanwin of substitution in place of the ya' or the vowel, there are two opinions. All of this is established in the science of grammar (ʿilm al-nahw). It was also read as "ghawashun (غَواشٌ)" with a damma, like the reading of ʿAbd Allah: ﴿and His are the ships raised high﴾.

﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds — We do not charge a soul except [with] its capacity; those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.﴾ When He informed of the threat against the disbelievers, He informed of the promise to the believers. The predicate of ﴿those who﴾ is either the clause ﴿We do not charge a soul﴾ and what is among them, or the clause that begins with ﴿those﴾ and what follows it. The clause ﴿We do not charge﴾ would then be an interjection between the subject and the predicate. Its benefit is that, when He mentioned ﴿and did righteous deeds﴾, He pointed out that this deed is within their capacity and not beyond their power. It also serves as a reminder to the disbelievers that Paradise, despite its vast extent, is reached through easy deeds without hardship.
