He said: The reference of ﴿these﴾ is to the people of the Garden, and the addressees are the people of the Heights, while those who are addressed are the people of the Fire. The meaning is: ﴿Are these﴾ the weak in the world, about whom you swore that Allah does not regard them? It is said to them: "Enter the Garden." Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿Are these﴾ is a speech of an angel by the command of Allah, a reference to the people of the Heights and an address to the people of the Fire. Al-Naqqash said: When they rebuked them with their words ﴿Of no avail to you was your multitude﴾, the people of the Fire swore that the people of the Heights would enter the Fire with them. So the angels called out to them ﴿Are these...﴾. Then the people of the Heights called out: "Enter the Garden." It has also been said: the reference of ﴿these﴾ is to the people of the Heights, and the speakers are the companions of the Heights, who then return to addressing themselves, so some of them say to others: ﴿Enter the Garden.﴾ This was said by al-Hasan. It has also been said: the reference is to the believers whom the disbelievers used to swear would not enter the Garden, and the speaker is either Allah or the angels. It has also been said: the one referred to by ﴿these﴾ is the people of the Heights, and the speaker is Malik, the keeper of the Fire, by the command of Allah, Exalted. Abu Mijlaz said: The people of the Heights are the angels, and they are the speakers, saying ﴿Are these...﴾ as a reference to the people of the Garden. Similarly comes the saying of one who said: The people of the Heights are prophets and martyrs. Al-Hasan and Ibn Hurmuz read ﴿adkhilū﴾ (أدخلوا) from the causative form (adkhala), meaning: "Cause yourselves to enter," or it is an address to the angels, after which He addresses humankind. ʿIkrima read ﴿dakhalū﴾ as a report in the past tense. Talha, Ibn Wathhab and al-Nakhaʿi read ﴿udkhilū﴾ as a passive report. On these two readings, the statement ﴿no fear shall be upon you﴾ is in the sense of: "said to them, no fear shall be upon you." Al-Zamakhshari said: It is said to the people of the Heights: "Enter the Garden," after they have been detained on the Heights and have looked at the two groups, recognized them by their marks, and said what they say. The benefit of this is to show that reward is according to the measure of deeds, that rank and delay are according to them, and that no one precedes with Allah, Exalted, except by his precedence in deeds, nor lags behind except by his lagging in them. It is also to make the listeners desire the condition of the foremost and strive to attain their excellence, and to show that each person will know that Day by his own mark which made him deserving of being marked as one of the people of good or of evil, so that the wrongdoer restrains from his wrongdoing and the doer of good increases in his goodness, and so that it becomes known that everyone will rebuke the sinners, even the least of people in deeds. End of quotation. This is an excessive use of rhetorical discourse with no real benefit, and in it is a hidden trace of Mu'tazilism (i'tizal). It is related from Hudhayfa that the people of the Heights will desire intercession, so they come to Adam, who refers them to Noah. Then the prophets refer them among themselves until they come to Muhammad (ﷺ), who intercedes for them. He is granted intercession, and they enter the Garden, where they are cast into the river of life, and they become radiant, and they are called "the poor of the Garden." Salim, the freedman of Abu Hudhayfa, said: "I wish that I were among the people of the Heights."

﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of the Garden: "Pour upon us some water, or some of what Allah has provided you." They will say: "Allah has forbidden both to the disbelievers."﴾ This requires that each of the two groups hears the speech of the other. This is rationally possible despite the distance between them, from high to low. It is also possible that this happens with sight and observation from Allah, and that is more humiliating and painful for the disbelievers. It is also possible that this happens while there is a barrier and a wall between them. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that when the people of the Heights reached the Garden, the people of the Fire, after despair, hoped for relief. They said: "O Lord! We have relatives among the people of the Garden, so permit us to see them and speak with them." So they look at them and at what they are in of bliss, and they recognize them. The people of the Garden look at their relatives among the people of Hell but do not recognize them, for their faces have blackened and they have become a different creation. The people of the Fire call out to the people of the Garden by their names and inform them of their relatives. A man calls to his brother, saying: "O my brother! I have been burned, so help me!" He replies: "Allah has forbidden both to the disbelievers." It is possible that the particle ("an") is verbal and explanatory. Ibn ʿAbbas's statement indicates that this calling was out of hope and desire for its fulfillment. Al-Qadi said: It is with despair, because they have known the permanence of their punishment and that it will not be lightened for them. But one who is despairing of something may still seek it, as the proverb says: "The drowning man clings to the foam," even if he knows it will not save him. End of quotation. ﴿Pour upon us﴾ (afīḍū) is more appropriate than "give us to drink" (usqūnā), because it implies abundance, as one says: "Allah poured His blessings upon him," meaning He expanded them. Their request for water is due to the intensity of their burning and scorching, and because it is customary for it to extinguish fire. Or it is ﴿of what Allah has provided you﴾, because the human constitution cannot do without food, since it strengthens it. Or they hoped for mercy through eating some food. The ("or") is in its proper sense, in that they asked for one of the two things, and ﴿or of what Allah has provided you﴾ comes in general terms. The conjunction with "or" indicates that the first item is not included within the generality. It has also been said: "or" is in the sense of "and," because of their saying "Allah has forbidden both". It has also been said: the meaning is that He forbade each of them, so "or" is in its proper sense, and ﴿what Allah has provided you﴾ is general, so it includes food, fruit and drinks other than water. Restricting it to fruit, or to food, or to drinks other than water, are three opinions: the second is that of al-Suddi, and the third is that of al-Zamakhshari, who said: ﴿Or of what Allah has provided you﴾ refers to other than these, such as drinks, since they are included in the ruling of pouring. So he said: It is permissible that what is meant is: "Pour upon us from what Allah has provided you of food and fruit," like the saying of the poet:

*I fed her straw and cold water.*

They only request this while despairing of being answered, out of bewilderment about their condition, as the distressed and tested person does. End of quotation. His statement "and they only request" to the end is the words of al-Qadi, which we have already cited. It is permissible that what is meant is: "Pour upon us from what Allah has provided you of food and fruit," which allows two interpretations. One is that ﴿pour﴾ [al-Baqara 2:199] is implicitly meaning "throw," so that ﴿upon us, some water, or some of what Allah has provided you﴾ is correctly conjoined. The other, which is the apparent meaning of his words, is that he supposes a verb after ("or") that reaches ﴿of what Allah has provided you﴾, namely "throw." These are two positions of the grammarians regarding what is conjoined to something by a conjunctive particle, where the verb does not reach it. The sound one of the two is implicit inclusion (tadmīn), not supposition (iḍmār), as we have established in the science of Arabic grammar. The meaning of "forbidding" here is prevention, as in the saying:

*Forbidden to my eyes that they should taste sleep.*

Their report of this is from the command of Allah.

﴿Those who took their religion as diversion and play, and whom the life of this world deceived.﴾ The explanation of similar words has already been given in Surat al-An'am.

﴿So today We forget them as they forgot the meeting of this their Day, and as they used to deny Our signs.﴾ This is a report from Allah about what He does to them. Ibn ʿAbbas and a group said: He leaves them in punishment, as they left looking forward to the meeting of this Day. Qatada said: They were forgotten regarding good, but not forgotten regarding evil. Al-Zamakhshari said: He treats them as forgetful people treat their servants from among the good, not mentioning them with it: ﴿as they forgot the meeting of this their Day﴾, as they acted toward its meeting like forgetful people, not bringing it to mind and not caring for it. Al-Hasan, al-Suddi, and most of the scholars also said: "We leave them in their punishment, as they left action for the meeting of their Day." End of quotation. If "forgetting" is understood as neglect on the part of the disbelievers, then it is, on Allah's part, a calling of the punishment by the name of the sin. ﴿And as they used to﴾ is conjoined to ﴿as they forgot﴾, and the "mā" in both is verbal. It appears that the kāf in ("kamā") is causal.

﴿And We have certainly brought them a Book which We have detailed with knowledge, as guidance and mercy for a people who believe.﴾ The pronoun in ﴿We have certainly brought them﴾ refers to those previously mentioned, and so the Book in this case is a genus, meaning: "with a Book" of divine origin, since the pronoun is general regarding the disbelievers. Yahya ibn Sallam said: The pronoun refers to those who deny Muhammad (ﷺ), and this is the beginning of a new statement, and the speech is complete at His saying ﴿they deny﴾. The Book is the Qur'an. ﴿We have detailed it﴾, knowing how to detail it regarding rulings, admonitions, stories and all its other meanings. It has also been said: ﴿We have detailed it﴾ by clarifying the truth from falsehood. It has also been said: We have sent it down in various sections. Ibn Muhaysin and al-Jahdari read ﴿faḍḍalnāhu﴾ with a dotted ḍād (ض), meaning: "We have preferred it over all the Books, knowing that it is worthy of being preferred over them." In al-Tahrir it is stated that it was preferred over the other revealed Books by thirty qualities which were not in any other. ﴿Detailed﴾ is an attribute of ﴿a Book﴾. The apparent view is that ﴿with knowledge﴾ is a circumstantial clause of the subject of ﴿detailed﴾. It has also been said: the estimate is "comprising knowledge," so it is a circumstantial clause of the object. ﴿Guidance and mercy﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause. It has also been said that it is an object for the sake of which (maf'ūl li-ajlihi). It was also read in the nominative, meaning: "it is guidance and mercy." Zayd ibn ʿAli read ﴿guidance and mercy﴾ in the genitive, as an apposition to "a Book" or as an attribute. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' (may Allah have mercy on them both) explained the genitive reading as an attribute of "a Book."

﴿Do they await anything but its ta'wil?﴾ That is, the final outcome of the matter and its consequence. This was said by Qatada, Mujahid and others. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Its outcome on the Day of Resurrection. al-Suddi said: In this world, like the event of Badr, and also on the Day of Resurrection. al-Zamakhshari said: What it leads to of making clear its truthfulness and the manifestation of its soundness, the threats and promises it contains. The root of ta'wil (interpretation/ultimate meaning) is hamza, waw and lam, from "āla yaʾūlu" (to return/lead to). al-Khattabi said: "I returned the thing to its beginning (awwal)," so the word is derived from "first" (awwal). End of quotation. This is an error, because the two roots differ.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 48–53 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿On the Day its interpretation (ta'wil) comes, those who had forgotten it before will say: "The messengers of our Lord had indeed come with the truth. Do we have any intercessors who might intercede for us, or could we be sent back so that we might do other than what we used to do?"﴾. That is: the outcome of what He announced of promise and threat becomes manifest. This takes place on the Day of Resurrection, when those who abandoned the followers of the Messenger ask, "Do we have any intercessors?", a question about the means of deliverance at a time when there is no deliverance. There is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning: "The messengers of our Lord had indeed come with the truth, but we did not believe them, or we did not follow them," ﴿so do we have any intercessors?﴾. Here "the messengers" means the prophets, who on the Day of Resurrection report that what their messengers brought them was the truth. It has also been said that "the messengers" are the angels of punishment, at the moment of direct witnessing (mu'ayanah) of what they had been warned about.

The majority of reciters read ﴿أوْ نُرَدُّ﴾ (aw nuraddu) with a ḍammah on the dāl, and (fa-na'mala) with a fatḥah on the lām, as a verbal sentence (jumlah fi'liyyah) coordinated with a nominal sentence (jumlah ismiyyah). Both preceded by an interrogative, so the two answers are in the accusative. That is: "Are there intercessors for us so that they intercede for us in deliverance from the punishment, or can we be returned to the world so that we may do righteous deeds?"

Al-Hasan is reported, as transmitted by al-Zamakhshari, to have read (fa-na'mala) with a fatḥah on the dāl and a ḍammah on the lām. Al-Hasan is also reported, as transmitted by Ibn 'Atiyyah and others, to have read both with a ḍammah. (fa-na'mulu) is coordinated with (nuraddu). Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abu Haywah read both with a fatḥah, so (nuradda) is in the accusative, coordinated with (fa-yashfa'ū lanā) as an answer upon an answer. The intercessors would then be in one of two matters: either for deliverance from the punishment or for being returned to the world to resume righteous deeds. The intercession would then extend to either the return or the deliverance, and (fa-na'malu) is coordinated with (fa-nuraddu).

It is possible that (aw nuraddu) is of the type of (la-alzamanna-ka, aw taqḍiyanī ḥaqqī), "I will surely keep you company until you either pay me my due," on the reckoning of one who assigns it the meaning of (ḥattā taqḍiyanī ḥaqqī, "until you pay me my due"), or (kay taqḍiyanī ḥaqqī, "so that you pay me my due"). In that case the obligation is made to end upon the payment of the due, or is made to be caused by it. Then the intercession would be for the return only. As for the reckoning of Sibawayh, "Verily I will surely keep you company unless you pay me," it does not appear that the meaning of "aw" here is the meaning of "illā" (unless), for then the meaning would become: "Do intercessors intercede for us except that we be returned?" and this is an unclear exception.

As to whether their saying "Do we have intercessors?" is made in hope or in despair, there is the same disagreement as in their call, ﴿"Pour down upon us water"﴾ (an afīḍū). Al-Qadi said: this (their saying) indicates two rulings: that they were able to believe and repent, and for this reason they asked for a second return. Those of the Hereafter are not obligated (mukallafūn), contrary to the Mujbirah (determinists) and al-Najjar, for if they were so, they would not have asked for return; rather they would have repented and believed.

﴿They have lost their souls, and what they used to fabricate has strayed far from them﴾. That is: they lost in the trade of their souls, since they bought the base and perishing of the worldly life in exchange for the precious and enduring of the Hereafter. What they had fabricated against God, namely what He had not said nor commanded them, became null for them, and He refuted them in taking gods besides God. (p. 307)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 48–53 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And the companions of the Heights will call out to men whom they recognize by their marks, saying: "Of no avail to you was your multitude, nor what you used to be arrogant about."﴾ It is possible that this calling and those men are in the Fire, and that their recognizing them was in this world through signs. It is also possible that the calling takes place while they are being driven to the Fire, and that their marks are blackened faces and disfigured forms. Abu Mijlaz said: "The angels call out to men in the Fire." According to his interpretation, the people of the Heights are angels, whereas the majority hold that they are human beings. The word ﴿men﴾ indicates that they are not specified. End of quotation. ﴿Of no avail﴾ is an interrogative of rebuke and reproach. It has also been said that it is negative, and the "mā" in ﴿what you used to be﴾ [al-A'raf 7:37] is verbal (masdariyya), meaning: "and your being arrogant." A group read ﴿tastakthirun﴾ with a thāʾ (ث), with three dots, from "multiplicity" (al-kathra).

﴿Are these the ones of whom you swore that Allah would not grant them mercy? Enter the Garden; no fear shall be upon you, nor shall you grieve.﴾ The apparent meaning is that this is part of what the people of the Heights say, and the reference is to the people of the Garden, whom the leaders used to belittle and despise because of their poverty and their scarce portions in the world. Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿Are these﴾ is a speech of an angel by the command of Allah, a reference to the people of the Heights and an address to the people of the Fire. It has also been said: the reference of ﴿these﴾ is to the people of the Heights, and the speakers are the companions of the Heights, who then return to addressing themselves, so some of them say to others: ﴿Enter the Garden.﴾ This was said by al-Hasan. It has also been said: the reference is to the believers whom the disbelievers used to swear would not enter the Garden, and the speaker is either Allah or the angels. It has also been said: the one referred to by ﴿these﴾ is the people of the Heights, and the speaker is Malik, the keeper of the Fire, by the command of Allah, Exalted. Abu Mijlaz said: The people of the Heights are the angels, and they are the speakers, saying ﴿Are these...﴾ as a reference to the people of the Garden. It is related from Hudhayfa that the people of the Heights will desire intercession, so they come to Adam, who refers them to Noah. Then the prophets refer them among themselves until they come to Muhammad (ﷺ), who intercedes for them. He is granted intercession, and they enter the Garden, where they are cast into the river of life, and they become radiant, and they are called "the poor of the Garden." We have relatives among the people of the Garden, so permit us to see them and speak with them." So they look at them and at what they are in of bliss, and they recognize them. Ibn ʿAbbas's statement indicates that this calling was out of hope and desire for its fulfillment. **Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 48–53 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿On the Day its interpretation (ta'wil) comes, those who had forgotten it before will say: "The messengers of our Lord had indeed come with the truth. Do we have any intercessors who might intercede for us, or could we be sent back so that we might do other than what we used to do?"﴾. That is: the outcome of what He announced of promise and threat becomes manifest. This takes place on the Day of Resurrection, when those who abandoned the followers of the Messenger ask, "Do we have any intercessors?", a question about the means of deliverance at a time when there is no deliverance. There is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning: "The messengers of our Lord had indeed come with the truth, but we did not believe them, or we did not follow them," ﴿so do we have any intercessors?﴾. Here "the messengers" means the prophets, who on the Day of Resurrection report that what their messengers brought them was the truth. It has also been said that "the messengers" are the angels of punishment, at the moment of direct witnessing (mu'ayanah) of what they had been warned about.

The majority of reciters read ﴿أوْ نُرَدُّ﴾ (aw nuraddu) with a ḍammah on the dāl, and (fa-na'mala) with a fatḥah on the lām, as a verbal sentence (jumlah fi'liyyah) coordinated with a nominal sentence (jumlah ismiyyah). Both preceded by an interrogative, so the two answers are in the accusative. That is: "Are there intercessors for us so that they intercede for us in deliverance from the punishment, or can we be returned to the world so that we may do righteous deeds?"

Al-Hasan is reported, as transmitted by al-Zamakhshari, to have read (fa-na'mala) with a fatḥah on the dāl and a ḍammah on the lām. Al-Hasan is also reported, as transmitted by Ibn 'Atiyyah and others, to have read both with a ḍammah. (fa-na'mulu) is coordinated with (nuraddu). Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abu Haywah read both with a fatḥah, so (nuradda) is in the accusative, coordinated with (fa-yashfa'ū lanā) as an answer upon an answer. The intercessors would then be in one of two matters: either for deliverance from the punishment or for being returned to the world to resume righteous deeds. The intercession would then extend to either the return or the deliverance, and (fa-na'malu) is coordinated with (fa-nuraddu).

It is possible that (aw nuraddu) is of the type of (la-alzamanna-ka, aw taqḍiyanī ḥaqqī), "I will surely keep you company until you either pay me my due," on the reckoning of one who assigns it the meaning of (ḥattā taqḍiyanī ḥaqqī, "until you pay me my due"), or (kay taqḍiyanī ḥaqqī, "so that you pay me my due"). In that case the obligation is made to end upon the payment of the due, or is made to be caused by it. Then the intercession would be for the return only. As for the reckoning of Sibawayh, "Verily I will surely keep you company unless you pay me," it does not appear that the meaning of "aw" here is the meaning of "illā" (unless), for then the meaning would become: "Do intercessors intercede for us except that we be returned?" and this is an unclear exception.

As to whether their saying "Do we have intercessors?" is made in hope or in despair, there is the same disagreement as in their call, ﴿"Pour down upon us water"﴾ (an afīḍū). Al-Qadi said: this (their saying) indicates two rulings: that they were able to believe and repent, and for this reason they asked for a second return. Those of the Hereafter are not obligated (mukallafūn), contrary to the Mujbirah (determinists) and al-Najjar, for if they were so, they would not have asked for return; rather they would have repented and believed.

﴿They have lost their souls, and what they used to fabricate has strayed far from them﴾. That is: they lost in the trade of their souls, since they bought the base and perishing of the worldly life in exchange for the precious and enduring of the Hereafter. What they had fabricated against God, namely what He had not said nor commanded them, became null for them, and He refuted them in taking gods besides God. (p. 307)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 48–53 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And the companions of the Heights will call out to men whom they recognize by their marks, saying: "Of no avail to you was your multitude, nor what you used to be arrogant about."﴾ It is possible that this calling and those men are in the Fire, and that their recognizing them was in this world through signs. It is also possible that the calling takes place while they are being driven to the Fire, and that their marks are blackened faces and disfigured forms. Abu Mijlaz said: "The angels call out to men in the Fire." According to his interpretation, the people of the Heights are angels, whereas the majority hold that they are human beings. The word ﴿men﴾ indicates that they are not specified. Ibn al-Qushayri said: The companions of the Heights call out to the leaders of the polytheists, before their forms are erased, in the Fire: "O Walid ibn al-Mughira! O Abu Jahl ibn Hisham! O As ibn Wa'il! O Utba ibn Abi Mu'ayt! O Umayya ibn Khalaf! O Ubayy ibn Khalaf! O all the other leaders of the disbelievers! Of no avail to you was your multitude in the world, the wealth, the children, the helpers, the chamberlains and the armies, nor what you used to be arrogant about, regarding faith." End of quotation. ﴿Of no avail﴾ is an interrogative of rebuke and reproach. It has also been said that it is negative, and the "mā" in ﴿what you used to be﴾ [al-A'raf 7:37] is verbal (masdariyya), meaning: "and your being arrogant." A group read ﴿tastakthirun﴾ with a thāʾ (ث), with three dots, from "multiplicity" (al-kathra).

﴿Are these the ones of whom you swore that Allah would not grant them mercy? Enter the Garden; no fear shall be upon you, nor shall you grieve.﴾ The apparent meaning is that this is part of what the people of the Heights say, and the reference is to the people of the Garden, whom the leaders used to belittle and despise because of their poverty and their scarce portions in the world. They used to swear by Allah, Exalted, that He would not admit them [p. 304] into the Garden. This was said by al-Zamakhshari, and Ibn Atiyya mentioned it from some of the interpreters. He said: The reference of ﴿these﴾ is to the people of the Garden, and the addressees are the people of the Heights, while those who are addressed are the people of the Fire. The meaning is: ﴿Are these﴾ the weak in the world, about whom you swore that Allah does not regard them? It is said to them: "Enter the Garden." Ibn ʿAbbas said: ﴿Are these﴾ is a speech of an angel by the command of Allah, a reference to the people of the Heights and an address to the people of the Fire. Al-Naqqash said: When they rebuked them with their words ﴿Of no avail to you was your multitude﴾, the people of the Fire swore that the people of the Heights would enter the Fire with them. So the angels called out to them ﴿Are these...﴾. Then the people of the Heights called out: "Enter the Garden." It has also been said: the reference of ﴿these﴾ is to the people of the Heights, and the speakers are the companions of the Heights, who then return to addressing themselves, so some of them say to others: ﴿Enter the Garden.﴾ This was said by al-Hasan. It has also been said: the reference is to the believers whom the disbelievers used to swear would not enter the Garden, and the speaker is either Allah or the angels. It has also been said: the one referred to by ﴿these﴾ is the people of the Heights, and the speaker is Malik, the keeper of the Fire, by the command of Allah, Exalted. Abu Mijlaz said: The people of the Heights are the angels, and they are the speakers, saying ﴿Are these...﴾ as a reference to the people of the Garden. Similarly comes the saying of one who said: The people of the Heights are prophets and martyrs. Al-Hasan and Ibn Hurmuz read ﴿adkhilū﴾ (أدخلوا) from the causative form (adkhala), meaning: "Cause yourselves to enter," or it is an address to the angels, after which He addresses humankind. ʿIkrima read ﴿dakhalū﴾ as a report in the past tense. Talha, Ibn Wathhab and al-Nakhaʿi read ﴿udkhilū﴾ as a passive report. On these two readings, the statement ﴿no fear shall be upon you﴾ is in the sense of: "said to them, no fear shall be upon you." Al-Zamakhshari said: It is said to the people of the Heights: "Enter the Garden," after they have been detained on the Heights and have looked at the two groups, recognized them by their marks, and said what they say. The benefit of this is to show that reward is according to the measure of deeds, that rank and delay are according to them, and that no one precedes with Allah, Exalted, except by his precedence in deeds, nor lags behind except by his lagging in them. It is also to make the listeners desire the condition of the foremost and strive to attain their excellence, and to show that each person will know that Day by his own mark which made him deserving of being marked as one of the people of good or of evil, so that the wrongdoer restrains from his wrongdoing and the doer of good increases in his goodness, and so that it becomes known that everyone will rebuke the sinners, even the least of people in deeds. End of quotation. This is an excessive use of rhetorical discourse with no real benefit, and in it is a hidden trace of Mu'tazilism (i'tizal). It is related from Hudhayfa that the people of the Heights will desire intercession, so they come to Adam, who refers them to Noah. Then the prophets refer them among themselves until they come to Muhammad (ﷺ), who intercedes for them. He is granted intercession, and they enter the Garden, where they are cast into the river of life, and they become radiant, and they are called "the poor of the Garden." Salim, the freedman of Abu Hudhayfa, said: "I wish that I were among the people of the Heights."

﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of the Garden: "Pour upon us some water, or some of what Allah has provided you." They will say: "Allah has forbidden both to the disbelievers."﴾ This requires that each of the two groups hears the speech of the other. This is rationally possible despite the distance between them, from high to low. It is also possible that this happens with sight and observation from Allah, and that is more humiliating and painful for the disbelievers. It is also possible that this happens while there is a barrier and a wall between them. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that when the people of the Heights reached the Garden, the people of the Fire, after despair, hoped for relief. They said: "O Lord! We have relatives among the people of the Garden, so permit us to see them and speak with them." So they look at them and at what they are in of bliss, and they recognize them. The people of the Garden look at their relatives among the people of Hell but do not recognize them, for their faces have blackened and they have become a different creation. The people of the Fire call out to the people of the Garden by their names and inform them of their relatives. A man calls to his brother, saying: "O my brother! I have been burned, so help me!" He replies: "Allah has forbidden both to the disbelievers." It is possible that the particle ("an") is verbal and explanatory. Ibn ʿAbbas's statement indicates that this calling was out of hope and desire for its fulfillment. Al-Qadi said: It is with despair, because they have known the permanence of their punishment and that it will not be lightened for them. But one who is despairing of something may still seek it, as the proverb says: "The drowning man clings to the foam," even if he knows it will not save him. End of quotation. ﴿Pour upon us﴾ (afīḍū) is more appropriate than "give us to drink" (usqūnā), because it implies abundance, as one says: "Allah poured His blessings upon him," meaning He expanded them. Their request for water is due to the intensity of their burning and scorching, and because it is customary for it to extinguish fire. Or it is ﴿of what Allah has provided you﴾, because the human constitution cannot do without food, since it strengthens it. Or they hoped for mercy through eating some food. The ("or") is in its proper sense, in that they asked for one of the two things, and ﴿or of what Allah has provided you﴾ comes in general terms. The conjunction with "or" indicates that the first item is not included within the generality. It has also been said: "or" is in the sense of "and," because of their saying "Allah has forbidden both". It has also been said: the meaning is that He forbade each of them, so "or" is in its proper sense, and ﴿what Allah has provided you﴾ is general, so it includes food, fruit and drinks other than water. Restricting it to fruit, or to food, or to drinks other than water, are three opinions: the second is that of al-Suddi, and the third is that of al-Zamakhshari, who said: ﴿Or of what Allah has provided you﴾ refers to other than these, such as drinks, since they are included in the ruling of pouring. So he said: It is permissible that what is meant is: "Pour upon us from what Allah has provided you of food and fruit," like the saying of the poet:

*I fed her straw and cold water.*

They only request this while despairing of being answered, out of bewilderment about their condition, as the distressed and tested person does. End of quotation. His statement "and they only request" to the end is the words of al-Qadi, which we have already cited. It is permissible that what is meant is: "Pour upon us from what Allah has provided you of food and fruit," which allows two interpretations. One is that ﴿pour﴾ [al-Baqara 2:199] is implicitly meaning "throw," so that ﴿upon us, some water, or some of what Allah has provided you﴾ is correctly conjoined. The other, which is the apparent meaning of his words, is that he supposes a verb after ("or") that reaches ﴿of what Allah has provided you﴾, namely "throw." These are two positions of the grammarians regarding what is conjoined to something by a conjunctive particle, where the verb does not reach it. The sound one of the two is implicit inclusion (tadmīn), not supposition (iḍmār), as we have established in the science of Arabic grammar. The meaning of "forbidding" here is prevention, as in the saying:

*Forbidden to my eyes that they should taste sleep.*

Their report of this is from the command of Allah.

﴿Those who took their religion as diversion and play, and whom the life of this world deceived.﴾ The explanation of similar words has already been given in Surat al-An'am.

﴿So today We forget them as they forgot the meeting of this their Day, and as they used to deny Our signs.﴾ This is a report from Allah about what He does to them. Ibn ʿAbbas and a group said: He leaves them in punishment, as they left looking forward to the meeting of this Day. Qatada said: They were forgotten regarding good, but not forgotten regarding evil. Al-Zamakhshari said: He treats them as forgetful people treat their servants from among the good, not mentioning them with it: ﴿as they forgot the meeting of this their Day﴾, as they acted toward its meeting like forgetful people, not bringing it to mind and not caring for it. Al-Hasan, al-Suddi, and most of the scholars also said: "We leave them in their punishment, as they left action for the meeting of their Day." End of quotation. If "forgetting" is understood as neglect on the part of the disbelievers, then it is, on Allah's part, a calling of the punishment by the name of the sin. ﴿And as they used to﴾ is conjoined to ﴿as they forgot﴾, and the "mā" in both is verbal. It appears that the kāf in ("kamā") is causal.

﴿And We have certainly brought them a Book which We have detailed with knowledge, as guidance and mercy for a people who believe.﴾ The pronoun in ﴿We have certainly brought them﴾ refers to those previously mentioned, and so the Book in this case is a genus, meaning: "with a Book" of divine origin, since the pronoun is general regarding the disbelievers. Yahya ibn Sallam said: The pronoun refers to those who deny Muhammad (ﷺ), and this is the beginning of a new statement, and the speech is complete at His saying ﴿they deny﴾. The Book is the Qur'an. ﴿We have detailed it﴾, knowing how to detail it regarding rulings, admonitions, stories and all its other meanings. It has also been said: ﴿We have detailed it﴾ by clarifying the truth from falsehood. It has also been said: We have sent it down in various sections. Ibn Muhaysin and al-Jahdari read ﴿faḍḍalnāhu﴾ with a dotted ḍād (ض), meaning: "We have preferred it over all the Books, knowing that it is worthy of being preferred over them." In al-Tahrir it is stated that it was preferred over the other revealed Books by thirty qualities which were not in any other. ﴿Detailed﴾ is an attribute of ﴿a Book﴾. The apparent view is that ﴿with knowledge﴾ is a circumstantial clause of the subject of ﴿detailed﴾. It has also been said: the estimate is "comprising knowledge," so it is a circumstantial clause of the object. ﴿Guidance and mercy﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause. It has also been said that it is an object for the sake of which (maf'ūl li-ajlihi). It was also read in the nominative, meaning: "it is guidance and mercy." Zayd ibn ʿAli read ﴿guidance and mercy﴾ in the genitive, as an apposition to "a Book" or as an attribute. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' (may Allah have mercy on them both) explained the genitive reading as an attribute of "a Book."

﴿Do they await anything but its ta'wil?﴾ That is, the final outcome of the matter and its consequence. This was said by Qatada, Mujahid and others. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Its outcome on the Day of Resurrection. al-Suddi said: In this world, like the event of Badr, and also on the Day of Resurrection. al-Zamakhshari said: What it leads to of making clear its truthfulness and the manifestation of its soundness, the threats and promises it contains. The root of ta'wil (interpretation/ultimate meaning) is hamza, waw and lam, from "āla yaʾūlu" (to return/lead to). al-Khattabi said: "I returned the thing to its beginning (awwal)," so the word is derived from "first" (awwal). End of quotation. This is an error, because the two roots differ.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 48–53 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿On the Day its interpretation (ta'wil) comes, those who had forgotten it before will say: "The messengers of our Lord had indeed come with the truth. Do we have any intercessors who might intercede for us, or could we be sent back so that we might do other than what we used to do?"﴾. That is: the outcome of what He announced of promise and threat becomes manifest. This takes place on the Day of Resurrection, when those who abandoned the followers of the Messenger ask, "Do we have any intercessors?", a question about the means of deliverance at a time when there is no deliverance. There is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning: "The messengers of our Lord had indeed come with the truth, but we did not believe them, or we did not follow them," ﴿so do we have any intercessors?﴾. Here "the messengers" means the prophets, who on the Day of Resurrection report that what their messengers brought them was the truth. It has also been said that "the messengers" are the angels of punishment, at the moment of direct witnessing (mu'ayanah) of what they had been warned about.

The majority of reciters read ﴿أوْ نُرَدُّ﴾ (aw nuraddu) with a ḍammah on the dāl, and (fa-na'mala) with a fatḥah on the lām, as a verbal sentence (jumlah fi'liyyah) coordinated with a nominal sentence (jumlah ismiyyah). Both preceded by an interrogative, so the two answers are in the accusative. That is: "Are there intercessors for us so that they intercede for us in deliverance from the punishment, or can we be returned to the world so that we may do righteous deeds?"

Al-Hasan is reported, as transmitted by al-Zamakhshari, to have read (fa-na'mala) with a fatḥah on the dāl and a ḍammah on the lām. Al-Hasan is also reported, as transmitted by Ibn 'Atiyyah and others, to have read both with a ḍammah. (fa-na'mulu) is coordinated with (nuraddu). Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abu Haywah read both with a fatḥah, so (nuradda) is in the accusative, coordinated with (fa-yashfa'ū lanā) as an answer upon an answer. The intercessors would then be in one of two matters: either for deliverance from the punishment or for being returned to the world to resume righteous deeds. The intercession would then extend to either the return or the deliverance, and (fa-na'malu) is coordinated with (fa-nuraddu).

It is possible that (aw nuraddu) is of the type of (la-alzamanna-ka, aw taqḍiyanī ḥaqqī), "I will surely keep you company until you either pay me my due," on the reckoning of one who assigns it the meaning of (ḥattā taqḍiyanī ḥaqqī, "until you pay me my due"), or (kay taqḍiyanī ḥaqqī, "so that you pay me my due"). In that case the obligation is made to end upon the payment of the due, or is made to be caused by it. Then the intercession would be for the return only. As for the reckoning of Sibawayh, "Verily I will surely keep you company unless you pay me," it does not appear that the meaning of "aw" here is the meaning of "illā" (unless), for then the meaning would become: "Do intercessors intercede for us except that we be returned?" and this is an unclear exception.

As to whether their saying "Do we have intercessors?" is made in hope or in despair, there is the same disagreement as in their call, ﴿"Pour down upon us water"﴾ (an afīḍū). Al-Qadi said: this (their saying) indicates two rulings: that they were able to believe and repent, and for this reason they asked for a second return. Those of the Hereafter are not obligated (mukallafūn), contrary to the Mujbirah (determinists) and al-Najjar, for if they were so, they would not have asked for return; rather they would have repented and believed.

﴿They have lost their souls, and what they used to fabricate has strayed far from them﴾. That is: they lost in the trade of their souls, since they bought the base and perishing of the worldly life in exchange for the precious and enduring of the Hereafter. What they had fabricated against God, namely what He had not said nor commanded them, became null for them, and He refuted them in taking gods besides God. (p. 307)
