He replies: "Allah has forbidden both to the disbelievers." It is possible that the particle ("an") is verbal and explanatory. Ibn ʿAbbas's statement indicates that this calling was out of hope and desire for its fulfillment. Al-Qadi said: It is with despair, because they have known the permanence of their punishment and that it will not be lightened for them. But one who is despairing of something may still seek it, as the proverb says: "The drowning man clings to the foam," even if he knows it will not save him. End of quotation. ﴿Pour upon us﴾ (afīḍū) is more appropriate than "give us to drink" (usqūnā), because it implies abundance, as one says: "Allah poured His blessings upon him," meaning He expanded them. Their request for water is due to the intensity of their burning and scorching, and because it is customary for it to extinguish fire. Or it is ﴿of what Allah has provided you﴾, because the human constitution cannot do without food, since it strengthens it. Or they hoped for mercy through eating some food. The ("or") is in its proper sense, in that they asked for one of the two things, and ﴿or of what Allah has provided you﴾ comes in general terms. The conjunction with "or" indicates that the first item is not included within the generality. It has also been said: "or" is in the sense of "and," because of their saying "Allah has forbidden both". It has also been said: the meaning is that He forbade each of them, so "or" is in its proper sense, and ﴿what Allah has provided you﴾ is general, so it includes food, fruit and drinks other than water. Restricting it to fruit, or to food, or to drinks other than water, are three opinions: the second is that of al-Suddi, and the third is that of al-Zamakhshari, who said: ﴿Or of what Allah has provided you﴾ refers to other than these, such as drinks, since they are included in the ruling of pouring. So he said: It is permissible that what is meant is: "Pour upon us from what Allah has provided you of food and fruit," like the saying of the poet:

*I fed her straw and cold water.*

They only request this while despairing of being answered, out of bewilderment about their condition, as the distressed and tested person does. End of quotation. His statement "and they only request" to the end is the words of al-Qadi, which we have already cited. It is permissible that what is meant is: "Pour upon us from what Allah has provided you of food and fruit," which allows two interpretations. One is that ﴿pour﴾ [al-Baqara 2:199] is implicitly meaning "throw," so that ﴿upon us, some water, or some of what Allah has provided you﴾ is correctly conjoined. The other, which is the apparent meaning of his words, is that he supposes a verb after ("or") that reaches ﴿of what Allah has provided you﴾, namely "throw." These are two positions of the grammarians regarding what is conjoined to something by a conjunctive particle, where the verb does not reach it. The sound one of the two is implicit inclusion (tadmīn), not supposition (iḍmār), as we have established in the science of Arabic grammar. The meaning of "forbidding" here is prevention, as in the saying:

*Forbidden to my eyes that they should taste sleep.*

Their report of this is from the command of Allah.

﴿Those who took their religion as diversion and play, and whom the life of this world deceived.﴾ The explanation of similar words has already been given in Surat al-An'am.

﴿So today We forget them as they forgot the meeting of this their Day, and as they used to deny Our signs.﴾ This is a report from Allah about what He does to them. Ibn ʿAbbas and a group said: He leaves them in punishment, as they left looking forward to the meeting of this Day. Qatada said: They were forgotten regarding good, but not forgotten regarding evil. Al-Zamakhshari said: He treats them as forgetful people treat their servants from among the good, not mentioning them with it: ﴿as they forgot the meeting of this their Day﴾, as they acted toward its meeting like forgetful people, not bringing it to mind and not caring for it. Al-Hasan, al-Suddi, and most of the scholars also said: "We leave them in their punishment, as they left action for the meeting of their Day." End of quotation. If "forgetting" is understood as neglect on the part of the disbelievers, then it is, on Allah's part, a calling of the punishment by the name of the sin. ﴿And as they used to﴾ is conjoined to ﴿as they forgot﴾, and the "mā" in both is verbal. It appears that the kāf in ("kamā") is causal.

﴿And We have certainly brought them a Book which We have detailed with knowledge, as guidance and mercy for a people who believe.﴾ The pronoun in ﴿We have certainly brought them﴾ refers to those previously mentioned, and so the Book in this case is a genus, meaning: "with a Book" of divine origin, since the pronoun is general regarding the disbelievers. Yahya ibn Sallam said: The pronoun refers to those who deny Muhammad (ﷺ), and this is the beginning of a new statement, and the speech is complete at His saying ﴿they deny﴾. The Book is the Qur'an. ﴿We have detailed it﴾, knowing how to detail it regarding rulings, admonitions, stories and all its other meanings. It has also been said: ﴿We have detailed it﴾ by clarifying the truth from falsehood. It has also been said: We have sent it down in various sections. Ibn Muhaysin and al-Jahdari read ﴿faḍḍalnāhu﴾ with a dotted ḍād (ض), meaning: "We have preferred it over all the Books, knowing that it is worthy of being preferred over them." In al-Tahrir it is stated that it was preferred over the other revealed Books by thirty qualities which were not in any other. ﴿Detailed﴾ is an attribute of ﴿a Book﴾. The apparent view is that ﴿with knowledge﴾ is a circumstantial clause of the subject of ﴿detailed﴾. It has also been said: the estimate is "comprising knowledge," so it is a circumstantial clause of the object. ﴿Guidance and mercy﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause. It has also been said that it is an object for the sake of which (maf'ūl li-ajlihi). It was also read in the nominative, meaning: "it is guidance and mercy." Zayd ibn ʿAli read ﴿guidance and mercy﴾ in the genitive, as an apposition to "a Book" or as an attribute. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' (may Allah have mercy on them both) explained the genitive reading as an attribute of "a Book."

﴿Do they await anything but its ta'wil?﴾ That is, the final outcome of the matter and its consequence. This was said by Qatada, Mujahid and others. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Its outcome on the Day of Resurrection. al-Suddi said: In this world, like the event of Badr, and also on the Day of Resurrection. al-Zamakhshari said: What it leads to of making clear its truthfulness and the manifestation of its soundness, the threats and promises it contains. The root of ta'wil (interpretation/ultimate meaning) is hamza, waw and lam, from "āla yaʾūlu" (to return/lead to). al-Khattabi said: "I returned the thing to its beginning (awwal)," so the word is derived from "first" (awwal). End of quotation. This is an error, because the two roots differ.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 48–53 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿On the Day its interpretation (ta'wil) comes, those who had forgotten it before will say: "The messengers of our Lord had indeed come with the truth. Do we have any intercessors who might intercede for us, or could we be sent back so that we might do other than what we used to do?"﴾. That is: the outcome of what He announced of promise and threat becomes manifest. This takes place on the Day of Resurrection, when those who abandoned the followers of the Messenger ask, "Do we have any intercessors?", a question about the means of deliverance at a time when there is no deliverance. There is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning: "The messengers of our Lord had indeed come with the truth, but we did not believe them, or we did not follow them," ﴿so do we have any intercessors?﴾. Here "the messengers" means the prophets, who on the Day of Resurrection report that what their messengers brought them was the truth. It has also been said that "the messengers" are the angels of punishment, at the moment of direct witnessing (mu'ayanah) of what they had been warned about.

The majority of reciters read ﴿أوْ نُرَدُّ﴾ (aw nuraddu) with a ḍammah on the dāl, and (fa-na'mala) with a fatḥah on the lām, as a verbal sentence (jumlah fi'liyyah) coordinated with a nominal sentence (jumlah ismiyyah). Both preceded by an interrogative, so the two answers are in the accusative. That is: "Are there intercessors for us so that they intercede for us in deliverance from the punishment, or can we be returned to the world so that we may do righteous deeds?"

Al-Hasan is reported, as transmitted by al-Zamakhshari, to have read (fa-na'mala) with a fatḥah on the dāl and a ḍammah on the lām. Al-Hasan is also reported, as transmitted by Ibn 'Atiyyah and others, to have read both with a ḍammah. (fa-na'mulu) is coordinated with (nuraddu). Ibn Abi Ishaq and Abu Haywah read both with a fatḥah, so (nuradda) is in the accusative, coordinated with (fa-yashfa'ū lanā) as an answer upon an answer. The intercessors would then be in one of two matters: either for deliverance from the punishment or for being returned to the world to resume righteous deeds. The intercession would then extend to either the return or the deliverance, and (fa-na'malu) is coordinated with (fa-nuraddu).

It is possible that (aw nuraddu) is of the type of (la-alzamanna-ka, aw taqḍiyanī ḥaqqī), "I will surely keep you company until you either pay me my due," on the reckoning of one who assigns it the meaning of (ḥattā taqḍiyanī ḥaqqī, "until you pay me my due"), or (kay taqḍiyanī ḥaqqī, "so that you pay me my due"). In that case the obligation is made to end upon the payment of the due, or is made to be caused by it. Then the intercession would be for the return only. As for the reckoning of Sibawayh, "Verily I will surely keep you company unless you pay me," it does not appear that the meaning of "aw" here is the meaning of "illā" (unless), for then the meaning would become: "Do intercessors intercede for us except that we be returned?" and this is an unclear exception.

As to whether their saying "Do we have intercessors?" is made in hope or in despair, there is the same disagreement as in their call, ﴿"Pour down upon us water"﴾ (an afīḍū). Al-Qadi said: this (their saying) indicates two rulings: that they were able to believe and repent, and for this reason they asked for a second return. Those of the Hereafter are not obligated (mukallafūn), contrary to the Mujbirah (determinists) and al-Najjar, for if they were so, they would not have asked for return; rather they would have repented and believed.

﴿They have lost their souls, and what they used to fabricate has strayed far from them﴾. That is: they lost in the trade of their souls, since they bought the base and perishing of the worldly life in exchange for the precious and enduring of the Hereafter. What they had fabricated against God, namely what He had not said nor commanded them, became null for them, and He refuted them in taking gods besides God. (p. 307)

Indeed your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then established Himself over the Throne. ﴿إنَّ رَبَّكُمُ اللَّهُ الَّذِي خَلَقَ السَّماواتِ والأرْضَ في سِتَّةِ أيّامٍ ثُمَّ اسْتَوى عَلى العَرْشِ﴾

When Exalted is He mentioned matters concerning the origin of human creation and the command given to His Prophet, the division of people into believers and disbelievers, and their return and gathering to Paradise or Hellfire, He then mentioned the origin of the world and its bringing into existence, and drew attention to the proofs that indicate His oneness (tawhid), the perfection of His power, knowledge and decree. Then, after that, He moved on to prophethood and messengership, since the Qur'an revolves around establishing four matters: tawhid, power, the Return (ma'ad) and prophethood. The words "your Lord" are a general address to both the believer and the disbeliever.

Bakkar ibn... (narrated) "inna rabbakumu Allah" with the ha' in the accusative as an appositive (ʿatf bayan). The apparent meaning is that He "created the heavens and the earth in six days." On this apparent meaning, the majority of people interpreted it, and they began the creation on Sunday.

In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ took my hand and said: Allah created the clay on Saturday, created the mountains in it on Sunday, created the trees on Monday, created the disliked things on Tuesday, created light on Wednesday, spread the living creatures in it on Thursday, and created Adam after the 'Asr prayer on Friday, the last of creation, in the last hour of the hours of Friday, between after 'Asr and night."

And ʿAdi ibn Zayd al-ʿAbbadi said:
"He decreed His creation in six days, and the last day He fashioned the man."

This is the choice of Muhammad ibn Ishaq. Ibn al-Anbari said: "This is the consensus (ijma') of the people of knowledge."

ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, Kaʿb, al-Dahhak and Mujahid said, and al-Tabari chose it: He began the creation on Sunday, and this is what the People of the Torah say. It was also said: on Monday, and this is what the People of the Gospel say. Ibn ʿAbbas, Kaʿb, Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: the measure of each of those days is a thousand years. There is no difference, with respect to His power, between His creating all of that in a single moment or in successive periods. The explanation of these meanings, as some commentators claimed, is an assertion without proof, so we will not blacken our book by mentioning it, and He, Exalted is He, alone has knowledge of that.

Some commentators went to the view that the sense of His saying "in six days" is "in the measure of six days," so the six days themselves were not the times in which creation occurred. This is like His saying: ﴿ولَهم رِزْقُهم فِيها بُكْرَةً وعَشِيًّا﴾ [Maryam: 62] ("And for them is their provision therein, morning and evening"), where what is meant is the measure of morning and evening in this world, since there is no night or day in Paradise. The one who took this view did so because the day is distinguished from the night only by the rising and setting of the sun, and the sun and moon had not yet been created, so how could days be conceived of as created?

What I say is: whenever it is possible to take a word in its apparent sense, or in a sense close to its apparent sense, it is better than taking it in a sense that the intellect cannot encompass, or in a sense that entirely contradicts the apparent meaning. This can be done by making His saying "in six days" a time-frame (zarf) for the creation of the earth, not a time-frame for the creation of the heavens and the earth together. Then "in six days" is the duration of the creation of the earth with its dust, its mountains, its trees, its disliked things, its light, its living creatures and Adam, peace be upon him. This agrees with the established hadith in the Sahih. The six days remain in their literal sense in terms of their number and in terms of their being days, by considering that the day is distinguished from the night by the rising and setting of the sun.

As for His establishing Himself over the Throne, a group took it in its apparent sense of settling Himself physically upon the Throne. The majority of the early scholars (salaf), namely al-Sufyanan, Malik, al-Awza'i, al-Layth, Ibn al-Mubarak and others, regarding the hadiths of the attributes, held to belief in them and letting them pass as they are, as Allah intended, without specifying a particular meaning. Another group interpreted that in several ways. Sufyan al-Thawri said: "He did an action regarding the Throne and named it istiwa'."

It is reported from Abu al-Fadl ibn al-Nahwi that he said: "al-ʿArsh (the Throne)" is the verbal noun of "ʿarasha, yaʿrishu, ʿarshan," and what is meant by "the Throne" in His saying "then established Himself over the Throne" is this. This view is contradicted by what is established in the Shariʿah, that the Throne is a specific created body. The matter of istiwa' is mentioned in the science of the fundamentals of religion (usul al-din), and al-Qaffal Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi went deeply into establishing what can be established concerning it, and he mentioned that in al-Tahrir, so it should be consulted there.

The word "al-ʿArsh" is shared (mushtarak) among many meanings. So al-ʿArsh is the throne of kingship, as in: ﴿ورَفَعَ أبَوَيْهِ عَلى العَرْشِ﴾ [Yusuf: 100] ("And he raised his parents upon the throne"), and ﴿نَكِّرُوا لَها عَرْشَها﴾ [al-Naml: 41] ("Disguise her throne for her"). Al-ʿArsh is also the roof, and everything that is high and provides shade is an ʿarsh. Al-ʿArsh is also kingship, authority and might. Zuhayr said:
"You two restored ʿAbs, when its throne had been broken, and Dhubyan, when its feet had slipped with their sandals."

Another said:
"If they kill you, I have broken their thrones, through ʿUtaybah ibn al-Harith ibn Shihab."

Al-ʿArsh is also the wooden frame with which a well is lined after its bottom has been lined with stones. Al-ʿArsh is also four small stars below al-ʿAwwa', called ʿajuz al-asad (the rump of the lion), and it is called ʿarsh al-simak. Al-ʿArsh is also what meets the sole of the foot, in which are the toes.

Istawa is also used in the sense of "settled (istaqarra)," in the sense of "rose high (ʿala)," in the sense of "intended (qasada)," in the sense of "equaled (sawa)," and in the sense of "became equal (tasawa)." It was also said: in the sense of "seized power (istawla)," and they recited:
"They both, by their merit together, have seized the throne of kings without falsehood."

Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: "We do not know istawa to mean istawla."

The pronoun in His saying "then established Himself over the Throne" may refer to the creation (khalq) implied by His saying "created," so that the meaning is: "then His creation established itself over the Throne." Likewise in His saying: ﴿الرَّحْمَنُ عَلى العَرْشِ اسْتَوى﴾ [Taha: 5] ("The Most Merciful, over the Throne, established Himself"), it is not necessary to take the pronoun in "istawa" as referring to al-Rahman, since it is possible that al-Rahman is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the pronoun in "istawa" refers to the creation implied by His saying: ﴿تَنْزِيلًا مِمَّنْ خَلَقَ الأرْضَ والسَّماواتِ العُلا﴾ [Taha: 4] ("A revelation from He who created the earth and the high heavens"), meaning: "He is the Most Merciful; His creation established itself over the Throne." Because when He mentioned the creation of the heavens and the earth, He mentioned the creation of what is greater, larger and more spacious than the heavens and the earth. And given the possibilities regarding the Throne, regarding istawa, and regarding the returning pronoun, it is not necessary to take the verse in its apparent sense, along with the rational proofs that they put forward to establish the impossibility of that.

Al-Hasan said: "His command established itself." A man asked Malik ibn Anas about this verse, saying: "How did He establish Himself?" He lowered his head for a long while, and sweat came over him. Then he said: "The istiwa' is known, the how (kayf) is unintelligible, belief in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation (bid'ah). I do not think you are other than a misguided person." Then he ordered that he be taken out.

﴿يُغْشِي اللَّيْلَ النَّهارَ يَطْلُبُهُ حَثِيثًا﴾ "He covers the night over the day, which pursues it swiftly." (Yughshi al-layl al-nahar yatlubuhu hathithan)

Taghshiyah means covering. The meaning is that night removes the light of day, so that the foundation of life in this world is completed by the coming of night and day. Night is for rest, and day is for movement. The context of the speech indicates that day is covered by night (yughshi Allah al-layl al-nahar). The two are objects (mafʿulan), because the doubling (tadʿif) and the hamza are both transitive markers. Al-Akhawan (the two brothers, i.e., Hamzah and al-Kisa'i) read with doubling, and Abu Bakr read it with the ghayn sukun like the rest of the seven, and with fatha on the ya' and sukun on the ghayn, and fatha on the shin and damma on the lam, Humayd ibn Qays. So said Abu ʿAmr al-Dani about him, while Abu al-Fath ʿUthman ibn Jinni said on the authority of Humayd: with fatha on "al-layl" and rafʿ on "al-nahar." Ibn ʿAttiyah said: "Abu al-Fath is more reliable." This statement, that Abu al-Fath is more reliable, is an assertion that is not correct, since the rank of Abu ʿAmr al-Dani in the readings, in knowing them, in controlling their transmissions, and his specialization in that to a degree that no one among the leading reciters comes close to, let alone the grammarians who were not reciters, nor did they transmit the Qur'an from anyone, nor was the Qur'an transmitted from them. This is in addition to his exceptional piety, his precision in transmission, his avoidance of boldness, and his abundant share of Arabic. I have seen his book on Kalla and his book on the idgham of Abu ʿAmr al-Kabir, which show his knowledge of what leading grammarians and reciters hardly ever know. As for his other works, may Allah have mercy on him. What Abu ʿAmr al-Dani transmitted from Humayd is more probable in meaning, because it agrees with the reading of the majority, since "al-layl" in their reading, although in the accusative, is the doer in meaning, since the hamza of transitivity or the doubling made it an object. It cannot be a second object in meaning, because the two accusatives are both reached by the verb, and one of them is the doer in meaning, so the first of them must necessarily be the doer, as this is necessary in "mallaktu Zaydan ʿAmran," since the order of precedence is what makes clear that it is the doer in meaning, just as this is necessary in "darab Musa ʿIsa" (Musa struck ʿIsa).

The clause "yatlubuhu" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the doer in meaning, which is "al-layl," since it is the one spoken of before the transitivity, and its estimate is "hathithan" (urging on). It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial clause from "al-nahar," with the estimate "mahthuthan" (being urged). It is also permissible that it be an adjective (naʿt) of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a swift pursuit," i.e., "a hath," or "muhith." The attribution of the pursuit to night is metaphorical, and it is an expression for its constant succession, so it is as if it is seeking it without catching it; rather, it is right behind it, such that it almost catches it. He put "al-layl" first here, as He put it first in His saying: ﴿يُولِجُ اللَّيْلَ في النَّهارِ﴾ [al-Hajj: 61] ("He causes the night to enter into the day"), and in: ﴿ولا اللَّيْلُ سابِقُ النَّهارِ﴾ [Ya-Sin: 40] ("nor does the night outrun the day"), and in: ﴿وجَعَلَ الظُّلُماتِ والنُّورَ﴾ [al-An'am: 1] ("and made the darknesses and the light").

Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: He described this movement with swiftness and intensity, because the succession of night and day occurs through the motion of the greatest sphere (al-falak al-aʿzam), and that motion is the most swift of motions and the most complete in intensity, to the extent that researchers into the conditions of existents said: when a man is running at full, strong speed, before he lifts his foot and sets it down, the greatest sphere moves three thousand miles. For this reason He said: ﴿يَطْلُبُهُ حَثِيثًا﴾, and a parallel to it is ﴿لا الشَّمْسُ يَنْبَغِي لَها﴾ [Ya-Sin: 40] ("It is not for the sun to overtake the moon") and so on. He likened that course and that motion to swimming in water, and the intent is to draw attention to the speed, the ease, and the perfect continuity. End of quote, and in it there is some abridgment.

﴿والشَّمْسَ والقَمَرَ والنُّجُومَ مُسَخَّراتٍ بِأمْرِهِ﴾ "And the sun, the moon and the stars are subjected by His command." Musakhkharat is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the whole group, meaning: and He created the sun, etc. Ibn ʿAmir read with rafʿ in the four (nouns) as an inchoative and predicate (mubtada' and khabar). Aban ibn Thaʿlab read with rafʿ only on "wa al-nujum musakhkharat," as an inchoative and predicate. The meaning of "bi-amrihi" is by His will and His direction. It is related to "musakhkharat," meaning: He created them running in accordance with His wisdom and His management, and just as He wills to turn them, that is called a command (amr) by way of comparison, as if they were commanded with that. Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: The sun has two kinds of motion. One of them is according to its own essence, and that is completed in a full year, and by means of it the solar year occurs. The second is its motion according to the motion of the greatest sphere, and that is completed in a day with its night. So they say that night and day do not occur by the motion of the sun, but occur by the motion of the outermost heaven, which is called the Throne. For this reason, when He indicated the Throne by His saying: ﴿ثُمَّ اسْتَوى عَلى العَرْشِ﴾, and connected it with His saying: ﴿والشَّمْسَ والقَمَرَ والنُّجُومَ مُسَخَّراتٍ بِأمْرِهِ﴾, as an indication that the greatest sphere, which is the Throne, moves the spheres and the stars against their natural tendency, from east to west, and that He, Exalted is He, placed in the body of the sun a dominating power, by which it became strong enough to overpower all the spheres and stars and move them against the requirement of their natures. These are rationally based investigations, and the wording of the Qur'an hints at them, and knowledge is with Allah. End of quote.

He spoke at length on His saying ﴿subjected by His command﴾, with a great deal drawn from ʿilm al-hayʾa (the science of astronomy and cosmology), a discipline which we have not studied. He said: "Its practitioners say it is a noble science in which one becomes acquainted with wondrous particulars of the creation of God, the Exalted, by which the faith of the believer increases, for knowledge of the particulars and details of things is not like knowledge of them in their totality." It was also said that ﴿by His command﴾ means by the effectiveness of His will, since the purpose is to show the greatness of His power, as in His saying: ﴿Come, willingly or unwillingly﴾ [Fussilat: 11] and His saying: ﴿Our word to a thing is only that We say to it﴾ [al-Nahl: 40]. It was also said that the command (al-amr) is speech.

The apparent meaning is that supplication (du'a) is intimate communication with God through calling upon Him, to seek things and to ward off things. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "worship." "Taḍarru'an wa khufyah" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), meaning: humbly and secretly, or possessing humility and concealment in your supplication.

In the authentic hadith: "Indeed you do not call upon one who is deaf or absent. Indeed you call upon One who is All-Hearing, Near." The Companions, when the Messenger informed them of this, had been raising their voices in remembrance. God commanded supplication coupled with humility, submission, and concealment, for that is more likely to be answered and further from ostentation (riyā'). Supplication in secret is better than supplication aloud. For this reason God praised Zakariyya, peace be upon him, saying: ﴿When he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾ [Maryam: 3]. In another hadith: "The best remembrance is the hidden one." The principles of the Sharia establish that secrecy in acts of righteousness that are not obligatory is greater in reward than doing them openly.

Al-Ḥasan said: "We met people for whom no deed on earth was such that they could make it secret and it would become public, ever. Muslims would strive in supplication and no voice of theirs would be heard, except a whisper between them and their Lord." End of quote.

If al-Ḥasan had lived to this strange age, in which there appeared people who call themselves "shaykhs," who wear garments of fame among the common folk for piety, abandon earning a livelihood, and establish for themselves invocations not found in the Sharia, which they recite aloud in mosques. They gather servants for themselves who bring people to them for their service and the plundering of their wealth. They spread reports of miracles (karāmāt) about them and claim dreams for them, which they record in books. They urge abandoning knowledge and occupation with the Sunna. They claim arrival at God through matters they establish from seclusions and invocations that no revealed Book nor sent Prophet brought. They exalt themselves over people by sitting alone on prayer rugs, extending their hands for kissing, speaking little, lowering their heads, and appointing an attendant who says: "The Shaykh is occupied in seclusion," "The Shaykh has drawn," "The Shaykh has said," "The Shaykh saw," "The Shaykh looked at you," "The Shaykh was mentioning you last night," and similar expressions by which they deceive the common folk and captivate the minds of the ignorant. This is if the Shaykh and his attendant are spared from the belief that has now prevailed among the Sufis of this age, namely the doctrine of incarnation (ḥulūl) or the doctrine of unity (waḥda). In that case, he is wholly detached from the Sharia of Islam. It is astonishing that stipends are arranged for such people, that lodges are built for them, that endowments are established upon them, and that people serve them while they are empty of all other virtues. But people are more inclined toward their likes than toward others.

We have lengthened this discussion, hoping that a Muslim will read it and benefit from it.

Abu Bakr read "khīfah" with the kasra replacing the ḍamma on the kha', and both are dialects (lughatān). This is evident from the words of Abu 'Ali, and it cannot be achieved except by claiming a transposition (qalb), which contradicts the original form. Ibn Sida reported in al-Muḥkam that a group read "wa khīfah" from fear (khawf), meaning: call upon Him with humility and fear. Abu Hatim said: al-A'mash read it, so they claim.

﴿Indeed He does not love the transgressors.﴾ Ibn Abi 'Abla read "Inna Allāh," replacing the pronoun with the explicit noun. This expression is general and includes first supplication that departs from these two qualities, namely lacking humility and lacking concealment. That is, one calls upon Him while afflicted with arrogance and pride, or it is his habit in gatherings and schools so that it becomes his craft and custom, and humility and submissiveness do not reach him. Or one calls upon Him with extreme loudness and shouting, like the supplication of people at gatherings in shrines and visitation sites. The scholars said: transgression in supplication takes several forms, among them: excessive loudness and shouting; asking to attain the rank of a prophet; asking for the impossible and similar excess; and asking for an act of disobedience. Ibn Jurayj and al-Kalbi said: transgression is raising the voice in supplication. It is also reported from him that shouting in supplication is disliked and an innovation (bid'ah). It was said: it is excessive prolixity in supplication. Al-Qurtubi said, having mentioned several forms of transgression in supplication: among them is calling upon God with what is neither in the Noble Book nor in the Sunna, choosing rhymed phrases and rhymed words, which he found in notebooks belonging to these people, meaning the shaykhs, which are not to be relied upon, and making them his motto, abandoning what the Messenger of God supplicated with. All of this prevents the answering of supplication.

Ibn Jubayr said: transgression in supplication is that one calls down disgrace, polytheism, and curse upon believers.

In the Sunan of Ibn Majah: "'Abdullah ibn Mughaffal heard his son say: O God, I ask You for the white palace on the right of Paradise when I enter it. He said: O my son, ask God for Paradise and seek refuge with Him from the Fire, for I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: There will be a people who will transgress in supplication." Ibn 'Atiyyah and al-Zamakhshari added in this hadith: "It is sufficient for a person to say: O God, I ask You for Paradise and what draws near to it of speech and action, and I seek refuge with You from the Fire and what draws near to it of speech and action." Then he recited: ﴿Indeed He does not love the transgressors.﴾

[p-312] This is a prohibition against causing corruption on the earth and bringing its essence into existence. It applies to all its kinds: corrupting souls, lineages, wealth, minds and religions. The meaning of "after its reformation" is after Allah has set its creation in the form suited to the benefits of creatures and the welfare of the responsible (mukallafun). What has been related from the exegetes (mufassirun) specifying a particular type of corruption and reformation should be understood as illustration (tamthil), since claiming that any of this is restricted to one thing has no evidence. Examples include: wrongdoing after justice, disbelief after faith, disobedience after obedience, or with disobedience, so that Allah withholds rain and destroys the crops after they were reformed by rain and abundance; or He kills the believer after he has remained alive; or through denying the messengers after the revelation; or through polluting flowing water and cutting trees and fruit out of harm; or through debasing the dinars and dirhams; or through the trade of rulers; or through associating partners with Allah after the sending of the messengers, the establishment of the laws and the clarification of the religion.

﴿And call upon Him in fear and in hope﴾. Since supplication (du'a') from Allah has a particular standing, He repeated it. First He said: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret﴾ [al-A'raf: 55]. These two states are outward attributes, because humility, submissiveness and lowering the voice are not inner acts of the heart. That is, be anxious and apprehensive, and hopeful and aspiring. He began with the acts of the limbs, then secondly with the acts of the hearts. ﴿Khawfan wa tama'an﴾ is in the accusative as two verbal nouns (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), or in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu). Joining one to the other requires that fear and hope be equal, so that they are for a person like the two wings of a bird, carrying him on a straight path. If one of them stands alone, the person perishes. Many scholars have said that fear should predominate over hope during the long span of life, but when death comes hope should predominate. Many other scholars held that fear should be the stronger. From this is the wish of al-Hasan al-Basri that he be the last man to enter Paradise. Salim, the freedman of Abu Hudhayfa, wished to be among the people of al-A'raf, because his view was that they are sinners. Salim was of such rank in religion and virtue that Umar ibn al-Khattab said something whose meaning is: If Salim, the freedman of Abu Hudhayfa, were alive, I would have appointed him to the caliphate. Far off is the one who held that the meaning is fear of rejection and hope of acceptance.

﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: like His saying: ﴿And indeed I am the Forgiving to whoever repents, believes and does righteousness﴾ [Ta-Ha: 82], end of quote. He means that mercy is specific to the doer of good, who is one who repents, believes and does righteousness. All of this is the Qur'an being interpreted according to his Mu'tazili doctrine. Mercy (rahmah) is feminine, so the analogy is that it should be predicated with feminine agreement, saying qariba. It was said that it is masculine because rahmah here means ruhm (womb) and tarahhum (compassion). It was said that it is masculine because rahmah means forgiveness and pardon, as said by al-Nadr ibn Shumayl and preferred by al-Zajjaj. It was said that it means rain, as said by al-Akhfash, or reward, as said by Ibn Jubayr. In these views, rahmah is a substitute for a masculine noun. It was said that the masculine form is by way of attribution (nasab), meaning "possessing nearness." It was said that qarib is an adjective for an omitted masculine noun, meaning "a near thing." It was said that qarib is modelled on fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, like khadib (dyed) and jarih (wounded), just as fa'il was made similar to it in some of its rulings, so that its plural is fu'ala', as in asir/usara' and qatil/qutala', just as they said rahim/ruhama' and 'alim/'ulama'. It was said that it is a verbal noun (masdar) of the pattern fa'il, like daghith (the cry of the hare) and naqiq. When it is a verbal noun, it is valid to predicate it of masculine, feminine, singular, dual and plural with the verbal noun form. It was said that the feminine of rahmah is not real, as said by al-Jawhari. This is not good except when the verb precedes it. But when it follows, only the feminine is permitted: one says al-shamsu tali'atun (the sun is rising), and tali' is not permitted except in poetic necessity. This differs with the preceding case, where it is permitted to say a-tali'atun al-shamsu and a-tali'un al-shamsu, just as it is permitted to say tala'at al-shamsu and tala'a al-shamsu, and tala'a is not permitted except in poetry. It was said that fa'il here means maf'ul, i.e., muqarrabatun (brought near), and it becomes like kaffun khadib (a dyed hand) and 'aynun kahil (a kohl-darkened eye). This is said by al-Kirmani, and it is not good, because what occurs of that is only from the unaugmented triliteral, whereas this means muqarraba, which is from the augmented triliteral, and in any case it is not a regular pattern. Al-Farra' said: when it is used of kinship and relationship, it takes a feminine ta' marbuta with the feminine, and it must: one says hadhihi qarибatu fulan (this is so-and-so's close relative). If it is used of nearness in distance or time, it may come with a ta' with the feminine, or without a ta', so one says: dāruka minni qarib (your house is near me), and fulanatun minna qarib (so-and-so is near to us), and from this is this verse, and the saying of the poet:

"On an evening when Afra' is not near to you, so that she draws close, nor is Afra' far from you."

So in this line he combined both forms. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is the statement of al-Farra' in his book, and it has come in the books of some exegetes altered, end of quote. Al-Zajjaj refuted him and said: this is an error by al-Farra', because the rule for masculine and feminine is that they follow their verbs. He who argued for him said: this is the speech of the Arabs. Allah says: ﴿And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ [al-Ahzab: 63]. And the poet said:

"Woe to him if he should be sought, and neither Umm Hashim nor Basbasa, the daughter of Yashkur, is near."

Abu 'Ubayda said: qarib in the verse is not an adjective of rahmah, but an adverb (zarf) of it and a place, so it comes this way for feminine, dual and plural. Likewise bu'd (far). If they make it an adjective in the sense of muqtarib (near), they say qariba, qaribatan and qaribat. Ali ibn Sulayman said: this is an error. If it were as he said, qarib would be in the accusative, as you say inna Zaydan qariban minka (Zayd is indeed near you), end of quote. It is not an error, because it would have been used with latitude in the adverb, using it not as an adverb, just as you say Hind khalfaka (Hind is behind you) and Fatimah amamaka (Fatimah is in front of you) with the nominative, when you use latitude with khalf and amam. The accusative is required only when both remain in the adverbial sense and are not used with latitude. They also permitted qariban minka Zayd (near you is Zayd), with qarib as the subject of inna and Zayd as the predicate, so qarib is used with latitude and is used as a noun, not as an accusative adverb. The apparent view is that the nearness of mercy to the doer of good is not restricted by time; rather it is near to him absolutely. Al-Tabari mentioned that at the moment the spirits separate from the bodies, mercy reaches them.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 57 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And it is He who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy, until, when they have carried heavy clouds, We drive them to a dead land, and We send down water therewith and bring forth with it fruits of every kind. Thus do We bring forth the dead; perhaps you will remember.﴾ ﴿As for the good land, its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord, and that which is bad yields nothing but scanty growth. Thus do We vary the signs for a people who are grateful.﴾ [al-A'raf: 58] ﴿Indeed, We sent Noah to his people, and he said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day."﴾ [al-A'raf: 59] ﴿The eminent ones of his people said: "Indeed, we see you in manifest error."﴾ [al-A'raf: 60] ﴿He said: "O my people, there is no error in me, but I am a Messenger from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ [al-A'raf: 61] ﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord and advise you, and I know from Allah what you do not know."﴾ [al-A'raf: 62] ﴿Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, to warn you and that you may fear Allah and perhaps receive mercy?﴾ [al-A'raf: 63] ﴿But they denied him, so We saved him and those with him in the ark, and We drowned those who denied Our signs. Indeed, they were a blind people.﴾ [al-A'raf: 64] ﴿And to 'Ad, their brother Hud. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. Will you not then fear Him?"﴾ [al-A'raf: 65] ﴿The eminent ones among his people who disbelieved said: "Indeed, we see you in foolishness, and indeed, we think you are among the liars."﴾ [al-A'raf: 66] ﴿He said: "O my people, there is no foolishness in me, but I am a Messenger from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ [al-A'raf: 67] ﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I am a sincere, trustworthy adviser to you.﴾ [al-A'raf: 68] ﴿Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, to warn you? And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah and increased you in stature. So remember the bounties of Allah that perhaps you may prosper.﴾ [al-A'raf: 69] ﴿They said: "Have you come to us that we should worship Allah alone and abandon what our fathers used to worship? So bring us what you threaten us with, if you are of the truthful."﴾ [al-A'raf: 70] ﴿He said: "Indeed, there has befallen you from your Lord abomination and wrath. Do you dispute with me over names you have named, you and your fathers, for which Allah has sent down no authority? So wait; indeed, I am with you among those who wait."﴾ [al-A'raf: 71] ﴿So We saved him and those with him by mercy from Us, and We cut off the root of those who denied Our signs and were not believers.﴾ [al-A'raf: 72] ﴿And to Thamud, their brother Salih. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. There has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord. This is the she-camel of Allah as a sign for you, so leave her to eat on Allah's earth, and do not touch her with harm, lest a painful punishment seize you.﴾ [al-A'raf: 73] ﴿And remember when He made you successors after 'Ad and settled you in the land, taking for yourselves palaces from its plains and hewing out the mountains as houses. So remember the bounties of Allah, and do not commit corruption on the earth, spreading mischief.﴾ [al-A'raf: 74] ﴿The eminent ones who were arrogant among his people said to those who were oppressed, to those among them who believed: "Do you know that Salih is one sent from his Lord?" They said: "Indeed, we believe in what he has been sent with."﴾ [al-A'raf: 75] ﴿Those who were arrogant said: "Indeed, we disbelieve in what you believe."﴾ [al-A'raf: 76] ﴿So they hamstrung the she-camel, defied the command of their Lord, and said: "O Salih, bring us what you threaten us with, if you are of the messengers."﴾ [al-A'raf: 77] ﴿So the earthquake seized them, and they became prostrate in their homes.﴾ [al-A'raf: 78] ﴿He turned away from them and said: "O my people, I certainly conveyed to you the message of my Lord and advised you, but you do not love sincere advisers."﴾ [al-A'raf: 79] ﴿And Lot, when he said to his people: "Do you commit an immorality no one in the worlds has committed before you?﴾ [al-A'raf: 80] ﴿Indeed, you approach men with desire instead of women. Rather, you are a people who exceed the limits."﴾ [al-A'raf: 81] ﴿The answer of his people was only that they said: "Expel them from your town. Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure."﴾ [al-A'raf: 82] ﴿So We saved him and his family, except for his wife; she was among those who remained behind.﴾ [al-A'raf: 83] ﴿And We rained upon them a rain. So observe how was the end of the criminals.﴾ [al-A'raf: 84] ﴿And to Midian, their brother Shu'ayb. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. There has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord. So give full measure and weight, do not deprive people of their things, and do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation. That is better for you, if you are believers."﴾ [al-A'raf: 85]

Aqalla al-shay' (he lifted and carried the thing): he carried it and raised it without hardship. From this comes iqlal al-batn 'an al-fakhdh (the lifting of the belly away from the thigh) in bowing and prostration, and from it al-qullah (a jar), because the camel carries it without hardship. Its origin is from al-qullah, so the one who lifts (al-muqill) sees what he raises as little, and he "found it light" (istaqalla bihi) and "lifted it" (aqallahu). Al-sawq (driving) is carrying a thing with force. Al-nakid is little hardship/difficulty. The poet said: (p. 315)

"Do not fulfil the promise if you promise, and if you give, you give a worthless and grudging gift."

Nakida al-rajul: he was asked insistently and was embarrassed. The poet said:

"Give what you have given in good grace; there is no good in the one who is refused and the one who refuses."

Al-ala' (bounties): its singular is ilan, like mi'an. Al-Zajjaj recited:

"White, he does not fear emaciation, nor does he sever kinship, nor does he betray the bond of ilan."

Ila can mean "time," or alan like qafan, or aliy like hisy, or ilw like jirw. Waqa'a (to fall, to befall): the Nadr ibn Shumayl said: it means "struck and issued," like the falling of the mallet. Others said: it means "descended." Al-waqi'ah is a calamity among hardships, and al-waqa'i' are wars. Al-miqa'ah is the hammer. One of our men of letters said:

"The man of excellence is like gold, sometimes under the hammer, and sometimes on the crown of a king."

Thamud is the name of a tribe, named after their father. Its mention will come in the tafsir, Allah willing. Al-naqah is the female of camels; its alif is changed from waw. Its plural in the paucity form is anwuq and anyiq, and there is qalb and ibdal in it. In the plurality form it is niyaq and nuq. Istanwaqa al-jamal means the male camel came to resemble the female camel. Al-sahl is the land that is soft and low, and it is the opposite of the hazn (rough, elevated land). Al-qasr is the dwelling that is confined to a specific plot of land, unlike the houses of tents (buyut al-'amud). It is named so because people cannot climb it, or because most people cannot build it. Al-nahf: carving and hewing in a hard thing, like stone or wood. The poet said:

"As for the day, it is in fetters and chains, and the night is in a belly hewn from teak."

'Aqartu al-naqah: I killed it, so it is ma'qurah and 'aqir. From this is "he hamstrung his horse" (man 'aqara jawadah). Ibn Qutaybah said this. Al-Azhari said: among the Arabs, al-'aqr is cutting the hamstring of the camel. When it was the cause of slaughter, the word al-'aqr was applied to slaughter, using the name of the cause for the effect, even if there was no cutting of the hamstring. Imru' al-Qays said:

"On the day I slaughtered my mount for the maidens, how strange was its saddle that was carried."

Others said: al-'aqr means wounding. He said:

"She said, when the saddle-bag tilted with us together: 'You have wounded my camel, O Imru' al-Qays, so dismount!'"

'Ata ya'tu 'utuwwan: he was arrogant. Al-rajfah is the overwhelming calamity by which a person trembles, that is, he is shaken, agitated and quakes. From it comes "his shoulders tremble" (tarjufu bawadiruh). The root of rajf is agitation: "the earth trembled" (rajafat al-ard), "the sea is rajjaf because of its agitation," "the people spread bad news by spreading the wrong thing and became agitated" (arjafa al-nas bi al-shar), and from it al-arajif (rumours). "The mountain shook them" (rajafa bihimu al-jabal). The poet said:

"When I saw that the time of Hajj had come, and the camels of the people were still trembling in the encampment."

Al-judum: sticking to the ground on the chest with the shins contracted, as the hare and the bird crouch. Ghabara: remained. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"So I remained after them in a barren life, and I think I will be a follower who is left behind."

This is the well-known meaning in the language, and from it comes "the menstruation remained" (ghabara al-hayd). Abu Bakr al-Hudhali said:

"And free from every stain of menstruation, the corruption of a nursing woman, and the sickness of the mughil."

Ghubr al-laban in the udder is its remainder. The people of language also recorded ghabara with the meaning of "passed." Al-A'sha said:

"He bit, due to what the one who consoles him has lost of his mother, in the bygone time."

It also means "went away," as in "he went away from us for a time" (ghabara 'anna zamanan), i.e., went away. Al-Zajjaj said this. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Umar remained (ghabara) a long age until he became old." Al-matar (rain) is well known. Abu 'Ubayd said: matar is used for mercy, and amtara is used for punishment. This conflicts with the words: ﴿This is a cloud bringing us rain﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 24], for they only meant mercy. Both are transitive: it is said "the sky rained upon them" (matarathumu al-sama') and "amtarathum." Shu'ayb: the name of a prophet, and his lineage will come in the tafsir, Allah willing.

﴿And it is He who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy﴾. When the Exalted mentioned the proofs of His perfect divinity, power and knowledge from the upper world, He followed them with proofs from the lower world. These are confined to the effects of the upper world, among them the wind, the clouds and the rain, and in the mineral, plant and animal kingdoms. The conditions of plants result from the descent of rain, and that is what is mentioned in the verse. Along with that, it implies evidence for the truth of the gathering, resurrection, raising and the Last Day. These two verses combined the principles of origin and return. The predicate was made a relative clause in "Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who..." and in "And He is the One who..." This indicates that this is known to the hearer, established, with the attribution already fixed and known to him. The construction did not come as "Indeed, your Lord created" nor "He sends the winds."

He (Ibn Kathir) recited "al-riyaha nushuran" in two plurals. With a dammah on the shin, it is the plural of nashir, according to the pattern of nasab (relation), i.e., "possessing spreading out after folding," like labin and tamir. They said nazil and nuzul, and sharif and shurf. This is a rare plural of fa'il. Or it is nushur from life, or it is the plural of nashur, like sabur and subur. This is a regular plural, not the plural of nushur in the sense of mansur, contrary to those who permitted that, because fu'ul, like rukub in the sense of marcub, is not regular. Even though it is not regular, it is not made into the pattern fi'l. Al-Hasan, al-Sulami, Abu Raja' (with differing report from them), al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, Abu Yahya, and Abu Nawfal al-A'rabiyyan, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr recited it so. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Abd Allah, Zirr, Ibn Wathhab, al-Nakha'i, Talha ibn Musarrif, al-A'mash, Masruq and Ibn 'Amir recited it as a plural too, but they pronounced the shin with sukun to lighten the dammah, like rusl. Masruq, as reported by Abu al-Fath, recited nashran with a fatha on the nun and shin; it is an ism jam' (collective noun), like ghayab and nashi' in ghaibah and nashi'ah. Ibn Kathir recited al-rih in the singular, nushuran, with nun and its dammah and the dammah of the shin. Nushuran may be a plural in the sense of a hal (state) from the singular, because it is intended as a genus, like the saying: "The Arabs are the white ones." It may also be a singular, like naqah surh. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited nashran with a fatha on the nun and sukun on the shin as a verbal noun (masdar), like nashr, contrary to tawa, or like nashara meaning "lived," from the saying "Allah revived the dead, and they lived" (anshara Allah al-mawta fa-nashharu), i.e., they came to life. The poet said:

"Until people say, from what they have seen: 'How strange for the dead one who has come back to life!'"

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Sulami recited "al-riyah" in the plural, and Ibn Abi 'Abla recited "bushuran" with dammah on the ba' and shin. It was reported from 'Asim, and it is the plural of bashirah, like nadhirah and nudhur. 'Asim recited the same, except that he made the shin sukun to lighten the dammah. Al-Sulami also recited "bashran" with fatha on the ba' and sukun on the shin, which is the verbal noun of the regular verb bashara, reported from 'Asim. Ibn al-Sumayfa' and Ibn Qutayb recited "bushra" with a long alif, like rujca, and it is a verbal noun. These are eight recitations: four in the nun and four in the ba'. Whoever recites with the ba' as a plural or as a verbal noun with the alif of feminine, it is in the place of hal from the object. Or if it is a verbal noun without the alif of feminine, that is possible, and it is possible that it is a hal from the subject. Whoever recites with the nun as a plural or as a collective noun, it is hal from the object. Or if it is a verbal noun, it is possible that it is a hal from the subject, and it is possible that it is a hal from the object, or a verbal noun for "yursil" (sends) by meaning, because its sending is its release, and that is the meaning of spreading. It is as if it were said: "by spreading the winds, spreading." The describing of the wind with spreading has one of two meanings, unlike folding and life. Abu 'Ubaydah said about spreading: they are scattered in directions. The poet said, describing the wind with reviving and dying:

"The south wind blew for him and revived for him the mirage; its breeze gives life to the waters."

Al-Rayda and al-Murid: it is the wind. Another said:

"Indeed I hope the wind will die, so I may sit today and rest."

The meaning of ﴿before His mercy﴾ is His favour, which is the rain. It is among the greatest and most beneficial of blessings in its effects. Specifying it as the forerunner of mercy by saying "before my hands" (*bayna yadayya*) is a metaphor (*majaz al-isti'arah*, figurative usage), since the literal meaning of "before a person's hands" is what lies in front of him in terms of his state.

Al-Kirmani said: "He said here *yursilu* (He sends), because before it is ﴿and call upon Him in fear and in hope﴾ [al-A'raf: 56], and both of these are in the future tense, so the future tense suits it. In al-Furqan and Fatir, He said *arsala* (He sent), because before it is ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord extends the shade?﴾ [al-Furqan: 45], and after it is ﴿And it is He who lets loose the two seas﴾ [al-Furqan: 53]. Likewise in al-Rum: ﴿And of His signs is that He sends﴾ [al-Rum: 46], to agree with what precedes it in the future tense. In Fatir, before it is ﴿Praise be to Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, who made the angels messengers having wings﴾ [Fatir: 1], and that is in the past tense, so the past tense suits it." End of the summary.

﴿Until, when they bear heavy clouds, We drive them to a dead land﴾. This is the end point (*ghayah*) of the sending of the winds. The meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, sends the winds as bearers of good news, or as good news, to drive the clouds at the time they carry them to a dead land. *Sahab* (cloud) is a collective noun (*ism jins*), between which and its singular form there is the feminine marker *ta'*, so it is treated as masculine, as in His saying: ﴿and the subjugated cloud﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164], and as in His saying: ﴿He drives the clouds gently, then joins them together﴾ [al-Nur: 43]. It is also treated as feminine, described with adjectives, and referred to with plural pronouns, as in His saying: ﴿and He produces the heavy clouds﴾ [al-Ra'd: 12], and His saying: ﴿and the palm trees, tall and towering﴾ [Qaf: 10]. He made it heavy with the water within it. He attributed the driving to Himself, exalted is He, using the plural of majesty (*nun al-'azamah*), out of regard for the great favour contained in it. The pronoun in ﴿We drive it﴾ is in the masculine out of regard for the word, as we have said, since it is treated as masculine.

Al-Suddi said: "Allah, exalted is He, sends the winds, and they come to the clouds from between the two horizons (*al-khafiqayn*), the edge of the sky and the earth where they meet, and from there they bring it out. Then it spreads out, and He spreads it in the sky. The gates of the sky are opened, the water flows over the clouds, and then the cloud rains after that." He said: "This detail has not been reported from the Prophet ﷺ." End of quotation.

The position of the People of the Truth (*ahl al-haqq*) is that Allah, exalted is He, is the One who subjects the winds and turns them wherever He wills by His will, and His decree has no partner in that. The philosophers have a way of explaining the occurrence of winds, which Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi mentioned and refuted in four respects, which can be found in his discourse. The astrologers (*al-munajjimun*) also have a discourse on this, which he refuted. At its end he said: "Thus it is established by this proof that the mover of the winds is Allah, exalted is He, and by rational proof the soundness of His saying is confirmed: ﴿And He is the One who sends the winds﴾."

From Ibn 'Imran: the winds are eight, four of which are punishment: *al-qasif* (the shattering), *al-'asif* (the violent), *al-sarsar* (the piercing cold), and *al-'aqim* (the barren). And four of which are mercy: *al-nashirat* (the spreading), *al-mubashshirat* (the bearers of good news), *al-mursalat* (the sent), and *al-dhariyat* (the scatterers).

The *lam* in ﴿li-baladin﴾ (to a dead land), in my view, is the *lam* of communication (*lam al-tabligh*), as in your saying: "I said to you." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It means *li-ajl baladin* (for the sake of a land)," making the *lam* a *lam* of cause (*lam al-'illah*). But no difference appears between your saying "I drove wealth to you" (*suqtu laka malan*) and "I drove wealth for your sake" (*suqtu li-ajlika malan*). The first means "I delivered it to you and made it reach you," while the second does not necessarily imply that it reached him. Rather, the one to whom the water reached may be other than the one for whose sake the driving was done. Do you not see the soundness of a speaker saying: "For Zayd's sake I drove your property to you"?

Describing the land as dead is a fine metaphor for its aridity and lack of vegetation, as if, in terms of the absence of benefit from it, it were like a body without a soul. Since this is the place where Allah's mercy is near and His kindness is manifest, He mentioned the most specific kind of land, which is *al-balad* (the town), where people gather and settle. In Surah Ya-Sin, since the aim was to show the great signs that indicate resurrection, the construction came with the general term, which is His saying: ﴿And a sign for them is the dead earth﴾ [Ya-Sin: 33], and after it: ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip from it the day﴾ [Ya-Sin: 37], and ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring﴾ [Ya-Sin: 41]. ʿĀṣim, Abu 'Amr, and al-A'mash pronounced the *ya'* of *al-mayyit* with sukun (*sakkana ya' al-mayyit*).

﴿Then We sent down water with it﴾. The apparent reading is that the *ba'* is locative (*zarfiyyah*, meaning "in"), and the pronoun refers to "a dead land," meaning: "Then We sent down water in it." This is the nearest previous mention, and it is appropriate for the pronoun to refer to it, so it is not made to refer to a more distant mention. It was also said: the *ba'* is causal (*sababiyyah*), and the pronoun refers to the cloud. It was also said: it refers to the verbal noun (*masdar*) understood from "We drove it," so the meaning is: "by the cloud," or "by the driving." The third view is weak, because it refers to something not mentioned while there is a mentioned antecedent that is fit to be referred to. It was also said: it refers to the cloud, and the *ba'* means *min* (from), meaning: "Then We sent down water from it," as in His saying: ﴿a spring from which the servants of Allah drink﴾ [al-Insan: 6], meaning "from it." This is not good, because it is a substitution of particles (*tadmin min al-huruf*).

﴿Then We brought forth with it every kind of fruit﴾. The disagreement concerning "with it" is like the disagreement mentioned earlier concerning "with it." It was also said: the first refers to the cloud and the second refers to the land, shifting from one pronoun to another without a separating element, as in His saying: ﴿Satan made their deeds fair to them and gave them false hope﴾ [Muhammad: 25], where the subject of "gave them false hope" is Allah, exalted is He.

﴿Thus We bring forth the dead, that perhaps you may remember﴾. That is: like this bringing forth, We bring forth the dead from their graves alive until the gathering. Perhaps you may remember by the bringing forth of fruits and their creation your own coming out for resurrection, since the acts of bringing forth are alike. So this visible bringing forth is the parallel of the promised bringing forth.

Al-Bayhaqi and others narrated from Razin al-'Uqayli, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, how will Allah restore the creation, and what is the sign of that in His creation?' He said: 'Did you not pass by the valley of your people barren, and then you passed by it green?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'That is the sign of Allah in His creation.'" End of quotation.

Is the comparison in the general act of bringing forth, and is the indication of the power to bring forth fruits a proof of the power to bring forth the dead, or is it in the manner of bringing forth, namely that rain descends upon them and they come to life just as rain descends upon a dead land and its plants come to life? Both are possibilities. It has been narrated from Abu Hurayrah that rain will fall upon them from water beneath the Throne called the water of life, for forty years, and they will grow as crops grow. When their bodies are complete, He will breathe the spirit into them. Then He will cast upon them a sleep, and they will sleep. When the second Trumpet is blown, they will rise, finding the taste of sleep, and they will say: "Woe to us! Who has raised us from our resting place?" Then the caller will call out to them: "This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke the truth."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 58:

﴿And the good land – its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord, and that which is bad comes forth only meagerly.﴾ *Al-ṭayyib* (the good) is the land that is excellent in its soil and noble in its earth. ﴿And that which is bad﴾ is the salty place (*al-sabakh*) that produces nothing of benefit; it is the inferior part of the land. When He said, ﴿So We brought forth thereby fruits of every kind﴾ [Al-A'raf: 57], He completed this meaning by describing how vegetation emerges from the noble land and from the salty land. This is God's customary way of making lands grow. In the sentence there is an elided circumstantial phrase (*ḥāl maḥdhūfah*, an omitted adverbial qualifier), meaning: its vegetation comes forth complete and good. It was omitted for the sake of conveying the meaning, because of the indication of ﴿And the good land﴾ upon it, and because it is contrasted with His saying ﴿except meagerly﴾, and because of the indication of ﴿by the permission of its Lord﴾. For what God permits to come forth comes forth only in the best condition. The phrase ﴿by the permission of its Lord﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial phrase. He specified the emergence of the vegetation of the good land with ﴿by the permission of its Lord﴾ as a way of praising and honoring it, and attributing it to Him, exalted is He, with the noble and good attribution, even though both kinds of vegetation come forth by His permission. The meaning of ﴿by the permission of its Lord﴾ is "by His facilitation." In the second sentence, the described noun (*al-mawṣūf*) is also elided, and the estimated wording is: "and the land that is bad," because of the indication of ﴿And the good land﴾ upon it. Each of the two sentences contains an elision. He varied between the two relative pronouns for eloquence and variety: in the first He said *al-ṭayyib* (the good), and in the second He said *alladhī khabutha* (that which is bad). The presentation of the predicate here is a verb, unlike the first, in order to balance the wording; this makes two words: "the two words" in His saying ﴿And the good land﴾. *Al-ṭayyib* (good) and *al-khabīth* (bad) are often opposites in the Qur'an: ﴿Say: not equal are the bad and the good﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 100]; ﴿He makes lawful for them the good things and forbids them the bad﴾ [Al-A'raf: 157]; ﴿Spend of the good things you have earned and of what We have brought forth for you from the earth, and do not aim at the bad [to spend from]﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 267], and others besides these. The subject in ﴿does not come forth﴾ refers back to *alladhī khabutha* (that which is bad). We have already said that it is an attribute of an elided described noun, and the land itself does not come forth. So it is by elision of a genitive-construct element (*ḥadhf muḍāf*): either from the first, meaning "and the vegetation of that which is bad," or from the second, meaning "its vegetation does not come forth." When the element was elided, the pronoun that had been in the genitive, because it is now the subject, became concealed (*istakanna*). It was said: these two sentences were intended as an illustration (*tamthīl*). Ibn Abbas and Qatadah said: it is an example for the soul of the believer, which returns to its body easily and good, just as it departed when it died, and for the soul of the disbeliever, which returns only with difficulty, just as it departed when it died. End of quotation. This would then refer, in meaning, back to His saying ﴿Thus do We bring forth the dead﴾ [Al-A'raf: 57], meaning: according to these two attributes.

Al-Suddi said: it is an illustration for hearts. When the Qur'an was sent down, it was like the descent of rain on the earth. The heart of the believer is like the good earth, which accepts the water and benefits from what comes forth. The heart of the disbeliever is like the salty land, which does not benefit from the water it receives. Al-Nahhas said: it is an illustration of the quick-understanding and the dull. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is a parable for those among the responsible people in whom admonition and warning take effect, and for those in whom nothing of that has any effect. From Mujahid: the descendants of Adam are bad and good. This illustration came in the wake of mentioning the rain, its sending down upon the dead land, and the bringing forth of fruits by it, by way of digression (*istiṭrād*). End of quotation. What we advanced earlier is more apparent: that the intent is to inform about God's act of making vegetation come forth in the good land and in the bad land, without an intention to illustrate with anything of what they mentioned. Ibn Abi Ablah, Abu Haywah and Isa ibn Umar read ﴿its vegetation comes forth﴾ in the passive voice (*mabniyyan lil-maf'ūl*). Ibn al-Qa'qa' read *nakadan* with a fatha on the kaf. Al-Zajjaj said: this is the reading of the people of Medina. Ibn Musarrif read it with a sukun on it. Both are verbal nouns (*maṣdarān*), meaning "possessing meagerness." That the vegetation of that which is bad is restricted in its emergence to the state of meagerness is an intensive exaggeration (*mubālaghah shadīdah*) in its being unable to be otherwise and in the impossibility of its existence except in this way, ﴿except meagerly﴾. It is an indication of one in whom the attribute of badness has become firmly established, far from any inclination toward good.

﴿Thus do We vary the signs for a people who give thanks.﴾ That is: like this variation, repetition and diversification, We diversify the signs and repeat them. They are the proofs indicating God's oneness, His overwhelming and complete power, and His acting by choice. Since the sending of the winds as bearers of good tidings and scattering them, mentioned earlier, was a cause of the existence of vegetation, which is the cause of the existence of life and its continuance, this was the greatest of God's blessings upon creation. So He said ﴿for a people who give thanks.﴾ That is: this is a blessing which hardly anything can equal. He specified the grateful because they are the ones who benefit from these blessings as they should, and they are the ones who benefit from the signs and their variation, for whoever does not reflect upon blessings does not give thanks and does not benefit from the signs. It was read *yuṣarrifu* with the ya' (third-person), in consideration of the third-person form (*al-ghaybah*) in His saying ﴿by the permission of its Lord﴾.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 59–63:

﴿Indeed We sent Noah to his people, and he said: "O my people, worship God; you have no god other than Him. Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day."﴾ When He mentioned in this surah the origin of humankind, which is Adam, peace be upon him, and related some of his news as He related it, and digressed from that to the Return (al-ma'ad) and the destiny of the people of happiness to Paradise and the people of misery to the Fire, and commanded him to leave those who took their religion as play and amusement, and the ones to whom the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was first sent did not respond to him or affirm what he brought from God, God related to him the circumstances of the messengers who came before him and the circumstances of those sent to them, as consolation for him and as a model to follow. He began with Noah, for he is "the lesser Adam" (Adam al-asghar) and the first messenger sent to the inhabitants of the earth. His nation was the most persistent in denying him and the least in responding. His lineage's ascent to Adam has already been mentioned. He was a carpenter, whom God sent to his people when he was forty years old. This is what Ibn 'Abbas said. It was also said: fifty. (p. 320) Muqatil said: a hundred. It was said: two hundred and fifty. It was said: three hundred. 'Awn ibn Shaddad said: three hundred and fifty. Wahb said: four hundred. This is considerable disagreement, ranging from forty to four hundred and what lies between them. It is narrated that the Flood occurred in the year one thousand six hundred of his life, and that he was the first messenger after Adam to forbid marriage with daughters, sisters, paternal aunts and maternal aunts. All of creation today is from the offspring of Noah, peace be upon him. It is related from al-Zuhri that the Arabs, Persians, Romans, the people of the Levant and Yemen are from the offspring of Sam ibn Noah; and the Indians, the Sindhis, the Zanj, the Abyssinians, the Zutt, the Nubians and every black-skinned people are from the offspring of Ham ibn Noah; and the Turks, the Berbers, the peoples beyond China, Gog and Magog, and the Slavs are from the offspring of Japheth ibn Noah.

﴿Laqad arsalna﴾ (the lam here is the lam of oath, and "laqad" is the emphatic particle): "ولَقَدْ أرْسَلْنا" is a resumptive clause (istinaf, a new sentence that begins a fresh statement) without a conjunction (waw). In Hud it is "والمُؤْمِنُونَ" and "ولَقَدْ" with the conjunction of coordination. Al-Kirmani said: Since the mention of the Messenger had been repeated several times in Hud, and the mention of Noah had been made implicitly in His words "and upon the ark" (وعَلى الفُلْكِ), because he was the first to build it, the coordination (ʿatf) occurs in both surahs. End of quote. The lam is the answer to a suppressed oath, by which God emphasized this report. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, why do they hardly ever use this lam except with qad? And rarely from them is the saying of the poet:

"I swore to her by God an oath of a wicked man: they slept..."

I say: That is because the oath-clause is only brought as emphasis for the clause sworn to, which is its answer, so it was liable to convey the meaning of anticipation (tawaqquʿ), which is the meaning of qad when the listener hears the word of oath. End of quote. Some of our companions say: if one swears to a clause that begins with a affirmative past verb that is inflected, and it is close to the present time, one affirms it with the lam together with qad, which indicates proximity to the present time; and if one does not intend proximity, one uses the lam alone without qad.

Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿arsalna﴾ means "we sent." Others said: "We entrusted him with a message to deliver," so according to this the message includes sending. Here (in this surah) it says "fa-qala" (so he said) with the conjunctive fa, and likewise in "the believers" in the story of 'Ad, Salih and Shu'ayb. Here it says it without fa, though the original is fa. It is omitted in the two stories for breadth of expression and sufficiency with the semantic connection. In the story of Noah in Hud: ﴿Innee lakum﴾ [Hud: 25] is with the verb of saying suppressed, meaning: "so he said, 'Indeed I...'" In his calling out to his people there is an alerting to what he is about to convey to them, an appeal for their sympathy, and a reminder that they are his people; so it is fitting that they should not oppose him. The object of the verb of saying is the clause of the command to worship God alone and to abandon their gods called Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq, Nasr and others. The clause that draws attention to the attribute calling for the worship of God, which is His singularity in divinity, the One whose beneficence is hoped for and whose vengeance is feared, as opposed to their gods, is not introduced with a conjunction, because it is an explanation and elucidation of the reason for His exclusive right to be worshipped.

Ibn Wththab, al-A'mash, Abu Ja'far and al-Kisa'i read (ghayrihi) with the genitive, following the form of (ilahin) as a substitute (badal, apposition) or a qualifier (na't, adjective). The rest of the seven readers read (ghayruhu) with the nominative, in coordination with the position of ﴿min ilahin﴾, because "min" is an extra particle here. Ibn 'Umar's son 'Isa read (ghayrahu) with the accusative as an exception (istithna', exceptive construction). The genitive and nominative are more eloquent. "Min ilahin" is the subject (mubtada', topic), and "lakum" is in the position of the predicate (khabar, comment). It was also said that the predicate is omitted, meaning: "in existence," and "lakum" is a specification and restriction.

﴿Akhafu﴾ (I fear): It was said it means "I am certain and sure," because he knew that the punishment would descend upon them if they did not believe. It was said the fear is in its proper sense, meaning caution, because he allowed that they might believe, and that they might persist in their disbelief. ﴿A tremendous day﴾ is the Day of Resurrection, or the day the punishment befalls them in this world, which is the Flood. In this sentence is the display of compassion and tenderness toward them.

It is related from al-Zuhri that the Arabs, Persians, Romans, the people of the Levant and Yemen are from the offspring of Sam ibn Noah; and the Indians, the Sindhis, the Zanj, the Abyssinians, the Zutt, the Nubians and every black-skinned people are from the offspring of Ham ibn Noah; and the Turks, the Berbers, the peoples beyond China, Gog and Magog, and the Slavs are from the offspring of Japheth ibn Noah.
