Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 64:

﴿The chiefs among his people said: "Indeed, we see you in manifest error."﴾ (Al-A'raf: 60) Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Ibn 'Amir recited (al-mala'u) with a waw, and it is written thus in the codices of the people of Syria, end of quote. But this is not well known from Ibn 'Amir. Rather, his recitation is like the recitation of the rest of the Seven Readers, with a hamza. None responded to him from his people except their nobles and leaders, and they are the ones who opposed the messengers, because their minds were submerged in worldly life and in the pursuit of leadership and superiority over others in both. As for "nara-ka" (we see you), the more apparent view is that it is from seeing with the heart. It was also said that it is from seeing with the eye. The meaning of "in manifest error" (Al-A'raf: 60) is: in going astray from the path of rightness and in ignorance of what you follow, clear and evident. The answer clause came emphasized by inna and by the lam, and fi (in) denotes a container, so it is as if error came as a vessel for him, and he was within it (p. 321), and he did not come as one who is astray or one who possesses error.

﴿He said: "O my people, there is no error in me, but I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds. I convey to you the messages of my Lord and I advise you, and I know from God what you do not know."﴾ (Al-A'raf: 61–62) The negation from him did not follow the wording of what they had said. So the structure did not come as "I am not in manifest error," but came in the most beautiful form: a negation that error could adhere to him or become mixed with him, not even a single instance of error. How could he be "in error" when not even one act of error clings to him? This is more emphatic than negating error from him, since no single instance of it attaches to him. In his calling them a second time, and in turning away from their harshness, there is evidence of the breadth of his chest and of his gentleness toward them.

When he negated from them any mixing of error with him, this indicated that he was upon the straight path. So it was proper for him to use a corrective particle, as you say: "Zayd is not astray, but he is guided." Here "lakin" (but) falls between two opposites, because a person is never free of one of two states: error or guidance, and the error of prophethood does not coexist with it. In his saying "from the Lord of the worlds" (Al-A'raf: 61) there is an alert that He is their Lord, since they are part of the worlds. That is: from your Lord, the Owner of your affairs, who watches over you for your benefit, in that He sent to you a messenger calling you to devote worship to Him alone. "I convey to you" (Al-A'raf: 62) is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) by way of explanation of his being a messenger, or it is a clause in the position of a qualifier for "messenger," considered in terms of being a predicate of a first-person pronoun. As you say: "I am a man who commands the good," where you observe the wording of "I," and it is also permissible to say "who commands the good," observing the wording of "man." The more common practice is to observe the pronoun of the speaker or addressee, so the pronoun returns as a pronoun of speaker or addressee. God the Exalted said: "Rather, you are a people being tested" (An-Naml: 47), with the ta', and if it were read with the ya' it would also be correct Arabic, observing the wording of "qawm" (people), which is third person.

Abu 'Amr recited "uballighukum" (Al-A'raf: 62) in both places here and in al-Ahqaf with a light form (takhfif), while the rest of the Seven recited it with doubling (tashdid). The hamza and the doubling both serve to make the verb transitive. He used the plural "risalat" (messages) in consideration of what was revealed to him over long periods of time, or in consideration of the different meanings: command, prohibition, deterrence, admonition, glad tidings, and warning, or in consideration of what was revealed to him and to those before him. It was said: in the scrolls of Idris, which are thirty scrolls, and in the scrolls of Shith, which are fifty scrolls. The discussion of "nasaha" (to advise) and its transitivity has already passed. Al-Zamakhshari said: In the addition of the lam there is emphasis and an indication of the purity of the advice, and that it was directed to the one advised with attention given only to his benefit. For many an advisor benefits himself by intending both benefits together, but there is no advice more beneficial than the advice of God the Exalted and His messengers. Al-Farra' said: The Arabs hardly say "nasahtuka" (I advised you); rather they say "nasahtu laka" (I advised for you). Al-Nabigha said:

*I advised the Banu 'Awf, but they would not accept.*

In his saying "what you do not know" (Al-A'raf: 62) there is an ambiguity for them, and it is general. But he presented it in the manner of things known, which they should fear, and which they had never heard of: a nation punished. So it implies threat and warning. It may be that he meant what you do not know of God's attributes, His power, and the severity of His seizing of those who take a god besides Him, or he meant what you do not know of what has been revealed to me. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is necessary that Noah, peace be upon him, and every prophet sent to creation had a miracle that breaks habit. Some of them we know by their miracle, and some we do not know. How excellent is the arrangement of these verbs! He said first: (p. 322) "I convey to you the messages of my Lord" (Al-A'raf: 62), and this is the beginning of his dealing with them, which is conveyance, as He said: "Your duty is only to convey" (Ash-Shura: 48). Then he said: "and I advise you" (Al-A'raf: 62), that is: I sincerely make clear to you the right course and the safety of the outcome if you worship God alone. Then he said: "and I know from God what you do not know" of His seizing of you, and this is the end of your affair if you do not single Him out in worship. Thus he alerted them to the beginning and the end of his dealings with them.

﴿Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, so that he may warn you and that you may become mindful of God, and perhaps you will be shown mercy?﴾ (Al-A'raf: 63) Their saying "Indeed, we see you in manifest error" (Al-A'raf: 60) includes their deeming it unlikely and inconceivable that what he informed them of, namely the fear of punishment for them, and that God sent him to them to worship Him alone and abandon their gods. They wondered at this. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: The cause of their finding it unlikely was the sending of Noah. The hamza is for denial and rebuke, that is: this is not something to be wondered at, since God has complete authority to send whom He wills to whom He wills. Al-Zamakhshari said: The waw is for conjunction (atf), and the conjoined element is omitted, as if it were said: "Did you deny and wonder that a reminder has come to you?" End of quote. This is a statement contrary to the statement of Sibawayh and the grammarians, because they say that the waw is for conjoining what follows to what precedes in the speech, with no omission there. It seems the original was "a-u'jibtum" (did you wonder), but he gave priority to the interrogative hamza and placed it before the conjunctive particles, because the interrogative has the front position in speech. The discussion of this question has already passed in a similar case, and he himself returned from this view to the position of the majority. "Reminder" (dhikr) may mean admonition, revelation, a miracle, a book that is miraculous, or clarification; these are sayings. The better view is that his saying "upon a man" (Al-A'raf: 63) contains an elision (hadhf): that is, "upon the tongue of a man," as He said: "what You promised us upon Your messengers" (Al 'Imran: 194). It was also said: "upon" here means "with." It was also said: there is no elision and no implication (tadmin) in the particle; rather "upon a man" is in its literal sense, because "has come to you" (Al-A'raf: 63) means "has descended to you." They were wondering at the prophethood of Noah and saying: "We have not heard of this among our forefathers of old" (Al-Mu'minun: 24), meaning the sending of a human being. And: "If our Lord had willed, He would have sent down angels" (Fussilat: 14). He mentioned the coming, which is the informing of what is feared and the warning against the evil consequence of disbelief, and the existence of God-consciousness among them, and the hope of mercy. It seems these are a chain of causes arranged in sequence: the reminder came to warn of what is feared; warning of what is feared is for the sake of the existence of God-consciousness among them; and God-consciousness exists in hope of mercy and its attainment. So he gave as the cause of the coming all these arranged causes, because what is arranged upon a cause is itself a cause.

﴿So they denied him, and We saved him and those with him in the ship, and We drowned those who denied Our signs. Indeed, they were a blind people.﴾ (Al-A'raf: 64) God the Exalted informed that they denied him, despite the excellence of his gentleness toward them, his return to them, and his compassion for them. So the outcome of this was nothing but denial of him regarding what he brought from God. "Those with him in the ship" (Al-A'raf: 64) are those who believed in him and affirmed him, and they were forty men. It was said: eighty men and forty women. This was said by al-Kalbi, and to them is attributed the town known as the town of the Eighty, which is in Mosul. It was said: ten, among them his three sons. It was said: nine, of whom three were his sons. In His saying "and We drowned those who denied" there is information about the cause of the drowning, which is denial. "Our signs" (Al-A'raf: 64) requires that Noah had signs and miracles indicating his sending. "In the ship" is connected to what the relative clause describing it connects to, that is: "those who settled with him in the ship." It may also be connected to "We saved him," meaning: We saved them in the ship from the flood. In this case the particle "fi" may be causal, as in the saying "a woman entered Hell because of a cat" (a hadith), meaning: because of a cat. "Blind" (ʿamin) comes from "the heart became blind," that is: not perceiving insight. The fact that it came in the pattern fa'il (ʿamin rather than ʿamin) indicates the permanence of this attribute. Had the meaning been transient, it would have come in the form fā'il, as "ḍā'iq" for "ḍayyiq" and "thāqil" for "thaqil" when the meaning intended is the occurrence of tightness and heaviness. Ibn 'Abbas said: their hearts became blind to knowledge of the oneness of God, prophethood, and the Return. Mu'adh al-Nahwi said: "a man ʿamm in his affair" means one who does not see it, while "a'mā" refers to sight. He said:

*There is no blindness (ʿamm) in tomorrow, but I am [speaking] from knowledge.*

Sometimes "ʿamā" (blindness) and "aʿmā" (blind) are used like "akhḍar" and "khiḍr" (green). Al-Layth said: "a man ʿamm" means one who is blind of heart.

And to ʿĀd [We sent] their brother Hūd. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. Will you not then be wary?"

ʿĀd is the name of a tribe (ḥayy), and for this reason he gave it sarf (the nunation of the noun, so it is declined as a triptote). Others made it the name of a tribe (qabīlah) and so withheld sarf from it. The poet said:

*"Had ʿĀd been witnessed in the era of ʿĀd, Mubārak al-Jallād would have snatched them away."*

The tribe was named after their father, who was ʿĀd ibn ʿAwṣ ibn Iram ibn Sām ibn Nūḥ, peace be upon him. As for Hūd, our shaykh Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ubbadī the grammarian said: "It is well known that Hūd is an Arab. What appears from the words of Sībawayh, when he counted him together with Nūḥ and Lūṭ, both of whom are non-Arabs, is that he considered him a non-Arab." End of quote. The noble genealogist Abū al-Barakāt al-Juwānī mentioned that Yaʿrub ibn Qaḥṭān ibn Hūd is the one whom the Yemenis claim was the first to speak Arabic and who settled the land of Yemen; he is the father of all of Yemen, and the Arabs were named "Arabs" after him. End of quote. According to this, Hūd would not be an Arab. Hūd is the son of ʿĀbir ibn Shālikh ibn Arfakhshad ibn Sām ibn Nūḥ. The word ﴿brother﴾ (akhāhum) is coordinated with (Nūḥan) and means one of them. Hūd was not from the sons of ʿĀd, as we have mentioned. This is like saying "O brother of the Arabs" to one of them.

It was also said that he was from ʿĀd: Hūd ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Riyāḥ ibn al-Jalūd ibn ʿĀd ibn ʿAwṣ ibn Iram ibn Sām ibn Nūḥ. According to this view, he was from ʿĀd, and the name of his mother was Murjānah. He was a merchant, the most similar of Allah's creatures to Ādam, peace be upon both of them. It is narrated that ʿĀd had thirteen tribes who dwelt in the sands of ʿĀlij. These were the first ʿĀd, and they were owners of gardens, crops and buildings, and their lands were the most fertile lands. Allah became displeased with them and turned their lands into deserts. Their territory extended from the regions of ʿUmān to Ḥaḍramawt and to Yemen. They worshipped idols. When they perished, Hūd and those who believed with him went to Makkah, and they remained there until they died.

The Qur'an did not say (fa-qāla) with the fāʾ; this is because it is the answer to an implied question, meaning: "So what did he say to them?" The answer is ﴿O my people﴾. Likewise (qāla al-mala'), ﴿the chiefs said﴾ [al-A'raf: 66].

In His words ﴿Will you not then be wary?﴾ there is an appeal to tenderness (istiʿṭāf) and an urging (taḥḍīḍ) to attain taqwā. Since what befell the people of Nūḥ in the matter of the Flood was an event the like of which had not appeared in the world, He said: ﴿Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day﴾ [al-A'raf: 59]. The event of Hūd was preceded by the event of Nūḥ, and the people's memory of it was still recent, so Hūd suffices with his words ﴿Will you not then be wary?﴾. The meaning is: you know that when the people of Nūḥ did not fear Allah and worshipped other than Him, that punishment befell them, the report of which became famous in the world. Thus His words ﴿Will you not then be wary?﴾ are an allusion to warning with that well-known event.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 66–72 (part 1 of 2):

﴿The chiefs of those among his people who disbelieved said: "Indeed, we see you in foolishness, and indeed we think you are among the liars."﴾ He described ﴿al-mala'﴾ (the chiefs, the notables) with ﴿those who disbelieved﴾, and did not use this description for the people of Nuh. The reason is that among the notables of the people of Hud there were those who believed in him, including Marthad ibn Sa'd ibn Ufayr (p-٣٢٤). Among the notables of the people of Nuh there was no believer. Consider their words ﴿And we do not see that anyone has followed you except those who are the lowest among us﴾ [Hud: 27] and their words ﴿Shall we believe you when the lowest have followed you?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 111]. It is possible that this description was given for blame and was not intended as a distinction. As for ﴿lanaraka﴾ (we see you), it may be from seeing with the eye or from seeing with the heart, as was discussed earlier in the story of Nuh. ﴿Fi safahah﴾ (in foolishness) means: in lightness of judgement and feebleness of intellect, in that you abandon the religion of your people for another religion. The use of ﴿fi﴾ (in) implies that foolishness contains him, like a ﴿zarf﴾ (container, locative complement) that encloses a thing. Since the speech of Nuh to his people was stronger than the speech of Hud, in strengthening his words ﴿Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great day﴾ [al-A'raf: 59], their reply was harsher, namely ﴿Indeed, we see you in manifest error﴾ [al-A'raf: 60]. The speech of Hud was gentler, in his words ﴿Will you not then be mindful?﴾ [al-A'raf: 65], so their reply to him was gentler than the reply of the people of Nuh to Nuh, in their words ﴿Indeed, we see you in foolishness﴾. Then they followed that with their words ﴿And indeed, we think you are among the liars﴾. This indicates that he had told them of the punishment that would befall them if they did not fear God. Or they attached the ﴿zann﴾ (supposition) to his words ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾ [al-A'raf: 73], meaning: we have gods, so confining them to one is a lie. It has been said that ﴿zann﴾ here means certainty, or means the preponderance of one of two possibilities. These are two opinions among the exegetes, and the second is that of al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj. Al-Kirmani said: Nuh warned the disbelievers of a general deluge and occupied himself with building the ship, so they said ﴿Indeed, we see you in manifest error﴾ [al-A'raf: 60], in that you tire yourself in repairing a great ship in a desert where there is no water, and nothing has appeared that indicates this. This is accompanied by the worship of idols, and they attributed foolishness to his people, so he answered them with the same.

﴿He said: "O my people, there is no foolishness in me, but I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds. I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I am a sincere and trustworthy adviser to you."﴾ The manner of this negation has been mentioned in his words ﴿There is no error in me﴾ [al-A'raf: 61]. There he said ﴿and I advise you﴾ [al-A'raf: 62], and here he said ﴿and I am a sincere and trustworthy adviser to you﴾. Since the last of their reply was a ﴿jumla ismiyya﴾ (nominal sentence), his reply came likewise. They said ﴿And indeed, we think you are among the liars﴾, and he said ﴿and I am a sincere and trustworthy adviser to you﴾, and he brought the description of trustworthiness (amanah), which is the great trust that man bore, and there is no trust greater than the trust of messengership and conveying its burdens to those who are charged. The meaning is: I am known among you for sincere counsel, so it is not right for you to accuse me, and for trustworthiness in what I say, so it is not fitting that I be called a liar. Ibn 'Atiyya said: His words ﴿amin﴾ (trustworthy) may mean trustworthy concerning the revelation and the remembrance sent down from God. It may also mean that he is trustworthy over them, over their unseen affairs, and in desiring good for them. The Arabs say: "So-and-so is sincere in his breast and trustworthy in what is unseen to so-and-so." It may also mean from safety, that is: my side is safe for you from lying and deceit. Al-Qushayri said: How different is the one whose Lord repelled charges from him by saying ﴿Your companion has not strayed nor erred﴾ [al-Najm: 2] and ﴿Your companion is not a madman﴾ [al-Takwir: 22], from one who repelled charges from himself by saying ﴿There is no error in me﴾ [al-A'raf: 61] and ﴿There is no foolishness in me﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: In the response of the prophets, peace be upon them, to those who attributed error and foolishness to them, with what they answered them of speech that issues from forbearance, overlooking, and refraining from retaliating in kind, despite knowing that their opponents were the root of foolishness and its lowest level, there is a fine manners and a great character. God's relating of that about them is a lesson to His servants on how to address the foolish, and how to overlook them and let their skirts trail over what they do.

﴿"Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, so that he may warn you?"﴾ [al-A'raf: 63]. Here he gave only one cause, namely warning, which is frightening with punishment, and he omitted what follows from warning, namely piety and hope for mercy.

﴿"And remember when He made you successors (khulafa') after the people of Nuh"﴾. That is: the inhabitants of the earth after them. This was said by al-Suddi and Ibn Ishaq. Or it means: He made you kings in the earth, and appointed you to it as successors. This was said by al-Zamakhshari. Hud's reminding them of this indicates the nearness of their time to the time of Nuh, by His words ﴿after the people of Nuh﴾. The word ﴿idh﴾ (when) is a ﴿zarf﴾ (adverbial of time) according to al-Hawfi, in which case the object of ﴿udhkuru﴾ (remember) is omitted, meaning: remember the bounties of God upon you at the time of such-and-such. The governing element of ﴿idh﴾ is what the blessings contain of a verb. According to al-Zamakhshari's view, ﴿idh﴾ is a ﴿maf'ul bihi﴾ (direct object), in the accusative governed by ﴿udhkuru﴾, meaning: remember the time of your being made.

﴿"And He increased you in stature (basṭah) in creation"﴾. The apparent meaning of the histories is that ﴿basṭah﴾ means extension, height, and beauty in forms and shapes (p-٣٢٥). So it is possible that ﴿al-khalq﴾ (creation) means the created beings, and it is possible that it is a verbal noun, meaning: He increased you in your creation in ﴿basṭah﴾, that is, He extended, lengthened, and beautified your creation. It was said: the shortest of them was sixty cubits, and the tallest was a hundred cubits. This was said by al-Kalbi and al-Suddi. Abu Hamza al-Yamani said: seventy cubits. Ibn 'Abbas said: eighty cubits. Muqatil said: twelve cubits. Wahb said: the head of one of them was like a great dome, and his eye would be a nest in which hyenas gave birth, and likewise his nostril. If ﴿al-khalq﴾ means the created beings, then ﴿al-khalq﴾ refers to the people of Nuh, or the people of their time, or all people. These are the opinions. It was also said: the increase is in physical bulk, namely reaching what a person's hand can reach when he raises it. It was said: the increase is in strength and robustness, not in bulk. It was also said: the increase in ﴿basṭah﴾ is that they were from one tribe, sharing in strength, supporting one another, and loving one another. It is possible that the meaning is ﴿wa-zadakum basṭah﴾, that is: power and dominance over created beings and control.

﴿"So remember the bounties of God, that you may prosper"﴾. He first reminded them of His favour upon them in making them successors and increasing them in ﴿basṭah﴾, and secondly reminded them of His bounties upon them in general, not restricted to the time of their being made successors. The apparent meaning of ﴿udhkuru﴾ (remember) is that it is from ﴿dhikr﴾ (remembrance), namely that they should not forget His bounties, but that His bounties should be before them in remembrance, in hope that they would prosper. The linking of hope for success to mere remembrance is not evident, so it requires an omitted element on which the hope for success is consequent. Its estimated meaning, God knows best, is: so remember the bounties of God and devote worship to Him alone. Consider His words ﴿Have you come to us that we should worship God alone?﴾. In their mention of ﴿the bounties of God﴾ there is a mention of the Benefactor upon them, who deserves to be worshipped alone and to have all else discarded. It was also said: ﴿udhkuru﴾ here means ﴿ushkuru﴾ (give thanks).

﴿They said: "Have you come to us that we should worship God alone and abandon what our fathers used to worship? So bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful."﴾ The apparent meaning is that they denied that they should abandon their idols and devote worship to God alone, while acknowledging God, out of love for what they had grown up upon and attachment to what they found their fathers upon. It is possible that they were deniers of God, and their words ﴿that we should worship God alone﴾ mean: according to your words, O Hud, and your claim. This was said by Ibn 'Atiyya, who added: the first interpretation is more apparent regarding them and regarding the worshippers of idols, and none of the disbelievers denies the lordship of God except one who claims it for himself, like Pharaoh and Nimrod. End of quote. In Hud's words to his people ﴿So remember the bounties of God﴾ there is a decisive proof that none should be worshipped except the Benefactor, and their idols are inanimate objects with no power over anything at all. Worship is the utmost extent of veneration, so it befits only one from whom the utmost of benefaction proceeds. When he pointed out this argument, and they had no way to answer it, they resorted to pure imitation, saying ﴿Have you come to us that we should worship God alone?﴾. The word ﴿al-maji'﴾ (coming) here may be literal, in that he had been absent from his people, alone in worshipping his Lord, and then God sent him to them, so he came to them from his place of seclusion. It may also be that their saying was in mockery, because they believed that God sends only angels, so it was as if they said: have you come to us from the heaven as an angel comes? They did not mean the literal coming, but rather confronting and intending, as one says: "He went to abuse me," not meaning the literal going. It was as if they said: have you intended us that we should worship God alone, and confronted us with its obligations? In their words ﴿So bring us what you threaten us with﴾ there is evidence that he used to threaten them with the punishment of God if they persisted in disbelief. Their saying this indicates their determination to deny him, their contempt for the matter of prophethood, and their hastening of the punishment, since in their view it would never occur at all. Their earlier words ﴿Indeed, we see you in foolishness﴾ and ﴿And indeed, we think you are among the liars﴾ have already been mentioned. Since they believed him to be a liar, they said ﴿So bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful﴾, meaning: in your prophethood and sending, or in the claim that the punishment will descend upon us.

﴿He said: "There has already fallen upon you from your Lord a ruin (rijs) and wrath"﴾, meaning: it has befallen you and become decreed against you. Zayd ibn Aslam and most of the exegetes said: ﴿al-rijs﴾ here means punishment, from ﴿al-irtijas﴾ (trembling, agitation). Ibn 'Abbas said: it means anger. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: it cannot be punishment, because the punishment had not yet occurred at that time. Al-Qaffal said: it is possible that the increase in disbelief by the rust (rayn) upon the hearts is meant, that is, because of their persistence in disbelief there fell upon you from God a rust upon your hearts, like His words ﴿so it increased them in ruin to their ruin﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125], since ﴿al-rijs﴾ is anger, or rust. Thus His words ﴿There has fallen﴾ are in their literal sense of the past tense, even if the punishment is meant, in which case it is the use of the past tense for the future to express the certainty of its occurrence.

﴿"Do you dispute with me over names that you and your fathers have named, for which God has sent down no authority?"﴾ This is a denunciation by him of their disputing with him over what is not fitting to dispute, namely the mention of words under which there is no referent deserving worship, so the dispute became void for that reason. The meaning of ﴿sammaytumuha﴾ (you named them) is: you and your fathers named them, that is, you and your fathers invented them recently, and they are Samud, Sada, and al-Haba'. Marthad ibn Sa'd mentioned them in his poetry, saying:

The 'Ad disobeyed their messenger, so they became thirsty, the sky would not moisten them.
For them is an idol called Samud, opposite it Sada and al-Haba'.
So the Messenger showed us the path of guidance, and we saw guidance, and blindness was removed.
Indeed the god of Hud is my god; upon God is reliance and hope.

So the dispute at that time would be over the words, not their referents. It is possible that the dispute took place over the named things, which are the idols, in which case he used the names and meant the things named, and this would be by omission of a ﴿mudaf﴾ (governed noun), that is, ﴿Do you dispute with me⦆ concerning the essences of names. The meaning would be: ﴿you named them﴾ as gods, and worshipped them besides God. It was said: they named each idol with a name as they pleased, and they claimed that one of them gives them rain, another cures them of sickness, another accompanies them on journeys, and another brings them provision.

﴿"God has sent down no authority for them"﴾. The clause ﴿mā nazzala Allāh﴾ (God did not send down) is in the position of a ﴿ṣifa﴾ (qualifying description). The meaning is: you have no proof or evidence for that. Here the verb is ﴿nazzala﴾, while in another place it is ﴿anzala﴾, and both are eloquent, and transitivity by doubling (the middle radical) and by the hamza is equivalent.

﴿"So wait, I am with you among those who wait."﴾ This is an extreme of threat and warning, meaning: wait for the outcome of your affair in worshipping other than God and in denying His messenger. This is an extreme of certainty about what will befall them, and that it will occur without doubt.

﴿Then We saved him and those with him by a mercy from Us﴾, meaning those who believed with him, ﴿by a mercy﴾ preceding them from God, and a grace upon them, in that He made them believe, and this was the cause of their salvation from what afflicted their people of punishment.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 66–72 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And We cut off the last remnant of those who denied Our signs﴾: this is a metaphor (kinaya) for their total annihilation by destruction through punishment. The discussion of dabir (the last remnant, the tail end, of a people) has already occurred in His words: ﴿So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off﴾ [al-An'am: 45]. His words ﴿who denied﴾ are an alert to the reason for the cutting off of their remnant. His words ﴿Our signs﴾ are evidence that Hud had miracles (mu'jizat), but they were not specified for us by name.

﴿And they were not believers﴾: this sentence emphasizes His words ﴿who denied Our signs﴾. It may also be a report from Allah, exalted is He, that they were among those whom Allah knew would not believe if they remained alive; that is, they were not among those who would accept faith at all. Had Allah known that they would believe, He would have spared them. This is because one who denies the signs may afterward believe in them and his condition may become good; but as for the one whom Allah has sealed with disbelief, he will never believe, ever. In this there is an implicit reference to those among them who did believe, such as Marthad ibn Sa'd and those who were saved along with Hud, peace be upon him. It is as if He said: "And We cut off the remnant of the people who denied, from among them, and they were not like those of them who believed," so as to indicate that the destruction was specific to the deniers and that Allah saved the believers. This is what al-Zamakhshari said. The commentators have mentioned here the story of the destruction of 'Ad and have mentioned in it matters that have no connection to the wording of the Qur'an and were not authentically related from the Messenger (ﷺ), so I have passed over mention of them entirely. As for what has a connection to the wording of the Qur'an, it will come in its appropriate places, God willing.

They said ﴿And indeed, we think you are among the liars﴾, and he said ﴿and I am a sincere and trustworthy adviser to you﴾, and he brought the description of trustworthiness (amanah), which is the great trust that man bore, and there is no trust greater than the trust of messengership and conveying its burdens to those who are charged. The meaning is: I am known among you for sincere counsel, so it is not right for you to accuse me, and for trustworthiness in what I say, so it is not fitting that I be called a liar. Ibn 'Atiyya said: His words ﴿amin﴾ (trustworthy) may mean trustworthy concerning the revelation and the remembrance sent down from God. It may also mean that he is trustworthy over them, over their unseen affairs, and in desiring good for them. The Arabs say: "So-and-so is sincere in his breast and trustworthy in what is unseen to so-and-so." It may also mean from safety, that is: my side is safe for you from lying and deceit. Al-Qushayri said: How different is the one whose Lord repelled charges from him by saying ﴿Your companion has not strayed nor erred﴾ [al-Najm: 2] and ﴿Your companion is not a madman﴾ [al-Takwir: 22], from one who repelled charges from himself by saying ﴿There is no error in me﴾ [al-A'raf: 61] and ﴿There is no foolishness in me﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: In the response of the prophets, peace be upon them, to those who attributed error and foolishness to them, with what they answered them of speech that issues from forbearance, overlooking, and refraining from retaliating in kind, despite knowing that their opponents were the root of foolishness and its lowest level, there is a fine manners and a great character. God's relating of that about them is a lesson to His servants on how to address the foolish, and how to overlook them and let their skirts trail over what they do.

﴿"Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, so that he may warn you?"﴾ [al-A'raf: 63]. Here he gave only one cause, namely warning, which is frightening with punishment, and he omitted what follows from warning, namely piety and hope for mercy.

﴿"And remember when He made you successors (khulafa') after the people of Nuh"﴾. That is: the inhabitants of the earth after them. This was said by al-Suddi and Ibn Ishaq. Or it means: He made you kings in the earth, and appointed you to it as successors. This was said by al-Zamakhshari. Hud's reminding them of this indicates the nearness of their time to the time of Nuh, by His words ﴿after the people of Nuh﴾. The word ﴿idh﴾ (when) is a ﴿zarf﴾ (adverbial of time) according to al-Hawfi, in which case the object of ﴿udhkuru﴾ (remember) is omitted, meaning: remember the bounties of God upon you at the time of such-and-such. The governing element of ﴿idh﴾ is what the blessings contain of a verb. According to al-Zamakhshari's view, ﴿idh﴾ is a ﴿maf'ul bihi﴾ (direct object), in the accusative governed by ﴿udhkuru﴾, meaning: remember the time of your being made.

﴿"And He increased you in stature (basṭah) in creation"﴾. The apparent meaning of the histories is that ﴿basṭah﴾ means extension, height, and beauty in forms and shapes (p-٣٢٥). So it is possible that ﴿al-khalq﴾ (creation) means the created beings, and it is possible that it is a verbal noun, meaning: He increased you in your creation in ﴿basṭah﴾, that is, He extended, lengthened, and beautified your creation. It was said: the shortest of them was sixty cubits, and the tallest was a hundred cubits. This was said by al-Kalbi and al-Suddi. Abu Hamza al-Yamani said: seventy cubits. Ibn 'Abbas said: eighty cubits. Muqatil said: twelve cubits. Wahb said: the head of one of them was like a great dome, and his eye would be a nest in which hyenas gave birth, and likewise his nostril. If ﴿al-khalq﴾ means the created beings, then ﴿al-khalq﴾ refers to the people of Nuh, or the people of their time, or all people. These are the opinions. It was also said: the increase is in physical bulk, namely reaching what a person's hand can reach when he raises it. It was said: the increase is in strength and robustness, not in bulk. It was also said: the increase in ﴿basṭah﴾ is that they were from one tribe, sharing in strength, supporting one another, and loving one another. It is possible that the meaning is ﴿wa-zadakum basṭah﴾, that is: power and dominance over created beings and control.

﴿"So remember the bounties of God, that you may prosper"﴾. He first reminded them of His favour upon them in making them successors and increasing them in ﴿basṭah﴾, and secondly reminded them of His bounties upon them in general, not restricted to the time of their being made successors. The apparent meaning of ﴿udhkuru﴾ (remember) is that it is from ﴿dhikr﴾ (remembrance), namely that they should not forget His bounties, but that His bounties should be before them in remembrance, in hope that they would prosper. The linking of hope for success to mere remembrance is not evident, so it requires an omitted element on which the hope for success is consequent. Its estimated meaning, God knows best, is: so remember the bounties of God and devote worship to Him alone. Consider His words ﴿Have you come to us that we should worship God alone?﴾. In their mention of ﴿the bounties of God﴾ there is a mention of the Benefactor upon them, who deserves to be worshipped alone and to have all else discarded. It was also said: ﴿udhkuru﴾ here means ﴿ushkuru﴾ (give thanks).

So bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful."﴾ The apparent meaning is that they denied that they should abandon their idols and devote worship to God alone, while acknowledging God, out of love for what they had grown up upon and attachment to what they found their fathers upon. It is possible that they were deniers of God, and their words ﴿that we should worship God alone﴾ mean: according to your words, O Hud, and your claim. This was said by Ibn 'Atiyya, who added: the first interpretation is more apparent regarding them and regarding the worshippers of idols, and none of the disbelievers denies the lordship of God except one who claims it for himself, like Pharaoh and Nimrod. End of quote. Worship is the utmost extent of veneration, so it befits only one from whom the utmost of benefaction proceeds. When he pointed out this argument, and they had no way to answer it, they resorted to pure imitation, saying ﴿Have you come to us that we should worship God alone?﴾. They did not mean the literal coming, but rather confronting and intending, as one says: "He went to abuse me," not meaning the literal going. It was as if they said: have you intended us that we should worship God alone, and confronted us with its obligations? Their saying this indicates their determination to deny him, their contempt for the matter of prophethood, and their hastening of the punishment, since in their view it would never occur at all. Since they believed him to be a liar, they said ﴿So bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful﴾, meaning: in your prophethood and sending, or in the claim that the punishment will descend upon us.

The 'Ad disobeyed their messenger, so they became thirsty, the sky would not moisten them.
For them is an idol called Samud, opposite it Sada and al-Haba'.

Indeed the god of Hud is my god; upon God is reliance and hope.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 66–72 (part 2 of 2):

The discussion of dabir (the last remnant, the tail end, of a people) has already occurred in His words: ﴿So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off﴾ [al-An'am: 45]. His words ﴿who denied﴾ are an alert to the reason for the cutting off of their remnant. His words ﴿Our signs﴾ are evidence that Hud had miracles (mu'jizat), but they were not specified for us by name.

﴿And they were not believers﴾: this sentence emphasizes His words ﴿who denied Our signs﴾. It may also be a report from Allah, exalted is He, that they were among those whom Allah knew would not believe if they remained alive; that is, they were not among those who would accept faith at all. Had Allah known that they would believe, He would have spared them. This is because one who denies the signs may afterward believe in them and his condition may become good; but as for the one whom Allah has sealed with disbelief, he will never believe, ever. In this there is an implicit reference to those among them who did believe, such as Marthad ibn Sa'd and those who were saved along with Hud, peace be upon him. It is as if He said: "And We cut off the remnant of the people who denied, from among them, and they were not like those of them who believed," so as to indicate that the destruction was specific to the deniers and that Allah saved the believers. This is what al-Zamakhshari said. The commentators have mentioned here the story of the destruction of 'Ad and have mentioned in it matters that have no connection to the wording of the Qur'an and were not authentically related from the Messenger (ﷺ), so I have passed over mention of them entirely. As for what has a connection to the wording of the Qur'an, it will come in its appropriate places, God willing.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 66–72 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And We cut off the last remnant of those who denied Our signs﴾: this is a metaphor (kinaya) for their total annihilation by destruction through punishment. The discussion of dabir (the last remnant, the tail end, of a people) has already occurred in His words: ﴿So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off﴾ [al-An'am: 45]. His words ﴿who denied﴾ are an alert to the reason for the cutting off of their remnant. His words ﴿Our signs﴾ are evidence that Hud had miracles (mu'jizat), but they were not specified for us by name.

﴿And they were not believers﴾: this sentence emphasizes His words ﴿who denied Our signs﴾. It may also be a report from Allah, exalted is He, that they were among those whom Allah knew would not believe if they remained alive; that is, they were not among those who would accept faith at all. Had Allah known that they would believe, He would have spared them. This is because one who denies the signs may afterward believe in them and his condition may become good; but as for the one whom Allah has sealed with disbelief, he will never believe, ever. In this there is an implicit reference to those among them who did believe, such as Marthad ibn Sa'd and those who were saved along with Hud, peace be upon him. It is as if He said: "And We cut off the remnant of the people who denied, from among them, and they were not like those of them who believed," so as to indicate that the destruction was specific to the deniers and that Allah saved the believers. This is what al-Zamakhshari said. The commentators have mentioned here the story of the destruction of 'Ad and have mentioned in it matters that have no connection to the wording of the Qur'an and were not authentically related from the Messenger (ﷺ), so I have passed over mention of them entirely. As for what has a connection to the wording of the Qur'an, it will come in its appropriate places, God willing.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 66–72 (part 1 of 2):

﴿The chiefs of those among his people who disbelieved said: "Indeed, we see you in foolishness, and indeed we think you are among the liars."﴾ He described ﴿al-mala'﴾ (the chiefs, the notables) with ﴿those who disbelieved﴾, and did not use this description for the people of Nuh. The reason is that among the notables of the people of Hud there were those who believed in him, including Marthad ibn Sa'd ibn Ufayr (p-٣٢٤). Among the notables of the people of Nuh there was no believer. Consider their words ﴿And we do not see that anyone has followed you except those who are the lowest among us﴾ [Hud: 27] and their words ﴿Shall we believe you when the lowest have followed you?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 111]. It is possible that this description was given for blame and was not intended as a distinction. As for ﴿lanaraka﴾ (we see you), it may be from seeing with the eye or from seeing with the heart, as was discussed earlier in the story of Nuh. ﴿Fi safahah﴾ (in foolishness) means: in lightness of judgement and feebleness of intellect, in that you abandon the religion of your people for another religion. The use of ﴿fi﴾ (in) implies that foolishness contains him, like a ﴿zarf﴾ (container, locative complement) that encloses a thing. Since the speech of Nuh to his people was stronger than the speech of Hud, in strengthening his words ﴿Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great day﴾ [al-A'raf: 59], their reply was harsher, namely ﴿Indeed, we see you in manifest error﴾ [al-A'raf: 60]. The speech of Hud was gentler, in his words ﴿Will you not then be mindful?﴾ [al-A'raf: 65], so their reply to him was gentler than the reply of the people of Nuh to Nuh, in their words ﴿Indeed, we see you in foolishness﴾. Then they followed that with their words ﴿And indeed, we think you are among the liars﴾. This indicates that he had told them of the punishment that would befall them if they did not fear God. Or they attached the ﴿zann﴾ (supposition) to his words ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾ [al-A'raf: 73], meaning: we have gods, so confining them to one is a lie. It has been said that ﴿zann﴾ here means certainty, or means the preponderance of one of two possibilities. These are two opinions among the exegetes, and the second is that of al-Hasan and al-Zajjaj. Al-Kirmani said: Nuh warned the disbelievers of a general deluge and occupied himself with building the ship, so they said ﴿Indeed, we see you in manifest error﴾ [al-A'raf: 60], in that you tire yourself in repairing a great ship in a desert where there is no water, and nothing has appeared that indicates this. This is accompanied by the worship of idols, and they attributed foolishness to his people, so he answered them with the same.

﴿He said: "O my people, there is no foolishness in me, but I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds. I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I am a sincere and trustworthy adviser to you."﴾ The manner of this negation has been mentioned in his words ﴿There is no error in me﴾ [al-A'raf: 61]. There he said ﴿and I advise you﴾ [al-A'raf: 62], and here he said ﴿and I am a sincere and trustworthy adviser to you﴾. Since the last of their reply was a ﴿jumla ismiyya﴾ (nominal sentence), his reply came likewise. They said ﴿And indeed, we think you are among the liars﴾, and he said ﴿and I am a sincere and trustworthy adviser to you﴾, and he brought the description of trustworthiness (amanah), which is the great trust that man bore, and there is no trust greater than the trust of messengership and conveying its burdens to those who are charged. The meaning is: I am known among you for sincere counsel, so it is not right for you to accuse me, and for trustworthiness in what I say, so it is not fitting that I be called a liar. Ibn 'Atiyya said: His words ﴿amin﴾ (trustworthy) may mean trustworthy concerning the revelation and the remembrance sent down from God. It may also mean that he is trustworthy over them, over their unseen affairs, and in desiring good for them. The Arabs say: "So-and-so is sincere in his breast and trustworthy in what is unseen to so-and-so." It may also mean from safety, that is: my side is safe for you from lying and deceit. Al-Qushayri said: How different is the one whose Lord repelled charges from him by saying ﴿Your companion has not strayed nor erred﴾ [al-Najm: 2] and ﴿Your companion is not a madman﴾ [al-Takwir: 22], from one who repelled charges from himself by saying ﴿There is no error in me﴾ [al-A'raf: 61] and ﴿There is no foolishness in me﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: In the response of the prophets, peace be upon them, to those who attributed error and foolishness to them, with what they answered them of speech that issues from forbearance, overlooking, and refraining from retaliating in kind, despite knowing that their opponents were the root of foolishness and its lowest level, there is a fine manners and a great character. God's relating of that about them is a lesson to His servants on how to address the foolish, and how to overlook them and let their skirts trail over what they do.

﴿"Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, so that he may warn you?"﴾ [al-A'raf: 63]. Here he gave only one cause, namely warning, which is frightening with punishment, and he omitted what follows from warning, namely piety and hope for mercy.

﴿"And remember when He made you successors (khulafa') after the people of Nuh"﴾. That is: the inhabitants of the earth after them. This was said by al-Suddi and Ibn Ishaq. Or it means: He made you kings in the earth, and appointed you to it as successors. This was said by al-Zamakhshari. Hud's reminding them of this indicates the nearness of their time to the time of Nuh, by His words ﴿after the people of Nuh﴾. The word ﴿idh﴾ (when) is a ﴿zarf﴾ (adverbial of time) according to al-Hawfi, in which case the object of ﴿udhkuru﴾ (remember) is omitted, meaning: remember the bounties of God upon you at the time of such-and-such. The governing element of ﴿idh﴾ is what the blessings contain of a verb. According to al-Zamakhshari's view, ﴿idh﴾ is a ﴿maf'ul bihi﴾ (direct object), in the accusative governed by ﴿udhkuru﴾, meaning: remember the time of your being made.

﴿"And He increased you in stature (basṭah) in creation"﴾. The apparent meaning of the histories is that ﴿basṭah﴾ means extension, height, and beauty in forms and shapes (p-٣٢٥). So it is possible that ﴿al-khalq﴾ (creation) means the created beings, and it is possible that it is a verbal noun, meaning: He increased you in your creation in ﴿basṭah﴾, that is, He extended, lengthened, and beautified your creation. It was said: the shortest of them was sixty cubits, and the tallest was a hundred cubits. This was said by al-Kalbi and al-Suddi. Abu Hamza al-Yamani said: seventy cubits. Ibn 'Abbas said: eighty cubits. Muqatil said: twelve cubits. Wahb said: the head of one of them was like a great dome, and his eye would be a nest in which hyenas gave birth, and likewise his nostril. If ﴿al-khalq﴾ means the created beings, then ﴿al-khalq﴾ refers to the people of Nuh, or the people of their time, or all people. These are the opinions. It was also said: the increase is in physical bulk, namely reaching what a person's hand can reach when he raises it. It was said: the increase is in strength and robustness, not in bulk. It was also said: the increase in ﴿basṭah﴾ is that they were from one tribe, sharing in strength, supporting one another, and loving one another. It is possible that the meaning is ﴿wa-zadakum basṭah﴾, that is: power and dominance over created beings and control.

﴿"So remember the bounties of God, that you may prosper"﴾. He first reminded them of His favour upon them in making them successors and increasing them in ﴿basṭah﴾, and secondly reminded them of His bounties upon them in general, not restricted to the time of their being made successors. The apparent meaning of ﴿udhkuru﴾ (remember) is that it is from ﴿dhikr﴾ (remembrance), namely that they should not forget His bounties, but that His bounties should be before them in remembrance, in hope that they would prosper. The linking of hope for success to mere remembrance is not evident, so it requires an omitted element on which the hope for success is consequent. Its estimated meaning, God knows best, is: so remember the bounties of God and devote worship to Him alone. Consider His words ﴿Have you come to us that we should worship God alone?﴾. In their mention of ﴿the bounties of God﴾ there is a mention of the Benefactor upon them, who deserves to be worshipped alone and to have all else discarded. It was also said: ﴿udhkuru﴾ here means ﴿ushkuru﴾ (give thanks).

﴿They said: "Have you come to us that we should worship God alone and abandon what our fathers used to worship? So bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful."﴾ The apparent meaning is that they denied that they should abandon their idols and devote worship to God alone, while acknowledging God, out of love for what they had grown up upon and attachment to what they found their fathers upon. It is possible that they were deniers of God, and their words ﴿that we should worship God alone﴾ mean: according to your words, O Hud, and your claim. This was said by Ibn 'Atiyya, who added: the first interpretation is more apparent regarding them and regarding the worshippers of idols, and none of the disbelievers denies the lordship of God except one who claims it for himself, like Pharaoh and Nimrod. End of quote. In Hud's words to his people ﴿So remember the bounties of God﴾ there is a decisive proof that none should be worshipped except the Benefactor, and their idols are inanimate objects with no power over anything at all. Worship is the utmost extent of veneration, so it befits only one from whom the utmost of benefaction proceeds. When he pointed out this argument, and they had no way to answer it, they resorted to pure imitation, saying ﴿Have you come to us that we should worship God alone?﴾. The word ﴿al-maji'﴾ (coming) here may be literal, in that he had been absent from his people, alone in worshipping his Lord, and then God sent him to them, so he came to them from his place of seclusion. It may also be that their saying was in mockery, because they believed that God sends only angels, so it was as if they said: have you come to us from the heaven as an angel comes? They did not mean the literal coming, but rather confronting and intending, as one says: "He went to abuse me," not meaning the literal going. It was as if they said: have you intended us that we should worship God alone, and confronted us with its obligations? In their words ﴿So bring us what you threaten us with﴾ there is evidence that he used to threaten them with the punishment of God if they persisted in disbelief. Their saying this indicates their determination to deny him, their contempt for the matter of prophethood, and their hastening of the punishment, since in their view it would never occur at all. Their earlier words ﴿Indeed, we see you in foolishness﴾ and ﴿And indeed, we think you are among the liars﴾ have already been mentioned. Since they believed him to be a liar, they said ﴿So bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful﴾, meaning: in your prophethood and sending, or in the claim that the punishment will descend upon us.

﴿He said: "There has already fallen upon you from your Lord a ruin (rijs) and wrath"﴾, meaning: it has befallen you and become decreed against you. Zayd ibn Aslam and most of the exegetes said: ﴿al-rijs﴾ here means punishment, from ﴿al-irtijas﴾ (trembling, agitation). Ibn 'Abbas said: it means anger. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: it cannot be punishment, because the punishment had not yet occurred at that time. Al-Qaffal said: it is possible that the increase in disbelief by the rust (rayn) upon the hearts is meant, that is, because of their persistence in disbelief there fell upon you from God a rust upon your hearts, like His words ﴿so it increased them in ruin to their ruin﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125], since ﴿al-rijs﴾ is anger, or rust. Thus His words ﴿There has fallen﴾ are in their literal sense of the past tense, even if the punishment is meant, in which case it is the use of the past tense for the future to express the certainty of its occurrence.

﴿"Do you dispute with me over names that you and your fathers have named, for which God has sent down no authority?"﴾ This is a denunciation by him of their disputing with him over what is not fitting to dispute, namely the mention of words under which there is no referent deserving worship, so the dispute became void for that reason. The meaning of ﴿sammaytumuha﴾ (you named them) is: you and your fathers named them, that is, you and your fathers invented them recently, and they are Samud, Sada, and al-Haba'. Marthad ibn Sa'd mentioned them in his poetry, saying:

The 'Ad disobeyed their messenger, so they became thirsty, the sky would not moisten them.
For them is an idol called Samud, opposite it Sada and al-Haba'.
So the Messenger showed us the path of guidance, and we saw guidance, and blindness was removed.
Indeed the god of Hud is my god; upon God is reliance and hope.

So the dispute at that time would be over the words, not their referents. It is possible that the dispute took place over the named things, which are the idols, in which case he used the names and meant the things named, and this would be by omission of a ﴿mudaf﴾ (governed noun), that is, ﴿Do you dispute with me⦆ concerning the essences of names. The meaning would be: ﴿you named them﴾ as gods, and worshipped them besides God. It was said: they named each idol with a name as they pleased, and they claimed that one of them gives them rain, another cures them of sickness, another accompanies them on journeys, and another brings them provision.

﴿"God has sent down no authority for them"﴾. The clause ﴿mā nazzala Allāh﴾ (God did not send down) is in the position of a ﴿ṣifa﴾ (qualifying description). The meaning is: you have no proof or evidence for that. Here the verb is ﴿nazzala﴾, while in another place it is ﴿anzala﴾, and both are eloquent, and transitivity by doubling (the middle radical) and by the hamza is equivalent.

﴿"So wait, I am with you among those who wait."﴾ This is an extreme of threat and warning, meaning: wait for the outcome of your affair in worshipping other than God and in denying His messenger. This is an extreme of certainty about what will befall them, and that it will occur without doubt.

﴿Then We saved him and those with him by a mercy from Us﴾, meaning those who believed with him, ﴿by a mercy﴾ preceding them from God, and a grace upon them, in that He made them believe, and this was the cause of their salvation from what afflicted their people of punishment.
