End of quote. In Hud's words to his people ﴿So remember the bounties of God﴾ there is a decisive proof that none should be worshipped except the Benefactor, and their idols are inanimate objects with no power over anything at all. Worship is the utmost extent of veneration, so it befits only one from whom the utmost of benefaction proceeds. When he pointed out this argument, and they had no way to answer it, they resorted to pure imitation, saying ﴿Have you come to us that we should worship God alone?﴾. The word ﴿al-maji'﴾ (coming) here may be literal, in that he had been absent from his people, alone in worshipping his Lord, and then God sent him to them, so he came to them from his place of seclusion. It may also be that their saying was in mockery, because they believed that God sends only angels, so it was as if they said: have you come to us from the heaven as an angel comes? They did not mean the literal coming, but rather confronting and intending, as one says: "He went to abuse me," not meaning the literal going. It was as if they said: have you intended us that we should worship God alone, and confronted us with its obligations? In their words ﴿So bring us what you threaten us with﴾ there is evidence that he used to threaten them with the punishment of God if they persisted in disbelief. Their saying this indicates their determination to deny him, their contempt for the matter of prophethood, and their hastening of the punishment, since in their view it would never occur at all. Their earlier words ﴿Indeed, we see you in foolishness﴾ and ﴿And indeed, we think you are among the liars﴾ have already been mentioned. Since they believed him to be a liar, they said ﴿So bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful﴾, meaning: in your prophethood and sending, or in the claim that the punishment will descend upon us.

﴿He said: "There has already fallen upon you from your Lord a ruin (rijs) and wrath"﴾, meaning: it has befallen you and become decreed against you. Zayd ibn Aslam and most of the exegetes said: ﴿al-rijs﴾ here means punishment, from ﴿al-irtijas﴾ (trembling, agitation). Ibn 'Abbas said: it means anger. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: it cannot be punishment, because the punishment had not yet occurred at that time. Al-Qaffal said: it is possible that the increase in disbelief by the rust (rayn) upon the hearts is meant, that is, because of their persistence in disbelief there fell upon you from God a rust upon your hearts, like His words ﴿so it increased them in ruin to their ruin﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125], since ﴿al-rijs﴾ is anger, or rust. Thus His words ﴿There has fallen﴾ are in their literal sense of the past tense, even if the punishment is meant, in which case it is the use of the past tense for the future to express the certainty of its occurrence.

﴿"Do you dispute with me over names that you and your fathers have named, for which God has sent down no authority?"﴾ This is a denunciation by him of their disputing with him over what is not fitting to dispute, namely the mention of words under which there is no referent deserving worship, so the dispute became void for that reason. The meaning of ﴿sammaytumuha﴾ (you named them) is: you and your fathers named them, that is, you and your fathers invented them recently, and they are Samud, Sada, and al-Haba'. Marthad ibn Sa'd mentioned them in his poetry, saying:

The 'Ad disobeyed their messenger, so they became thirsty, the sky would not moisten them.
For them is an idol called Samud, opposite it Sada and al-Haba'.
So the Messenger showed us the path of guidance, and we saw guidance, and blindness was removed.
Indeed the god of Hud is my god; upon God is reliance and hope.

So the dispute at that time would be over the words, not their referents. It is possible that the dispute took place over the named things, which are the idols, in which case he used the names and meant the things named, and this would be by omission of a ﴿mudaf﴾ (governed noun), that is, ﴿Do you dispute with me⦆ concerning the essences of names. The meaning would be: ﴿you named them﴾ as gods, and worshipped them besides God. It was said: they named each idol with a name as they pleased, and they claimed that one of them gives them rain, another cures them of sickness, another accompanies them on journeys, and another brings them provision.

﴿"God has sent down no authority for them"﴾. The clause ﴿mā nazzala Allāh﴾ (God did not send down) is in the position of a ﴿ṣifa﴾ (qualifying description). The meaning is: you have no proof or evidence for that. Here the verb is ﴿nazzala﴾, while in another place it is ﴿anzala﴾, and both are eloquent, and transitivity by doubling (the middle radical) and by the hamza is equivalent.

﴿"So wait, I am with you among those who wait."﴾ This is an extreme of threat and warning, meaning: wait for the outcome of your affair in worshipping other than God and in denying His messenger. This is an extreme of certainty about what will befall them, and that it will occur without doubt.

﴿Then We saved him and those with him by a mercy from Us﴾, meaning those who believed with him, ﴿by a mercy﴾ preceding them from God, and a grace upon them, in that He made them believe, and this was the cause of their salvation from what afflicted their people of punishment.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 66–72 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And We cut off the last remnant of those who denied Our signs﴾: this is a metaphor (kinaya) for their total annihilation by destruction through punishment. The discussion of dabir (the last remnant, the tail end, of a people) has already occurred in His words: ﴿So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off﴾ [al-An'am: 45]. His words ﴿who denied﴾ are an alert to the reason for the cutting off of their remnant. His words ﴿Our signs﴾ are evidence that Hud had miracles (mu'jizat), but they were not specified for us by name.

﴿And they were not believers﴾: this sentence emphasizes His words ﴿who denied Our signs﴾. It may also be a report from Allah, exalted is He, that they were among those whom Allah knew would not believe if they remained alive; that is, they were not among those who would accept faith at all. Had Allah known that they would believe, He would have spared them. This is because one who denies the signs may afterward believe in them and his condition may become good; but as for the one whom Allah has sealed with disbelief, he will never believe, ever. In this there is an implicit reference to those among them who did believe, such as Marthad ibn Sa'd and those who were saved along with Hud, peace be upon him. It is as if He said: "And We cut off the remnant of the people who denied, from among them, and they were not like those of them who believed," so as to indicate that the destruction was specific to the deniers and that Allah saved the believers. This is what al-Zamakhshari said. The commentators have mentioned here the story of the destruction of 'Ad and have mentioned in it matters that have no connection to the wording of the Qur'an and were not authentically related from the Messenger (ﷺ), so I have passed over mention of them entirely. As for what has a connection to the wording of the Qur'an, it will come in its appropriate places, God willing.

**Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah al-A'raf, verse 73:**

﴿And to Thamud, their brother Salih. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him."﴾

*Thamud*: the name of a tribe, named after their eldest forefather, who was Thamud, the brother of Jadis. They were the two sons of Jathir ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh (peace be upon him). Their dwellings were al-Hijr, between the Hijaz and al-Sham, extending to Wadi al-Qura. It is also said that they were named Thamud after the scarcity of water (*thamad*) they had, *thamad* meaning little water. The poet said:

*"Judge as the judgment of the girl of the tribe when she looked at a white-winged dove coming to the little water."*

The Thamud were Arabs living in ease and abundance of livelihood, but they opposed the command of Allah, worshipped other than Him, and spread corruption. So Allah sent to them Salih as a prophet, from among the most central of them in lineage and the best of them in noble descent. He called them to Allah until he grew gray-haired, and only a few followed him. This was stated by Wahb. Allah sent him when he was approaching puberty. When his people perished, he moved with those who were with him to Makkah, and they remained with him until they died. Their graves are between Dar al-Nadwa and al-Hijr.

Salih is Salih ibn Asif ibn Kashih ibn Arum ibn Thamud ibn Jathir ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh. Thus he was genealogically traced by the noble genealogist al-Jawwani, who was the final authority in the science of lineage (*'ilm al-nasab*). In some tafsirs, between Salih and Asif, an extra father, Ubayd, has been inserted, so they said: Salih ibn Ubayd ibn Asif. There is also a deficiency in the forefathers, and a corruption of Jathir into "Abir" in their saying. Al-Jawwani said in the *al-Muqaddima al-Fadiliyya*: The descendants of Jathir ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh and Jadis, and the descendants of Thamud ibn Jathir, are Fallakh, Hay'a, Tanuq and Arum, and from his offspring is Salih the Prophet (ﷺ), ibn Asif ibn Kashih ibn Arum ibn Thamud.

Ibn Wathhab (?) and al-A'mash read: (*wa-ila Thamudin*) with a kasra on the dal and tanwin, treated as declinable in the whole Qur'an. They took it as the name of a clan (*hayy*). The majority did not allow it to take the declension (*sarf*), taking it as the name of a tribe. The brotherhood here is one of kinship, because his lineage and theirs goes back to Thamud ibn Jathir. Each of these prophets, Nuh, Hud and Salih, came with the same command to worship Allah and to alert that there is no god but Him, since their people worshipped idols and took gods alongside Allah, as Quraysh and the Arabs did. So in these narratives there is a rebuke and a warning to them that they may be struck with the like of what befell those people, of total destruction through punishment. The story of Nuh was famous and spread throughout the horizons. The stories of Hud and Salih were well known among the Arabs and others, to the extent that the ancient poets of the Jahiliyya mentioned them and compared the corrupters of their own people to the corrupters of the people of Hud and Salih. One of their ancient poets said:

*"Among us are people who will never build for their people, even if their people build what they corrupt, they perish."*

*"They became like Qayl ibn Anz among his clan, when they were destroyed by what 'Ad had woven for them."*

*"Or after him, like Qudar when people followed him in error, they too perished."*

It is said that Ibn Anz was from the people of Hud, and his report will come when the mention of the sending of the wind on the people of Hud comes, if Allah wills. Qudar is the son of Salif, the slayer of Salih's she-camel, and his report will come, if Allah wills.

﴿Indeed there has come to you a clear sign (*bayyina*) from your Lord﴾, that is: a manifest and evident sign and a witness to the truth of my prophethood. This attribute (*bayyina*) became so frequently used as a noun in the Qur'an that it governed verbs, as in His saying: "until there came to them the clear sign" and His saying: "with the clear proofs and the scriptures" [Al 'Imran: 184]. The meaning is: the clear sign, and with the clear signs. It is close to being like *al-Abtah* and *al-Abraq* (place names), since the relative is hardly ever stated with them. His saying: ﴿Indeed there has come to you a clear sign from your Lord﴾ is as if it were an answer to their saying: ﴿Bring us what you claim, as a sign showing your truthfulness, and that you are sent to us﴾ [al-A'raf: 77]. And ﴿from your Lord﴾ is connected to *ja'at-kum* (has come to you), or it is in the position of an attribute of a sign, by an omitted supposition, that is: from the signs of your Lord.

﴿This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you﴾. When He had been vague in His saying ﴿Indeed there has come to you a clear sign from your Lord﴾ (p-328), He made clear what the sign is. It is as if it were said to him: what is the clear sign? He said: ﴿This is the she-camel of Allah﴾, and He attributed it to Allah as an honour and a specification, like "the House of Allah" and "the Spirit of Allah." And because He created it without the intermediary of a male and a female, and because no one owns it but Him, and because it is a proof against the people, and because He placed in it signs, He mentioned it in the story of the people of Salih. ﴿For you﴾ is an explanation of the one for whom it is a sign obligating belief upon him, and they are Thamud, because they witnessed it, while the rest of people were informed about it. It is as if He said: "for you" specifically. The word ﴿sign﴾ (*ayah*) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*). Its governing element is *ha'* (the particle of pointing), with what it carries of the meaning of drawing attention, or the demonstrative noun with what it carries of the meaning of indication, or an implied verb indicated by the sentence, as if it were said: "look at it while it is a sign." These are three opinions mentioned in the science of grammar.

Al-Hasan said: it was a she-camel that was chosen from among their camels and was not milked. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said that he took a she-camel from the rest of the camels, and Allah made for it a drinking day, and for them a drinking day, and the sign lay in its drinking and its milking. It is said: he brought it out of his own accord. The majority said: it was a sign that was asked for. When he warned and admonished them, they asked him for a sign. He said: "What sign do you want?" They said: "Come out with us to our festival on a known day of the year, and call upon your God and we will call upon our gods. If yours is answered for you, we will follow you, and if ours is answered for us, you will follow us." Salih said: "Yes." So he went out with them, and they called upon their idols and asked them to answer, but they did not answer them. Then their chief, Jund'a ibn Amr ibn Jawwas, pointed to a single rock on the side of the mountain called al-Kathiba, and said: "Bring out for us from this rock a she-camel that is pregnant, hollow-sided, large-hoofed and ten-months pregnant (*'ushara*)." The *mukhtarija* is the one that resembles the Bactrian camels. So Salih (peace be upon him) took their covenant: "If I do that, you will surely believe and surely confirm." They said: "Yes." So he prayed two rak'as and called upon his Lord, and the rock quaked like a woman in labour with her child, then it moved and split open to a she-camel as they had described, whose size no one knows except Allah, while they were watching. Then it gave birth to a young camel (*saqb*) like it in size. Jund'a believed, along with a group of his people. The nobles of Thamud wanted to believe, but Dhu'ab ibn Amr ibn Labid and al-Hubab, the companions of their idols, and Rayyan, son of their soothsayer, who were among the nobles of Thamud, forbade them. The story of this she-camel and its young camel is well known among the pre-Islamic Arabs, and they mentioned the young camel in their poetry. One of them, describing people who were killed together in a battle, said:

*"As if a cloud had struck them, its thunderbolts for its birds are a creeping."*

*"Above them cried the young camel of the sky, fleeing, with its harness not stripped, nor was the spoil taken."*

Abu Musa al-Ash'ari said: I came to the land of Thamud and measured the chest of the she-camel, and found it to be sixty cubits.

﴿So leave her to eat in the land of Allah﴾. When He attributed the she-camel to Allah, He attributed the place of its grazing to Allah, since the land and what grows in it belong to Him, may He be exalted, not to you, nor is its growth from you. In this statement there is an indication that this she-camel is a blessing from Allah whose benefit is obtained without the hardship of providing fodder or sustenance, and this is the way of camels, as came in the hadith: "He said: What about a lost camel? He said: What is it to you? It has its water-skin and its sandal (its feet are its protection). It comes to water and eats the trees until its owner finds it." The word ﴿eat﴾ (*ta'kul*) is apocopated (*majzum*) as an answer to the imperative. Abu Ja'far, in one narration, read (*ta'kulu*) with a *raf* (nominative), and its position is then a circumstantial clause. The she-camel was with its young one grazing the trees and drinking water. She came to the water on alternate days, and when it was her day, she would put her head into the well and would not raise it until she had drunk all that was in it. Then she would step aside, and they would milk as much as they wished until their vessels were full, and they would drink and store.

﴿And do not touch her with harm, lest a painful punishment seize you﴾. He forbade them from touching her with any kind of harm. This is a warning from the lesser to the greater (*tanbih bi-l-adna 'ala al-a'la*): if He forbade them from touching her with harm out of honour for the sign of Allah, then His prohibition against slaughtering her, hamstringing her, and preventing her from water and pasture is more fitting and more worthy. The words ﴿touch﴾ and ﴿seize﴾ here are a metaphor. This is a severe threat to whoever touches her with harm. The painful punishment is what befell them when they hamstrung her, and what He prepared for them in the Hereafter.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 74:

﴿And remember when He made you successors after ʿĀd and settled you in the land, taking for yourselves palaces in its plains and hewing out the mountains as houses. So remember the bounties of Allah, and do not commit corruption in the land, causing mischief.﴾ (p-329) Ṣāliḥ reminded his people with what Hūd had used to remind his people. He first mentioned particular blessings, namely that they were made successors after the nation that preceded them, and Hūd mentioned to his people what they had been singled out for, namely the increase in stature in creation; and Ṣāliḥ mentioned to his people what they had been singled out for, namely taking palaces from the plains and hewing out the mountains as houses. Then he mentioned general blessings by his saying ﴿So remember the bounties of Allah﴾. The meaning of ﴿and settled you in the land﴾ is that He caused you to descend in it and dwell in it. The *mabaʾah* (dwelling place) is a residence in the land, and it derives from *bāʾa*, meaning "returned," and its mention has preceded. "The land" here refers to al-Ḥijr, the area between the Ḥijāz and Syria. And *tattakhidhūna* (taking) is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) or an explanation of His saying ﴿and settled you in the land﴾, so it has no place in terms of i'rāb (grammatical analysis). The apparent meaning is that some of the plains they took and built palaces in, that is, they built palaces in them and established them there, and they did not occupy all their plains with palaces. Al-Zamakhsharī said: ﴿from its plains palaces﴾ means they build them from the softness of the earth, by what they make from it of *al-rihṣ* (mortar/plaster), *al-labin* (mud bricks), and *al-ājurr* (baked bricks), meaning that the palaces they built had parts made of the softness of the earth, like *al-jayyār* (plaster/mortar), baked brick, and gypsum (*al-jiṣṣ*). This is like His saying ﴿And the people of Mūsā took after him a calf made from their ornaments﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 148], meaning that the image's material was from ornaments, just as the palaces' material was from the plains of the earth and the parts from which they were made. The apparent meaning of *al-ittikhādh* here is making/fashioning, so *tattakhidhūna* takes one object. It was said that it takes two objects, and the prepositional phrase is the second. Al-Ḥasan read ﴿wa-tanḥitūna﴾ with a fatḥah on the ḥāʾ. Al-Zamakhsharī added that he read (*wa-tanḥātūna*) with the fatḥah extended, saying, like His saying:

*yanbāʿu min dhafrī ghaḍūbin jasratin*

End of quotation. Ibn Muṣarrif read it with a yāʾ from below and a kasrah on the ḥāʾ, and Abū Mālik read it with a bāʾ from below and a fatḥah on the ḥāʾ. Whoever reads with a yāʾ, it is an *iltifāt* (shift of person). ﴿Buyūtan﴾ is in the accusative as a *ḥāl muqaddarah* (anticipated circumstantial clause), since the mountains were not houses at the time of hewing, like your saying: "Carve this reed for me as a pen, and sew this for me as a robe (*qibāʾ*)." It was said that it is a second object by implicitly making *wa-tanḥitūna* carry the meaning of *wa-tattakhidhūna*. It was also said that it is an object of *tanḥitūna*, and ﴿al-jibāla﴾ is in the accusative by dropping *min*, meaning "from the mountains." Al-Aʿmash read (*tiʿthaw*) with a kasrah on the tāʾ, based on their saying *anta tiʿlamu*, and it is a dialect. ﴿Mufsidīn﴾ is an emphatic circumstantial clause (ḥāl muʾakkidah). Ibn ʿAbbās said: the palaces were for their summer, and the houses in the mountains were for their winter. It was said: they hewed the mountains because of the length of their lifespans, as the palaces would be ruined before their death. Wahb said: a man would build a structure, and a hundred years would pass over it and it would fall into ruin; then he would rebuild it, and a hundred years would pass over it and it would fall into ruin; then he would rebuild it, and a hundred years would pass over it and it would fall into ruin, so that annoyed them, and they took the mountains as houses.

The chieftains of his people who were arrogant said to those who had been deemed weak, those among them who believed: "Do you know that Salih is one sent from his Lord?" ﴿قالَ المَلَأُ الَّذِينَ اسْتَكْبَرُوا مِن قَوْمِهِ لِلَّذِينَ اسْتُضْعِفُوا لِمَن آمَنَ مِنهم أتَعْلَمُونَ أنَّ صالِحًا مُرْسَلٌ مِن رَبِّهِ﴾ Ibn 'Amir recited (وقالَ المَلَأُ) with a conjunctive waw (wa-qala al-mala'), while the majority recited (قالَ) without the waw. ﴿الَّذِينَ اسْتَكْبَرُوا﴾ (alladhina istakbaru, "who were arrogant") is a descriptive qualifier of al-mala' (the chieftains), either for specification, since among their nobles there were those who believed, such as Jundu' ibn 'Amr, or for censure. ﴿اسْتَكْبَرُوا﴾ (istakbaru) may mean that they sought grandeur for themselves, and it derives from al-kibr (greatness/pride), so that istaf'ala denotes seeking, which is its usual function. Or istaf'ala may have the meaning of fa'ala, i.e., they became great because of abundance of wealth and status, in which case it is like 'ajiba and musta'jaba (both meaning "to be amazed"). ﴿اسْتُضْعِفُوا﴾ (ustud'ifu, "were deemed weak") means that the leaders of the disbelievers regarded them as weak and humiliated them, and they were the common people, the followers of the messengers. (liman) "for those who" is a substitution (badal, a grammatical apposition) for alladhina ustud'ifu. The pronoun in (minhum) "among them": if it refers to the oppressed (al-mustad'afin), then it is a partial substitution (badal ba'd min kull, substitution of part for whole), and the alladhina ustud'ifu are then two groups, believers and disbelievers. If it refers to (qawmihi) "his people", then it is a complete substitution (badal kull min kull), the oppression is restricted to the believers, the alladhina ustud'ifu are a single group, and man amana serves as an explanation of the oppressed from among his people. The lam in (lilladhina) "to those who" is the lam of communication (li-l-tabligh), and the statement spoken is an interrogative (istifham) in the manner of mockery and belittling. In their saying ﴿مِن رَبِّهِ﴾ (min rabbihi, "from his Lord") there is a specification of Salih, and they did not say "from our Lord" nor "from your Lord."

They replied: "Indeed we are believers in that with which he has been sent." ﴿قالُوا إنّا بِما أُرْسِلَ بِهِ مُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ This is the answer of the oppressed. Their turning away from saying "he is sent" (huwa mursal) to saying "indeed we believe in that with which he has been sent" is most eloquent, since the matter of his prophethood is known, clear, and accepted, and no doubt enters it because of the extraordinary, great miracle he brought. So there is no need for him to be asked about his mission, nor for anyone to inquire about knowledge of his being sent. Therefore they informed them that they believe in what he was sent with, because after the clarity of his mission nothing is required except affirmation of what he brought. Their statement also included the knowledge that he is sent from God, exalted is He.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 76–79 (part 1 of 2):

﴿The arrogant among his people said: "Indeed, we disbelieve in what you believe."﴾ "What you believed in" is, in meaning, what he was sent with, but in wording it is more general. They intended the rejection, since the believers had made it known and taken it as settled.

﴿So they hamstrung the she-camel.﴾ The hamstringing is attributed to all of them, although it was carried out by some of them, because her slaughter was by collective agreement and consensus. It is related that Qudar did not hamstring her except after consulting the men, the women and the boys, and they all agreed to it. The reason for her slaughter was that when the heat came she would stand at the top of the valley, and their livestock would flee from her and descend into its bottom. When the cold came she would remain in the bottom of the valley, and their herds would flee to its top. This was difficult for them. She also used to drink their water entirely, while they milked her as much as God willed, until they grew weary of her and said: "What shall we do with the milk? Water is more beloved to us than it." Salih once said to them: "Indeed, in this month a child will be born whose birth will be your destruction at his hands." So a child was born to ten men, and the nine of them slaughtered their children, and the tenth, Salif son of Qudar, survived. Qudar was red, blue-eyed and short, and for this reason one of the pre-Islamic poets said:

"She will bear you boys, ill-omened, all of them like the red one of ʿAd; then she nurses and weans."

The commentators said: this is an error; it should be "the red one of Thamud," who was Qudar. He would grow in one day as much as others grew in a year. Whenever the nine saw him they said: "If our sons had lived, they would have been like this." Because of Salih's words they killed their children, and so they agreed to kill him. They lay in wait for him in a cave in order to ambush him. The account of the ambush and what befell them will come in Surat al-Naml, God willing.

It is also related that the cause of the hamstringing was that two women of Thamud, enemies of Salih, namely ʿUnayza daughter of Ghanm, the mother of Mijlaz, wife of Duʾab son of ʿAmr, who was called Umm Ghanm, an old woman with beautiful daughters and wealth in camels, cattle and sheep; and Sadūf daughter of al-Muhayya, a beautiful and wealthy woman with many livestock, summoned Qudar to hamstring her, in exchange for which ʿUnayza would give him whichever of her daughters he wished. He was powerful and well-protected among his people. Sadūf summoned a man of Thamud called al-Hubab to the same end and offered herself to him if he did it, but he refused. So she summoned a cousin of hers called Musaddaʿ son of Muharrij son of al-Muhayya for this purpose and offered herself to him. Qudar and Musaddaʿ responded and enticed seven men, so they became nine men. They watched for the she-camel when she came back from the water. Qudar hid at the base of one rock and Musaddaʿ at the base of another. She passed by Musaddaʿ, who shot her with an arrow which lodged in the muscle of her leg. Umm Ghanm ʿUnayza came out with her daughter, who was among the most beautiful of women, and unveiled her before Qudar. Then the she-camel passed by him, and he attacked her with the sword and cut her hamstring. She fell and gave one cry, and he stabbed her in the throat and slaughtered her. It is narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that "when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by al-Hijr during the expedition of Tabuk, he commanded them not to drink from its water nor to draw water from it. They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we have already cooked and kneaded [dough with it].' So he commanded them to throw away that cooked food and the dough, to pour out that water, and he commanded them to draw water from the well which the she-camel of Salih used to come to drink from."

And it is narrated from Jabir that "when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by al-Hijr during the expedition of Tabuk, he said to his companions: 'None of you should enter the town, nor drink from its water, nor enter upon these punished people unless you are weeping, lest there befall you what befell them.'"

And in another hadith: "He passed by a grave and said: 'Do you know what this is?' They said: 'No.' He said: 'This is the grave of Abu Righal, who was Abu Thaqif. He was from Thamud, and the calamity struck his people, while he was in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), and he was safe. When he came out of the Sacred Precinct, there befell him what befell them, so he was buried here, and a golden branch was placed with him.'" He said: "So the people hastened with their swords and dug until they brought out the branch."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 76–79 (part 2 of 2):

It is narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that "when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by al-Hijr during the expedition of Tabuk, he commanded them not to drink from its water nor to draw water from it. They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we have already cooked and kneaded [dough with it].' So he commanded them to throw away that cooked food and the dough, to pour out that water, and he commanded them to draw water from the well which the she-camel of Salih used to come to drink from."

In accordance with this hadith, Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm held, in his (school of) thought, that it is not permissible to perform wudu with the water of the land of Thamud, except if it is from the spring which the she-camel used to come to.

And it is narrated from Jabir that "when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by al-Hijr during the expedition of Tabuk, he said to his companions: 'None of you should enter the town, nor drink from its water, nor enter upon these punished people unless you are weeping, lest there befall you what befell them.'"

And in another hadith: "He passed by a grave and said: 'Do you know what this is?' They said: 'No.' He said: 'This is the grave of Abu Righal, who was Abu Thaqif. He was from Thamud, and the calamity struck his people, while he was in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), and he was safe. When he came out of the Sacred Precinct, there befell him what befell them, so he was buried here, and a golden branch was placed with him.'" He said: "So the people hastened with their swords and dug until they brought out the branch."

[p-333] He is Lut (Lot) son of Haran, brother of Ibrahim (Abraham), peace be upon him, and Nahur. They are the sons of Tarih son of Nahur, and the account of his lineage has already been presented. His statement "they are the people of Sodom and the rest of the overturned cities (al-mu'tafikah)" means that God sent him to them. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: God sent him to a nation called Sodom. (Lut) is in the accusative by an implied verb, "and We sent," coordinated with the prophets before him. (Idh) is governed by "We sent." Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyyah also allowed that it is in the accusative governed by an implied "remember" (udhkur). Al-Zamakhshari added that (idh) is a substitute for Lut, meaning: "Remember the time when he said to his people." The discussion has already been given about whether (idh) can be used as a direct object of "remember," and that this is a deviation from its usual use. The interrogative is for the purpose of denunciation, rebuke, condemnation, and making them stop from this ugly act. The "indecency" (al-fahisha) here is the mounting of males among human beings in their backsides. Since the ugliness of this act is well known and fixed in minds, its indecency is mentioned with the definite article (al-). Or the (al) may be for the whole class, as an intensification, as if because of its extreme ugliness all indecencies are included in it. Since the Arabs were far removed from this act entirely, [the Qur'an did not say it in that way]. This differs from fornication (zina), for He said about it: ﴿And do not approach fornication; indeed, it is an indecency﴾ [al-Isra: 32], where it is mentioned indefinitely, meaning "an indecency among indecencies." Many Arabs used to commit it, and they did not find its doing or mention in their poetry objectionable. The negated sentence indicates that they were the first to commit this ugly act and that they were its originators. The emphasis in (min ahad) lies in that (min) is added to stress the negation of the category, and in the use of the general term "the worlds" in the plural.

Umar ibn Dinar said: "No male was seen mounting a male before the people of Lut." It is narrated that some of them used to mount others. Al-Hasan said: "They used to mount strangers. Their land, al-Urdunn (Jordan), was visited from every side because of its fertility. Iblis (Satan), in the form of a youth, said to them: 'If you want to repel the strangers, do this to them.' So he enabled them over himself as a lesson. Then it spread, and they made lawful what they made lawful." Whoever held that the meaning is "those of their time" has gone too far, and whoever held that the meaning of "what preceded you" is "to its practice and its witnessing" has also gone too far. Calling this act "indecency" is evidence that it falls under the same rule as fornication: the married offender is stoned and the unmarried offender is flogged (the muhsan being the one who is married). 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr did this. Seven of them were brought to him; he stoned four who were married and flogged three, while Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas were with him and did not object. This is the view of al-Shafi'i. Malik said: the offender is stoned whether married or not, and likewise the passive partner if he has reached puberty. According to him, the married one is stoned, and the unmarried one is disciplined (ta'zir, discretionary punishment) and imprisoned. This is the view of Ibn 'Atiyyah, Ibn al-Musayyab, al-Nakha'i, and others. It is also narrated from Malik that the offender receives discretionary punishment whether married or not, and this is the view of Abu Hanifa. Khalid ibn al-Walid burned a man called al-Fuja'a who did this deed, and that was by the opinion of Abu Bakr and Ali. It is also said that the companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) were unanimous in this, and Ali ibn Abi Talib was among them. It is narrated that Ibn al-Zubayr burned them in his time, and Khalid al-Qasri in Iraq, and Hisham.

Here, (ma sabaqakum) is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya) referring to the subject [of the verb], or to (al-fahisha), because in (sabaqakum biha) there is a pronoun referring to them and a pronoun referring to it. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is an independent new sentence (mustaʼnafa). He first denounced them by saying (atata'unna al-fahisha), then rebuked them for it, saying: "You are the first to do it." Or it is an answer to an implied question, as if they had said: "Why should we not do it?" So he said: "No one has preceded you in it, so do not do what no one has preceded you in." Al-Zamakhshari also said: the (ba') is for transitivity, from your saying "sabaqtuhu bi'l-kura" (I outran him with the ball) when you struck the ball before him. And from it is his statement, peace be upon him: "'Ukkasha outran you with it." End of quote. But the meaning of transitivity here is very problematic, because the transitive (ba') in a verb that is transitive to one object makes the first object perform that action on what the (ba') governs; it is like the hamza (causative). The explanation is that when you say (sakaktu al-hajara bi'l-hajar), its meaning is "I caused the stone to strike the stone," i.e., you made the stone strike the stone. Likewise, (dafa'tu Zaydan bi-'Amr 'an Khalid) means "I caused Zayd to repel 'Amr from Khalid," i.e., you made Zayd repel 'Amr from Khalid. So the first object has an effect on the second. This meaning cannot be achieved here, because it is not valid to assume "I caused Zayd to outrun the ball," except by a strained metaphor, namely that your striking the ball was the first cause of a strike that had preceded it in time, so they did not coincide.

﴿Indeed, you approach men with desire instead of women. Rather, you are a people who exceed all bounds.﴾ This explains His words: ﴿Do you commit an abomination?﴾ [Al-A'raf: 80]. The verb *ta'tuna* (you approach) here is taken from the phrase *atā al-mar'ah*, meaning he had intercourse with the woman. The form is interrogative, in the sense of rebuke and denunciation. Nafi' and Hafs read *innakum* (indeed you) as a declarative, new sentence. *Shahwatan* (out of desire) is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*). This is the view of al-Hawfi and Ibn 'Atiyya, and al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa' also permitted it. The meaning is: aroused, following desire, not heeding its ugliness. It may also be a accusative of purpose (*maf'ūl min ajlih*). This is the view of al-Zamakhshari, and Abu al-Baqa' began with it. The meaning is: for the sake of appetite, with nothing moving you to this except mere desire. No blame is greater than this, because it describes them as beasts, with no motive from reason such as seeking offspring or the like. *Min dūn al-nisā'* (instead of women) is in the position of a circumstantial phrase, meaning: separate from women. Al-Hawfi said: *min dūn al-nisā'* is connected to *shahwah*. *Bal* (rather) here marks a shift from one account to another, indicating that they transgress the limits in their aggression. It was also said that it is a turning away from their affirmation and rebuke, or from informing about them with this shameful sin to passing judgment on them by the state that gives rise to ugly deeds and calls to following desires, which is excess (*isrāf*). This is excess that corrupts. Since excess was their habit, they exceeded even in satisfying desire and went beyond what was customary to something else. Compare: ﴿Rather, you are a people who transgress﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 166]. It was also said that *bal* turns away from an omitted clause, whose supposed sense is: "You have not been just; rather, you..." Al-Kirmani said: *bal* is a rejection of an answer they might claim as an excuse, meaning: you have no excuse and no argument. ﴿Rather, you...﴾. Here the phrase is ﴿musrifūn﴾ (excessive) in the form of the active participle, to indicate permanence, and to match the rhyme endings of preceding verses, which close with nouns. In al-Naml the phrase is ﴿tajhalūn﴾ (you are ignorant) in the imperfect, to indicate the renewal of ignorance in them, and to match the preceding verse endings, which close with verbs.

﴿Yet the answer of his people was only that they said: "Expel them from your town."﴾ The pronoun in ﴿akhrijūhum﴾ (expel them) refers to Lot and those who believed in him. Since this surah was revealed after surah al-Naml, the thing that the explicit text explains in al-Naml was left implicit here. In al-Naml it is His words: ﴿Expel the family of Lot from your town﴾ [Al-Naml: 56]. The "family of Lot" were his two daughters, Ra'wa' and Raifa', and those believers who followed him. It was also said that with him there were only his two daughters, as He said: ﴿We found in it no house of the submitting ones﴾ [Al-Dhariyat: 36]. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the pronoun refers to the family of Lot and his household, even though no mention of them had preceded, since the meaning requires them. Al-Hasan read *jawāb* with the nominative (*jawābu*). End of quotation. Here the conjunction is *wāw* (and), and it bears one of its three possible senses, that of immediate succession, which is intended in al-Naml in His words: ﴿you are ignorant﴾ [Al-Naml: 55], followed by ﴿then﴾ [Al-Naml: 56]. And in al-'Ankabut: ﴿and you commit in your gatherings what is abhorrent, then﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 29]. Immediacy here is an intensification of the rejection, since they did not delay in answering. Rather, they rushed to answer quickly, and the answer did not correspond to his words. This is because when he denounced their abomination, magnified its matter, and attributed to them excess, they hurried to say something unrelated to his speech, namely the command to expel. A parallel is the answer of the people of Abraham, who said: ﴿Burn him and support your gods﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 68], until he disgraced them with His words: ﴿Fie upon you and upon what you worship besides God! Will you not reason?﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 67]. So they gave an answer that did not match his speech. The town is Sodom. It was named after Sodom son of Baqim, whose name is proverbially used for hardened rulers. Lot migrated with his paternal uncle Abraham from the land of Babylon. Abraham settled in the land of Palestine, and settled Lot in al-Urdunn (Jordan).

﴿Indeed they are people who purify themselves.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: they keep themselves clean from anal intercourse with men and women. It was also said: they approach women during their times of purity. Ibn Bahr said: they watch for the purity of women and then have intercourse with them during it. It was also said: they keep themselves pure from our deeds. This is the meaning of the statement of Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. It was also said: they wash from major impurity and purify themselves with water. They reproached them with this. This type of expression is called in the science of rhetoric (*'ilm al-bayān*) *ta'rīḍ* (allusion), which is a speech that suggests blame while actually praising, like the verse:

*"And there is no fault in them, except that their swords are notched from the clashing of battalions."*

For this reason Ibn 'Abbas said: they disparaged them with what is praised about them. The apparent view is that His words *innahum* (indeed they) are a reason for the expulsion, meaning: because they do not agree with us in what we are upon. Whoever does not agree with us must be expelled. Al-Zamakhshari said: their words ﴿Indeed they are people who purify themselves﴾ are mockery of them and of their purity from abominations, and boasting of the filth they were in, just as Satan says of the sinners to some of the pious when they admonish them: "Keep this ascetic away from us, and relieve us of this self-denier."

﴿So We saved him and his family, except his wife, who was among those who remained behind.﴾ That is: ﴿We saved him and his family﴾ from the punishment that befell his people. His family were the believers with him, or his two daughters, according to the disagreement mentioned above. He excepted his wife from his family, so she was not saved. Her name was Wahila. She was a hypocrite, concealing disbelief and allied with the people of Sodom. The meaning of ﴿among those who remained behind﴾ is among those who stayed in their homes and were destroyed. On this view, His words ﴿was among those who remained behind﴾ are an explanation and emphasis of what the exception implies, namely that God did not save her. Abu 'Ubayda said: ﴿except his wife﴾ suffices to show that she was not saved. Then he began describing her by a quality that has no bearing on salvation or destruction, namely that she was among those advanced in years who lived on from one era to another, so she was *ghābira*, that is, advanced in age, as in the verse: *"except an old woman among those who remained behind"*, until she died along with her people. End of quotation. ﴿Among those who remained behind﴾ uses the masculine plural to include the feminine, giving precedence to males over females. Al-Zajjaj said: among those who were absent from salvation, so it is an emphasis of what the exception implies. End of quotation. *Kānat* (she was) means "became," or "was in God's knowledge," or remains on its apparent sense, restricting her being left behind to past time. There are several views.

﴿And We rained upon them a rain﴾. *Amṭarnā* (We rained) is construed with the sense of *arsalnā* (We sent), which is why it takes *'alā* (upon), as in His words: ﴿So We rained upon them stones from heaven﴾. The "rain" here is stones. It is mentioned in more than one verse that the earth swallowed them and stones rained upon them. It was also said that the overturned cities were five towns, or six, or four. Gabriel uprooted them with his wing, lifted them until the people of heaven heard the braying of donkeys and the crowing of roosters, then he reversed them, making their upper part lower, and sent them down to the earth. Stones followed them despite this, and destroyed whoever was among them on a journey, or outside the lands. Lot's wife, when she heard the roar, said: "O my people!" and turned around, and a rock struck her and killed her. The apparent view is that the rain covered them all. It was also said that the people of the cities were swallowed by the earth, and stones rained upon those of them who were travelling. Mujahid was asked whether any of them had been saved. He said: No, except a man who was a merchant in Mecca. The stone stood still over him for forty days until he finished his trade, and when he left the sacred precinct (*Ḥaram*) it struck him and he died. Their number was one hundred thousand.

Since this surah was revealed after surah al-Naml, the thing that the explicit text explains in al-Naml was left implicit here. In al-Naml it is His words: ﴿Expel the family of Lot from your town﴾ [Al-Naml: 56]. The "family of Lot" were his two daughters, Ra'wa' and Raifa', and those believers who followed him. It was also said that with him there were only his two daughters, as He said: ﴿We found in it no house of the submitting ones﴾ [Al-Dhariyat: 36]. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the pronoun refers to the family of Lot and his household, even though no mention of them had preceded, since the meaning requires them. Al-Hasan read *jawāb* with the nominative (*jawābu*). End of quotation. Here the conjunction is *wāw* (and), and it bears one of its three possible senses, that of immediate succession, which is intended in al-Naml in His words: ﴿you are ignorant﴾ [Al-Naml: 55], followed by ﴿then﴾ [Al-Naml: 56]. And in al-'Ankabut: ﴿and you commit in your gatherings what is abhorrent, then﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 29]. Immediacy here is an intensification of the rejection, since they did not delay in answering. Rather, they rushed to answer quickly, and the answer did not correspond to his words. This is because when he denounced their abomination, magnified its matter, and attributed to them excess, they hurried to say something unrelated to his speech, namely the command to expel. A parallel is the answer of the people of Abraham, who said: ﴿Burn him and support your gods﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 68], until he disgraced them with His words: ﴿Fie upon you and upon what you worship besides God! Will you not reason?﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 67]. So they gave an answer that did not match his speech. The town is Sodom. It was named after Sodom son of Baqim, whose name is proverbially used for hardened rulers. Lot migrated with his paternal uncle Abraham from the land of Babylon. Abraham settled in the land of Palestine, and settled Lot in al-Urdunn (Jordan).

﴿Indeed they are people who purify themselves.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: they keep themselves clean from anal intercourse with men and women. It was also said: they approach women during their times of purity. Ibn Bahr said: they watch for the purity of women and then have intercourse with them during it. It was also said: they keep themselves pure from our deeds. This is the meaning of the statement of Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid. It was also said: they wash from major impurity and purify themselves with water. They reproached them with this. This type of expression is called in the science of rhetoric (*'ilm al-bayān*) *ta'rīḍ* (allusion), which is a speech that suggests blame while actually praising, like the verse:

*"And there is no fault in them, except that their swords are notched from the clashing of battalions."*

For this reason Ibn 'Abbas said: they disparaged them with what is praised about them. The apparent view is that His words *innahum* (indeed they) are a reason for the expulsion, meaning: because they do not agree with us in what we are upon. Whoever does not agree with us must be expelled. Al-Zamakhshari said: their words ﴿Indeed they are people who purify themselves﴾ are mockery of them and of their purity from abominations, and boasting of the filth they were in, just as Satan says of the sinners to some of the pious when they admonish them: "Keep this ascetic away from us, and relieve us of this self-denier."

﴿So We saved him and his family, except his wife, who was among those who remained behind.﴾ That is: ﴿We saved him and his family﴾ from the punishment that befell his people. His family were the believers with him, or his two daughters, according to the disagreement mentioned above. He excepted his wife from his family, so she was not saved. Her name was Wahila. She was a hypocrite, concealing disbelief and allied with the people of Sodom. The meaning of ﴿among those who remained behind﴾ is among those who stayed in their homes and were destroyed. On this view, His words ﴿was among those who remained behind﴾ are an explanation and emphasis of what the exception implies, namely that God did not save her. Abu 'Ubayda said: ﴿except his wife﴾ suffices to show that she was not saved. Then he began describing her by a quality that has no bearing on salvation or destruction, namely that she was among those advanced in years who lived on from one era to another, so she was *ghābira*, that is, advanced in age, as in the verse: *"except an old woman among those who remained behind"*, until she died along with her people. End of quotation. ﴿Among those who remained behind﴾ uses the masculine plural to include the feminine, giving precedence to males over females. Al-Zajjaj said: among those who were absent from salvation, so it is an emphasis of what the exception implies. End of quotation. *Kānat* (she was) means "became," or "was in God's knowledge," or remains on its apparent sense, restricting her being left behind to past time. There are several views.

﴿And We rained upon them a rain﴾. *Amṭarnā* (We rained) is construed with the sense of *arsalnā* (We sent), which is why it takes *'alā* (upon), as in His words: ﴿So We rained upon them stones from heaven﴾. The "rain" here is stones. It is mentioned in more than one verse that the earth swallowed them and stones rained upon them. It was also said that the overturned cities were five towns, or six, or four. Gabriel uprooted them with his wing, lifted them until the people of heaven heard the braying of donkeys and the crowing of roosters, then he reversed them, making their upper part lower, and sent them down to the earth. Stones followed them despite this, and destroyed whoever was among them on a journey, or outside the lands. Lot's wife, when she heard the roar, said: "O my people!" and turned around, and a rock struck her and killed her. The apparent view is that the rain covered them all. It was also said that the people of the cities were swallowed by the earth, and stones rained upon those of them who were travelling. Mujahid was asked whether any of them had been saved. He said: No, except a man who was a merchant in Mecca. The stone stood still over him for forty days until he finished his trade, and when he left the sacred precinct (*Ḥaram*) it struck him and he died. Their number was one hundred thousand.

﴿Then look at how was the end of the criminals.﴾ This address is to the Messenger, or to the listener who hears their story: how was the final fate of those who committed crime. It contains a warning and a deterrent, lest this community take that same path. ﴿The criminals﴾ is general, covering the people of Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot, and others. It is from the sight of reflection (*naẓar al-tafakkur*), or from the sight of the eye regarding those whose traces of dwellings and homes remain, such as Thamud and the people of Lot, as He said: ﴿And [We destroyed] 'Ad and Thamud, and it has become clear to you from their dwellings﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 38].

﴿Indeed, you approach men with desire instead of women. Rather, you are a people who exceed all bounds.﴾ This explains His words: ﴿Do you commit an abomination?﴾ [Al-A'raf: 80]. The verb *ta'tuna* (you approach) here is taken from the phrase *atā al-mar'ah*, meaning he had intercourse with the woman. The form is interrogative, in the sense of rebuke and denunciation. This is the view of al-Hawfi and Ibn 'Atiyya, and al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa' also permitted it. The meaning is: aroused, following desire, not heeding its ugliness. It may also be a accusative of purpose (*maf'ūl min ajlih*). This is the view of al-Zamakhshari, and Abu al-Baqa' began with it. The meaning is: for the sake of appetite, with nothing moving you to this except mere desire. No blame is greater than this, because it describes them as beasts, with no motive from reason such as seeking offspring or the like. *Min dūn al-nisā'* (instead of women) is in the position of a circumstantial phrase, meaning: separate from women. Al-Hawfi said: *min dūn al-nisā'* is connected to *shahwah*. *Bal* (rather) here marks a shift from one account to another, indicating that they transgress the limits in their aggression. It was also said that it is a turning away from their affirmation and rebuke, or from informing about them with this shameful sin to passing judgment on them by the state that gives rise to ugly deeds and calls to following desires, which is excess (*isrāf*). This is excess that corrupts. Since excess was their habit, they exceeded even in satisfying desire and went beyond what was customary to something else. Compare: ﴿Rather, you are a people who transgress﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 166]. It was also said that *bal* turns away from an omitted clause, whose supposed sense is: "You have not been just; rather, you..." Al-Kirmani said: *bal* is a rejection of an answer they might claim as an excuse, meaning: you have no excuse and no argument. ﴿Rather, you...﴾. Here the phrase is ﴿musrifūn﴾ (excessive) in the form of the active participle, to indicate permanence, and to match the rhyme endings of preceding verses, which close with nouns. In al-Naml the phrase is ﴿tajhalūn﴾ (you are ignorant) in the imperfect, to indicate the renewal of ignorance in them, and to match the preceding verse endings, which close with verbs.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 85:**

﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb. He said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him."﴾. Al-Farra' said: "Madyan is the name of a town and region," and he recited:

*"The monks of Madyan, had they seen you, would have come down."*

On this reading, the phrase means "and to the people of Madyan." It has also been said that Madyan is the name of a tribe, named after its father, Madyan ibn Ibrahim. This was said by Muqatil and Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. As for Shu'ayb, it has been said that he was the son of Lot's daughter, and it has been said that he was the husband of Lot's daughter. This connection is what links his story with the story of Lot. The name Shu'ayb is Arabic, a diminutive of *sha'b* or *shi'b*. The majority hold that Madyan is non-Arabic. If it is Arabic, it may be *fay'al* from *madyan* (meaning "he settled in the place"), which is a rare pattern, or it may be *maf'al* from *dana*, in which case its sound form is irregular, like *Maryam*, *mikwara*, and *mitybah*. In every case it is diptote (not declined with nunation), whether it is the name of a land or of a tribe, and whether it is foreign or Arabic.

Scholars differed about Shu'ayb's lineage. 'Ata', Ibn Ishaq, and others said he was Shu'ayb ibn Miykil ibn Yashjur ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim, and his name in Syriac was Bayrut. Al-Sharqi ibn al-Qutami said he was Shu'ayb ibn 'Anqa' ibn Thuwayb ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim. Abu al-Qasim Isma'il ibn Muhammad ibn al-Fadl ibn 'Ali al-Talhi al-Isbahani, in his book *al-Idah fi al-Tafsir*, said he was Shu'ayb ibn Thuwayb ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim. It has also been said that he was Shu'ayb ibn Jadhy ibn Sijn ibn al-Lam ibn Ya'qub. Ibn Sam'an said the same, except that he put Lawa in place of al-Lam. Al-Lam is not known among the sons of Ya'qub, so it may be a scribal error for Lawi. It has also been said that he was Shu'ayb ibn Safwan ibn 'Anqa' ibn Thuwayb ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim. Al-Sharif al-Nassabah al-Jawwani, who was the final authority in this field, said: he is Shu'ayb ibn Hubaysh ibn Wa'il ibn Malik ibn Haram ibn Judham, whose name was 'Amir, the brother of Najm. These two were the sons of al-Harith ibn Murrah ibn Udad ibn Zayd ibn Yashjub ibn 'Uraybi ibn Zayd ibn Kahlan ibn Saba' ibn Yashhub ibn Ya'rub ibn Qahtan ibn 'Abir, who is Hud, peace be upon him. Between him and Hud, in this last lineage, there are eighteen fathers. In some of the lineages mentioned, there are seven fathers between them, because it mentions that he is Shu'ayb ibn Thuwayb ibn Madyan ibn Ibrahim, and Ibrahim is the son of Terah ibn Nahor ibn Saru'ugh ibn Arghu ibn Falikh ibn 'Abir, who is Hud, peace be upon him.

Shu'ayb was called "the orator of the prophets" because of the excellence of his address to his people. Qatadah said: he was sent twice, once to Madyan and once to the companions of al-Ayka (the thicket). He was attached to Madyan. The word *akhahum* ("their brother") is governed by *arsalna* ("We sent"). This supports the view of those who made Lot the object of *arsalna* and considered him coordinated with the prophets mentioned before him.

﴿There has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord.﴾ Al-Hasan recited *ayatun min rabbikum* ("a sign from your Lord"). This is evidence that he came with a miracle, since every prophet must have a miracle that indicates the truth of his prophethood. However, the verse does not specify here what the miracle was, or of what kind it was, just as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had very many miracles that are not specified in the Qur'an. Some people said: Shu'ayb was a prophet, but he had no clear evidence, and the "clear evidence" here means admonition. Al-Zajjaj rejected this view and said: prophethood is not accepted without a miracle. Among his miracles was that he gave Moses his staff, and that staff became a serpent (*tinnin*). Al-Zamakhshari said: among the miracles of Shu'ayb is what has been related about the staff of Moses fighting the serpent when he (Shu'ayb) gave him his flock, and the birth of speckled sheep only, when he promised that the speckled ones among their offspring would be his, and the falling of the staff of Adam into his hand seven times, and other signs. All these occurred before Moses, peace be upon him, was made a prophet, so they were miracles for Shu'ayb. Al-Zajjaj also said: Shu'ayb said to Moses, peace be upon him, "These sheep will give birth to young that have black and white markings, and I have given them to you," and it happened as he had reported. All these circumstances were a miracle for Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, because at that time Moses, peace be upon him, had not yet claimed the mission. End of quotation. What al-Zamakhshari said, following al-Zajjaj, is the opinion of the Mu'tazila. The reason is that *irhas* (a miraculous sign preceding prophethood, appearing through one who will later become a prophet and messenger) is disputed as to whether it is permissible. The Mu'tazila say it is not permissible, and therefore they attributed these miracles to Shu'ayb. The People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah) say it is permissible, so these are an *irhas* for Moses before he received revelation. The arguments for both positions are mentioned in the books of the principles of religion.

﴿So give full measure and weight, and do not deprive people of their due.﴾ He first commanded them to do a specific thing, which is to give full measure and weight, and then he forbade them from a general thing, which is his saying "their due" (*ashya'ahum*). The word *al-kayl* ("measure") is a verbal noun used to refer to the instrument by which something is measured, as in his saying in Hud, "the measure and the scale" (*al-mikyal wa al-mizan*). This matches his saying *wa al-mizan*. Or it remains a verbal noun, and *al-mizan* is meant as a verbal noun, like *al-mi'ad*, not the instrument, and so they match. Or *al-mizan* is taken with an omitted modifier, meaning "the weighing by the scale," and *al-kayl* means "the measuring vessel," so they match. *Al-bakhs* (depriving) was explained earlier in his saying ﴿and let him not diminish from it anything﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282]. *Ashya'ahum* ("their due") is general for everything that belongs to them. It has been said it means their wealth. Al-Tibrizi said it means their rights. The attribution of things to people is evidence that they own them, against the antinomian heretics (al-Ibahiyyah al-Zanadiqah). They used to deprive people in their dealings, and they were stingy, leaving nothing without reducing it, and from this word the tax is called *bakhs*. It is reported that when a stranger entered their town, they would take his good dirhams and say they were counterfeit, and they would cut them into pieces, then take them at a clear loss and give him counterfeit coins in exchange. This sin had spread among them in that era, together with their disbelief, on account of which the earthquake (al-Rajfah) overtook them.

﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reform.﴾ The explanation of this sentence was given shortly before in this surah.

﴿That is better for you, if you are believers.﴾ The reference is to giving full measure and weight, and leaving off depriving people and causing corruption. *Khayr* is the comparative form (*af'al al-tafdil*), meaning "better than" cheating, depriving, and corruption. This is because the benefit of this for you is very immediate, and it quickly passes from you, since people cut off their dealings with you and beware of you. When you give full measure and abandon depriving and corruption, your conduct becomes beautiful, your reputation becomes good, and people come to you for trade and gain. That is better than what you were doing, because trade and profits endure through justice in transactions and adherence to trusts. It has been said that *dhalikum* ("that") refers to the faith implied in his saying ﴿worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him﴾, and to leaving off depriving in measure and weight. It has also been said that *khayr* here is not in its comparative sense, and for this reason Ibn 'Atiyyah explained it by saying: that is beneficial with Allah, bringing you His success and good pleasure. The apparent meaning of his saying ﴿if you are believers﴾ is that they were disbelievers, and the beginning of the verse and the end of the story indicate this. So the meaning is that this will not be good for you and beneficial with Allah except on condition of faith and monotheism, since no deed benefits without faith. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿if you are believers﴾ means if you are those who believe me in what I say: ﴿That is better for you﴾.

(p-338) The apparent meaning is a prohibition against sitting on every path to threaten people and to bar them from the way of the religion, which is what they used to do. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Suddi said: "They used to sit on the roads leading to Shu'ayb, threatening whoever wanted to come to him and barring him, and saying, 'He is a liar, so do not go to him.' This was like what Quraysh did with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Al-Suddi said: "This is a prohibition against tax collectors, toll collectors and the like, who take people's wealth unjustly." Abu Hurayrah said: "It is a prohibition against robbery and highway banditry, and this was among their practices." It is also reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "On the night I was taken on the Night Journey, I saw a piece of wood on the road. No garment passed by it without it tearing it, and nothing passed by it without it piercing it. I said, 'What is this, O Jibril?' He said, 'This is an example of a people from your community who sit on the road and cut it off.' Then he recited: ﴿And do not sit on every path, threatening.﴾"

In this view and the one before it there is a connection to His saying: ﴿And do not diminish people's things﴾ [al-A'raf: 85]. However, no clear connection appears between these two views and His saying: ﴿and barring from the way of Allah those who believe in Him﴾; rather, that connection fits the first view.

Al-Qurtubi said: "Our scholars said: Like them today are these tax collectors (al-makkasun) who take from people what is not obligatory for them by law of the financial levies, by force and compulsion, and who guarantee what it is not permissible to guarantee in its origin, such as zakat, inheritances, entertainments, and those who are stationed on the roads, and other things that have become widespread in existence and are practised in all lands. This is among the greatest, largest and most vile of sins, for it is anger, injustice and oppression against people, spreading evil, practising it, persisting in it and approving of it. The greatest of this is the appointment of the law and the judgment for the judiciary. To Allah we belong and to Him we return. Nothing remains of Islam except its outward form, and nothing of the religion except its name." End of his words.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) linked property and honour with blood in his saying at the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Indeed your blood, your property and your honour are sacred to you." How much people have been lax in taking property and in backbiting! The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is killed defending his property is a martyr." It is strange that those who pretend to righteousness, religion and knowledge unanimously refrain from denouncing these unlawful levies and guarantees, and some of them claim that he has control over existence and is a guide to Allah, such that he supplicates and is answered in what he wants, and guarantees Paradise for whoever is among his companions and followers. Yet despite this, he frequents the holders of these unlawful levies and humbles himself before them to get some trivial thing removed from the tax they have collected. This is an impudence that does not come from one who has smelled the scent of faith or has attached himself to anything of Islam.

Some poets said:

"We are all alike in our faults, so the best of us is not worth a date-fibre's thread."

On the above views, sitting on every path is literal. Al-Zamakhshari took the sitting and the path figuratively, saying: "Do not follow Satan in his saying: ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾ [al-A'raf: 16], so that you sit on every path," meaning every method of the methods of the religion. The evidence that the path means the way of truth is His saying: ﴿and barring from the way of Allah.﴾ If you say: the path of truth is one, as in ﴿And this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow the other ways, lest they separate you from His way﴾ [al-An'am: 153], how then is it said "every path"? I say: the path of truth is one, but it branches into many knowledges, limits and varied rulings, so whenever they saw someone beginning on any part of it, they prevented and barred him. End of his words.

The indication that the path means the way of truth from His saying ﴿and barring from the way of Allah﴾ does not appear, as he mentioned. Rather, the apparent meaning is a difference: "every path" is general and "the way of Allah" is specific. So ﴿every path﴾ is literal, meaning the roads, and ﴿the way of Allah﴾ is figurative for the religion of Allah. The preposition (bi-) in ﴿bi-kulli sirat﴾ ("on every path") is locative, like Zayd bi-al-Basrah, meaning "in every path," just as "in Basrah." The clauses ﴿tu'iduna﴾ ("threatening"), ﴿wa-tasudduna﴾ ("and barring") and ﴿tabghunaha﴾ ("and seeking it") [Al 'Imran: 99] are circumstantial (hal) clauses, meaning "threatening, barring and seeking." Al-i'ad (threatening) is mentioning the infliction of harm on the one threatened. The object of the threat was not mentioned so that the soul may go in every direction of evil, because awa'da (to threaten) is used only for evil, and when it is mentioned, the verb is transitive to it with bi-.

Abu Mansur al-Jawaliqi said: "When they wanted to mention what they threaten with the verb awa'tu (I threatened), they used bi-, and they say awa'tuhu bi-al-darb ("I threatened him with beating"), not awa'tuhu al-darb."

The barring (sadd) can be literal, meaning preventing the access to the Messenger to hear his words. It can also be figurative for threatening by the one who bars in some way, or for promising the one barred benefits in return for abandoning it. The phrase ﴿man amana﴾ ("those who believe") is the object of ﴿tasudduna﴾ according to the rule of the second verb taking the governance (i'mal al-thani). The object of ﴿tu'iduna﴾ is a deleted pronoun. The apparent referent of the pronoun in (bihi) is ﴿sabil Allah﴾ ("the way of Allah"), and it is masculine because sabil can be masculine or feminine. It was also said that it refers to Allah. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: to what does the pronoun in amana bihi refer? I say: to every path. Its estimate is: 'you threaten those who believe in it and bar from it,' so he put the apparent noun which is 'the way of Allah' in the place of the pronoun, as an increase in condemning their affair, indicating the greatness of what they bar from." End of his words.

This is a strained grammatical analysis (i'rab), not suitable for the Qur'an to be interpreted by, because it involves inversion and rearrangement and putting an apparent noun in the place of a pronoun without need. Also, returning the pronoun to the farthest mentioned noun when it is possible to return it to the nearest mentioned noun is a permissible, good and preferable option. He made ﴿man amana﴾ an object of ﴿tu'iduna﴾, so it becomes an instance of the first verb governing, which is rare.

The grammarians have said that this did not occur in the Qur'an because of its rarity. If it were the first verb governing, the wording would require mention of the pronoun in the second verb, and the construction would be (wa-tasudduna-hu) or (wa-tasudduna-hum), since this pronoun may not be deleted according to most grammarians, except by necessity. According to some grammarians it may be deleted in rare speech. The other verse indicates that ﴿man amana﴾ is the object of ﴿tasudduna﴾: His saying: ﴿Say: O People of the Book, why do you bar from the way of Allah those who believe﴾ [Al 'Imran: 99]. Such a pronoun is not deleted except in poetry. Some have permitted its deletion rarely, with these additional burdensome estimates, so it is worthy of being rejected, because of the far-fetched complexity that is distant from eloquence.

Ibn 'Atiyyah permitted that the pronoun return to Shu'ayb according to the view of one who regards sitting on the road as a means of turning people away from Shu'ayb. This is far-fetched, because the speaker of ﴿and do not sit﴾ is Shu'ayb, so the wording would have been "man amana bi" ("those who believe in me"). It is not permissible here to be an iltifat (shift of person). If you say: "O Hind, I am telling you: do not humiliate the one I honour," meaning "the one who honoured me," it is not correct.

The explanation of similar words in His saying ﴿and seeking it crooked﴾ was mentioned earlier in Al 'Imran.

(p-340) ﴿And remember when you were few, so He multiplied you.﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: "(idh) is an object that is not a time adverb, meaning: remember in gratitude the time when you were few in number, so Allah multiplied you and increased your number." End of his words. Others mentioned that it is in the accusative as a time adverb, so it is not possible for ﴿remember﴾ to govern it, since the imperative "remember" is future and idh is an adverb for the past. The fewness and multiplicity here, relative to individuals, or to poverty and wealth, or to the shortness and length of lives, are three opinions, the first of which is most apparent. It was said: Madyan ibn Ibrahim married the daughter of Lut, and she gave birth, so Allah bestowed blessing and growth upon her descendants, and they multiplied and spread. Al-Zamakhshari said: "When you were few and humble, He made you mighty with multitude of numbers and equipment." End of his words. There is no necessity to delete the attribute "humble," nor to interpret the saying ﴿so He multiplied you﴾ as meaning "in number." Do you not see that fewness does not entail humiliation, nor does multiplicity entail might? A poet said:

"They reproach us that our number is few, so I said to her: Noble people are few."

"What harms us that we are few, when our neighbour is mighty, and the neighbour of the many is humbled?"

It was also said: the intended meaning is the combination of the four opinions, for He multiplied their number, their provisions, lengthened their lives and made them mighty after they had been the opposite of these.

﴿And see how was the end of the corrupters.﴾ This is a threat to them and a reminder of the end of those who corrupted before them, and an example for them of those upon whom punishment fell, from the people of Noah, Hud, Salih and Lut, who were close in time to what overturned the overturned cities.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 87:

﴿And if there is a group among you who have believed in that with which I have been sent, and a group who have not believed, then be patient until Allah judges between us. And He is the best of judges.﴾ This statement is among the finest of gentle courtesies in discourse, for the one who is certain (of the truth) appears in the form of one in doubt. This is because a group had indeed believed in him, as evidenced by the words of the arrogant ones who turned away from faith (p-341): ﴿O Shu'ayb, we will surely expel you and those who believed with you from our city﴾ [al-A'raf: 88]. It is also an excellent form of division (taqsim), since his people cannot be free of the two categories. That with which he was sent here refers to what he commanded them of: devoting worship to Allah alone, giving full measure and weight, and what he forbade them of: diminishing (people's rights), corruption, and sitting in wait as mentioned. The object of (lam yu'minu, "did not believe") is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, and its estimated form is (lam yu'minu bihi, "did not believe in it"). The address in His words (minkum, "among you") is to his people, and it is fitting that His words (fasbiru, "then be patient") be an address to both groups of his people, those who believed and those who did not. (Baynana, "between us") means between all of them. Thus this is a promise to the believers of victory, which is the outcome of patience, so they were patient over what they were denied and harmed, until Our help came to them, and a threat to the disbelievers of punishment and loss.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: The meaning is: and if you, O my people, have disagreed with me and divided my affair by your disbelief, so one group believed and one group disbelieved, then be patient, O disbelievers, until the judgment of Allah comes between me and you. In His words "fasbiru" there is the force of threat and warning. This is the apparent meaning of the statement. And the address in the whole verse is to the disbelievers. Al-Naqqash said, and Muqatil ibn Sulayman said: The meaning of "fasbiru" is: O company of disbelievers. He said: This is the view of the majority. End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari began with this view, saying: "Fasbiru" means "then wait and expect," "until Allah judges between us" means between the two groups, by making the righteous victorious over the falsifiers and making them prevail over them. This is a threat to the disbelievers of Allah's vengeance upon them, due to His words: ﴿So wait, indeed We are with you waiting﴾ [al-Tawba: 52]. End of quote.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: Mundhir ibn Sa'id related from Abu Sa'id that the address in His words ﴿fasbiru﴾ is to the believers, in the sense of a promise to them. Muqatil ibn Hayyan also said this. End of quote.

Al-Zamakhshari also relied on this, saying: "Or it is an exhortation to the believers and an encouragement to patience and to bearing what harm the polytheists inflicted upon them, until Allah judges between them and takes vengeance on them from them." End of quote.

What we mentioned first, that it is an address to both groups, is the view of Abu 'Ali, and al-Zamakhshari mentioned it third, saying: "It may also be an address to both groups, so that the believers may be patient over the harm of the disbelievers, and the disbelievers may be patient over what distresses them of the faith of those among them who believed, until Allah judges, distinguishing the evil from the good." End of quote. This is in keeping with his habit of mentioning possibilities in speech that give the impression they are his own words, while they are opinions of earlier scholars.

﴿And He is the best of judges﴾ because His judgment is just, and there is no fear that there is in it any unfairness or injustice.

[p. 342]

**"The chiefs of his people who were arrogant said: 'We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb, and those who believed with you, from our town, or you will return to our religion.' He said: 'Even though we are unwilling?'"** ﴿قالَ المَلَأُ الَّذِينَ اسْتَكْبَرُوا مِن قَوْمِهِ لَنُخْرِجَنَّكَ يا شُعَيْبُ والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مَعَكَ مِن قَرْيَتِنا أوْ لَتَعُودُنَّ في مِلَّتِنا قالَ أوَلَوْ كُنّا كارِهِينَ﴾

**"We would have fabricated a lie against God if we returned to your religion after God has rescued us from it. It is not for us to return to it, unless God, our Lord, wills it. Our Lord encompasses all things in knowledge. In God we have put our trust. Our Lord, decide between us and our people with truth, for You are the best of deciders."** ﴿قَدِ افْتَرَيْنا عَلى اللَّهِ كَذِبًا إنْ عُدْنا في مِلَّتِكم بَعْدَ إذْ نَجّانا اللَّهُ مِنها وما يَكُونُ لَنا أنْ نَعُودَ فِيها إلّا أنْ يَشاءَ اللَّهُ رَبُّنا وسِعَ رَبُّنا كُلَّ شَيْءٍ عِلْمًا عَلى اللَّهِ تَوَكَّلْنا رَبَّنا افْتَحْ بَيْنَنا وبَيْنَ قَوْمِنا بِالحَقِّ وأنْتَ خَيْرُ الفاتِحِينَ﴾

**"The chiefs of his people who disbelieved said: 'If you follow Shu'ayb, then you will surely be losers.'"** ﴿وقالَ المَلَأُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِن قَوْمِهِ لَئِنِ اتَّبَعْتُمْ شُعَيْبًا إنَّكم إذًا لَخاسِرُونَ﴾ [al-A'raf: 90]

**"So the earthquake seized them, and they became prostrate in their homes."** ﴿فَأخَذَتْهُمُ الرَّجْفَةُ فَأصْبَحُوا في دارِهِمْ جاثِمِينَ﴾ [al-A'raf: 91]
