**"We did not send a prophet to any town except that We seized its people with adversity and hardship, so that they might humble themselves."** ﴿وما أرْسَلْنا في قَرْيَةٍ مِن نَبِيٍّ إلّا أخَذْنا أهْلَها بِالبَأْساءِ والضَّرّاءِ لَعَلَّهم يَضَّرَّعُونَ﴾ [al-A'raf: 94]

**"Then We replaced the bad condition with good until they multiplied and said: 'Our forefathers were touched by hardship and ease,' so We seized them suddenly while they did not perceive."** ﴿ثُمَّ بَدَّلْنا مَكانَ السَّيِّئَةِ الحَسَنَةَ حَتّى عَفَوْا وقالُوا قَدْ مَسَّ آباءَنا الضَّرّاءُ والسَّرّاءُ فَأخَذْناهم بَغْتَةً وهم لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ [al-A'raf: 95]

**"Or are the people of the towns secure that Our punishment will not come upon them in the forenoon while they are playing?"** ﴿أوَأمِنَ أهْلُ القُرى أنْ يَأْتِيَهم بَأْسُنا ضُحًى وهم يَلْعَبُونَ﴾ [al-A'raf: 98]

Thus God seals the hearts of the disbelievers."** ﴿تِلْكَ القُرى نَقُصُّ عَلَيْكَ مِن أنْبائِها ولَقَدْ جاءَتْهم رُسُلُهم بِالبَيِّناتِ فَما كانُوا لِيُؤْمِنُوا بِما كَذَّبُوا مِن قَبْلُ كَذَلِكَ يَطْبَعُ اللَّهُ عَلى قُلُوبِ الكافِرِينَ﴾ [al-A'raf: 101]

[p. 342]

*ʿāda* (عادَ): "to return to what it was upon," and it also comes in the sense of *ṣāra* (to become). The poet said:

*tuʿidu fīkum jazra l-jazūri ridāḥunā / wa-yarjiʿna bi-l-asyāfi munkasirātin*
"Our spears make you return the carving of the slaughtered camel, and they come back with their swords broken."

*ḍuḥā* (ضُحًى): a noun of time that is inflected when indefinite, and not inflected when it refers to a specific day. It is the time when the sun rises high after it has risen, and it is feminine. The grammarians deviated in its diminutive, saying *ḍuḥayy* without the feminine *tāʾ*. You say *ataytuhu ḍuḥan* and *ḍuḥāʾ*; if you open the *ḍād* you lengthen the vowel. *Al-thuʿbān* (الثُّعْبانُ): the large male of the serpents, derived from *thaʿabta bi-l-makān*, meaning you made the place gush with water. *Al-mathʿab* is the place where water gushes out, because the serpent moves like water when it bursts forth. *Al-irjāʾ* (الإرْجاءُ): delay. *Al-madīna* (المَدِينَةُ): a well-known word, derived from *madana*, so it is of the form *faʿīla*. As for the one who holds that it is *mafʿala* from *dāna*, his view is weak, because the Arabs agree on the hamza in its plural: they say *madāʾin* with a hamza, and *madāyin* with a *yāʾ* is not transmitted. There is no necessity that it be *mafʿala*, and their plural of it as *fuʿul* (*mudun*), as they say *ṣuḥuf* for *ṣaḥīfa*, settles that it is *faʿīla*.

*"The chiefs of his people who were arrogant said: 'We will surely expel you, O Shuʿayb, and those who believed with you, from our town, or you will return to our religion.'"* That is, the disbelievers (*al-kuffār*) **"who were arrogant"** toward faith. They swore to one of two things: the expulsion of Shuʿayb and his followers, or their return to their religion. The oath may be upon the action of the one swearing and upon the action of others. They equated his expulsion and the expulsion of his followers with returning to the religion. This indicates the difficulty of leaving one's homeland, since they linked that with returning to disbelief. In "expulsion" and "return" there is an antithesis in meaning (*ṭibāq maʿnawī*). *ʿāda*, as mentioned, has two usages: one is in the sense of *ṣāra*, and the second is in the sense of *rajaʿa ilā mā kāna ʿalayhi*. On the first, there is no difficulty in His statement "or you will return," since it becomes a verb attributed to Shuʿayb and his followers, and it does not indicate that Shuʿayb was in their religion. On the second meaning, there is a difficulty, because Shuʿayb was never in their religion, but their followers were in it. This is answered in several ways. The first: that by Shuʿayb's "return" to the religion is meant his state of silence about them before he was sent as a prophet, not a state of misguidance, for he used to conceal his religion until God revealed to him. The second: that this is from the category of giving the ruling of the group precedence over the individual. When they conjoined his followers with his pronoun in the expulsion, they extended their ruling to him in the return, even though Shuʿayb was innocent of what his followers were upon before faith. The third: that their chiefs said that in a manner of deception toward the common people and creating the impression that he had been one of them.

*"He said: 'Even though we are unwilling?'"* That is, would one of these two matters occur from you in every state, even in the state of our aversion to it? The interrogation is to make clear the enormity of the disobedience in what they swore **"[to expel us] from our homes unjustly, or to acknowledge return to their religion."** Al-Zamakhsharī said: "The *hamza* is for interrogation, and the *wāw* is the *wāw* of circumstance; its estimate is: 'Will you return us to your religion while we are in a state of aversion, or while we are unwilling?'" End of quote. So he made the interrogation specific to the return to their religion, and it is not so; rather, the interrogation is about one of the two matters, expulsion or return. He made the *wāw* a *wāw* of circumstance, estimating: "Will you return us while we are in a state of aversion?" But it is not the *wāw* of circumstance that the grammarians express by the term *wāw al-ḥāl*; rather, it is the *wāw* of conjunction, conjoined to an elided circumstance, like his saying: *"Return the beggar, even with a burnt hoof."* The meaning is not "return him in a state of giving him charity with a burnt hoof," but rather "return him accompanied by charity, even if accompanied by a burnt hoof." We have previously elaborated on the discussion of such a construction.

*"We would have fabricated a lie against God if we returned to your religion after God has rescued us from it."* This is an informational statement restricted in meaning by a condition, whose answer of the condition is elided in terms of grammatical structure. Its estimate is: *"If we return to your religion, then we have fabricated [a lie]."* His statement "We have fabricated a lie against God" is not the answer of the condition, except according to the view of one who permits placing the answer of the condition before the condition, so this may be interpreted accordingly. They allowed two possibilities for this sentence. The first is that it be an independent informational statement. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It carries the sense of amazement, as if they said: 'How false we would be against God if we returned to disbelief after Islam!' Because the apostate is more guilty of fabrication than the original disbeliever, meaning the original one, since the disbeliever fabricates a lie against God by claiming that God has a rival, while there is no rival to Him; the apostate is like him in that, and goes beyond him in claiming that what was obscure to him of the distinction between truth and falsehood has been made clear to him." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The apparent meaning is that it is an informational statement, that is: 'We were already engaged in a great matter in returning to disbelief.'" The second possibility is that it be an oath, with the *lām* elided, that is, "By God, we have certainly fabricated," which al-Zamakhsharī mentioned. Ibn ʿAṭiyya cited it as a possibility, saying: "It may be an oath in the form of a supplication, like the words of the poet:

*baqqaytu wafrī wa-nḥaraftu ʿani l-ʿulā / wa-laqītu aḍyāfī bi-wajhin ʿabūsi*
"I have kept my wealth intact and turned aside from nobility, and I have met my guests with a scowling face."

And as you say: 'I have fabricated against God that I spoke to so-and-so.'" Ibn ʿAṭiyya did not recite the verse that restricts his saying "I have kept intact" and what follows it by a condition, which is his saying:

*in lam ashunna ʿalā Ibni Hindin ghāratan / lam takhlu yawman min nihābi nufūsi*
"If I do not launch a raid upon the son of Hind, [my life] will not be free one day from the plundering of souls."

Since the matter of religion is the greatest for the believer and preferred over the matter of this world, they did not heed the expulsion, even though one of the two matters is greatest for the believer and preferred over the lie. The disbelievers swore that it would occur, saying: *"We have certainly fabricated a lie against God if we return to your religion."* The explanation of "return" as "becoming" has already been mentioned, and its interpretation, if it carries the sense of "returning to what the person was in," is in relation to the Prophet, who is protected from major and minor sins.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 88–89 (part 2 of 2):

﴿It is not for us to return to it unless God, our Lord, wills﴾. That is, it is not fitting for us, nor is it possible for us, to return to your religion, unless God, our Lord, wills it, so that we return to it. This exception is meant to attribute the totality of affairs to God's will and volition. The return of the believers to their religion is permissible without Shu'ayb, because he was protected from it by prophethood. Thus the exception follows the principle of giving the ruling of the plural precedence over the singular, even though that one individual is not included in the ruling of the plural.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is possible that it means the exception of what God could make the believers worship of the acts of devotion performed by the disbelievers. When they said to him, 'We will not return to your religion,' he then feared that God might be worshipped through some of the disbelievers' acts, so that a heretic would oppose them with this and say, 'This is a return to our religion.' So he made an exception for God's will regarding what could be worshipped." End of quote. This possibility is not sound, because His saying ﴿after God has saved us from it﴾ refers only to deliverance from disbelief and sins, not from acts of righteousness.

Ibn 'Atiyyah also said: "It is possible that by this he means the sense of remote improbability, as you say, 'I will not do that until the raven turns white' and 'until the camel passes through the eye of the needle.' It is known that this is impossible, so it is a conditional tied to something impossible. This is an interpretation that the commentators have reported without realizing its problem." End of quote. This interpretation belongs only to the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school), whose doctrine is that disbelief and belief are not by the will of God, exalted is He.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, what is the meaning of His saying ﴿It is not for us to return to it unless God wills﴾, when God, exalted is He, is too exalted to will the apostasy of the believers and their return to disbelief? I say: its meaning is 'unless God wills our abandonment and withholds from us His favour, since He knows that it will not benefit us.' Then it would be in vain, and vanity is an ugliness that the Wise does not do. The evidence for this is His saying ﴿Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾, that is, He knows everything that has been and will be. He, exalted is He, knows the states of His servants, how their hearts change, how they turn, how they harden after softness, sicken after health, and return to disbelief after belief. It is also possible that His saying ﴿unless God wills﴾ is a closing off of their hope of return, because God's willing their return to disbelief is an impossibility outside of wisdom." End of quote. These two interpretations are on the Mu'tazilite doctrine.

It has been said: this exception is only a form of submission and good manners. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The connection of this interpretation lies in the future-tense sense of the exception, and if the statement were 'if God wills,' this interpretation would be stronger." End of quote. But it does not strengthen this interpretation, for there is no difference between ﴿unless God wills﴾ and ﴿unless if God wills﴾, because 'in' (in) makes the past tense refer to the future, just as 'an' (an) makes the present tense refer to the future, and both verbs are in the future.

The one who held that the pronoun in ﴿in it﴾ refers to the town and not to the religion is further from the truth.

﴿Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾. The explanation of its counterpart in al-An'am, in the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, has already been given.

﴿In God we have put our trust﴾. That is, in repelling what you threaten us with, and in protecting us from error. This involves submission to God and holding fast to His kindness, and this supports the first interpretation of ﴿unless God wills﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: "He keeps us firm in faith and grants us success in increasing certainty."

﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth, and You are the best of deciders﴾. That is: judge. The fatih and the fattah mean the judge in the dialect of Himyar. It has been said: in the dialect of Murad. One of them said:

"Oh, convey to the Banu 'Usam a messenger:
I am independent of your judgment (futahatikum)."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "I did not know the meaning of this word until I heard the daughter of Dhu Yazan say to her husband, 'Come, let me judge (ufatihka) between you,' that is, let me judge you." Al-Farra' said: "The people of Oman call the judge the fatih." Al-Suddi and Ibn Bahr said: "Judge between us." Abu Ishaq said: "It is also possible that the meaning is: make our matter manifest, until what is between us and our people is opened up and that is uncovered, by sending down upon their enemy a punishment that shows that the truth is with them."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "He used to pray much. When it lasted long and his people persisted in their disbelief and he despaired of their righteousness, he prayed against them, and God answered his prayer and destroyed them with the earthquake." Al-Hasan said: "Every prophet who wanted his people destroyed was commanded to pray against them, and then He answered him and destroyed them."

[p. 342]

*ʿāda* (عادَ): "to return to what it was upon," and it also comes in the sense of *ṣāra* (to become). The poet said:

*tuʿidu fīkum jazra l-jazūri ridāḥunā / wa-yarjiʿna bi-l-asyāfi munkasirātin*
"Our spears make you return the carving of the slaughtered camel, and they come back with their swords broken."

*ḍuḥā* (ضُحًى): a noun of time that is inflected when indefinite, and not inflected when it refers to a specific day. It is the time when the sun rises high after it has risen, and it is feminine. The grammarians deviated in its diminutive, saying *ḍuḥayy* without the feminine *tāʾ*. You say *ataytuhu ḍuḥan* and *ḍuḥāʾ*; if you open the *ḍād* you lengthen the vowel. *Al-thuʿbān* (الثُّعْبانُ): the large male of the serpents, derived from *thaʿabta bi-l-makān*, meaning you made the place gush with water. *Al-mathʿab* is the place where water gushes out, because the serpent moves like water when it bursts forth. *Al-irjāʾ* (الإرْجاءُ): delay. *Al-madīna* (المَدِينَةُ): a well-known word, derived from *madana*, so it is of the form *faʿīla*. As for the one who holds that it is *mafʿala* from *dāna*, his view is weak, because the Arabs agree on the hamza in its plural: they say *madāʾin* with a hamza, and *madāyin* with a *yāʾ* is not transmitted. There is no necessity that it be *mafʿala*, and their plural of it as *fuʿul* (*mudun*), as they say *ṣuḥuf* for *ṣaḥīfa*, settles that it is *faʿīla*.

*"The chiefs of his people who were arrogant said: 'We will surely expel you, O Shuʿayb, and those who believed with you, from our town, or you will return to our religion.'"* That is, the disbelievers (*al-kuffār*) **"who were arrogant"** toward faith. They swore to one of two things: the expulsion of Shuʿayb and his followers, or their return to their religion. The oath may be upon the action of the one swearing and upon the action of others. They equated his expulsion and the expulsion of his followers with returning to the religion. This indicates the difficulty of leaving one's homeland, since they linked that with returning to disbelief. In "expulsion" and "return" there is an antithesis in meaning (*ṭibāq maʿnawī*). *ʿāda*, as mentioned, has two usages: one is in the sense of *ṣāra*, and the second is in the sense of *rajaʿa ilā mā kāna ʿalayhi*. On the first, there is no difficulty in His statement "or you will return," since it becomes a verb attributed to Shuʿayb and his followers, and it does not indicate that Shuʿayb was in their religion. On the second meaning, there is a difficulty, because Shuʿayb was never in their religion, but their followers were in it. This is answered in several ways. The first: that by Shuʿayb's "return" to the religion is meant his state of silence about them before he was sent as a prophet, not a state of misguidance, for he used to conceal his religion until God revealed to him. The second: that this is from the category of giving the ruling of the group precedence over the individual. When they conjoined his followers with his pronoun in the expulsion, they extended their ruling to him in the return, even though Shuʿayb was innocent of what his followers were upon before faith. The third: that their chiefs said that in a manner of deception toward the common people and creating the impression that he had been one of them.

*"He said: 'Even though we are unwilling?'"* That is, would one of these two matters occur from you in every state, even in the state of our aversion to it? The interrogation is to make clear the enormity of the disobedience in what they swore **"[to expel us] from our homes unjustly, or to acknowledge return to their religion."** Al-Zamakhsharī said: "The *hamza* is for interrogation, and the *wāw* is the *wāw* of circumstance; its estimate is: 'Will you return us to your religion while we are in a state of aversion, or while we are unwilling?'" End of quote. So he made the interrogation specific to the return to their religion, and it is not so; rather, the interrogation is about one of the two matters, expulsion or return. He made the *wāw* a *wāw* of circumstance, estimating: "Will you return us while we are in a state of aversion?" But it is not the *wāw* of circumstance that the grammarians express by the term *wāw al-ḥāl*; rather, it is the *wāw* of conjunction, conjoined to an elided circumstance, like his saying: *"Return the beggar, even with a burnt hoof."* The meaning is not "return him in a state of giving him charity with a burnt hoof," but rather "return him accompanied by charity, even if accompanied by a burnt hoof." We have previously elaborated on the discussion of such a construction.

*"We would have fabricated a lie against God if we returned to your religion after God has rescued us from it."* This is an informational statement restricted in meaning by a condition, whose answer of the condition is elided in terms of grammatical structure. Its estimate is: *"If we return to your religion, then we have fabricated [a lie]."* His statement "We have fabricated a lie against God" is not the answer of the condition, except according to the view of one who permits placing the answer of the condition before the condition, so this may be interpreted accordingly. They allowed two possibilities for this sentence. The first is that it be an independent informational statement. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It carries the sense of amazement, as if they said: 'How false we would be against God if we returned to disbelief after Islam!' Because the apostate is more guilty of fabrication than the original disbeliever, meaning the original one, since the disbeliever fabricates a lie against God by claiming that God has a rival, while there is no rival to Him; the apostate is like him in that, and goes beyond him in claiming that what was obscure to him of the distinction between truth and falsehood has been made clear to him." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The apparent meaning is that it is an informational statement, that is: 'We were already engaged in a great matter in returning to disbelief.'" The second possibility is that it be an oath, with the *lām* elided, that is, "By God, we have certainly fabricated," which al-Zamakhsharī mentioned. Ibn ʿAṭiyya cited it as a possibility, saying: "It may be an oath in the form of a supplication, like the words of the poet:

*baqqaytu wafrī wa-nḥaraftu ʿani l-ʿulā / wa-laqītu aḍyāfī bi-wajhin ʿabūsi*
"I have kept my wealth intact and turned aside from nobility, and I have met my guests with a scowling face."

And as you say: 'I have fabricated against God that I spoke to so-and-so.'" Ibn ʿAṭiyya did not recite the verse that restricts his saying "I have kept intact" and what follows it by a condition, which is his saying:

*in lam ashunna ʿalā Ibni Hindin ghāratan / lam takhlu yawman min nihābi nufūsi*
"If I do not launch a raid upon the son of Hind, [my life] will not be free one day from the plundering of souls."

Since the matter of religion is the greatest for the believer and preferred over the matter of this world, they did not heed the expulsion, even though one of the two matters is greatest for the believer and preferred over the lie. The disbelievers swore that it would occur, saying: *"We have certainly fabricated a lie against God if we return to your religion."* The explanation of "return" as "becoming" has already been mentioned, and its interpretation, if it carries the sense of "returning to what the person was in," is in relation to the Prophet, who is protected from major and minor sins.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 88–89 (part 2 of 2):

﴿It is not for us to return to it unless God, our Lord, wills﴾. That is, it is not fitting for us, nor is it possible for us, to return to your religion, unless God, our Lord, wills it, so that we return to it. This exception is meant to attribute the totality of affairs to God's will and volition. The return of the believers to their religion is permissible without Shu'ayb, because he was protected from it by prophethood. Thus the exception follows the principle of giving the ruling of the plural precedence over the singular, even though that one individual is not included in the ruling of the plural.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is possible that it means the exception of what God could make the believers worship of the acts of devotion performed by the disbelievers. When they said to him, 'We will not return to your religion,' he then feared that God might be worshipped through some of the disbelievers' acts, so that a heretic would oppose them with this and say, 'This is a return to our religion.' So he made an exception for God's will regarding what could be worshipped." End of quote. This possibility is not sound, because His saying ﴿after God has saved us from it﴾ refers only to deliverance from disbelief and sins, not from acts of righteousness.

Ibn 'Atiyyah also said: "It is possible that by this he means the sense of remote improbability, as you say, 'I will not do that until the raven turns white' and 'until the camel passes through the eye of the needle.' It is known that this is impossible, so it is a conditional tied to something impossible. This is an interpretation that the commentators have reported without realizing its problem." End of quote. This interpretation belongs only to the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school), whose doctrine is that disbelief and belief are not by the will of God, exalted is He.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask, what is the meaning of His saying ﴿It is not for us to return to it unless God wills﴾, when God, exalted is He, is too exalted to will the apostasy of the believers and their return to disbelief? I say: its meaning is 'unless God wills our abandonment and withholds from us His favour, since He knows that it will not benefit us.' Then it would be in vain, and vanity is an ugliness that the Wise does not do. The evidence for this is His saying ﴿Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾, that is, He knows everything that has been and will be. He, exalted is He, knows the states of His servants, how their hearts change, how they turn, how they harden after softness, sicken after health, and return to disbelief after belief. It is also possible that His saying ﴿unless God wills﴾ is a closing off of their hope of return, because God's willing their return to disbelief is an impossibility outside of wisdom." End of quote. These two interpretations are on the Mu'tazilite doctrine.

It has been said: this exception is only a form of submission and good manners. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The connection of this interpretation lies in the future-tense sense of the exception, and if the statement were 'if God wills,' this interpretation would be stronger." End of quote. But it does not strengthen this interpretation, for there is no difference between ﴿unless God wills﴾ and ﴿unless if God wills﴾, because 'in' (in) makes the past tense refer to the future, just as 'an' (an) makes the present tense refer to the future, and both verbs are in the future.

The one who held that the pronoun in ﴿in it﴾ refers to the town and not to the religion is further from the truth.

﴿Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾. The explanation of its counterpart in al-An'am, in the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, has already been given.

﴿In God we have put our trust﴾. That is, in repelling what you threaten us with, and in protecting us from error. This involves submission to God and holding fast to His kindness, and this supports the first interpretation of ﴿unless God wills﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: "He keeps us firm in faith and grants us success in increasing certainty."

﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth, and You are the best of deciders﴾. That is: judge. The fatih and the fattah mean the judge in the dialect of Himyar. It has been said: in the dialect of Murad. One of them said:

"Oh, convey to the Banu 'Usam a messenger:
I am independent of your judgment (futahatikum)."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "I did not know the meaning of this word until I heard the daughter of Dhu Yazan say to her husband, 'Come, let me judge (ufatihka) between you,' that is, let me judge you." Al-Farra' said: "The people of Oman call the judge the fatih." Al-Suddi and Ibn Bahr said: "Judge between us." Abu Ishaq said: "It is also possible that the meaning is: make our matter manifest, until what is between us and our people is opened up and that is uncovered, by sending down upon their enemy a punishment that shows that the truth is with them."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "He used to pray much. When it lasted long and his people persisted in their disbelief and he despaired of their righteousness, he prayed against them, and God answered his prayer and destroyed them with the earthquake." Al-Hasan said: "Every prophet who wanted his people destroyed was commanded to pray against them, and then He answered him and destroyed them."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 7, verses 90–93:**

﴿And the chiefs of those among his people who disbelieved said: "If you follow Shu'ayb, then you will indeed be losers."﴾ That is: some of them said to others, namely their elders said to their followers, discouraging them from faith: ﴿"If you follow Shu'ayb"﴾ in what he commands you and forbids you. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, what is the response of the oath that the lam introduced in ﴿"If you follow"﴾, and what is the response of the conditional? I say: His saying ﴿"then you will indeed be losers"﴾ stands in place of both responses. End of quotation. What the grammarians say is that the response of the conditional is omitted, because the response of the oath indicates it, and for this reason the verb of the condition must be in the past tense. If al-Zamakhshari meant by his saying "stands in place of both responses" that it is sufficient in place of mentioning the response of the conditional, then this is close to correct. But if he meant that from the standpoint of grammatical craft it is as he claimed, then it is not so, because a clause cannot both have no place in the i'rab (grammatical analysis) and have a place in it. Here (idhan) means emphasis; it is the particle that is a response, and the conditional may accompany it, and it may not. Some grammarians claimed that in this position it is an adverb of time, whose governing element is (la-khasirun), and the nun is a substitute for the omitted element. The estimate is: "that you, if you follow him, are indeed losers." So when what it was attached to was omitted, the nun was introduced as a substitute for that, and it coincided with the alif, so two sakin letters met, and the alif was dropped because of their meeting. The substitution here is like the substitution in (yawma'idhin) and (hina'idhin) and the like. What this claimant held is nothing, because the substitution is not established, and the omission in (idhan), which is for the future, has a place, so this is to be understood in that way. (La-khasirun): Ibn Abbas said: "defrauded." Ata said: "ignorant." Al-Dahhak said: "incapable." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Losers for your exchanging misguidance for guidance, in accordance with His saying: ﴿Those are the ones who bought misguidance in exchange for guidance, so their trade did not profit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16]." It was also said: "You will suffer loss by following him, the benefits of short-measure and fraud, because he forbids you from it and urges you to full measure and fairness." End of quotation.

﴿So the quake seized them, and they became prostrate in their homes in the morning﴾ [al-A'raf: 78]. The explanation of this sentence has already passed. Ibn Abbas and others said: When he prayed against them, a gate of Hell was opened upon them with a severe heat that seized their breath, so shade and water did not benefit them. When they entered the caves to cool themselves, they found them hotter than the outside, so they came out fleeing to the open desert. A cloud overshadowed them, in which was a pleasant wind, and they called out to one another: "Upon you the shade!" So they all gathered beneath it, and it closed over them, and God kindled it into fire, and the earth quaked beneath them, and they burned as locusts burn when roasted, until they became ashes. It is also narrated that the wind was withheld from them for seven days, then the heat was imposed upon them. Yazid al-Jarīrī said: The wind was imposed upon them for seven days, then a mountain was raised for them from afar, and a man came to it, and beneath it were rivers and springs, so they all gathered beneath it, and that mountain fell upon them. Qatadah said: Shu'ayb was sent to the People of the Thicket and they were destroyed by the overshadowing cloud, and to the People of Madyan, and Gabriel cried out to them one cry, and they all perished. Ibn Atiyyah said: It is possible that one group of Shu'ayb's people perished by the quake and another group perished by the overshadowing cloud. Al-Tabari said: It reached me that a man from them, called Amr ibn Jalha, when he saw the cloud, said, the poet said:

O people, indeed Shu'ayb is a messenger, so leave behind you Sumayr and Imran ibn Shaddad.

Indeed I see a cloud, O people, that has risen, calling with a voice over the stony valley.

And indeed you will not see in it any healthy one tomorrow, except the Raqim walking between the hills.

Sumayr and Imran were their soothsayers, and al-Raqim was their dog. And from Abu Abd Allah al-Bajali: Abjad, Hawwaz, Huttī, Kalaman, Sa'fas, and Qarshat are names like the kings of Madyan, and Kalaman was their king at the time the punishment came upon them, in the time of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him. When he died, his daughter wept for him, saying:

Kalaman has broken my pillar; his destruction is in the midst of the dwelling place.

The lord of the people, death came upon him as fire in the midst of a shade.

Their dwelling was made a fire upon them, like something dissolved to nothing.

﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb, as if they had never dwelt therein﴾, that is: as if they had never lived at ease, comfortable in their homes. In this is the force of reporting their destruction and the descent of what is hateful upon them, and an admonition to take lesson from them, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We made them stubble, as if they had not flourished yesterday﴾ [Yunus: 24], and like the saying of the poet:

As if there had never been between al-Hajun and al-Safa any companion, and no night-talker had conversed in Mecca.

Ibn Atiyyah said: "And ghanīna in the place" is said of residence that is accompanied by luxury and a comfortable life. This is what I have deduced from the poems in which the Arabs used this word, and he recited several verses on this, then said: As for the poet's saying:

We enjoyed ourselves for a time with poverty and wealth, then time gave each of us a cup of both.

its meaning is "we became self-sufficient and content," although this word is not connected to a place. End of quotation. Ibn Abbas said: "as if they had not been given life." Qatadah said: "as if they had not enjoyed." Al-Akhfash said: "as if they had not lived." Also Qatadah, Ibn Zayd, and Muqatil said: "as if they had not existed." Al-Zajjaj said: "as if they had not dwelt." Ibn Qutaybah said: "as if they had not stayed." (Alladhina) is the subject, and the comparative clause is its predicate. Al-Zamakhshari said: In this beginning there is the meaning of restriction, as if it were said: "Those who denied Shu'ayb" are the specific ones who were destroyed and uprooted, as if they had never stayed in their homes, because those who followed Shu'ayb were saved by God, exalted is He. End of quotation. Abu al-Baqa permitted that the predicate be ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb﴾, they were the losers, and ﴿as if they had never dwelt﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (kadhdhabu). He also permitted that "those who denied" be an attribute of the statement of "those who disbelieved among his people," and that it be a substitute for it, and on these two possibilities (ka'anna) is a hal. End of quotation. These are contrived aspects, and the apparent meaning is that they are independent sentences having no connection to what precedes them in terms of i'rab.

﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb, they were the losers﴾. This also is a subject and its predicate. Al-Zamakhshari said: In it is the meaning of restriction, that is, they are the specific ones singled out for the great loss, not those who followed him, for they are the winners. In this resumption of the beginning and this repetition is an intensification in refuting the statement of the chiefs to their followers, a mockery of their opinion, a derision of their counsel to their people, and a magnification of what befell them. End of quotation. These two sentences inform of what God did to them in their statement. They said: ﴿"We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb"﴾ [al-A'raf: 88], so the report came of their expulsion by destruction, and what expulsion is greater than their expulsion? And they said: ﴿"If you follow Shu'ayb, then you will indeed be losers"﴾, so God, exalted is He, ruled against them that they were the losers. Abu al-Baqa permitted in the i'rab of (alladhina) here that it be a substitute for the pronoun in (yaghnaw), or an accusative by implied "I mean." But the beginning we have mentioned is stronger and more eloquent.

﴿Then he turned away from them and said: "O my people, I have indeed conveyed to you the messages of my Lord, and I advised you"﴾. The explanation of its counterpart has passed in the story of Salih, peace be upon him.

﴿"So how can I grieve over a disbelieving people?"﴾ That is: how can I grieve over one who does not deserve to be grieved over? He indicated the cause that does not provoke grief, which is disbelief, since it is the greatest thing by which a believer is opposed, for they are opposites, as it came: "their two fires do not see each other." It seems he found in himself tenderness toward them, since his hope concerning them was that they would believe, and he could not. So he consoled himself by recalling the reason for consolation from them and for harshness, and he mentioned the most abominable of what they committed against him in description, which is disbelief in God, the thing that prompts the denial of the messengers, and fierce hostility, to the point that they would not dwell with him, and they threatened him with expulsion and with something worse, which is their return to their religion. Makki said: Shu'ayb set out with those who followed him to Mecca and they settled there. Ibn Wathhab, Ibn Musarrif, and al-A'mash read (ayisi) with a kasra on the hamza, and this is a dialect already mentioned in al-Fatiha.

What the grammarians say is that the response of the conditional is omitted, because the response of the oath indicates it, and for this reason the verb of the condition must be in the past tense. If al-Zamakhshari meant by his saying "stands in place of both responses" that it is sufficient in place of mentioning the response of the conditional, then this is close to correct. But if he meant that from the standpoint of grammatical craft it is as he claimed, then it is not so, because a clause cannot both have no place in the i'rab (grammatical analysis) and have a place in it. Here (idhan) means emphasis; it is the particle that is a response, and the conditional may accompany it, and it may not. Some grammarians claimed that in this position it is an adverb of time, whose governing element is (la-khasirun), and the nun is a substitute for the omitted element. The estimate is: "that you, if you follow him, are indeed losers." So when what it was attached to was omitted, the nun was introduced as a substitute for that, and it coincided with the alif, so two sakin letters met, and the alif was dropped because of their meeting. The substitution here is like the substitution in (yawma'idhin) and (hina'idhin) and the like. What this claimant held is nothing, because the substitution is not established, and the omission in (idhan), which is for the future, has a place, so this is to be understood in that way. (La-khasirun): Ibn Abbas said: "defrauded." Ata said: "ignorant." Al-Dahhak said: "incapable." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Losers for your exchanging misguidance for guidance, in accordance with His saying: ﴿Those are the ones who bought misguidance in exchange for guidance, so their trade did not profit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16]." It was also said: "You will suffer loss by following him, the benefits of short-measure and fraud, because he forbids you from it and urges you to full measure and fairness." End of quotation.

﴿So the quake seized them, and they became prostrate in their homes in the morning﴾ [al-A'raf: 78]. The explanation of this sentence has already passed. Ibn Abbas and others said: When he prayed against them, a gate of Hell was opened upon them with a severe heat that seized their breath, so shade and water did not benefit them. When they entered the caves to cool themselves, they found them hotter than the outside, so they came out fleeing to the open desert. A cloud overshadowed them, in which was a pleasant wind, and they called out to one another: "Upon you the shade!" So they all gathered beneath it, and it closed over them, and God kindled it into fire, and the earth quaked beneath them, and they burned as locusts burn when roasted, until they became ashes. It is also narrated that the wind was withheld from them for seven days, then the heat was imposed upon them. Yazid al-Jarīrī said: The wind was imposed upon them for seven days, then a mountain was raised for them from afar, and a man came to it, and beneath it were rivers and springs, so they all gathered beneath it, and that mountain fell upon them. Qatadah said: Shu'ayb was sent to the People of the Thicket and they were destroyed by the overshadowing cloud, and to the People of Madyan, and Gabriel cried out to them one cry, and they all perished. Ibn Atiyyah said: It is possible that one group of Shu'ayb's people perished by the quake and another group perished by the overshadowing cloud. Al-Tabari said: It reached me that a man from them, called Amr ibn Jalha, when he saw the cloud, said, the poet said:

O people, indeed Shu'ayb is a messenger, so leave behind you Sumayr and Imran ibn Shaddad.

Indeed I see a cloud, O people, that has risen, calling with a voice over the stony valley.

And indeed you will not see in it any healthy one tomorrow, except the Raqim walking between the hills.

Sumayr and Imran were their soothsayers, and al-Raqim was their dog. And from Abu Abd Allah al-Bajali: Abjad, Hawwaz, Huttī, Kalaman, Sa'fas, and Qarshat are names like the kings of Madyan, and Kalaman was their king at the time the punishment came upon them, in the time of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him. When he died, his daughter wept for him, saying:

Kalaman has broken my pillar; his destruction is in the midst of the dwelling place.

The lord of the people, death came upon him as fire in the midst of a shade.

Their dwelling was made a fire upon them, like something dissolved to nothing.

﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb, as if they had never dwelt therein﴾, that is: as if they had never lived at ease, comfortable in their homes. In this is the force of reporting their destruction and the descent of what is hateful upon them, and an admonition to take lesson from them, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We made them stubble, as if they had not flourished yesterday﴾ [Yunus: 24], and like the saying of the poet:

As if there had never been between al-Hajun and al-Safa any companion, and no night-talker had conversed in Mecca.

Ibn Atiyyah said: "And ghanīna in the place" is said of residence that is accompanied by luxury and a comfortable life. This is what I have deduced from the poems in which the Arabs used this word, and he recited several verses on this, then said: As for the poet's saying:

We enjoyed ourselves for a time with poverty and wealth, then time gave each of us a cup of both.

its meaning is "we became self-sufficient and content," although this word is not connected to a place. End of quotation. Ibn Abbas said: "as if they had not been given life." Qatadah said: "as if they had not enjoyed." Al-Akhfash said: "as if they had not lived." Also Qatadah, Ibn Zayd, and Muqatil said: "as if they had not existed." Al-Zajjaj said: "as if they had not dwelt." Ibn Qutaybah said: "as if they had not stayed." (Alladhina) is the subject, and the comparative clause is its predicate. Al-Zamakhshari said: In this beginning there is the meaning of restriction, as if it were said: "Those who denied Shu'ayb" are the specific ones who were destroyed and uprooted, as if they had never stayed in their homes, because those who followed Shu'ayb were saved by God, exalted is He. End of quotation. Abu al-Baqa permitted that the predicate be ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb﴾, they were the losers, and ﴿as if they had never dwelt﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (kadhdhabu). He also permitted that "those who denied" be an attribute of the statement of "those who disbelieved among his people," and that it be a substitute for it, and on these two possibilities (ka'anna) is a hal. End of quotation. These are contrived aspects, and the apparent meaning is that they are independent sentences having no connection to what precedes them in terms of i'rab.

﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb, they were the losers﴾. This also is a subject and its predicate. Al-Zamakhshari said: In it is the meaning of restriction, that is, they are the specific ones singled out for the great loss, not those who followed him, for they are the winners. In this resumption of the beginning and this repetition is an intensification in refuting the statement of the chiefs to their followers, a mockery of their opinion, a derision of their counsel to their people, and a magnification of what befell them. End of quotation. These two sentences inform of what God did to them in their statement. They said: ﴿"We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb"﴾ [al-A'raf: 88], so the report came of their expulsion by destruction, and what expulsion is greater than their expulsion? And they said: ﴿"If you follow Shu'ayb, then you will indeed be losers"﴾, so God, exalted is He, ruled against them that they were the losers. Abu al-Baqa permitted in the i'rab of (alladhina) here that it be a substitute for the pronoun in (yaghnaw), or an accusative by implied "I mean." But the beginning we have mentioned is stronger and more eloquent.

﴿Then he turned away from them and said: "O my people, I have indeed conveyed to you the messages of my Lord, and I advised you"﴾. The explanation of its counterpart has passed in the story of Salih, peace be upon him.

﴿"So how can I grieve over a disbelieving people?"﴾ That is: how can I grieve over one who does not deserve to be grieved over? He indicated the cause that does not provoke grief, which is disbelief, since it is the greatest thing by which a believer is opposed, for they are opposites, as it came: "their two fires do not see each other." It seems he found in himself tenderness toward them, since his hope concerning them was that they would believe, and he could not. So he consoled himself by recalling the reason for consolation from them and for harshness, and he mentioned the most abominable of what they committed against him in description, which is disbelief in God, the thing that prompts the denial of the messengers, and fierce hostility, to the point that they would not dwell with him, and they threatened him with expulsion and with something worse, which is their return to their religion. Makki said: Shu'ayb set out with those who followed him to Mecca and they settled there. Ibn Wathhab, Ibn Musarrif, and al-A'mash read (ayisi) with a kasra on the hamza, and this is a dialect already mentioned in al-Fatiha.

﴿Then he turned away from them and said: "O my people, I have indeed conveyed to you the messages of my Lord, and I advised you"﴾. The explanation of its counterpart has passed in the story of Salih, peace be upon him.

﴿"So how can I grieve over a disbelieving people?"﴾ That is: how can I grieve over one who does not deserve to be grieved over? He indicated the cause that does not provoke grief, which is disbelief, since it is the greatest thing by which a believer is opposed, for they are opposites, as it came: "their two fires do not see each other." It seems he found in himself tenderness toward them, since his hope concerning them was that they would believe, and he could not. So he consoled himself by recalling the reason for consolation from them and for harshness, and he mentioned the most abominable of what they committed against him in description, which is disbelief in God, the thing that prompts the denial of the messengers, and fierce hostility, to the point that they would not dwell with him, and they threatened him with expulsion and with something worse, which is their return to their religion. Ibn Wathhab, Ibn Musarrif, and al-A'mash read (ayisi) with a kasra on the hamza, and this is a dialect already mentioned in al-Fatiha.

﴿And We did not send a prophet to any town without seizing its people with misfortune and hardship, that perhaps they would humble themselves.﴾ When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned what befell the earlier nations of His might and punishment upon them at the end of their affair, when admonition no longer benefited them, He mentioned that this was His custom with the followers of the prophets when they persisted in denying them. After "illa" (except, only) comes a past-tense verb, which is "akhadhna" (We seized). A past-tense verb does not follow "illa" unless a verb precedes it or it is accompanied by "qad." The example of a preceding verb is this verse, and the example of "qad" is your saying: "Zayd is not but qad qama" (Zayd is none but has risen). The clause "akhadhna" is a circumstantial clause (ḥaliyyah), meaning: except while seizing its people. This is an "istithna' mufarragh" (exceptive construction lacking its complement) in terms of circumstances. The explanation of a similar instance of His saying "illa akhadhna" to its end has already been given.

﴿Then We replaced the evil with good.﴾ That is, in place of the evil condition of misfortune and hardship, We gave the good condition of ease and blessing. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and Qatadah said: the place of hardship is ease. It is also said: the place of evil is good. "Makan" (place) is the object of the "ba'" (in), meaning: with the place of evil. The word "makan" implies that hardship had settled among them, as if it had become a place for hardship among them. Some grammarians parsed "makan" as an adverb of place (ẓarf), meaning: in the place of. ﴿Until they multiplied (ʿafaw)⦆, that is, they increased and multiplied. Mujahid said: their wealth and children increased. Ibn Bahr said: until they turned away, from "ʿafa 'an dhanbihi" (he pardoned his sin), meaning he turned away from it. al-Hasan said: they grew fat. Qatadah said: they were delighted by their multitude. This was a gradual leading on by Him, because He seized them with hardship so that they might take heed and refrain, but they did not do so; then He seized them with ease so that they might give thanks.

﴿And they said: Hardship and ease have touched our fathers.﴾ Blessing made them insolent and wanton, so they said: this is the custom of time, hardship and ease. Similar things had befallen our fathers, not through trial and purpose, but by mere chance, not as the prophets inform us. They made their forefathers and what had befallen them an example for themselves and for what would befall them. Therefore, we should not deny this custom of the actions of time.

﴿So We seized them suddenly while they did not perceive.﴾ The discussion of a similar verse has already preceded, when they corrupted things under both interpretations; they were seized by this seizing.

﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and been mindful of Allah, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth. But they denied, so We seized them for what they had earned.﴾ That is: had they been among those whom Allah's knowledge had preordained to be clothed in belief in what the prophets brought and in acts of obedience, which are the fruit of belief, so that the blessings of heaven would be made easy for them. But they were among those whom His knowledge had preordained to deny the prophets, and so they were seized for their transgression. Belief, denial, reward and punishment were all decreed by destiny (qadar). Belief and denial are attributed to the servant as acquisition (kasb), while the one who brings both into existence is Allah, exalted is He, who is not questioned about what He does.

al-Zamakhshari said: the definite article in "al-qura" (the towns) refers back to the towns indicated by His saying: "And We did not send a prophet to any town." It is as if He said: "And if the people of those towns who denied and were destroyed had believed, their disbelief would have been replaced, and they would have avoided sins in place of committing them, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth." We would have given them good in every way. It is also said: He meant rain and plants. "But they denied, so We seized them" for the evil of their earnings. It is permissible that the definite article in "al-qura" is for the genus. End of quotation. In his saying "and were mindful of sins" there is a trace of Mu'tazili tendency. Allah connected the opening of blessings to belief and piety, and connected to denial alone, which is the opposite of belief, destruction, and He did not mention the opposite of piety, because denial is not benefited by good with it, unlike belief, which benefits even if acts of obedience are not performed with it.

The apparent meaning of His saying "blessings from the heaven and the earth" is not a specific thing, which is why it came indefinite. It is said: the blessings of heaven are rain and the blessings of earth are fruits. al-Suddi said: the meaning is: We would have opened upon them the gates of heaven and earth with provision. It is also said: the blessings of heaven are the answering of supplication, and the blessings of earth are the facilitating of needs. It is also said: the blessings of heaven are rain and the blessings of earth are livestock and cattle, and the attainment of safety and security. It is also said: the blessings are growth and increases. So from heaven, through rain, wind and sun, and from earth, through plants and preservation of what has grown. This is what human nature perceives; Allah has other servants whose number is not counted, and Allah knows best. This is because heaven functions as a father and earth as a mother, and from both all goods come about through the creation and management of Allah. The seizing is a seizing of destruction for sins.

Ibn 'Amir, 'Isa al-Thaqafi and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read "la-fattahna" with a doubled ta'. The meaning of "fath" (opening) here is facilitation for them, as ease is given to closed doors by opening them. From this comes "fataḥtu 'ala al-qari'" (I prompted the reciter) when you facilitate for him by feeding him what is difficult for him to memorize of the Qur'an when he wishes to recite.

﴿Did the people of the towns then feel secure that Our punishment would come upon them by night while they were sleeping?﴾ The hamza (interrogative particle) entered upon "amina" (felt secure) for interrogation, in the manner of rebuke, reproach, denial and threat to the disbelievers contemporary with the Messenger ﷺ, that there would descend upon them the like of what descended upon those. The "fa" (then) connects this clause to what precedes it. al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, what is the element it is connected to, and why was the first connected with "fa" and the second with "wa"? I say: the element connected to is His saying "So We seized them suddenly," and His saying "And if the people of the towns had believed... they earned," which came as a parenthetical insertion between the conjunct and the element conjoined to. It is connected with "fa" because the meaning is: they did and made, so We seized them suddenly; after that, did the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment would come upon them by night, and did they feel secure that Our punishment would come upon them in the forenoon? End of quotation. What al-Zamakhshari mentioned, that the conjunctive particle after the interrogative hamza, which conjoins what follows it to what precedes the hamza in sentences, is a return to the position of the majority in this matter, and an interpretation of this verse contrary to what he had established as his own position in other verses, namely that he assumes an omitted element between the hamza and the conjunctive particle, by which the conjunction of what follows the particle to it becomes sound, and that the hamza and the conjunctive particle are situated in their places without considering the conjunctive particle as preceding the hamza in the assumed structure, and that he placed the interrogative first out of concern, because it has the front of speech. Our discussion with him on this question has already preceded. "Baʾsuna" means Our punishment, and "bayatan" means at night. Its explanation has been given at the beginning of the surah. It is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf), meaning at the time of their sleeping, or as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). That is the time of heedlessness and sleep, so the coming of punishment at that time, which is the time of rest and gathering, is extremely difficult, since it came at the time of safety.

﴿Or did the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment would come upon them in the forenoon while they were at play?﴾ That is, in a state of heedlessness, aversion, and preoccupation with what is of no benefit, as if they were playing. "Duḥan" (in the forenoon) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, meaning at the time of forenoon brightness. Each adverb of time is qualified by what suits it of the state: night is qualified by sleep, and forenoon by play. "Na'imun" (sleeping) came as the active participle because it is a state of settledness and stability for those who spend the night, and "yal'abun" (playing) came in the imperfect because they are occupied with actions that renew gradually at that time. Nafi' and the two sons (Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir) read "aw amina" with a sukun on the waw, making "aw" a conjunctive particle, whose meaning is classification, not permission or choice, contrary to those who held that. Warsh omitted the hamza of "amina" and transferred its vowel to the preceding sukun waw. The rest read with the interrogative hamza before it and the conjunctive waw. The phrase "people of the towns" is repeated because of what this carries of making hear, conveying, threatening, and warning the hearer with what would not be present in a pronoun if it had come; or "they felt secure," for whenever the purpose is glorification, magnification, and dread, the apparent noun is used.

﴿Did they then feel secure from the plan of Allah? None feels secure from the plan of Allah except the losing people.﴾ [al-A'raf: 99] The conjunction with "fa" and the attribution of the verb to the pronoun came because the conjoined clause is a repetition of His saying "Did the people of the towns feel secure," and "or did they feel secure," and an emphasis on its content. So it was fitting to repeat the clause accompanied by "fa." "Makr" (plan) is a verbal noun attributed to its agent, and it is a metaphor for His seizing the servant from where he does not perceive. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "makra Allah" (the plan of Allah) is the attribution of a created thing to the Creator, as you say "the she-camel of Allah" and "the house of Allah." What is meant is an action by which the plan of the disbelievers is requited, and it was attributed to Allah because it is the punishment for the sin, for the Arabs call punishment, from whatever direction it comes, by the name of the sin upon which the punishment falls. This is explicit in His saying "they plotted" and "Allah plotted." End of quotation. 'Ata' al-'Awfi said: the plan of Allah is His punishment and His recompense for their plotting. It is also said: His plan is His gradual leading on through blessing and health, and His seizing them when they are heedless. Warsh omitted the hamza of "amina" and transferred its vowel to the preceding sukun waw. The rest read with the interrogative hamza before it and the conjunctive waw. The phrase "people of the towns" is repeated because of what this carries of making hear, conveying, threatening, and warning the hearer with what would not be present in a pronoun if it had come; or "they felt secure," for whenever the purpose is glorification, magnification, and dread, the apparent noun is used.

﴿Did they then feel secure from the plan of Allah? None feels secure from the plan of Allah except the losing people.﴾ [al-A'raf: 99] The conjunction with "fa" and the attribution of the verb to the pronoun came because the conjoined clause is a repetition of His saying "Did the people of the towns feel secure," and "or did they feel secure," and an emphasis on its content. So it was fitting to repeat the clause accompanied by "fa." "Makr" (plan) is a verbal noun attributed to its agent, and it is a metaphor for His seizing the servant from where he does not perceive. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "makra Allah" (the plan of Allah) is the attribution of a created thing to the Creator, as you say "the she-camel of Allah" and "the house of Allah." What is meant is an action by which the plan of the disbelievers is requited, and it was attributed to Allah because it is the punishment for the sin, for the Arabs call punishment, from whatever direction it comes, by the name of the sin upon which the punishment falls. This is explicit in His saying "they plotted" and "Allah plotted." End of quotation. 'Ata' al-'Awfi said: the plan of Allah is His punishment and His recompense for their plotting. It is also said: His plan is His gradual leading on through blessing and health, and His seizing them when they are heedless. He repeated "plan" attributed to Allah to confirm that the requital of the plan would fall upon them.

﴿And We did not send a prophet to any town without seizing its people with misfortune and hardship, that perhaps they would humble themselves.﴾ When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned what befell the earlier nations of His might and punishment upon them at the end of their affair, when admonition no longer benefited them, He mentioned that this was His custom with the followers of the prophets when they persisted in denying them. After "illa" (except, only) comes a past-tense verb, which is "akhadhna" (We seized). A past-tense verb does not follow "illa" unless a verb precedes it or it is accompanied by "qad." The example of a preceding verb is this verse, and the example of "qad" is your saying: "Zayd is not but qad qama" (Zayd is none but has risen). The clause "akhadhna" is a circumstantial clause (ḥaliyyah), meaning: except while seizing its people. This is an "istithna' mufarragh" (exceptive construction lacking its complement) in terms of circumstances. The explanation of a similar instance of His saying "illa akhadhna" to its end has already been given.

﴿Then We replaced the evil with good.﴾ That is, in place of the evil condition of misfortune and hardship, We gave the good condition of ease and blessing. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and Qatadah said: the place of hardship is ease. It is also said: the place of evil is good. "Makan" (place) is the object of the "ba'" (in), meaning: with the place of evil. The word "makan" implies that hardship had settled among them, as if it had become a place for hardship among them. Some grammarians parsed "makan" as an adverb of place (ẓarf), meaning: in the place of. ﴿Until they multiplied (ʿafaw)⦆, that is, they increased and multiplied. Mujahid said: their wealth and children increased. Ibn Bahr said: until they turned away, from "ʿafa 'an dhanbihi" (he pardoned his sin), meaning he turned away from it. al-Hasan said: they grew fat. Qatadah said: they were delighted by their multitude. This was a gradual leading on by Him, because He seized them with hardship so that they might take heed and refrain, but they did not do so; then He seized them with ease so that they might give thanks.

﴿And they said: Hardship and ease have touched our fathers.﴾ Blessing made them insolent and wanton, so they said: this is the custom of time, hardship and ease. Similar things had befallen our fathers, not through trial and purpose, but by mere chance, not as the prophets inform us. They made their forefathers and what had befallen them an example for themselves and for what would befall them. Therefore, we should not deny this custom of the actions of time.

﴿So We seized them suddenly while they did not perceive.﴾ The discussion of a similar verse has already preceded, when they corrupted things under both interpretations; they were seized by this seizing.

﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and been mindful of Allah, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth. But they denied, so We seized them for what they had earned.﴾ That is: had they been among those whom Allah's knowledge had preordained to be clothed in belief in what the prophets brought and in acts of obedience, which are the fruit of belief, so that the blessings of heaven would be made easy for them. But they were among those whom His knowledge had preordained to deny the prophets, and so they were seized for their transgression. Belief, denial, reward and punishment were all decreed by destiny (qadar). Belief and denial are attributed to the servant as acquisition (kasb), while the one who brings both into existence is Allah, exalted is He, who is not questioned about what He does.

al-Zamakhshari said: the definite article in "al-qura" (the towns) refers back to the towns indicated by His saying: "And We did not send a prophet to any town." It is as if He said: "And if the people of those towns who denied and were destroyed had believed, their disbelief would have been replaced, and they would have avoided sins in place of committing them, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth." We would have given them good in every way. It is also said: He meant rain and plants. "But they denied, so We seized them" for the evil of their earnings. It is permissible that the definite article in "al-qura" is for the genus. End of quotation. In his saying "and were mindful of sins" there is a trace of Mu'tazili tendency. Allah connected the opening of blessings to belief and piety, and connected to denial alone, which is the opposite of belief, destruction, and He did not mention the opposite of piety, because denial is not benefited by good with it, unlike belief, which benefits even if acts of obedience are not performed with it.

The apparent meaning of His saying "blessings from the heaven and the earth" is not a specific thing, which is why it came indefinite. It is said: the blessings of heaven are rain and the blessings of earth are fruits. al-Suddi said: the meaning is: We would have opened upon them the gates of heaven and earth with provision. It is also said: the blessings of heaven are the answering of supplication, and the blessings of earth are the facilitating of needs. It is also said: the blessings of heaven are rain and the blessings of earth are livestock and cattle, and the attainment of safety and security. It is also said: the blessings are growth and increases. So from heaven, through rain, wind and sun, and from earth, through plants and preservation of what has grown. This is what human nature perceives; Allah has other servants whose number is not counted, and Allah knows best. This is because heaven functions as a father and earth as a mother, and from both all goods come about through the creation and management of Allah. The seizing is a seizing of destruction for sins.

Ibn 'Amir, 'Isa al-Thaqafi and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read "la-fattahna" with a doubled ta'. The meaning of "fath" (opening) here is facilitation for them, as ease is given to closed doors by opening them. From this comes "fataḥtu 'ala al-qari'" (I prompted the reciter) when you facilitate for him by feeding him what is difficult for him to memorize of the Qur'an when he wishes to recite.

﴿Did the people of the towns then feel secure that Our punishment would come upon them by night while they were sleeping?﴾ The hamza (interrogative particle) entered upon "amina" (felt secure) for interrogation, in the manner of rebuke, reproach, denial and threat to the disbelievers contemporary with the Messenger ﷺ, that there would descend upon them the like of what descended upon those. The "fa" (then) connects this clause to what precedes it. al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, what is the element it is connected to, and why was the first connected with "fa" and the second with "wa"? I say: the element connected to is His saying "So We seized them suddenly," and His saying "And if the people of the towns had believed... they earned," which came as a parenthetical insertion between the conjunct and the element conjoined to. It is connected with "fa" because the meaning is: they did and made, so We seized them suddenly; after that, did the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment would come upon them by night, and did they feel secure that Our punishment would come upon them in the forenoon? End of quotation. What al-Zamakhshari mentioned, that the conjunctive particle after the interrogative hamza, which conjoins what follows it to what precedes the hamza in sentences, is a return to the position of the majority in this matter, and an interpretation of this verse contrary to what he had established as his own position in other verses, namely that he assumes an omitted element between the hamza and the conjunctive particle, by which the conjunction of what follows the particle to it becomes sound, and that the hamza and the conjunctive particle are situated in their places without considering the conjunctive particle as preceding the hamza in the assumed structure, and that he placed the interrogative first out of concern, because it has the front of speech. Our discussion with him on this question has already preceded. "Baʾsuna" means Our punishment, and "bayatan" means at night. Its explanation has been given at the beginning of the surah. It is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf), meaning at the time of their sleeping, or as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). That is the time of heedlessness and sleep, so the coming of punishment at that time, which is the time of rest and gathering, is extremely difficult, since it came at the time of safety.

﴿Or did the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment would come upon them in the forenoon while they were at play?﴾ That is, in a state of heedlessness, aversion, and preoccupation with what is of no benefit, as if they were playing. "Duḥan" (in the forenoon) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, meaning at the time of forenoon brightness. Each adverb of time is qualified by what suits it of the state: night is qualified by sleep, and forenoon by play. Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 99–100:

﴿Has it not become clear to those who inherit the land after its former people that, if We willed, We could afflict them for their sins?﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: (yahdi) means "makes clear," as in His saying ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them﴾ [Fussilat: 17], meaning: We made clear to them the path of guidance. The subject of yahdi may take several forms. The first is that it refers to Allah, and the reading of those who recite (nahdi) with a nun supports this. The second is that it is a pronoun referring to what is understood from the context of the preceding speech, meaning: "Has there not become clear (yahdi) what happened to the past nations, the people of the towns and others?" On these two views, "that if We willed" and what follows it occupy the position of the object of yahdi, meaning: "Has Allah not made clear," or "What has preceded of the stories of the towns and the outcome of their affairs has not made clear to the inheritors that We could afflict them for their sins if We willed that," meaning: their knowledge of Our affliction of them, or Our power to afflict them. The meaning is: "You are sinners like them, and you know what befell them. Do you not fear that what befell them may befall you? That is not beyond Us if We will it." The third view is that the subject of yahdi is His saying ﴿that if We willed﴾, so that the verbal noun is formed from the apodosis of law (lau), and the estimated meaning is: "Have We not made clear and manifest to the inheritors their end, their outcome, and Our affliction of them for their sins if We willed that," meaning: their knowledge of Our affliction of them, or Our power to afflict them. On both estimates, when (an) is the object, the (an) here is the lightened form of the heavy (inna), because guidance in this sense carries the meaning of knowledge; its noun is an omitted pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), and the predicate is the clause introduced by (law). (Nashaʾ) has the meaning of (shiʾna), not the (law) which denotes that something would have occurred for the occurrence of something else; when the imperfect follows it, it turns its meaning into the past. The object of (nashaʾ) is omitted, indicated by the apodosis of (law). The apodosis is ﴿We afflicted them﴾, and it does not come with the (lam), although the verb is affirmative, since omitting it is permissible. This is like His saying ﴿If We willed, We would have made it salty﴾ [al-Waqiʿa: 70]. The more common usage is with the (lam), as in His saying ﴿If We willed, We would have made it into debris﴾ [al-Waqiʿa: 65] and ﴿If We had willed, We would have raised him thereby﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 176]. "Those who inherit the land" means: those who are left in it after the destruction of its people. Its apparent sense is an address to those in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) among the polytheists of Quraysh and others. Ibn ʿAbbas said: he means the people of Makkah.

﴿And We seal their hearts, so they do not hear﴾. Apparently this is a resumptive (independent) sentence, meaning: "And We Ourselves seal their hearts." The meaning is that whoever Allah has made clear the paths of guidance for, and has mentioned to him examples of those whom Allah destroyed for their sins, and who nevertheless persists in his error without restraint, Allah seals his heart, so his hearing turns away from hearing the truth. Ibn al-Anbari said: it may be coordinated with (asabna) if it has the meaning of (nuṣību), so that the past tense is placed in the position of the future when the usage is clear, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills, will give you better than that﴾ [al-Furqan: 10], meaning: if He wills, which is indicated by His saying ﴿and will give you palaces﴾ [al-Furqan: 10]. End. Thus he made (law) conditional with the meaning of (an), and did not make it the (law) which denotes that something would have occurred for the occurrence of something else. For this reason he made (asabna) mean (nuṣību). An example of (law) being used in place of (an) is the poet's verse:

Let not those who hope in you deceive you, unless you show the character of the noble, even if you are destitute.

Al-Zamakhshari refuted what Ibn al-Anbari said on the level of meaning, but with the assumption that (wa-naṭbaʿu) means (ṭabaʿnā), so that he coordinated the present tense with the past tense that is the apodosis of (law nashaʾ). Thus he interpreted the coordinated element, which is the apodosis, as referring to the future, and interpreted the coordinating element as referring to the past. Al-Zamakhshari interpreted the coordinated element and referred it to the past. The result of al-Zamakhshari's refutation is that neither of the two estimates is valid. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "Can (wa-naṭbaʿu) be in the sense of (ṭabaʿnā), just as (law nashaʾ) is in the sense of (law shiʾna), and be coordinated with (asabnāhum)?" I say: this meaning does not fit, because the people were already sealed upon their hearts, described by the attribute of those before them in committing sins and being afflicted by them, and this interpretation leads to their being free of this attribute, and to Allah, if He willed, making them attributed with it. End. This refutation, on its face, is sound. Its summary is that what is coordinated with the apodosis is an apodosis, whether we interpret the coordinated element or the coordinating element. The apodosis of (law) has not yet occurred, whether (law) is the particle for what would have occurred upon the occurrence of something else, or in the sense of the conditional (in). The affliction has not occurred, while the sealing upon hearts has occurred. Therefore it is not valid to coordinate it with the apodosis. But if (wa-naṭbaʿu) is interpreted as meaning "and We continue to seal their hearts," coordination becomes possible, because the continuance has not yet occurred, even though the sealing has occurred. Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: al-Zamakhshari's explanation, even on the strongest of the possibilities, is weak, because being sealed upon in disbelief was not incompatible with the validity of coordination, and he had established that the meaning is: "Or has it not become clear to those whom We leave in the land after We destroyed those before them in it, that We could destroy them after them?" This is the meaning of His saying ﴿that if We willed﴾, We would have afflicted them, that is, for the punishment of their sins, ﴿and We seal their hearts﴾, that is, We did not destroy them with punishment, ﴿and We seal their hearts, so they do not hear﴾, that is, they do not accept, do not take warning, and are not restrained. We have said that what is meant is either destruction or sealing upon the heart, because destruction does not combine with sealing upon the heart; when He destroys someone, it is impossible for Him to seal his heart. End. The coordination in (wa-naṭbaʿu) with (wa) is not prevented by what he mentioned, because making the meaning "either destruction or sealing" and the apparent sense of coordination with (wa) do not indicate this meaning. If you make (wa) mean (aw), it is possible, and likewise the phrase "if We did not destroy them with punishment and We seal upon their hearts" would be contrary to coordination with (wa). Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi cited some of the statements of the exegetes which show that being sealed upon in disbelief does not prevent the validity of coordination. He said: Abu ʿAli, meaning al-Jubba'i, and Allah knows best, said: the sealing (ṭabʿ) is a mark on the heart, a black spot, which indicates that its bearer will not prosper. Al-Asamm said: meaning, what they are upon is imposed on them, so they do not repent except at the moment of seeing, and their repentance is not accepted. Abu Muslim said: the sealing is forsaking (khidhlān); the disbeliever is forsaken, so he sees the sign and does not believe in it, and chooses what he has become accustomed to and familiar with. With these statements, coordination is possible only on the interpretation that (wa) means (aw). Al-Zamakhshari permitted two other possibilities for the coordination of (wa-naṭbaʿu), one of which is weak and the other is wrong. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, "With what is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and We seal upon their hearts﴾ connected?" I say: it has several possibilities. Either it is coordinated with what is indicated by the meaning of ﴿Has it not become clear to them﴾ [al-Sajda: 26], as if it were said: "They are heedless of the guidance, and We seal upon their hearts," or it is coordinated with ﴿inherit the land﴾. End. His saying that it is coordinated with something implied, namely "they are heedless of the guidance," is weak, because it is an ellipsis (iḍmār) that is not needed, since it is valid for it to be a resumptive sentence within coordination of sentences (ʿaṭf al-jumal), being coordinated with the whole sentence introduced by the interrogative particle. Al-Zamakhshari and others said this. His saying that it is coordinated with (yarithūna) is wrong, because if it were coordinated with yarithūna, it would be a relative clause (ṣila) of (alladhīna), since what is coordinated with a relative clause is a relative clause. Then the components of the relative clause would be separated by something foreign to it, namely His saying ﴿that if We willed, We would have afflicted them for their sins﴾, whether we estimate ﴿that if We willed﴾ to be in the position of the subject of (yahdi) or in the position of its object. It is then a complement of (yahdi) with no connection to any part of the relative clause of (alladhīna), and this is not permissible. The meaning of His saying ﴿We afflicted them for their sins﴾ is: We punished them for their sins; or ﴿afflicted them﴾ is taken as implicitly meaning ﴿destroyed them﴾, so it is a figure of speech by ellipsis (majāz al-iḍmār) or implicit meaning (tadmīn). The meaning of "not hearing" is: the negation of acceptance and of the admonition that follows from the existence of hearing. He made the absence of its benefit an absence of it.
