In both possibilities, the complement is connected to ḥaqīq.

Since he had mentioned that he is a messenger from Allah, and that he does not say anything about Allah except the truth, he began to mention the miracle and the extraordinary sign that proves the truth of his messengership. The address in ﴿I have brought you﴾ is to Pharaoh and his assembly who were present with him. The meaning of "with a clear proof" (bi-bayyina) is a sign that is clear in indicating what I shall mention. As for the bayyina (clear proof), it is said to be the nine signs mentioned in His words ﴿among nine signs to Pharaoh and his people﴾ [al-Naml: 12]. Some scholars said that the context of the verse requires that the bayyina be the staff and the white hand, as is shown by what follows, His words ﴿so he threw down his staff﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas and most scholars said it is the staff. In His words ﴿from your Lord﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 3] there is an allusion that Pharaoh is not a lord for them; rather their Lord is the One who sent Musa with the proof from Him. ﴿So send﴾, meaning: release, and sending is the opposite of holding back. ﴿With me the Children of Israel﴾, meaning: so that they may go back to their homelands and the birthplace of their fathers, the holy land. This is because, when Yusuf (Joseph, peace be upon him) died and the tribes (asbat) ended, Pharaoh overpowered their descendants and enslaved them in hard labor, and they used to pay him tribute. Allah rescued them through Musa, peace be upon him. The period between the day Yusuf entered Egypt and the day Musa entered it was four hundred years. The apparent meaning is that Musa did not ask Pharaoh in this verse for anything except the sending of the Children of Israel with him. In other verses, he called him to acknowledge the lordship of Allah the Exalted and to affirm His unity. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So say, "Would you like to purify yourself, and I would guide you to your Lord so that you would fear Him?"﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 18]. Every prophet calls to the unity of Allah the Exalted. Allah the Exalted also said, relating Pharaoh's words: ﴿Shall we believe in two humans like us, while their people are our servants?﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 47]. This and similar verses are evidence that he asked him to believe, contrary to those who said that Musa did not call him to faith nor to adherence to his law. The Children of Israel were not from the people of Pharaoh and the Copts. Do you not see that the rest of the Copts, who are the majority, were not returned to by Musa?

(p-356) ﴿He said, "If you have brought a sign, then produce it, if you are of the truthful."﴾ When Musa, peace be upon him, presented his messengership to Pharaoh and mentioned the proof of his truthfulness, which is his coming with a clear sign and a miraculous extraordinary event, Pharaoh demanded from him a breach of habit that proves truthfulness. This demand may be understood as a test of whether he could do it, or it may be understood as a challenge, since it was fixed in Pharaoh's mind that Musa could not bring a sign. The meaning is: "If you have brought a sign from your Lord, then bring it before me so that your claim may be valid and your truthfulness established."

﴿So he threw down his staff, and behold, it was a clear serpent.﴾ He began with the staff rather than the other miracles, because it is a miracle that contains many miracles. It was said that among them: he struck with it the door of Pharaoh, and Pharaoh was frightened by the knocking, so his hair turned white and he dyed it black; he was thus the first to dye hair black. Among them also: its transformation into a serpent, and the transformation of a piece of wood into flesh and blood with life inside it, which is among the greatest miracles. Its transformation into a serpent produced a terror that nothing else produces. Among them: his striking the rock with it so that it gushed forth springs; his striking the earth with it so that it produced plants. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. Among them: his fighting with it against thieves and beasts that targeted his flock; its blazing at night like the blaze of a candle; its becoming like a rope for drawing water from a deep well; its swallowing the ropes and staves of the magicians; and its nullifying what they had made by their deception and sorcery. Throwing (ilqaʾ) is literal when applied to bodies, and metaphorical when applied to meanings, as in "he threw the question" (alqā al-masʾala).

Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Suddi said: the staff became a great serpent, with a mane, its mouth open, between whose jaws there were eighty cubits. It was said: forty. This was mentioned by Makki from Farqad. One of its jaws was on the ground and the other on the wall of the palace. They also mentioned, concerning Pharaoh's agitation, fear, and flight, and his promise to Musa that he would believe if it returned to its former state, and the great number of Pharaoh's people who died of fright, matters that the verse does not touch upon and that are not established in a sound hadith. Allah knows best about them. The meaning of "clear" (mubin) is manifest, with no imagination involved; rather, it was a serpent in reality. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "idha" (behold) is a place adverb according to al-Mubarrad, since it is a predicate referring to a body. The correct view held by our shaykhs is that it is a place adverb, as al-Mubarrad said, and this is attributed to Sibawayh. His words "since it is a predicate referring to a body" do not apply to this position, since in this place it is not a predicate about a body. Rather, the predicate is his words "a serpent." If you said "fa-idha hiya" (and behold it) without more, it would not be a complete sentence. His words "since it is a predicate referring to a body" should be understood as similar to: "I went out, and behold, a lion," according to the interpretation of one who makes it a place adverb. What he mentioned, that the correct view held by people is that it is a time adverb, is the position of al-Riyashi, and it is also attributed to Sibawayh. The position of the Kufans is that idha al-fujaʾiyya (the sudden "idha") is a particle, not a noun.

﴿He drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the onlookers.﴾ That is, he pulled his hand out. It is said that it was from his pocket (*jayb*), which is the apparent meaning, based on His words: ﴿Put your hand into your pocket﴾ (Q. 27:12). It is also said that it was from his sleeve. And "to the onlookers" means to those who look. Mentioning this indicates how great its whiteness was, because it would not appear to onlookers unless its whiteness was wondrous and beyond the ordinary, so that people would gather to it as spectators gather to marvels. Mujahid said: "white" like milk, or whiter. It is narrated that it would appear (p. 358) luminous and transparent like the sun, then he would return it, and it would go back to the color of Musa's skin. Adam, peace be upon him, had a very dark complexion. Ibn 'Abbas said: it became a brilliant light which illuminated what was between the heaven and the earth, with a sheen like the flash of lightning. So they fell prostrate on their faces. Al-Kalbi said: we have been told that Musa, peace be upon him, said: "O Pharaoh, what is this in my hand?" He said: "It is a staff." So Musa threw it down, and behold, it was a serpent. It is also narrated that Pharaoh saw Musa's hand and said to Pharaoh: "What is this?" He said: "Your hand." Then he put it into his pocket, and he was wearing a woolen cloak; he took it out, and behold, it was white with a luminous whiteness, whose ray overpowered the ray of the sun. How wondrous are these two miraculous signs: one of them is in itself, and that is the white hand; the other is not in itself, and that is the staff. Together they contain the transformation of atoms and the transformation of accidents, so both were evidence for the possibility of both matters, and that both of them are possible to occur. Abu Muhammad ibn 'Atiyya said: Musa, peace be upon him, presented these two verses for confrontation, called to God with them, broke the habit with them, and challenged people to the religion with them. If we make the tahaddi (challenge) mean the call to religion in general, then he challenged with them; and if we make the tahaddi mean the call after being unable to counter the miracle and that miracle becoming manifest, then the staff alone is singled out for that, because confrontation and the miracle occurred in it. It is also said: the tahaddi is the call to bring the like of the miracle (mu'jiza), and this is a third sense. On this basis, Musa's challenge is with both verses together, because the apparent meaning of his matter is that he presented them both together, even if he did not explicitly call for bringing their like. End of quote. And this is words that are confused.

﴿The chiefs of Pharaoh's people said: "Indeed, this is a knowing sorcerer."﴾ In al-Shu'ara' it is: ﴿He said to the chiefs around him: "Indeed, this is a knowing sorcerer."﴾ (Q. 26:34). The reconciliation between them is that Pharaoh and his people said this statement, so here it reports their words, and there it reports his words. Or he said it first, and the chiefs took it from him and said it to their followers. Or they said it on his behalf to the people, by way of transmission, as kings do: one of them sees an opinion and speaks it to those close to him from the elite, then the elite convey it to the common people. The proof of this is that they responded to him with his words: "Put him off" (*arjih*). Magic at that time was at the highest rank. When they saw the staff turn into a serpent and the dark hand become white, and they denied prophethood and defended against it, they intended to disparage him by describing him with sorcery and belittling his status, since they could not attribute to him, regarding what appeared at his hand, anything other than sorcery. They exaggerated in describing him by saying "knowing" ('alim), meaning one who has reached the utmost limit in knowledge of magic, its deceptions, its imaginings, and its arts. The use of the word "this" (*hadha*) is most frequent when it is from the speech of disbelievers, in belittlement and astonishment, as He said: ﴿Is this the one who mentions your gods?﴾ (Q. 21:36); ﴿Is this the one whom God has sent as a messenger?﴾ (Q. 25:41); ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾ (Q. 6:25); ﴿This is nothing but a human like you﴾ (Q. 23:24); ﴿Indeed, these two are two sorcerers﴾ (Q. 20:63); ﴿If this is indeed the truth from You﴾ (Q. 8:32). They turn away from naming that thing to using a demonstrative, and they emphasized the attribution of sorcery to him by using "indeed" (*inna*) and the lam.

﴿He wants to drive you out of your land, so what do you advise?﴾ Their souls sensed what their affair was leading to: their expulsion from their land, their homes emptied of them, and their dwellings ruined. So they hastened (p. 359) to report that. And the matter was as they sensed, when God drowned Pharaoh and his household and emptied their dwellings of them. They drew attention to this difficult description, which is equivalent to killing souls, as He said: ﴿Had We prescribed for them, "Kill yourselves or leave your homes," few of them would have done it﴾ (Q. 4:66). He meant their expulsion either by his making them rule over you, sending your servants and the cultivators of your land with him wherever he travels, which leads to the ruin of your homes; or by their fearing that he would fight them with those who gather to him from the Children of Israel and overcome their kingdom. Al-Naqqash said: they used to take from the Children of Israel a tribute like the jizya, so they saw that their kingdom would be lost with the removal of that. In Surat al-Shu'ara' it is: ﴿with his sorcery﴾ (Q. 26:35), but here it is omitted, because the first verse here is built on brevity, so it suits omission; and because the word "sorcerer" indicates sorcery. And ﴿so what do you advise?﴾ is from the speech of Pharaoh or from the speech of the chiefs, either addressed to Pharaoh and his companions, or addressed to him alone, as individual great men are addressed with the plural form. It is from *amr* (command). Ibn 'Abbas said: its meaning is "what do you point out?" Al-Zamakhshari said: from "amartuhu fa-amarani bi-kadha," meaning I consulted him and he advised me with an opinion. The majority read *ta'murun* with a fatha on the nun here and in al-Shu'ara', while Kardam narrated from Nafi' with a kasra on the nun in both. The word *madha* may be entirely an interrogative, and it may be a second object of *ta'murun*, by way of extension, by dropping the preposition from it, as one says *amartuka al-khayra* ("I commanded you the good"), with the first object omitted because the meaning is understood, i.e., "what thing do you command me?" The original would be "with what thing." It is also permissible for *ma* to be an interrogative subject, with *dha* in the sense of *alladhi* as its predicate, and *ta'murun* as the relative clause of *dha*; then the two objects of *ta'murun* are omitted: the first is the first-person pronoun, and the second is the pronoun returning to the relative, so the sense is "what is the thing that you command me with," i.e., you command me with it. Both grammatical analyses of *madha* are permissible in the reading of the one who reads with a kasra on the nun, except that he omitted the first-person ya' and left the kasra as an indication of it. Ibn 'Atiyya estimated the pronoun returning to *dha*, when it is a relative with a preposition, and said: in *ta'murun* there is a pronoun returning to *alladhi*, its estimate being "you command with it." End of quote. This is not good, because it fails the condition for permitting the omission of a pronoun governed by a preposition. That condition is that the pronoun not be in the nominative position, that the preposition govern the relative noun, or the qualified noun, or the noun it is added to, and that the verb associated with the two prepositions be identical in form and meaning, and that the meaning of the preposition be identical too. Ibn 'Atiyya's view is that he estimated it according to the original, then it was extended so that the verb reached it without an intermediary preposition, then it was omitted after the extension.

﴿They said: "Put him off, and his brother"﴾. That is, those present at the debate with Musa among the wise chiefs and nobles of Pharaoh's household said this. It was said: no one who was of illegitimate birth sat with Pharaoh; they were nobles, and for this reason they advised him to postpone and did not advise killing. They said: if you kill him, doubt will enter the people's minds; rather, overcome him with argument. It was read with hamza and without hamza. It was said both mean the same thing. It was said the meaning is "imprison him." It was said: *arjih* without hamza means "make him hopeful," taking it from *rajawta* with the hamza of the verb, i.e., "make him and his brother hopeful, and do not kill them until his lie appears, for if you kill them, it will be thought that they were truthful." Harun had not been mentioned at the beginning of the story, but it has become clear from another verse that the two of them went together and were sent to Pharaoh. And since he agreed with him in his claim (p. 360) and was his supporter, they advised postponing both of them. Ibn Kathir and Hisham read *arjiʾhu* with hamza and a damma on the ha', connected with a waw; Abu 'Amr did likewise except that he did not connect; this was narrated from Hisham, and from Yahya from Abu Bakr. Warsh and al-Kisa'i read *arjihi* without hamza, with a kasra on the ha', connected with a ya'. 'Asim and Hamza read without hamza and with the ha' sukun. Qalun read without hamza and with the kasra of the ha' brief. Ibn Dhakwan in one narration read like the reading of Warsh and al-Kisa'i; in the well-known narration from him it is *arjiʾhi* with hamza and kasra on the ha', without connection; it has been said of him that he connects it with a ya'. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Ibn 'Amir read *arjiʾhi* with a kasra on the ha' with a hamza before it. Al-Farisi said: this is an error. End of quote. Ibn 'Atiyya's attribution of this reading to Ibn 'Amir is not good, because the one who narrated it is in fact Ibn Dhakwan, not Hisham, so he should have specified, saying: Ibn 'Amir in the narration of Ibn Dhakwan. Some said: Abu 'Ali said: the damma of the ha' with the hamza is not permissible other than that. He said: the narration of Ibn Dhakwan from Ibn 'Amir is an error. Ibn Mujahid said after him: this is not permissible, because the ha' is not given a kasra except when a kasra or a sukun ya' comes before it. Al-Hawfi said: among the reciters there are those who give a kasra with the hamza, and it is not good. Abu al-Baqa' said: it is read with a kasra on the ha' with the hamza, and it is weak, because the hamza is a sound consonant with sukun, so there is nothing before the ha' that requires a kasra. Its explanation is that he made the ha' follow the kasra of the jim, and the barrier is not strong. It also comes out on the supposition that the hamza is replaced by a ya', or that the hamza, since it is often replaced by a weak letter, is treated like a weak letter in giving a kasra to what follows it. What al-Farisi and others claimed, that this reading is an error and not permissible, is a corrupt opinion, because it is a established, mutawatir reading, transmitted by the great authorities from the imams, and the community accepted it. It has a grammatical justification, and the hamza is not like other sound letters, because it is liable to change by substitution and the transfer of the vowel and other things. So there is no basis for denying this reading.

﴿And send to the cities gatherers﴾ ﴿who will bring you every knowing sorcerer﴾. "The cities" (*al-madain*) means the cities of Egypt and its villages. "The gatherers" (*al-hashirun*): Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the police (*ashab al-shurta*). Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: when Pharaoh saw of the signs of God, mighty and majestic, what he saw, he said: "We will not overcome Musa except with someone from his own people." So he took boys from the Children of Israel and sent them to a village. Al-Baghawi said: it is al-Farama. They taught them sorcery, as children are taught in the school, and they taught them a great deal of sorcery. Pharaoh had set a appointment with Musa; then he summoned them and asked them, saying: "What have you done?" They said: "We have taught them of sorcery what no people on earth can withstand with it, unless it is a matter from heaven, for we have no power against it." The two brothers (Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr) read *bi-kulli saḥḥārin* here and in Yunus, while the rest read *sahir* (sorcerer), and in al-Shu'ara' they all agreed on *saḥḥār*. *Saḥḥār* (very skilled sorcerer) is suitable with "knowing" (*alim*), because both are forms of intensification. And since "Indeed, this is a knowing sorcerer" had already preceded, it was suitable here to answer it with His words: ﴿every knowing sorcerer﴾.

The sorcerers came to Pharaoh and said: "Indeed, there will surely be a reward for us if we are the victors."

There is an omission in the speech, which the meaning requires, and its estimated form is: "So send [messengers] to gather [people]." They gathered the sorcerers and ordered them to come. The transmitters of reports differed greatly regarding their number, in a contradictory manner that astonishes the intellect when it is recorded in books. Some say nine hundred thousand sorcerers, and others say seventy sorcerers, and what lies between these is among the specified, contradictory numbers.

"And came" [وجاء] and "said" [قالوا] are without a conjunction, because it is in the estimation of an answer to a questioner who asked what they said when they came: they said, "Indeed, there will surely be a reward for us" [إن لنا لأجرا], that is, a payment (ju'l).

Al-Hawfi said: "They said" [وقالوا] is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) for the sorcerers, and the governing element is "came" [جاء].

The two Haramayn (Ibn Kathir and Nafi') and Hafs read "Indeed" [إن] as a declarative statement. The stipulation of a reward and its obligation, on the estimation of victory, does not mean any reward whatsoever; rather the meaning is "a great reward" [لأجرا عظيما]. For this reason al-Zamakhshari said: "The indefiniteness is for magnification, like the saying of the Arabs: 'Indeed he has camels [إن له لإبلا] and indeed he has sheep [وإن له لغنما]', meaning abundance."

Abu 'Ali permitted that "Indeed" [إن] be an interrogative, with the hamza omitted from it, like the reading of the rest who retained it, and they are al-Akhawan (al-Kisa'i and Hamza), Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr and Abu 'Amr. Among them are those who made both [hamzas] clear, and among them those who softened the second, and among them those who inserted an alif between them. The disagreement is in the books of readings.

In the sorcerers' address to Pharaoh with this, there is evidence of their presumption over him through his need of them, and of what befalls the knowledgeable person about a thing of haughtiness over one who needs him, and over one who does not know the like of his knowledge. "We" [نحن] is either an emphasis for the pronoun or a separator (fasl). The response of the conditional is omitted; al-Hawfi said: its response is what preceded.

"He said: 'Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near.'" That is: "Yes, indeed there is a reward for you." [وإنكم] So he conjoined this clause to the omitted clause after "Yes" [نعم], which stands in its place. The meaning: "among those brought near to me," that is, I will not limit to you the payment and the reward for Musa's defeat; rather I add to you that you will be among those brought near, so that along with the reward you gain honor, elevation, rank, standing and station. The one who is content and gladdened by it is only so when he gains that honor. In Pharaoh's hastening to promise them and bring them near to him there is evidence of the intensity of his need for them, and that they knew he was helpless; for this reason he needed the sorcerers to repel Musa, peace be upon him.

"They said: 'O Musa, either you throw, or we will be the throwers.'" Al-Zamakhshari said: "Their offering him the choice is good manners, which they observed with him, as craftsmen do when they meet, like two debaters before they engage in disputation, and two wrestlers before they take up wrestling." End. Al-Qurtubi said: "They behaved courteously with Musa, peace be upon him, by their saying 'either you throw', and that was the cause of their faith." What appears is that their offering him the choice is not a matter of courtesy; rather it is from the category of presumption, for what they knew of sorcery, and creating the illusion of victory, and confidence in themselves, and lack of concern for and no humbling before the matter of Musa. As al-Farra said to Sibawayh when al-Rashid gathered Sibawayh and al-Kisa'i: "Do you ask and I answer, or do I begin and you answer?" So here the offering of choice came by way of presumption in oneself and ease with what one has, and lack of concern for debating him, and confidence that he is the victor. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Their saying 'and either we will be the throwers' contains what indicates their eagerness to be the first to throw, through emphasis of their connected pronoun with the detached one, definiteness of the predicate, and insertion of the separator (fasl)." End.

They permitted, in "that you throw" [أن تلقي] and in "that we be" [أن نكون], the accusative, meaning: choose and act, either your throwing or our throwing, and the meaning here is initiative and precedence: your throwing is what is begun, or our throwing; so it is the subject (mubtada'), or "either your command is the throwing", that is, the initiative with it, or "either our command is the throwing", in which case it is the predicate of an omitted subject. "That" [أن] entered because the verb alone cannot be an object or a subject, unlike His saying: "And others are deferred to the command of God: either He punishes them or He turns to them in forgiveness" [Al-Tawba: 106]. There the verb after "either" [إما] is a second predicate for "and others", or a qualifier, so it is not one of the places of "that" [أن]. The object of "you throw" [تلقي] is omitted, that is: either you throw your staff; and likewise the object of "the throwers" [الملقين], that is: the throwers of the staffs and the ropes.

"He said: 'Throw.'" Musa, peace be upon him, granted them precedence, trusting in the truth and knowing that God would nullify it, as God related of him: "Musa said: 'What you have brought is sorcery; indeed God will nullify it'" [Yunus: 81]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Musa, peace be upon him, permitted them what they were eager for, out of disdain for their affair and confidence in what he was about of heavenly support, and that a miracle is never overcome by sorcery." End. The meaning: throw your ropes and your staffs. The apparent sense is that he commanded them to throw. It has been said: it is a threat, that is: you will soon see what disgrace befalls you.

"So when they threw, they bewitched the eyes of the people and terrified them, and they produced a great sorcery." That is: they showed the eyes, through tricks and imaginings, what has no reality, as God the Exalted said: "It was imagined to him from their sorcery that they were running" [Ta-Ha: 66].

In His saying "they bewitched the eyes of the people" there is an indication that sorcery does not transform an eye; it is only a matter of imagining. "And they terrified them" [واسترهبوهم], that is, they frightened them; istafala here has the meaning of af'ala, like aballa and istaballa. Al-Rahba is fear and dread. Al-Zamakhshari said: "'And they terrified them' [واسترهبوهم] and they frightened them with a severe fright, as if they had sought their dread." End. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "'And they terrified them' is in the meaning of 'and they frightened them', so their act demanded and solicited dread from the people." End. What the two said does not appear correct, for solicitation and seeking do not necessarily entail the occurrence of what is sought; the apparent sense here is that dread occurred. Therefore we say that istaf'ala here agrees with af'ala. Abu al-Baqa' explicitly stated that the meaning of "they terrified them" is that they asked them for dread.

He described the sorcery as great for the strength of what was imagined, or for the abundance of its implements of ropes and staffs. It was narrated that they came with ropes of leather and hollow pieces of wood filled with mercury, and they lit a fire in the valley, so the ropes were heated by the fire from beneath and by the sun from above; they moved and some of them mounted others. This is of the category of trickery and deception. Other of their tricks were narrated as well. In the speech there is an omission, its estimated form being: "He said: 'Throw!' so they threw." Then "when they threw": the fa' is conjunctive upon this omitted element. Al-Hawfi said: "The fa' is the response of the command." End. And this is not intelligible as he said. We say: it is described as great because of what appeared of its effect on the apparent organs, which are the eyes, by what befell them of imagining the staffs and ropes to be snakes; and on the inward organs, which are the hearts, by what befell them of terror and fear. And since the dread arose from the seeing of the eyes, the clause indicating it was placed later.

"So when they threw, they bewitched the eyes of the people and terrified them, and they produced a great sorcery." That is: they showed the eyes, through tricks and imaginings, what has no reality, as God the Exalted said: "It was imagined to him from their sorcery that they were running" [Ta-Ha: 66].

In His saying "they bewitched the eyes of the people" there is an indication that sorcery does not transform an eye; it is only a matter of imagining. "And they terrified them" [واسترهبوهم], that is, they frightened them; istafala here has the meaning of af'ala, like aballa and istaballa. Al-Rahba is fear and dread. Al-Zamakhshari said: "'And they terrified them' [واسترهبوهم] and they frightened them with a severe fright, as if they had sought their dread." End. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "'And they terrified them' is in the meaning of 'and they frightened them', so their act demanded and solicited dread from the people." End. What the two said does not appear correct, for solicitation and seeking do not necessarily entail the occurrence of what is sought; the apparent sense here is that dread occurred. Therefore we say that istaf'ala here agrees with af'ala. Abu al-Baqa' explicitly stated that the meaning of "they terrified them" is that they asked them for dread.

He described the sorcery as great for the strength of what was imagined, or for the abundance of its implements of ropes and staffs. It was narrated that they came with ropes of leather and hollow pieces of wood filled with mercury, and they lit a fire in the valley, so the ropes were heated by the fire from beneath and by the sun from above; they moved and some of them mounted others. This is of the category of trickery and deception. Other of their tricks were narrated as well. In the speech there is an omission, its estimated form being: "He said: 'Throw!' so they threw." Then "when they threw": the fa' is conjunctive upon this omitted element. Al-Hawfi said: "The fa' is the response of the command." End. And this is not intelligible as he said. We say: it is described as great because of what appeared of its effect on the apparent organs, which are the eyes, by what befell them of imagining the staffs and ropes to be snakes; and on the inward organs, which are the hearts, by what befell them of terror and fear. And since the dread arose from the seeing of the eyes, the clause indicating it was placed later.

The sorcerers came to Pharaoh and said: "Indeed, there will surely be a reward for us if we are the victors."

There is an omission in the speech, which the meaning requires, and its estimated form is: "So send [messengers] to gather [people]." They gathered the sorcerers and ordered them to come. The transmitters of reports differed greatly regarding their number, in a contradictory manner that astonishes the intellect when it is recorded in books. Some say nine hundred thousand sorcerers, and others say seventy sorcerers, and what lies between these is among the specified, contradictory numbers.

"And came" [وجاء] and "said" [قالوا] are without a conjunction, because it is in the estimation of an answer to a questioner who asked what they said when they came: they said, "Indeed, there will surely be a reward for us" [إن لنا لأجرا], that is, a payment (ju'l).

Al-Hawfi said: "They said" [وقالوا] is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) for the sorcerers, and the governing element is "came" [جاء].

The two Haramayn (Ibn Kathir and Nafi') and Hafs read "Indeed" [إن] as a declarative statement. The stipulation of a reward and its obligation, on the estimation of victory, does not mean any reward whatsoever; rather the meaning is "a great reward" [لأجرا عظيما]. For this reason al-Zamakhshari said: "The indefiniteness is for magnification, like the saying of the Arabs: 'Indeed he has camels [إن له لإبلا] and indeed he has sheep [وإن له لغنما]', meaning abundance."

Abu 'Ali permitted that "Indeed" [إن] be an interrogative, with the hamza omitted from it, like the reading of the rest who retained it, and they are al-Akhawan (al-Kisa'i and Hamza), Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr and Abu 'Amr. Among them are those who made both [hamzas] clear, and among them those who softened the second, and among them those who inserted an alif between them. The disagreement is in the books of readings.

In the sorcerers' address to Pharaoh with this, there is evidence of their presumption over him through his need of them, and of what befalls the knowledgeable person about a thing of haughtiness over one who needs him, and over one who does not know the like of his knowledge. "We" [نحن] is either an emphasis for the pronoun or a separator (fasl). The response of the conditional is omitted; al-Hawfi said: its response is what preceded.

"He said: 'Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near.'" That is: "Yes, indeed there is a reward for you." [وإنكم] So he conjoined this clause to the omitted clause after "Yes" [نعم], which stands in its place. The meaning: "among those brought near to me," that is, I will not limit to you the payment and the reward for Musa's defeat; rather I add to you that you will be among those brought near, so that along with the reward you gain honor, elevation, rank, standing and station. The one who is content and gladdened by it is only so when he gains that honor. In Pharaoh's hastening to promise them and bring them near to him there is evidence of the intensity of his need for them, and that they knew he was helpless; for this reason he needed the sorcerers to repel Musa, peace be upon him.

"They said: 'O Musa, either you throw, or we will be the throwers.'" Al-Zamakhshari said: "Their offering him the choice is good manners, which they observed with him, as craftsmen do when they meet, like two debaters before they engage in disputation, and two wrestlers before they take up wrestling." End. Al-Qurtubi said: "They behaved courteously with Musa, peace be upon him, by their saying 'either you throw', and that was the cause of their faith." What appears is that their offering him the choice is not a matter of courtesy; rather it is from the category of presumption, for what they knew of sorcery, and creating the illusion of victory, and confidence in themselves, and lack of concern for and no humbling before the matter of Musa. As al-Farra said to Sibawayh when al-Rashid gathered Sibawayh and al-Kisa'i: "Do you ask and I answer, or do I begin and you answer?" So here the offering of choice came by way of presumption in oneself and ease with what one has, and lack of concern for debating him, and confidence that he is the victor. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Their saying 'and either we will be the throwers' contains what indicates their eagerness to be the first to throw, through emphasis of their connected pronoun with the detached one, definiteness of the predicate, and insertion of the separator (fasl)." End.

The object of "you throw" [تلقي] is omitted, that is: either you throw your staff; and likewise the object of "the throwers" [الملقين], that is: the throwers of the staffs and the ropes.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 117–120:

﴿And We revealed to Musa: "Throw down your staff," and behold, it swallowed up what they were faking.﴾ ﴿So the truth was established, and what they had been doing was proved void.﴾ ﴿They were overcome there and returned humiliated.﴾ ﴿And the magicians were cast down, prostrating.﴾ ﴿They said: "We believe in the Lord of the worlds,﴾ [Al-A'raf: 121] ﴿the Lord of Musa and Harun."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 122] ﴿Pharaoh said: "Have you believed in Him before I gave you permission? This is surely a plot you have plotted in the city, to drive its people out of it. But you will soon know.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 123] ﴿I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, then I will crucify you all."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 124] ﴿They said: "Indeed, to our Lord we will return.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 125] ﴿You take revenge on us only because we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us. Our Lord, pour upon us patience, and cause us to die as Muslims."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 126] ﴿The chiefs of Pharaoh's people said: "Will you leave Musa and his people to spread corruption in the land and abandon you and your gods?" He said: "We will kill their sons and spare their women, and we are certainly dominant over them."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 127] ﴿Musa said to his people: "Seek help in Allah and be patient. Indeed the earth belongs to Allah; He gives it as inheritance to whomever He wills of His servants, and the final outcome is for the righteous."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 128] ﴿They said: "We were harmed before you came to us and after you came to us." He said: "It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land, and see how you will act."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 129] ﴿And We certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years of drought and shortage of fruits, so that they might take heed.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 130] ﴿But when good came to them, they said: "This is ours." And if an evil afflicted them, they ascribed omens to Musa and those with him. Surely their omen is with Allah, but most of them do not know.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 131] ﴿They said: "Whatever sign you bring us to bewitch us with, we will not believe in you."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 132] ﴿So We sent upon them the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood as distinct signs; but they were arrogant, and they were a guilty people.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 133] ﴿And when the plague fell upon them, they said: "O Musa, call upon your Lord for us by what He has promised you. If you remove the plague from us, we will surely believe in you and send the Children of Israel with you."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 134] ﴿But when We removed the plague from them, until a term which they were to reach, they immediately broke their word.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 135] ﴿So We took revenge upon them and drowned them in the sea, because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 136] ﴿And We caused the people who had been oppressed to inherit the eastern and western parts of the land which We had blessed. The good word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel because they were patient. And We destroyed what Pharaoh and his people had been building and what they had been erecting.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 137] ﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea, and they came upon a people devoted to idols of theirs. They said: "O Musa, make for us a god just as they have gods." He said: "Indeed you are a people who are ignorant.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 138] ﴿Indeed, these people's practice is doomed, and what they have been doing is void."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 139]

[p. 363] Laqifa al-shay' laqfan wa laqafanan: he seized it quickly and devoured it, or swallowed it. A man who is thaqif laqif is quick to grasp. Laqif thaqif means one who is clearly skilled in dexterity and alertness. Laqima, lahima and laqifa have the same meaning. From it come iltaqaftu and talaqqaftu talaqquفan (I snatched it up).

Maha: a noun, contrary to al-Suhayli, who claimed it may come as a particle. It is a conditional particle. Its use as an interrogative is rare, in the verse of the poet:

Maha li al-laylata maha liyah
awda bi na'layya wa sirbaliyah

Some claimed that when it is a conditional noun, it may come as a time adverb. Whether it is simple or composed of ma ma or mah ma is a matter of disagreement mentioned in grammar. It should be understood as in the poet's verse:

Amawiyyu mah man yastami' fi sadiqihi
aqawila hadha al-nasi mawiyyu yandam

meaning that it has no composition, rather mah means "restrain," and man is the conditional noun.

Al-jarad: a known creature, whose singular is jaradah with the feminine ta', for both male and female, and the distinction is made by the adjective. The morphologists mentioned that it is derived from al-jarad (stripping/denuding), and they said: derivation in common nouns is very rare.

Al-qummil: Abu Ubayda said it is al-hamnan, singular hamnanah, a type of tick. Its explanations by the exegetes will come later.

Al-difda': the known animal, its dal may be pronounced with kasra or fatha, it is feminine, and its plural with alif and ta' is anomalous; they said difda'at.

Al-naks: annulment. Al-yamm: the sea. Dhu al-Rummah said:

Dawiyyatun wa duja layl ka'annahuma
yammun tarattana fi hafatihi al-Rum

This root was discussed under fatayammamu, but Ibn Qutayba said: al-yamm is the sea in Syriac, or it was said in Hebrew.

Al-tadmir: destruction and ruining of a building. Al-tatbir: destruction, from which comes al-tibr (gold ore), because people rush for it. Ibn Atiyya and al-Kirmani said: al-tatbir is destruction and evil end, and its root is breaking, from which comes tibr al-dhahab (gold ore), because it is its fragments.

﴿And We revealed to Musa: "Throw down your staff," and behold, it swallowed up what they were faking.﴾ The apparent meaning is that it was a revelation of information, as it is narrated that Jibril, peace be upon him, came to him and said that the Truth commands you to throw down your staff. Its being a revelation of information contains reassurance of the heart and good news of victory. Others said it was a revelation of inspiration, cast into his heart. "An" may be explanatory, or it may be the governing "an," meaning "that you throw." In the speech there is an omission before the sudden clause, meaning: so he threw it, ﴿and behold, it swallowed up﴾. The sudden clause is then a report of what followed the throwing, and it is not itself the revealed content in the mention. As for one who holds that the fa' in phrases like "I went out and behold, a lion" is superfluous, it is possible on his view that this clause is itself revealed in the mention, except that the omitted element after it is estimated: so he threw it and it swallowed what they had brought.

Hafs read taluqfu with a sukun on the lam, from laqifa. The rest of the seven read talaqqafu, the present tense of laqqafa, with one of its two ta's omitted, since the original is tatalaqqafu. Al-Bazzi read with the idgham (assimilation) of the present-tense ta' into the ta' of the root. Ibn Jubayr read talqamu with a mim, meaning it swallows like a morsel. "Ma" is a relative pronoun, meaning what they fake, i.e., what they turn away from truth to falsehood and falsify. They said: or it is a verbal (masdarīya) ma, meaning it swallows their deceit, calling the object by the verbal noun.

It is narrated that when Friday came, Musa, peace be upon him, went out leaning on his staff, with his hand in his brother's hand, and the magicians had been arrayed for him in a great number. When they threw down and were frightening, Allah revealed to him and he threw. Behold, it was a great serpent, until it was like a mountain. It was said: it grew until it crossed the Nile. It was said: it grew until it crossed with its tail the Sea of Qulzum. It was said: the gathering was at Alexandria, and it grew until it passed the city of al-Buhayra. It is narrated that they began to enchant, and their ropes and staffs grew, and Musa's staff grew until it blocked the horizon and swallowed them all. Then it returned to being a staff, and Allah annihilated the staffs and ropes. Musa stretched out his hand toward the serpent and it returned to being a staff as it was. At that point the magicians knew that this was not from human beings, so they fell down prostrate, believing in Allah and His Messenger. Al-Zamakhshari said: Allah by His power annihilated those enormous bodies, or He divided them into subtle particles. The magicians said: if this were magic, our ropes and staffs would have remained.

﴿So the truth was established, and what they had been doing was proved void.﴾ Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan said: it became manifest and clear. The people of meanings said: "waqa'" is the manifestation of a thing by its existence, coming down to its place of rest. The judge said: "fa waqa'a al-haqq" indicates a strength of manifestation and firmness such that falsehood cannot be attributed to it, just as in reality nothing can become other than what has occurred. With the establishment of the truth, the matter was resolved, and those objects they had brought, namely the ropes and staffs, disappeared. Al-Zamakhshari said: among the strange interpretations is "fa waqa'a fi qulubihim," meaning it had an effect on their hearts, from the saying "fa's wa qi'," meaning a plain axe. End quote. And ﴿what they had been doing﴾ covers the magic of the magicians and the efforts of Pharaoh and his party.

﴿They were overcome there and returned humiliated.﴾ That is, all of them were overcome in their gathering place, or at that time, ﴿and returned﴾ humbled. This is because the "returning" (inqilab), if it was before the magicians believed, then they are partners in the pronoun of "wanqalabu" (they returned). If it was after belief, then they are not included in the pronoun and no humiliation befell them that Allah describes them with, because they believed and were martyred. This holds if the returning is literal. But if the meaning of becoming is considered, then the pronoun in "wanqalabu" includes the magicians and others, and for this reason al-Zamakhshari explained it as: and they became humbled and bewildered.

Some claimed that when it is a conditional noun, it may come as a time adverb. Whether it is simple or composed of ma ma or mah ma is a matter of disagreement mentioned in grammar. It should be understood as in the poet's verse:

Amawiyyu mah man yastami' fi sadiqihi
aqawila hadha al-nasi mawiyyu yandam

meaning that it has no composition, rather mah means "restrain," and man is the conditional noun.

Al-jarad: a known creature, whose singular is jaradah with the feminine ta', for both male and female, and the distinction is made by the adjective. The morphologists mentioned that it is derived from al-jarad (stripping/denuding), and they said: derivation in common nouns is very rare.

Al-qummil: Abu Ubayda said it is al-hamnan, singular hamnanah, a type of tick. Its explanations by the exegetes will come later.

Al-difda': the known animal, its dal may be pronounced with kasra or fatha, it is feminine, and its plural with alif and ta' is anomalous; they said difda'at.

Al-naks: annulment. Al-yamm: the sea. Dhu al-Rummah said:

Dawiyyatun wa duja layl ka'annahuma
yammun tarattana fi hafatihi al-Rum

This root was discussed under fatayammamu, but Ibn Qutayba said: al-yamm is the sea in Syriac, or it was said in Hebrew.

Al-tadmir: destruction and ruining of a building. Al-tatbir: destruction, from which comes al-tibr (gold ore), because people rush for it. Ibn Atiyya and al-Kirmani said: al-tatbir is destruction and evil end, and its root is breaking, from which comes tibr al-dhahab (gold ore), because it is its fragments.

﴿And We revealed to Musa: "Throw down your staff," and behold, it swallowed up what they were faking.﴾ The apparent meaning is that it was a revelation of information, as it is narrated that Jibril, peace be upon him, came to him and said that the Truth commands you to throw down your staff. Its being a revelation of information contains reassurance of the heart and good news of victory. Others said it was a revelation of inspiration, cast into his heart. "An" may be explanatory, or it may be the governing "an," meaning "that you throw." In the speech there is an omission before the sudden clause, meaning: so he threw it, ﴿and behold, it swallowed up﴾. The sudden clause is then a report of what followed the throwing, and it is not itself the revealed content in the mention. As for one who holds that the fa' in phrases like "I went out and behold, a lion" is superfluous, it is possible on his view that this clause is itself revealed in the mention, except that the omitted element after it is estimated: so he threw it and it swallowed what they had brought.

Hafs read taluqfu with a sukun on the lam, from laqifa. The rest of the seven read talaqqafu, the present tense of laqqafa, with one of its two ta's omitted, since the original is tatalaqqafu. Al-Bazzi read with the idgham (assimilation) of the present-tense ta' into the ta' of the root. Ibn Jubayr read talqamu with a mim, meaning it swallows like a morsel. "Ma" is a relative pronoun, meaning what they fake, i.e., what they turn away from truth to falsehood and falsify. They said: or it is a verbal (masdarīya) ma, meaning it swallows their deceit, calling the object by the verbal noun.

It is narrated that when Friday came, Musa, peace be upon him, went out leaning on his staff, with his hand in his brother's hand, and the magicians had been arrayed for him in a great number. When they threw down and were frightening, Allah revealed to him and he threw. Behold, it was a great serpent, until it was like a mountain. It was said: it grew until it crossed the Nile. It was said: it grew until it crossed with its tail the Sea of Qulzum. It was said: the gathering was at Alexandria, and it grew until it passed the city of al-Buhayra. It is narrated that they began to enchant, and their ropes and staffs grew, and Musa's staff grew until it blocked the horizon and swallowed them all. Then it returned to being a staff, and Allah annihilated the staffs and ropes. Musa stretched out his hand toward the serpent and it returned to being a staff as it was. At that point the magicians knew that this was not from human beings, so they fell down prostrate, believing in Allah and His Messenger. Al-Zamakhshari said: Allah by His power annihilated those enormous bodies, or He divided them into subtle particles. The magicians said: if this were magic, our ropes and staffs would have remained.

﴿So the truth was established, and what they had been doing was proved void.﴾ Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan said: it became manifest and clear. The people of meanings said: "waqa'" is the manifestation of a thing by its existence, coming down to its place of rest. The judge said: "fa waqa'a al-haqq" indicates a strength of manifestation and firmness such that falsehood cannot be attributed to it, just as in reality nothing can become other than what has occurred. With the establishment of the truth, the matter was resolved, and those objects they had brought, namely the ropes and staffs, disappeared. Al-Zamakhshari said: among the strange interpretations is "fa waqa'a fi qulubihim," meaning it had an effect on their hearts, from the saying "fa's wa qi'," meaning a plain axe. End quote. And ﴿what they had been doing﴾ covers the magic of the magicians and the efforts of Pharaoh and his party.

﴿They were overcome there and returned humiliated.﴾ That is, all of them were overcome in their gathering place, or at that time, ﴿and returned﴾ humbled. This is because the "returning" (inqilab), if it was before the magicians believed, then they are partners in the pronoun of "wanqalabu" (they returned). If it was after belief, then they are not included in the pronoun and no humiliation befell them that Allah describes them with, because they believed and were martyred. This holds if the returning is literal. But if the meaning of becoming is considered, then the pronoun in "wanqalabu" includes the magicians and others, and for this reason al-Zamakhshari explained it as: and they became humbled and bewildered.

﴿And the magicians were cast down, prostrating.﴾ Since the pronoun before was shared, the believers were singled out and mentioned separately. The meaning is: they fell prostrate as if someone had cast them down, because of the intensity of their falling. It was said: they could not restrain themselves from what they saw, so it was as if they had been cast down. Their prostration was to Allah, the Exalted, because of what they saw of Allah's power. They became certain of the prophethood of Musa, peace be upon him, and magnified this kind of power of Allah, the Exalted. It was said: Allah cast them down prostrating, so that the guidance that had been granted to them made them fall in prostration. It was said: they prostrated in agreement with Musa and Harun, for both of them had prostrated to Allah in gratitude for the establishment of the truth, so they agreed with them when they recognized the truth; thus it was as if the two had cast them down. Qatada said: at the beginning of the day they were disbelieving magicians, and at its end they were righteous martyrs. Al-Hasan said: you see one who was born in Islam and grew up among Muslims, selling his religion for such and such, while these were disbelievers who grew up in disbelief, and they gave up their souls for the sake of Allah, the Exalted.

They said, "We believe in the Lord of the worlds, [﴿the Lord of Moses and Aaron﴾]." That is, [they were] prostrating and saying [this]. They said it in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the pronoun in ﴿prostrating﴾ [Al-A'raf: 120], or relating to the magicians. Under either reading, they were engaged in prostration to God, giving thanks for the knowledge and faith, and for the statement that expresses the affirmation whose seat is the hearts. Since prostration is the greatest nearness a servant can have to his Lord, they hastened to speak the words that are indispensable in the presence of the One who is able to hear them, because entry into faith is indicated only by speech. They said "Lord of the worlds" in agreement with Moses' statement, "Indeed, I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds" [Al-A'raf: 104]. Since this phrase could give the impression of someone other than God, as in Pharaoh's saying, "I am your lord, the Most High" [Al-Nazi'at: 24], they made explicit by apposition (badal) that the Lord of the worlds is "the Lord of Moses and Aaron," and that they had separated from Pharaoh and rejected his lordship. Apparently all the magicians said this, though it is said that rather (p-365) their leaders said it. Ibn Ishaq named the leaders among them as Sabur, Azur, Khatkhat and Musaffa, and Ibn Makula also related this. Muqatil said the eldest of them was Shamun. They mentioned Moses before Aaron, although Aaron was older than Moses, it is said by three years, because Moses is the one who debated Pharaoh, and the two miracles appeared in his hand and his staff. Also, because the words "and Aaron" form a fasila (a verse-ending rhyme). In Ta-Ha, it came as ﴿the Lord of Aaron and Moses﴾ [Ta-Ha: 70], because Moses is the fasila there. It is possible that each of them occurred in succession from one group and another, so the act of some was attributed to the whole group in one surah, and the act of others to the whole group in another surah. The theologians (mutakallimun) said: the verse shows the virtue of knowledge, because when they were complete in the knowledge of magic, they knew that what Moses brought was truth outside the category of magic. Had it not been for knowledge, they would have supposed it to be magic, and that he was a greater magician than they were.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 123–124:

﴿Pharaoh said: "Did you believe in Him before I gave you permission?"﴾ Hafs read ﴿āmantum﴾ as a statement in every place in the Qur'an, meaning: you did this shameful act. He rebuked them with this and reproved them. Al-'Arabiyyan (Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir's counterpart, i.e., the two Basran and Kufan readers as named in the tradition), Nafi' and al-Bazzi read it with a hamza of interrogation and a lengthened madda after it, estimated as two alifs, except that Warsh softens the second hamza. No one inserted an alif between the realized and the softened forms. Likewise in Ta-Ha and al-Shu'ara'. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr read them in those places with the interrogative and realized the hamza, with an alif after it. Qunbul read here with the interrogative hamza replaced by a waw, because of the damma of the nun of Fir'awn, and the realization of the hamza after it, or its softening, or its replacement, or its elision: four modes. He read in Ta-Ha like Hafs and in al-Shu'ara' like al-Bazzi. This interrogative conveys denial and disapproval. The pronoun in ﴿bihi﴾ refers to God, Exalted, because of their saying ﴿"We believe in the Lord of the worlds"﴾ [al-A'raf: 121]. It was said that it may refer to Musa. In Ta-Ha and al-Shu'ara', the pronoun in His saying ﴿lahu﴾ refers to Musa, because of His saying: ﴿"Indeed, he is your chief"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 71]. It was said: "Amantu bihi" and "amantu lahu" are one and the same in His saying ﴿"before I gave you permission"﴾. This is evidence of the weakness of his affair, because he made their sin consist in departing from permission, and did not make it the very act of faith except on a condition.

﴿"Indeed, this is a plot you have plotted in the city, to drive its people out from it."﴾ That is: this deed of yours is a stratagem you and Musa devised in Egypt before you left it for this desert, and you colluded upon it for an aim of yours, which is to drive the Copts out of it and settle the Children of Israel. He said this to confuse the people, lest they follow the magicians in faith. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas that Musa, peace be upon him, met with the chief of the magicians, Shim'un, and Musa said to him: "Tell me, if I overcome you, will you believe in me?" He said: "Yes." Pharaoh learned of this and said what he said. End. When Pharaoh feared that the faith of the magicians would become a proof for his people, he immediately put forward two kinds of doubts: the first, that this is a collusion on their part and not that what he brought is true; the second, that this was a request from them to the king.

﴿"But you will soon know."﴾ This is a threat and a warning. The object of ﴿taʿlamūn﴾ is omitted; that is, what will befall you is left vague in the complement of ﴿taʿlamūn﴾. Then he specified what would be done to them, saying with an oath: ﴿"I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, then I will surely crucify you all."﴾ When the proof became manifest, he returned to the custom of wicked kings when they are defeated: punishing whoever opposes them, even if he is in the right. The meaning of ﴿min khilaf﴾ is: a right hand and a left foot, or the reverse. It was said: he was the first to do this. It was also said: the meaning is "because of the opposition that appeared from you." Crucifixion (ṣalb) is hanging on a wood. This threat which Pharaoh made against the magicians is not stated in the Qur'an as having been carried out and inflicted upon them, but it is related in the stories that he cut off some and crucified some, and the saying of Qatadah has preceded. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that they became magicians in the morning and were martyrs by evening. Mujahid, Humayd al-Makki and Ibn Muhaysin read ﴿la-aqta'anna﴾ as the present of the triliteral qata'a, and ﴿la-usallibannakum﴾ as the present of the triliteral ṣalaba, with a damma on the lam of ﴿la-uṣallibannakum﴾; it is also narrated with a kasra. Here ﴿thumma﴾ (then) occurs, while in the two surahs ﴿wa-la-uṣallibannakum﴾ [Ta-Ha: 71] occurs with waw. This indicates that waw is intended to convey the meaning of thumma, from the fact that crucifixion comes after amputation; and transitivity may or may not be accompanied by an interval.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 125:**

﴿They said: "Indeed, to our Lord we are returning."﴾ This is a expression of submission and reliance upon Allah, the Exalted, and of trust in what is with Him. The meaning is: "Indeed, we will return to the reward of our Lord on the Day of Recompense for what we will suffer of hardships." Or: "Indeed, we will turn back to the meeting with our Lord and His mercy, and our deliverance from you and from your meeting." Or: "Indeed, we are mortals who will return to Allah, so we are not concerned with death, since you cannot do to us except what we must necessarily endure." So the first "returning" is meant for the Day of Recompense, and these two "returnings" are meant for this world. It is unlikely that the pronoun in "(wa-inna)" ("and indeed we") is meant to include themselves and Pharaoh, i.e., "we will all return to Allah, and He will judge between us," in light of His saying: ﴿And you do not resent us﴾ [al-A'raf: 126], since this pronoun is specific to the believing magicians. The more appropriate view is that the pronouns are unified. The one who permitted this interpretation was al-Zamakhshari. In their saying ﴿to our Lord﴾ there is a disavowal of Pharaoh and of his lordship. As for the difference in al-Shu'ara' ("there is no harm"), this surah abridged the story, while al-Shu'ara' expanded it. In it the conditions of Pharaoh are mentioned from its beginning to its end. It begins with His saying: ﴿Did We not raise you among us as a child?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 18], and ends with His saying: ﴿Then We drowned the others﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 66]. Therefore, there occur in it additions that did not occur in this surah, nor in Ta-Ha. This was said by al-Kirmani.

﴿And you do not resent us except that we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us﴾ [al-A'raf: 126]. Al-Dahhak said: "And you do not find fault with us." Others said: "And you do not dislike us." Al-Zamakhshari said: "And you do not blame us." Ibn 'Atiyya said: "And you do not count against us a sin and hold us accountable for it." On these interpretations, His saying ﴿except that we believed﴾ [al-A'raf: 126] occupies the position of the object, and it is of the type of the exhaustive exception (al-istithna' al-mufarragh, an exception where the excluded element is left unstated and the exception stands in the place of the missing object). This construction occurs in the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿Say: "O People of the Scripture, do you resent us except that we believe"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 59], and ﴿And they did not resent them except that they believed﴾ [al-Buruj: 8]. This verb in the Arabic language is transitive with ʿalā (on), as one says "naqamtu ʿalā al-rajul, anqimu" ("I resented the man, I resent") when one prevails over him. What appears from its being transitive with min (from) is that the meaning is "and you do not resent us," i.e., "you do not obtain anything from us," like His saying: "fa-yantaqimu Allahu minhu" ("so Allah takes vengeance from him"), i.e., He afflicts him with something hateful. The verb "fa'ala" and "if'talla" (here, the form "naqama" and "intaqama") are then of one meaning, like "qadara" and "iqtadara" (both meaning to have power over). On this reading, His saying ﴿except that we believed﴾ [al-A'raf: 126] is an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi, an object expressing the reason for the action), and also an exhaustive exception. The meaning is: "You do not obtain from us, and do not punish us, for anything except that we believed in the signs of our Lord." On this meaning the commentary of 'Ata' points, for 'Ata' said: "That is, we have no sin with you for which you punish us, except that we believed." The "signs" are the miracles which Musa (peace be upon him) brought. Whoever makes "lamma" (when) an adverb of time (zarf) makes its governing element ﴿we believed﴾ [al-A'raf: 126]. Whoever makes it a particle (harf) makes its answer omitted, because what precedes it indicates it, meaning: "When they came to us, we believed." In this statement of theirs there is a denial of Pharaoh's claim to lordship, and a disassociation from their own belief in it. Belief in Allah is the root of all glories and virtues. This exception is similar to the saying:

"They have no fault, except that their swords, by them, are notched from clashing with the battalions."

Abu al-Yusr Hashim, Ibn Abi 'Abla, and al-Hasan and Abu Haywa read (wa-ma tanqam) with a fatha on the qaf, as the present tense of naqima with a kasra. Both are dialects, but the more eloquent is the reading of the majority.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 126:**

﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience and take us in death as those who submit (Muslims).﴾ When Pharaoh threatened them with the cutting off of hands and feet and crucifixion, they asked God Most High to grant them patience for whatever might befall them, if it should befall them. There is nothing in this request that indicates that this threat was carried out against them, contrary to those who claimed that it does. Nor is there in His words "and take us in death as Muslims" any evidence that the threatened punishment did not befall them, contrary to those who claimed that it does, because they asked God that their death come from Him and not by this cutting off and killing. The discussion of the phrase "pour upon us patience" has already preceded. "They asked for death upon Islam," which is the submission (*inqiyad*) to the religion of God and to what He commanded.

﴿The chiefs of the people of Pharaoh said: Will you leave Moses and his people to cause corruption in the land and to abandon you and your gods?﴾ [Al-A'raf: 127]

(p. 367) Ibn ʿAbbas said: When the magicians believed, six hundred thousand of the Children of Israel followed Moses. Muqatil said: Moses remained in Egypt after the belief of the magicians for a year, or thereabouts, showing them the signs. The words of the chiefs included an incitement of Pharaoh against Moses and his people, and an urging of him to kill them and torment them so that none of them would depart from the religion of Pharaoh. By "his people" they mean those among the Children of Israel who followed him, so the interrogative (*istifham*) in this case is one of denial and astonishment. It was also said that it is a request for information (*istikhbar*), and its purpose is that they might know what is in Pharaoh's heart towards Moses and those who believed in him. Muqatil said: "Corruption" is their fear that he would kill the sons of the Copts and let their women live, by way of retaliation against them, just as they had done to the Children of Israel. It was also said: "Corruption" is their calling the people to oppose Pharaoh and to abandon his worship.

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read *wa-yadharaka* (with the *ya'* and a *fatha* on the *ra'*) as a conjunction (*ʿatf*) upon *li-yufsidu* (*liyufsidu*), meaning: for corruption and for your abandoning and the abandoning of your gods. The abandonment was for that purpose, and they began first with the general cause, which is corruption, and then followed it with the specific cause, in order to show that this abandonment by Pharaoh of Moses and his people also tends toward something specific to Pharaoh. By this they kindled the fire of his anger against Moses and his people, so that this would be more lasting against them, since they were the nobles, and with the abandonment of Moses and his people in Egypt, his kingdom and his honour would go. It is also possible that the accusative (*nasb*) is by way of answer to the interrogative, and the meaning is: How can there be a combination between your abandoning Moses and his people for corruption and their abandoning you from worshipping your gods? That is, this is something that cannot occur.

Nuʿaym ibn Maysara and al-Hasan, in one report from him, read *wa-yadharuka* with a *damma* on the *ra'* (*raf'*), as a conjunction upon *a-tadharu* (*atadharu*), with the meaning *a-tadharuhu wa-yadharuka*, that is: Do you permit him that? Or it is a resumption (*istiʾnaf*), or a circumstantial clause (*ḥal*) with the assumption of *wa-huwa yadharuka* (while he abandons you). Al-Ashhab al-ʿUqayli and al-Hasan, in one report from him, read *wa-yadharka* with a jussive (*jazm*) as a conjunction upon the presumed form (*ʿatf ʿala al-tawahhum*), as if they had presumed the utterance *yufsidu* in the jussive as the answer to the interrogative, as in the words of God: ﴿So that I may give charity and be among the righteous﴾ [Al-Munafiqun: 10]. Or it is a lightening (*takhfif*) of *wa-yadharaka*. Anas ibn Malik read *wa-nadharuka* with a *nun* and a *damma* on the *ra'*: they threatened him with abandoning him and abandoning his gods. Or it is by way of an informative sense, meaning: the matter tends toward this. Ubayy and ʿAbdullah read: *fi al-ard*, and "they have abandoned you so that they worship you" (*wa-qad tarakūka an yaʿbudūka*) and "(your gods)" (*wa-ālihatak*). Al-Amash read: "and he has abandoned you and your gods" (*wa-qad tarakaka wa-ālihatak*).

The majority read *wa-ālihatak* in the plural. The apparent meaning is that Pharaoh had gods that he worshipped. Sulayman al-Taymi said: It has reached me that he used to worship the cow. It was also said: He used to worship a stone which he hung on his chest like a ruby or the like. It was also said: The annexation (*idafa*) is in the sense that he prescribed for them the worship of gods of cattle, idols and other things, and made himself the Supreme God. According to this, his words ﴿I am your supreme lord﴾ [Al-Nazi'at: 24] are only in reference to a relation between him and the others among the objects of worship. It was said: They were Copts who worshipped the stars and claimed that they answered the prayer of whoever called upon them, and Pharaoh claimed that the sun had responded to him and made him king over them.

Ibn Masʿud, Ali, Ibn ʿAbbas, Anas and a group other than them read *wa-ilahatak* (*wa-ilahatak*), and they explained it in two ways. The first: its meaning is "and your worship," in which case it is a verbal noun (*masdar*). Ibn ʿAbbas said: Pharaoh was worshipped and did not worship. The second: its meaning is "and your object of worship," which is the sun that he used to worship. The sun is called *ilaha* as a proper name (*ʿalam*) for it, and it is of the diptote form (*mamnu'at al-sarf*).

[Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 127–128:]

﴿He said: "We will kill their sons and spare their women, and indeed we are dominant over them."﴾ The reason he did not hasten to fight Moses and his people is that he was filled with terror of Moses. The meaning is that he said: "We will repeat against them what we did to them before, killing their sons, so that the group through whom the corruption occurs will be reduced." The superiority here is in rank and power in this world. The word ﴿dominant﴾ implies belittling them, meaning: we dominate them with a domination too minor for us to concern ourselves with it, since we remain in the same dominance we had before. Or it means that Moses's victory will have no effect on our kingdom and our control. And so that the common people would not imagine that he is the boy whom the astrologers and soothsayers spoke of, the one through whom our kingdom would be destroyed. That would discourage them from obeying us and call them to follow him, and he is still awaited.

Al-Kufiyyun and the two Basran readers (al-ʿArabiyyan) read ﴿sanuqattilu﴾ and ﴿yuqattilun﴾ with shaddah (intensive doubling of the qaf). Nafiʿ read both with a light form, and Ibn Kathir read ﴿sanaqtulu﴾ without shaddah but ﴿yuqattilun﴾ with shaddah. [p. 368]

﴿Moses said to his people: "Seek help in Allah and be patient."﴾ When Pharaoh threatened them, they became distressed and impatient, so Moses, peace be upon him, calmed them, ordered them to seek help from Allah and to be patient, consoled them, promised them victory, and reminded them of what Allah had promised the Children of Israel: the destruction of the Copts and the inheritance of their land and dwellings.

﴿Indeed the earth belongs to Allah; He gives it as an inheritance to whomever He wills of His servants.﴾ That is: the land of Egypt, with the definite article (al-) in it being for a known reference, and it is the land in which they were. It was also said: the earth is the earth of this world, so it is general. It was also said: the intended meaning is the land of Paradise, based on His saying: ﴿And He has given us the land, that we may take up residence in Paradise wherever we will﴾ [Az-Zumar: 74]. The verb ﴿seek help﴾ here takes the preposition bi (in), whereas in ﴿You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatihah: 5] it takes no preposition, and it has come in the supplication: "O Allah, we ask You for help."

﴿And the good outcome is for the righteous.﴾ It was said: it means victory and triumph. It was said: the Hereafter. It was said: happiness and martyrdom. It was said: Paradise. Al-Zamakhshari said: the praiseworthy final end is for the righteous, from among them and from among the Copts, and the will [of Allah] encompasses them as well. End of quotation. A group read ﴿yurithuha﴾ with a fatha on the ra. Al-Hasan read ﴿yurrithuha﴾ with a shaddah on the ra for intensification, and this reading is narrated from Hafs. Ibn Masʿud and Ubayy read ﴿wal-ʿaqibata﴾ in the accusative, as a conjunction (ʿatf, coordination) with ﴿anna al-ard﴾ (that the earth). In Moses's promise there is good news for his people of victory and a good end. The result of seeking help is the inheritance of the land for them, and the result of patience is the praiseworthy outcome and victory over those who oppose them. For this reason the command came with two things, each of which produces one result. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, why was this sentence left without the conjunction waw and attached to what precedes it? I say: it is a new, independent sentence (istiʾnaf, resumptive sentence). As for ﴿And the chiefs said﴾, it is conjoined to what precedes it in His saying: ﴿The chiefs of Pharaoh's people said﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 109]. End of quotation.

﴿He said: "We will kill their sons and spare their women, and indeed we are dominant over them."﴾ The reason he did not hasten to fight Moses and his people is that he was filled with terror of Moses. The meaning is that he said: "We will repeat against them what we did to them before, killing their sons, so that the group through whom the corruption occurs will be reduced." ﴿And the good outcome is for the righteous.﴾ It was said: it means victory and triumph. It was said: the Hereafter. It was said: happiness and martyrdom. It was said: Paradise. Al-Zamakhshari said: the praiseworthy final end is for the righteous, from among them and from among the Copts, and the will [of Allah] encompasses them as well. End of quotation. A group read ﴿yurithuha﴾ with a fatha on the ra. Al-Hasan read ﴿yurrithuha﴾ with a shaddah on the ra for intensification, and this reading is narrated from Hafs.
