﴿They said: "We were harmed before you came to us and after you came to us."﴾ That is, through our being tested by the slaughter of our sons, out of fear of what Pharaoh anticipated, namely the loss of his kingdom at the hands of the boy who would be born among us. ﴿Before you came to us﴾: al-Zamakhshari said: from before Musa's birth until he received prophethood. ﴿And after you came to us﴾ is a repetition of that for them. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Zamakhshari added: and what they were subjected to, enslaved and humiliated in it, with various kinds of servitude and labour, and the punishments inflicted upon them. End of quotation. Ibn 'Atiyya said: As for what came after his coming, they mean by it Pharaoh's threats and all the other intimidation they suffered during that period. Al-Hasan said: by taking the poll tax (jizya) from them before Musa was sent to them, and after his sending, more than that. Al-Kalbi said: they used to make bricks for him and he would give them straw, but when Musa came he imposed the straw upon them as a debt. The women used to spin flax for him and weave it. Jarir said: he subjected them to forced labour from the beginning of the day until midday before Musa's coming, and when Musa came he subjected them to forced labour all day without food or drink. 'Ali ibn 'Isa said: ﴿before﴾ refers to enslavement and the killing of the sons, and ﴿after﴾ refers to threats and expulsion. The same was narrated from 'Ikrima. It was also said: ﴿before you came to us﴾ refers to the covenant of God regarding deliverance, and ﴿after you came to us﴾ refers to that (deliverance) which they said in the context of complaining about Pharaoh and seeking help against him through Musa. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi said: they said this when (Pharaoh) pursued them and drove them to the sea, their hearts became constricted, and they saw a sea before them and a dense enemy behind them. When Musa led them away at night and they reached the sea, they turned around and saw the dust raised by Pharaoh's animals, and so they uttered this statement: "This is the sea before us, and this is Pharaoh behind us, who has overtaken us with those with him." End of quotation. This view is far-fetched, and the context of the verses indicates sequence. It came after this: ﴿And We had seized the people of Pharaoh with years (of drought)﴾ [al-A'raf: 130]. Ibn 'Atiyya said: This is a statement consistent with what is known of the Children of Israel: their restlessness toward their prophets, the weakness of their certainty, and their lack of patience in religion. End of quotation. It was said: Their saying this does not indicate aversion to Musa's coming, because that would lead to disbelief. They only said it because he had promised them the removal of harms, so they assumed that it would occur immediately. Thus their saying this is an appeal for compassion, not aversion.

* *

﴿He said: "It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land, and then He will observe how you act."﴾ (p. 369) This is a hope expressed by the Prophet of God Musa, peace be upon him. Prophets like him strengthen the hearts of their followers, so that they remain patient until the object of the hope occurs. There is no contradiction between this hope and His saying: ﴿And the good outcome is for the righteous﴾ [al-A'raf: 128], in that hope is not definitively certain to be fulfilled, whereas the report that the good outcome is for the righteous is inevitably certain to occur. For if the outcome refers to the Hereafter, then the absence of contradiction is very clear. And if the outcome refers to this world, there is no explicit statement about the outcome of these particular people. So Musa followed the path of good manners toward God and framed his speech in the form of hope. Al-Tibrizi said: It is possible that this was revealed to Musa, so ﴿'asa﴾ (it may be) is for certainty; or it was not revealed, in which case it is an expression of his own hope. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is an explicit statement of the good news he had hinted at before, and an unveiling of it, namely the destruction of Pharaoh and their succession to the land of Egypt after him. Ibn 'Atiyya said: Musa's appeal to them with his saying ﴿It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy﴾, and his promise to them of succession in the land, indicates that this calls for souls that are averse (to it), and this supposition is strengthened concerning the Children of Israel, and their taking this path without a story. The land here is the land of Egypt; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. God fulfilled this hope by the occurrence of its object: He drowned Pharaoh, gave them dominion over Egypt, and David and Solomon died (as kings there). It was also said: the land of Syria, for they conquered Jerusalem with Joshua, took possession of Syria, and David and Solomon died (there). The meaning of ﴿then He will observe how you act﴾ is: regarding your succession, whether you do good or evil. This is a sentence that functions as an exhortation and encouragement to obey God, the Exalted. In a hadith: "Indeed, the world is sweet and green, and indeed God makes you successors in it, and He observes how you act." Al-Zamakhshari said: He sees what you do, the good and the bad, and the gratitude for blessings and the ingratitude for them, so that He may reward you according to what is found in you. End of quotation. In it there is a hint of Mu'tazilism (the Mu'tazila being a rationalist theological school that held that God's knowledge and actions must be understood in a particular way). 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, who was one of the great Mu'tazilis and their ascetics, entered upon al-Mansur, the second caliph of the Abbasid dynasty, before he became caliph, and on his table there was one loaf, or two loaves. He asked for more for 'Amr, but none was found. So 'Amr recited this verse. Then he entered upon him after he had become caliph, and mentioned that to him, and said: ﴿then He will observe how you act﴾ remains (unrecited).

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 130:

﴿And We certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years of drought and shortage of fruits, so that perhaps they would take heed.﴾

Al-akhdh (seizing) is taking hold with the hand, and its meaning here is testing, during the period in which Musa had remained among them calling them to Allah. The meaning of bil-sinin is: with famine and barrenness. The word sanah is used for a year, and it is also used for drought, the opposite of abundance; in this sense it is among the words that became dominant, like al-najm (the star) and al-Dabaran. From it they derived verbs in this sense, so they said asnata al-qawm when the people suffered drought. From this usage is the saying of the poet:

"And the men of Makkah are in drought, emaciated."

And Hatim said:

"Indeed we spend wealth without miserliness, and the harm of the years does not trouble us."

In the word sinin there are two dialects, the more well-known of which is to inflect it with waw in the nominative and with ya' in the genitive and accusative. The grammarians have strained to give a reason for why it takes this plural form. The other dialect is to put the case inflection on the nun and to keep the ya' in all three cases; this was transmitted by Abu Zayd and al-Farra'. Al-Farra' said: in this dialect it is declinable among Banu 'Amir, and indeflectable among others. The discussion of this is more thorough in the books of grammar.

This drought lasted seven years, according to Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. As for the years, they fell upon their desert dwellers and their livestock, and as for the shortage of fruits, it was in their settled towns. This is the custom of Allah among the nations: He tests them with calamities so that they may be restrained and remember, through it, the blessings they were in. For hardship brings repentance, fear, softness of heart, and a return to seeking Allah's kindness and grace. Likewise He did to Quraysh when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed against them: "O Allah, make it upon them years like the years of Yusuf."

It is narrated that everything dried up for them, until the Nile of Egypt, and they were reduced in fruits until a palm tree would bear only a single date. The meaning of "so that perhaps they would take heed" is an expectation of their remembrance and alertness, indicating that this testing was only because of their persistence in disbelief and their denial of the signs of Allah, so that they might be restrained.

(p-370) ﴿So when good came to them, they said, "This is ours by right"; and if an evil afflicted them, they ascribed it as an omen to Moses and those with him.﴾ They were tested with drought and loss of crops in the hope that they would take heed, but what was hoped for did not happen. Whenever they were blessed with plenty and good health, they said, "We are deserving of this," and whenever something that displeased them befell them, they regarded it as an ill omen from Moses and claimed that it was because of him. The lam in (lanā, "ours") is said to be the lam of entitlement, as in when you say "the saddle is for the horse." Their taking Moses and those with him as an ill omen means that, had they not been among us, it would not have befallen us, just as the disbelievers said to the Messenger (ﷺ), "This is from you," in His words: ﴿And if an evil afflicts them, they say, "This is from you."﴾ [al-Nisa': 78]. The conditional was introduced with idhā (when) for the coming of good, because it is something whose occurrence is certain: God's bounty is the familiar, far-reaching and general bounty toward His creation, such that His favour to His creation is general even in times of trial. The conditional was introduced with in (if) for the affliction of evil, because it is something possible, to show that the affliction of evil is something that may or may not occur, "for His mercy is more far-reaching." Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "Why is it said ﴿when good came to them﴾ with idhā and the definite 'good', but ﴿if an evil afflicts them﴾ with in and the indefinite 'evil'?" I answer: because the genus of good occurs as something almost obligatory, owing to its abundance and breadth, whereas evil only occurs rarely, and only a little of it befalls. From this is the saying of one of them: "You have counted the days of hardship, so why not count the days of ease?" End of quotation. Isa ibn Umar and Talha ibn Musarrif read tatayyarū with a taʾ and a light ṭāʾ as a past verb, and it is the answer to ﴿if an evil afflicts them﴾. According to Sibawayh this is restricted to poetry, meaning that the conditional verb is in the present tense and the answering verb has a past form, as in the poet's words:

مَن يَكِدْنِي بِسَيِّئٍ كُنْتُ مِنهُ كالشَّجى بَيْنَ حَلْقِهِ والوَرِيدِ

(Whoever plots evil against me, I will be from him like a bone lodged in his throat, between his gullet and his jugular.)

Some grammarians permit it in ordinary speech. As for what is reported that Mujahid read tashā'amū in place of tatayyarū, that should be understood as an interpretation rather than as Qur'an, since it contradicts the consonantal text of the codex.

* *

﴿Certainly, their omen is with God, but most of them do not know.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: "Their omen" means what befalls them, that is, what has been determined for them in the decree of what they will encounter. It is derived from the augury of birds (zajr al-ṭayr). What is with God of decree for a person is called a "bird" because it was believed that whatever befalls him is in accordance with what is seen in the bird; so the word is used metaphorically. Thus said Ibn Atiyya. Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, the cause of their good and evil is with God, the Exalted, namely His judgment and His will. God, the Exalted, is the One who wills what befalls them of good and evil, and the ill omen or blessing of any one of them is not due to a cause within himself, as in His words: ﴿Say, "All is from God."﴾ [al-Nisa': 78]. It may also mean: "Certainly, the cause of their ill omen is with God, and it is their deeds, which are recorded with Him; because of them what displeases them befalls them, and they are punished for them after their death, by what God the Exalted has promised them in His words: ﴿The Fire, to which they are exposed﴾ [Ghafir: 46], and so on. There is no omen more ill than this." Al-Hasan read ﴿Certainly, their bird is with God﴾ (ṭayruhum), and he judged that knowledge is negated for most of them, because a few of them did know, such as the believer of Pharaoh's family and Asiya the wife of Pharaoh. Ibn Atiyya said: It is possible that the pronoun in ṭāʾiruhum refers to the whole world, and the restriction to "most" is then taken at face value; it is also possible that he means "but most of them" is not near to being known, owing to their immersion in ignorance, and on this view there are a few among them who are prepared to know, were God to grant them success. End of quotation. These are two distant possibilities, and more distant than them is his saying: "Or it may be intended as a collective and the expression is figurative."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 132:

﴿And they said, "Whatever sign you bring us to enchant us with, we will not believe you."﴾ The pronoun in (وقالوا, "and they said") refers to the people of Pharaoh. Being struck by droughts and the loss of fruits only increased them in transgression and in obstinacy in their disbelief and their denial. They did not content themselves with attributing what befell them of evils to anything other than the cause being Moses and those with him, until they confronted him with this statement, which indicates that even if he were to bring the signs he had brought, they would not believe in them. They used (مَهْما, "whatever"), which requires generality, and then specified it with (آيَة, "sign") as a sarcastic naming of that thing a sign, as they said in His words: ﴿Indeed, we killed the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, the Messenger of Allah﴾ [an-Nisa: 157], and their calling it a sign means: according to your claim. For this reason they gave as the reason for the bringing of it their words ﴿to enchant us with it﴾. They emphasized the negation of faith by beginning the sentence with (نَحْنُ, "we") and by introducing the (ب, "bi") into (بِمُؤْمِنِينَ, "believers"), meaning: our belief in you will never occur.

(مَهْما, "whatever") is in the nominative as a subject, or it is in the accusative by an implied verb which the conditional verb explains, so it falls under the category of (الاشتغال, "preoccupation"), meaning: whatever thing arrives, bring it to us. The pronoun in (بِهِ, "with it") refers to (مَهْما), and the pronoun in (بِها, "with it") also refers to the meaning of (مَهْما), because what is intended by it is "whatever sign," just as it referred to what is in His words: ﴿Whatever sign We abrogate or cause to be forgotten﴾ [al-Baqarah: 106], and as Zuhayr said:

Whatever is in a man of disposition, even if he conceals it, will be known among people.

He made the feminine agreement according to the meaning. Az-Zamakhshari said: This word is among those words which whoever has no skill in the science of Arabic distorts, placing it other than its proper place, and thinks that (مَهْما) means (مَتى ما, "whenever"), and says "whatever you come to me, I will give you," and this is from his own invention, and is not in any way from the speech of the founder of Arabic. Then he goes on to interpret "whatever sign you bring us" as meaning a time, and thereby he deviates from the signs of Allah Most High without realizing it. This and similar things necessitate sitting humbly before the reader of the book of Sibawayh. End of quote. What az-Zamakhshari denied, that (مَهْما) does not come as an adverb of time, was held by Ibn Malik, which he mentioned in at-Tashil and his other works, except that he did not restrict its meaning to being an adverb of time only; rather he said: (مَا and مَهْما) may come as two adverbs of time. And in his lengthy rajaz poem called ash-Shafiyya al-Kafiyya he said:

And (مَهْما and مَا) have come as two adverbs in the evidences, whoever relies on them is sufficient.

And he said in explaining this line: All the grammarians make (مَا and مَهْما) like (مِنْ, "from") in requiring freedom from the adverbial sense, although their use as two adverbs is established in the usage of the eloquent Arabs. He cited verses from the Arabs, claiming among them that (مَا and مَهْما are adverbs of time) (p-٣٧٢). His son, Shaykh Badr ad-Din Muhammad, refuted him in them. We ourselves have interpreted some of them and mentioned that in our book at-Takmil li-Sharh at-Tashil, our composition. It is sufficient as a refutation that he transmitted from all the grammarians a view contrary to what he said. But whoever pursues knowledge needs to sit before the teachers. As for whoever explains (مَهْما) in the verse as an adverb of time, he is, as az-Zamakhshari said, one who deviates from the signs of Allah. As for az-Zamakhshari's words, "This and similar things" to the end of his statement, it indicates that he sat humbly before the reader of the book of Sibawayh, and that is correct. He travelled from Khwarazm in his old age to Makkah, may Allah Most High honor it, to read the book of Sibawayh with a man from our companions, from the people of the island of al-Andalus, who was residing in Makkah, namely the Shaykh, the Imam, the scholar, the consulted one Abu Bakr Abdullah ibn Talha ibn Muhammad ibn Abdullah al-Andalusi, from the people of Babara in the lands of the island of al-Andalus. Az-Zamakhshari read the entire book of Sibawayh to him and related it to him by reading, from the Imam, the memorizer Abu Ali al-Husayn ibn Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Ghassani al-Jayyani, who said: I read it to Abu Marwan Abd al-Malik ibn Siraj ibn Abdullah ibn Siraj al-Qurtubi, who said: I read it to Abu al-Qasim ibn al-Iflili, from Abu Abdullah Muhammad ibn Asim al-Asimi, from ar-Rabahi with its chain. Az-Zamakhshari also has a qasida praising Sibawayh and his book. This indicates that he did indeed study the book of Sibawayh, contrary to what some of our companions believed, that he had only looked at fragments of the speech of Abu Ali al-Farisi and Ibn Jinni. Abu al-Hajjaj Yusuf ibn Ma'zuz composed a book refuting az-Zamakhshari concerning his book al-Mufassal, and pointing out his errors in which he opposed the imam of the discipline, Abu Bishr Amr ibn Uthman Sibawayh. May Allah have mercy on them all.

﴿So We sent upon them the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood as distinct signs, but they were arrogant and were a criminal people.﴾

Al-Akhfash said: al-Tufan (the flood) is the plural of tufana according to the Basrans. According to the Kufans, it is a verbal noun (masdar), like rujhan. Abu Zayd related the verbal noun of ṭāfa as ṭawfan and ṭawafan, and did not relate ṭawafan. Even if it is a verbal noun, it is not intended as a verbal noun here.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: it is the drowning water. Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Ibn Jubayr, Abu Malik and Muqatil said: it is the rain that was sent upon them continuously, night and day, for eight days. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah preferred this view. It was also said: this was with intense darkness, so they could not see the sun or the moon, and no one could leave his house.

It was also said: they were rained upon until they nearly perished. The houses of the Copts and the houses of the Children of Israel were close together, so the houses of the Copts filled with water until they stood in it up to their collarbones. Whoever sat down drowned. Not a drop entered the houses of the Children of Israel. The water spread over their land and stood still, preventing them from farming, building and any activity, and it lasted over them for seven days.

It was also said: the flooding of the Nile overflowed upon them until it covered the land, both plains and mountains.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: it is a general term for anything that sweeps over, but the Arabs use it most often for water and heavy rain. From this is the verse of the poet:

*The rough winds and the flood of rain have changed the traces of its newness.*

And Abu al-Najm said:

*A destructive flood extended its reach, *** a month of heavy showers and a month of hail.*

Mujahid, ʿAtaʾ, Wahb and Ibn Kathir said: here it means the sweeping death (al-mawt al-jarif). Aisha narrated it from the Messenger (ﷺ), and if it is authentic, it must be adopted. It was related from Mujahid and Wahb that it is the plague, in the language of Yemen. Abu Qilabah said: it is smallpox, and it was the first punishment that befell them, and it remained in the land. It was also said: it is a punishment that descended from the sky and encircled them. It was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that it is an ambiguous term, meaning something that God made to encircle them. They said to Musa: "Pray to your Lord to remove this from us, and we will believe in you." He prayed, and it was lifted from them, but they did not believe. That year, plants and crops grew for them in a way never seen before. They remained for a month, then God sent the locusts upon them, and they ate most of their crops and fruits. Then they ate everything, even the doors, the roofs of the houses and the clothing, but none of it entered the houses of the Children of Israel. They fled to Musa and promised him repentance, so he lifted it from them for seven days. Musa (peace be upon him) went out to the open land and pointed with his staff toward the east and the west, and the locusts returned to the regions from which they had come. They said: "We will not abandon our religion." They remained for a month, and then He sent the lice upon them.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and ʿAtaʾ said: it is al-daba', which is young locusts before they grow wings and cannot fly. Ibn Jubayr related from Ibn ʿAbbas that it is the weevil that falls on wheat. Al-Hasan and Ibn Jubayr said: they are small black creatures. Habib ibn Abi Thabit said: it is the dung beetle (al-jiʿlan). Abu ʿUbaydah said: it is al-hamnan, a kind of tick. ʿAtaʾ al-Khurasani and Zayd ibn Aslam said: it is the well-known lice, and this is a dialectal form of it, supported by the reading of al-Hasan with a fatḥa on the qaf and a sukun on the mim, namely "al-qamal." It was also said: it is fleas, related by Ibn Zayd. It was narrated that Musa walked to a heap of sand, struck it with his staff, and all of it spread as lice throughout Egypt. They ate what the locusts had left and licked the ground. The lice would enter between the skin of a Copt and his shirt, and they would fill with food at night. One of them would grind ten sacks of grain and hardly anything would come back from it. They spread over their skin, their hair and the eyelashes of their eyes, and clung to their bodies. They cried out and fled to Musa (peace be upon him), and he lifted it from them. They said: "Now we have realized that you are a sorcerer. By the might of Pharaoh, we will never believe you."

God then sent the frogs upon them after a month. They filled their vessels, their food, and their beds. They threw themselves into the pots while they were boiling and into the ovens while they were blazing. When one of them spoke, a frog would leap into his mouth. Ibn Jubayr said: one of them would sit among the frogs up to his chin. They said to Musa: "Have mercy on us this time, and we will repent with sincere repentance and will not return." He took covenants from them, and he lifted it from them, but they broke the covenant. So God sent the blood upon them.

The majority of scholars said: their water turned into blood, so that when an Israelite put water into the mouth of a Copt, it became blood in his mouth. Pharaoh became so thirsty that he was nearly destroyed, and he would suck on green trees, but when he chewed them, their sweet water became salty and bitter. Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab said: the Nile flowed over them with blood. Zayd ibn Aslam said: the blood was nosebleeds, which God sent upon them.

The meaning of "detailing the signs" (tafṣīl al-āyāt) is making them clear and removing their ambiguity. Tafṣīl in terms of separation means distinguishing, and in terms of meanings it means that He distinguished them from one another, so they became clear, and some of them were distinguished from others. Thus it is not unclear to a rational person that these are among the signs of God, which no one else can bring about, and that they are a lesson for them and a punishment for their disbelief. Ibn Qutaybah said: He called them "detailed" because there was an interval of time between one sign and another. It was said that each sign would remain from Saturday to Saturday, and then, after it was lifted, they would remain for a month in well-being. It was also said: eight days, and then the next sign would come. Wahb said: there were forty days between every two signs. Nawf al-Bikali said: Musa (peace be upon him) remained among the people of Pharaoh, after the sorcerers believed, for twenty years, showing them the signs. The wisdom of detailing them over time is that He tests their conditions: whether they would fulfil what they had pledged or break it, so that the proof would be established against them.

The phrase ﴿distinct signs﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). What the verse indicates is that He sent upon them what it mentions. As for the manner of sending, and the duration and forms of what was sent upon them, these depend on reports from the Israelite narratives (al-Isra'iliyyat), since nothing of this is established in the Prophetic hadith. Along with the sending of these kinds of signs, they were arrogant toward faith and toward accepting God's command. ﴿But they were a criminal people﴾ is a statement from Him, the Exalted, about them, regarding their committing crimes against God and against His servants.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 134–135:

﴿When the punishment (al-rijz) befell them, they said, "O Musa, invoke your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you. If you remove the punishment from us, we will certainly believe in you and will certainly send the Children of Israel with you."﴾ The apparent meaning is that the punishment (al-rijz) here is what was sent upon them: the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood. If the apparent meaning is intended, then their request to Musa came after all of them had befallen them, not after only one type of them. It is also possible that the meaning of ﴿when it befell them﴾ is one type of punishment, so that their request came between one type and another. The meaning of ﴿befell them﴾ is: descended upon them and settled. Some said: al-rijz is the plague (al-ta'un), which descended upon them, and seventy thousand Qibti (Egyptians) died from it in one night. In their words ﴿invoke your Lord for us﴾, the attribution of "Lord" to Musa is a non-acknowledgment that He is their Lord, since they did not say "invoke our Lord." The meaning of ﴿by what He has covenanted with you﴾ is: by what He has singled you out with, so that He made you a prophet; or by what He instructed you to invoke Him with, so that He would answer you as He answered you in the signs; or by the knowledge He entrusted to you. The apparent view is that ﴿by what He has covenanted﴾ is connected to ﴿invoke your Lord for us﴾, and the object of the supplication is omitted, its estimated sense being: ﴿invoke your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you﴾ to remove this punishment. The clause ﴿if you remove﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath (qasam), in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "they said", i.e. they said that while swearing ﴿if you remove﴾; or it is the answer to an omitted oath that is coordinated, i.e. and they swore: if you remove. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and others permitted that the preposition (ba') in ﴿by what He has covenanted with you﴾ be the ba' of oath, i.e. they said ﴿invoke your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you﴾ to remove the punishment, swearing ﴿by what He has covenanted with you, if you remove﴾; or: and they swore ﴿by what He has covenanted with you, if you remove﴾. The meaning is: if you remove it by your supplication. In their words ﴿we will certainly believe in you﴾ there is an indication that he demanded of them belief, just as he demanded of them the sending of the Children of Israel. They mentioned belief first, because it is the greatest intended aim, from which obedience arises. In attributing the removal (kashf) to Musa there is a deviation from attributing it to God the Exalted, because they did not acknowledge that.

﴿Then when We removed the punishment from them until a term (ajal) which they were to reach, behold, they broke their word.﴾ There is an omission in the speech, indicated by the meaning, which is: so Musa supplicated, and He removed the punishment from them. God the Exalted attributed the removal to Himself because He is the true remover. When it was from their words, they attributed it to Musa, and that is a metaphorical attribution (isnad majazi); and when it was a report from God, He attributed it to Himself, because that is a literal attribution (isnad haqiqi). Since the punishment belonged to another sentence, not one attributed to them, it was good to state it explicitly rather than by a pronoun, and it would have been permissible for the construction outside the Qur'an to be ﴿then when We removed from them﴾. The meaning of ﴿until a term which they were to reach﴾ is: until a limit of time which they will certainly reach, so they will be punished in it, and what preceded for them of respite and removal of punishment will not benefit them, until its arrival. This was said by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn 'Atiyya said: he means by it the end point of each one of them according to what belongs to him of destruction and death; this is the necessary implication of the wording, as you say "I postponed such-and-such until such-and-such a time," and you do not mean a specific time. Yahya ibn Salam said: the ajal here is drowning. He said: I only said this because I saw that most of this group had perished by drowning, so I believed that the indication here is to drowning. This is not necessary, because some of them must have died before the drowning, and some of them were delayed; and He removed the punishment from them until a term which they reached. End of quotation. In al-Tahrir: "until a term" means until the end of the period of their respite, which is the period set for their belief. It was said: drowning; it was said: death. If the term is explained as death or drowning, then it is not correct for the removal of punishment to be until that time, i.e. the time of the occurrence of death or drowning, because there has intervened between the removal and the drowning [a period], or because death is a time, and that is the time of breaking the word. So on this view the estimated sense should be: until the nearest term which they will reach. As for when the term is the period set for their belief and the sending of the Children of Israel, there is no need to omit a modifier (mudaf). They said: ﴿until a term﴾ is connected to "We removed" (kashafna), and it is not possible to take it as connected to it, because what the particle (lamma) governs has its answer ordered upon the beginning of its occurrence, and a limit (ghaya) contradicts being conditioned on the beginning of an occurrence; so the beginning and the continuation must be conceived until the limit is realised. That is why a limit cannot be applied to a verb that is momentary rather than extended. You do not say "when I killed Zayd until Thursday such-and-such happened," nor "when I jumped until Friday such-and-such occurred." Some of them made ﴿until a term﴾ part of the punishment, i.e. the punishment being for a term, and the meaning is: the punishment was deferred; and this interpretation is strengthened by the answer of lamma coming with the sudden "idha" (idha al-fuja'iyya), i.e. when We removed from them the punishment prescribed upon them (until a term), they were suddenly taken by breaking their word. In the sense of making the removal limited by the term reached, the suddenness cannot occur except on the interpretation of the removal as continuing up to the limit, so that the suddenness of breaking the word is then possible. Al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿behold, they break their word﴾ is the answer to what is limited; so when We removed from them, they were suddenly upon breaking and hastened to it, and did not delay it; but when it was removed from them, they broke it. End of quotation. The limit cannot apply with the apparent sense of this estimate. ﴿They are to reach it﴾ is a clause in the position of a qualifier (sifa) of ajal, and it is more majestic than a qualifier by a single word, due to the repetition of the pronoun; so in the excellence of the construction it is not like the single word would be if said outside the Qur'an: "until a term reaching it." The occurrence of idha al-fuja'iyya as the answer to lamma is among what indicates that lamma is a particle of necessity for necessity, as Sibawayh says, not an adverb, as some claimed, because it requires a governing element, and the sentence is complete, not admitting an implied element, and what follows idha al-fuja'iyya does not govern what precedes it. Abu Hashim and Abu Haywa read (yankithun) with a kasra on the kaf.

﴿So We took retribution from them and drowned them in the sea because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them.﴾ That is, We brought upon them *al-niqmah* (retribution), which is the opposite of *al-ni'mah* (blessing). If *al-intiqam* (vengeance) is the drowning itself, then the *fa'* is explanatory (*tafsiriyyah*), according to those who affirm this meaning for the *fa'*. Otherwise the meaning is "We intended to take vengeance upon them." The *ba'* in "*bi-annahum*" indicates cause (*sababiyyah*). The "signs" (*al-ayat*) are the miracles that appeared at the hand of Musa, peace be upon him. The apparent reference of the pronoun in "*'anha*" is to the signs, meaning that they were heedless of what the signs contained of guidance and salvation, and did not reflect upon them. That heedlessness is the cause of the denial. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the retribution indicated by "*fa-intaqamna*," meaning: they were heedless of the retribution and of its descending upon them (p-٣٧٦). According to the first opinion, heedlessness is understood as turning away from something, because heedlessness of it and denying it cannot coexist, since heedlessness requires the absence of awareness of a thing, while denying it requires knowing it. Also, if the attribute of heedlessness were intended, they would be excused, because that is not within the servant's choice.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 7, Verse 137:**

﴿And We caused the people who had been oppressed to inherit the eastern and western parts of the land, which We had blessed.﴾ When Musa (peace be upon him) said, ﴿Perhaps your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land﴾ [al-A'raf: 129], it happened as Musa had hoped. He drowned their enemies in the sea and made the Children of Israel successors in the land. ﴿Those who had been oppressed﴾ are the Children of Israel, whom Pharaoh enslaved and put to service. Al-istid'af (oppression, from istid'af, meaning to seek to weaken someone by force) is a term whose usage became so common that people said istad'afahu, meaning he found him weak. ﴿The eastern and western parts of the land﴾: one group said it means the whole earth. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is by way of majaz (figurative usage, in which a word is used beyond its literal sense), because God gave them possession of many lands. As for the literal meaning (haqiqa), God gave possession to their descendants, namely Sulayman ibn Dawud. Al-Hasan also said: ﴿the eastern parts of the land﴾ is al-Sham (Syria) and ﴿its western parts﴾ is the land of Egypt, which God gave them by destroying the Pharaohs and the 'Amaliq (Amalekites). al-Zamakhshari also said this, and said: they took possession of these lands as they wished, in their eastern and western regions. Al-Hasan also said, as did Qatada and others, that it is the land of al-Sham. In the book of al-Naqqash, from al-Hasan: it is the land of Egypt, and the blessing in it is in water and trees. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Another commentator added to this, saying: with fertility, rivers, abundance of trees and good fruit. It was also said: the blessing is through the coming of the prophets, their frequent stays there and their burial there, and this follows from those who said it is the land of al-Sham. It was also said: ﴿We blessed﴾ means We made goodness in it lasting and constant, and this points to Egypt. al-Layth said: it is Egypt, which God blessed with the good things that come from its Nile, and with abundance of grain and fruits. From 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), in a long hadith, that the Nile of Egypt is the lord of rivers. It is also narrated that there were gardens on both banks of this Nile, from its beginning to its end, in both lands, between Aswan and Rashid, and the trees were continuous, with nothing cut off from anything else. Abu Basra al-Ghifari said: Egypt is the treasury of the whole earth. Do you not see the words of Yusuf (peace be upon him): ﴿Set me over the treasures of the land﴾ [Yusuf: 55]? It is also related that 'Isa (peace be upon him) stayed there for twelve years, because God revealed to Maryam: "Go to Egypt and its land." It is mentioned that it is the high ground of which God said: ﴿And We gave them refuge on a high ground, a place of settlement and flowing water﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 50]. Ibn 'Umar said: the blessings are ten, nine of which are in Egypt and one in the rest of the earth. The accusative (intisab) of ﴿mashariq﴾ is because it is the second object (maf'ul thani) of ﴿awrathna﴾, and ﴿allati barakna﴾ is a qualifier (na't) of ﴿mashariq al-ard wa-maghariba﴾. As for al-Farra's view that the accusative of ﴿mashariq﴾ and what is conjoined to it is adverbial of place (zarfiyya, an adverbial indicating location), with the verb governing them being ﴿yustad'afun﴾, and ﴿allati barakna﴾ being the second object, meaning "the land in which We blessed," this is artificial and a departure from the apparent sense without evidence. As for those who permitted ﴿allati﴾ to be a qualifier of "the land," his view is weak because of the separation by conjunction between the modified noun and its qualifier.

* *

﴿And the good word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel because of their patience.﴾ That is, it passed and continued. From the expression tamma 'ala al-amr, meaning he persisted in the matter. Mujahid said: the meaning is what had already been decreed for them in His knowledge and speech from eternity, namely deliverance from their enemy and victory over him. al-Mahdawi, followed by al-Zamakhshari, said: the word (kalima) is His statement, ﴿And We wished to show favour to those who were oppressed in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 5], up to His words ﴿what they had feared﴾ [al-Qasas: 6]. It was also said: it is His statement ﴿Perhaps your Lord will destroy your enemy﴾ [al-A'raf: 129] and what follows. It was said: the word is blessing, and al-husna is the feminine of al-ahsan (the best), and it is a qualifier of the word. It was good because it is a promise of something beloved. This was said by al-Kirmani. The meaning is: upon those who remained of the believing Children of Israel, ﴿because of what they endured﴾, that is, because of their patience. al-Hasan read ﴿kalimat﴾ in the plural, and this reading is also narrated from 'Asim and Abu 'Amr. al-Zamakhshari said: a parallel to this is ﴿He had seen of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾ [al-Najm: 18]. End of quote. He means a parallel to describing a plural with a feminine singular adjective. What al-Zamakhshari said, that al-Kubra is a qualifier of ayat Rabbihi, is not decisive, since it may be that it is the object of the verb ra'a, meaning "the greatest sign," in which case it is originally a qualifier of a feminine singular noun that is not made plural, and this is more eloquent in description. [p. 377]

﴿And We destroyed what Pharaoh and his people had made, and what they had built up.﴾ That is, We ruined their palaces and buildings through destruction. Tadmir means annihilation and the ruining of buildings. It was also said: what Pharaoh devised in the matter of Musa (peace be upon him) and the suppression of his word. It was also said: the intended meaning is the destruction of the people of the palaces and the strongholds, and when the inhabitant perishes, the dwelling perishes with him. ﴿And what they had built up﴾, that is, what they raised of solid structures, like the tower of Haman and others. al-Hasan said: the intended meaning is the trellises of vines, and from this comes ﴿gardens trellised and untrellised﴾ [al-An'am: 141]. Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr read ya'rishun (with a damma on the ra'), and the rest of the seven readers, along with al-Hasan, Mujahid and Abu Raja', read ya'rishun with a kasra on the ra' here and in al-Nahl. This is the dialect of the Hijaz. al-Yazidi said: it is the more eloquent form. Ibn Abi 'Abla read ya'arrishun with a damma on the initial letter, a fatha on the 'ayn and a shadda on the ra'. al-Hasan derived from this verse that one should not rebel against the kings of the earth, but rather be patient toward them and against them, for God will destroy them. It is narrated from him and from others: when people meet trial with its like, God leaves them to it, and when they meet it with patience and waiting for relief, relief comes. al-Zamakhshari said: I have been told that some people read yaghrisun (they plant), from gharasa al-ashjar (he planted trees), and I do not think it is anything but a misreading. This is the end of what God related of the account of Pharaoh and the Copts, their denial of God's signs, their wrongdoing and their opposition. Then He followed it with the account of the Children of Israel and what they introduced after their deliverance from Pharaoh's kingdom and his enslavement, their witnessing of the great signs, their crossing of the sea, their worship of the calf, their request to see God openly, and other kinds of disbelief and disobedience, so that the state of the human being may be known, and that he is, as described, "a great wrongdoer, a great ingrate" [cf. Ibrahim: 34], except those whom God protects, and "few of My servants are grateful" [Saba': 13]. And in order to console the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for what he saw from the Children of Israel in Madina.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 138–139:

﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea﴾. When He had mentioned the kinds of His blessings upon the Children of Israel by destroying their enemy, He followed with the greatest blessing: the sight of this tremendous sign and their crossing of the sea in safety. The sea is the Sea of Qulzum (the Red Sea), and whoever said it is the Nile of Egypt was mistaken. The meaning of (jāwaznā) is "We carried them across the sea"; it is said "jāwaza al-wādiya" when one crosses the valley, and the bāʾ (bi-) is for transitivity. It is said "jāwaza bi-ghayrihi al-baḥr" meaning "he brought him across the sea," so it is as if He said "wa-juznā bi-Banī Isrāʾīla," i.e., "We made them cross the sea." The form fāʿala is used in the sense of the bare form faʿala; it is said jāwaza and jāza with one meaning. Al-Ḥasan, Ibrāhīm, Abū Rajāʾ and Yaʿqūb read (wa-jawwaznā), and this is among the cases where faʿʿala has the sense of the bare faʿala, like qaddara and qadara. The doubling here is not for transitivity. It is related that Mūsā (peace be upon him) brought them across on the Day of ʿĀshūrāʾ, after Allah had destroyed Firʿawn and his people, and they fasted in gratitude to Allah. Mūsā was given the Torah on the Day of Naḥr, so between the two events there were eleven months.

* *

﴿Then they came upon a people devoted to idols of their own﴾. Qatādah and Abū ʿAmr al-Jawnī said: they were from Lakhm and Judhām, who used to dwell in the countryside. It was also said: they were camping at al-Raqqah, the Raqqat Miṣr, which is a village in the countryside of Egypt known for being on the seashore, from which one reaches al-Fayyūm. It was also said: they were the Canaanites whom Mūsā had been commanded to fight. The meaning of (fa-ataw) is "they passed by," as in "atat ʿalayhi sunūn" (years passed over him). The meaning of (yaʿkufūna) is "they remain and persist in worshipping idols." The two Akhawān (Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī), Abū ʿAmr, and in the narration of ʿAbd al-Wārith read it with a kasra on the kāf, while the rest of the Seven read it with a ḍammah, and both are eloquent. As for al-aṣnām (idols), it was said they were literally cows. Ibn Jurayj said they were images of cows made of stone, wood and the like, and that was the beginning of the affair of the Calf.

* *

﴿They said: "O Mūsā, make for us a god just as they have gods."﴾ The apparent meaning is that asking for the like of this is disbelief, rebellion and obstinacy. They followed their habit of being contentious with their prophets and asking for what is not fitting. Among their earlier words was ﴿We will not believe you until we see Allah plainly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 55], and other things that are disbelief. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: (p-378) The apparent meaning is that they admired what they saw of the gods of those people, and wished that this be part of the sharīʿah of Mūsā and of what is drawn near to Allah the Exalted. Otherwise it is far-fetched that they would say to Mūsā "make for us a god," meaning one to be worshipped alone. End of quote. In a hadith: "They passed through the Battle of Ḥunayn by a great green lote-tree, and it was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, make for us a Dhāt Anwāṭ'." Dhāt Anwāṭ was a lote-tree belonging to some polytheists, on which they hung their weapons, and they had a day when they gathered at it. The one who said this wanted the Messenger to legislate that in Islam, and the Messenger (peace be upon him) saw that as a means to worshipping that tree, so he denounced it and said: "Allahu akbar! You have said, by Allah, what the Children of Israel said."

﴿Make for us a god﴾, a creator and governor. Because what Mūsā would make cannot be a creator of the worlds and its governor, the closest meaning is that they asked him to designate for them images and figures, through whose worship they would draw near to Allah the Exalted. Of the worship of idols it has been reported that they said: ﴿We only worship them so that they bring us nearer to Allah in position﴾ [al-Zumar: 3]. All the prophets, peace be upon them, agreed that worshipping other than Allah is disbelief, whether one believes it to be a god of the worlds or believes that worshipping it brings one nearer to Allah. End of quote. It appears that this did not come from all of them, for among them were the seventy chosen men, and one of them would not have uttered this false request. Rather, it was attributed to the Children of Israel when it occurred from some of them, following the Arab custom in such matters. And the (mā) in (kamā) [is]: al-Zamakhsharī said it is a mā that is kāffah (restrictive), which is why the sentence follows it. Others said it is a mā ḥarfiyyah ṣilah (verbal relative particle), meaning "as they have gods," so its ṣilah is omitted, following the rule of Ibn Mālik that when the ṣilah of mā is omitted, its ma'mūl must be retained, as in their saying: "I will not speak to you as long as there is a star in the sky," meaning "as long as it is established that there is a star in the sky." Here ālihah (gods) would be the subject of the omitted verb. It was also said that it is a nominal relative, with the lām and its complement forming the ṣilah, and the pronoun referring to it is hidden in the genitive phrase; the implied meaning is "like that which they have, and ālihah is a substitute for that hidden pronoun."

﴿He said: "Indeed you are a people who act in ignorance."﴾ Mūsā (peace be upon him) marvelled at their words immediately after seeing the great signs and dazzling miracles, and described them with absolute ignorance, emphasizing it with inna, because there is no greater ignorance than this statement, nor a more shameful one. He used the verb (tajhalūna, "you act in ignorance") and did not say (jahiltum, "you were ignorant"), to indicate that this was for them like a nature and an instinct, from which they do not move, in past or future.

﴿Indeed these people—what they are in is destroyed, and what they have been doing is vain﴾. The reference of (hāʾulāʾ) is to those devoted to worshipping idols. The meaning of mutabbar is destroyed, ruined, broken; its root meaning is breaking. al-Kalbī said: "nullified." Abū al-Yasaʿ said: "misguided." al-Suddī and Ibn Zayd said: "destroyed, evil, of bad outcome." (Mā hum fīhi) encompasses all their circumstances. The vanishing of their deed is its dissolution such that it does not benefit, even if it was intended to draw near to Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [al-Furqan: 23]. al-Zamakhsharī said: In placing (hāʾulāʾ) as the subject of (inna), and in fronting the predicate of the subject within the sentence that is the predicate of inna, and in naming them as those who are exposed to ruin, and that it does not go beyond them at all, and that it is a striking blow for them, there is a warning against the outcome of what they asked for and a making hateful to them of what they loved. End of quote. What he said, that the predicate of the subject in the sentence that is the predicate of inna has been made definite, is not necessarily so, for the better way of parsing such a construction is that the predicate of inna is mutabbarun, and what follows it is raised as a passive-voice subject (mafʿūl lam yusamma fāʿiluhu). Likewise (mā kānū) is the subject of (bāṭilun), so that he would then have given information about the subject of inna with a single noun, not a sentence, as in the example inna Zaydan maḍrūbun ghulāmuhu. The better parsing is that ghulāmuhu is raised as a passive-voice subject, and maḍrūbun is the predicate of inna. The other possibility, that it is a subject with maḍrūbun as its predicate, is permissible but less preferred.

How excellent was Moses' address to them. He first attributed ignorance to them, then second informed them that the worshippers of idols are not upon anything, but rather the outcome of their affair is destruction and the nullification of their deeds. Third, he denied and marvelled that he, peace be upon him, should fall into seeking for them a god other than Allah. That is, "Shall I seek for you a deity (ilah) other than the One deserving worship and divinity?" He is the One who honoured you and singled you out with blessings that He did not give to the nations that preceded you, and no one else did. So how could I seek for you a god other than Him?

The meaning of ﴿عَلَى الْعَالَمِينَ﴾ ("above the worlds") is "above the two worlds of their time," or "by the great number of prophets among them." Ibn al-Qushayri said: "By destroying their enemy, and by the signs that He specially granted them."

The word ﴿غَيْرَ﴾ ("other than") is in the accusative as an object of ﴿أَبْغِيكُمْ﴾ ("I seek for you"). That is, "I seek for you other than Allah." The word ﴿إِلَهًا﴾ ("a deity") is a specification (tamyiz, a noun clarifying the preceding vague term) for ﴿غَيْرَ﴾, or a circumstantial accusative (hal), or it is in the accusative of the state (ʿala al-hal). It may also be the object, and the sense would be "I seek for you a god other than Allah." In that case ﴿غَيْرُ﴾ would be an attribute (sifah), and when it was placed first it became accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: "﴿غَيْرَ﴾ is in the accusative by a hidden verb. This is the apparent reading, and it is possible that it is accusative as a circumstantial state." Its accusative cannot clearly be by a hidden verb, because ﴿أَبْغِي﴾ already governs it, or governs ﴿إِلَهًا﴾. If one imagines that it is accusative by a hidden ﴿أَبْغِي﴾ which this apparent reading explains, that is not valid, because the explanatory clause has no connecting element, neither a pronoun nor any other linking word. Had the construction been ﴿أَغَيْرَ اللَّهِ أَبْغِيكُمُوهُ﴾ ("Shall I seek other than Allah for you, it?"), it would have been valid. The clause ﴿وَهُوَ فَضَّلَكُمْ﴾ ("while He has favoured you") may be a circumstantial clause (hal), or it may be a new independent sentence.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 141:

﴿And [remember] when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who subjected you to a terrible torment: they slaughtered your sons and spared your women. In that was a tremendous trial from your Lord.﴾ The majority of readers recited (anjaynākum), and a group recited (najjaynākum) with a shaddah, and Ibn ʿĀmir recited (anjākum). Upon the reading (anjākum), the verse follows His saying (wa-huwa faḍḍalakum, "and He preferred you"), and Moses addressed his people with it. In the reading with nūn, God Most High addressed them with it. Al-Ṭabarī said: the address is to those who were in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ), as a rebuke to them for what their forebears did and for what they brought.

The explanation of the like of this verse was given earlier, at the beginning of al-Baqarah. Nāfiʿ recited (yaqtulūna), from qatala, while the majority recited it from qattala with a shaddah.

**(p. 380)** It is narrated that Musa, peace be upon him, promised the Children of Israel, while he was in Egypt, that if Allah destroyed their enemy he would bring them a Book from Allah containing an explanation of what they should do and what they should avoid. When Fir'awn perished, Musa asked his Lord, exalted is He, for the Book. He was commanded to fast thirty days, which was the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah. When he completed the thirty days, he noticed a change in the smell of his mouth (*khuluf*, the odor of a fasting person's breath), so he used the siwak (tooth-stick). The angels said, "We used to smell the fragrance of musk from your mouth, and you have spoiled it with the siwak." It is also said that Allah revealed to him: "Do you not know that the odor of the mouth of one who fasts is more fragrant to Allah than the scent of musk?" So he was commanded to add ten more days from Dhu al-Hijjah because of this.

It is also said that Allah commanded him to fast thirty days and to do during them what would bring him closer to Allah, the Exalted. Then the Torah was sent down to him during the ten days, and He spoke to him in them. The mention of the forty nights is summarized in al-Baqarah and detailed here.

Al-Kalbi said: When Musa crossed the sea with the Children of Israel and Fir'awn drowned, the Children of Israel said to Musa, "Bring us a Book from our Lord, as you promised us, and as you claimed you would bring it to us within a month." Musa chose seventy men from his people to go with him. When they had made ready, Allah, the Exalted, said to Musa, "Inform your people that you will not come to them for forty nights." That was when the period had been completed with ten. When Musa set out with the seventy, he commanded them to wait for him at the foot of the mountain. Musa ascended the mountain, and Allah spoke to him for forty days and forty nights, and wrote the Tablets for him. Then the Children of Israel counted twenty nights and twenty days, and said, "Musa has broken his promise to us." Al-Samiri made the calf for them, and they worshipped it.

It is also said that the ten were added after the month for the intimate converse (*munajah*, private conversation with Allah). It is said that he turned aside on his way, so the ten were added. It is also said that they were added as a punishment for his people for worshipping the calf. It is also said that Musa was informed of his absence (from his people) as thirty nights, and when He added the ten to his absence, they did not know of this, and their souls were troubled by the addition beyond what he had told them. Then al-Samiri said, "Musa has died and will not return," and he led them astray with the calf, and they followed him. This is what Ibn Jurayj said.

The benefit of the detail, they said, is that the thirty were for preparation for the intimate converse, and the ten were for the sending down of the Torah and His speaking to him.

Abu Muslim said: He hastened to the appointed time of his Lord before his people, because of His saying: ﴿And what hastened you away from your people, O Musa?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 83] and the rest of the verse. So it is permissible that he came to Mount Sinai at the completion of the thirty. Then, when he was informed of the news of his people with al-Samiri, he returned to his people before the completion of the period of the promise, then he went back to the appointed time for ten more.

It was said: There is no impossibility that there were two promises: the first, which Musa attended, and the second, which the chosen men attended so they could hear the speech of Allah. The promise thus differed because the attendees differed.

The thirty were the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah, and the ten were from Dhu al-Hijjah. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Masruq, and Mujahid.

The difference in the recitation of *wa-wa'adna* has already been mentioned. They said that *thalathin* (thirty) is in the accusative as a second object (*maf'ul thani*) with an elided *mudaf* (genitive construction). Abu al-Baqa' estimated it as "the arrival of thirty" or "the completion of thirty." Ibn Atiyya said: *thalathin* is in the accusative on the assumption of "We set a term for him" or "the intimate converse of thirty," and it is not in the accusative as an adverb of time (*zarf*).

The *ha'* in *wa-atmamnaha* refers to the promise (*al-muwa'adah*) understood from *wa'adna*. Al-Hawfi said: the *ha'* and the *alif* are in the accusative with *atmamnaha*, and both refer to *thalathin*, but this is not apparent, because the thirty was not deficient so as to be completed with ten. The specifier of *ashr* (ten) is elided, meaning "ten nights," because what precedes it indicates it. In the codex of Ubayy, the reading is *wa-tammamnaha* with the doubled *mim* (intensive form).

The *mi'qat* (appointed time) is the time that has been fixed for something and set for it. The phrase ﴿mi'qat rabbihi﴾ came with the word *rabbihi* (his Lord) and did not come in the form of *wa'adna*, so the construction would have been *fatamma miqatuna* (our appointed time was completed). This is because the word *rabbihi* indicates that He is the one who sets right his affairs, watches over his matter, owns him, and disposes of him. It was said: The difference between *al-mi'qat* and *al-waqt* (time) is that *al-mi'qat* is the time in which a deed is determined to be done, while *al-waqt* is the time of a thing.

*Arba'in* (forty) is in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), as Al-Zamakhshari said, "the circumstantial element in it." He said: He came with *tamma* (was completed) reaching this number. In this case, *arba'in* is not the circumstantial element; rather, the circumstantial element is this elided word. This contradicts His saying *wa-arba'ina laylatan* (and forty nights), which is in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative.

**\* \***

**(p. 381)** ﴿And Musa said to his brother Harun, "Take my place among my people, act rightly, and do not follow the way of the corrupters."﴾ It was read irregularly (*shadhdh*) as *Harunu* with a *damma* as a vocative (*nida'*), meaning "O Harun." When he intended to depart for the intimate converse and to be absent for it, He commanded him to be his successor among his people, and to act rightly in himself or in what must be rectified of the affairs of his people. He forbade him to follow the way of those who corrupt. In the prohibition is evidence of the existence of corrupters, and for this reason He forbade him from following their way. His command to him to do what is right and his prohibition from following the way of the corrupters is for emphasis, not because it was feared that he would do the opposite of rectification or follow that way, because the station of prophethood is exempt from that.

The meaning of *ukhlufni* (take my place) is "be independent in the matter," and that is during his lifetime, since he went to the intimate converse with his Lord. The meaning is not that you will be my successor after my death. Do you not see that Harun, peace be upon him, died before Musa, peace be upon them both? In the saying of the Messenger (ﷺ) to Ali, "You are to me as Harun was to Musa," there is no evidence that he was his successor after his death, since Harun was not a successor after the death of Musa. Rather, the Messenger (ﷺ) appointed Ali as a deputy over his household when the Messenger, peace be upon him, travelled on some of his military campaigns, just as he appointed Ibn Umm Maktum over Madinah. So there is no evidence in that that he would be a successor after the death of the Messenger.

﴿When Moses came at Our appointed time and his Lord spoke to him﴾. That is, at the time He had set for him, that is, upon the completion of the forty (nights), just as you say, "I came to him on the tenth of the month, with ten days having passed." The meaning of the lam (li, "for") is specificity (ikhtisas). The majority hold that he alone was singled out for speech, since he came for the appointed time. Al-Qadi said: he and the seventy heard the speech of God. Ibn 'Atiyya said: He created for him a perception (idrak) by which he heard the speech subsisting in the Eternal Essence, which is an attribute of the Essence. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said: God brought Moses near until he heard the scratching of the pens on the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz). Al-Zamakhshari said: "And his Lord spoke to him" without an intermediary, as He speaks to an angel. His speaking means that He creates speech articulated in some of the bodies, just as He created it preserved in the Tablet. It is narrated that Moses heard speech from every direction. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas: "He spoke to him for forty days and forty nights, and He wrote the Tablets for him." It was also said: He spoke to him only at the beginning of the forty. Wahb said: He spoke to him in a thousand stations, and after each station a light would appear on his face for three days, and he did not approach women from the time God spoke to him. Here they have brought up the dispute concerning the speech of God, which is well known, and the proofs of those who differ are mentioned in the books of the foundations of religion (usul al-din). "And His speaking" is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon "came." It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal). He turned from saying "And We spoke to him" to saying "and his Lord spoke to him," for the same reason that He turned to saying "so the appointed time of his Lord was completed" and "when his Lord manifested Himself."
* *
﴿He said: "My Lord, show me (Yourself) that I may look upon You."﴾ Al-Suddi and Abu Bakr al-Hudhali said: When He spoke to him and singled him out with this rank, his aspiration soared toward the rank of vision, and he longed for it, so he asked his Lord to show Himself to him. Al-Zajjaj said: The speech inspired him with longing, and his patience was overcome, so it drove him to ask for vision. Al-Rabi' said: He had not been commissioned concerning vision, so he thought that asking at that time was permissible. Al-Suddi said: Satan crept into the earth and emerged before him, and said, "It is only a devil speaking to you." So he asked for vision. Had vision not been permissible, he would not have asked for it. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The vision of God is permissible by reason according to the Ash'ariyya (the Ash'arite school) and the People of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna wa'l-Jama'a); for insofar as He exists, He can be seen. The Law has established the vision of God in the Hereafter and has prohibited it in this world by the apparent texts of the Shari'a. So Moses, peace be upon him, did not ask for something impossible, but for something permissible. His saying: ﴿"You will not see Me, but look at the mountain..."﴾ is not the answer to one who asks for the impossible, for God said to Noah, peace be upon him: ﴿"So do not ask Me about what you have no knowledge of. I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant."﴾ [Hud: 46]. Had Moses asked for the impossible, the answer would have contained some rebuke and despair. Al-Karmani and others said: There is an elision in the speech, its estimate being: "You will not see Me in this world." It was also said: "You will not be able to see Me." It was also said: "You will not see Me by your asking." It was also said: "You will not see Me, but you will see Me when I manifest Myself to the mountain." Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, how could Moses, peace be upon him, ask for that when he is among the most knowledgeable of people about God, His attributes, what is permissible for Him and what is not, and His exaltation above the quality of perception by some of the senses, which is valid only for what is in a direction and is neither a body nor an accident? It is impossible for Him to be in a direction. The denial of the Jabriyya (the determinists) that He is impossible in the intellects is not binding, for this is not the first of their obstinacy and their recklessness. And how could he be the one seeking it, when he said, when the quake seized those who said, "Show us God openly," ﴿"Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did? It is only Your trial by which You send astray whom You will..."﴾ [al-A'raf: 155], so he disavowed their deed and called them foolish and misguided. I say: His request for vision was only to silence those whom he called foolish and misguided, and to disavow their deed, and to put the proof in their mouths. For when they asked for vision, he denied it to them, informed them of their error, and alerted them to the truth. But they persisted and went on in their obstinacy, saying, "There is no way out; we will not believe you until we see Him." So he wanted them to hear the text from God about the impossibility of that, namely His saying "You will not see Me," so that they would be certain and the doubt that had entered them would be removed. Therefore he said: ﴿"My Lord, show me (Yourself) that I may look upon You."﴾ If you say: Why did he not say, "Show them that they may look upon You"? I say: Because God, glorified be He, spoke to Moses while they were listening. When they heard the speech of the Lord of Might, they wanted Moses to see His Essence so that they might see Him along with him, just as He had caused him to hear His speech and they heard it with him. It was a desire based on a corrupt analogy. Therefore Moses said, ﴿"Show me (Yourself) that I may look upon You"﴾. Also, because when he was rebuked for what he asked, and denied it despite his prophethood, his special status and his nearness to God, and was told, "This will not happen," then others would be more deserving of denial. Also, because the Messenger is the imam of his community, so what is addressed to him or what he addresses is relevant to them. His saying ﴿"look upon You"﴾, with its sense of confrontation (muqabala), which is pure likening (tashbih) and corporealization (tajsim), is evidence that it is a rendering of their proposal and a reporting of their words. Glorified is the author of al-Jumal (Sahib al-Jumal) above making God an object seen and confronted by the faculty of sight. How much more so for one who is more deeply versed in knowledge of God than Wasil ibn 'Ata', 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, al-Nazzam, Abu al-Hudhayl, the two Shaykhs, and all the Muslims. The second object of "show me" is elided, meaning: "Show me (Yourself)," make me able to see You by manifesting Yourself to me, that I may look upon You. End.
﴿He said: "You will not see Me."﴾ Ibn 'Atiyya said: It explicitly states the prohibition of vision in this world. But "lan" (will not) does not negate the future absolutely; so if we kept to this negation alone, it would imply that Moses would never see Him, not even in the Hereafter. But there has come from another source the widely transmitted hadith (hadith mutawatir) that the people of faith will see God on the Day of Resurrection, so Moses, peace be upon him, is more deserving of seeing Him. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, what is the meaning of "lan"? I say: It emphasizes the negation that "la" gives, for "la" negates the future; you say, "I will not do it tomorrow," and when you emphasize its negation you say, "I will certainly not do it tomorrow." The meaning is that his doing it contradicts my state, like His saying: ﴿"They will never create a fly, even if they gathered together for it."﴾ [al-Hajj: 73], and His saying ﴿"Vision does not perceive Him"﴾ [al-An'am: 103] is a negation of vision in the future. And "You will not see Me" is emphasis and clarification. If you say, why did He say "You will not see Me" and not "You will not look at Me," given His saying "Show me that I may look upon You"? I say: When he said "show me," meaning "make me able to see," which is perception, He knew that the request was for vision, not for looking without perception. So He said, "You will not see Me," and did not say, "You will not look at Me."
* *
﴿"But look at the mountain; if it remains firm in its place, then you will see Me."﴾ Mujahid and others said: "But I will manifest Myself to the mountain, which is stronger than you and more powerful. If it remains firm and endures the patience of My majesty, then I will enable you to see Me." Ibn 'Atiyya said: According to this, God only made the mountain an example for him. Another group said: The meaning is: "I will begin for you upon the mountain; if it remains firm in awe of My greatness, then you will see Me." End. Making vision conditional upon the mountain's remaining firm indicates its absence if it does not remain firm. He thereby pointed out that the mountain, despite its might and hardness, if it does not remain firm, then the human being, with his weak constitution, is even more unlikely to remain firm. This was a consolation to the heart of Moses and a lightening of the weight of the prohibition. Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, how is the "but" (istidrak) in His saying ﴿"But look at the mountain"﴾ connected to what precedes it? I say: It connects to it in the sense that gazing at Me is impossible, so do not seek it; but rather, upon you is another kind of looking: that you look at the mountain which quakes with you and with those for whose sake you sought vision; how I will deal with it, and how I will make it crumble (dakk) because of your request for vision, so that you may magnify what you have undertaken, by what I show you of its great effect. It is as if, glorified and exalted be He, when vision was sought, He realized what He had illustrated when the attribution of a son to Him was mentioned in His saying: ﴿"And the mountains would collapse in ruins"﴾ [Maryam: 90] ﴿"because they attribute a son to the Most Merciful"﴾ [Maryam: 91]. ﴿"If it remains firm in its place"﴾, as it was steady and established, moving in its directions, ﴿"then you will see Me"﴾ is an allusion to the existence of vision on account of the existence of what will not happen, namely the mountain's remaining in its place until He crumbles it to dust and levels it with the earth. This is a speech interwoven, part into part, delivered in a wondrous style and a marvelous arrangement. Do you not see how He moved from the looking to the looking by the word "but," and then how He followed with the threat of the quake occurring because of the request for looking, under the condition of the existence of vision, I mean His saying: ﴿"If it remains firm in its place, then you will see Me."﴾ End. This is according to the method of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) in denying the vision of God. They have in this several views, four in number. The first: what they narrated from al-Hasan and others, that Moses did not know that vision was impermissible, though he knew of God's justice, His Lordship, and His unity; so it is not far-fetched that knowledge of the impossibility or permissibility of vision depended on hearing (sam'). This was refuted, and it is said that this would imply that his knowledge of God was of a lesser rank than the knowledge of the lowliest Mu'tazila, and that is false by consensus. The second: al-Jubba'i and his son Abu Hashim said: He asked for vision on behalf of his people, for they used to press him often about it, not for himself. When he was refused, it became clear that there is no way to it. This was refuted: if it were so, He would have said, "Show them that they may look upon You," and it would have been said, "You will not see Me." Also, if it were impossible, He would have forbidden them from it as He forbade them from making gods for them with His saying, ﴿"Indeed you are a people who are ignorant"﴾ [al-A'raf: 138]. Al-Ka'bi said: He asked for the striking signs by which doubts and suspicions about knowing Him vanish, as you say regarding the knowledge of the people of the Hereafter. This was refuted: it requires an elision of a noun, and the context of the speech rejects that, for He had shown him signs with no limit after them, such as the staff and others. Al-Asamm said: The intent is that He mention from the revealed proofs (al-dala'il al-sam'iyya) what indicates the impossibility of vision, so that the rational proof is reinforced by the revealed proof. The "al" in "al-jabal" (the mountain) is for definiteness (al-'ahd), and it is the greatest mountain in Madyan, called Arrarayn. Ibn 'Abbas said: The mountains stretched themselves up for the manifestation, and Arrarayn humbled itself, so He manifested Himself to it.
* *

[p. 382] [p. 383]

(p-384) *Al-tajalli* means manifestation. *Al-dakk* is the verbal noun of *dakaktu al-shay'*, meaning I crushed and pulverized the thing; it is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle. *Al-dakk* and *al-daqq* have the same meaning. Ibn 'Aziz said: *dakkan* means level with the ground. *Al-khurur* means falling. *Afaqa* means that his senses and his reason returned to him. *Al-lawh* is well known; it is prepared for writing and other purposes, and its root meaning is shining, since written things shine and appear on it. *Al-huli* is well known; it is what women adorn themselves with, of silver, gold, jewels and other precious stones. *Al-khuwar* is the lowing of a cow. *Al-asaf* is grief; it is said: *asifa, ya'safu*. *Al-jarr* is pulling. *Al-ishmat* is joy at what befalls a person of hardship. *Al-sukut* and *al-sukat* are silence.

* *

﴿So when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He crushed it to dust, and Moses fell down unconscious.﴾ Two things followed the manifestation: first, the mountain was crushed and its parts scattered; second, Moses fell down in a swoon. This was said by Ibn Zayd and the majority of the exegetes. Al-Suddi said: he fell down dead, but the word *afaqa* (he recovered) rules this out. The manifestation in the sense of physical appearance is impossible for God, the Exalted. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: when His light fell upon it, it was crushed. Al-Mubarrad said: the meaning is that there appeared to the mountain from the dominion of God that by which it was crushed. It was also said: a part of the Throne appeared to the mountain, and it collapsed from awe of it. It was said: His command appeared. It was said: (manifested) to the people of the mountain, meaning Moses and the seventy who were with him. Al-Dahhak said: God manifested from the light of the veils the like of the nostril of a bull. 'Abdullah ibn Salam and Ka'b al-Ahbar said: what manifested of God's greatness to the mountain was no more than the size of the eye of a needle. Al-Zamakhshari said: when His power became manifest to it and His command and will confronted it. End of quotation. Those theologians who interpret, such as al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Tayyib and others, said: God created for the mountain life, sensation and perception by which it could see; then He manifested Himself to it, that is, appeared and became visible, and the mountain was crushed because of the intensity of the sight. When Moses saw what was in the mountain, he swooned. This meaning is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. The apparent sense is that manifestation is attributed to Him, the Exalted, in a manner befitting Him, without movement and without any description that indicates corporeality. Ibn 'Abbas said: it became dust. Muqatil said: scattered pieces. It was also said: it became six mountains, three in Medina: Uhud, Warqan and Radwa; and three in Mecca: Thawr, Thabir and Hira. Anas narrated this from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It was said: its upper part went away and its lower part remained. It was said: it became dust scattered by the winds. Sufyan said: it is narrated that it spread out over the earth and reached the sea beneath the earths. Ibn al-Kalbi said: so it continues to sink into it until the Day of Resurrection. The majority said: *dakkan*, that is, crushed, or having crushing. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *dakka'*, on the pattern of *hamra'*. *Al-dakka'* is a she-camel without a hump, and the meaning is: He made it level ground, likened to the humpless she-camel. Al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham said: spread out your hand *dakka'*, that is, stretch it out level. Al-Zamakhshari said: *al-dakka'* is the name of a raised elevation that rises from the earth like a mound. End of quotation. This agrees with the view of those who said that it did not disappear entirely, but its upper part went away and most of it remained. Yahya ibn Wathhab read *dukkan*, that is, pieces, the plural of *dakka'*, like *ghuzz*, the plural of *ghazza'*. It is in the accusative as a second object of *ja'alahu*. The view of al-Akhfash that its accusative is of the type of *qa'adtu juluusan* is weak. (*Sa'qan*) is a concomitant state. One says *sa'aqahu*, so he was struck senseless, and this is of the verbs that are transitive by movement, like *shatara Allahu 'aynahu*, so his eye was cut off. The apparent meaning is that Moses and the mountain could not bear to see God, the Exalted, when He manifested Himself, and for this reason the mountain was crushed, and Moses, peace be upon him, swooned. 'Iyad ibn Musa related from al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Tayyib that Moses, peace be upon him, saw God, and for this reason he fell down in a swoon; and that the mountain saw its Lord, and for this reason it became crushed, through perceiving the immensity of God's manifestation to it. Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah related from Ka'b who said: God, the Exalted, divided His speech and His vision between Muhammad and Moses, may God bless them both and grant them peace: Moses spoke with Him twice, and Muhammad (ﷺ) saw Him twice. The exegetes mentioned his seeing the angels of the seven heavens and the bearers of the Throne, their forms and their numbers; God knows best their soundness.
