﴿So when he recovered, he said: Glory be to You, I repent to You﴾. That is, from the request to see Him in this world. This was said by Mujahid. Or: from asking for it before permission was given. Or: for my minor sins, related by al-Kirmani. Or he said that in the manner of turning back to God, the Exalted, and returning to Him at the appearance of signs, as is the custom of the believer when seeing great things, and it is not a repentance from some specific thing; this was indicated by Ibn 'Atiyyah. Al-Zamakhshari said: *Glory be to You*: I exalt You above what is not permitted for You, of seeing and other things. *I repent to You*: from asking to see You. If you say: if the request to see was for the purpose you mentioned, then from what did he repent? I say: from his carrying out that great utterance, even though it was for a correct purpose, uttered by his tongue without permission from God, the Exalted. Look at God's magnifying of the matter of seeing in this verse: how He made the mountain tremble at those who sought it, and made it crushed, and how He struck them down, and He did not spare His interlocutor from denying that, as an exaggeration in magnifying the matter. And how he glorified his Lord, seeking refuge in Him, and repented from having that word carried out on his tongue, and said: *I am the first of the believers*. Then he marvelled at those who call themselves Muslims, by calling themselves People of the Sunnah and the Community, how they took this great matter as a doctrine. Do not let their concealment with *bilkafa* deceive you, for it is among the sayings of their shaykhs. The matter is as one of the just scholars (*'adliyyah*) said about them:

*For a group who named their desire a sunnah, and a group of asses, by my life, saddled with pack-saddles.*
*They likened Him to His creation, and feared the reproach of the people, so they hid behind bilkafa.*

This is an interpretation according to the method of the Mu'tazilah, and an abuse of the People of the Sunnah and the Community according to his habit. Some scholars of the Sunnah composed on the metre and rhythm of these two verses. Our teacher, the eminent Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Ibrahim ibn al-Zubayr, recited them to us in Granada by licence, if not by hearing, and I transcribed them from his hand. He said: al-Qadi, the man of letters and scholar Abu al-Khattab Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Khalil al-Sakuni recited to us, while I read to him, from his brother al-Qadi Abu Bakr, from his composition:

*You likened the ignorance of the community of Ahmad, and the people of insight, to the saddled asses.*
*You claimed they likened their worshipped One, and feared, so they hid behind bilkafa.*
*You shot them from a bow you had made straight, like the shooting of a youth who tears the Mushaf tomorrow.*
*The loss is due upon you; look, being fair, at the verse of al-A'raf, for it is the fair one.*
*Do you think Moses came with an ignorance he did not come with, and that your shaykhs did not come with it from knowledge?*
*And with the verse of al-A'raf, woe to you, you were forsaken, so you stopped short of the lofty steps.*
*Had your pact in Islam been sound, you would not have spoken of the doctrine abandoned, the denial of attributes.*
*Indeed, faces will be looking towards Him; with this the Book came; you said: this is folly.*
*So the denial is specific to a dwelling after which for you there is no... may you have no father, a promise that will not be broken.*

And our judge of judges, Abu al-Qasim 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Qadi al-Qudat Abi Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Wahhab ibn Khalaf al-'Ulami recited to us in Cairo, for himself:

*They said: He wills, and His will is not to be; they swerved, but from the path of knowledge.*

﴿And I am the first of the believers﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: first among the believers of the Children of Israel. It was said: first among the people of his time, if unbelief had spread over the horizons. Abu al-'Aliyah said: that You are not seen in this world. Al-Zamakhshari said: that You are not seen and not perceived by any of the senses. He also said: in Your greatness and majesty, and that nothing can stand against Your might and power. End of quotation. His first interpretation follows the method of the Mu'tazilah. The theologians of the People of the Sunnah have mentioned proofs for the vision of God, the Exalted, both from transmitted and rational evidence, which are established in the books of the principles of religion, along with the arguments of the opponents.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 144:

﴿He said, "O Musa, I have chosen you above the people by My messages and by My speech. So take what I have given you and be among the grateful."﴾ When Musa (peace be upon him) asked to see Allah and was denied, Allah enumerated to him the great forms of His favours upon him and commanded him to occupy himself with giving thanks for them. This is a consolation from Allah to him. The meaning of *al-istifa'* (choosing) has already been explained. The word *'ala al-nas* (above the people) is general in form, but its meaning is specific, that is, above the people of your time. Alternatively, it may remain general, and what is meant is the combination of the two ranks, the messagehood and the speech. This is the view of Ibn 'Atiyya. It should be understood that this refers to the occurrence of speech on earth, since it is established that Adam was a prophet to whom Allah spoke. It has also been interpreted as referring to [speech] in Paradise. Our Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) [was also spoken to], and it appears from the hadith of the Night Journey (al-Isra') that Allah the Exalted spoke to him. The words *"wa bi-kalami"* (and by My speech) indicate that he heard the speech directly from Allah and not from anyone else, because the angels descend upon the messengers with Allah's speech. He placed *"bi-risalati"* (by My messages) before *"wa bi-kalami"* (and by My speech) because messagehood is earlier in time, or because he moved from a noble thing to a nobler one. The two Harams (Ibn Kathir and Nafi') read *bi-risalati* in the singular, and it is intended as a verbal noun, that is, *bi-irsali* (by My sending). Or it may be by elision of a modifier, that is, *bi-tabligh risalati* (by conveying My message), because the signified meaning of *risala* (message) is different from the signified meaning of the verbal noun. The rest of the seven readers read it in the plural, because what he was sent with comprises kinds and types. The majority read *"wa bi-kalami"* (and by My speech), which may be a verbal noun, that is, *wa bi-taklimi* (and by My speaking to you), or it may be by elision of a modifier, that is, *wa bi-sama'i kalami* (and by hearing My speech). Abu Raja' read *"bi-risalati wa bi-kalimi"* with *kalima* in the plural, that is, *wa bi-sama'i kalimi* (and by hearing My words). Al-A'mash read *"bi-risalati wa taklumi"*, and al-Mahdawi related from him *wa taklimi* in the pattern *taf'ili*. Allah commanded him to take what He had given him of prophethood, because the command to take carries added emphasis and the reward of obeying. The meaning is: take what I have given you with diligence in conveying it and earnestness in benefiting by it. ﴿And be among the grateful﴾ for what We have given you. In this there is an indication of contentment and satisfaction with what Allah has given, and of thankfulness for it.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 145:

﴿And We wrote for him on the Tablets of everything﴾. It has been said that Musa (عليه السلام) was struck senseless (ṣaʿiqa) on the Day of Friday, the Day of ʿArafah, and regained consciousness on it, and that the Torah was given to him on the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr). The apparent sense of His words "And We wrote" is the attribution of the writing to Himself. It has been said that He wrote with His own hand, and the people of the heavens heard the scratching (ṣarīr) of the pen on the Tablet. It has been said that He made them manifest and created them on the Tablets. It has been said that He commanded the pen to inscribe for Musa on the Tablets. It has been said that Jibril (عليه السلام) wrote them with the pen with which the Reminder (al-Dhikr) was written, and drew upon the river of light. In these two opinions, the writing is attributed to Himself in a form of honour, since that act issued from His command. It has been said that the meaning of "We wrote" is "We prescribed," as in His saying: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183]. The pronoun in "for him" (lahu) refers to Musa. "Al-Alwah" (the Tablets) is a plural of paucity (jamʿ qillah), and the definite article (alif-lam) in it is for defining the reality (taʿrīf al-māhiyyah). If it was he who cut and split them, then the alif-lam is for previous reference (al-ʿahd).

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "The alif-lam has replaced the pronoun that would be supposed to connect al-Alwah and Musa (عليه السلام); its estimated form is 'in his Tablets' (fī alwāḥihi). This is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, Paradise is the refuge﴾ [al-Naziʿat: 41], meaning 'its refuge' (maʾwāhu)." End of quote. That the alif-lam is a replacement for the pronoun is not the doctrine of the Basrans (al-Baṣriyyūn), and it is not necessary that it be a replacement for the pronoun. It is not like His saying ﴿Indeed, Paradise is the refuge﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 41], because the clause is a predicate about "man" (min), so the clause needs a connecting element (rābiṭ). The Kufans (al-Kūfiyyūn) said: the alif-lam is a replacement for the pronoun, as if it were said "its refuge" (maʾwāhu). The Basrans said: the connecting element is omitted, i.e., "it is the refuge for him."

The apparent form of "al-Alwah" is plural. It has been said that they were seven. This is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. It has been said that they were eight; this was mentioned by al-Karmani. It has been said that they were nine; this was said by Muqatil. It has been said that they were ten; this was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih. It has been said that they were two; this is also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, and it was chosen by al-Farrāʾ. This is weak, because indicating two by a plural form, by analogy, has a condition mentioned in grammar, and that condition is absent here.

al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said: "The Torah was sent down, and it was a load of seventy camels. A portion of it could be read in a year, and only four men read it: Musa, Yusha, ʿUzayr, and ʿIsa." They differed over what it was made of. From Ibn ʿAbbas and Abu al-ʿĀliyah: "chrysolite (zabarjad)." From Ibn Jubayr: "red ruby (yāqūt aḥmar)." Also from Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid: "green emerald (zumurrud akhḍar)." Also from Abu al-ʿĀliyah: "of hail (barad)." From Muqatil: "of emerald and ruby." From al-Hasan: "of wood, whose length was ten cubits (adhruʿ)." From Wahb: "of a hard, solid rock, which he was commanded to cut, and it became soft for him, so he cut it with his hand and split it with his fingers." It has been said: "of light," narrated by al-Karmani.

The meaning is: from every matter needed in their law (sharīʿah), ﴿an admonition﴾ for deterrence and reflection, ﴿and a detailed explanation of everything﴾ from the obligations, the lawful and the unlawful, the commands and prohibitions, the stories, the creeds, the reports, and the unseen matters. Ibn Jubayr and Mujahid said: "of everything they were commanded with and forbidden from." al-Suddi said: "the lawful and the unlawful." Muqatil said: "It was written in the Tablets: 'I am Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Do not associate anything with Me, do not cut off the roads, do not swear by My name falsely, for whoever swears falsely by My name, I will not purify him. Do not kill, do not commit adultery, and do not disobey your parents.'"

The apparent sense is that the object of "We wrote" (kataba) is: "We wrote in them an admonition from everything and a detailed explanation of everything." This was said by al-Hawfi, who said: "He put 'admonition' in the accusative by 'We wrote,' and 'detailed explanation' is conjoined to 'admonition,' and 'of everything' is connected to 'detailed explanation.'" End of quote. al-Zamakhsharī said: "﴿from everything﴾ is in the accusative position as the object of 'And We wrote,' ['admonition'] and ['detailed explanation'] is an apposition (badal) of it, and the meaning is: We wrote for him everything that the Children of Israel needed in their religion, of admonitions and detailed explanations of the rulings." End of quote.

A third possibility is, in my view, admissible: that the object of "We wrote" is in the place of a prepositional phrase (majrūr), as you say "I ate from the loaf of bread" (akaltu min al-raghīf), and "min" is partitive (lil-tabʿīḍ). That is, "We wrote for him things from everything." "Admonition and detailed explanation" is in the accusative as an object of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlih), meaning: We wrote for him those things for admonition and for detailed explanation of their rulings.

* *

﴿So take hold of them with strength and command your people to take the best of them. I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient﴾. That is: We said, "Take them," conjoined to "We wrote." It is permissible that "So take hold of them" is a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿So take what I have given you﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 144]. The pronoun in "take hold of them" (fa-khudhha) refers to "what" (mā) according to its meaning, not its wording. But if it is according to the implied "We said" (fa-qulnā), then it refers to "the Tablets" (al-alwāḥa), i.e., the Tablets, or to "everything," since it has the sense of "things," or to "the Torah," or to "the messages." These are possibilities that have been stated, the most apparent of which is the first.

As for the meaning of "with strength" (bi-quwwah): Ibn ʿAbbas said: "with diligence and striving, the action of the people of firm resolve (ulū al-ʿazm)." Abu al-ʿĀliyah and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said: "with obedience." Juwaybir said: "with gratitude." Ibn ʿĪsā said: "with determination and strength of heart, because if one takes it with weak intention, it leads to slackness." This last statement goes back to the statement of Ibn ʿAbbas: Musa was commanded to take with more firmness than what his people were commanded.

His saying "the best of them" (bi-aḥsanihā): its apparent meaning is that it is the elative form (ʿaf'al al-tafḍīl). Among them are the good and the better, such as retaliation (qiṣāṣ), pardon, self-defence (intiṣār), and patience. It has been said: the best of them are the obligations and the voluntary acts, and their goodness is the permissible. It has been said: the best of them is the abrogating (nāsikh), and their goodness is the abrogated (mansūkh). It is not conceivable that the abrogated is good except with regard to what it was before abrogation. As for after abrogation, it is not described as good, because it is not legislated. It has been said: "the best" is what is commanded, not what is forbidden. al-Zamakhsharī said, on his saying "Summer is hotter than winter": "This is on the imagination that there is heat in winter." End of quote. It is possible that both are shared in goodness with respect to pleasures and the appetites of the self, so what is commanded is better in terms of compliance and the reward that results from it, and what is forbidden is good in terms of pleasure and desire. So there is a shared measure of goodness between them, even though their objects differ.

It has been said: "the best of them" is the one most resembling what the word can bear of meanings. When a word has several possible meanings, it is interpreted by the most preferable of them in truth and the closest to it. It has been said: "ḥusnihā" here is not the elative form; rather the meaning is "with its goodness," as the poet said:

*A house whose pillars are mightier and loftier.*

That is: "mighty and lofty." This was said by Quṭrub and Ibn al-Anbārī. On this view, they were commanded to take with its goodness, which is what leads to reward, not the prohibitions that lead to punishment when done. It has been said: "ahsan" here is an extra element (ṣilah), and the meaning is: "take them." This is weak, because nouns are not to be added. "Ya'khudhū" (they take) is apocopated (majzūm) as the answer to the imperative. The phrase "and command your people" should be interpreted, because it does not follow from commanding his people to take the best of them that they "take the best of them," so no conditional and response structure results from it. "With the best of them" is connected to "they take," and this is by the application of the second (of two verbs competing for a complement, i.e., "ʿamal al-thānī"), because "with the best of them" is required by both "command" and "they take." It is possible that the verb "they take" is apocopated by the implicit lām of command, i.e., "let them take," because the meaning of "command your people" is "say to your people." This is according to the view of al-Kisāʾī. The object of "they take" is omitted for understanding of the meaning, i.e., "they take themselves with the best of them." It is possible that the bāʾ is extra, i.e., "they take the best of them," like His saying: "They should not recite with the suras" (lā yaqrāʾna bi-l-suwar). The first mode is better.

Observe the difference in the objects of the two commands. Musa was commanded to take all of it, so it was said: ﴿So take hold of them with strength﴾, and he was emphasised in taking by "with strength." As for them, they were commanded that they ﴿take the best of them﴾, and it was not emphasised, to show that the rank of prophethood is harder in obligation than the rank of the follower. For this reason, the night prayer (qiyām al-layl) and other obligations specific to him were made obligatory upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

"Showing" (al-irāʾah) here is from seeing with the eye, and for this reason it transitively takes two objects. "The abode of the defiantly disobedient" (dār al-fāsiqīn): it is Egypt. This was said by ʿAlī, Qatādah, Muqatil, and ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī. The defiantly disobedient are Pharaoh and his people.

al-Zamakhsharī said: "How they were left desolate by them, and were destroyed because of their disobedience, so that you may take heed and not disobey as they disobeyed, lest you be punished with the like of their punishment." End of quote. It has also been said: the meaning is "I will show you the places where the disbelievers met their end." That is because when He drowned Pharaoh and his people, He revealed to the sea, "Cast their bodies to the shore," and it did so. The Children of Israel looked at them, and He showed them the fallen places of the defiantly disobedient. al-Kalbī said: "what they passed by when travelling, from the fallen places of ʿĀd and Thamūd and the generations who were destroyed." Qatādah also said: "the Levant (al-Shām)," and the intended people are the ʿAmāliqah, whom Musa was commanded to fight. Mujahid and al-Hasan said: "the abode of the defiantly disobedient is Hell (Jahannam)," and the intended are the disbelievers in Musa and others. Ibn Zayd said: "I will show you from the sight of the heart," i.e., "I will make you know the ways of the former peoples and what punishment befell them." It has been said: "the abode of the defiantly disobedient" means "what their affair came to (mā dāra ilayhi amruhum)." This is not grasped except by reports that knowledge conveys. This is close to the statement of Ibn Zayd. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "If it were from sight of the heart, it would have transitively taken the hamzah to three objects. If someone said: the third object is implied by the meaning, so it is implicit, i.e., 'destroyed' (mudammarah) or 'ruined' (kharibah) or 'set ablaze' (musaʿʿarah), according to the view of whoever said it is Hell, it is said to him: it is not permissible to omit this object or to limit it to the lesser. Because it (the verb) enters upon the subject and predicate." End of quote. Omitting the third object in the chapter of "ʿalama" (to inform/know) for the indication of meaning is permissible. So it is permissible in answer to "Did you inform Zayd that ʿAmr was departing?" to say "You informed Zayd that ʿAmr [was departing]," and "departing" (muntaliqan) is omitted for indication by the preceding speech. As for his reasoning, "because it enters upon the subject and predicate," the predicate does not show prohibition, because the predicate of the subject may be omitted for brevity, and the second and third in the chapter of "ʿalama" may each be omitted for brevity. In his saying "because it enters upon the subject and predicate," there is a figurative usage: it means "before transference by hamzah, it was entering upon the subject and predicate."

al-Ḥasan recited: "sa-ūrīkum" with a quiescent wāw after the hamzah, according to what the orthography of the Muṣḥaf requires. This recitation has been explained in two ways. The first is what Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinnī) mentioned: that he prolonged the ḍammah and stretched it, so that a wāw arose from it. He said: "It is good to allow the wāw in this place, since it is a place of threat and severity, so he lengthened the sound in it," so it is like His saying "adnū fa-anẓūr" (I draw near and look) and "raʾā fa-anẓur" (he saw and I look). This explanation is weak, because lengthening of this kind belongs to the necessity of poetry. The second is what al-Zamakhsharī mentioned. He said: "al-Ḥasan recited sa-ūrīkum, and it is a widespread dialect in the Ḥijāz. One says: awrinī kadhā (show me such-and-such) and awraytuhu (I showed it to him), so its explanation is that it is from awraytu al-zand (I struck the fire-stick so it sparked), as if the meaning is 'he made it clear to me,' and 'he lit it for me so that I could see clearly.'" End of quote. It is also in the dialect of the people of al-Andalus, as if they took it from the dialect of the Ḥijāz, and it remains on their tongues to this day. It should be examined whether this dialect is truly in the dialect of the Ḥijāz or not.

Ibn ʿAbbās and Qasāmah ibn Zuhayr recited: "sa-ūrithukum" (I will make you inherit). al-Zamakhsharī said: "This is a good recitation, which the saying of the Exalted confirms: ﴿And We caused to inherit the people who had been oppressed﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 137]."

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 146:

﴿I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant in the earth without right﴾. When He mentioned ﴿I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-A'raf: 145], He mentioned what He does to them, exalted is He, by turning them away from His signs because of their defiance and their going beyond their proper bounds into a description that is not theirs. Then He mentioned, exalted is He, some of their conditions for which they deserved the name of defiance (fisq). Ibn Jubayr said: "I will turn them away from taking admonition and from reasoning by the proofs and signs, [which are] these miracles and the marvels of creation." Qatadah said: "I will prevent them from disparagement, slander, distortion, alteration and change." So the signs here are the Qur'an, for it is specifically protected from that. Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: "I will prevent them from pondering over them and from looking at them with the correct gaze that leads to the truth." Al-Zajjaj said: "I will make their recompense: I will turn them away from repelling retribution, meaning that if punishment befalls them, He will not repel it from them. So the signs according to this view are the punishments that struck them, by which they became an example and a lesson." According to these statements, ﴿those who are arrogant﴾ is general, i.e., everyone who has this attribute. It was also said: this is part of the address to Musa, and the signs are the nine that were given to him, and the arrogant are Pharaoh and his people. God turned their hearts away from taking admonition from them because of their immersion in the pleasures of this world. Al-Zamakhshari adopted some of the views of the exegetes and said: "I will turn away from My signs by sealing the hearts of the arrogant and forsaking them, so they do not reflect upon them nor take admonition from them, out of heedlessness and immersion in what occupies them from them of their desires." In this there is a warning to the addressees of the end of those who are turned away from the signs because of their arrogance and disbelief in them, lest they become like them and He treat them as He treated them. End. ﴿Those who are arrogant against belief﴾: Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "They are the disbelievers, and the meaning of this verse is: I will make the turning away from the signs a punishment for the arrogant for their arrogance." End. It was also said: they are those who despise people and regard themselves as superior to them. In the authentic hadith: "Arrogance is to reject the truth and to look down on people." ﴿Without right﴾ is connected to ﴿they are arrogant﴾, i.e., with what is not right, and with what they hold of their religion. Arrogance may also be with right, like the arrogance of the one who is right toward the one who is wrong, according to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿mighty toward the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 54]. It is also permissible that it be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), so it is connected to an omitted element, i.e., ﴿while being connected with what is not right﴾, and the meaning is: not deserving; because arrogance with right belongs to God alone, since He is the One who has the power and the superiority that no one else has.

﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it﴾. He described them with this blameworthy description, which is arrogance against belief, to the point that if every sign were presented to them, they would not regard it as a sign so that they would believe in it. This is a sealing from Him, exalted is He, upon the group whom He decreed would not believe. Malik ibn Dinar recited: ﴿wa-in yuraw﴾ with a dammah on the ya'.

* *

﴿And if they see the path of right guidance, they will not take it as a path; and if they see the path of error, they will take it as a path﴾. God showed them the two paths, and they saw them, and they preferred error over right guidance, as in His saying: ﴿so they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat: 17]. Al-Akhawan (Hamzah and al-Kisa'i) read ﴿al-Rashad﴾, and the rest of the seven read ﴿al-Rushd﴾. From Ibn 'Amir in one narration: following the sheen with the dammah of the ra'. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read ﴿al-Rashad﴾, and these are verbal nouns like al-saqam, al-suqm and al-saqam. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala said: al-Rushd is righteousness in judgment, and with both vowelled with fath it means religion. Ibn Abi 'Ablah read ﴿lā yattakhidhūhā﴾ and ﴿yattakhidhūhā﴾ with feminine agreement with sabil, and sabil is both masculine and feminine. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: This is my way﴾ [Yusuf: 108]. When He denied them belief, which is an act of the heart, He metaphorically made right guidance and error into two paths, and He mentioned that they abandon the path of right guidance and travel the path of error. The placing first of the conditional clause containing the path of right guidance before its counterpart fits, since it comes before it.

﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it﴾: here He mentioned what necessitates belief, which is the signs, and its opposite was made to follow from it; and He followed that with what necessitates right guidance, and its opposite followed from it. Then the clause after them came explicitly stating their taking the path of error and confirming the implied meaning of the conditional clause before it, since abandoning the path of right guidance necessarily entails taking the path of error, for they are either guidance or misguidance; so they are opposites: when one is negated, the other is established.

* *

﴿That is because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them﴾. That is, that turning away from the signs is the cause of their denial of them and their heedlessness of reflecting upon them and contemplating their indication. The meaning: their denial persisted and became their habit, until those signs no longer occurred to their minds, so heedlessness of them and forgetfulness of them arose, until they no longer mentioned them or anything of them. The apparent sense is that the turning away is caused by denial and heedlessness on the part of all of them. It is also possible that the turning away is caused by denial, and the phrase ﴿and they were heedless of them﴾ is a new informative statement from Him, exalted is He, about them, i.e., it is their nature that they were heedless of the signs and of pondering them, so heedlessness led to their denial of them. The apparent sense is that ﴿that﴾ is the subject and its predicate is ﴿because they﴾, i.e., that turning away occurs because they denied. It was permitted that it be in the accusative, and Ibn 'Atiyyah estimated it as "We did that," and al-Zamakhshari estimated it as "God turned them away with that very turning." In His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant in the earth without right﴾ there is an indication that the turning away is caused by this arrogance; and in His saying: ﴿That is because they denied﴾ there is an informing that that turning away is caused by denial. The combination of the two is that arrogance is the first cause from which denial arose, so the turning away is attributed both to the first cause and to what it caused.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 147:

﴿And those who denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter, their deeds have become void. Will they be recompensed except for what they used to do?﴾ He, the Most High, mentioned the outcome of the matter of the deniers in the Hereafter. He stated that He nullifies their deeds, meaning He gives them no regard. The original meaning of ḥabt (nullification, lit. "spoiling") is that what came before it was sound. Here, however, ḥubūṭ is used for cases where their deeds were running along a sound path according to their beliefs, so the nullification applies to them according to their beliefs. For the one who denies the signs may have deeds in which there is kindness to people, forgiveness, and pardon toward one who wronged him, and none of this is rewarded in the Hereafter. Thus the nullification of deeds includes both the one whose deeds are righteous and the one whose deeds are corrupt from the outset. By mentioning "the meeting of the Hereafter," He drew attention to the place of their exposure and their recompense, and as a threat and warning to them, and to the fact that it is certain to occur without doubt. The idafa (genitive construction) of "meeting" (liqāʾ) to "the Hereafter" (al-ākhira) is the idafa of a verbal noun (maṣdar) to its object, meaning "and their meeting the Hereafter." Al-Zamakhshari said: It may also be the idafa of the maṣdar to its object, meaning "and their meeting the Hereafter and their witnessing its conditions," and the idafa of the maṣdar to the adverbial noun (ẓarf), in the sense of "the meeting of what God the Most High promised in the Hereafter," end of quote. The great grammarians permit the idafa to the ẓarf, because the ẓarf is in the sense of "in" (fī), while the idafa, in their view, is only in the sense of "the lām" or the sense of "min," as explained in the science of grammar. If the governing element is given wider scope, it is permissible for it to put the ẓarf in the accusative as an object, and it is then permissible for its verbal noun to be made idafa to that ẓarf with its extended governing element. Some grammarians permitted the idafa to be in the sense of "fī," as the apparent meaning of al-Zamakhshari's words indicates, but this view is rejected in the science of grammar. As for ﴿Will they be recompensed﴾, it is an interrogative in the sense of affirmation (taqrīr), meaning: they deserve punishment because of the evil of their actions. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: The apparent meaning is that it is an interrogative in the sense of negation, and for this reason "except" (illā) has entered. But the interrogative used in the sense of affirmation is affirmative in meaning, so the entry of illā is unlikely, and perhaps it is not permissible.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 148:

﴿And the people of Musa took, after him, from their ornaments a calf, a body with a lowing sound.﴾ (If "taking" (ittikhadh) means taking it as a worshipped god, then attributing it to the people is correct, and it is mentioned that they all worshipped it except Harun. For this reason he said: ﴿My Lord, forgive me and my brother﴾ [al-A'raf: 151].) It has also been said that only some of them worshipped it, not all of them, because of His saying: ﴿And among the people of Musa is a community that guides by the truth﴾ [al-A'raf: 159]. If "taking" means making, as in His saying: ﴿Like the spider, which takes a house﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 41], meaning it made and fashioned it, then the one who made it was only al-Samiri, whose name was Musa ibn Zafar, from a village called Samira. The act was attributed to the people of Musa figuratively, as they say: "The Banu Tamim killed so-and-so," when in fact only one of them killed him, and because they were content with it.

The meaning of ﴿from after him﴾ is: after his departure for the appointed meeting (munajat). The phrase ﴿from their ornaments﴾ is connected to ittakhadha, and the phrase "from after him" is connected to it as well, even though they are two prepositions (harfay jarr) with one form (lafz). This is permitted because their meanings differ: the first min denotes the starting point (ibtida' al-ghaya), and the second denotes partition (tab'id). Abu al-Baqa' permitted that ﴿from their ornaments﴾ be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), so that it is connected to an omitted element, because if it came after it would be a qualifier (sifa), meaning: a calf made of their ornaments.

Al-Akhawan read ﴿min hiliyyihim﴾ with a kasra on the ha', by assimilation to the vowel of the lam (itba'an li-harakat al-lam), as they said: ʿaṣā (a stick, with the vowel of the lam influencing the preceding consonant as in such forms). This is the reading of the companions of ʿAbd Allah, Yahya ibn Wathhab, Talha, and al-A'mash. The rest of the Seven, al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, and Shayba read it with a damma on the ha', and it is the plural of ḥalý (ornament), like thady and thudiyy. Its pattern is fu'ul. A yaʾ and a waw came together, and one of them was preceded by a sukun, so the waw was changed into a yaʾ and assimilated into the yaʾ, and the letter before it was given a kasra so that the yaʾ would be sound.

Ya'qub read ﴿min hulyihim﴾ with a fatha on the ha' and a sukun on the lam. It is a singular noun intended as a generic (yurad bihi al-jins), or a collective noun (ism jins) whose singular is ḥalya, like tamr and tamra. The attribution of the ornaments to them is either because they possessed them from what was on the people of Pharaoh when they drowned and the sea cast them up, so it was like war spoils (ghanima), and for this reason Harun was ordered to gather it until Musa returned and gave his judgment about it. Or they possessed it, since it was from their wealth which the Copts had seized through the poll tax (jizya) that they had imposed on them, so the Children of Israel devised a way to retrieve it from them by way of borrowing (ʿariya). Or they did not possess it, but their hands had disposed of it by way of borrowing, and the attribution to them is valid because such attribution may be made on the basis of the slightest connection.

Yahya ibn Sallam transmitted from al-Hasan that they borrowed the ornaments from the Copts for a wedding. It has been said: for a day of adornment. When Pharaoh and his people perished, the ornaments remained with them, and they were forbidden to them, so the Children of Israel began to sell it and destroy it. Then al-Samiri said to Harun: "It is a loan and it is not ours." Harun then commanded a crier to call for the return of the loan, so that Musa could give his opinion about it when he came. They gathered it, and Harun deposited it with al-Samiri, who was a goldsmith, and he fashioned for them the image of a calf from the ornaments. It has also been said that what prevented them from returning the loan was their fear that the Copts would discover their nocturnal departure (suran), since God had commanded Musa to travel by night with them.

The calf (al-ʿijl) is the young of a cow, recently born. The meaning of jasadan is a lifeless body (juththa jamad). It has been said: a body without a head, of solid gold (dhahaban musmatan). It has been said: he made it hollow. Al-Zamakhshari said: jasadan means a body with flesh and blood like other bodies. Al-Hasan said: al-Samiri took a handful of dust from the hoofprint of Jibril, peace be upon him, on the day the sea was split, and threw it into the mouth of the calf, so it became a calf that had a lowing sound. End of quotation. This is weak, I mean the claim that it was flesh and blood, because reports have come that Musa burned it with files (bardahu bi-al-mabarid) and cast it into the sea, and flesh is not burned with files, rather it would be killed and cut up. Ibn al-Anbari said: the mention of "jasad" indicates that there was no spirit in it. The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿it has a lowing sound﴾ indicates that there was a spirit in it, since only that which has a spirit lows. It has been said: when he made it hollow, he contrived its sound by placing pipes inside its hollow in a particular shape and placing it in the path of the winds, so the wind entered those pipes and a sound resembling lowing appeared. It has been said: he placed beneath it someone who blew into it from a place that it was not noticed, so a sound from its inside was heard like lowing. Al-Kirmani said: he placed in the belly of the calf a chamber that opened and closed, and when he wanted it to low, he sent in a boy who lowed, with a signal between them when he wanted it. It has been said: it is possible that God made it low in order to test the Children of Israel. Its lowing is said to have been once only and not repeated, transmitted by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas. It has been said: it lowed several times, and when it lowed they prostrated, and when it fell silent they raised their heads. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and most of the exegetes.

ʿAli, Abu al-Sammal, and a group read (ju'ar) with a jim and a hamza, from ja'ara, meaning to cry out with intense voice. The word jasadan is in the accusative. Al-Zamakhshari said it is in apposition (badal). Al-Hawfi said it is a qualifier (naʿt). Abu al-Baqa' permitted both, and also that it be an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan). He only said "jasadan" because it is possible for it to be made as a drawing or inscribed on a wall or a stone or other than that, like pictures rendered by drawing, writing, painting, and carving. So God clarified that it had a body.

* *

﴿Did they not see that it does not speak to them, nor guide them to a way?﴾ If the meaning of ittakhadha is "made and fashioned," then there must be an omitted element on which this rebuke is based, which is: so they worshipped it and made it a god for themselves. If the omitted element is "a god," meaning: they took ﴿a calf, a body with a lowing sound﴾ as a god, then there is no need to omit a clause. This is a rhetorical question of denunciation (istifham inkar), in that they worshipped an inanimate object or a helpless animal, bearing the marks of craftsmanship, that cannot speak or guide. Reason has established that whoever is in this condition cannot be a god. This is a kind of rhetorical eloquence called the rational argument (al-ihtijaj al-nazari), and some call it the theological method (al-madhhab al-kalami). The apparent meaning of "yarawa" is "they knew." God negated these two attributes from it without the rest of the attributes of divinity, because the absence of power and the absence of these two attributes, which are knowledge and power, entail the rest of the attributes. For this reason these two attributes were singled out for negation.

﴿They took it, and they were wrongdoers﴾, meaning: they proceeded to do what they did of this abominable matter, and they were placing a thing in other than its proper place. That is, wrongdoing is their characteristic, so they were not the first to place a thing in other than its proper place, and worshipping the calf was not the first of the evil deeds they introduced. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it is possible that the waw is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), meaning in "wa-kanu" (and they were). The first possibility is more eloquent in reproach, namely the report that describing them as wrongdoers is their habit, so their wrongdoing is not restricted to this shameful act.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 149:

﴿And when they regretted and saw that they had gone astray, they said: If our Lord does not have mercy on us and forgive us, we will surely be among the losers.﴾ Some grammarians mentioned that the Arabs' saying *suqita fi yadihi* (سُقِطَ في يَدِهِ, "he was struck with regret" or "he was left helpless") is a verb that does not inflect (*la yatasarraf*), so no present tense (*mudari'*), active participle (*ism fa'il*), or passive participle (*maf'ul*) is formed from it. Its original form, however, was inflected: one says *saqata al-shay'*, meaning "the thing fell from a height." So in origin it is an inflected intransitive verb (*mutasarrif lazim*). Al-Jurjani said: *suqita fi yadihi* is one of the expressions whose usage has fallen out of use, just as the usage of the Almighty's saying has fallen out of use: ﴿So We struck upon their ears﴾ [al-Kahf: 11].

Ibn Atiyya said: "There is weakness in this statement. In the speech of the Arabs, *al-siqat* (السِّقاط) means much error and regret over it." From this is the saying of Ibn Abi Kahil:

*"How can they hope for my downfall after gray hair has spotted my head and baldness has come?"*

It is related from Abu Marwan ibn Siraj, one of the imams of language in al-Andalus, that he used to say: "The Arabs' saying *suqita fi yadihi* — its meaning has baffled me."

Abu Ubayda said: it is said of one who regretted a matter and was unable to deal with it: *suqita fi yadihi*. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that regret fell into their hands, that is, into their hearts and souls, just as one says: "a calamity occurred in their hands," although it is impossible for it to be in the hand, by way of likening what occurs in the heart and soul to what occurs in the hand and is seen with the eye.

Ibn Atiyya said: The Arabs say of one who was striving toward a direction or seeking a goal, and then something came to him that turned him from his direction and brought him to a position of helplessness, and he became certain that he was powerless: *suqita fi yadi fulan* ("it fell into the hand of so-and-so"). Regret may or may not accompany it. He said: The link that connects these expressions to the meaning we mentioned is that the striving, or the effort, or the defense, has fallen into the hand of the one referred to, so it remains in his hand and does not go beyond it, and it has no effect outside.

Al-Zamakhshari said: When their regret and grief over the worship of the calf intensified, since it is the way of one whose regret and grief intensify to bite his hand in distress, his hand becomes one into which (something) has fallen, because his mouth has come to rest upon it. *Suqita* is predicated of ﴿in their hands﴾, and this is of the category of metonymy (*kinaya*), end of quote. The correct reading is: *suqita* is predicated of *ma* ("what"): *fi aydihim* ("in their hands").

Al-Wahidi reported from some of them that it is derived from *al-saqit* (السَّقِيط), which is what covers the earth in the early morning, resembling snow. It is said of it: *suqitat al-ard* ("the earth was covered"), just as it is said: *thullijat al-ard wa thullijna*, meaning "snow fell upon the earth and upon us." The meaning of *suqita fi yadihi* and *al-saqit* and *al-suqt* is that it melts with the slightest heat and does not remain. One upon whom *al-saqit* fell in his hand gains nothing from it, so it became a proverb for everyone who lost in his outcome and did not obtain anything of his aim, and whose final state was regret. It was also said: it is the habit of one who regrets to lower his head and place his chin on his hand, leaning upon it, and to be in a posture such that, if his hand were removed, he would fall on his face. So the hand is the thing into which he has fallen. The meaning of *fi* here is *ala* ("upon"), that is, he fell upon his hand. And the meaning of *fi aydihim* is *ala aydihim* ("upon their hands"), like His saying: ﴿And I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees﴾ [Ta-Ha: 71], end of quote.

The complement of *suqita* is the phrase ﴿in their hands﴾, because the hand is the instrument by which one takes hold and controls. *Suqita* is in the passive voice, and what has been placed in the position of the subject is the prepositional phrase, just as you say: *julisa fi al-dar* ("he was seated in the house") and *duhika min Zayd* ("Zayd was laughed at"). It was also said: *suqita* implies an object, which here is the verbal noun that is *al-isqat* (the causing to fall), just as one says: *dhuhiba bi Zayd* ("Zayd was taken away"), end of quote. The correct view is that the object here is the pronoun of the verbal noun that is *al-suqut* (the falling), because the verbal noun of *suqita* is not *al-isqat*, and the verbal noun itself is not the unnamed object (*maf'ul lam yusamma fa'iluh*), but rather its pronoun.

A group of readers, including Ibn al-Sumayqa, read *saqata fi aydihim* in the active voice. Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, the biting (of the hand) fell into them. Al-Zajjaj said: the regret fell into their hands. Ibn Atiyya said: It is possible that loss and disappointment fell into their hands. Ibn Abi Ablah read *usqita fi aydihim*, in the quadriliteral form in the passive voice.

*Wa ra'aw* means "they knew": ﴿that they had gone astray﴾. Al-Qadi said: The latter element must be placed first, because regret and grief occur only after recognition. It is as if He, Exalted, said: "When they saw that they had gone astray and were struck with regret, because of the great grief that befell them." End of quote. This wording is not needed, for it is possible for regret to precede the clarification of error, because when a person doubts the deed he has undertaken, whether it is right or wrong, regret arises in him, and afterward his reflection and thinking are completed, and he knows that it was an error.

﴿They said: If our Lord does not have mercy on us﴾: this is a turning toward God, Exalted, and an acknowledgment of the enormity of what they had done. Similarly Adam and Eve said: ﴿And if You do not forgive us and have mercy on us﴾ [al-A'raf: 23]. Since this sin, which is taking a god other than God, is the greatest of sins, they began with mercy, which encompasses everything, and from which forgiveness of sin follows. As for the story of Adam, there was a dialogue between him and God, Exalted, and rebuke for what they had done, the eating of the tree's fruit after He had forbidden them to approach it, let alone eat its fruit. So they hastened to seek forgiveness and followed it with mercy, since the forgiveness of what the rebuke was directed at confirmed what was requested first.

Al-Akhawan (Hamza and al-Kisa'i), al-Sha'bi, Ibn Wathhab, al-Jahdari, Ibn Musarrif, al-A'mash and Ayyub read *tarhamna* and *taghfir* in the second person, with the vocative *rabbana* (O our Lord). The rest of the seven readers, Mujahid, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, Shayba ibn Nassah and others read ﴿yarhamna Rabbuna wa yaghfir lana﴾ with *ya* in both and *Rabbuna* in the nominative case.

In the codex of Ubayy: *qalu Rabbana la-in tarhamna wa taghfir lana*, with the vocative placed first, which is *Rabbana*.

It is possible that both statements came from all of them in succession, or that one came from one group and the other from another group. Whoever was overcome by fear and was strong enough to address (God) directly addressed Him, seeking to be relieved of his great sin. Whoever was overcome by shame expressed his words in the manner of one who is too shy to address directly, and so he attributed the verb to the third person (absent). In their saying *Rabbuna* there is a fine appeal for compassion, since the Lord (*al-Rabb*) is the Owner, the one who watches over the affairs of His servants and sets right among them what has become corrupt.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 150:**

﴿When Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved, he said: "Evil is what you have done in my absence after me. Did you hasten ahead of your Lord's command?"﴾ That is, he returned from the intimate conversation with his Lord. It is related that when he drew near the encampment of the Children of Israel, he heard their voices and said: "These are the voices of people at play." When he became certain of their devotion to the worship of the calf, anger and grief overcame him and he threw down the Tablets. Al-Tabari said: God, exalted is He, informed him before his return that they had been tested with the calf, and for this reason he returned angry. This view is supported by His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have tested your people after you, and al-Samiri has led them astray﴾ [Ta-Ha: 85], and the verse continues.

*Ghadban* (angry) is an intensive form (*sifat al-mubalagha*). Anger (*al-ghadab*) is the boiling of the heart due to the occurrence of something painful. It is mentioned that he (peace be upon him) was among the quickest of people to anger, yet he was quick to calm down. Ibn al-Qasim said: I heard Malik say: "When he became angry, smoke rose from his cap, and the hair of his body raised his robe."

*Asifan*: from *asifa*, so he is *asif*, as one says *fariqa*, so he is *fariq*, indicating the permanence of the attribute. Had it been taken in the sense of a temporary state, it would have been on the pattern *fa'il*, and one would say *a'sif*. *Al-Asif* means the sorrowful. This is the statement of Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Suddi. Or it means the distressed (*al-jaza'*), as Mujahid said. Or the one filled with longing (*al-mutalahhif*), or the one of intense anger (*al-shadid al-ghadab*), as al-Zamakhshari said. Ibn Atiyya said: most often it means the sorrowful or the angered, as Ibn Qutayba said. Or the regretful, as al-Qutabi also said. Or they are close in meaning, as al-Wahidi said. He said: When something you dislike comes to you from one below you, you become angry; if from one above you, you become sorrowful. So their worship of the calf angered him, and God's trial of them grieved him. He had informed him of this by His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have tested your people after you﴾ [Ta-Ha: 85].

The discussion of *bi'sama* has preceded at the beginning of al-Baqara (p-395). The address is either to al-Samiri and the worshippers of the calf, meaning: evil is what you did in my stead, when you worshipped the calf instead of the worship of God, exalted is He. Or it is addressed to the notables of the Children of Israel: Harun and the believers, in that they did not restrain those who worshipped other than God.

*Khalaftumuni* indicates posteriority in time. The meaning here is: after what you saw from me of the oneness of God, His negation of partners from Him, and the sincere worship of Him. Or: after I used to lead the Children of Israel to monotheism and restrain them from what their eyes longed for, the worship of cows. It is incumbent upon a successor (*khalaf*) to follow the course of the one he succeeds and not oppose him. It is said: *khalafahu* with good or evil, when he does an action in the absence of the one who came before him.

*A'ajiltum* is a question of denunciation (*istifham inkar*). Al-Zamakhshari said: It is said: *'ajila 'an al-amr* when one leaves it incomplete; its opposite is *tamma 'alayhi*. And *a'jalahu 'anhu* (someone else caused him to leave it). It is implied in a meaning previously mentioned, so it takes the same transitive construction, as one says: *'ajiltu al-amr*. The meaning is: you hastened away from your Lord's command, which was waiting for Musa while keeping his covenant and what he had enjoined upon you. So you formed the judgment that the appointed time had reached its end, and I had not returned to you. You spoke to yourselves about my death and changed, as the nations changed after their prophets. It is related that al-Samiri said to them when he brought out the calf to them: "This is your god and the god of Musa; Musa will not return, and he has died." End of quotation.

Ibn Atiyya said: its meaning is: did you outrun the decree of your Lord and hasten my coming before the time He had appointed? End of quotation.

Ya'qub said: It is said: *'ajiltu al-shay'* (I preceded the thing), and *a'jiltu al-rajul* (I made the man hasten), meaning I drove him to haste. End of quotation.

It is also said: its meaning is: did you hasten the appointment of your Lord of forty nights? It is said: did you hasten the wrath of your Lord? It is said: did you hasten with the worship of the calf? It is said: haste (*al-'ajala*) is advancing with a thing before its time, and it is said that it is blameworthy. This is weakened by His saying: ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased﴾ [Ta-Ha: 84]. Haste-speed (*al-sur'a*) is hurrying toward a thing before its time, and that is praiseworthy.

\* \*

﴿And he threw down the Tablets and seized his brother by the head, drawing him toward himself﴾. That is: the Tablets, the Torah, and he had been carrying them. He placed them on the ground in anger at what his people had done by worshipping the calf, and out of zeal for the religion of God. As has preceded, he was very quick to anger. They said: Harun was gentler in character than him, and for this reason he was more beloved to the Children of Israel than he was. It is also said: he threw them in bewilderment because of the calamity that overwhelmed him concerning their affair.

From Ibn Abbas: when Musa (peace be upon him) threw them, they broke. Most of them were lifted up, the part in which was the detailed explanation of everything, and what remained in his copy was guidance and mercy, and that is what he took afterward. It is related that six-sevenths of them were lifted and one-seventh remained. This was said by a group of exegetes. Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi said: It is not authentic that he hurled them with a breaking throw. End of quotation.

The apparent meaning is that he threw them from his two hands, because his two hands were occupied with them, and he wanted to seize his brother and drag him. That cannot be achieved except by freeing his hands to drag him. In His saying: ﴿When the anger subsided from Musa, he took up the Tablets﴾ [al-A'raf: 154] there is evidence that they were not broken, and evidence that nothing was lifted from them.

The apparent meaning is that he seized his head, that is, he held his head and dragged him toward himself. It is said: by the hair of his head. It is said: by its locks and beard. It is said: by his beard. It is said: by his ear. It is said: he did not take hold literally; it was only a gesture. Harun feared that the observer of the two of them would suppose it was out of anger, so he forbade him and begged him.

The apparent meaning is that the cause of this seizing was his anger at his brother. And how could they worship the calf when he had appointed him as his successor over them, commanded him to reform, and not to follow the way of those who corrupt? And how did he not rebuke them and restrain them from that? This apparent meaning is supported by His saying: ﴿When the anger subsided from Musa﴾ [al-A'raf: 154], and His saying: ﴿Do not seize my beard nor my head. Indeed, I feared that you would say: "You have caused division among the Children of Israel and did not observe my word"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 94].

Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, by the hair of his head, dragging him toward himself by his locks. This was because of the severity of the matter that befell him, which startled him and took away his clear judgment, and because he suspected his brother had been negligent in restraining them. It is also said: that seizing and dragging was so that he could tell him privately that the Tablets had been revealed to him in his conversation with God, and he wanted to conceal them from the Children of Israel. So Harun forbade him, lest his secret become apparent to the Children of Israel through his humiliation. It is also said: he drew him close in order to learn what was with him, and Harun disliked this lest they think he was being humiliated. His brother made clear to him that they had made him weak. It is also said: that was done in the manner of honor, not in the manner of insult, as the Arabs do by seizing a man's brother's beard.

\* \*

(p-396) ﴿He said: "Son of my mother! Indeed, the people have made me weak and nearly killed me. So do not let the enemies gloat over me, and do not place me among the wrongdoing people."﴾ He called him with a call of pleading for gentleness and tenderness. He was his full brother. It is the custom of the Arabs to be gentle and tender by mentioning the mother, as one of them said:

*"O son of my mother, and O full brother of my soul."*

Another said: *"O son of my mother, may my soul and my wealth be your ransom."*

Also, their mother was a believer. They said: their father was cut off from kinship by unbelief, as God said to Nuh (peace be upon him): ﴿Indeed, he is not of your family﴾ [Hud: 46]. Also, since her right was greater, because of her hardships in bearing him, raising him, and her compassion for him, he reminded him of her right.

The two Harams (Mecca and Medina), Abu Amr, and Hafs read *Ibn Umma* with a fatha on the mim. The Kufans said: its origin is *ya ibn umma'ah*, so the alif was dropped for lightness, as it was dropped in *ya ghulam*, whose origin is *ya ghulaman*, and the silent *ha'* (*ha' al-sakt*) was dropped because it is a continuous reading (*daraj*). On this view, the noun is inflected, since the alif is converted from the ya of the first person; so it is in apposition (*mudaf ilayhi*) with *ibn*. Sibawayh said: they are two nouns built on fatha like one noun, like *khamsata 'ashar* and the like. So according to his view, it is not a genitive construction with *ibn*, and the vowel is a built vowel.

The rest of the seven read with a kasra on the mim. The analogy of the Kufans' view is that it is inflected, and the ya of the first person was dropped and the kasra was used in place of it, just as they used the fatha in place of the alif converted from the ya of the first person. Sibawayh said: it is built, and it is annexed to the ya of the first person, as they said: *ya ahada 'ashar aqbilu* (O eleven, come forward). The ya was dropped and they used the kasra in place of it, as they used it in *ya qawmi*. If the two words had remained in annexation, it would not be permissible to drop the ya, because the noun is not the vocative but the genitive of the vocative. So it is not permissible to drop the ya from it.

It was also read with the ya of annexation retained. The best of the dialects is using the kasra in place of the ya of annexation, then converting the ya to alif and making the kasra before it a fatha, then dropping the ta' and making the mim a fatha, then retaining the ta' with fatha or with sukun. These dialects are permissible in *ibnat ummi* and in *ibn 'ammi* and *ibnat 'ammi*.

It was also read *ya ibn ummi* with the ya retained, and *ibn imm* with a kasra on the alif and the mim.

The object of the verb of saying is the vocative, and the sentence after it is intended to alleviate what Musa had felt of anger, and to excuse him by saying that he had not fallen short in restraining them through admonition and warning, and what his capacity could achieve. But they made him weak, so they did not heed his admonition, and they nearly killed him. This shows that he had exaggerated in denouncing them until they resolved to kill him.

The meaning of *istad'afuni* (they made me weak) is that they found me, so it is equivalent to finding a thing in the sense of what is derived from it, that is, they considered me weak. This was mentioned in His saying: ﴿To those who were made weak﴾ [al-A'raf: 75].

When he disclosed to him what they had done in making him weak and nearly killing him, he asked him to leave aside what would please them by his action, and said: ﴿So do not let the enemies gloat over me﴾. That is: do not make them rejoice over what you do to me, so that I become blameworthy in their eyes and in yours. A poet said:

*"And death is preferable to the gloating of enemies."*

Ibn Muhaysin read *tushmit* with a fatha on the ta' and a kasra on the mim, with *al-a'da'a* in the accusative. Mujahid read likewise, except that he made the mim a fatha. *Shammata* is transitive like *ashmata*. Abu al-Fath explained Mujahid's reading as intransitive, meaning: "So do not gloat, you, O Lord." This is permissible, as in His saying: ﴿God mocks them﴾ [al-Baqara: 15] and similar. Then he returned to the intended meaning and supplied a verb which governs *al-a'da'* in the accusative, like the reading of the majority. End of quotation.

This is a departure from the apparent meaning and an artificial construction in grammar. It has been related that *shammata* is transitive as a dialect, so there is no need to strain that it is intransitive together with the accusative *al-a'da'*. Also, His saying: ﴿God mocks them﴾ [al-Baqara: 15] is only in the manner of reciprocation for their saying: ﴿We are only mockers﴾ [al-Baqara: 14], so He said: ﴿God mocks them﴾ [al-Baqara: 15]. Similar is His saying: ﴿They plot, and God plots﴾ [al-Anfal: 30]. Such a construction is not permissible initially without reciprocation.

From Mujahid: *fa-la tashmat* with a fatha on the ta' and the mim, and *al-a'da'u* in the nominative. From Humayd ibn Qays likewise, except that he read the mim with a kasra, taking it as an intransitive verb, so *al-a'da'u* is its subject. Its apparent meaning is that he forbade the enemies from gloating over him. This is of the type of *la ara'annaka huna*. The intended meaning is his forbidding of his brother: that is, do not bring upon me something disliked so that they gloat over me.

He began first by asking his brother not to let the enemies gloat over him, because what causes gloating is an apparent disliked action that is visible to them, so they gloat over it. He began with the more emphatic matter. Then he asked him not to make him, or consider him, one of the wrongdoers, since making him with them and believing him to be one of them is an inward act, not apparent to the Children of Israel. Or the meaning is: do not make me, in your displeasure with me, a companion of theirs and associated with them.

"My Lord, forgive me and my brother, and admit us into Your mercy, and You are the most merciful of the merciful." When his brother had apologized to him, he asked forgiveness for himself and for him. They said: his asking forgiveness for himself was because of his act with his brother and his hastiness in throwing down the tablets, and his asking forgiveness for his brother was for his brother's act in being patient with the Children of Israel. They said: it is possible that the forgiveness sought is for something he does not know, and Allah knows best. Al-Zamakhshari said: when his brother apologized to him and mentioned the gloating of the enemies, "He said: My Lord, forgive me and my brother," so as to satisfy his brother and to show to the people who gloat his pleasure with him, so that their gloating would not be complete. He asked forgiveness for himself for what had proceeded from him toward his brother, and for his brother for what perhaps his brother had neglected during the time of the caliphate. He asked that they not be separated from His mercy, and that it continue to encompass them both in this world and the Hereafter. End of quote. As for his statement, "and for his brother, perhaps he neglected during the time of the caliphate": if "an" is with a fatha on the hamza, then it is the light form of the heavy one (an-mukhaffafah), and its meaning is close to this. If it is with a kasra on the hamza, then it is conditional, and it is not valid in that case for it to enter upon "asa" (perhaps), because conditional particles do not enter upon a rigid verb.

"Indeed, those who took the calf will be overtaken by wrath from their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world. Thus do We recompense the fabricators." The apparent meaning is that this is from the speech of Allah the Exalted, informing about what will befall the worshippers of the calf, and addressing Moses regarding what will befall them. It was said: it is from the remainder of Moses' speech up to His words, "And he said: You only took..." (Al-Ankabut 25), and Allah confirmed it with His words, "Thus do We recompense the fabricators." The first is apparent because of His words, "Thus do We recompense the fabricators," in a single sequence with the speech before it, and the meaning is that they took it as a god, based on His words, "So He brought out for them a calf, a body that lowed, and they said: This is your god and the god of Moses" (Ta-Ha 88). It was said: the wrath is in the Hereafter and the humiliation is in this world, and they are a group of the Jews who were made to drink in the love of the calf and did not repent. It was said: they are those among them who died before Moses returned from the appointed time. Abu al-Aliyah, and al-Zamakhshari following him, said: it is what they were commanded regarding killing themselves. Al-Zamakhshari said: the humiliation is their going out from their homes, because the humiliation of exile is a struck proverb, end of quote. It would be better to say: the continuation of their being cut off from their homes, because their departure had preceded the worship of the calf. Ata al-Awfi said: it refers to the killing of the Banu Qurayzah and the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir, because they sided with the worshippers of the calf. It was said: it is what befell their descendants in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of captivity, expulsion, the poll-tax and other things. Al-Zamakhshari combined these two sayings, saying: it is what befell their sons, namely the Banu Qurayzah and al-Nadir, of the wrath of Allah the Exalted by killing and expulsion, and of the humiliation by imposing the poll-tax, end of quote. The apparent view is that His words, "in the life of this world," are connected to "will befall them."
