Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 154:

﴿And when the anger subsided from Moses, he took up the tablets, and in their inscription was guidance and mercy for those who fear their Lord.﴾ The subsiding of his anger was - and Allah knows best - due to the excuse offered by his brother, and to the fact that he (Aaron) had not fallen short in forbidding the Children of Israel from worshipping the calf, and to Allah's promise to him to take vengeance upon them. The "subsiding" of anger (sukut al-ghadab) is a metaphor (isti'arah): it likens the quieting of anger to the cessation of speech by a speaker, which is his silence. Yunus ibn Habib said: the Arabs say, "The valley flowed, then fell silent" (sala al-wadi thumma sakata). Al-Zajjaj said: the verbal noun (masdar) of "sakata al-ghadab" is "sakana" (calmed), and the verbal noun of "sakata al-rajul" is "sukut"; this implies that it is a verb in its ordinary sense, and not from the silence of people. It has also been said that it is an instance of inversion (al-qalb), meaning: "when Moses fell silent from the anger," like: "I inserted the stone into myself" and "I put the cap onto my head." (End of quotation.) This should not be accepted, because inversion is not a general rule; it occurs only in a few expressions, and the correct view is that it is not applied analogically. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is a figure of speech (mathal). It is as if anger was urging him to do what he did and saying to him: "Say to your people such-and-such, throw down the tablets, and take your brother by the head towards you." He refrained from speaking thus and abandoned the incitement. Every person of sound nature and correct taste has found this expression admirable and eloquent only for this reason, and because it belongs to the branches of eloquence. Otherwise, what is the reading of Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah, "wa lamma sakana 'an Musa al-ghadab" (and when the anger calmed down from Moses), that the soul finds in it none of that stirring nor any trace of that awe? It was also read: "uskita" (in the fourth form, passive), and so it is in the codex of Hafsah; the implied agent is Allah, or his brother through his apology or self-exoneration to him; that is, Allah or Aaron silenced it. In the codex of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) it reads: "wa lamma sabara" (and when he was patient), and in the codex of Ubayy it reads: "wa lamma inshaqqa" (and when it split). The meaning is: when his anger was extinguished, he took up the tablets of the Torah which he had thrown from his hand. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas that he threw them and they broke, so he fasted forty days, and they were returned to him in two tablets without his losing any part of them. "In their inscription" means: in what was copied from the broken tablets, or in what was inscribed on them, or in what remained of them after the lifted part, which was a seventh of them. The more apparent meaning is: in what was transcribed from them and transferred from them. The lam in "li-rabbihim" is for reinforcement, so that the verb reaches its previously mentioned object. The Kufans said it is redundant (za'idah). Al-Akhfash said it is the lam of purpose (lam al-maf'ul lahu), meaning: "for the sake of their Lord, they fear," not for show or reputation. Al-Mubarrad said it is connected to a verbal noun, the meaning being: "those whose dread is for their Lord." This does not hold according to the method of the Basrans, because it involves deleting the verbal noun while retaining its complement, which they consider permissible only in poetry; moreover, this reckoning takes the speech out of eloquence.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 155:**

﴿And Musa chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time.﴾ (اخْتارَ) is on the pattern افْتَعَلَ (ifta'ala), from الخَيْرِ (al-khayr, "the good"), and means choosing and selecting. Among the verbs that take two objects, one directly and the other through a preposition, are those that are restricted to what is transmitted: اخْتارَ, واسْتَغْفَرَ, وأمَرَ, وكَنّى, ودَعا, وزَوَّجَ, وصَدَقَ. The preposition may then be dropped and the verb takes the object directly, so one says: اخْتَرْتُ زَيْدًا مِنَ الرِّجالِ (I chose Zayd from among the men) and اخْتَرْتُ زَيْدًا الرِّجالَ. The poet said:

*"I chose you from among the people when their characters had decayed, and the one who was hoped for had become weak in his resolve."*

That is, اخْتَرْتُكَ مِنَ النّاسِ (I chose you from among the people). (p-399) سَبْعِينَ (seventy) is the first object and قَوْمَهُ (his people) is the second object, with the implied meaning مِن قَوْمِهِ (from among his people). Whoever parses قَوْمَهُ as the first object and سَبْعِينَ as a badal (apposition, here a partitive apposition of part to whole) from it, with the pronoun omitted, meaning سَبْعِينَ رَجُلًا مِنهُمُ (seventy men from among them), must posit a second object, namely the one chosen from, and so this i'rab (grammatical analysis) is remote and involves an artificial deletion both in the linking pronoun of the apposition and in the object from which the choice is made.

They differed about this appointed time: was it the appointed time for the private conversation and the descent of the Torah, or something else? Nawf al-Bikali said, and it was related by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and this is the first view, in which he explained some of what happened in his circumstances: that he chose six men from each tribe, and they came to seventy-two. He said, "Let two remain behind, for I was only commanded with seventy," and they disputed over it. He said, "Whoever remains behind will have the reward of whoever attends." Kaleb ibn Yuqna and Yusha' ibn Nun remained behind. He took the seventy with him after commanding them to fast, purify themselves, and purify their garments. Then he went out with them to Mount Sinai (Tur Sina') for the appointed time of his Lord. His Lord had commanded him to come to Him with seventy of the Children of Israel. When Musa approached the mountain, the pillar of cloud descended upon it until it covered the whole mountain, and Musa drew near and entered it. He said to the people, "Come forward," and they came forward, until when they entered the cloud they fell down in prostration. They heard Him speaking to Musa, commanding and forbidding him: "Do this and do not do that." Then the cloud cleared, and they came toward Him and asked to see God. He admonished them, rebuked them, and denounced them. They said: ﴿O Musa, we will not believe you until we see God openly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 55].

Al-Zamakhshari said: He said, ﴿My Lord, show me Yourself, that I may look upon You﴾ [al-A'raf: 143], intending that they should hear the refusal and denial from His side. He was answered, ﴿You will not see Me﴾, and the mountain shook with them and they were struck down. End of quotation. It was also said that this was a different appointed time from the appointed time of the private conversation and the descent of the Torah. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: The Children of Israel said to Musa, "A group among us claims that God does not speak to you. So take with you some of us who will go with you so that they may hear His speech and believe." God revealed to him that he should choose from his people seventy of their best, then ascend the mountain with them, you and Harun, and appoint Yusha' as your successor. He did so. When they heard His speech, they asked Musa to let them see God openly, and the quake seized them. Al-Suddi said: It was an appointed time that God set for Musa, to meet with some people of the Children of Israel so that they might make excuses to Him for worshipping the calf. Ibn 'Abbas, as related from him by 'Ali ibn Talhah, said: It was an appointed time that God set for Musa, and He commanded him to choose from his people seventy men to supplicate their Lord, and they supplicated, saying, "O God, give us what You have not given anyone before us or after us." God disliked that, and the quake seized them. It was related from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, as narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah, that Musa, Harun, and his two sons Shabbar and Shubayr set out until they reached a mountain in which there was a couch. Harun stood on it and his soul was taken. Musa returned to his people, and they said: "You killed him and envied us for his character and gentleness." He said, "How could I kill him when his two sons are with me?" He said: "Choose whomever you wish." So seventy were chosen, and they came to where Harun was and said: "Who killed you, O Harun?" He said: "No one killed me, but God took me in death." They said: "O Musa, we will not disobey you any longer," and the quake seized them, and they began to fall over right and left. End of quotation.

The wording لِمِيقاتِنا (for Our appointed time) in this report attributed to 'Ali indicates that it was at a time set by God, Exalted, and Ibn al-Sa'ib said: Musa would not come to his Lord except by His permission. What appears to be the case is that this appointed time is different from the appointed time of Musa mentioned in ﴿And when Musa came at Our appointed time and his Lord spoke to him﴾ [al-A'raf: 143], because the two stories are plainly different and what happened in them differs: in that one, God spoke to Musa and he asked to see Him, and God referred him to His manifestation to the mountain; the mountain did not stand firm and became dust, and Musa fainted. In this one, the seventy were chosen for God's appointed time, the quake seized them, and it did not seize Musa. Moreover, there is a great gap between the parts of the narrative, were it one story.

* *

﴿So when the quake seized them, he said: My Lord, had You willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me as well.﴾ The cause of the quake is disputed, and it is connected with the interpretation of the appointed time. Was the quake a punishment for their silence and their overlooking the worship of the calf? Or a punishment for their asking to see God? Or a punishment for their excessiveness in the aforementioned supplication? Or was its cause the hearing of Harun's speech while he was dead? These are the views. Al-Suddi said: It was a punishment for the worship of the calf by these seventy, (p-400) by their choosing the calf, and this was hidden from Musa at the time of the choosing until God informed him. As for the seizure by the quake, it may have resulted in death, or it may have resulted in a swoon; both are views. Al-Suddi also said: Musa said, "How shall I return to the Children of Israel when their best have been destroyed? What shall I say? And how will they trust me with anyone?" So God restored them to life. It was also said that the trembling seized them until it nearly separated their joints and broke their backs, and Musa feared death; at that point he wept and supplicated, and it was lifted from them. Al-Zamakhshari said: This is a wish on his part for their destruction before he saw what he saw of the consequence of asking to see God, as a regretful person says when he sees the bad outcome of a matter: "If God had willed, He would have destroyed me before this." End of quotation. So the meaning of his words ﴿before﴾ is before the request to see God. This is an interpretation by al-Zamakhshari based on the premise that this appointed time is the appointed time of private conversation and of asking to see God, and we have mentioned that the more evident view is otherwise. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: When Musa saw that, he grieved over them and knew that the affair of the Children of Israel would be split apart if he did not bring the people back. So he began to plead with his Lord: "My Lord, had You willed, You would have destroyed them before this condition, and me as well, and that would have been lighter for me, for this time of their destruction brings corruption upon me and harm to me." End of quotation. The object of شِئْتَ (You willed) is elided, its implied meaning being: "had You willed our destruction." The response of لَوْ (had) is أهْلَكْتَهم (You would have destroyed them), and it came without the lam (لام, the lam of response). This is eloquent, but with the lam it is more common, as in ﴿Had You willed, You would have taken for it a fee﴾ [al-Kahf: 77], and ﴿Had your Lord willed, He would have made them all believe﴾ [Yunus: 99]. Apart from this instance, no occurrence without the lam is preserved in the Qur'an, nor in His saying ﴿If We willed, We would have struck them﴾ [al-A'raf: 100], and ﴿If We willed, We would have made it bitter﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 70]. The element elided in مِن قَبْلُ (before) is: before the choosing and the seizure of the quake, that is, at the time of their overlooking the worship of the calf, or of their own worship of it. His saying وإيّايَ (and me as well) means: at the time of my killing of the Coptic man. "You covered and forgave then, so how is it now, when my returning without them is corruption for the Children of Israel?" Ibn 'Atiyyah said most of this. He conjoined وإيّايَ (and me) to the pronoun in أهْلَكْتَهم (You would have destroyed them), and conjoining a pronoun requires separating it, which is why he began with their pronoun; the reason is that they are the ones the quake seized, who died or were struck senseless. He was neither killed nor struck senseless, and he did not stop at saying ﴿You would have destroyed them before﴾ until he included himself with them, though he did not share with them in the consequence of destruction, out of submission to God's will and power, and that had God willed to destroy the disobedient and the obedient, no barrier would have prevented Him.

﴿Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?﴾ It was said: This is an interrogative in the manner of presenting an argument in the form of a plea and humble entreaty. The pronoun in أتُهْلِكُنا (will You destroy us) refers to him and the seventy. As for بِما فَعَلَ السُّفَهاءُ (for what the foolish did), there is disagreement about it, depending on the cause of the seizure by the quake: the request to see God, or the worship of the calf, or their saying "You killed Harun," or their excessiveness in supplication, or their own worship of the calf. It was also said: the pronoun in أتُهْلِكُنا refers to him and to the Children of Israel, and بِما فَعَلَ السُّفَهاءُ means: by dispersal, disbelief, and disobedience their destruction will come about. Al-Zamakhshari said: He means himself and them, for he only requested the vision to rebuke the foolish, and they requested it out of folly and ignorance. What appears to me is that it is an interrogative of inquiry, following the destruction of the chosen ones, who were the best of the Children of Israel, with what others did, since it is permissible in reason for that to happen. Do you not see God's saying: ﴿And beware of a trial that will not strike only those among you who did wrong﴾ [al-Anfal: 25], and the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him, when he was asked: "Will we be destroyed while there are righteous people among us?" He said: "Yes, when wickedness increases." And as it is reported: "A people will be swallowed up by the earth." It was said: "And among them are the righteous?" He said: "They will be raised according to their intentions," or words to this effect. It was reported from 'Ali that they were brought back to life and all of them were made prophets.

﴿It is only Your trial, by which You lead astray whom You will and guide whom You will.﴾ That is: their trial is only Your trial. The pronoun in هي (it) is explained by the context of the speech, meaning: You are the one who tried them. One group said: When God informed him that the seventy had worshipped the calf, he was astonished and said: "It is only Your trial." It was also said: When Musa was informed of the Children of Israel's worship of the calf and its description, he said: "My Lord, who led them astray?" He said: "I did." Musa said: "Then You led them astray; it is only Your trial." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It may be that he refers by it to their saying ﴿Show us God openly﴾ [al-Nisa': 153], since it was a trial from God that caused the quake. In this verse there is a refutation of the Mu'tazilah (a theological school that denied God's creation of misguidance). Al-Zamakhshari said: That is, Your test and affliction, when You spoke to me and let them hear Your speech. They inferred from the speech the vision by a corrupt inference, until they were tried and went astray. "You lead astray thereby those who are ignorant and not firm in Your knowledge, and You guide those who are learned and firm by the firm word." He made that misguidance from God, Exalted, and guidance from Him, because His trial was only a cause for them to go astray and to be guided. So it is as though He led them astray by it and guided them, by way of extended usage. End of quotation. This is in line with the Mu'tazilah's way of denying that God causes misguidance.

﴿You are our Protector, the one who manages our affairs. So forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the best of forgivers.﴾ He asked for forgiveness for himself and for them, and for mercy. Since his people were already included in his words "You are our Protector," and in his request for forgiveness and mercy for himself and for them, and since his people were people of sins, he emphasized his entreaty to his Lord, Exalted, for forgiveness of those sins. He emphasized this and drew attention to it with his words "and You are the best of forgivers." Since he and his brother Harun, peace be upon him, were among those protected from sins, when he asked forgiveness for himself and his brother and asked for mercy, he did not emphasize the mercy, but said "and You are the most merciful of the merciful." Thus he drew attention to the fact that God, Exalted, is the most merciful of the merciful. Do you not see His saying ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾ [al-A'raf: 156]? God, Exalted, is the best of forgivers because others pardon sin only to seek praise or reward, or to remove a base quality from the heart, namely the quality of resentment, whereas the Creator, glory be to Him and exalted, is far above His forgiveness being for any such reason.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 156:

﴿And prescribe for us in this world good, and in the Hereafter; indeed we have turned back to You.﴾ That is: establish for us a good end and a pleasant life, or righteous deeds that bring about a good reputation in this world. In the Hereafter, it means Paradise and the vision of God, and reward for the good of this world. The better view is to understand "good" (ḥasanah) as whatever is good of blessing, obedience, and other things. The good of the Hereafter is Paradise, and there is no good beyond it. "Indeed we have turned back to You" (inna hudna ilayka) is a justification for the request for forgiveness and for the good, and for the prescription of good. That is: we have repented to You. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Abu al-Aliyah, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, and al-Suddi, from hada, yahudu (to become a Jew, to return). Ibn Bahr said: we have drawn near through repentance. It was also said: we have inclined. From this is the saying of the poet:

*Salma and her neighbours have known that I am, by God's grace, one who inclines toward her.*

That is, one who leans. Zayd ibn Ali and Abu Wajzah read hidna with a kasrah on the hā, from hada, yahidu, when it means to move. That is: we moved ourselves and drew ourselves to Your obedience. The pronoun is then the subject. It may also be understood as a passive verb whose subject is not named: we were moved toward You and inclined. The ḍammah on hudna admits both readings. These sentences include that He, exalted is He, is their Lord and their Guardian, and that they are repentant servants, humbly submissive to Him. Thus the might of lordship fits that He should move the repentant, submissive servants to ask for forgiveness, mercy, and prescription.

﴿He said: My punishment I afflict with whom I will, and My mercy has encompassed all things.﴾ The apparent sense is that this is a resumed statement informing about His punishment and His mercy. Included in His words "I afflict with it whom I will" are the people of the quake (al-rajfah). It was said: the punishment here is the quake, and "whom I will" refers to its people. The meaning is that there is no objection to Him, that is, whomever I will, I punish. It was said: "whom I will" means whom I will not pardon. It was said: "whom I will" of My creatures, as I afflicted your people with it. It was said: "whom I will" of the disbelievers. It was said: the will refers to hastening or deferring, not to abandoning or neglecting. Al-Zamakhshari said: "whom I will" refers to those whose punishment is obligatory upon Me in wisdom, and for whom pardon has no justification because it would be a corruption. This is the way of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school). Ibn Abbas said: "I afflict whom I will" for a minor sin. He also said: "encompassed all things" refers to the sins of the believers. Abu Rawq said: it is mutual compassion among creatures. Ibn Zayd said: it is repentance in general. Al-Hasan said: in this world it is general, through provision, and in the Hereafter it is specific to the believers. Al-Zamakhshari said: as for My mercy, of its nature and quality is that it encompasses all things; no Muslim, nor disbeliever, nor obedient, nor disobedient, but is moving about in My blessing. This is an elaboration of al-Hasan's statement, that in this world it is general through provision. Zayd ibn Ali, al-Hasan, Tawus, and Amr ibn Fa'id read (man asa'a), from al-isa'ah (evil-doing), "whom I will" meaning "whoever does evil." Abu Amr al-Dani said: this reading is not sound from al-Hasan and Tawus, and Amr ibn Fa'id was a bad man. Sufyan ibn Uyaynah once recited it and approved of it; then Abd al-Rahman al-Muqri came up to him, shouted at him and made him hear. Sufyan said: I did not know, and I did not perceive what the people of innovation say. The Mu'tazilah have a connection to this reading from the perspective of enforcing the threat, and from the perspective of man's creation of his own acts: if he does evil, there is no act of God in it. Escaping this is like escaping all other apparent meanings.

* *

﴿So I will prescribe it for those who fear God and give zakat.﴾ That is: I will decree it and ordain it. The pronoun refers to mercy, since it is the nearest mentioned thing. In my opinion it may also refer to "good" in His saying "prescribe for us in this world good, and in the Hereafter," that is, "I will prescribe the good." This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Nawf al-Bikali, Qatadah, and Ibn Jurayj, and the meaning is close. When Iblis heard "My mercy has encompassed all things," he aspired to it. When he heard "I will prescribe it for those who fear God and give zakat," he despaired. The Jews and Christians remained, and when the description continued, it became clear that the intended people are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). The Christians and Jews despaired of the verse. The scholars of tafsir said: God presented these qualities to the people of Moses, but they did not bear them. When the delegation of the Children of Israel went out to the appointed time, it was said to them: the earth has been made for you a mosque and a purifier, except at a latrine, a grave, or a bath; and the tranquility (sakinah) has been placed in your hearts. They said: We cannot; so place the tranquility in the ark, and the prayer in the church, and we do not recite the Torah except from a written text, and we do not pray except in the church. Then God, exalted is He, said: "So I will prescribe it for those who fear God and give zakat," from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). Nawf al-Bikali said: Moses, peace be upon him, said: My Lord, You made my delegation for the community of Muhammad. Nawf said: so praise God who made the delegation of the Children of Israel for you.

As for the meaning of "fear God" (yattaqūn), Ibn Abbas and a group said: it means shirk (associating partners with God). Another group said: it means sins. Whoever says it means shirk alone has gone over to the view of the Murji'ah (the school that separates faith from action). The verse refutes him with the condition of deeds in His saying "and give zakat." Whoever says it means sins without exception has gone over to the view of the Mu'tazilah. Ibn Atiyah said: the correct view is that the word is general, but we do not say that avoiding sins is a necessity; rather we say that the instances of sins are subject to the Will. The meaning of "fear God" is that they place between themselves and what they fear a barrier and a protection. God mentioned the high rank so that the hearers might race toward it. End quote. "And give zakat": the apparent meaning is the zakat of wealth, and this is what Ibn Abbas said. It is also reported from him: "give" refers to the deeds by which they purify themselves. Al-Hasan said: the purification of deeds is through sincerity. End quote.

Since the obligations return to two kinds: abstentions (turūk) and acts (af'āl), and acts are of two kinds: those related to wealth, and those related to the person himself. These two are knowledge and action. Knowledge is recognition, and action is affirmation by the tongue and action by the limbs. By "fear God" He indicated the abstentions, and by the preferred act He indicated wealth through zakat. He indicated what remains by His saying: "and those who believe in Our signs." This is similar to His saying: "Guidance for those who fear God, who believe in the unseen" (Q 2:2–3). The commentators understood from His saying "those who fear God" (Q 6:69) to the end of the attributes that those who are described by these are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). It is possible that this is a case of difference between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined. Then His saying "for those who fear God and give zakat" would be for those who did this before the Messenger, and His saying "and those who believe in Our signs" would be for those who did this after the mission. Here he interpreted "signs" as the Qur'an, which is the inimitable Book.

﴿Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel, who commands them to do what is right and forbids them what is wrong, makes lawful for them the good things and makes unlawful for them the foul things, and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them. So those who believe in him, honor him, support him, and follow the light that has been sent down with him, they are the successful.﴾ ﴿Say: O mankind, I am the Messenger of God to you all, of Him to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. There is no deity except Him; He gives life and causes death. So believe in God and His Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, who believes in God and His words, and follow him that you may be guided.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 158] ﴿And among the people of Moses is a community who guide by the truth and by it act justly.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 159] ﴿And We divided them into twelve tribes, as nations. And We revealed to Moses when his people asked him for water: Strike the rock with your staff. And there gushed forth from it twelve springs. Every people knew its drinking place. And We shaded them with clouds and sent down upon them manna and quail: Eat of the good things with which We have provided you. And they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 160] ﴿And when it was said to them: Dwell in this town and eat from it wherever you wish, and say: "Remission," and enter the gate prostrating, We will forgive you your sins. We will increase the doers of good.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 161] ﴿But those who did wrong among them changed the word from what had been said to them, so We sent upon them a punishment from the sky because they were wronging.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 162] ﴿And ask them about the town that was by the sea, when they transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath, when their fish came to them on their Sabbath day openly, and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath they did not come to them. Thus We tested them for what they were defiantly doing.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 163]

Al-ta'zir (honoring, supporting). Yunus ibn Habib said: al-ta'zir is praise and commendation. Al-inbijas is sweat. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: inbajasat means "she sweated," and infajarat means "she flowed." Al-Wahidi said: al-inbijas is al-infijar; it is said: bajasa and inbajasa. Al-hut (fish) is well known; its plural for the few is ahwat, and for the many is hitan, and this is a regular pattern for fu'l with a waw-medial root, like 'ud, a'wad and 'idan.

﴿Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel, who commands them to do what is right and forbids them what is wrong﴾ This is from the remainder of the address of the Exalted to Moses, peace be upon him. In it is good news to him of the sending of Muhammad, a description of his attributes, and also information to him that He will send down a book called the Gospel. The meaning of following (ittiba') is emulating him in what he brought, in belief, speech and action. Here he combined the messengerhood (risalah) and prophethood (nubuwwah), because messengerhood among the children of Adam is greater in honor than prophethood, or because it is relative to the human being, and sovereignty is more general, so it was begun with. The unlettered (ummi) is one of the character of the Arab nation: "We are an unlettered nation, we neither write nor calculate." Most Arabs neither write nor read, as al-Zajjaj said. That he was unlettered is among the miraculous signs. It was also said: it is a relative noun referring to Umm al-Qura, which is Mecca. It was narrated from Ya'qub and others that he read al-ummiyya with a fatha on the hamza, and this was explained as a change in the relative form, the original being with a damma, as is said of the relative to Umayya: Umawi, with a fatha; or that it is related to the verbal noun from umm, meaning the intended, i.e., because this Prophet is a destination for people and a place of return. Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: that is Mecca, and he is attributed to it, but it was mentioned to intend the sanctuary or the place. The meaning of yajiduna-hu ("they find him") is that they find his description and attribute. Al-Tabrizi said: in the Torah, namely: I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers like you, and I will put My word in his mouth, and he will tell them whatever I command him; and in it: As for the Prophet, I have blessed him greatly, greatly, and I will keep him for a great nation. And in the Gospel: "He will give you another Paraclete (al-Faraqlit), who will give you the teacher of the whole age." And the Messiah said: "I go, and there will come to you the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, who does not speak from himself, and he will praise me and bear witness to me." It is possible that ﴿commands them to do what is right﴾ to the end is connected to yajiduna-hu, so it would be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) by way of metaphor, a hypothetical circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah). It is also possible that it is from the description of the Prophet, as if it were said: the one who commands what is right and forbids what is wrong, and so on and so forth. Abu 'Ali said: yamuruhum (he commands them) is an explanation of what was written of his mention, like His saying: ﴿He created him from dust﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59]. It is not permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in yajiduna-hu, because the pronoun refers to the masculine noun, and a noun and a masculine cannot command. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' said: ﴿commands them to do what is right﴾, i.e., to abandon rivals (to God), to noble character, and to maintain ties of kinship. Muqatil said: it is faith; it was also said: it is the truth. Al-Zajjaj said: it is everything recognized by the Sharia. And the wrong (al-munkar): Ibn 'Abbas said: worship of idols and severing of kinship ties. Muqatil said: polytheism. It was also said: falsehood; it was said: corruption and the beginnings of bad character; it was said: speaking about the attributes of God without knowledge, disbelief in what was sent down, severing of kinship and disobedience to parents.

﴿and makes lawful for them the good things﴾ The difference concerning the good things was already mentioned at His saying: ﴿Eat of the good things﴾ [Al-A'raf: 160], whether they are the lawful or the palatable, and both have been said here. Al-Zamakhshari said: what was forbidden to them of good things, such as fats and others, or what is good in the Sharia; and meat of what the name of God was mentioned upon of the slaughtered animals, and what its earnings were free from unlawful gain (al-suht). End of quote. It was also said: what the Arabs used to forbid of the bahira, the sa'iba, the wasila and the ham. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi considered far-fetched the view of those who said they are the made-lawful things, because of its implicit meaning: "and makes lawful for them the made-lawful things." He said: this is pure denial, and because the speech would lose its benefit, since we do not know what was made lawful for us or how much it is. He said: rather, what must be intended is what is agreeable according to natural disposition, because consuming it gives pleasure, and the basic principle regarding benefits is permissibility. So the verse indicates that everything the soul finds agreeable and the nature finds pleasurable is lawful, except what is excluded by a separate proof.

﴿and makes unlawful for them the foul things﴾ It was said: the prohibited things; it was said: what the Arabs find repugnant, such as the scorpion, the snake and insects; it was said: blood, carrion and the flesh of swine. And from Ibn 'Abbas: what is in Surat al-Ma'ida up to His saying: ﴿That is wickedness﴾ [Al-Ma'ida: 3].

﴿and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them﴾ Talha read: "and removes from them their burden." The explanation of al-isr (burden) was already mentioned at the end of Surat al-Baqara. Here Qatada, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, al-Hasan and others explained it as heaviness. Ibn 'Amir read: aşarahum, the plural of isr; and it was read: uşrahum, with a fatha and with a damma on the hamza. Whoever read it in the plural considered the related matters of the burden, since they are many; and whoever read it in the singular, because it is a collective noun. The shackles are like what they were obliged to from difficult matters, such as cutting off the place of impurity from the skin and garment, burning the spoils, retaliation (qisas) being mandatory upon the killer, whether intentional or by mistake, leaving off occupation on the Sabbath day, and the prohibition of veins in meat. From 'Ata': the Children of Israel, when they stood for prayer, would wear sackcloth and bind their hands to their necks, and a man might pierce his collarbone, put the end of a chain in it and fasten it to a pillar, restraining himself for worship. It is narrated that Moses, peace be upon him, saw on the Sabbath day a man carrying reeds, and he struck his neck. This image is like what they say: "I made this a collar on your neck," and they say: "He collared it with the collar of the dove." Al-Hudhali said:

"It is not like this, O mother of Malik, the house; but the chains have encircled the necks.
So the youth became like the elder who is not capable of anything except justice, and the blamers have rested."

There are no chains there; he meant that Islam obligated him to matters he had not been committed to before that, as he said: "Faith is the fetter of treachery." Ibn Zayd said: the shackles are what is meant in His saying: ﴿Their hands are chained﴾ [Al-Ma'ida: 64]; whoever believes, the call is removed from him and its shackling.

﴿So those who believe in him, honor him, support him, and follow the light that has been sent down with him, they are the successful﴾ "Honor him" (ta'zirun) means they praised him and extolled him. Al-Zamakhshari said: they restrained him so that no enemy could prevail over him. Al-Jahdari, Qatada, Sulayman al-Taymi and 'Isa read it with the lighter form. Ja'far ibn Muhammad read: "wa 'azzazuhu," with two zayns. And "the light" is the Qur'an, as Qatada said. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is a metaphor for the whole Sharia. It was also said: ma' ("with") means 'alayhi ("upon him"), i.e., the one sent down upon him. It was also said: it is by elision of a noun, i.e., sent down with his prophethood, because his being a prophet was accompanied by the Qur'an and joined with it. According to these two statements, the verb governing the adverbial phrase is unzila ("was sent down"). It is permissible in my view that ma'ahu be an adverbial phrase in the position of a circumstantial clause, and the governing element is elided, its estimate being: "sent down being with him," and it is a hypothetical circumstantial clause, like His saying: "I passed by a man with a falcon, hunting with it tomorrow." The state of sending down was not that he was with it, but he became with it afterward, just as the hunting had not occurred at the time of passing. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is also permissible that it be connected to ittaba'u ("follow"), i.e., and follow the Qur'an sent down together with following the Prophet and acting by his Sunna and by what he commanded, i.e., follow the Qur'an as those accompanying him followed him. And in His saying: ﴿So those who believe in him﴾ to the end there is an indication to those among the notable Children of Israel who believed in the Messenger, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and others from the People of the Two Books.

(p-٤٠٥)﴿Say: "O mankind, I am the Messenger of God to you all, of Him to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. There is no god but He; He gives life and causes death."﴾ When the Exalted related to Moses, peace be upon him, the description of Muhammad (ﷺ), and informed him that whoever reached him and believed in him would prosper, He commanded His Prophet to proclaim his call and his message to mankind in general, and to summon them to belief in God, His Messenger, His words, and following him. The call of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is general to both humans and jinn, as al-Hasan said and as the hadiths indicate. The phrase *alladhi* (the one to whom) is in the accusative position as a praise (*madh*) or in the nominative. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be in the genitive as an attribute (*sifah*) of God, saying: "even though the attribute and the thing described are separated by His words *ilaykum* (to you)." Abu al-Baqa' said: "It is remote for it to be an attribute of God or a substitute (*badal*) from Him, because of the separation it involves between them by *ilaykum* and by the circumstantial clause (*hal*)." *Ilaykum* is related to *rasul* (Messenger), and *jami'an* (all) is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in *ilaykum*. This description requires submission and obedience to the One who sent him, since to Him belongs the dominion, so He is the one who disposes as He wills. In restricting divinity (*uluhiyyah*) to Him there is the negation of partnership, because whoever possesses the dominion of this world cannot have anyone share it with Him; so He alone is characterized by divinity. He mentioned giving life and causing death, since these are two attributes that none can exercise except God, and they point to bringing into existence and annihilating whatever He wills. It is best that these be independent sentences in terms of grammatical analysis (*i'rab*), even though some of them are connected to one another in meaning. Al-Zamakhshari said: "*La ilaha illa huwa* (there is no god but He) is a substitute (*badal*) for the relative clause (*silah*) which is *lahu mulku as-samawati wal-ard* (to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth), and likewise *yuhyi wa yumit* (He gives life and causes death). In *la ilaha illa huwa* there is an explanation (*bayan*) of the sentence before it, because whoever possesses the world is truly the God. In *yuhyi wa yumit* there is an explanation of His exclusivity in divinity, because no one other than Him can give life or cause death." End of quotation. The substitution of sentences for sentences that do not share a governing operator is something we do not know. Al-Hawfi said: "*Yuhyi wa yumit* is in the position of the predicate (*khabar*), because *la ilaha* is in the nominative position as the subject (*mubtada'*), and *illa huwa* is a substitute (*badal*) according to its position." He said: "The sentence is also in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the name of God, the Exalted," meaning from the pronoun of the name of God. This is a strained grammatical analysis.

﴿So believe in God and His Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, who believes in God and His words, and follow him, that you may be guided.﴾ When He mentioned that he is the Messenger of God, He commanded them to believe in God, and with this He shifted (*iltifat*) from the first-person pronoun to the apparent noun, for the rhetorical eloquence in that, namely that he is the Prophet previously mentioned in His words: *alladhina yattabi'unar-rasulan-nabiyyal-ummiyy* (those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet) [al-A'raf: 157], and that he is the one commanded to be followed, present with the qualities mentioned earlier. The apparent meaning is that His words (*kalimatihi*) are the divine books that were revealed to those who preceded him and to him. Since belief in God is the foundation from which belief in the Messenger and the Prophet branches out, He began with it, then followed it with belief in the Messenger, then followed that with an indication of the miracle (*mu'jiz*) that demonstrates his prophethood, which is that he was unlettered. There appeared from him, in his own person, miracles such as the Qur'an, which comprises the knowledge of the first and the last, together with his upbringing in a land devoid of people of knowledge; he did not read a book, did not write, did not accompany a scholar, and did not leave Mecca for an absence that would imply learning. It has been said: *wa kalimatihi* (and His words) refers to the miracles that appeared from outside his person, such as the splitting of the moon and the gushing of water from between his fingers, and these are called "words of God" because they were extraordinary and strange events, just as Jesus, peace be upon him, was called "a word" because his coming into being was a strange and extraordinary matter. Mujahid and ‘Isa read *wa kalimatihi* in the singular form (*kalimah*), and used the singular to mean the plural, as in the saying: "The truest word (*kalimah*) spoken by the Arabs is the word of Labid." They also say of a poem: *kalimah* and *kalimat fulan* (a word of so-and-so). Mujahid and al-Suddi said: the intended meaning of *kalimatihi* and *kalimatihi* is Jesus, in accordance with His words: *wa kalimatuhu alqaha ila Maryam* (and His word which He cast to Mary) [an-Nisa': 171]. It has also been said: it is the word *kun* (be) by which Jesus and all other existents came into being. Al-A'mash read *alladhi yu'minu billahi wa ayatihi* (who believes in God and His signs) in place of *kalimatihi*. Since they were commanded to believe in God and His Messenger, and that is belief in the creed, they were commanded to follow him in what he brought, and this is a term that includes all the obligations of the Sharia, and He linked the hope of guidance to following him.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 159:

﴿And among the people of Musa is a community who guide by the truth and by it act justly.﴾ When He commanded belief in Allah and His Messenger and commanded following him, He mentioned that among the people of Musa there were those who were granted success in guidance, who acted justly and did not deviate. Guidance was not attained by anyone except by following the Law (shari'ah) of Musa before the mission of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and by following the Law of the Messenger of Allah after his mission. So this is information about those among the people of Musa who had these attributes, and the meaning is that they were not all astray; rather, among them were those who were guided. Sa'ib said: they are a group from the People of the Book who believed in our Prophet (ﷺ), such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions. Others said: they are a community from the Children of Israel who held fast to the Law of Musa before its abrogation (naskh, the cancelling of one ruling by a later one), and did not alter it, and did not kill the prophets. Al-Zamakhshari said: they are the believing repentant ones among the Children of Israel. When he mentioned those among them who had deviated, he mentioned a community of believing repentant people who guide people with the word of truth, direct them to uprightness, and show them the right way, and by the truth they judge justly among them and do not oppress. Or he meant those he described from among those who reached the Prophet (ﷺ) and believed in him from among their descendants. End of quote. Ibn Atiyyah said: it is possible that he meant the group who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ), as a means of attracting the faith of all of them; and it is possible that he meant the description of believing repentant ones among the Children of Israel, and those who were guided, feared Allah, and acted justly. End of quote. As for what is narrated from Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj: that they are a people from the Children of Israel who went away and entered a tunnel, walking in it for a year and a half beneath the earth, until they emerged beyond China, and there they still establish the Law. This is in long accounts mentioned by al-Zamakhshari, and the author of al-Tahrir wal-Tahbir, who stopped at them, saying: "perhaps it is not authentic." In His saying ﴿and among the people of Musa﴾ there is an indication of fewness, and that most of them do not guide by the truth nor act justly by it. And they, until now, are such. Likewise, a vast number of Christians have entered Islam, whose number none knows except Allah the Exalted; as for the Jews, few of them have believed.

﴿And We divided them into twelve tribes, as distinct communities﴾. That is, We divided the people of Musa (Moses) into them. Its meaning is: We separated them and distinguished them from one another. This entails that the affairs of each tribe were referred to its chief, so that Musa's burden would be lightened, and so that they would not envy one another and chaos would not break out. For this reason He caused twelve springs to gush forth for them, so that they would not dispute and fight over the water, and for this reason He appointed for each tribe a leader (naqib) to whom their affairs would be referred. The explanation of asbat (tribes) has already been given. Aban ibn Taghlib, on the authority of Asim, read ʿashrata with the ṭā' lightened (qaṭṭaʿnāhum, with the ṭā' pronounced lightly). Ibn Wathhab, al-Aʿmash and Talha ibn Sulayman read ʿashrata with a kasra on the shīn, and on their authority the fatḥa (vowel a) is also reported. Abu Hayyan and Talha ibn Musarrif read it with a kasra, which is the dialect of Tamim, while the majority read it with sukūn (no vowel), which is the dialect of the Hijaz. Ithnatay ʿashrata (twelve) is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the object).

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that qaṭṭaʿnā be taken in the sense of ṣayyarnā (We made), and that ithnatay ʿashrata be in the accusative as a second object (maf'ūl thānin) of qaṭṭaʿnāhum. The grammarians did not count qaṭṭaʿnā among the verbs of the category of ẓanantu (verbs of the heart that take two objects). Al-Hawfi affirmed this and said: ithnatay ʿashrata is an object of qaṭṭaʿnāhum, that is, We made twelve [parts]. The specification (tamyīz, a noun clarifying an ambiguous number) of ithnatay ʿashrata is omitted because the meaning is understood. Its estimated form is: twelve groups and tribes. Asbatan (tribes) is a badal (apposition) of ithnatay ʿashrata, and umaman (communities) is also an apposition.

Abu al-Baqa' said: asbatan is a na't (adjective), or a badal after a badal. It is not permissible for asbatan to be a tamyīz, because it is a plural, and the tamyīz of this type of number is only singular. Al-Zamakhshari held that asbatan is a tamyīz. He said: If you ask, the specified noun after ten is singular, so what is the reason for its coming in the plural? Why was it not said: ithnā ʿashara sibṭan (twelve tribe, singular)? I answer: If that were said, it would not be precise, because the intended meaning is: We divided them into twelve clans, and every clan is asbāṭ, not a sibṭ. So he put asbāṭ in the place of clan. A parallel to this is the verse:

"Between the spears of Malik and Nahshal"

Umaman is an apposition of ithnatay ʿashrata, in the sense of: and We divided them into communities, because each of the asbāṭ was a great nation and a dense multitude, and each one aims at something different from what the other aims at, so they hardly unite. End of quotation. As for what he claimed, that every clan is asbāṭ, this contradicts what the people have mentioned. They stated that the asbāṭ among the Children of Israel were like the tribes among the Arabs, and they said: asbāṭ is the plural of sibṭ, and they are the groups. The asbāṭ from the descendants of Isaac are in the position of the tribes from the descendants of Ishmael. Thus, according to his view, the saying of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿And what was sent down to Abraham and Ishmael and Isaac and Jacob and the tribes﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:136] would mean "the clans." As for his saying "a parallel to this is," it is not a parallel, because this is the dual of a plural, which is not permitted except in cases of poetic necessity. It seems he is pointing out that if the plural was not considered to have the sense of a kind of spear, its dualization in this way would not be correct; here he took account of asbāṭ, though it is a plural, in the sense of clan, and so it was specified with it, just as it is specified with the singular.

Al-Hawfi said: It is permissible that it be by omission, and the estimated form is: twelve groups, and asbāṭan is a na't (adjective) of firqa (group), then the modified noun was deleted and the adjective was put in its place. Umaman is a na't of asbāṭ. The numeral was feminine, though it refers to asbāṭ, which is masculine, because it has the meaning of firqa or umma (group or nation), as in the saying: thalāthat anfusin (three persons), meaning men, and ʿashara abṭun (ten bellies), with regard to the clan. End of quotation. A parallel to the specified singular being described by a plural, out of regard for the meaning, is the poet's saying:

"In it are forty-two milch camels, black like the crow with glossy black feathers"

He did not say sawdāʾ (feminine singular). It was also said: he made each one of the twelve into asbāṭ, as you say: to Zayd are dirhams, to so-and-so are dirhams, and to ʿUmar are dirhams, so these are twenty dirhams. It was also said: the estimate is: We divided them into groups, twelve, so no specification is needed. Al-Baghawi said: there is a reordering in the sentence, its estimated form being: We divided them into tribes, communities, twelve. All these estimates are forced, and the most consistent with the rules of Arabic is the view with which we began.

﴿And We revealed to Musa, when his people asked him for water: Strike the rock with your staff. And there gushed from it twelve springs. Every people knew their drinking place. And We shaded them with clouds, and sent down upon them manna and quails. Eat of the good things with which We have provided you. And they did not wrong Us, but they wronged themselves﴾. The explanation of the like of these sentences has already been given in al-Baqarah. As for inbajasat (gushed forth): if its meaning is what Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlaʾ said, it was said that it would appear at every point of the rock, like the breast of a woman, and Musa struck it, and it first sweated, then flowed. If it is synonymous with infajarat (burst forth), then there is no difference. Al-Zamakhshari said: here al-unās is a collective noun with no broken plural, like rukhāʾ, thunāʾ, thuʾām, and its sisters. It is also possible to say that the original form is a broken plural with kasra, and the ḍamma is a substitute for the kasra, just as it was substituted from fatḥa in forms like sukārā and ghuyārā. End of quotation. What he said is not correct, for two reasons. The first: it is not spoken as ināsun with a kasra on the hamza, so that it would be a broken plural and the ḍamma a replacement for the kasra; unlike sukārā and ghuyārā, where the analogical form is fuʿālā with a fatḥa on the first radical, and this is attested in both. The second: sukārā, ghuyārā, ʿujālā and what comes like them do not have a ḍamma that replaces a fatḥa; rather Sibawayh stated explicitly in his book that it is the broken plural of a root, just as fuʿālā is a broken plural of a root, even though the ḍamma is not as productive as the fatḥa. Sibawayh said in defining the broken plurals of adjectives: some of them are broken into fuʿālā, such as the saying of some: sukārā and ʿujālā. Sibawayh also said in the chapter on patterns: fuʿālā in nouns is like ḥubārā, sumānā and lubādā, and it is not an adjective unless the singular is broken into the plural with it, like ʿujālā, kusālā and sumānā. These are two explicit statements from Sibawayh that it is a broken plural. Since it is a broken plural from the start, it is not valid to claim that its original form is fuʿālā and that the vowel was changed. Al-Mubarrad held that it is a collective noun, meaning fuʿālā with a ḍamma on the first letter, and not a broken plural. Al-Zamakhshari did not follow what Sibawayh said, nor what al-Mubarrad said, because according to al-Mubarrad it is a collective noun (ism jamʿ), so the ḍamma on its first letter is original, not a replacement for the fatḥa. Rather he introduced a third opinion.

ʿIsa al-Hamdani read: ﴿min ṭayyibāti mā razaqnākum﴾ (of the good things with which We have provided you), with the pronoun in the singular (razaqtukum, with the first person singular verb).

This story and its explanation were covered in al-Baqarah, and it seems that this passage is an abridged version of that one. However, there are some differences. There: "And when We said, 'Enter'," and here: "And when it was said to them, 'Dwell'." There: "raghadan" (freely, in abundance), which is absent here. There: "wa-sanazid" (and We will increase), and here: "sanazid." There: "fa-anzalna 'ala alladhina zalamu" (then We sent down upon those who did wrong), and here: "fa-arsalna 'alayhim" (then We sent upon them). Between the two passages there is variation in some wording, without any contradiction. As for "wa-qila lahum" (and it was said to them) here, versus "wa-idh qulna" (and when We said) there, the agent is omitted here because it is known, namely Allah Most High. There: "udkhulu" (enter), and here: "uskunu" (dwell). Dwelling is a necessary consequence of entering, so they were commanded there with the beginning of the matter, and here with what follows from entering. There: "fa-kulu" (so eat), with the fa' (fa' of consequence, indicating sequence), and here: "wa-kulu" with the waw. The waw is used in one of its possible senses, that what follows happened after what precedes. It has also been said: entering is a momentary action that calls for a following result, so the fa' of sequence is apt after it. Dwelling is a continuing state, so commanding eating together with it, rather than immediately after it, is apt, and so the waw, which joins both matters in one time, is apt. This is one of its possible meanings, and some grammarians claim that it is more appropriate and more common in this sense. It has also been said: "raghadan" was mentioned after the command to enter, because that is a state of arrival, in which eating is more pleasant and complete, and they are more in need of it. This differs from dwelling, which is a state of settling and tranquility, so eating is not more pleasant in it, nor are they more in need of it.

[p. 409] As for the advancing and postponing in "wa-qulu" and "wa-udkhulu," al-Zamakhshari said: "It makes no difference whether they put the 'Hittah' (a request for the removal of sins) before entering the gate or after it; they are all combining the two in performance." End of quote. His statement "it makes no difference whether they put it first or after" is not correct Arabic. The proper form would be "sawa'un aqaddamu am akhkharu-ha," as Allah Most High said: ﴿It is all the same for us whether we bear it with patience or not﴾ [Ibrahim: 21]. It may be said that placing the command to enter the gate in prostration before the phrase "udkhulu hadhihi al-qaryah" (enter this town) is fitting, because entering in prostration is an act that signifies submission and humility, whereas "Hittah" is a word. An act is stronger than a word in showing submission, so it is fitting that it be mentioned with the beginning of the matter, which is entering. Also, the command "udkhulu" came before it, so the command to enter the town is followed by the command to enter its gate in a posture of submission. Furthermore, entering the town is not possible except by entering its gate, so the gate of the town is, as it were, a substitute for the town, with the governing verb repeated with it. This differs from the command to dwell.

As for "sanazid" here, al-Zamakhshari said: "It is a promise of two things, forgiveness and increase, and omitting the waw does not harm this, because it is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) that follows from an assumed question: 'And what comes after forgiveness?' So it was said to them, 'We will increase the good-doers.'" The "min-hum" (from among them) is an explanation of the increase. "Arsalna" and "anzalna" and "yazlimun" and "yafsuqun" are all of one kind.

al-Hasan read "Hittatan" in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning "the removal of our sins, a removal." It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative governed by "qulu" with an omitted element, the sense being: "and say a word, Hittatan," that is, "a word of removal," so "dha" (possessor of) is omitted and "Hittah" becomes a descriptive for the omitted verbal noun, as you say: "I said a good thing," meaning "a good word," and "I said a true thing," meaning "a true word."

The Kufans, Ibn Kathir, al-Hasan and al-A'mash read "naghfir" with the nun, and "lakum khati'atikum" as a sound plural. However, al-Hasan lightened the hamza and assimilated the ya' into it. Abu Amr read "naghfir" with the nun, "lakum khataya-kum" on the pattern of "qada-ya-kum." Nafi' and Mahbub, on the authority of Abu Amr, read "tughfar" with the ta' in the passive voice, "lakum khati'atukum" as a sound plural. Ibn Amir read "tughfar" with a ta' with damma, in the passive, "lakum khati'atukum" in the singular and with hamza. Ibn Hurmuz read "taghfir" with an open ta', in the sense that the Hittah itself forgives, since it is the cause of forgiveness.

Ibn Atiyya said: "Baddala" means to change the wording without removing its whole meaning, while "abdala" means to remove something and bring another wording. This distinction is worthless, since "baddala" and "abdala" have come in the readings with one meaning. It is read: ﴿So We desired that their Lord would exchange for them something better than him in purity﴾ [al-Kahf: 81], and ﴿It may be that their Lord, if he divorces you, will exchange for him wives better than you﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5], and ﴿It may be that our Lord will give us in exchange something better than it﴾ [al-Qalam: 32], with the lightened and the intensified forms, and the meaning is one: removing a thing and bringing something else in its place. Then the intensified form has also come where the whole thing is removed, as Allah Most High said: ﴿Those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds﴾ [al-Furqan: 70], ﴿And We replaced for them their two gardens with two gardens﴾ [Saba': 16], ﴿Then We replaced the evil with good﴾ [al-A'raf: 95]. And on this is the speech of the Arabs, in prose and in verse.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 161–163 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And ask them about the town that was by the sea, when they transgressed concerning the Sabbath, when their fish came to them on their Sabbath day openly, and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath, they did not come to them. Thus did We test them because they used to defy (Our command).﴾ The pronoun in "wa-s'alhum" (and ask them) refers to the Jews who were present in the presence of the Messenger (ﷺ). It is related that some of the Jews who opposed the Messenger said to him: "There was no disobedience or defiance among the Children of Israel regarding what they were commanded." So this verse was revealed, rebuking them, establishing their lie, and informing them of what befell their forebears of destruction and transformation. The Jews used to conceal this story, so it is among the things that cannot be known except through a Book or revelation. Thus, when one who had not read their Book informed them of it, it was known that it came from revelation. His saying "'an al-qaryah" (about the town) contains an ellipsis, meaning "about the people of the town." The town is Ayla, as stated by Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, al-Suddi, Ikrimah, Abdullah ibn Kathir, and al-Thawri. Or it is Madyan. Ikrimah related from Ibn Abbas: "Or the shore of Madyan." It was also reported from Qatadah, who said: "It is Maqna, with a sukun on the qaf." Ibn Zayd said: "It is Maqnat, the shore of Madyan, and it is also called Ma'anna, with a fathah on the 'ayn and a shaddah on the nun." Or it is Tiberias, as stated by al-Zuhri. Or Ariha. Or Bayt al-Maqdis, and this is far-fetched because of His saying "hadirat al-bahr" (a town by the sea). Or it is a town in Syria that was not named specifically. It was reported from al-Hasan: "And Ma'anna." End of quotation. "Hadirat al-bahr" (a town by the sea): located near the sea, built on its shore. It is possible that by "hadirah" he means it in a manner of glorifying it, i.e., it is the principal town among the towns by the sea. So the estimated meaning is "the principal town of the towns of the sea," meaning the people of the towns of the sea would gather there for their buying, selling, and needs. "Idh ya'dukna fi as-sabt" (when they transgressed concerning the Sabbath), i.e., they exceeded God's command regarding work on the Sabbath day. He had already prohibited work on it and occupation with hunting or other things. However, in this incident their disobedience consisted of... It was read "yu'iddun" (they prepare), from i'dad (preparing), and they used to prepare the tools of hunting on the Sabbath day, while they were commanded not to occupy themselves on it with anything other than worship. Shahr ibn Hawshab and Abu Nuhayk read "ya'uddun," with a fathah on the 'ayn and a shaddah on the dal, and its original form is ya'tadun, and the ta' was assimilated into the dal (idgham, assimilation of letters), like the reading of the one who read: "la ta'uddu fi as-sabt" (do not transgress concerning the Sabbath). "Idh" (when) is an adverb of time, and its governing element is... Al-Hawfi said: "Idh is related to salhum (ask them)." End of quotation. But this is not conceivable, because idh is an adverb of past time, and salhum is in the future. If it were a future adverb, the meaning would not be correct, because the transgressors, who are the people of the town, are absent, so it is not possible to ask them, and what is asked about is the people of the town who transgressed. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Idh ya'dun is a badal (substitute) for al-qaryah, and what is meant by al-qaryah is its people, as if it were said: 'And ask them about the people of the town at the time of their transgression on the Sabbath.' It is badal al-ishtimal (a substitution of inclusion)." End of quotation. This is not permissible, because idh is among the adverbs that are not inflected and that a prepositional particle does not enter upon. Making it a badal permits 'an to enter upon it, because a badal is intended as a repetition of the governing element, and if 'an were introduced upon it, it would not be permissible. It is only treated as inflected by having some temporal adverbs added to it, such as in "yawma idh kana kadha" (the day when such-and-such was). As for the view of one who holds that it is inflected by being a direct object of "udhkur" (remember), it is the view of one who was unable to interpret it in the way that befits keeping it as an adverb. Abu al-Baqa' said concerning "'an al-qaryah": that is, "about the story of the town," and this omitted element is what governs the adverb which is "idh ya'dun." It was also said: it is an adverb of "al-hadirah" (the principal town), and he allowed that because it existed at that time, then it was ruined. End of quotation. The apparent meaning is that His saying "fi as-sabt" (on the Sabbath) and "yawma sabtihim" (on their Sabbath day) refers to the day itself, and the meaning of "i'tadaw fihi" (they transgressed in it) is, by their disobedience and opposition, as we previously mentioned. Al-Zamakhshari said: "As-sabt is a verbal noun from sabatat al-yahud, when the Jews glorified their Sabbath by abstaining from hunting and occupying themselves with worship. So its meaning is: they transgress in glorifying this day." Likewise His saying: "yawma sabtihim" (on their Sabbath day) means the day of their glorification. This is indicated by His saying: "wa-yawma la yasbituna" (and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath). "Idh ta'tihim" (when it came to them): the governing element is "idh ya'dun," i.e., "idh 'adaw fi as-sabt idh atat-hum" (when they transgressed on the Sabbath when it came to them), because idh is an adverb of past time, which turns the present tense verb into the past. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It may also be a badal after a badal." End of quotation, meaning a badal from al-qaryah after the badal of "idh ya'dun." We have mentioned that this is not permissible. He attributed "as-sabt" to them because they were specifically subject to rulings concerning it. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz read: "hitanuhum yawma as-batihim" (their fish on the day of their sabbath observance). Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said in Kitab al-Lawami', in which he mentioned this reading from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz: "It is a verbal noun from asbata ar-rajul, when a man entered upon the Sabbath." Isa ibn Umar and Asim, with a variant, read: "la yasbutuna" (they do not observe the Sabbath), with a damma on the kasrah of the ba', which is the reading of the majority. Ali, al-Hasan, and Asim, with a variant, read: "yusbituna" (they do not rest), with a damma on the ya' of the present tense, from asbata, meaning he entered upon the Sabbath. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is reported from al-Hasan: 'la yusbatuna' (they are not made to observe the Sabbath), with a damma on the ya', in the passive form, i.e., the Sabbath is not imposed on them, and they are not commanded to observe it." The governing element of "yawma" (on the day) is "la ta'tihim" (did not come to them). In this there is evidence that what follows la (not) governs what precedes it, and on this there are three positions: permissibility absolutely, prohibition absolutely, and a distinction: if la is the answer to an oath, it is prohibited; otherwise it is permitted. This last is the correct view. "Kadhalika" (thus): i.e., like that trial by the command of the fish, "nablu-hum" (We test them), i.e., We tested them and examined them. It was also said: "kadhalika" is related to what precedes it, i.e., "wa-yawma la yasbituna la ta'tihim kadhalika" (and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath they did not come to them, thus), i.e., they did not come with a coming similar to that coming, which was that they came openly, in great numbers; rather, only some of them came, which is few. So according to the first view regarding "kadhalika," the fish's coming is entirely negated, as is related in the stories that it would disappear altogether. According to the second view, most of it would disappear, and only a little would remain, with which they would toil in hunting. This was stated by Qatadah. This coming of the fish may be by sending from God, like the sending of clouds, or by inspiration of an inner impulse, as He revealed to the bee, or by a sense on that day, in the manner in which God makes animals aware on Friday of the matter of the Hour, as has come in the hadith: "There is no creature except that it is attentive on Friday until the sun rises, out of fear of the Hour." It is possible that this coming of the fish was a sense of safety. The meaning of "shurra'an" (openly) is approaching them, drawn up in rows, as you say: "I aimed the spear toward him," i.e., I advanced with it toward him. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Shurra'an means openly, upon the surface of the water." It is reported from al-Hasan: "They come forward to their doors, as if they were fat rams." It is said: "Shara'a 'alayna fulan" when someone approached us and came over us, and "shara'tu 'ala fulan fi baytihi fa-ra'aytuhu yafʿalu kadha" (I looked in on so-and-so in his house and saw him doing such-and-such). The narrators of stories said: "It approaches until it is possible to take it by hand. This displeased them, and they found a way to disobedience by digging trenches through which the sea water would flow in a channel. When the fish came on the Sabbath day and got into the trench, they threw a stone into the channel and prevented it from going out to the sea. When Sunday came, they took it." This was the first way of finding a pretext. Ibn Ruman said: "A man among them would take a thread and place a noose in it, throw it onto the fish's tail, and at the other end of the thread a stake was driven in. He would leave it like that until he took it on Sunday. Then people found a way to it, seeing that one who did this was not tested, until the catching of fish increased and it was carried about in the markets, and the wicked openly hunted it and said: 'The sanctity of the Sabbath has gone.'"

This story and its explanation were covered in al-Baqarah, and it seems that this passage is an abridged version of that one. However, there are some differences. There: "And when We said, 'Enter'," and here: "And when it was said to them, 'Dwell'." There: "raghadan" (freely, in abundance), which is absent here. There: "wa-sanazid" (and We will increase), and here: "sanazid." There: "fa-anzalna 'ala alladhina zalamu" (then We sent down upon those who did wrong), and here: "fa-arsalna 'alayhim" (then We sent upon them). Between the two passages there is variation in some wording, without any contradiction. As for "wa-qila lahum" (and it was said to them) here, versus "wa-idh qulna" (and when We said) there, the agent is omitted here because it is known, namely Allah Most High. There: "udkhulu" (enter), and here: "uskunu" (dwell). Dwelling is a necessary consequence of entering, so they were commanded there with the beginning of the matter, and here with what follows from entering. There: "fa-kulu" (so eat), with the fa' (fa' of consequence, indicating sequence), and here: "wa-kulu" with the waw. The waw is used in one of its possible senses, that what follows happened after what precedes. It has also been said: entering is a momentary action that calls for a following result, so the fa' of sequence is apt after it. Dwelling is a continuing state, so commanding eating together with it, rather than immediately after it, is apt, and so the waw, which joins both matters in one time, is apt. This is one of its possible meanings, and some grammarians claim that it is more appropriate and more common in this sense. It has also been said: "raghadan" was mentioned after the command to enter, because that is a state of arrival, in which eating is more pleasant and complete, and they are more in need of it. This differs from dwelling, which is a state of settling and tranquility, so eating is not more pleasant in it, nor are they more in need of it.

[p. 409] As for the advancing and postponing in "wa-qulu" and "wa-udkhulu," al-Zamakhshari said: "It makes no difference whether they put the 'Hittah' (a request for the removal of sins) before entering the gate or after it; they are all combining the two in performance." End of quote. His statement "it makes no difference whether they put it first or after" is not correct Arabic.
