Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 161–163 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And ask them about the town that was by the sea, when they transgressed concerning the Sabbath, when their fish came to them on their Sabbath day openly, and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath, they did not come to them. Thus did We test them because they used to defy (Our command).﴾ The pronoun in "wa-s'alhum" (and ask them) refers to the Jews who were present in the presence of the Messenger (ﷺ). It is related that some of the Jews who opposed the Messenger said to him: "There was no disobedience or defiance among the Children of Israel regarding what they were commanded." So this verse was revealed, rebuking them, establishing their lie, and informing them of what befell their forebears of destruction and transformation. The Jews used to conceal this story, so it is among the things that cannot be known except through a Book or revelation. Thus, when one who had not read their Book informed them of it, it was known that it came from revelation. His saying "'an al-qaryah" (about the town) contains an ellipsis, meaning "about the people of the town." The town is Ayla, as stated by Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, al-Suddi, Ikrimah, Abdullah ibn Kathir, and al-Thawri. Or it is Madyan. Ikrimah related from Ibn Abbas: "Or the shore of Madyan." It was also reported from Qatadah, who said: "It is Maqna, with a sukun on the qaf." Ibn Zayd said: "It is Maqnat, the shore of Madyan, and it is also called Ma'anna, with a fathah on the 'ayn and a shaddah on the nun." Or it is Tiberias, as stated by al-Zuhri. Or Ariha. Or Bayt al-Maqdis, and this is far-fetched because of His saying "hadirat al-bahr" (a town by the sea). Or it is a town in Syria that was not named specifically. It was reported from al-Hasan: "And Ma'anna." End of quotation. "Hadirat al-bahr" (a town by the sea): located near the sea, built on its shore. It is possible that by "hadirah" he means it in a manner of glorifying it, i.e., it is the principal town among the towns by the sea. So the estimated meaning is "the principal town of the towns of the sea," meaning the people of the towns of the sea would gather there for their buying, selling, and needs. "Idh ya'dukna fi as-sabt" (when they transgressed concerning the Sabbath), i.e., they exceeded God's command regarding work on the Sabbath day. He had already prohibited work on it and occupation with hunting or other things. However, in this incident their disobedience consisted of... It was read "yu'iddun" (they prepare), from i'dad (preparing), and they used to prepare the tools of hunting on the Sabbath day, while they were commanded not to occupy themselves on it with anything other than worship. Shahr ibn Hawshab and Abu Nuhayk read "ya'uddun," with a fathah on the 'ayn and a shaddah on the dal, and its original form is ya'tadun, and the ta' was assimilated into the dal (idgham, assimilation of letters), like the reading of the one who read: "la ta'uddu fi as-sabt" (do not transgress concerning the Sabbath). "Idh" (when) is an adverb of time, and its governing element is... Al-Hawfi said: "Idh is related to salhum (ask them)." End of quotation. But this is not conceivable, because idh is an adverb of past time, and salhum is in the future. If it were a future adverb, the meaning would not be correct, because the transgressors, who are the people of the town, are absent, so it is not possible to ask them, and what is asked about is the people of the town who transgressed. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Idh ya'dun is a badal (substitute) for al-qaryah, and what is meant by al-qaryah is its people, as if it were said: 'And ask them about the people of the town at the time of their transgression on the Sabbath.' It is badal al-ishtimal (a substitution of inclusion)." End of quotation. This is not permissible, because idh is among the adverbs that are not inflected and that a prepositional particle does not enter upon. Making it a badal permits 'an to enter upon it, because a badal is intended as a repetition of the governing element, and if 'an were introduced upon it, it would not be permissible. It is only treated as inflected by having some temporal adverbs added to it, such as in "yawma idh kana kadha" (the day when such-and-such was). As for the view of one who holds that it is inflected by being a direct object of "udhkur" (remember), it is the view of one who was unable to interpret it in the way that befits keeping it as an adverb. Abu al-Baqa' said concerning "'an al-qaryah": that is, "about the story of the town," and this omitted element is what governs the adverb which is "idh ya'dun." It was also said: it is an adverb of "al-hadirah" (the principal town), and he allowed that because it existed at that time, then it was ruined. End of quotation. The apparent meaning is that His saying "fi as-sabt" (on the Sabbath) and "yawma sabtihim" (on their Sabbath day) refers to the day itself, and the meaning of "i'tadaw fihi" (they transgressed in it) is, by their disobedience and opposition, as we previously mentioned. Al-Zamakhshari said: "As-sabt is a verbal noun from sabatat al-yahud, when the Jews glorified their Sabbath by abstaining from hunting and occupying themselves with worship. So its meaning is: they transgress in glorifying this day." Likewise His saying: "yawma sabtihim" (on their Sabbath day) means the day of their glorification. This is indicated by His saying: "wa-yawma la yasbituna" (and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath). "Idh ta'tihim" (when it came to them): the governing element is "idh ya'dun," i.e., "idh 'adaw fi as-sabt idh atat-hum" (when they transgressed on the Sabbath when it came to them), because idh is an adverb of past time, which turns the present tense verb into the past. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It may also be a badal after a badal." End of quotation, meaning a badal from al-qaryah after the badal of "idh ya'dun." We have mentioned that this is not permissible. He attributed "as-sabt" to them because they were specifically subject to rulings concerning it. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz read: "hitanuhum yawma as-batihim" (their fish on the day of their sabbath observance). Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said in Kitab al-Lawami', in which he mentioned this reading from Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz: "It is a verbal noun from asbata ar-rajul, when a man entered upon the Sabbath." Isa ibn Umar and Asim, with a variant, read: "la yasbutuna" (they do not observe the Sabbath), with a damma on the kasrah of the ba', which is the reading of the majority. Ali, al-Hasan, and Asim, with a variant, read: "yusbituna" (they do not rest), with a damma on the ya' of the present tense, from asbata, meaning he entered upon the Sabbath. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is reported from al-Hasan: 'la yusbatuna' (they are not made to observe the Sabbath), with a damma on the ya', in the passive form, i.e., the Sabbath is not imposed on them, and they are not commanded to observe it." The governing element of "yawma" (on the day) is "la ta'tihim" (did not come to them). In this there is evidence that what follows la (not) governs what precedes it, and on this there are three positions: permissibility absolutely, prohibition absolutely, and a distinction: if la is the answer to an oath, it is prohibited; otherwise it is permitted. This last is the correct view. "Kadhalika" (thus): i.e., like that trial by the command of the fish, "nablu-hum" (We test them), i.e., We tested them and examined them. It was also said: "kadhalika" is related to what precedes it, i.e., "wa-yawma la yasbituna la ta'tihim kadhalika" (and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath they did not come to them, thus), i.e., they did not come with a coming similar to that coming, which was that they came openly, in great numbers; rather, only some of them came, which is few. So according to the first view regarding "kadhalika," the fish's coming is entirely negated, as is related in the stories that it would disappear altogether. According to the second view, most of it would disappear, and only a little would remain, with which they would toil in hunting. This was stated by Qatadah. This coming of the fish may be by sending from God, like the sending of clouds, or by inspiration of an inner impulse, as He revealed to the bee, or by a sense on that day, in the manner in which God makes animals aware on Friday of the matter of the Hour, as has come in the hadith: "There is no creature except that it is attentive on Friday until the sun rises, out of fear of the Hour." It is possible that this coming of the fish was a sense of safety. The meaning of "shurra'an" (openly) is approaching them, drawn up in rows, as you say: "I aimed the spear toward him," i.e., I advanced with it toward him. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Shurra'an means openly, upon the surface of the water." It is reported from al-Hasan: "They come forward to their doors, as if they were fat rams." It is said: "Shara'a 'alayna fulan" when someone approached us and came over us, and "shara'tu 'ala fulan fi baytihi fa-ra'aytuhu yafʿalu kadha" (I looked in on so-and-so in his house and saw him doing such-and-such). The narrators of stories said: "It approaches until it is possible to take it by hand. This displeased them, and they found a way to disobedience by digging trenches through which the sea water would flow in a channel. When the fish came on the Sabbath day and got into the trench, they threw a stone into the channel and prevented it from going out to the sea. When Sunday came, they took it." This was the first way of finding a pretext. Ibn Ruman said: "A man among them would take a thread and place a noose in it, throw it onto the fish's tail, and at the other end of the thread a stake was driven in. He would leave it like that until he took it on Sunday. Then people found a way to it, seeing that one who did this was not tested, until the catching of fish increased and it was carried about in the markets, and the wicked openly hunted it and said: 'The sanctity of the Sabbath has gone.'"

This story and its explanation were covered in al-Baqarah, and it seems that this passage is an abridged version of that one. However, there are some differences. There: "wa-sanazid" (and We will increase), and here: "sanazid." There: "fa-anzalna 'ala alladhina zalamu" (then We sent down upon those who did wrong), and here: "fa-arsalna 'alayhim" (then We sent upon them). Between the two passages there is variation in some wording, without any contradiction. As for "wa-qila lahum" (and it was said to them) here, versus "wa-idh qulna" (and when We said) there, the agent is omitted here because it is known, namely Allah Most High. There: "udkhulu" (enter), and here: "uskunu" (dwell). Dwelling is a necessary consequence of entering, so they were commanded there with the beginning of the matter, and here with what follows from entering. The waw is used in one of its possible senses, that what follows happened after what precedes. It has also been said: entering is a momentary action that calls for a following result, so the fa' of sequence is apt after it. Dwelling is a continuing state, so commanding eating together with it, rather than immediately after it, is apt, and so the waw, which joins both matters in one time, is apt. This is one of its possible meanings, and some grammarians claim that it is more appropriate and more common in this sense. It has also been said: "raghadan" was mentioned after the command to enter, because that is a state of arrival, in which eating is more pleasant and complete, and they are more in need of it. This differs from dwelling, which is a state of settling and tranquility, so eating is not more pleasant in it, nor are they more in need of it.

According to the second view, most of it would disappear, and only a little would remain, with which they would toil in hunting. This was stated by Qatadah. This coming of the fish may be by sending from God, like the sending of clouds, or by inspiration of an inner impulse, as He revealed to the bee, or by a sense on that day, in the manner in which God makes animals aware on Friday of the matter of the Hour, as has come in the hadith: "There is no creature except that it is attentive on Friday until the sun rises, out of fear of the Hour." It is possible that this coming of the fish was a sense of safety. The meaning of "shurra'an" (openly) is approaching them, drawn up in rows, as you say: "I aimed the spear toward him," i.e., I advanced with it toward him. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Shurra'an means openly, upon the surface of the water." It is reported from al-Hasan: "They come forward to their doors, as if they were fat rams." It is said: "Shara'a 'alayna fulan" when someone approached us and came over us, and "shara'tu 'ala fulan fi baytihi fa-ra'aytuhu yafʿalu kadha" (I looked in on so-and-so in his house and saw him doing such-and-such). The narrators of stories said: "It approaches until it is possible to take it by hand. This displeased them, and they found a way to disobedience by digging trenches through which the sea water would flow in a channel. When the fish came on the Sabbath day and got into the trench, they threw a stone into the channel and prevented it from going out to the sea. When Sunday came, they took it." This was the first way of finding a pretext. Ibn Ruman said: "A man among them would take a thread and place a noose in it, throw it onto the fish's tail, and at the other end of the thread a stake was driven in. He would leave it like that until he took it on Sunday. Then people found a way to it, seeing that one who did this was not tested, until the catching of fish increased and it was carried about in the markets, and the wicked openly hunted it and said: 'The sanctity of the Sabbath has gone.'"

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 164:

﴿And when a community among them said: "Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy or punish with a severe punishment?" They said: "As an excuse before your Lord, and perhaps they will fear Him."﴾ That is, a group of the people of the town, from among their righteous ones (p-412) who had tried admonishing them and found that the admonition was not benefiting them. Apparently, the one who speaks is other than those addressed: "Why do you admonish a people," so there are three groups: those who transgressed, a group that admonished and forbade, and a group that withdrew and neither forbade nor transgressed. This last group is not the one that said to the admonishers, "Why do you admonish?" It is also reported that they were two groups: a group that disobeyed, and a group that forbade and admonished, and that a company of the disobedient said to the admonishers, mockingly: "Why do you admonish a people whom you yourselves know Allah is going to destroy or punish?" Ibn 'Atiyya said: "The first opinion is more correct, and it is supported by the pronouns in His words: ﴿as an excuse before your Lord, and perhaps they will fear Him﴾, for this address requires an addressee." End of quote. He means that if the disobedient group were the speakers, the admonishers would have said: "An excuse before their Lord, and perhaps they..." or in the second person: "An excuse before your Lord, and perhaps you will fear Him."

The meaning of "destroy them" (muhlikuhum) is to cut them off and purge the land of them. ﴿Or punish them with a severe punishment﴾ because of their persistence in disobedience. The punishment may be in this world, and it may be in the Hereafter. Even if there were three groups, the speakers said this only because they knew that admonition would not benefit them, given its repetition upon them and their non-acceptance of it. It is also possible that there were two groups: disobedient and obedient, and that some of the obedient said to others, when they saw that admonition had no effect and changed nothing among the disobedient: "Why do you admonish?"

The majority (al-Jumhur) read مَعْذِرَةٌ (ma'dhiratun) with a nominative ending (marfu') , meaning: our admonition is establishing an excuse before Allah, so that we may not be attributed with some negligence in forbidding evil, and because we hope that they will refrain from sins. Zayd ibn 'Ali, 'Asim in some of what is reported from him, 'Isa ibn 'Umar and Talha ibn Musarrif read مَعْذِرَةً (ma'dhiratan) with an accusative ending (mansub), meaning: we admonished them as an excuse. Sibawayh said: "If a man said to a man, 'An excuse before Allah and before you for such-and-such,' he would put it in the accusative." End of quote. Here Sibawayh prefers the nominative, saying: "They did not intend to offer an excuse in a new, independent sense, but when it was said to them, 'Why do you admonish?' they answered, 'Our admonition is an excuse.'" Abu al-Baqa' said: "Whoever reads it in the accusative does so as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: our admonition is for the sake of an excuse." It was also said that it is a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: "we make an excuse, an excuse," and al-Zamakhshari stated both.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah al-A'raf (7), verse 165:**

﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We saved those who forbade evil, and We seized those who did wrong with a severe punishment, because they had been defiantly disobedient.﴾

The pronoun in *nasu* (they forgot) refers to those who were forbidden, meaning they abandoned what the righteous had reminded them of. Abandonment is described as forgetting for emphasis (mubalaghah), since the strongest form of abandoning something is for it to be forgotten. *Ma* (what) is a relative pronoun meaning *alladhi* (that which).

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "It is possible that by *dhikr* (reminder) is meant the reminder itself, and it is possible that by it is meant what was contained in the reminder." End of quote. These two possibilities do not appear clear to me.

*Al-su'* (evil) is general, covering acts of disobedience, but according to the narratives it is specifically the hunting of fish here. *Alladhina zalamu* (those who did wrong) are the disobedient, and the verse points out the cause of their punishment, which is wrongdoing (*zulm*).

Mujahid said: *ba'is* means severe and painful. al-Akhfash said: it means destructive. Nafi', Abu Ja'far, Shaybah and others read *bi'sin*, on the pattern of *jayyid*. Ibn 'Amir also read it this way, except that he hamzated it like *bi'r*. Both readings are explained as a verb that was made into a name, as in the saying: "I forbid you from *qil wa qal*" (gossip). It is also possible that it was used as a descriptive word on the pattern of *fi'l*, like *hilf*, so its origin would not be a verb. al-Kisa'i explained it in another way, namely that the original form was *ba'is*, the hamza was lightened, so two *ya'* sounds met, one was deleted, and the first letter was given a kasrah, as in *raghif* and *shahid*. Others explained it as being on the pattern of *fi'l* with its first letter given a kasrah by assimilation (*itba'*), then the kasrah was deleted, as they say *fakhidh*, and then they lightened the hamza.

al-Hasan read *ba'is* both with hamza and without hamza, and from Nafi' and Abu Bakr it is similar to this, except that without hamza it is from Nafi', as you say *bi'sa al-rajul* (what a wretched man). Abu Hatim considered this weak and said: "There is no basis for it, because one does not say *marartu bi-rajulin bi'sa* unless one says *bi'sa al-rajul* or *bi'sa rajulan*." al-Nahhas said: "This is rejected from Abu Hatim's statement. The grammarians have reported: *in fa'alta kadha wa kadha fa-biha wa ni'mat*, meaning: *wa ni'mati al-khislah* (what a fine quality), and the estimated meaning is: *bi'sa al-'adhab* (what a wretched punishment)."

It was also read as *ba'isa* on the pattern of *shahida*, reported by Ya'qub al-Qari', and Abu al-Fadl al-Razi attributed it to 'Isa and Zayd ibn 'Ali.

Jurayyah ibn 'A'id and Nasr ibn 'Asim, in one transmission, read *ba'asa* on the pattern of *daraba*, as a past-tense verb. From al-A'mash and Malik ibn Dinar: *ba'as*, whose origin is *ba'as*, with the hamza made sukun, making it a verb that does not inflect. A group read *bayasa*, with a fatha on the *ba'*, the *ya'* and the *sin*. al-Zahrawi reported from Ibn Kathir and the people of Makkah: *bi'isa*, with a kasrah on the *ba'* and a light hamza, but he did not specify whether the hamza is kasrah or sukun. A group read *basa*, with a fatha on the *ba'* and sukun on the alif. Kharijah from Nafi' and Talhah read *(bayisin)*, on the pattern of *kayl* in its pronunciation, though its original form was *fay'al*, hamzated, but they lightened the hamza by changing it to *ya'*, assimilated, then deleted, like *mayyit*.

Nasr, in the transmission of Malik ibn Dinar from him, read *(ba'sin)* on the pattern of *jabal*. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Musarrif read *ba'-ssa*, on the pattern of *kabbada* and *hadhdhara*. Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat said:

*"Would that I could meet Ruqayyah alone, without the ba'ass."*

Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, and al-A'mash read *(bay'isin)* on the pattern of *dayghamin*. Imru' al-Qays ibn 'Abis al-Kindi said:

*"Both were a chief, fierce (bay'is), striking on the day of battle the helmet."*

'Isa ibn 'Umar and al-A'mash, with a variant from him, read *bay'ish* on the pattern of *saygal*, a woman's name, with a kasrah on the hamza and a kasrah on the qaf, and both are irregular because it is a form restricted to weak-letter roots, like *sayyid* and *mayyit*. Nasr ibn 'Asim, in one transmission, read *baysin* on the pattern of *mayt*, and it was explained as being from *bu's* (misery), with no basis in hamza. It was also explained as lightening the hamza by changing it to *ya'*, then assimilating it. And from him also: *bi'sa*, by changing the *ya'* into a hamza and assimilating it into the hamza. This was reported from al-A'mash. A group read *ba''asa*, with fatha on all three letters and a shadda on the hamza.

The rest of the seven readers, Nafi' in the transmission of Abu Qurrah, 'Asim in the transmission of Hafs, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, Mujahid, al-A'raj, al-A'mash in one transmission, and the people of the Hijaz read *ba'isin* on the pattern of *ra'is*. It was explained as a descriptive word on the pattern of *fa'il* used for intensification, from *ba'is* on the pattern of *fa'il*. This is the reading of Abu Raja' from 'Ali. Or it is a verbal noun described by it, like *nakir* and *qadir*. Abu al-Is'ba' al-'Adwani said:

*"Angry at me, and I see no severe evil (ba'is) from either of them for me."*

The people of Makkah read it the same way, except that they put a kasrah on the *ba'*. This is the dialect of Tamim for *fa'il* words whose 'ayn is a throat letter, where they put a kasrah on the first letter, whether it is a noun or an adjective. al-Hasan and al-A'mash, as alleged by 'Isma, read *ba'isin* on the pattern of *tarim* and *hazim*.

These are twenty-two readings. Summarised: they were read as triliteral and quadriliteral forms. The triliteral as nouns are *bi'sin, baysin, bisin, ba'sin, ba'sin* and *bayasa*, and as verbs *bisa, bi'isa, ba'isa, ba'asa, ba'sa* and *bu'isa*. The quadriliteral as nouns are *bay'isin, bi'ysin, bay'ishin, baysin, bayiyisin, ba'iyisin, ba'ish* and *ba'ish*, and as a verb *ba'asa*.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 166–168:**

﴿So when they persisted in what they had been forbidden, We said to them: "Be apes, despised."﴾ That is, they became defiant. *Utuww* (insolence, obstinacy) means defiance and refusal in a matter. The rest of the verse has already been explained in al-Baqarah. The apparent meaning is that the punishment, the transformation, and the destruction fell only on the transgressors regarding the Sabbath. The community that said, ﴿Why do you admonish a people﴾ [al-A'raf 7:164], were among the group who forbade the evil and were saved. They asked their brethren about the reason for admonishing them, although it was entirely useless with them, since God was going to destroy them or punish them. In that case, admonition becomes like preaching to the stubborn, for they mock whoever admonishes them, and this often leads to the admonisher's harm. According to the view of those who claim that the community that said, "Why do you admonish a people," were the disobedient, they said this mockingly, meaning: "You claim that God will destroy them or punish them." In that case, this community would be among those destroyed and transformed. The apparent meaning of His words, ﴿So when they persisted﴾, is that they were first seized with punishment when they forgot what they had been reminded of, and then, when they persisted, they were transformed. It has also been said that ﴿So when they persisted﴾ repeats His words, ﴿So when they forgot﴾. The "severe punishment" (*al-'adhab al-ba'is*) is the transformation.

﴿And when your Lord declared that He would surely send against them, until the Day of Resurrection, those who would afflict them with a terrible punishment.﴾ When God mentioned the ugliness of their deeds and their defiance, He informed that He had decreed for them humiliation and disgrace until the Day of Resurrection. *Ta'adhdhana* is more than *adhdhana*, which means "to inform." This was the view of al-Hasan and Ibn Qutayba, and was preferred by al-Zajjaj and Abu 'Ali. 'Ata' said: *ta'adhdhana* means "decreed." Qutrub said: "promised." Abu 'Ubayda said: "informed," which returns to the meaning of "informed." Mujahid said: "ordered," and it was also reported from him. It has been said: "swore," and this is reported from al-Zajjaj. Al-Zamakhshari said: *ta'adhdhana* means "resolved," and *rabbuka* is the subject. It is the form *tafa''ala* from *al-iidhan*, which means informing, because one resolved upon a matter speaks to himself and informs himself of his act. It is treated as the verb of an oath, like "God knows" and "God bears witness," and therefore it is answered with what an oath is answered with, which is *la-yab'athanna* ("He will surely send"). The meaning is: "And when your Lord decreed and wrote upon Himself." Ibn 'Atiyya said: The form *ta'adhdhana* requires acquisition (*taksub*), from *adhina*, meaning "knew and was able." When it is attributed to other than God, it carries the sense of acquisition that befalls created beings, but when attributed to God, it means "knowledge," a attribute not acquired but subsisting in His essence. So the meaning is: "And when God knew, He will surely send." The strength of the expression implies that this knowledge from Him is accompanied by execution and enforcement, as you say about a matter you have fully resolved upon: "God knows I will surely do such and such." This was the view of Abu 'Ali al-Farisi. Al-Tabari and others said: *ta'adhdhana* means "informed." This is problematic from the standpoint of morphology, since the attribution of *ta'adhdhana* to the agent differs from that of *a'lama*, and there is a difference between them in transitivity and other respects. End of quote, and there is some abridgement in it.

Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: He informed the prophets of the Children of Israel. *La-yab'athanna* means "He will surely send," and "He will surely empower." This is in line with His words, ﴿We sent against you servants of Ours﴾. The pronoun in ﴿against them﴾ refers to the Jews, as the majority held. Or it refers to both the Jews and the Christians, as Mujahid said. It has also been said that it refers to the offspring of those transformed and those among them who remained. It has also been said that it refers to the Jews of Khaybar, Qurayza, and al-Nadir. On this basis, the disagreement arises over who is meant by ﴿those who would afflict them﴾. It has been said: Bukhtunassar and whoever humiliated them after him until the Day of Resurrection. It has been said: the Magians (Majus), to whom the Jews paid the *jizya* (poll tax levied on non-Muslim subjects) until God sent Muhammad (ﷺ), who imposed it upon them, so it will continue to be imposed upon them until the end of time. It has been said: the Arabs, who used to collect the *kharaj* (tax on land and produce) from the Jews. This was said by Ibn Jubayr. Al-Suddi said: God sent the Arabs against them, who took the *jizya* from them and killed them. Ibn 'Abbas said: The one sent against them is Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community. No prophet ever collected the *kharaj* except Musa, who collected it for thirteen years, then he withheld it for the Prophet (ﷺ). The "terrible punishment" (*su' al-'adhab*) is the *jizya*, or the *jizya* and *maskana* (humiliation), both reported from Ibn 'Abbas, or fighting until they embrace Islam or pay the *jizya* "by hand" while they are humbled. It has also been said that it is expulsion and banishment from their homeland. This is according to the view of those who said that the pronoun in ﴿against them﴾ refers to the people of Khaybar, Qurayza, and al-Nadir. This verse indicates that the Jews have no state and no honor, and that humiliation and disgrace will not leave them. Since it was a report in the time of the Messenger (peace be upon him), and we have witnessed the matter as it is, it was a report of an unseen matter that is true, and thus it is a miracle. As for what has come concerning the followers of the Dajjal (the Antichrist) that they are the Jews, this is by naming them after what they were characterized by, since at that time they will submit to the divinity of the Dajjal. So there is no contradiction between this report, if it is authentic, and the verse. In the book of Ibn 'Atiyya: It has been related to me that a group of the Romans became impoverished in their region, so they sold the Jews who were neighboring them and took possession of them.

Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: He informed the prophets of the Children of Israel. *La-yab'athanna* means "He will surely send," and "He will surely empower." This is in line with His words, ﴿We sent against you servants of Ours﴾. The pronoun in ﴿against them﴾ refers to the Jews, as the majority held. Or it refers to both the Jews and the Christians, as Mujahid said. It has also been said that it refers to the offspring of those transformed and those among them who remained. It has also been said that it refers to the Jews of Khaybar, Qurayza, and al-Nadir. On this basis, the disagreement arises over who is meant by ﴿those who would afflict them﴾. It has been said: Bukhtunassar and whoever humiliated them after him until the Day of Resurrection. It has been said: the Magians (Majus), to whom the Jews paid the *jizya* (poll tax levied on non-Muslim subjects) until God sent Muhammad (ﷺ), who imposed it upon them, so it will continue to be imposed upon them until the end of time. It has been said: the Arabs, who used to collect the *kharaj* (tax on land and produce) from the Jews. This was said by Ibn Jubayr. Al-Suddi said: God sent the Arabs against them, who took the *jizya* from them and killed them. Ibn 'Abbas said: The one sent against them is Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community. No prophet ever collected the *kharaj* except Musa, who collected it for thirteen years, then he withheld it for the Prophet (ﷺ). The "terrible punishment" (*su' al-'adhab*) is the *jizya*, or the *jizya* and *maskana* (humiliation), both reported from Ibn 'Abbas, or fighting until they embrace Islam or pay the *jizya* "by hand" while they are humbled. It has also been said that it is expulsion and banishment from their homeland. This is according to the view of those who said that the pronoun in ﴿against them﴾ refers to the people of Khaybar, Qurayza, and al-Nadir. This verse indicates that the Jews have no state and no honor, and that humiliation and disgrace will not leave them. Since it was a report in the time of the Messenger (peace be upon him), and we have witnessed the matter as it is, it was a report of an unseen matter that is true, and thus it is a miracle. As for what has come concerning the followers of the Dajjal (the Antichrist) that they are the Jews, this is by naming them after what they were characterized by, since at that time they will submit to the divinity of the Dajjal. So there is no contradiction between this report, if it is authentic, and the verse. In the book of Ibn 'Atiyya: It has been related to me that a group of the Romans became impoverished in their region, so they sold the Jews who were neighboring them and took possession of them.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on Surah 7, verse 169:**

﴿Indeed, your Lord is swift in punishment﴾ [Al-A'raf: 167]. This is a statement implying that punishment will descend upon them swiftly.

﴿And indeed He is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾ [Al-A'raf: 167]. This is an encouragement for those among them who believed and for others, and a promise to those who repent and make amends.

﴿And We divided them in the earth into nations: some of them are righteous and some of them are otherwise﴾ [Al-A'raf: 168]. That is, they were divided into separate groups dispersed across the regions of the earth, such that there is hardly a land in which there is not a remnant of them. This is their condition everywhere, under humiliation and abasement, whether the people of that land are Muslims or disbelievers. "Umaman" (nations) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). Al-Ḥawfi said it is a second object (mafʿūl thānī), and this view was mentioned earlier in His saying "We divided them into twelve [tribes]." "The righteous" are those among them who believed in ʿIsa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both, or those who believed in Medina. "Otherwise" refers to those who fall below the righteous, namely the disbelievers. "Dhalika" (that) is a reference to righteousness, meaning: "and among them are those below the people of righteousness." This is because the division is not balanced except under this interpretation, with the omission of a modifier (muḍāf), or the meaning is that by "that" is meant "those," as if He said: "and among them (p. 415) are a people below those." The grammarians have mentioned that the singular demonstrative may be used for the dual and the plural, so that "dhalika" would mean "those" according to this usage, and the division is balanced. The words "the righteous" and "dūna dhalika" (otherwise/below that) are ambiguous. If by righteousness is meant faith, then "dūna dhalika" means the disbelievers. If by righteousness is meant worship, goodness and the consequences of faith, then "dūna dhalika" refers to believers who did not reach the rank of righteousness that those others attained. The more apparent of the two possibilities is the first, because of His saying "so that they may return" (la'allahum yarji'un), since the apparent meaning of His saying "And We tested them" is that they are the people who are below those, namely those who held firmly to Judaism and departed from faith. "Dūna dhalika" is an adverbial expression whose original use is for place, then it is used for a lowering in rank. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "If by righteousness is meant faith, then 'dūna dhalika' has the meaning of 'other than,' by which the disbelievers are meant," (end of quote). If he meant that "dūn" is synonymous with "ghayr" (other than), then this is not correct. If he meant that whoever is below something necessarily is other than it, then this is correct. "Dūna" is an adverb in a position of nominative as an adjective (naʿt) to an omitted noun being described. In a detailed statement with "min" (among), it is permissible to omit the described noun and place its description in its stead, as in this example and in the saying of the Arabs: "Some of us departed and some of us stayed" (minnā ẓaʿana wa minnā aqāma).

﴿And We tested them with good things and bad things﴾ [Al-A'raf: 168]. That is, with health, ease and abundance, and the bad things are their opposites.

﴿So that they might return﴾ [Al-A'raf: 168], to obedience, and repent from disobedience.

﴿Then there succeeded them a succession who inherited the Book, taking the goods of this lower life and saying, "It will be forgiven us"﴾. That is, after those mentioned there came a successor (khalf). Al-Zajjaj said: "The generation that comes after a generation is called a khalf." Al-Farra' said: "Khalf is a generation, and khalf is one who is made a successor." Thaʿlab said: "All people say: 'a khalf of righteousness' for the righteous and 'a khalf of evil' for the wicked." And from this is the saying of the poet:

*They have gone, those among whose protection one lived, and I remain in a khalf like the skin of a mangy camel.*

And the proverb: "He was silent a thousand [years] and then spoke a khalf," meaning: he was silent for a long time, then spoke with corrupt speech. From al-Farra': "Khalf is used in a derogatory sense, while khalaf is a good successor." The poet said:

*You left behind a khalf and did not leave a khalaf; you were with them, not you, the destruction.*

Khalf may also be used for the bad, as in the saying:

*Is not that the one-eyed khalf?* And for the good, khalf is also used. On this is the verse of Hassan:

*For us is the first step over them, and our khalf follows our first in obedience to God.*

Ibn al-Sikkit said: "It is said 'this is a khalf of righteousness' and 'this is a khalf of evil.' It is permissible to say 'these are a khalf of righteousness' and 'these are a khalf of evil,' and its singular and plural are the same." The poet said:

*Indeed we found a khalf, the worst of successors, a servant who, when the load is heavy, stands aside.*

(p. 416) (end of quote). He combined both dialects in the word for destruction in this verse. Al-Naḍr ibn Shumayl said: "Both vocalizations (al-taḥrīk and al-iskān) are used in the Qur'an for 'al-radā' (destruction), but for 'al-ṣāliḥ' (righteous) only the vowelled form is used." Most lexicographers agree with this except al-Farra' and Abu ʿUbayda, who permitted the sukun in ṣāliḥ. Khalaf is either a verbal noun of khalafa; for this reason it is not dualized, pluralized or feminized, even if what precedes it is dualized, pluralized or feminized. As for the plural of khālif (one who succeeds), like rākib/rakb (rider/riders) and shārib/shurb (drinker/drinkers), this was stated by Ibn al-Anbari, but it is not correct, since it follows the singular, whereas a collective noun (ism al-jam') does not follow the singular. Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Zayd said: "Here they are the Jews." Al-Zamakhshari said: "They are those who lived in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ. 'They inherited the Book' means the Torah, which remained in their hands after their predecessors; they read it and understood its commands, prohibitions, forbidden and permitted matters, but did not act upon it." Al-Tabari said: "They are the sons of the Jews." From Mujahid: they are the Christians. And from him also: they are this nation (the Muslims). Al-Hasan read "wūrrithū" (were given as inheritance) with a damma on the waw and a shadda on the ra'. According to these views, the "Book" may be understood as the Torah, the Gospel, or the Qur'an. "The goods of this lower life" refers to what they took of bribes and corrupt gains. "ʿArḍ" (goods) is what appears and does not last. In His saying "the goods of this lower life," there is a disparagement and belittling of what they took, and that they, despite their knowledge of the threats in their Book against sins, would prefer, for the sake of the common people, to alter and distort the Book, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then they say, "This is from God," to acquire for it a small price﴾ [Al-Baqara: 79]. "Al-adna" (the lower) comes from "dunuw" (nearness), which means closeness, because that is near, transient and passes away. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Or it may be from the nearness, decline and paltriness of the state." "And they say, 'It will be forgiven us'" is a definite claim, on God's part, of forgiveness for their sins, meaning: God will not hold us accountable for that. The fitting response, given that they inherited the Book, would be to act upon what is in it, and that if they were judged to be sinners, they should not be certain of forgiveness while persisting in committing it. "Lanā" (for us) occupies the position of the object of the passive verb (the agent not named). It is also said that the pronoun refers to the verbal noun of "yaʾkhudhūn" (taking), meaning: "it (the taking) will be forgiven for us."

﴿And if there comes to them goods like it, they will take it﴾. The apparent meaning is that this is a resumptive statement (isti'nāf) informing about them, that they are immersed in sins; even if bribes and corrupt gains were available to them, they would not hesitate to take them again, and they are constantly persisting in sins, unconcerned with the threat that has come. The wicked person is one who follows his soul's desires and wishes for things from God. "ʿAraḍ" (with a fatḥa on the ra') is the goods of this world, as said by Abu ʿUbayda; it is said: "The world is present goods, which the pious and the wicked alike take from." "ʿArḍ" (with a sukun on the ra') means dirhams and dinars, which are the capital and the value of destroyed property. Al-Suddi said: "They used to bribe the judge, and when the briber had turned away, he would take a bribe." It was also said: "If a litigant brought them a payment as a bribe, they would take it, and they would overturn with the second bribe what they had decided with the first." The poet said:

*When oil is poured into the lamp, the case turns in favor of the one who lit the lamp.*

Another said:

*People have not opened doors, nor known anything more effective and successful in needs than a tray. If one covers it with a napkin and places it on a tray, he need not fear the doorkeeper's rebuff or the lock.*

And for this nation there is a generous share of this verse. The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "You will surely follow the ways of those before you." Whoever examines the condition of its scholars, judges and muftis will witness with his own eyes what the Truthful One reported. Al-Zamakhshari said: "The waw is for the circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning in 'and if there comes to them' (wa in ya'tihim): they hope for forgiveness while they persist, returning to the like of their saying, not forgetting. Forgiveness of sins is not valid except with repentance, and the persistent one has no forgiveness," (end of quote). Interpreting the waw as a circumstantial marker rather than a conjunction is the doctrine of the Mu'tazila (rationalist school). The apparent meaning is what we have previously mentioned, and it is not refuted by the claim that the conditional clause cannot be a circumstantial clause, because that is permissible.

﴿Was not a covenant of the Book taken from them, that they would not say of God except the truth, and they studied what is in it?﴾ This is a rebuke and an affirmation of what the Book contains concerning the taking of the covenant, that they would not lie about God. Ibn Zayd said: "The one with a right claim would come to them with a bribe (p. 417), and they would bring out the Book of God for him and rule in his favor by it. When the wrongdoer came, they took a bribe from him, brought out their own book which they had written with their hands, and ruled in his favor." The covenant is attributed to the Book because it stated that they should not say of God except the truth. Some said: it is their saying "It will be forgiven us," but this is not restricted to that; rather it is more general than this saying and others, so that the definite claim of forgiveness and others are included in it. "An lā yaqūlū" (that they not say) is in the nominative position as a substitute (badal) for "covenant of the Book." Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) for 'covenant of the Book,' and its meaning is the covenant mentioned in the Book." In this there is the claim that asserting forgiveness without repentance is a departure from the covenant of the Book, a fabrication against God, and a saying of what is not true about Him. If the covenant of the Book is interpreted as what was mentioned earlier, then "an lā yaqūlū" is in the accusative as an object of purpose, meaning "lest they say." It is also permissible for it to be an explanatory clause, with "lā yaqūlū" as a prohibition, as if it was said: "Did He not say to you, 'Do not say of God except the truth'?" He also said earlier: "the covenant of the Book" meaning His saying in the Torah: "Whoever commits a great sin, he will not be forgiven except by repentance." "And they studied what is in it" means what is in the Book regarding the condition of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. What the compeller (mujbir, i.e., the determinist) adopts is exactly the doctrine of the Jews, as you see. Malik ibn Dinar, may God have mercy on him, said: "There will come upon people a time when, if they fall short of what they were commanded, they will say: 'It will be forgiven us, we will not associate anything with God.' Their whole affair will be based on hope; the best of them will be those who flatter." These people from this nation are similar to those whom God mentioned, and he recited the verse. (End of quote.) This is in the manner of the Mu'tazila. His saying "except the truth" is evidence that they used to say falsehood in pursuit of the goods of this world. "And they studied" is conjoined to His saying "Was not a covenant taken from them." In this there is the greatest rebuke and reproach, namely that they repeated what is in the Book and knew what is in it with complete knowledge of the threat against speaking falsehood and fabricating against God. This conjunction is for the purpose of reaffirmation, because its meaning is: "A covenant of the Book has been taken from them, and they have studied what is in it." Like His saying: ﴿Did We not raise you among us as a child, and you remained [with us] for years?﴾ [Al-Shu'ara: 18], meaning: "We have raised you and you remained." Al-Tabari and others said: it is conjoined to His saying "and they inherited the Book," but this is far-fetched. It was also said: it is with the implied "qad" (indeed), meaning "and indeed they studied what is in it." That it is conjoined to the reaffirmation is the apparent view, because in it is the meaning of establishing the proof against them, in that they took the covenant of the Book, by having memorized its wording and repeated it, and they did not forget it and understood its meaning, yet they say nothing but falsehood. ʿAbd Allah al-Jaḥdarī recited "an lā taqūlū" with the second-person "t". ʿAli and al-Sulami read "wa-ddārasū," whose origin is "wa-tadārasū" (and they studied one another), like His saying "fa-ddārāʾtum" (you disputed one another), meaning "tadārāʾtum." This has been explained in Arabic grammar. This reading clarifies that the meaning of "and they studied what is in it" is repetition of its recitation and continual attention to it, and that the interpretation of those who understood "wa-darasū mā fīhi" as "they erased it by abandoning action and understanding it" is far-fetched, from the saying: "the wind erased the traces" when it wipes them away. If that were the meaning, one would say "rabʿ madrūs" (an erased campsite) and "khaṭṭ madrūs" (an erased line), but they say "rabʿ dāris" (a worn campsite) and "khaṭṭ dāris" with the meaning of "effaced."

﴿And the Last Abode is better for those who fear God. Will you not reason?﴾ That is: the reward of the Last Abode is better than that foul, vile bribe, which brings disgrace in this world and the next. The meaning of "those who are God-conscious" (yattaqūn) is those who guard against God's prohibitions. Abu ʿAmr and the people of Mecca read "yaʿqilūn" (they reason) with the "y," following the third-person pronouns preceding it. The majority read it with the second person (you reason), following the shift of address (iltifāt) towards them, or following the address to this nation, as if it were said: "Will you not reason about the condition of these people, and what they are upon of evil deeds, and marvel at their boldness in that?"

The apparent meaning is that *al-Kitab* ("the Book") is the one mentioned earlier in: ﴿ورِثُوا الكِتَابَ﴾ ("they inherited the Book"). The disagreement over it is therefore the same as the disagreement over that phrase, and it depends on the intended meaning of ﴿خَلْفٌ ورِثُوا﴾ ("a successor generation inherited it") [al-A'raf: 169]. It has also been said that *al-Kitab* here is generic (*li-l-jins*), meaning the divine scriptures. Holding fast to the Book necessarily entails establishing the prayer (*iqamat al-salah*), but the prayer is singled out for mention to magnify its status, since it is the pillar of the religion. Between the servant and shirk stands the abandonment of prayer.

ʿUmar, Abu al-ʿAliyah, and Abu Bakr (on the authority of ʿAsim) read ﴿يُمْسِكُونَ﴾ from *amsaka* (to hold). The majority read ﴿يُمَسِّكُونَ﴾, with the doubled letter, from *massaka*. Both are dialectal variants (*lughatan*), and Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr combined them when he said:

"So he did not hold fast (*tamassaka*) to the covenant they claimed,
except as the sieves (*al-gharabil*) hold (*yumsiku*) water."

*Amsaka* is transitive, as in ﴿ويُمْسِكُ السَّماءَ أنْ تَقَعَ عَلى الأرْضِ﴾ ("and He holds back the sky from falling upon the earth") [al-Hajj: 65]. On this reading the object is omitted, so the meaning is ﴿يُمْسِكُونَ أعْمالَهم﴾ ("they hold their deeds"), that is, they keep them under control (*yadbutunaha*). On this reading the *ba'* (with) may be either circumstantial (*hal*) or instrumental (*alah*). *Massaka*, with the doubled letter, has the sense of *tamassaka* (to hold fast), and the *ba'* with it is instrumental. The grammarians of morphology (*al-tasrifiyyun*) state explicitly that *fa''ala* can come with the meaning of *tafa''ala*.

ʿAbd Allah and al-Aʿmash read *istamsakū*, and in the codex of Ubayy it is *tamassakū bi-l-Kitab*.

The apparent reading is that ﴿والَّذِينَ﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf ikhbar*). Having mentioned the condition of those who did not hold fast to the Book, the verse now mentions the condition of those who did. On this reading ﴿والَّذِينَ﴾ is in the nominative as a subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate (*khabar*) is the sentence that follows it. This is like His saying: ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وعَمِلُوا الصّالِحاتِ إنّا لا نُضِيعُ أجْرَ مَن أحْسَنَ عَمَلًا﴾ ("Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, indeed We do not allow to be lost the reward of one who does good work") [al-Kahf: 30]. When the connecting element (*al-rabt*) is taken to be the generality in ﴿مَن أحْسَنَ عَمَلًا﴾, the same applies here, and the connecting element is the generality in ﴿المُصْلِحِينَ﴾.

Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' said: the connecting element is omitted, its estimated form being ﴿أجْرُ المُصْلِحِينَ﴾ as a parenthetical clause (*i'tiraḍ*), and the estimate is "they are rewarded" (*ma'jurun*) or "We reward them" (*na'juruhum*). End of quotation. But there is no necessity to claim an omission. Abu al-Baqa' also permitted that the connecting element be ﴿المُصْلِحِينَ﴾ itself, placed in the position of a pronoun, meaning ﴿لا نُضِيعُ أجْرَهُمُ﴾ ("We do not allow their reward to be lost"). End of quotation. This is according to the opinion of al-Akhfash, who permitted a connecting element in the form of a noun when it is the subject itself, so that he allowed "Zayd, Abu ʿAmr stood up" when Abu ʿAmr is Zayd's kunyah, as if he had said "Zayd, that is, he stood up."

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that ﴿والَّذِينَ﴾ be in the genitive position, coordinated with ﴿الَّذِينَ يَتَّقُونَ﴾ ("those who fear God"). Ibn ʿAtiyyah mentioned no other possibility. The resumptive reading is the apparent one, as we have said.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 171–174 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when We raised the mountain over them as though it were a canopy, and they thought it would fall upon them: "Take what We have given you with strength, and remember what is in it, that you may be mindful of God."﴾ ﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes, we testify." Lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection: "We were indeed unaware of this."﴾ ﴿Or lest you should say: "Our fathers only associated partners with God before, and we were their descendants after them. Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?"﴾ ﴿Thus do We detail the signs, that they may return.﴾ ﴿And recite to them the news of the one to whom We gave Our signs, but he detached himself from them, so Satan pursued him, and he became one of the misguided.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 175] ﴿Had We willed, We would have raised him by them, but he clung to the earth and followed his desire. His likeness is that of the dog: if you attack it, it pants, or if you leave it, it pants. That is the likeness of the people who denied Our signs. So relate the stories, that they may reflect.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 176] ﴿Evil is the likeness of the people who denied Our signs, and they were wronging themselves.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 177] ﴿Whomever God guides, he is the one guided, and whomever He misguides, those are the losers.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 178] ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and humankind. They have hearts with which they do not understand, eyes with which they do not see, and ears with which they do not hear. Those are like livestock; rather, they are further astray. Those are the heedless.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 179] ﴿To God belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them, and leave those who deviate concerning His names. They will be recompensed for what they used to do.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 180] ﴿And among those We created is a community that guides by the truth and acts justly by it.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 181] ﴿And those who denied Our signs, We will draw them gradually from where they do not know.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 182] ﴿And I will give them respite; indeed, My plan is firm.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 183] ﴿Have they not reflected? There is no madness in their companion; he is only a clear warner.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 184] ﴿Have they not looked into the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and at what God has created of things, and that perhaps their term has drawn near? Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾ [Al-A'raf: 185] ﴿Whomever God misguides, there is none to guide him, and He leaves them in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 186] ﴿They ask you about the Hour: "When will it take place?" Say: "Its knowledge is only with my Lord. None will reveal it at its time except Him. It is heavy upon the heavens and the earth. It will not come upon you except suddenly." They ask you as though you were well-informed about it. Say: "Its knowledge is only with God, but most people do not know."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 187]

The word "نَتْق" (naṭq) means pulling with force. Some have explained it by its result, which is uprooting. The Arabs say: "I pulled the butter out of the mouth of the waterskin" (nataqtu al-zubda min fami al-qirba). The "nāṭiq" is the womb that expels the child from the man. Al-Nabigha said:

*They were not deprived of the goodness of ransom, and their mother overflowed upon you with a male-begetting womb.*

In a hadith: "Choose for yourselves virgins, for their wombs are more expelling, their mouths sweeter, and they are more content with little."

"الانسلاخ" (inslakh) means to be stripped bare of a thing so that nothing of it clings to you, and from it comes: "the snake sloughed its skin" (insalakhat al-hayya min jildiha).

The dog (al-kalb) is a well-known animal. In the paucity plural it is "aklub," and in the abundance plural "kilab." Some irregular plurals are formed with the suffix alif-ta', as in "kilabat." This root has been discussed earlier in "mukallibin," and I repeat it for added benefit. "Lahatha al-kalb yalhathu" (with fatha on both letters, in past and present) means the dog extended its tongue. The verbal noun is "lahth" or "luhth" (with ḍamma). It is the state of the dog in fatigue and rest, thirst and quenching alike, unlike other animals, which pant only from exhaustion or thirst.

"لحد" and "ألحد" are two dialectal forms. It is said they have the same meaning: deviating from the truth and introducing into it what is not part of it. Ibn al-Sikkit said this. Others said: deviating from uprightness. The quadriliteral form is more common in usage than the triliteral. A poet said:

*The commander is not a miser who deviates.*

From this comes "laḥada al-qabr," meaning to incline the grave toward one of its sides. In their speech, when a single person does something, they say: "laḥadahu al-laḥid" (the one who dug the grave inclined it for him). It is also said "alḥada" means to incline and deviate, while "laḥada" means to lean on and take refuge in. Al-Kisa'i said this.

"متن" (matana) means to become firm and strong.

"أيّان" (ayyan) is an adverb of time, indeclinable, used mostly in interrogation. It is followed by a noun in the nominative as subject, and by an imperfect verb, not a perfect one, unlike "mata," which is followed by either. God says: "أيّان يُبْعَثُونَ" (When will they be raised?). And: "أيّان مُرْساها" (When will it arrive?). A poet said:

*When will my need be fulfilled, when? Do you not see its time has come?*

It is also used in conditional sentences, jussifying the two imperfect verbs, but this is rare. Sibawayh did not record it, but others did, and they cited the poet's words:

*When the lean she-camel spends the night in a barren land, wherever the wind turns her, she will alight.*

Another said:

*When we give you security, you will be secure in our absence, but if you do not attain security from us, you will remain wary.*

The kasra of its initial hamza is the dialect of Sulaym. In my view it is a simple, not compound, particle, and an inflexible, not derived, word. The author of "Kitab al-Lawami'" mentioned that "ayyan" was originally "ayyu awan" (which time). Since it was used so often, the hamza was dropped without analogy or compensation, the waw became ya', three ya's gathered, and one was removed, so it became what you see. That is the end of his words. Abu al-Fath claimed it is "fa'lan" and "fa'lal," derived from "ayy," meaning "which time" and "which act," from "awaytu ilayhi" (I took refuge in him), because the part takes refuge in the whole, leaning upon it. He ruled out that it is "fa'al" or "fa'\"al" from "ayna" (where), because "ayyan" is an adverb of time and "ayna" is an adverb of place. This required that it come from the word "ayy" with the addition of the nun. Also, "ayyan" is an interrogative, as is "ayy," and the default is non-compounding. Interrogative and conditional particles are inflexible, like "mata," "haythuma," "anna," and "idha."

"رسا يرسو" means to be fixed and stable.

"الحفي" (al-ḥafiyy) is one who seeks out a thing thoroughly, who cares about it and takes pains with it. "Fulan ḥafiyy bi" means he is kind to me and attentive. A poet said:

*When we met, the sword separated us, for the one who asks about us is earnest in her question.*

Another said:

*A question of one who is solicitous about his brother, as though he, in his remembrance of him, were drowsy or half-asleep.*

"الإحفاء" (al-iḥfa') means thoroughness, from which comes "iḥfa' al-shārib" (trimming the moustache thoroughly). "al-ḥāfī" means his feet became worn for thoroughness in walking. "al-ḥafāwa" means kindness and gentleness.

﴿And when We raised the mountain over them and they thought it would fall upon them﴾: that is, We pulled the mountain with force. "Fawqahum" (over them) is a delayed circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddara), and its governing element is omitted. Its estimate is: "being over them," since the state of pulling did not coincide with being above; rather, it became above them. Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' said: "fawqahum" is an adverbial of place for "nataqna" (We pulled). This is only possible if "nataqna" is taken to include a meaning of a verb that can govern "fawqahum," that is, "We raised the mountain over them by pulling," so it is like His words: ﴿And We raised the Mount above them﴾ [An-Nisa': 154]. The clause "ka'annahu ẓullah" (as though it were a canopy) is in the place of a circumstantial clause. The meaning is: "as though it were a canopy over them." A "ẓulla" is what shades from a roof or a cloud. The comparison should be understood as referring to a particular kind of canopy, because if every shading thing is called a canopy, then the mountain above them became a canopy, and if it became a canopy, how can it be compared to a canopy? So the meaning, God knows best, is: "as though, at the time of its elevation over them, it was a canopy of cloud," that is, the canopy that has no pillars beneath it, but whose holding aloft is by divine power, even though they are solid bodies. This is unlike the earthly canopy, which can only exist on pillars. When this earthly shadow was held above them without pillars, it was compared to the cloud canopy that has no pillars. It is also said: humans were accustomed to these earthly bodies as canopies, since they stood on pillars. When the mountain was raised without pillars, it was said: "as though it were a canopy," that is, as though it stood on pillars. It is read "ṭulla" with ṭa', from "aṭalla 'alayhi," meaning to look down upon it. And "ẓannū" (they thought) here remains in its original sense, by preferring one of the two permissible meanings. The commentators said: it means "they were certain." Al-Zamakhshari said: "they knew." That is not so; rather, it is a predominant assumption with the hope remaining, unless it is restricted to the condition that they did not understand the Torah, in which case it means "mastering." The cause of raising the mountain over them was mentioned earlier in the explanation of His words "And We raised the Mount over you" in al-Baqara, so there is no need to repeat it. The commentators repeated it here, including al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, and others. Al-Zamakhshari, at the mention of the cause here, said: when Musa, peace be upon him, displayed the tablets, in which was the Book of God, no tree, mountain, or stone remained without trembling. Therefore you do not see a Jew reading the Torah without swaying and nodding his head. That is the end of his words. This tendency has spread, as far as I have observed in Egypt, to the children of the Muslims. You see them in the maktab (Qur'anic school), when they recite the Qur'an, swaying and moving their heads. As for our lands in al-Andalus and the West, if a child moved while reciting the Qur'an, the teacher of the maktab would discipline him and say: "Do not move, lest you resemble the Jews in their study."

* *

﴿Take what We have given you with strength, and remember what is in it, that you may be mindful of God.﴾ Al-A'mash read "wa-idhdhakkarū" (with shadda, from "idhdhakar"). Ibn Mas'ud read "wa-tadhkurū," and it was also read "wa-tadhakkarū" with shadda, meaning "wa-tadhdhakkarū." The explanation of these phrases was given earlier in al-Baqara.

﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes."﴾ It has been narrated in the hadith through several chains: "He took from the back of Adam his descendants, and took from them the covenant that He is their Lord and that there is no god but Him, so they acknowledged that and committed themselves to it." The scholars differed about the manner of the taking out, the form of what was taken out, the place and the time. The establishing of these matters belongs to that hadith and its discussion. The apparent meaning of this verse contradicts the apparent meaning of that hadith, and its wording does not agree with the wording of the verse. Some groups have attempted to reconcile the verse and the hadith through interpretation that is strained. The best thing said about this verse is what al-Zamakhshari explained: it is of the type of figurative representation and imagery. The meaning is that God set up for them the proofs of His lordship and oneness, and their intellects and insights, which He placed within them and made distinguishing between error and guidance, bore witness to them. So it is as though He, glory be to Him, made them testify against themselves and established it for them, and said: "Am I not your Lord?" And it is as though they said: "Yes, You are our Lord. We testify against ourselves and acknowledge Your oneness." The scope of figurative speech is wide in the words of God and His Messenger, and in Arab speech. Its parallel is the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it "Be," and it is﴾ [An-Nahl: 40], and ﴿He said to it and to the earth: "Come, willingly or unwillingly." They said: "We come willingly."﴾ [Fussilat: 11]. And the saying of the poet:

*When the halters say to the belly, "Be stilled," the morning breeze says to it, "Be cool."*

And it is well known that there was no actual speech there. Rather, this is an illustration and a depiction of the meaning. The phrase *an taqulu* ("lest you say") is an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*, the object expressing the reason for an action). The meaning is: We established the proofs, which the intellects bear witness to as sound, out of concern that you might say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were unaware of this and were not warned about it." Its implied sense is: "We were heedless of this and were not alerted to it." Or [the purpose is] lest you say, "Only our fathers associated partners with God before us, and we were their offspring after them, so we followed them." This is because the establishment of proofs for monotheism (*tawhid*, the affirmation of God's oneness) and what they were alerted to remained present with them. Therefore they have no excuse for turning away from it, for clinging to blind imitation (*taqlid*), and for following their fathers. Likewise, their fathers have no excuse for associating partners with God, since the proofs of monotheism were set up for them as well.

(If you ask): Who are "the children of Adam" and "their offspring"? I say: By "the children of Adam" is meant the ancestors of the Jews who associated partners with God, the Most High, when they said, "Ezra is the son of God." By "their offspring" is meant those who were in the time of the Messenger of God from among their descendants, who followed their fathers. The evidence that this refers to the polytheists and their children is His statement, the Most High: ﴿Or lest you say: "Only our fathers associated partners with God before us"﴾. The evidence that it refers to the Jews is that the verses it is connected to, and the verses connected to them, are of the same pattern and style. This is seen in His statement: ﴿And ask them about the town﴾ [al-A'raf: 163]; ﴿And when a community among them said﴾ [al-A'raf: 164]; ﴿And when your Lord proclaimed﴾ [al-A'raf: 167]; ﴿And when We raised the mountain above them﴾; ﴿And recite to them the story of the one to whom We gave Our signs﴾ [al-A'raf: 175]. This is the end of al-Zamakhshari's words, and it is an elaboration of the words of those before him.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: Some people said: The verse points to this interpretation, which applies to the worldly life. [They] took the meaning of *awjada* (to bring into existence), and that the two acts of testimony [occur] when the person reaches legal responsibility (*taklif*), at which point he has been given understanding and the sign indicating the Creator has been set up for him. Al-Zajjaj inclined toward this view, and it is a meaning that the wording permits. [End of Ibn 'Atiyya's words.] Yet taking the apparent meaning of the hadith leads to the doctrine of metempsychosis (*tanasukh*, the transmigration of souls), so it must be interpreted.

The object of *akhadha* (took) is *dhurriyyatahum*, as al-Hawfi said. It is possible, in the reading of all of them, that the object of *akhadha* is omitted because the meaning is understood, and *dhurriyyatihim* is a substitute (*badal*) for the pronoun in *zuhurihim* (their backs), just as *min zuhurihim* is a substitute for *bani Adam* (the children of Adam). The omitted object is the covenant (*mithaq*), as He said: ﴿And We took from them a solemn covenant﴾ [al-Nisa': 154], and ﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: "You shall not worship except God"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83]. The sense of the passage is: And when your Lord took from the backs of the offspring of the children of Adam a covenant of monotheism, [affirming] that God is one and that He alone is to be worshipped. He used the metaphor that the covenant was taken from the back, as if the covenant, because of its difficulty, its binding nature, and the obligation it places upon one, were a heavy thing carried upon the back. This is an illustration of the meaning with certainty. He made them bear witness against themselves through the proofs He had set up for them, saying: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes."

The two 'Arabi readers (*al-'Arabiyan*, the two readers identified as such in the tradition) and Nafi' read *dhurriyyatihim* in the plural. Its grammatical inflection (*i'rab*, the grammatical case-endings) was discussed earlier. The remaining seven readers read *dhurriyyatahum* in the singular, with a *fatha* on the *ta'*. It must be the object of *akhadha*, and it involves an omitted *mudaf* (a noun in a genitive construction that is dropped), i.e., *mithaq dhurriyyatihim* (the covenant of their offspring). The covenant was taken from the offspring of the children of Adam because the children of Adam in his lineage did not include any polytheist; rather, polytheism arose among their descendants.

"That you may say on the Day of Resurrection: 'We were indeed unaware of this.'" That is, God said: "We bear witness against you." Or God and the angels said it, as al-Suddi reported. Or the angels said it. Or some of them bore witness against others, according to some sayings. The meaning of "of this" ("'an hadha") is: of this covenant and the acknowledgment of Lordship.

﴿Or lest you say: "Only our fathers associated partners with God before us, and we were their offspring after them."﴾ The meaning is that if no covenant had been taken from them, and no messenger had come to remind them of what the covenant contained regarding God's oneness and worship, they would have had two arguments: first, "We were heedless"; and second, "We were followers of our ancestors." So how would we perish, when the sin belongs only to the one who established the path for us and led us astray? Therefore the testimony came to cut off their arguments. Abu 'Amr read *an yaqulu* ("lest they say") with the *ya'* (third person), and the remaining seven read it with the *ta'* (second person).

﴿Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?﴾ This is part of the second statement. That is, they were the cause of our association of partners, because they established polytheism, took the lead in it, and left it as a precedent for us. The meaning is that He, the Most High, removed their pretext of argument by placing intellects within them and reminding them through the sending of messengers to them, and thus He cut off their excuses.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 171–174 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when We raised the mountain over them as though it were a canopy, and they thought it would fall upon them: "Take what We have given you with strength, and remember what is in it, that you may be mindful of God."﴾ ﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes, we testify." Lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection: "We were indeed unaware of this."﴾ ﴿Or lest you should say: "Our fathers only associated partners with God before, and we were their descendants after them. Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?"﴾ ﴿Thus do We detail the signs, that they may return.﴾ ﴿And recite to them the news of the one to whom We gave Our signs, but he detached himself from them, so Satan pursued him, and he became one of the misguided.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 175] ﴿Had We willed, We would have raised him by them, but he clung to the earth and followed his desire. His likeness is that of the dog: if you attack it, it pants, or if you leave it, it pants. That is the likeness of the people who denied Our signs. So relate the stories, that they may reflect.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 176] ﴿Evil is the likeness of the people who denied Our signs, and they were wronging themselves.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 177] ﴿Whomever God guides, he is the one guided, and whomever He misguides, those are the losers.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 178] ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and humankind. They have hearts with which they do not understand, eyes with which they do not see, and ears with which they do not hear. Those are like livestock; rather, they are further astray. Those are the heedless.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 179] ﴿To God belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them, and leave those who deviate concerning His names. They will be recompensed for what they used to do.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 180] ﴿And among those We created is a community that guides by the truth and acts justly by it.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 181] ﴿And those who denied Our signs, We will draw them gradually from where they do not know.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 182] ﴿And I will give them respite; indeed, My plan is firm.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 183] ﴿Have they not reflected? There is no madness in their companion; he is only a clear warner.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 184] ﴿Have they not looked into the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and at what God has created of things, and that perhaps their term has drawn near? Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾ [Al-A'raf: 185] ﴿Whomever God misguides, there is none to guide him, and He leaves them in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 186] ﴿They ask you about the Hour: "When will it take place?" Say: "Its knowledge is only with my Lord. None will reveal it at its time except Him. It is heavy upon the heavens and the earth. It will not come upon you except suddenly." They ask you as though you were well-informed about it. Say: "Its knowledge is only with God, but most people do not know."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 187]

The word "نَتْق" (naṭq) means pulling with force. Some have explained it by its result, which is uprooting. The Arabs say: "I pulled the butter out of the mouth of the waterskin" (nataqtu al-zubda min fami al-qirba). The "nāṭiq" is the womb that expels the child from the man. Al-Nabigha said:

*They were not deprived of the goodness of ransom, and their mother overflowed upon you with a male-begetting womb.*

In a hadith: "Choose for yourselves virgins, for their wombs are more expelling, their mouths sweeter, and they are more content with little."

"الانسلاخ" (inslakh) means to be stripped bare of a thing so that nothing of it clings to you, and from it comes: "the snake sloughed its skin" (insalakhat al-hayya min jildiha).

The dog (al-kalb) is a well-known animal. In the paucity plural it is "aklub," and in the abundance plural "kilab." Some irregular plurals are formed with the suffix alif-ta', as in "kilabat." This root has been discussed earlier in "mukallibin," and I repeat it for added benefit. "Lahatha al-kalb yalhathu" (with fatha on both letters, in past and present) means the dog extended its tongue. The verbal noun is "lahth" or "luhth" (with ḍamma). It is the state of the dog in fatigue and rest, thirst and quenching alike, unlike other animals, which pant only from exhaustion or thirst.

"لحد" and "ألحد" are two dialectal forms. It is said they have the same meaning: deviating from the truth and introducing into it what is not part of it. Ibn al-Sikkit said this. Others said: deviating from uprightness. The quadriliteral form is more common in usage than the triliteral. A poet said:

*The commander is not a miser who deviates.*

From this comes "laḥada al-qabr," meaning to incline the grave toward one of its sides. In their speech, when a single person does something, they say: "laḥadahu al-laḥid" (the one who dug the grave inclined it for him). It is also said "alḥada" means to incline and deviate, while "laḥada" means to lean on and take refuge in. Al-Kisa'i said this.

"متن" (matana) means to become firm and strong.
