(If you ask): Who are "the children of Adam" and "their offspring"? I say: By "the children of Adam" is meant the ancestors of the Jews who associated partners with God, the Most High, when they said, "Ezra is the son of God." By "their offspring" is meant those who were in the time of the Messenger of God from among their descendants, who followed their fathers. The evidence that this refers to the polytheists and their children is His statement, the Most High: ﴿Or lest you say: "Only our fathers associated partners with God before us"﴾. The evidence that it refers to the Jews is that the verses it is connected to, and the verses connected to them, are of the same pattern and style. This is seen in His statement: ﴿And ask them about the town﴾ [al-A'raf: 163]; ﴿And when a community among them said﴾ [al-A'raf: 164]; ﴿And when your Lord proclaimed﴾ [al-A'raf: 167]; ﴿And when We raised the mountain above them﴾; ﴿And recite to them the story of the one to whom We gave Our signs﴾ [al-A'raf: 175]. This is the end of al-Zamakhshari's words, and it is an elaboration of the words of those before him.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: Some people said: The verse points to this interpretation, which applies to the worldly life. [They] took the meaning of *awjada* (to bring into existence), and that the two acts of testimony [occur] when the person reaches legal responsibility (*taklif*), at which point he has been given understanding and the sign indicating the Creator has been set up for him. Al-Zajjaj inclined toward this view, and it is a meaning that the wording permits. [End of Ibn 'Atiyya's words.] Yet taking the apparent meaning of the hadith leads to the doctrine of metempsychosis (*tanasukh*, the transmigration of souls), so it must be interpreted.

The object of *akhadha* (took) is *dhurriyyatahum*, as al-Hawfi said. It is possible, in the reading of all of them, that the object of *akhadha* is omitted because the meaning is understood, and *dhurriyyatihim* is a substitute (*badal*) for the pronoun in *zuhurihim* (their backs), just as *min zuhurihim* is a substitute for *bani Adam* (the children of Adam). The omitted object is the covenant (*mithaq*), as He said: ﴿And We took from them a solemn covenant﴾ [al-Nisa': 154], and ﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: "You shall not worship except God"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83]. The sense of the passage is: And when your Lord took from the backs of the offspring of the children of Adam a covenant of monotheism, [affirming] that God is one and that He alone is to be worshipped. He used the metaphor that the covenant was taken from the back, as if the covenant, because of its difficulty, its binding nature, and the obligation it places upon one, were a heavy thing carried upon the back. This is an illustration of the meaning with certainty. He made them bear witness against themselves through the proofs He had set up for them, saying: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes."

The two 'Arabi readers (*al-'Arabiyan*, the two readers identified as such in the tradition) and Nafi' read *dhurriyyatihim* in the plural. Its grammatical inflection (*i'rab*, the grammatical case-endings) was discussed earlier. The remaining seven readers read *dhurriyyatahum* in the singular, with a *fatha* on the *ta'*. It must be the object of *akhadha*, and it involves an omitted *mudaf* (a noun in a genitive construction that is dropped), i.e., *mithaq dhurriyyatihim* (the covenant of their offspring). The covenant was taken from the offspring of the children of Adam because the children of Adam in his lineage did not include any polytheist; rather, polytheism arose among their descendants.

"That you may say on the Day of Resurrection: 'We were indeed unaware of this.'" That is, God said: "We bear witness against you." Or God and the angels said it, as al-Suddi reported. Or the angels said it. Or some of them bore witness against others, according to some sayings. The meaning of "of this" ("'an hadha") is: of this covenant and the acknowledgment of Lordship.

﴿Or lest you say: "Only our fathers associated partners with God before us, and we were their offspring after them."﴾ The meaning is that if no covenant had been taken from them, and no messenger had come to remind them of what the covenant contained regarding God's oneness and worship, they would have had two arguments: first, "We were heedless"; and second, "We were followers of our ancestors." So how would we perish, when the sin belongs only to the one who established the path for us and led us astray? Therefore the testimony came to cut off their arguments. Abu 'Amr read *an yaqulu* ("lest they say") with the *ya'* (third person), and the remaining seven read it with the *ta'* (second person).

﴿Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?﴾ This is part of the second statement. That is, they were the cause of our association of partners, because they established polytheism, took the lead in it, and left it as a precedent for us. The meaning is that He, the Most High, removed their pretext of argument by placing intellects within them and reminding them through the sending of messengers to them, and thus He cut off their excuses.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 171–174 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when We raised the mountain over them as though it were a canopy, and they thought it would fall upon them: "Take what We have given you with strength, and remember what is in it, that you may be mindful of God."﴾ ﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes, we testify." Lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection: "We were indeed unaware of this."﴾ ﴿Or lest you should say: "Our fathers only associated partners with God before, and we were their descendants after them. Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?"﴾ ﴿Thus do We detail the signs, that they may return.﴾ ﴿And recite to them the news of the one to whom We gave Our signs, but he detached himself from them, so Satan pursued him, and he became one of the misguided.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 175] ﴿Had We willed, We would have raised him by them, but he clung to the earth and followed his desire. His likeness is that of the dog: if you attack it, it pants, or if you leave it, it pants. That is the likeness of the people who denied Our signs. So relate the stories, that they may reflect.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 176] ﴿Evil is the likeness of the people who denied Our signs, and they were wronging themselves.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 177] ﴿Whomever God guides, he is the one guided, and whomever He misguides, those are the losers.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 178] ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and humankind. They have hearts with which they do not understand, eyes with which they do not see, and ears with which they do not hear. Those are like livestock; rather, they are further astray. Those are the heedless.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 179] ﴿To God belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them, and leave those who deviate concerning His names. They will be recompensed for what they used to do.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 180] ﴿And among those We created is a community that guides by the truth and acts justly by it.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 181] ﴿And those who denied Our signs, We will draw them gradually from where they do not know.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 182] ﴿And I will give them respite; indeed, My plan is firm.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 183] ﴿Have they not reflected? There is no madness in their companion; he is only a clear warner.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 184] ﴿Have they not looked into the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and at what God has created of things, and that perhaps their term has drawn near? Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾ [Al-A'raf: 185] ﴿Whomever God misguides, there is none to guide him, and He leaves them in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 186] ﴿They ask you about the Hour: "When will it take place?" Say: "Its knowledge is only with my Lord. None will reveal it at its time except Him. It is heavy upon the heavens and the earth. It will not come upon you except suddenly." They ask you as though you were well-informed about it. Say: "Its knowledge is only with God, but most people do not know."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 187]

The word "نَتْق" (naṭq) means pulling with force. Some have explained it by its result, which is uprooting. The Arabs say: "I pulled the butter out of the mouth of the waterskin" (nataqtu al-zubda min fami al-qirba). The "nāṭiq" is the womb that expels the child from the man. Al-Nabigha said:

*They were not deprived of the goodness of ransom, and their mother overflowed upon you with a male-begetting womb.*

In a hadith: "Choose for yourselves virgins, for their wombs are more expelling, their mouths sweeter, and they are more content with little."

"الانسلاخ" (inslakh) means to be stripped bare of a thing so that nothing of it clings to you, and from it comes: "the snake sloughed its skin" (insalakhat al-hayya min jildiha).

The dog (al-kalb) is a well-known animal. In the paucity plural it is "aklub," and in the abundance plural "kilab." Some irregular plurals are formed with the suffix alif-ta', as in "kilabat." This root has been discussed earlier in "mukallibin," and I repeat it for added benefit. "Lahatha al-kalb yalhathu" (with fatha on both letters, in past and present) means the dog extended its tongue. The verbal noun is "lahth" or "luhth" (with ḍamma). It is the state of the dog in fatigue and rest, thirst and quenching alike, unlike other animals, which pant only from exhaustion or thirst.

"لحد" and "ألحد" are two dialectal forms. It is said they have the same meaning: deviating from the truth and introducing into it what is not part of it. Ibn al-Sikkit said this. Others said: deviating from uprightness. The quadriliteral form is more common in usage than the triliteral. A poet said:

*The commander is not a miser who deviates.*

From this comes "laḥada al-qabr," meaning to incline the grave toward one of its sides. In their speech, when a single person does something, they say: "laḥadahu al-laḥid" (the one who dug the grave inclined it for him). It is also said "alḥada" means to incline and deviate, while "laḥada" means to lean on and take refuge in. Al-Kisa'i said this.

"متن" (matana) means to become firm and strong.

"أيّان" (ayyan) is an adverb of time, indeclinable, used mostly in interrogation. It is followed by a noun in the nominative as subject, and by an imperfect verb, not a perfect one, unlike "mata," which is followed by either. God says: "أيّان يُبْعَثُونَ" (When will they be raised?). And: "أيّان مُرْساها" (When will it arrive?). A poet said:

*When will my need be fulfilled, when? Do you not see its time has come?*

It is also used in conditional sentences, jussifying the two imperfect verbs, but this is rare. Sibawayh did not record it, but others did, and they cited the poet's words:

*When the lean she-camel spends the night in a barren land, wherever the wind turns her, she will alight.*

Another said:

*When we give you security, you will be secure in our absence, but if you do not attain security from us, you will remain wary.*

The kasra of its initial hamza is the dialect of Sulaym. In my view it is a simple, not compound, particle, and an inflexible, not derived, word. The author of "Kitab al-Lawami'" mentioned that "ayyan" was originally "ayyu awan" (which time). Since it was used so often, the hamza was dropped without analogy or compensation, the waw became ya', three ya's gathered, and one was removed, so it became what you see. That is the end of his words. Abu al-Fath claimed it is "fa'lan" and "fa'lal," derived from "ayy," meaning "which time" and "which act," from "awaytu ilayhi" (I took refuge in him), because the part takes refuge in the whole, leaning upon it. He ruled out that it is "fa'al" or "fa'\"al" from "ayna" (where), because "ayyan" is an adverb of time and "ayna" is an adverb of place. This required that it come from the word "ayy" with the addition of the nun. Also, "ayyan" is an interrogative, as is "ayy," and the default is non-compounding. Interrogative and conditional particles are inflexible, like "mata," "haythuma," "anna," and "idha."

"رسا يرسو" means to be fixed and stable.

"الحفي" (al-ḥafiyy) is one who seeks out a thing thoroughly, who cares about it and takes pains with it. "Fulan ḥafiyy bi" means he is kind to me and attentive. A poet said:

*When we met, the sword separated us, for the one who asks about us is earnest in her question.*

Another said:

*A question of one who is solicitous about his brother, as though he, in his remembrance of him, were drowsy or half-asleep.*

"الإحفاء" (al-iḥfa') means thoroughness, from which comes "iḥfa' al-shārib" (trimming the moustache thoroughly). "al-ḥāfī" means his feet became worn for thoroughness in walking. "al-ḥafāwa" means kindness and gentleness.

﴿And when We raised the mountain over them and they thought it would fall upon them﴾: that is, We pulled the mountain with force. "Fawqahum" (over them) is a delayed circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddara), and its governing element is omitted. Its estimate is: "being over them," since the state of pulling did not coincide with being above; rather, it became above them. Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' said: "fawqahum" is an adverbial of place for "nataqna" (We pulled). This is only possible if "nataqna" is taken to include a meaning of a verb that can govern "fawqahum," that is, "We raised the mountain over them by pulling," so it is like His words: ﴿And We raised the Mount above them﴾ [An-Nisa': 154]. The clause "ka'annahu ẓullah" (as though it were a canopy) is in the place of a circumstantial clause. The meaning is: "as though it were a canopy over them." A "ẓulla" is what shades from a roof or a cloud. The comparison should be understood as referring to a particular kind of canopy, because if every shading thing is called a canopy, then the mountain above them became a canopy, and if it became a canopy, how can it be compared to a canopy? So the meaning, God knows best, is: "as though, at the time of its elevation over them, it was a canopy of cloud," that is, the canopy that has no pillars beneath it, but whose holding aloft is by divine power, even though they are solid bodies. This is unlike the earthly canopy, which can only exist on pillars. When this earthly shadow was held above them without pillars, it was compared to the cloud canopy that has no pillars. It is also said: humans were accustomed to these earthly bodies as canopies, since they stood on pillars. When the mountain was raised without pillars, it was said: "as though it were a canopy," that is, as though it stood on pillars. It is read "ṭulla" with ṭa', from "aṭalla 'alayhi," meaning to look down upon it. And "ẓannū" (they thought) here remains in its original sense, by preferring one of the two permissible meanings. The commentators said: it means "they were certain." Al-Zamakhshari said: "they knew." That is not so; rather, it is a predominant assumption with the hope remaining, unless it is restricted to the condition that they did not understand the Torah, in which case it means "mastering." The cause of raising the mountain over them was mentioned earlier in the explanation of His words "And We raised the Mount over you" in al-Baqara, so there is no need to repeat it. The commentators repeated it here, including al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, and others. Al-Zamakhshari, at the mention of the cause here, said: when Musa, peace be upon him, displayed the tablets, in which was the Book of God, no tree, mountain, or stone remained without trembling. Therefore you do not see a Jew reading the Torah without swaying and nodding his head. That is the end of his words. This tendency has spread, as far as I have observed in Egypt, to the children of the Muslims. You see them in the maktab (Qur'anic school), when they recite the Qur'an, swaying and moving their heads. As for our lands in al-Andalus and the West, if a child moved while reciting the Qur'an, the teacher of the maktab would discipline him and say: "Do not move, lest you resemble the Jews in their study."

* *

﴿Take what We have given you with strength, and remember what is in it, that you may be mindful of God.﴾ Al-A'mash read "wa-idhdhakkarū" (with shadda, from "idhdhakar"). Ibn Mas'ud read "wa-tadhkurū," and it was also read "wa-tadhakkarū" with shadda, meaning "wa-tadhdhakkarū." The explanation of these phrases was given earlier in al-Baqara.

﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes."﴾ It has been narrated in the hadith through several chains: "He took from the back of Adam his descendants, and took from them the covenant that He is their Lord and that there is no god but Him, so they acknowledged that and committed themselves to it." The scholars differed about the manner of the taking out, the form of what was taken out, the place and the time. The establishing of these matters belongs to that hadith and its discussion. The apparent meaning of this verse contradicts the apparent meaning of that hadith, and its wording does not agree with the wording of the verse. Some groups have attempted to reconcile the verse and the hadith through interpretation that is strained. The best thing said about this verse is what al-Zamakhshari explained: it is of the type of figurative representation and imagery. The meaning is that God set up for them the proofs of His lordship and oneness, and their intellects and insights, which He placed within them and made distinguishing between error and guidance, bore witness to them. So it is as though He, glory be to Him, made them testify against themselves and established it for them, and said: "Am I not your Lord?" And it is as though they said: "Yes, You are our Lord. We testify against ourselves and acknowledge Your oneness." The scope of figurative speech is wide in the words of God and His Messenger, and in Arab speech. Its parallel is the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it "Be," and it is﴾ [An-Nahl: 40], and ﴿He said to it and to the earth: "Come, willingly or unwillingly." They said: "We come willingly."﴾ [Fussilat: 11]. And the saying of the poet:

*When the halters say to the belly, "Be stilled," the morning breeze says to it, "Be cool."*

And it is well known that there was no actual speech there. Rather, this is an illustration and a depiction of the meaning. The phrase *an taqulu* ("lest you say") is an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*, the object expressing the reason for an action). The meaning is: We established the proofs, which the intellects bear witness to as sound, out of concern that you might say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were unaware of this and were not warned about it." Its implied sense is: "We were heedless of this and were not alerted to it." Or [the purpose is] lest you say, "Only our fathers associated partners with God before us, and we were their offspring after them, so we followed them." This is because the establishment of proofs for monotheism (*tawhid*, the affirmation of God's oneness) and what they were alerted to remained present with them. Therefore they have no excuse for turning away from it, for clinging to blind imitation (*taqlid*), and for following their fathers. Likewise, their fathers have no excuse for associating partners with God, since the proofs of monotheism were set up for them as well.

(If you ask): Who are "the children of Adam" and "their offspring"? I say: By "the children of Adam" is meant the ancestors of the Jews who associated partners with God, the Most High, when they said, "Ezra is the son of God." By "their offspring" is meant those who were in the time of the Messenger of God from among their descendants, who followed their fathers. The evidence that this refers to the polytheists and their children is His statement, the Most High: ﴿Or lest you say: "Only our fathers associated partners with God before us"﴾. This is the end of al-Zamakhshari's words, and it is an elaboration of the words of those before him.
