The dog (al-kalb) is a well-known animal. In the paucity plural it is "aklub," and in the abundance plural "kilab." Some irregular plurals are formed with the suffix alif-ta', as in "kilabat." This root has been discussed earlier in "mukallibin," and I repeat it for added benefit. "Lahatha al-kalb yalhathu" (with fatha on both letters, in past and present) means the dog extended its tongue. The verbal noun is "lahth" or "luhth" (with ḍamma). It is the state of the dog in fatigue and rest, thirst and quenching alike, unlike other animals, which pant only from exhaustion or thirst.

"لحد" and "ألحد" are two dialectal forms. It is said they have the same meaning: deviating from the truth and introducing into it what is not part of it. Ibn al-Sikkit said this. Others said: deviating from uprightness. The quadriliteral form is more common in usage than the triliteral. A poet said:

*The commander is not a miser who deviates.*

From this comes "laḥada al-qabr," meaning to incline the grave toward one of its sides. In their speech, when a single person does something, they say: "laḥadahu al-laḥid" (the one who dug the grave inclined it for him). It is also said "alḥada" means to incline and deviate, while "laḥada" means to lean on and take refuge in. Al-Kisa'i said this.

"متن" (matana) means to become firm and strong.

"أيّان" (ayyan) is an adverb of time, indeclinable, used mostly in interrogation. It is followed by a noun in the nominative as subject, and by an imperfect verb, not a perfect one, unlike "mata," which is followed by either. God says: "أيّان يُبْعَثُونَ" (When will they be raised?). And: "أيّان مُرْساها" (When will it arrive?). A poet said:

*When will my need be fulfilled, when? Do you not see its time has come?*

It is also used in conditional sentences, jussifying the two imperfect verbs, but this is rare. Sibawayh did not record it, but others did, and they cited the poet's words:

*When the lean she-camel spends the night in a barren land, wherever the wind turns her, she will alight.*

Another said:

*When we give you security, you will be secure in our absence, but if you do not attain security from us, you will remain wary.*

The kasra of its initial hamza is the dialect of Sulaym. In my view it is a simple, not compound, particle, and an inflexible, not derived, word. The author of "Kitab al-Lawami'" mentioned that "ayyan" was originally "ayyu awan" (which time). Since it was used so often, the hamza was dropped without analogy or compensation, the waw became ya', three ya's gathered, and one was removed, so it became what you see. That is the end of his words. Abu al-Fath claimed it is "fa'lan" and "fa'lal," derived from "ayy," meaning "which time" and "which act," from "awaytu ilayhi" (I took refuge in him), because the part takes refuge in the whole, leaning upon it. He ruled out that it is "fa'al" or "fa'\"al" from "ayna" (where), because "ayyan" is an adverb of time and "ayna" is an adverb of place. This required that it come from the word "ayy" with the addition of the nun. Also, "ayyan" is an interrogative, as is "ayy," and the default is non-compounding. Interrogative and conditional particles are inflexible, like "mata," "haythuma," "anna," and "idha."

"رسا يرسو" means to be fixed and stable.

"الحفي" (al-ḥafiyy) is one who seeks out a thing thoroughly, who cares about it and takes pains with it. "Fulan ḥafiyy bi" means he is kind to me and attentive. A poet said:

*When we met, the sword separated us, for the one who asks about us is earnest in her question.*

Another said:

*A question of one who is solicitous about his brother, as though he, in his remembrance of him, were drowsy or half-asleep.*

"الإحفاء" (al-iḥfa') means thoroughness, from which comes "iḥfa' al-shārib" (trimming the moustache thoroughly). "al-ḥāfī" means his feet became worn for thoroughness in walking. "al-ḥafāwa" means kindness and gentleness.

﴿And when We raised the mountain over them and they thought it would fall upon them﴾: that is, We pulled the mountain with force. "Fawqahum" (over them) is a delayed circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddara), and its governing element is omitted. Its estimate is: "being over them," since the state of pulling did not coincide with being above; rather, it became above them. Al-Hawfi and Abu al-Baqa' said: "fawqahum" is an adverbial of place for "nataqna" (We pulled). This is only possible if "nataqna" is taken to include a meaning of a verb that can govern "fawqahum," that is, "We raised the mountain over them by pulling," so it is like His words: ﴿And We raised the Mount above them﴾ [An-Nisa': 154]. The clause "ka'annahu ẓullah" (as though it were a canopy) is in the place of a circumstantial clause. The meaning is: "as though it were a canopy over them." A "ẓulla" is what shades from a roof or a cloud. The comparison should be understood as referring to a particular kind of canopy, because if every shading thing is called a canopy, then the mountain above them became a canopy, and if it became a canopy, how can it be compared to a canopy? So the meaning, God knows best, is: "as though, at the time of its elevation over them, it was a canopy of cloud," that is, the canopy that has no pillars beneath it, but whose holding aloft is by divine power, even though they are solid bodies. This is unlike the earthly canopy, which can only exist on pillars. When this earthly shadow was held above them without pillars, it was compared to the cloud canopy that has no pillars. It is also said: humans were accustomed to these earthly bodies as canopies, since they stood on pillars. When the mountain was raised without pillars, it was said: "as though it were a canopy," that is, as though it stood on pillars. It is read "ṭulla" with ṭa', from "aṭalla 'alayhi," meaning to look down upon it. And "ẓannū" (they thought) here remains in its original sense, by preferring one of the two permissible meanings. The commentators said: it means "they were certain." Al-Zamakhshari said: "they knew." That is not so; rather, it is a predominant assumption with the hope remaining, unless it is restricted to the condition that they did not understand the Torah, in which case it means "mastering." The cause of raising the mountain over them was mentioned earlier in the explanation of His words "And We raised the Mount over you" in al-Baqara, so there is no need to repeat it. The commentators repeated it here, including al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, and others. Al-Zamakhshari, at the mention of the cause here, said: when Musa, peace be upon him, displayed the tablets, in which was the Book of God, no tree, mountain, or stone remained without trembling. Therefore you do not see a Jew reading the Torah without swaying and nodding his head. That is the end of his words. This tendency has spread, as far as I have observed in Egypt, to the children of the Muslims. You see them in the maktab (Qur'anic school), when they recite the Qur'an, swaying and moving their heads. As for our lands in al-Andalus and the West, if a child moved while reciting the Qur'an, the teacher of the maktab would discipline him and say: "Do not move, lest you resemble the Jews in their study."

* *

﴿Take what We have given you with strength, and remember what is in it, that you may be mindful of God.﴾ Al-A'mash read "wa-idhdhakkarū" (with shadda, from "idhdhakar"). Ibn Mas'ud read "wa-tadhkurū," and it was also read "wa-tadhakkarū" with shadda, meaning "wa-tadhdhakkarū." The explanation of these phrases was given earlier in al-Baqara.

﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes."﴾ It has been narrated in the hadith through several chains: "He took from the back of Adam his descendants, and took from them the covenant that He is their Lord and that there is no god but Him, so they acknowledged that and committed themselves to it." The scholars differed about the manner of the taking out, the form of what was taken out, the place and the time. The establishing of these matters belongs to that hadith and its discussion. The apparent meaning of this verse contradicts the apparent meaning of that hadith, and its wording does not agree with the wording of the verse. Some groups have attempted to reconcile the verse and the hadith through interpretation that is strained. The best thing said about this verse is what al-Zamakhshari explained: it is of the type of figurative representation and imagery. The meaning is that God set up for them the proofs of His lordship and oneness, and their intellects and insights, which He placed within them and made distinguishing between error and guidance, bore witness to them. So it is as though He, glory be to Him, made them testify against themselves and established it for them, and said: "Am I not your Lord?" And it is as though they said: "Yes, You are our Lord. We testify against ourselves and acknowledge Your oneness." The scope of figurative speech is wide in the words of God and His Messenger, and in Arab speech. Its parallel is the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it "Be," and it is﴾ [An-Nahl: 40], and ﴿He said to it and to the earth: "Come, willingly or unwillingly." They said: "We come willingly."﴾ [Fussilat: 11]. And the saying of the poet:

*When the halters say to the belly, "Be stilled," the morning breeze says to it, "Be cool."*

And it is well known that there was no actual speech there. Rather, this is an illustration and a depiction of the meaning. The phrase *an taqulu* ("lest you say") is an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*, the object expressing the reason for an action). The meaning is: We established the proofs, which the intellects bear witness to as sound, out of concern that you might say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were unaware of this and were not warned about it." Its implied sense is: "We were heedless of this and were not alerted to it." Or [the purpose is] lest you say, "Only our fathers associated partners with God before us, and we were their offspring after them, so we followed them." This is because the establishment of proofs for monotheism (*tawhid*, the affirmation of God's oneness) and what they were alerted to remained present with them. Therefore they have no excuse for turning away from it, for clinging to blind imitation (*taqlid*), and for following their fathers. Likewise, their fathers have no excuse for associating partners with God, since the proofs of monotheism were set up for them as well.

(If you ask): Who are "the children of Adam" and "their offspring"? I say: By "the children of Adam" is meant the ancestors of the Jews who associated partners with God, the Most High, when they said, "Ezra is the son of God." By "their offspring" is meant those who were in the time of the Messenger of God from among their descendants, who followed their fathers. The evidence that this refers to the polytheists and their children is His statement, the Most High: ﴿Or lest you say: "Only our fathers associated partners with God before us"﴾. The evidence that it refers to the Jews is that the verses it is connected to, and the verses connected to them, are of the same pattern and style. This is seen in His statement: ﴿And ask them about the town﴾ [al-A'raf: 163]; ﴿And when a community among them said﴾ [al-A'raf: 164]; ﴿And when your Lord proclaimed﴾ [al-A'raf: 167]; ﴿And when We raised the mountain above them﴾; ﴿And recite to them the story of the one to whom We gave Our signs﴾ [al-A'raf: 175]. This is the end of al-Zamakhshari's words, and it is an elaboration of the words of those before him.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: Some people said: The verse points to this interpretation, which applies to the worldly life. [They] took the meaning of *awjada* (to bring into existence), and that the two acts of testimony [occur] when the person reaches legal responsibility (*taklif*), at which point he has been given understanding and the sign indicating the Creator has been set up for him. Al-Zajjaj inclined toward this view, and it is a meaning that the wording permits. [End of Ibn 'Atiyya's words.] Yet taking the apparent meaning of the hadith leads to the doctrine of metempsychosis (*tanasukh*, the transmigration of souls), so it must be interpreted.

The object of *akhadha* (took) is *dhurriyyatahum*, as al-Hawfi said. It is possible, in the reading of all of them, that the object of *akhadha* is omitted because the meaning is understood, and *dhurriyyatihim* is a substitute (*badal*) for the pronoun in *zuhurihim* (their backs), just as *min zuhurihim* is a substitute for *bani Adam* (the children of Adam). The omitted object is the covenant (*mithaq*), as He said: ﴿And We took from them a solemn covenant﴾ [al-Nisa': 154], and ﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: "You shall not worship except God"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 83]. The sense of the passage is: And when your Lord took from the backs of the offspring of the children of Adam a covenant of monotheism, [affirming] that God is one and that He alone is to be worshipped. He used the metaphor that the covenant was taken from the back, as if the covenant, because of its difficulty, its binding nature, and the obligation it places upon one, were a heavy thing carried upon the back. This is an illustration of the meaning with certainty. He made them bear witness against themselves through the proofs He had set up for them, saying: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes."

The two 'Arabi readers (*al-'Arabiyan*, the two readers identified as such in the tradition) and Nafi' read *dhurriyyatihim* in the plural. Its grammatical inflection (*i'rab*, the grammatical case-endings) was discussed earlier. The remaining seven readers read *dhurriyyatahum* in the singular, with a *fatha* on the *ta'*. It must be the object of *akhadha*, and it involves an omitted *mudaf* (a noun in a genitive construction that is dropped), i.e., *mithaq dhurriyyatihim* (the covenant of their offspring). The covenant was taken from the offspring of the children of Adam because the children of Adam in his lineage did not include any polytheist; rather, polytheism arose among their descendants.

"That you may say on the Day of Resurrection: 'We were indeed unaware of this.'" That is, God said: "We bear witness against you." Or God and the angels said it, as al-Suddi reported. Or the angels said it. Or some of them bore witness against others, according to some sayings. The meaning of "of this" ("'an hadha") is: of this covenant and the acknowledgment of Lordship.

﴿Or lest you say: "Only our fathers associated partners with God before us, and we were their offspring after them."﴾ The meaning is that if no covenant had been taken from them, and no messenger had come to remind them of what the covenant contained regarding God's oneness and worship, they would have had two arguments: first, "We were heedless"; and second, "We were followers of our ancestors." So how would we perish, when the sin belongs only to the one who established the path for us and led us astray? Therefore the testimony came to cut off their arguments. Abu 'Amr read *an yaqulu* ("lest they say") with the *ya'* (third person), and the remaining seven read it with the *ta'* (second person).

﴿Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?﴾ This is part of the second statement. That is, they were the cause of our association of partners, because they established polytheism, took the lead in it, and left it as a precedent for us. The meaning is that He, the Most High, removed their pretext of argument by placing intellects within them and reminding them through the sending of messengers to them, and thus He cut off their excuses.

This commentary on the verses preceding 7:175 is part of a longer discussion, and I have translated the text as it stands.

﴿Thus do We detail the verses﴾ [al-A'raf: 174], meaning: in the same manner of detail with which We explained the preceding verses, We detail the following verses. All of them follow one pattern in detailing and clarifying the proofs and evidences of monotheism (p-422).

﴿So that they may return﴾ [al-A'raf: 174], meaning: that they may turn from their polytheism and their worship of other than God to His oneness and His worship, through this detailed and clarified exposition. A group read *yufassilu* with a *ya'*, meaning: He Himself details, that is, God, exalted is He.

﴿And recite to them the story of the one to whom We gave Our signs, but he withdrew from them, so Satan pursued him, and he became of the deviators﴾. Meaning: recite to those among the disbelieving Jews and others who were present. When God, exalted is He, had mentioned the covenant taken concerning His oneness and the affirmation of His lordship, and had mentioned their acknowledgment of it and their testifying against themselves, He mentioned the state of one who believed in Him and then, after that, disbelieved. This is like the state of the Jews, who were affirming and awaiting the mission of the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, because of what they had come to know from the books of God that had been revealed, which gave glad tidings of him and mentioned his attributes. When he was sent, they disbelieved in him, and they claimed that what proceeded from them was a way of their forefathers whom they followed. The exegetes differed concerning "the one to whom He gave His signs but he withdrew from them." Ikrimah said: he is anyone who withdrew from the truth after it had been given to him, from among the Jews, the Christians, and the *hanifs*. Ubadah ibn al-Samit said: they are the Quraysh, to whom the commands and prohibitions of God and the miracles came, but they withdrew from the signs and did not accept them. On these two views, the singular *alladhi* is intended as a plural. The majority said: he is a specific individual. It was said: he is Bal'am; and it was said: he is Bal'am ibn Ba'ur, and he is a man from the Canaanites who was given some of the books of God; and it was said: he knew the Greatest Name of God. The name of his father was disputed. Ibn Mas'ud said: he is Abraha. Ibn Abbas said: Ba'ura'. Mujahid and al-Suddi said: Ba'ra'uyah. It was narrated that his people asked him to invoke against Moses and those with him, but he refused and said: how can I invoke against one who is accompanied by angels? They insisted upon him until he did it. The exegetes have elaborated at length on his story and mentioned what only God knows. It was said: he is a man of the scholars of the Children of Israel. Ibn Mas'ud said: Moses, peace be upon him, sent him toward Madyan, calling to God and to His law. He knew some of the signs of God that they claimed for him, and he was one whose supplication was answered. When he departed from the religion of Moses, God stripped the signs from him. It was said: his name was Na'im, who lived in the time of Moses, and he was in Habt (a name of a town). Whenever he looked, he saw the Throne. In his assembly there were twelve thousand inkwells for the students, who wrote from him, and he was the first to write a book stating that the world has no maker. It was said: he was a man from the Children of Israel who was given three answered supplications with which he would pray for the welfare of the servants. He gave them all to his wife, who was ugly, and she asked him, so he prayed to God, and she became beautiful, and she inclined to another. He prayed to God against her, and she became a barking bitch. He had children by her, and they implored him, so he prayed to God, and she returned to her former state. Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, Ibn al-Musayyib, Zayd ibn Aslam, and Abu Rawq said: he is Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt al-Thaqafi, who read the books and knew that a prophet would be sent from the Arabs, and he hoped that it would be him. He used to versify wisdom and proverbs. When Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, was sent, he envied him, and he went to some of the kings. It was narrated that he came intending to embrace Islam, and he reached Badr a day or so after the battle, and he said: who killed these? It was said: Muhammad. He said: I have no need for the religion of one who killed these. He apostatized and returned, and said: now wine is lawful for me, though he had forbidden wine to himself. He joined a people from the kings of Himyar and drank with them until he died. His sister Fari'ah came to the Messenger of God and asked him to recite some of his poetry, so she recited several odes to him. He said: his poetry believed, and his heart disbelieved. He is the one about whom God, exalted is He, said: "And recite to them the story of the one to whom We gave Our signs, but he withdrew from them." Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib also said: he is Abu Amir ibn al-Nu'man ibn Sayfi, the monk, whom the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, named "the Depraved." He had become a monk in the Jahiliyyah and wore sackcloth. He is the one for whom the hypocrites built the Mosque of Harm. A dispute took place between him and the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Abu Amir said: May God make the liar among us die, a stray, alone. He sent word to the hypocrites to prepare themselves with strength and weapons. Then he went to Caesar and sought his aid to expel Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and his companions from Medina. He died in Syria, a stray, a fugitive, alone. It was also said otherwise. The better course in such matters, when reported from the exegetes (p-423), is to take their statements as examples rather than as restricting the verse to a specific individual, for restriction leads to confusion, contradiction, and disagreement. Regarding "We gave him Our signs," it depends on who is meant by "the one to whom We gave": is it the Greatest Name of God, or the signs from the books of God, or the proofs of monotheism, or from the signs of Moses, or knowledge of the coming of the Messenger? "Withdrawing from the signs" is an intensification of disowning them and distancing from them, meaning: he did not act upon what the blessing We bestowed upon him by bringing him Our signs required. It was made as if he had been clothed in them like a garment, and then he stripped himself of them. This is treating the meaning as if it were a definite statement. The statement of one who said that it is an inverted construction, meaning: the signs were stripped away from him, has no need to be invoked. Sufyan said: a man commits a sin and then forgets a door of knowledge.

The majority read *fa-atba'ahu al-shaytanu*, from *atba'a* (the fourth form), meaning: he overtook him and became with him. This is an intensification regarding him, as if he were the leader of Satan whom Satan follows. Likewise is "a piercing flame followed him" (*fa-atba'ahu shihabun thaqib*), meaning: it ran behind him. Al-Qutabi said: he followed him from behind, and *atba'a* means he overtook and caught up, as in God's words: "So they overtook them at sunrise" [al-Shu'ara: 60], meaning: they caught up with them. On this view, it is transitive to one object. Sometimes *atba'a* is transitive to two objects, as God said: "And their offspring followed them in faith" [al-Tur: 21]. Accordingly this is to be understood as: Satan made him follow his footsteps, meaning: Satan caused him to follow his steps, so the hamza in it is for transitivity, since the original is *tabi'a* (he followed), he followed the steps of Satan. Talhah, by a variant reading, and al-Hasan, as Harun reported from him, read *fa-ittaba'ahu* with a shadda, with the meaning of *tabi'ahu*. The author of *Kitab al-Lawami'* said: there is a difference between them: *tabi'ahu* is when one walks in his trail, and *ittaba'ahu* is when one walks in his concealment. As for *fa-atba'ahu* with the hamza elided, it is among those that are transitive to two objects, since it is derived from *tabi'ahu*, and in the common reading one of the two objects has been omitted. It was also said: *fa-atba'ahu* means *istatba'ahu*, that is, he made him a follower, so he became obedient and attentive to him. It was also said: its meaning is that the devils of mankind, the people of disbelief and error, followed him, "and he became of the deviators." The verb *kana* may be understood as retaining its meaning of past time as applied to the content of the sentence, or *kana* may mean *sara* (became), that is: he became of the erring disbelievers. Muqatil said: "of the erring." Al-Zajjaj said: "of the perished and corrupt."

﴿Had We willed, We would have raised him by them, but he clung to the earth and followed his desire﴾ [al-A'raf: 176]. Meaning: had We wished to honor him and elevate his rank by the signs We gave him, We would have done so. But he clung to the earth, meaning: he inclined toward the lusts of this world and desired them, and followed what arises from desire. The conjunction "but" here (*istidrak*) is used to draw attention to the cause for which he was not raised and not honored, as was done with others who were given guidance and preferred it and followed it. The meaning of "clung" (*akhlada*) is: he threw himself down to the earth, that is, to what is in it of pleasures and lusts. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and al-Suddi said this. It is also possible that by "clung to the earth" one means: he inclined toward baseness and vileness, as one says: so-and-so is in the dirt, an expression for the lowering of his rank through his stripping himself of the signs. Al-Kirmani said this. Abu Rawq said: his desire overpowered his intellect, so he chose his worldly life over his hereafter. Others said: the meaning is "We would have raised him by them, We would have seized him," as you say: "the wrongdoer was raised" when he perished. The pronoun in *bi-ha* refers to the disobedience in the stripping away. The description of his state begins with "but he clung." Ibn Abi Najih said: "We would have raised him" means "We would have taken him (in death) before he fell into disobedience and We would have raised him away from it," and the pronoun refers to the signs, and then the description of his state begins. The first explanation is clearer, and it is narrated from Ibn Abbas and a group. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned no other, and it is what the *istidrak* requires, for according to the view of destruction through disobedience or of death before falling into it, the meaning of *istidrak* is not valid. The pronoun in *la-rafa'nahu* in these statements refers to the one who was given the signs, though they differed on what the pronoun in *bi-ha* refers to. Others said: the pronoun in *la-rafa'nahu* refers to disbelief, understood from what preceded, and in *bi-ha* it refers to the signs, meaning: had We willed, We would have raised disbelief out of the signs. This meaning is narrated from Mujahid, and it is far-fetched and forced (p-424). Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: how was his elevation made contingent upon God's will and not made contingent upon his own action that merits elevation?" I answer: the meaning is: had he held fast to the signs and not stripped himself of them, We would have raised him by them. For God's will to raise him is consequent upon his adherence to the signs, so He mentioned the will while meaning what it follows from and is caused by. As if it were said: had he adhered to them, We would have raised him by them. Do you not see His words: "But he clung to the earth" [al-A'raf: 176], by which He contrasted the will with his clinging, which was his own act. Therefore "Had We willed" must mean what his act was. Had the statement been taken at face value, it would have been required to say: "Had We willed, We would have raised him, but We did not will." End of quotation. This is in the manner of the Mu'tazilites (*i'tizal*).

﴿So his likeness is like the likeness of the dog: if you attack it, it pants, or if you leave it, it pants﴾ [al-A'raf: 176]. That is, his description is: if you impose wisdom upon him, he does not take it up, and if you leave him, he does not take it up, like the description of the dog: if it is chased away, it pants, and if it is lying down, it pants. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

It was also said: he likened the one who is utterly consumed by this world, in his restlessness and agitation in pursuing it and his constant adherence to that, to the dog in this state of its own, which is constant for it whether it is roused or left alone. That state is that it never stops panting, and it is the lowest and most contemptible of its conditions, just as the one who is consumed by this world never stops being weary and restless in pursuing it. Al-Hasan said: "He is like the hypocrite, who does not turn back to the truth whether he is called or not called, whether he is given or not given, like the dog that pants whether it is chased or left alone." End of quotation.

In Kitab al-Hayawan (the Book of Animals), it is said: the verse indicates that the dog is the lowest and most abject of animals, because lowness is struck as an example through it in its lowest condition. If there were among the animal kind something lower than the dog, the parable would not have been struck except with it.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The majority of scholars said: he was likened in that he was astray before he was given the signs, and then he was given them, yet he remained astray and they did not benefit him. So he is like the dog in that it never ceases panting, whether a burden is placed upon it or it is left without a burden."

al-Suddi and others said: "This man's tongue hung out over his chest and he began to pant, as the dog pants."

al-Zamakhshari said: "The proper form of the speech should have been: 'Had We willed, We would have raised him up by them, but he clung to the earth, so We brought him low and lowered his station.' But his saying 'So his likeness is like the likeness of the dog' has come in the place of 'so We brought him low,' with the most eloquent bringing-low, because his being likened to the dog in its lowest and most contemptible condition carries that meaning." End of quotation.

In al-Zamakhshari's words, "The proper form of the speech..." to the end, there is bad manners toward the speech of Allah the Exalted. As for his saying "his saying 'So his likeness...'" to the end, it does not stand in the place of what was mentioned. But his saying "he clung to the earth" stands in the place of "so We brought him low," except that when He mentioned the favour shown to him, He attributed that to His own noble Self, saying: "We gave him Our signs, and had We willed, We would have raised him up by them." And when He mentioned what is a wrong against the person, He attributed it to him, saying: "﴿Then he withdrew from them﴾" and "﴿but he clung to the earth﴾" [al-A'raf: 176]. In reality, Allah the Exalted is the One who stripped him of the signs and made him cling to the earth. So it comes in the manner of His saying: "﴿So I wished to damage it﴾" [al-Kahf: 79], and His saying: "﴿So your Lord wished that they should reach maturity﴾" [al-Kahf: 82]. This attributes what was good to Allah and attributes what was otherwise to the person.

This conditional clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: panting in both states. So said al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Baqa'. But some commentators of the book al-Misbah said: "As for the conditional clause, it is hardly ever placed in full in the position of a circumstantial clause. One does not say: 'Zayd came to me, if he asks he is given,' as a circumstantial clause. Rather, if that were intended, the conditional clause would be made a predicate of a pronoun referring to what the circumstance is about, as in: 'Zayd came, he, and if he asks he is given,' so that what occupies the position of the circumstance is the nominal clause, not the conditional. Yes, they have placed clauses introduced by the conditional particle in the position of circumstance, but only after removing them from the reality of the condition. And that clause either has something contradicting it conjoined to it or it does not. The first (where a contradicting clause is conjoined) requires omitting the waw, as in: 'I came to you if you came to me and if you did not come to me,' since it is not hidden that the two contradictory conditions in such a position do not remain with the meaning of a condition, but turn into the meaning of equalization, like the two contradictory interrogatives in His saying: '﴿Whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾' [al-Baqarah: 6]. The second requires the waw, as in: 'I came to you and if you did not come to me.' Had he omitted the waw, it would truly be confused with the condition." End of quotation.

So His saying "﴿if you attack it, it pants, or if you leave it, it pants﴾" [al-A'raf: 176] is of the first kind, because attacking it and leaving it are contradictories.

﴿That is the likeness of the people who denied Our signs﴾ [al-A'raf: 176]. That is, that description is the description of those who denied Our signs: their state is like the state of the dog panting in both conditions. Just as He likened the description of the one given the signs who withdrew from them to the dog in its lowest condition, so He likened to it those who denied the signs, in that they were given them, the signs came to them clear, requiring that they be affirmed, but they met them with denial and withdrew from them. It is possible that this is a reference to the likeness of the one who withdrew, and it is possible that it is a reference to the description of the dog. It is also possible that the particle of comparison is omitted from that, meaning: the description of that is the description of those who denied. It is also possible that it is omitted from "the likeness of the people," meaning: that description is the description of the one who withdrew, or the description of the dog, like the likeness of those who denied Our signs. This makes the censure of the deniers more forceful, since they are made the original and the comparison is made to them.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "That is, this parable, O Muhammad, is the likeness of these people who were astray before you brought them guidance and the message, then you came to them with that, but they remained in their error and did not benefit from it. So their likeness is like the likeness of the dog."

al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿who denied Our signs﴾" [al-A'raf: 176] refers to the Jews after they read in the Torah the mission of the Messenger of Allah, and the mention of the miraculous Qur'an and what is in it, and they gave good news to the people of the approach of his sending, and they used to seek victory through him. Ibn 'Abbas said: "He means the disbelievers of Mecca, because they used to wish for a guide who would guide them and a caller who would call them to obedience to Allah. Then there came to them one whose truthfulness, integrity and prophethood were beyond doubt, and they denied him. So the comparison came about between them and the dog that, whether it is attacked or left, pants. For they were not guided by what they abandoned, and they were not guided by what the Messenger brought, so they remained in error in every condition, like the dog that pants in every state." End of quotation.

It is summarised: are these deniers of the signs general, or specific to the Jews, or to the disbelievers of Mecca? There are three opinions, and the most apparent is generality.

Translation:

﴿So relate the stories, that they may reflect﴾, i.e., recount the reports of the past generations, such as the report of Bal'am (Bal'am), or the one who was interpreted as being "al-Munsalikh" (the one who cast off his signs), since it is one of the stories that none knows except one who has studied the Books, for it is among their hidden reports. So in your telling of it there is the greatest miracle, "that they may reflect" upon what befell those who denied, so that this becomes a lesson for them and a deterrent from denial, and that they may become reports of ill repute that are related just as the report of that "Munsalikh" was related.

﴿Evil is the example of the people who denied Our signs﴾. *Sa'a* means *bi'sa* (how evil). It was previously explained to us that its original form is transitive. You say *sa'anī al-shay'u yasū'unī* (the thing grieved me). Then, when it was used in the manner of *bi'sa*, it was made to follow the pattern *fa'ala* and was given the rulings of *bi'sa*. *Mathalan* (as an example) is a *tamyīz* (specifier, accusative of specification) for the hidden pronoun in *sa'a*, which is the subject (*fā'il*). The pronoun is explained by this *tamyīz*, and it is one of the pronouns explained by what follows it. According to the Basrī school it is not dualised or pluralised. The Kufans differ on this, as is mentioned in the grammar books. The noun being dispraised (*al-makhsūs bi'l-dhamm*) must be of the same kind as the *tamyīz*, so it is necessary to posit an omission, either in the *tamyīz*, meaning *sa'a aṣḥābu mathali'l-qawm* (evil were the people of the example of the people), or in the noun being dispraised, meaning *sa'a mathalan mathalu'l-qawm* (evil as an example is the example of the people). This sentence is an emphasis of the preceding sentence.

Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: Its apparent meaning requires that this example be described as evil, and that is not permissible, because God, exalted is He, mentioned this example, so how could it be described as evil? Therefore what must be described as evil is what the example conveys of their denial of God's signs and their turning away from them, until they became, in the illustration of that, like the panting dog. End of quotation.

This is not so. There is no striking of an example here. *Mathal* is a shared term between "description" (waṣf) and "that which is struck as an example." The intended meaning here is description. So the meaning of *mathaluhu ka-mathali'l-kalb* (his example is like the example of the dog) is: his description is the description of the dog. This is not from the striking of an example. Rather, as He said: ﴿Their example is like the example of one who kindled a fire﴾ [al-Baqara: 17], meaning their description is like the description of the one who kindled. And like His saying: ﴿The example of the Garden which the righteous have been promised﴾ [al-Ra'd: 35], meaning its description. Once this is established, His saying ﴿evil as an example﴾ means *bi'sa waṣfan* (evil as a description), so it is not from striking an example at all.

Al-Hasan, 'Isa ibn 'Umar and al-A'mash read *sa'a mathalu* with a *raf'* (nominative) on *mathalu*, and *al-qawmi* with a *khafd* (genitive). The reading of al-Jahdari is disputed. It is said that it is like the reading of al-A'mash. It is also said that it is with a *kasra* on the *mīm*, a *sukūn* on the *thā'* and a *ḍamma* on the *lām*, in construction (*muḍāfan*) with *al-qawm*. The better reading of *al-mathal* in the nominative is that it be used on its own and taken as part of the category of *ta'ajjub* (exclamation of wonder), like *laqaḍuwa al-rajul* (how fine the man is), meaning: how evil is the example of the people. It is also permissible that it be like *bi'sa*, with the *tamyīz* omitted according to the view of those who permit that. The construction would be: *sa'a mathalu'l-qawm* (evil is the example of the people). Or the noun being dispraised could be ﴿those who denied﴾ [al-A'raf: 40] with an omitted *muḍāf* (a construct noun dropped), meaning: evil is the example of the people, the example of "those who" denied, so that *alladhīna* is in the nominative, since it has taken the place of the omitted *mathal*, and not in the genitive as a description of *al-qawm* with an omitted *tamyīz*.

﴿And they wronged themselves﴾. It may be that it is coordinated with the relative clause (*ṣila*), and it may be that it is a new statement (*isti'nāf ikhbār*) about them, that they were wronging themselves. Al-Zamakhshari, following his method that fronting the object indicates restriction, took it to mean: *wa-mā ẓalamū illā anfusahum bi'l-takdhīb* (they wronged no one but themselves, by denial). He said: The fronting of the object for *ikhtiṣāṣ* (specification) is as if it were said: they singled out themselves for wronging, and did not extend it to anything else.

[p. 426]

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 178:

﴿Whomever Allah guides, he is the one guided; and whomever He leaves astray, those are the losers.﴾ When the mention of the guided and the misguided had preceded, He, exalted is He, informed that He is the one who disposes of them as He wills, with guidance or misguidance. It is established from the school of the People of the Sunna that He, exalted is He, is the Creator of guidance and misguidance in the servant, and the Mu'tazila have interpretations concerning this and its like. Al-Jubba'i said, and it is the choice of al-Qadi: ﴿Whomever Allah guides﴾ to Paradise and reward in the Hereafter, ﴿then he is the one guided﴾ in this world, the one who follows the path of right guidance in what he has been charged with. So He made clear that He does not guide to the reward in the Hereafter except one who has this description, and whomever He leads astray from the path of Paradise: ﴿those are the losers﴾. Some of them said: there is an omission in the speech, meaning: ﴿Whomever Allah guides﴾ so that he accepts and is guided by His guidance, ﴿then he is the one guided, and whomever He leaves astray﴾ by not accepting, ﴿then he is the loser﴾. Some of them said: what is meant is whomever Allah has described as guided: ﴿then he is the one guided﴾; because that is praise, and Allah's praise is not realized except regarding one who is described with it. ﴿And whomever He leaves astray﴾, meaning: whomever He describes as being astray, ﴿then he is the loser﴾. Some of them said: whomever We have given the subtle favours and increase of guidance, ﴿then he is the one guided﴾; ﴿and whomever He leaves astray﴾ from that, because of what has preceded from him through his evil choice, so He removes those subtle favours from having an effect on him for this reason, ﴿then he is the loser﴾. All these interpretations are contrived and remote, and the apparent meaning of the verse refutes the Qadariyya and the Mu'tazila. The phrase ﴿then he is the one guided﴾ was taken in accordance with the wording of "man" (مَن), and the phrase ﴿then those are the losers﴾ was taken in accordance with the meaning of "man," and what made it good is that it is the closing word (fasila) of the verse.

﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind.﴾ This is a report from Him, exalted is He, that He created many of the two categories for Hell. The connection of this with what precedes it is that when He mentioned that He is the Guide and He is the one who leads astray, He followed it with mention of those created for loss and the Fire, and He described their attributes in what He mentioned. Within this is a warning to the disbelievers. The meaning is: for the punishment of Hell. The lam here is the lam of *ṣayrūrah* (the lam of ultimate outcome, *lam al-ʿāqibah*), according to those who affirm this meaning for it. Or, since their final destination is Hell, He made that a cause in the manner of metaphor (*majāz*). Ibn ʿAṭiyyah rejected the view of those who claimed that it is the lam of ṣayrūrah, saying: "This is not correct. The lam of consequence can only be conceived when the act of the doer was not intended for what the matter comes to. Here, however, the act was intended for what the matter comes to, namely their residence in Hell." End of quote. The reason for holding that it is the lam of consequence and ṣayrūrah is that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhāriyāt: 56]. So affirming that it is for causation contradicts His saying: ﴿except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhāriyāt: 56]. They cited as evidence for establishing the meaning of ṣayrūrah for the lam the words of the poet:

*Certainly every newborn is born for death,*
*and I do not see a living thing being made to live forever.*

And the words of another:

*For death do the mothers bear their young,*
*just as dwellings are built for the ruin of time.*

The claim that there is an inversion (*qalb*, transposition of word order) in it, and that its intended sense is "And We have certainly created Hell for many," is not sound, because inversion does not occur except in poetry according to the correct view. The word *kathīr* (many) does not indicate the majority. However, it is established in a hadith that the group sent to the Fire is the greater: in the saying of God to Adam: "Bring forth the group for the Fire from your offspring." So he brought forth from every thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine. And these created ones for Hell are those upon whose hearts God has set a seal, so faith never comes from them at all. Ibn Jubayr's interpretation that they are children of fornication is not good.

﴿They have hearts with which they do not understand, and they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear.﴾ Since they did not reflect upon any of the signs, nor look at them with a view to taking lesson, nor hear them with the hearing of reflection, they were treated as though they had lost understanding with their hearts, sight with their eyes, and hearing with their ears. The intended meaning is not the negation of these perceptions from these senses; rather, the intended meaning is the negation of benefit from them in what was required of them, namely faith. Miskin al-Darimi said:

*Blind when my neighbour goes out,*
*until the veil conceals my neighbour.*

*And deaf to what passes between us,*
*deliberately, though I have no deafness in my hearing.*

Mujahid explained this, saying: "﴿They do not understand with them﴾ anything of the affairs of the Hereafter; ﴿they do not see with them﴾ the guidance; ﴿they do not hear with them﴾ the truth." End of quote. In His saying ﴿They have hearts with which they do not understand﴾ is evidence that the heart is an instrument for understanding and knowledge, just as the eye is an instrument for seeing and the ear an instrument for hearing.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "He made them so because of their extreme immersion in disbelief and their intense stubbornness in it, and that there does not come from them except the deeds of the people of the Fire, as those created for the Fire, indicating their deep penetration into what brings about (the Fire) and their firm establishment in what qualifies them to enter the Fire." From this is the letter of ʿUmar to Khalid ibn al-Walid: "It has reached me that the people of Syria have made for you a bucket kneaded with wine, and I think you, O family of al-Mughirah, are the seed of the Fire (*dharʾ al-nār*)." It is said of one who is drowning in some matters: "So-and-so was created only for the Fire." The intended meaning is describing their state in the magnitude of what they undertook in denying the Messenger of God, while knowing that he is the promised Prophet, and that they are among the great number from whom faith scarcely comes at all, as if they were created for the Fire. End of quote. And this is an exaggeration in the explanation.

﴿Those are like livestock﴾, that is: in lacking understanding of consequences, in looking for lesson, and in listening for reflection; and they are concerned with nothing other than eating and drinking.

﴿Nay, they are more astray﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: "﴿Nay, they are more astray﴾ in the way (*sabīlan*) than livestock, regarding understanding, lesson, and reflection." It has been said: livestock perceive their benefits from their harms, so they adhere to some of what they perceive; and most of these people know that the Messenger is opposed, yet they rush into the Fire. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: "They are judged to be more astray because livestock are constituted in their make-up and creation not to reflect upon anything, whereas these people are prepared for understanding, and powers have been created in them which they could employ, and they were given a portion of sight. So by their heedlessness and turning away, they join themselves to livestock, and thus they are more astray in this respect." End of quote. It has also been said: "They are more astray because they disobey, whereas livestock do not disobey." It has been said: livestock know their Lord and glorify Him, whereas the disbelievers do not know Him nor call upon Him. And it is narrated: "Everything is more obedient to God than the son of Adam." Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Razi said: "Man and the rest of the animals share with him in the powers of nature: the growing, the nourishing and the generative; and in the benefits of the five outward and inward senses; and in the states of imagination, thought and recollection. Distinction between man and other beings is achieved only through the intellectual and reflective power which guides him to knowledge of the truth for its own sake and of the good for the sake of acting upon it. So when the disbelievers turned away from the purposes of the states of intellect and thought, and from knowing the truth and acting upon the good, they became like livestock. Then He said: ﴿Nay, they are more astray﴾, (p-427) because animals have no capacity to attain virtues, whereas man was given the capacity to attain them. Whoever turns away from acquiring great virtues while having the capacity to attain them is in a worse state than one who did not acquire them through inability. Therefore He said: ﴿Nay, they are more astray﴾." End of quote.

It has been said: livestock flee to their owners and to those who look after their welfare, whereas the disbeliever flees from his Lord who has bestowed upon him countless blessings. It has been said: livestock go astray if there is no guide with them, and rarely go astray if one is with them; and these people, the Messengers have come to them and the Books have been sent down to them, yet they increase in error. End of quote.

I say: this turn (*iḍrāb*) is not by way of nullifying the preceding report that they are likened to livestock. It is not permissible for the aspect of exaggeration in error to be the aspect of the likeness, because that would lead to the falsehood of one of the two statements, and that is impossible with respect to God, exalted is He. The discourse of earlier commentators indicates that He likened them to livestock in what was mentioned, and that they are more astray than livestock in that wherein the likeness occurred; and this is not permissible for the reason we have stated. So what is relied upon is that the aspect of likeness differs from the aspect of exaggeration in error, and that this turn is not by way of nullification. The meaning of the sentence ﴿Nay, they are more astray﴾ is a turn indicating a shift from one report to another report. The first sentence likened them to livestock in the absence of the benefits of perceptions which lead to complying with what the Messengers brought; the second sentence affirmed for them the exaggeration in error of the path they take. So the one described with exaggeration in error is their path, and the specification (*tamyīz*) is omitted; its estimate is: ﴿Nay, they are more astray﴾ *as a path* than they are. What confirms this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or do you think that most of them hear or understand? They are only like livestock﴾ [al-Furqan: 44], that is, in the absence of hearing for reflection and understanding; ﴿Nay, they are more astray as a way﴾ [al-Furqan: 44], that is, nay, their way is more astray. So the one judged first is not the one judged last, and the thing judged is also different.

﴿Those are the heedless﴾. In this sentence God, exalted is He, explained the cause of their being more astray than livestock, which is heedlessness. ʿAṭāʾ said: heedless of what God has prepared for His friends of reward and for His enemies of punishment.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 180:

﴿To Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them, and leave those who deviate concerning His names. They will be recompensed for what they used to do.﴾ Muqatil said: A man called upon Allah in his prayer, and at another time he called upon al-Rahman. Abu Jahl said: "Does not Muhammad and his companions claim that they worship one Lord? So what is the matter with this one who calls upon two?" So this verse was revealed. Its connection to what precedes it is that when He, the Exalted, mentioned that He had created many of the jinn and mankind for the Fire, He mentioned a category of them, namely: ﴿those who deviate concerning His names﴾, and they are the most insolent of the disbelievers: Abu Jahl and his like. Also, when He pointed out that their entry into Hell is due to heedlessness of the remembrance of Allah, and that deliverance from the punishment is the remembrance of Allah, He commanded the remembrance of Allah by His Most Beautiful Names and His Sublime Attributes. When the heart becomes heedless of the remembrance of Allah and turns to this world and its desires, it falls into greed, and moves from one desire to another, from one pursuit to another, and from one darkness to another. We have found this by experience, to the extent that one of them may pray all the prayers together at one time as qada' (make-up prayers). But when the door of the remembrance of Allah the Exalted opens for his heart, he is freed from the afflictions of heedlessness, complies with what Allah has commanded him, and avoids what He has forbidden.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Those which are the most beautiful names, because they do not indicate meanings that are beautiful, such as praise, sanctification and other than that," end of quote. So al-husna is the feminine of al-ahsan, and the description of a plural non-rational noun with what the singular is described by, as in His saying: ﴿And for her there are other uses﴾ [Ta-Ha: 18], and this is eloquent. Had it come in agreement with the plural, the well-formed construction would have been al-ukhar on the pattern of al-ukhar, as in His saying: ﴿then an equal number of other days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184]; because the plural of non-rational things is referred to and described with the feminine plural, even if the singular is masculine. It was also said: al-husna is a verbal noun (masdar) described by it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "And al-asma' here means the namings (al-tasmiyat) by consensus of the interpreters; nothing else is possible," end of quote. There is no precision in what he said, because "al-tasmiyah" is a verbal noun, and what is meant here is the words that are applied to Allah, the Exalted, and they are the descriptions that indicate differences of attributes, not differences of the one described, just as you say: Zayd came, the jurist, the brave, the generous. That the name by which He, the Exalted, commanded to be called upon is beautiful is what the Law has established and explicitly stated regarding its application to Allah. The meaning of ﴿so call upon Him by them﴾ is: call out to Him by them, as in your saying: O Allah, O Merciful, O Owner, and what resembles that. Al-Zamakhshari said: "So name Him by those names," making it of the type of "I called my son Abd Allah," i.e., I named him with this name. It has been disputed regarding a name that entails pure praise and to which no doubt or shared meaning attaches, except that it has not been reported explicitly whether Allah the Exalted may be described and named by it. Al-Qadi Abu Bakr al-Baqillani explicitly permitted it, and Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari explicitly prohibited it, and the jurists and the majority held this view, and it is the correct position. It has also been disputed regarding the verbs in the Qur'an, such as the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15] and ﴿They plot and Allah plots﴾ [al-Anfal: 30], whether from Him, the Exalted, the active participle may be applied to Him restricted by its object, so that it is said: Allah is mocking the disbelievers, and plotting against those who plot. A group permitted that, and a group prohibited it, and it is the correct position. As for applying the active participle without its restriction, there is consensus on its prohibition. At-Tirmidhi in his Jami' narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah the explicit mention of ninety-nine names listed one by one. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "Some of them are anomalous," and that hadith is not mutawatir, although Abu 'Isa said about it: "This is a gharib hadith; we do not know it except through the route of the hadith of Safwan ibn Salih, and he is trustworthy according to the people of hadith." What is mutawatir from it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah has ninety-nine names, one hundred less one; whoever counts them enters Paradise." And the meaning of "counts them" (ahsaha) is that he enumerates them, memorizes them, and that includes believing in them, glorifying them and reflecting on their meanings. This is the hadith of al-Bukhari, end of quote.

Calling this hadith mutawatir is not in accordance with the terminology of the muhaddithun regarding mutawatir; rather it is a khabar of individual transmission (khabar ahad).

In some of the supplications of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) there is: "O Hannan, O Mannan," but these two are not found in the Jami' of at-Tirmidhi. Scholars have composed works explaining Allah's Most Beautiful Names, such as Abu Hamid al-Ghazali, Ibn al-Hakam ibn Burjan, Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi, Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi and others. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is also possible that what is meant is: To Allah belong the Most Beautiful Descriptions, which are description by justice, goodness and benevolence, and the negation of resemblance to creation; so describe Him by them: ﴿and leave those who deviate﴾ in His attributes, who describe Him with the will of ugliness and the creation of indecency and wrongdoing, and with what (p-430) falls under anthropomorphism, such as seeing and the like." It was also said: The meaning of His saying: ﴿and leave those who deviate concerning His names﴾ is: leave them and do not argue with them nor confront them, said by Ibn Zayd; on this view the verse is abrogated by fighting. It was also said: its meaning is a warning, like His saying: ﴿Leave Me with whom I created alone﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 11], and His saying: ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves﴾ [al-Hijr: 3]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "And leave the naming of those who turn away from truth and rightness in it, so that they name Him by what is not fitting for Him, as we have heard the Bedouins, in their ignorance, say: O father of generosity, O white-faced one, O generous one; or that they refuse to name Him by some of His Most Beautiful Names, such as saying: O Allah, but not saying: O Merciful." It was also said: the meaning of deviation (ilhad) concerning His names is their naming their idols al-Lat, looking to the name Allah, and al-'Uzza, looking to al-'Aziz; said by Mujahid. They also name Allah "father" and their idols "lords," and similar. Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning of (yulhidun) is "they deny." Qatadah said: "they associate partners." al-Khattabi said: error concerning His names and turning away from them is deviation (ilhad). Hamzah recited yalhadun with a fatha on the ya' and the ha', and likewise in al-Nahl and al-Sajdah; this is the reading of Ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash, Talhah and 'Isa. The rest of the seven read with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the ha' in them. ﴿sayujzawn﴾ is a severe warning, and within the scope of His saying ﴿for what they used to do﴾ falls deviation concerning His names and all their other ugly actions.

﴿And among those We have created is a community that guides by the truth and by it acts justly.﴾ When He mentioned those whom He created for Hell, He mentioned their counterpart. The word ﴿among﴾ (*wa-mimman*) indicates partiality, and that most of the created beings are not guides to the truth nor do they act justly by it. It has been said: they are the scholars and the callers to the religion. It has also been said: they are the believers among the People of the Book, related by Ibn al-Kalbi and narrated from Qatada and Ibn Jurayj. It has been said: they are the Emigrants (*al-Muhajirun*), the Helpers (*al-Ansar*), and those who followed them in goodness. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the Community of Muhammad (ﷺ), and most of the exegetes hold this view. It is narrated concerning this that when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited it, he would say: "This is for you, and the people before you were given something similar," referring to ﴿And among the people of Musa there is a community who guide by the truth and by it act justly﴾ (7:159). And from him (ﷺ): "Indeed, among my community there will be a group upon the truth until 'Isa ibn Maryam (Jesus, son of Mary) descends."

The apparent meaning is that this sentence informs that among those whom We created there is a community described with such-and-such qualities. It therefore does not indicate a specification of particular persons or particular times. It is suitable for every guide to the truth from this community and from others, and in the time of the Messenger and in other times, just as its counterpart in His saying ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind﴾ (7:179) does not indicate the specification of persons or times. Rather, this is a division of the created being for the Fire and the created being for the Garden. For this reason it has been said that there is an omitted element in the speech, its estimated form being "[And among those] whom We created," which is indicated by the affirmation of its counterpart in His saying ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell﴾ (7:179).

Al-Jubba'i said: this verse indicates that no time is ever devoid of those who stand for the truth, act by it, and guide to it, and that they never agree upon falsehood at any period of time. End of quote. The verse does not indicate what al-Jubba'i claimed, and what he said contradicts what has been narrated: "The Hour will not come except upon the worst of creation," and "The Hour will not come until it is not said on earth: Allah, Allah," and "The Hour will not come until the Book of God is erased (*yusra*), so that not a single letter of it remains," or as he said.

﴿And those who denied Our signs, We will lead them gradually (*nastadrijuhum*) from where they do not know﴾ (7:182). Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad said: We will prolong their lives in their delusion. Abu 'Ubayda said: *istidraj* (gradual leading) is that you proceed toward a thing secretly, little by little, and do not rush upon it; its root is from *darajah* (degree, step), because the one ascending and the one descending ascend and descend step by step. From it comes *darraja al-kitab*, meaning he folded the book bit by bit, and *darraja al-qawm*, meaning the people died one after another. Ibn Qutayba said: it is that He makes them taste a little of His punishment, little by little, from where they do not know, and does not follow up on them with it nor confronts them openly. Al-Azhari said: We will seize them little by little from where they do not expect, because God Most High opens a door of blessing in which they rejoice and to which they incline, then seizes them in their heedlessness at the moment they are most unaware. End of quote. From it comes *darraja al-sabiyy* (the child walked), when he brings his steps close together. The meaning is: We will take from them a little at a time, degree after degree, through blessings bestowed upon them and respite granted to them, until they become deluded and think that no punishment will reach them.

Al-Jubba'i said: "We will lead them gradually to the punishments until they fall into them from where they do not know, as a gradual leading to that. Thus this punishment may be in this world, like killing, and it may be the punishment of the Hereafter."

Al-Zamakhshari said: The meaning of ﴿We will lead them gradually﴾ is: We will bring them down little by little to that which destroys them and multiplies their punishment, from where they do not know what is intended for them. This is that God continues to bestow blessings upon them while they are immersed in error. Whenever He renews a blessing for them, they become more arrogant and renew their disobedience, so they advance in sins through the succession of blessings, thinking that the continuous blessings are a favour from God and a drawing near, when in fact they are abandonment by Him and distancing. This is the *istidraj* of God, we seek refuge in God Most High from it, "from where they do not know." It has been said: by the *istidraj*; and it has been said: by destruction.

Al-Nakha'i and Ibn Thabbat read *sa-yastadrijuhum* with the *ya'* (third person). This may be an instance of *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person), and it may be that the subject is the pronoun of denial understood from *kadhdhabu* (they denied), i.e., "denial itself will lead them gradually."

Al-A'sha said, concerning *istidraj*:

*Even if you were in a well eighty cubits deep,
and you ascended the means of the heavens by a ladder,
the speech would lead you gradually until you shake it,
and you would know that I am not one struck dumb before you.*

﴿And I will give them respite; indeed My plan is firm﴾ (7:183) is coordinated with "We will lead them gradually," so it falls within the future. It has also been said: My punishment; and He called it a plan because it descends upon the servants from where they do not perceive. *Matin* (firm) means strong of anything, from *matuna matanatan*. This is a report about the deniers in general. It has been said: it was revealed concerning the mockers among Quraysh, whom God destroyed in a single night after granting them respite for a period.

Abd al-Hamid, from Ibn 'Amir, read *inna kaydi* with a *fatḥa* on the *hamza*, meaning "because my plan..." The majority read it with a *kasra*, as a new sentence.
