Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 184:

﴿Have they not reflected? There is no madness in their companion. He is only a clear warner.﴾ Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: The occasion of its revelation was that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) climbed al-Safa at night and began calling the clans of Quraysh: "O Banu so-and-so, O Banu so-and-so," warning them and inviting them to Allah, the Exalted. Some of the disbelievers said when they woke in the morning: "This man is mad; he kept shouting until morning." They used to say: "He is a mad poet." So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, negated what they said about him, then informed that he is a warner of the punishment of Allah. The verse prompts them to reflect on the matter of the Messenger (ﷺ) and on the absence of madness from him. This interrogative (istifham) has been said to mean reproach (tawbikh), and it has been said to mean encouragement to contemplate (tahrid). "Jinnah" (madness), as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿of the jinn and of mankind﴾ [al-Nas: 6]. The meaning is: from the touch of a jinn, or the derangement of a jinn. It has also been said that it is a state like "al-jilsah" (the sitting) and "al-rukbah" (the kneeling), meaning a verbal noun, i.e., "there is no madness (junun) in your companion." The apparent view is that "yatafakkaru" is suspended (mu'allaq) from the negated clause, which occupies the place of an accusative after the removal of the preposition, because reflection is an act of the heart, so suspending it is permissible. The meaning is: "Have they not contemplated and pondered the negation of this attribute from the Messenger? It is certainly negated, and no one who applies careful thought to attributing it to him could do so." It has also been said that there is a concealed, omitted element here, meaning: "so that they would know what madness is not in their companion." This was stated by al-Hawfi, who claimed that "tafakkaru" cannot be suspended, since it does not govern whole clauses. He said: "Reflection implies knowledge." Our companions said: when a verb of the heart is transitive by means of a preposition, the clause is considered to be in the place of a genitive after the removal of the preposition. As for those who claim that the verb which is transitive by itself to one object, or by a preposition to one object, is treated as implying the meaning of what is transitive to two objects, so that the clause occupies the place of two objects, then according to these two views there is no need for the concealed element that al-Hawfi proposed. It has also been said: the sentence is complete at "yatafakkaru," and then it begins anew as a statement of the negation of madness and the affirmation of warning. Abu al-Baqa' said: regarding "ma," there are two possibilities. One is that it is retained (as a negative particle), and there is an ellipsis in the speech, its estimated form being: "Have they not reflected on their saying that he has madness?" The second is that it is an interrogative, meaning: "Have they not reflected what kind of madness their companion has, given the coherence of his words and deeds?" It has also been said: it is in the sense of "alladhi" (which), its estimated form being: "Have they not reflected on what is with their companion?" On this view the speech came out according to their own assumption. He concluded. These are weak explanations from which the Qur'an should be kept free. Reflection (tafakkur) is used with what is established in the language as suspended, so one should not depart from that.

﴿Have they not considered the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and whatever things Allah has created?﴾ When He urged them to reflect on the condition of the Messenger (ﷺ), and this followed from establishing the proof of tawhid (the oneness of God), He followed it with what indicates the oneness of God and the existence of the wise Creator. Malakut (the dominion) means the great kingdom. Its explanation has already been given in His words: ﴿And thus did We show Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 75]. He did not limit himself to mentioning the contemplation of the dominion. Rather, he drew attention to the fact that every single existing thing is a place for contemplation, reflection and inference concerning the wise Creator and His oneness, as the poet said:

*And in everything there is a sign for Him, that indicates He is the One.*

﴿And that perhaps their term has drawn near?﴾ (Wa-an) is coordinated with (ma) in His words "and what [things] He created." They are rebuked for failing to contemplate the dominion of the heavens and the earth, which is the greatest of created things and the strongest evidence of the greatness of the Creator. Then he joined to it something general, namely His words: ﴿and whatever things Allah has created﴾, so the heavens and the earth were included within "what He created." Then he joined to it something specific to themselves, namely their failure to contemplate and reflect on the fact that their term (ajal) has drawn near, so that death would seize them while they were heedless of considering what has been mentioned, and their affair would end in loss and the punishment of the Fire. He alerted them to reflect on the nearness of the term, so that perhaps they would hasten toward it, and toward seeking the truth and what would save them from the punishment of Allah before the term catches them. Their term is the time of their death. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that by the nearness of the term is meant the nearness of the Hour. (An) here is the lightened form of the heavy (an), and its noun is an omitted pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), and its predicate is ʿasā together with what is connected to it. The predicate of a non-declarative sentence has occurred in verses like this one, and like His words: ﴿and the fifth [oath] that the wrath of Allah be upon her﴾ [al-Nur: 9]. So ﴿the wrath of Allah be upon her﴾ is a supplicatory sentence, and it is not declarative. Had (an) been the heavy form, ʿasā and a supplicatory sentence could not have come after it. It is not permissible to say: "I knew that Zayd ʿasā an yakhruja," nor "I knew that Zayd, may Allah curse him," while you intend a supplication. Abu al-Baqa permitted that (an) be the lightened form of the heavy (an), and also that it be the masdarī (verbal-noun) particle, meaning the one composed of two letters, which governs the imperfect verb. This is not correct, because they stated explicitly that it is joined to a fully inflected verb without restriction, meaning a past, present, or imperative verb, and so they made inflection a condition for it. ʿAsā is an invariable verb, so it cannot be a relative clause for (an). Here ʿasā is complete (tāmmah), and (an) would have a subject after it, as in your saying: ʿasā an taqūma (it is possible that you will stand). The name of yakūnu: al-Hawfi said it is ajaluhum, and qad iqtaraba is the predicate. Al-Zamakhshari and others said that the name of yakūnu is a pronoun of the matter, so qad iqtaraba ajaluhum is in a position of accusative as the predicate of yakūnu, and ajaluhum is the subject of iqtaraba. What al-Hawfi permitted is disputed. When you say kāna yaqūmu Zayd, some grammarians hold that Zayd is the noun, and yaqūmu is in an accusative position as the predicate, while others forbid this and make the pronoun of the matter the subject there. Ibn Malik preferred permission, and Ibn ʿUṣfūr preferred prohibition. We have discussed this question fully, with its divisions and proofs, in our commentary on the book al-Tashil.

﴿Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾ The meaning of this sentence and of what precedes it: a rebuke and reproach for their not having contemplated or reflected on anything of the dominion of the heavens and the earth, nor on the creatures of Allah the Exalted, nor on the nearness of their terms. Then He said: "Then in what statement or matter will their faith and affirmation occur," since they have not believed in a matter in which their salvation and entry into Paradise lie. A similar line is the poet's:

*So on behalf of which soul after my soul do I fight?*

The meaning: if I do not fight on behalf of my own self, how will I fight on behalf of another's? Likewise, if they do not believe in this statement, which is pure truth and in which lies their salvation and deliverance, how will they believe in some other statement? The meaning is that it is not in their nature to affirm what contains their deliverance. The pronoun in (baʿdahu) refers either to the Qur'an, or to the Messenger and his account and affair, or to the term; the opinions are three, since there is no action after death. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: with what is His saying ﴿then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾ connected? I say: with His saying ﴿it is possible that their term has drawn near﴾, as if it were said: perhaps their term has drawn near, so why do they not hasten to believe in the Qur'an before it is too late? What are they waiting for after the truth has become clear? And with what statement more deserving than this do they wish to believe?"

﴿Whomever Allah leaves astray, there is no guide for him﴾ He negated, in a general way, that there could be a guide for one whom Allah has led astray. Thus it implies despair of their faith and abhorrence of them.

﴿And He leaves them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ Al-Hasan, Qatadah, Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman, Abu Jaʿfar, al-Aʿraj, Shaybah, the two Haramis (Makkah and Madinah), and Ibn ʿAmir read (nadharuhum) with a nun and a raised raʾ. Abu ʿAmr and ʿAsim read it with a yaʾ and a raised raʾ, and this is a resumed statement of a cut-off verb, or a pronoun of "we" is implied before it, making it a nominal sentence. Ibn Musarrif, al-Aʿmash, the two Akhawan (brothers), and Abu ʿAmr, as Abu Hatim mentioned, read it with a yaʾ and a jazm (apocopation). Kharijah related from Nafiʿ it with a nun and a jazm. The quiescence of the raʾ is explained in two ways: first, that it became quiescent to avoid a succession of vowels, as in the reading of (wa-mā yush'irakum) and (yanṣurkum); in that case it is in the raised position. Second, that it is in the jussive mood, coordinated with the position of (fa-lā hādiya lahu), since it is in a jussive position. This is like His words: ﴿so it is better for you, and He will expiate﴾ [al-Baqarah: 271], in the reading of the one who read with jazm on the raʾ of (wa-nukaffir). And like the poet's line:

*Whichever way you go, I am your enemy, and so increase in your diminishing in life.*

﴿They ask you about the Hour: when will be its arrival?﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 187] The pronoun in (yasaluunaka) refers to the Quraysh. They said: "O Muhammad, we are your kin, so inform us of the time of the Hour." Ibn ʿAbbas said the pronoun refers to the Jews. Hasal ibn Abi Bashir and Shamwil ibn Zaydan said: "If you are a prophet, inform us of the time of the Hour, for we know it. If you are truthful, we will believe in you." So it was revealed. Its connection with what precedes is that when He mentioned tawhid, prophethood, decree and predestination, He followed that with mention of the return (al-maʿad). Also, since His words ﴿it is possible that their term has drawn near﴾ came earlier, and this was a motive for hastening to repentance, He brought the question about the Hour so that it would be known that its time is hidden from creation, and that this would be a cause for hastening to repentance. The Hour (al-sāʿah) is the Resurrection: the death of whoever is alive at that time, and the raising of all of them. The term "Hour" applies to it and the term "Resurrection" applies to it. Al-Saʿah is among the dominant names, like al-Najm (the Star) for the Pleiades. The majority read (ayyāna) with a fatha on the hamza, while al-Sulami read it with a kasra wherever it occurs. It was previously mentioned that this is the dialect of his people, Sulaym. (Mursāhā) is a verbal noun, meaning: when is its anchoring? Its establishing (ithbātuhā) means its fixing (iqrāruhā). Al-rusuww means the steadiness of a heavy thing, from which comes "rasā al-jabal" (the mountain became anchored) and "arsaytu al-safīnah" (I anchored the ship), and al-mursā is the place where it is anchored. Al-Zamakhshari said: mursāhā means its anchoring, or the time of its anchoring, that is, its fixing and establishing, end of quote. His estimate "or the time of its anchoring" is not good, because ayyāna is an interrogative noun asking about time, so it cannot be a predicate about time except metaphorically. For it would mean: "at what time is the time of its anchoring?" Ayyāna mursāhā is the subject, and Ibn ʿAṭiyyah related from al-Mubarrad that mursāhā is raised by an omitted verb, but there is no need for this omission. Ayyāna mursāhā is an interrogative sentence in the position of a substitute for "al-sāʿah" (the Hour), and the substitute is according to the intention of repeating the governing verb. That governing verb is suspended from its action, because the sentence contains an interrogative. Since the verb is suspended, and it is transitive by means of "ʿan," the sentence is in an accusative position after dropping the preposition, so it is a substitute, in the sentence, for the position of "ʿan al-sāʿah," because the position of the genitive is accusative. A parallel in substitution is the saying: "ʿArftu Zayd abū man huwa?" (I knew Zayd: who is his father?) according to the best view on the analysis of this question. That is, the interrogative sentence stands in the position of a substitute.

﴿Have they not considered the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and whatever things Allah has created?﴾ When He urged them to reflect on the condition of the Messenger (ﷺ), and this followed from establishing the proof of tawhid (the oneness of God), He followed it with what indicates the oneness of God and the existence of the wise Creator. Malakut (the dominion) means the great kingdom. Its explanation has already been given in His words: ﴿And thus did We show Abraham the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 75]. He did not limit himself to mentioning the contemplation of the dominion. Rather, he drew attention to the fact that every single existing thing is a place for contemplation, reflection and inference concerning the wise Creator and His oneness, as the poet said:

*And in everything there is a sign for Him, that indicates He is the One.*

﴿And that perhaps their term has drawn near?﴾ (Wa-an) is coordinated with (ma) in His words "and what [things] He created." They are rebuked for failing to contemplate the dominion of the heavens and the earth, which is the greatest of created things and the strongest evidence of the greatness of the Creator. Then he joined to it something general, namely His words: ﴿and whatever things Allah has created﴾, so the heavens and the earth were included within "what He created." Then he joined to it something specific to themselves, namely their failure to contemplate and reflect on the fact that their term (ajal) has drawn near, so that death would seize them while they were heedless of considering what has been mentioned, and their affair would end in loss and the punishment of the Fire. He alerted them to reflect on the nearness of the term, so that perhaps they would hasten toward it, and toward seeking the truth and what would save them from the punishment of Allah before the term catches them. Their term is the time of their death. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that by the nearness of the term is meant the nearness of the Hour. (An) here is the lightened form of the heavy (an), and its noun is an omitted pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), and its predicate is ʿasā together with what is connected to it. The predicate of a non-declarative sentence has occurred in verses like this one, and like His words: ﴿and the fifth [oath] that the wrath of Allah be upon her﴾ [al-Nur: 9]. So ﴿the wrath of Allah be upon her﴾ is a supplicatory sentence, and it is not declarative. Had (an) been the heavy form, ʿasā and a supplicatory sentence could not have come after it. It is not permissible to say: "I knew that Zayd ʿasā an yakhruja," nor "I knew that Zayd, may Allah curse him," while you intend a supplication. Abu al-Baqa permitted that (an) be the lightened form of the heavy (an), and also that it be the masdarī (verbal-noun) particle, meaning the one composed of two letters, which governs the imperfect verb. This is not correct, because they stated explicitly that it is joined to a fully inflected verb without restriction, meaning a past, present, or imperative verb, and so they made inflection a condition for it. ʿAsā is an invariable verb, so it cannot be a relative clause for (an). Here ʿasā is complete (tāmmah), and (an) would have a subject after it, as in your saying: ʿasā an taqūma (it is possible that you will stand). The name of yakūnu: al-Hawfi said it is ajaluhum, and qad iqtaraba is the predicate. Al-Zamakhshari and others said that the name of yakūnu is a pronoun of the matter, so qad iqtaraba ajaluhum is in a position of accusative as the predicate of yakūnu, and ajaluhum is the subject of iqtaraba. What al-Hawfi permitted is disputed. When you say kāna yaqūmu Zayd, some grammarians hold that Zayd is the noun, and yaqūmu is in an accusative position as the predicate, while others forbid this and make the pronoun of the matter the subject there. Ibn Malik preferred permission, and Ibn ʿUṣfūr preferred prohibition. We have discussed this question fully, with its divisions and proofs, in our commentary on the book al-Tashil.

﴿Then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾ The meaning of this sentence and of what precedes it: a rebuke and reproach for their not having contemplated or reflected on anything of the dominion of the heavens and the earth, nor on the creatures of Allah the Exalted, nor on the nearness of their terms. Then He said: "Then in what statement or matter will their faith and affirmation occur," since they have not believed in a matter in which their salvation and entry into Paradise lie. A similar line is the poet's:

*So on behalf of which soul after my soul do I fight?*

The meaning: if I do not fight on behalf of my own self, how will I fight on behalf of another's? Likewise, if they do not believe in this statement, which is pure truth and in which lies their salvation and deliverance, how will they believe in some other statement? The meaning is that it is not in their nature to affirm what contains their deliverance. The pronoun in (baʿdahu) refers either to the Qur'an, or to the Messenger and his account and affair, or to the term; the opinions are three, since there is no action after death. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: with what is His saying ﴿then in what statement after this will they believe?﴾ connected? I say: with His saying ﴿it is possible that their term has drawn near﴾, as if it were said: perhaps their term has drawn near, so why do they not hasten to believe in the Qur'an before it is too late? What are they waiting for after the truth has become clear? And with what statement more deserving than this do they wish to believe?"

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 187:

﴿Say: "Its knowledge is only with my Lord. None will reveal it at its time except Him."﴾ That is: Allah has singled out its knowledge for Himself. Since the question about the Hour was first general and then specified as a question about its time, the answer came in general terms about it, with His saying ﴿Say: "Its knowledge is only with my Lord"﴾. Then it was specified with respect to the time, so it was said: "None will reveal it at its time except Him." The knowledge of the Hour is among the five unseen matters that are stated explicitly, namely that Exalted is He alone knows it. The meaning is: none will make it manifest and disclose it at the time that has been decreed for it to occur, except Him. They said: the wisdom in concealing it is that people will always be on guard, so its concealment is more conducive to obedience and more restraining from disobedience, just as He concealed the specific term, which is the time of death, for this same reason. Al-Zamakhshari said: "None will reveal it at its time except Him," that is, it remains hidden, and none but Him alone reveals its matter and uncovers the hiddenness of its knowledge, when He brings it at its time suddenly; none of His creatures reveals it by informing about it before its coming, because its hiddenness continues for others until the time of its occurrence. End of quotation. It is a statement that contains excess and obscurity.

﴿It has become heavy upon the heavens and the earth.﴾ Ibn Jurayj said: its meaning is that it has become heavy upon the heavens and the earth themselves, because the heavens will split, the earth will be changed, and the mountains will be blown away. Al-Hasan said: it has become heavy because of its awesomeness and the terror of it upon the people of the heavens and the earth. Al-Suddi said: the meaning of "it has become heavy" is that it is hidden in the heavens and the earth, so none of the angels brought near or the prophets sent knows when it will be. What is hidden in its matter becomes heavy upon souls. End of quotation. Heaviness is used to express severity and difficulty, as He said: ﴿And they leave behind them a heavy day﴾ [al-Insan: 27], that is, a severe and difficult day. Its original construction is that it takes ʿalā (upon), so one says: "This matter became heavy upon me" (thaqula ʿalayya hādhā al-amr). A poet said: "Heavy upon the enemies." So it may be claimed that fī here means ʿalā, as some have said regarding His saying ﴿and I will crucify you upon the trunks of palm trees﴾ [Ta-Ha: 71], that is, the verb thaqulat is taken to imply a meaning that takes fī (by tadmin, "implicit meaning," where one verb is given the sense of another). Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, each of its people, from the angels and the two weighty creatures (humans and jinn), was concerned with the matter of the Hour, desired that its knowledge be made manifest to him, and its hiddenness was hard upon him and weighed heavily upon him. Or it has become heavy in them both, because its people anticipate it and fear its severities and terrors, and because nothing can bear it or stand up to it, so it is heavy in both of them.

﴿It will not come upon you except suddenly.﴾ That is, abruptly, while you are heedless and unaware of its arrival. This is a general address to all people. In a hadith: "Indeed the Hour will come upon a man while he is repairing his pool, a man while he is watering his livestock, a man while he is grazing his animals, a man while he is lowering and raising his scale."

﴿They ask you as if you were eager (ḥafiyy) about it.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Suddi and Mujahid said: "as if you were eager about their question," that is, loving of it. Also from Ibn ʿAbbas: "as if your asking about it pleases you." Also from him: "as if you were striving in the question and extremely attentive to what you are asked about." Ibn Qutayba said: "as if you were seeking its knowledge." Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd also said: its meaning is "as if you were eager about asking about it and occupied with it until you attained it," that is, you love it and prefer it; or it means that you dislike the question because it is among the knowledge of the unseen which Allah has singled out for Himself and has not given to anyone. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: that is, one who takes pains and is concerned. Al-Zamakhshari said: "as if you knew it," and its real meaning is "as if you were excessive in asking about it," because whoever is excessive in asking about a thing and probing into it, his knowledge of it becomes firmly established. This construction means exaggeration, and from it comes iḥfāʾ al-shārib (cutting the moustache closely) and iḥtifāʾ al-naʿl (stripping the sandal, meaning removing it entirely). Aḥfā fī al-masʾalah means "he pressed hard in the question," and ḥafiya bi-fulān and taḥaffā bihi mean he was extremely kind to him. End of quotation. As for ʿanhā (about it), it may be connected to yasʾalūnaka (they ask you), meaning "they ask you about it," and the complement of ḥafiyy is then omitted, the estimate being "as if you were eager about it," that is, concerned with its matter until you knew its reality and the time of its coming. Or it means "as if you were eager about them, or concerned with their affair, so you answer them about it because they claim that its knowledge is with you." Ḥafiyy does not take ʿan; Exalted is He said: ﴿Indeed He was ever gracious to me﴾ [Maryam: 47], and so it took bi (with). Or it may be connected to ḥafiyy by way of tadmin (implicit meaning), because whoever is eager about something has reached it and uncovered it, so the estimate is "as if you were one who uncovers about it by your eagerness." Or ʿan may have the meaning of bi, just as bi may have the meaning of ʿan in the poet's words: "If you ask me about the women, then indeed I..." (that is, about the women). ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) read: "as if you were eager with it" (kaʾannaka ḥafiyyun bihā), with bi in place of ʿan, meaning: knowing it, thoroughly knowledgeable of it.

﴿Say: "Its knowledge is only with Allah."﴾ That is, the knowledge of when it will come is with the knowledge of Allah. The use of ʿinda (with) in the sense of place is figurative, as you say: "Grammar is with Sibawayh," meaning in his knowledge. The repetition of the question and answer is for emphasis, and because of what came with it of the addition of His saying: "as if you were eager about it."

﴿But most people do not know.﴾ Al-Tabari said: they do not know that this matter is known only to Allah, but most of them think that it is among what human beings know. It was also said: they do not know that the Resurrection is true, because most of creation deny the return and say: ﴿There is none but our life of this world﴾ [al-Anʿam: 29], and so on. It was also said: they do not know that I have informed you that its time is known only to Allah. It was also said: they do not know the reason for which I concealed the knowledge of its time. The view of al-Tabari is more apparent.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 188:

﴿Say: "I possess no power to benefit or harm myself, except as God wills."﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: (p-436) The people of Mecca said: "Would your Lord not inform you of cheap goods before their prices rise, so that you could buy and profit? And of a land that will become barren, so that you could leave it for one that is fertile?" So this was revealed. It is also said that when he returned from the campaign against the Banu al-Mustaliq, a wind came upon the road and brought news of the death of Rifaʿa, and this was a source of anger for the hypocrites. Then he said: "Look for where my she-camel is." ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy said: "Are you not amazed at this man, who reports the death of a man in Medina but does not know where his own she-camel is?" The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Some hypocrites said such-and-such, and my she-camel is in the valley, her halter caught on a tree. Bring her back to me." Then this was revealed. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is quite evident. In this, he (peace be upon him) displayed servitude and disavowed what is specific to lordship, namely power and knowledge of the unseen, and exhibited utmost submission. So: "I do not possess the ability to bring about benefit for myself or to avert harm, so how could I possess knowledge of the unseen?" As He said in Surah Yunus: ﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ [Yunus: 48] ﴿Say: "I possess no power to harm or benefit myself, except as God wills. For every nation there is a term."﴾ [Yunus: 49] Here, however, he placed benefit before harm, because the preceding verse says: ﴿Whomever God guides is the one truly guided, and whomever He leads astray…﴾ [al-Araf: 178], where guidance is placed before misguidance. And after it comes: ﴿I would have acquired much good, and no harm would have touched me﴾, so placing benefit first is appropriate. In Yunus, harm was placed first, in accordance with the natural order, because worship of God is first out of fear of His punishment, and then out of hope for His reward. For this reason He said: ﴿They call upon their Lord in fear and in hope﴾ [al-Sajda: 16]. When benefit is placed first, this is due to the precedence of a word that is implied in it. Furthermore, in Yunus there is agreement with what comes before it, for there He says: ﴿There is no one for them, besides God, to be a protector or intercessor, and even if they offered every ransom, it would not be accepted from them﴾ [al-Anam: 70]. In Yunus it also says: ﴿And do not call upon, besides God, that which neither benefits you nor harms you﴾ [Yunus: 106]. Preceding that is: ﴿Then We save Our messengers and those who believe﴾ [Yunus: 103], ﴿Thus, it is incumbent upon Us to save the believers﴾ [Yunus: 103]. In al-Anbiya He said: ﴿Do you worship, besides God, that which can neither benefit you at all nor harm you?﴾ [al-Anbiya: 66], and preceding it is the statement of the disbelievers to Abraham in the debate: ﴿You certainly know that these do not speak﴾ [al-Anbiya: 65]. In al-Furqan: ﴿And they worship, besides God, that which neither benefits them nor harms them﴾ [al-Furqan: 55], and preceding it: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord extends the shade?﴾ [al-Furqan: 45], and many other blessings. This type of subtle feature of the Great Qur'an and its clear proofs is evident. The exception here is contiguous (istithna' muttasil; an exception that is included in the preceding category), meaning: "except what God wills of my being empowered with it, for then I possess it, and that is by the will of God." Ibn Atiyya said: "This exception is disjunctive (istithna' munqati'; an exception of something not included in the preceding category), and that is the end of his statement." But there is no need to claim disjunction when contiguity is possible.

* *

﴿And if I knew the unseen, I would have acquired much good, and no harm would have touched me.﴾ That is: my condition would have been the opposite of what it is, in acquiring abundant good, multiplying benefits, and avoiding evil and harm, so that nothing of them would touch me. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿And if I knew the unseen﴾ is the negation of knowledge of the unseen in its general sense, as is narrated from him: "I do not know what is behind this wall except that my Lord informs me." This is contrary to the view of those who claim unveiling (kashf; spiritual disclosure), who assert that by purifying their souls they gain insight into the hidden and can report the events that will occur. How often people claim this, especially in the land of Egypt, to the point that they attribute it to a man smeared with impurity, who spends his entire life without praying, without cleansing himself of his impurity, and who exposes his nakedness to people when he urinates, while being devoid of knowledge and righteous action. Some have specified this generality. Makki related from Ibn ʿAbbas: "If I knew the year of drought, I would have prepared for it from the year of abundance." Others said: "I would have chosen the times of victory." Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj said: "If I knew my term, I would have multiplied righteous deeds." It is also said: "If I knew the time of the Hour, I would have informed you so that you might be certain." It is also said: "If I knew the revealed scriptures, I would have acquired more revelation." And it is said: "If I knew what God wants from me before He informs me of it, I would have done it." These statements and what resembles them should be taken as examples, not as specifications of the general sense of the unseen. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿and no harm would have touched me﴾ is coordinated (maʿtuf; conjoined grammatically) with His words ﴿I would have acquired much good﴾, so it is part of the answer to "law" (jawab law; the apodosis of the conditional clause). This is clarified by the fact that His earlier words ﴿I possess no power to benefit or harm myself﴾ preceded, so He matched benefit with His words ﴿I would have acquired much good﴾, and matched harm with His words ﴿and no harm would have touched me﴾. Also, both of what results from supposing knowledge of the unseen are present: the acquisition of benefit and the avoidance of harm. We did not attach the negative particle (ma) to the answer of law, because the eloquent usage is not to attach it to both, as in His saying: ﴿And if they heard, they would not respond to you﴾ [Fatir: 14]. The apparent meaning is the generality of the news, without specifying the evil. It is said: the evil is their denial of him, even though he was called "the Trustworthy." It is said: it is drought. It is said: it is death. It is said: it is defeat at the encounter. It is said: it is loss in trade. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it is poverty. These statements should be taken as examples and not as an exhaustive list, for the apparent meaning regarding the unseen, both good and evil, is non-specification. It is also said: the speech ends at His words ﴿I would have acquired much good﴾, then He informed that no evil touched him, namely madness, with which they accused him. Mu'arraj al-Sadusi said: "Al-suʾ (evil) means madness in the dialect of Hudhayl." This view disrupts the structure of the speech and limits the answer of law to only ﴿I would have acquired much good﴾, whereas the supposition of knowledge of the unseen entails both matters, not just one of them, so the answer would be deficient.

﴿I am but a warner and a bringer of good news to a people who believe.﴾ When He negated from himself knowledge of the unseen, He informed of what he was sent with: warning, whose object is what is feared, and good news, whose object is what is loved. The apparent meaning is that both are related to the believers, because their benefit and value are only attained by them. He said: ﴿And signs and warnings avail not a people who do not believe﴾ [Yunus: 101]. It is also said: the meaning of ﴿to a people who believe﴾ is that it demands of them faith and invites them to it, and this applies to all people. It is also said: He informed that he is a warner, and the statement is complete, meaning that he is a warner to the entire world. Then He informed that he is a bringer of good news to those who believe in him, so this is a promise to whoever attains faith. It is also said: the object of the warning has been omitted, and the omission is indicated by the affirmation of its opposite. The sense is: a warner to the disbelievers and a bringer of good news to a people who believe, just as the conjoined element is omitted in His saying: ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl: 81], meaning "and the cold." He began with warning because those who asked about the Hour were disbelievers, either the polytheists of Quraysh or the Jews, so the emphasis on mentioning the attribute in His words ﴿I am but a warner﴾ was more important and more fitting to be placed first. And God knows best.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 189–194 (part 1 of 3):

﴿He is the One who created you from a single soul, and made from it its mate, so that he might find rest in her. Then when he covered her, she bore a light burden and went about with it. Then when she grew heavy, they called upon Allah, their Lord: "If You give us a righteous child, we will surely be among the thankful."﴾ ﴿Then when He gave them a righteous child, they assigned to Him partners in what He had given them. But exalted is Allah above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿Do they associate with Him what creates nothing, while they themselves are created?﴾ ﴿And they cannot give them help, nor can they help themselves.﴾ ﴿And if you call them to guidance, they will not follow you. It is all the same to you whether you call them or you remain silent.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those you call upon besides Allah are servants like you. So call upon them, and let them answer you, if you are truthful.﴾ ﴿Do they have feet to walk with? Or do they have hands to strike with? Or do they have eyes to see with? Or do they have ears to hear with? Say: "Call upon your partners, then plot against me, and give me no respite."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 195] ﴿Indeed, my Protector is Allah, who revealed the Book, and He protects the righteous.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 196] ﴿And those you call upon besides Him cannot help you, nor can they help themselves.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 197] ﴿And if you call them to guidance, they do not hear. You see them looking at you, but they do not see.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 198] ﴿Take what is easy, enjoin what is good, and turn away from the ignorant.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 199] ﴿And if a prompting from Satan touches you, seek refuge in Allah. Indeed, He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 200] ﴿Indeed, those who are mindful of Allah, when a passing thought from Satan touches them, remember, and then they see clearly.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 201] ﴿But their brothers (i.e., the devils) keep them in error, and they do not fall short.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 202] ﴿And when you do not bring them a sign, they say: "Why have you not chosen one?" Say: "I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord. This is insights from your Lord, and guidance and mercy for a people who believe."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 203] ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent, that you may receive mercy.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 204] ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and in fear, without loudness of speech, in the mornings and the evenings, and do not be among the heedless.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 205] ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord do not disdain His worship; they glorify Him and prostrate to Him.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 206]

Ṣamata yaṣmutu (صَمَتَ يَصْمُتُ) with a damma on the mim: ṣamtan wa ṣumātan, meaning he kept silent (سَكَتَ). As for Iṣmit (إصْمِتْ), it is a known desert (فَلاةَ مَعْرُوفَةٌ), and it is named by an imperative verb whose hamza has been cut off. This is the rule for naming with a verb that contains a hamzat al-wasl. The mim is kissed because change accompanies change, and so that it does not enter a pattern that does not occur among nouns.

Al-Batsh (البَطْشُ) is seizing with force. Batasha yabtishu (بَطَشَ يَبْطِشُ), with a damma or a kasra on the ta'. Al-Nazgh (النَّزْعُ) is the least movement, and "min al-Shaytan" (مِنَ الشَّيْطانِ) means the least whispering. This is what al-Zajjaj said. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is a movement that involves corruption, and it is rarely used except for the act of Satan, because his movements are swift and corrupting. It is also said that it is the dialect term for a strike that occurs at the time of anger. Al-Farra' said: al-Ighra' (الإغْراءُ) and al-Ighdab (الإغْضابُ) is al-Inṣat (الإنْصاتُ). Al-Farra' said: it is silence for listening. One says naṣata, anṣata, and intaṣata with one meaning. The verb anṣata has also come transitively in the poetry of al-Kumayt, who said:

"Your father is the one through whose aid he was helped, so he silenced every speaker after him against me."

He said: he means "fa-askata 'annī" (he silenced me).

Al-Āṣāl (الآصالُ) is the plural of aṣl (أصْلٌ), which is al-'Ashiyy (the evening), like 'unuq and a'nāq. Or it is the plural of aṣīl, like yamīn and aymān. There is no need for the claim that it is a plural of a plural, as some have held, since it is established that aṣl is singular. Although the plural of aṣīl could be uṣul, making it a plural like kathīb and kuthub. Whoever holds that āṣāl is the plural of aṣl, and that the singular of aṣl is aṣīl, is al-Farra'. It is said: "We came to them muṣilīn," meaning at the time of aṣīl.

﴿He is the One who created you from a single soul, and made from it its mate, so that he might find rest in her﴾. The connection of this verse to what precedes it: when the question of the unbelievers about the Hour and its time was raised, and among them were those who did not believe in resurrection, He mentioned the beginning of the creation of man and his origination, as a reminder that re-creation is possible, just as origination was possible. Since bringing him from nonexistence into existence has occurred in fact, his re-creation is more fitting to occur in fact. It is also said that the connection is this: when He explained those who distort His names and derive from them names for their gods and idols, and commanded contemplation and reasoning that leads to His uniqueness in divinity and lordship, He explained here that the origin of shirk is from Iblis, to Adam and his wife, when they wished for a righteous child. Allah answered their supplication, and then Iblis introduced shirk to them by saying: "Name him 'Abd al-Harith, for he will not die." So they did that. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said, in summary: when He commanded contemplation of the dominion that indicates oneness, and divided His creation into believer and unbeliever, and negated the power of any of His creatures to benefit or harm themselves, He returned to establishing monotheism. End of quote.

The majority hold that what is meant by "from a single soul" (مِن نَفْسٍ واحِدَةٍ) is Adam (peace be upon him). So the address in "khalaqakum" is general, and the meaning is that you branched from Adam (peace be upon him). The meaning of "and made from it its mate" (وجَعَلَ مِنها زَوْجَها) is Eve. As for "from it" (مِنها), it is either from the body of Adam, from one of his ribs, or it may be from its kind, as He said: "He made for you mates from yourselves" [An-Nahl: 72]. These two opinions were discussed in the beginning of Surat al-Nisa' in more detail than this. The report after this sentence is about Adam and Eve, and its explanation will come, God willing. On this opinion al-Zamakhshari interpreted the verse. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi rejected this opinion and refuted it in several ways. First: "Exalted is Allah above what they associate with Him" indicates that those who committed this shirk were a group. Second: He said after it: "Do they associate with Him what creates nothing, while they themselves are created?" This is a rebuttal of those who made idols partners, and no mention of Iblis has occurred in this verse. Third: if the intended one were Iblis, He would have said: "Do they associate with one who does not create?" Al-Razi then mentioned three other aspects from the viewpoint of reasoning, which can be found in his book.

Al-Hasan and a group said: the address is to all creation, and the meaning of "He is the One who created you from a single soul" is: from one form and one shape. "And made from it its mate" means from its kind. Then he mentioned the condition of the male and female of the creatures. The meaning of "they made for Him partners" (جَعَلا لَهُ شُرَكاءَ) is that they distorted him from the natural disposition (الفِطْرَةِ) to shirk, as it has come: "Every child is born upon the fitrah; then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian." Al-Qaffal said something similar to this opinion. He said: He is the One who created each one of you from a single soul, and made from its kind its mate, and mentioned the condition of the husband and wife. "They made for Him partners," meaning the husband and wife made partners for Allah in what He gave them, because at times they attribute that child to natures, as the naturalists say; at times to the stars, as the astrologers say; and at times to idols and images, as the worshippers of idols say. End of quote. On this view, there is no mention of Adam and Eve in the verse.

It is also said: the address in "khalaqakum" is specific, and it is to the idolaters of the Arabs, as they bring the newborn near to al-Lat, al-'Uzza, and the idols seeking blessing in them at the beginning, and they turn their hope to Allah the Exalted at the beginning of the creation of the child until its separation, then they associate partners. Thus astonishment arose from them. It is also said: the address is also specific, and it is to the Quraysh contemporaries of the Messenger (ﷺ). "From a single soul" (مِن نَفْسٍ واحِدَةٍ) means "from it," i.e., from its kind, a female mate, an Arab Qurashi woman, "so that he might find rest in her." The "righteous" (الصّالِحُ) is the sound child. "They made for Him partners" since they named their four children: 'Abd Manaf, 'Abd al-'Uzza, 'Abd Qusayy, and 'Abd al-Dar. The pronoun in "yushrikūn" (يُشْرِكُونَ) refers to them both and to their descendants who followed them in shirk. End of quote.

﴿So that he might find rest in her﴾ means to be at ease and inclined, and not to flee, because a kind is more inclined to its own kind and more comfortable with it. If "from it" is taken literally, then the rest and love are more intense, just as a person rests in his child and loves him with the love of his own self or more, because he is a part of him. The feminine form appeared in "from it" (مِنها) by considering the word "soul" (النَّفْسِ). Then the masculine form appeared in "li-yaskun" (لِيَسْكُنَ) by considering the meaning of "soul," to clarify that what is meant is the male, Adam or another, according to the differing interpretations. The male is the one who rests with the female and covers her, so the masculine form is more fitting to the meaning.

﴿Then when he covered her, she bore a light burden and went about with it﴾. If the report is about Adam, then Eve's creation was in the Garden, but the covering and the bearing took place on earth. "Covering" (التَّغَشِّي), "ghashayan," and "ityan" are euphemisms for intercourse. The meaning of "lightness" is that she did not suffer from it the hardship that afflicts some pregnant women. It may be that "ḥamlan" is a verbal noun, or that it refers to what is in the womb. "Al-ḥamal" with a fatḥa on the ḥā' is what is in a belly or on the top of a tree, and with a kasra it is what is on a back or on the top of something other than a tree. Ya'qub related it in regard to the load of a palm tree, and Abu Sa'id related "khamala" and "hamala" regarding a woman's pregnancy. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the light burden is the seed (المَنِيُّ) that the woman carries in her womb. Hammad ibn Salamah related from Ibn Kathir a reading "ḥimlan" with a kasra on the ḥā'. The majority read "fa-marrat bihi." Al-Hasan said: that is, she continued with it. It was said that this is inverted, meaning "fa-marra bihā," i.e., he continued with her. Al-Zamakhshari said: she went on with it until the time of its birth without any delivery or slipping. It was also said: "ḥamalat ḥamlan khafīfan" means the drop, "fa-marrat bihi": she stood with it, sat, and continued with it. End of quote.

Ibn 'Abbas, as reported by al-Naqqash, and Abu al-'Aliyah, Yahya ibn Ya'mur, and Ayyub read "fa-maratʼ bihi" with a light rā' from al-miriyah (المِرْيَةِ), meaning she doubted what befell her, whether it was pregnancy or illness. It was also said: its meaning is that she continued with it, but they disliked the doubling and lightened it, like "waqarana" for those who read "qarar" with a fatḥa. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As and al-Jahdari read "fa-mārat bihi" with an alif and a light rā', meaning she came, went, and turned with it, as you say: "mārat al-rīḥ mawran" (the wind moved about). Its pattern is fa'ala. Al-Zamakhshari said: from al-miriyah, like His saying: "Will you dispute with him?" [An-Najm: 12]. Its meaning, and the meaning of the lightened form "fa-marat," is: the thought of pregnancy entered her mind and she doubted it. Its pattern is fa'ala. 'Abd Allah read "fa-istamarrat bi-ḥamlihā" (she continued with her load). Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Ibn 'Abbas also, and al-Dahhak read "fa-istamarrat bihi." Ubayy ibn Ka'b and al-Jirmi read "fa-istamarat bihi." The apparent meaning is that it returns to al-miriyah, and he formed istaf'ala from it, just as he formed fa'ala from it in your saying: "marayt."

﴿Then when she grew heavy, they called upon Allah, their Lord: "If You give us a righteous child, we will surely be among the thankful."﴾ Meaning: she entered into heaviness, as you say: "asbaḥa" and "amsā" (he entered the morning and the evening), or she became one who has heaviness, as you say: "atmara al-rajul" and "albana" when he became one who has dates and milk. Al-Zamakhshari said: meaning the time of her heaviness had come, as in His saying: "aqrabat" (she drew near). It was read "uthqilat" in the passive voice. "Their Lord," meaning the owner of their affair, who is worthy to be called upon. The object of the supplication is omitted, indicated by the answer clause of the oath. That is, they called upon Allah and sought from Him that He grant them a righteous child. Then they swore that they would be among the thankful if He gave them a righteous child, because giving a righteous child is a blessing from Allah upon the parents, as has come in the hadith: "The deeds of the son of Adam come to an end except for three," and then he mentioned "a righteous child who prays for his parent." So thanks should be given for it, since it is one of the greatest blessings. The meaning of "ṣāliḥan" (righteous) is obedient to Allah the Exalted, that is, a child who is obedient, or a male child, because maleness is part of righteousness and excellence. Al-Hasan said: they named him "ghulam" (boy). Ibn 'Abbas said: a complete, sound human being. "Wa-la-nakūnanna" is the answer to an omitted oath, its estimate being: "and they swore: if You give us..." or "swearing: if You give us..." The accusative of "ṣāliḥan" is as a second object of "ātaytanā." In al-Mushkil by Makki, it is said that it is an adjective of a verbal noun, meaning a righteous son.

﴿فَلَمّا آتاهُما صالِحًا جَعَلا لَهُ شُرَكاءَ فِيما آتاهُما﴾ *[So when He gave them a righteous child, they ascribed to Him partners in what He had granted them.]* Whoever takes this verse to be about Adam and Hawwa' (Eve) makes the pronouns and reports refer to the two of them. These commentators mention dialogues that took place between Iblis (Satan) and Adam and Hawwa', but these are not established in the Qur'an or in a sound hadith, so I have omitted mentioning them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The pronoun in *ataytana* and *lanakunanna lahuma* and *li-kulli man tanasala min dhurriyyatihima* [refers to the two of them and to everyone born of their offspring]. So when He gave them what they asked for of a righteous, sound child, they ascribed to Him partners. That is, their children ascribed partners to Him, by omitting the *mudaf* (the governed noun, "children") and placing the *mudaf ilayhi* (the noun governed by it, "they") in its position. Likewise, *fima ataahuma*, that is, "in what He gave their children." This is indicated by the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿فَتَعالى اللَّهُ عَمّا يُشْرِكُونَ﴾ *[Exalted is Allah above what they associate with Him]*, where the pronoun is in the plural, while Adam and Hawwa' are free of shirk. The meaning of their associating partners in what Allah gave them is by naming their children 'Abd al-'Uzza, 'Abd Manaf, 'Abd Shams and similar names, instead of 'Abd Allah, 'Abd al-Rahman and 'Abd al-Rahim. End of his words.

In his words there is a dislocation of the speech from its context. Others who took the discourse to be about Adam and Hawwa' held that the shirk was their naming their third child 'Abd al-Harith, since two sons had died before him, both of whom they had named 'Abd Allah. Iblis advised them to name this third one 'Abd al-Harith, and so they named him that out of concern for his life. Thus the shirk they ascribed to Allah was only in the naming. The pronoun in *yushrikun* refers to Adam, Hawwa' and Iblis, since he was involved with them in naming the child 'Abd al-Harith.

It was also said: *ja'ala* (they made) refers to one of them, meaning Hawwa'. Alternatively, the address is to people in general, and the intended meaning of the verse is not the soul and its spouse, Adam and Hawwa'. Or the address is to the pagan Arabs, or to the Quraysh, as previously mentioned. In this case the speech coheres well, without strained interpretation or dislocation.

Al-Suddi and al-Tabari said: Then He informed Adam and Hawwa' in His words *fima ataahuma* and His words *fa-ta'ala Allahu 'amma yushrikun*, which is a separate statement intended to refer to the pagan Arabs. Ibn 'Atiyya said: This is an arbitrary judgment that the wording does not support. End of his words.

The pronoun in *lahu* refers to Allah. Whoever claims it refers to Iblis is far off the mark, because he has not been mentioned. Similarly, it is remote to take it as referring to the righteous child. The shirk was also explained as a share of worldly provision, and that they had been eating and drinking alone before him. Then He resumed: ﴿فَتَعالى اللَّهُ عَمّا يُشْرِكُونَ﴾ *[Exalted is Allah above what they associate with Him]*, meaning the disbelievers.

Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Ja'far, Shayba, 'Ikrima, Mujahid, Iban ibn Tha'laba, Nafi' and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim read *shirkan* as a verbal noun (*masdar*). This entails the omission of a governed noun, meaning *dha shirkin* (possessing a share). It is also possible that *shirk* was used to mean "partner," as in the saying "Zayd is justice" (i.e., Zayd is a man of justice). Al-Zamakhshari said: Or they introduced an association (*ishrak*) regarding the child. End of his words.

The two Akhawan (Hamza and al-Kisa'i), Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read *shuraka'a* in the plural. In this reading it is difficult to apply the verse to Adam and Hawwa', while the other interpretations fit it well.

In the Mushaf of Ubayy: *fa-lamma ataahuma salihan ashraka fihi* [when He gave them a righteous child, they associated it with Him]. Al-Sulami read *'amma tushrikun* with *ta'* (second person), a shift (*iltifat*) from the third person to the second person. The pronoun was in *waw* (plural), and there is a shift from the dual to the plural. The construction of the plural pronoun referring to those who came before has already been explained.

﴿أيُشْرِكُونَ ما لا يَخْلُقُ شَيْئًا وهم يُخْلَقُونَ﴾ *[Do they associate with Him what creates nothing, while they themselves are created?]*. That is: Do you associate with Allah the idols, which are unable to create anything, as Allah creates, while they are themselves created? That is, Allah creates them and brings them into existence just as He brings you into existence. Or its meaning may be: while they themselves are carved and fashioned. Thus their worshippers create them, yet they are unable to create anything, so they are weaker than their worshippers. The pronoun *hum* refers to the meaning of *ma* (what). The pronoun returned to the form of *ma* in *yakhluqu*, and he expressed the idols with *hum*, as if they had intellect, according to the disbelievers' belief about them and in accordance with their names.

It was also said: He used the pronoun for rational beings, because the category of those who worship includes devils, angels and some of the children of Adam, so the rational form was given precedence over every creature of Allah, the Exalted. It is also possible that *hum* refers to what the pronoun of the subject in *ayushrikun* refers to, meaning: these polytheists are created. That is, they ought to take heed that they are created, and so make their god their creator, not something that creates nothing. Al-Sulami read *atushrikun* with *ta'* at the beginning, so it is evident that *hum* refers to what *ma* refers to in its meaning.

﴿ولا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ لَهم نَصْرًا ولا أنْفُسَهم يَنْصُرُونَ﴾ *[And they cannot help them, nor can they help themselves.]* That is: the idols are unable to help those who worship them, nor can they help themselves if some calamity befalls them. Rather, it is their worshippers who defend them and protect them. And how could one who cannot help himself help others?

﴿وإنْ تَدْعُوهم إلى الهُدى لا يَتَّبِعُوكم سَواءٌ عَلَيْكم أدَعَوْتُمُوهم أمْ أنْتُمْ صامِتُونَ﴾ *[If you call them to guidance, they will not follow you. It is all the same to you whether you call them or remain silent.]* The apparent sense is that the address is to the disbelievers, shifting from the third person to the second as a *iltifat* and a rebuke for worshipping other than Allah. What shows that the address is to the disbelievers is His words after this: ﴿إنَّ الَّذِينَ تَدْعُونَ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ عِبادٌ أمْثالُكُمْ﴾ *[Indeed, those you call upon besides Allah are servants like you]*. The object pronoun refers to what these pronouns previously referred to, namely the idols. The meaning is: if you call these idols to what is guidance and right direction, or to guide you, just as you ask Allah for guidance and good, they will not follow you as you wish, nor will they respond to you. That is, they do not have this capacity, because they are inanimate and do not understand. Then He emphasized this with His words *sawa'un 'alaykum*, meaning: your calling them and your silence about them are the same. So how can one who is in this condition be worshipped?

It was also said: the address is to the Messenger and the believers, and the object pronoun refers to the disbelievers. That is: if you call the disbelievers to guidance, they will not accept from you. So your calling and your silence are the same, meaning they have no capacity to accept and no guidance.

The majority of readers read *la yattabi'ukum* with a doubled *ta'* here and in al-Shu'ara': ﴿يَتَّبِعُهُمُ الغاوُونَ﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:224] *[the misguided follow them]*, from *ittaba'a*, meaning: they will not follow your example. Nafi' read both places as *la yatbi'ukum*, unvoweled from *tabi'a*, meaning: they will not follow your traces.

The nominal sentence is conjoined to the verbal sentence because it has the sense of a verbal sentence. The implied construction is *am samattum* (or you are silent). Ibn 'Atiyya said: In His words *adaawtumuhum am antum samitun* he joined a noun to a verb, since the implied construction is *am samattum*. A similar statement is the words of the poet:

*Sawa'un 'alayka al-nafru am bitta laylatan*
*bi-ahli al-qibabi min Numayri ibn 'Amir*

[It is all the same to you whether the tribe departs, or you spend a night among the people of the tents from Numayr ibn 'Amir.]

End of his words. This is not a case of conjoining a noun to a verb. Rather, it is conjoining a verbal sentence to a nominal construction that is implicitly a verbal sentence. The original structure is: *sawa'un 'alayka anfarta am bitta laylatan* (it is all the same to you whether you departed or spent a night). He placed *al-nafr* (the departure) in the place of *anfarta* (you departed). The second clause was nominal to preserve the rhythm of the verse endings, and because the verb suggests occurrence while the active participle suggests stability and continuity. So when a grave matter befell them, they would resort to their idols, and when nothing happened, they would remain silent. It was said: there is no difference between your producing a supplication for them and your persisting in your silence, so they remain in their customary silence, which is a continuous state.

[p. 441]
[p. 442]

﴿Indeed, those whom you invoke besides Allah are servants like you. So call upon them, and let them respond to you, if you are truthful.﴾ This sentence serves as an emphasis on what precedes it, in negating that these idols have any power to benefit or harm. That is: those whom you invoke and call gods besides Allah, who created them and created you, are servants. He called the idols "servants" even though they are inanimate, because they used to believe that they could harm and benefit, and so this required that they be rational (p-443) and "like you." Al-Hasan said that it refers to their being owned by Allah. Al-Tabrizi said it refers to their being created. Muqatil said that the intended people were a group of Arabs from Khuza'a who used to worship the angels, so Allah informed them that they are servants like them, not gods. End of quote. On this view, the statement is an address about rational beings. Al-Zamakhshari said: "'Servants like you' is a mockery of them, meaning: the most they can be is living and rational. If that is established, then they are servants like you, with no superiority between you. Then he refuted that they are servants like you, saying: ﴿Do they have feet with which they walk?﴾ [al-A'raf: 195]." End of quote. But this is not as he claimed, because Allah has judged these who are invoked besides Allah to be servants like those who invoke them. So it cannot be said regarding the statement from Allah that "if that is established, it is established because it is established, and it is not valid to say." Then he refuted that they are servants like you, saying: ﴿Do they have feet?﴾ [al-A'raf: 195], because his saying ﴿Do they have feet?﴾ [al-A'raf: 195] is not a refutation of his saying ﴿servants like you﴾, since likeness is established either in their being created, or in their being owned and subjugated. Rather, that is a belittling of the idols' status, and that they are beneath you in lacking the limbs that were made for benefiting by them, while their being like you in what was mentioned is established. The denial of these limbs does not indicate the negation of likeness in what was mentioned. Moreover, refutation is not conceivable with respect to Him, the Exalted, because it implies the falsehood of one of the two statements, and that is impossible with respect to Allah the Exalted. We have already explained this in His saying: ﴿They are like cattle; rather, they are further astray﴾ [al-A'raf: 179].

Ibn Jubayr read "in" (إنْ) without emphasis, and "servants like you" with fatha on the dal and lam. The exegetes agreed on interpreting this reading as follows: "in" is the negating particle, and it operates like the Hijazi "ma" (al-Hijaziyya, the dialect in which "ma" negates and governs the subject in the nominative and the predicate in the accusative). So it raises the subject and puts the predicate in the accusative. Thus "servants like you" is an accusative predicate. They said the meaning with this reading is belittling the status of the idols and negating their likeness to humans; rather, they are lesser and more contemptible, since they are inanimate things that neither understand nor reason. The operation of "in" like the Hijazi "ma" is disputed. Al-Kisa'i and most of the Kufans permitted it, and among the Basrans Ibn al-Siraj, al-Farisi and Ibn Jinni. Al-Farra' and most of the Basrans prohibited it. The reports from Sibawayh and al-Mubarrad differ. The correct view is that its operation is a dialect, established in both prose and verse. We have explained this at length in the commentary on al-Tashil. Al-Nahhas said: "This is a reading that should not be recited, for three reasons. First, it contradicts the consonantal text (al-sawad, the written text of the Mushaf). Second, Sibawayh prefers the nominative for the predicate of 'in' when it means 'ma', saying 'in Zayd munTaliq', because the operation of 'ma' is weak, and 'in' with its meaning is even weaker. Third, al-Kisa'i held that in Arabic speech it does not mean 'ma' unless it is followed by an affirmative." End of quote. This speech of al-Nahhas is what should not be said, because it is a reading transmitted from a distinguished Successor (tabi'i), and it has a basis in Arabic grammar. As for the three aspects he mentioned, none of them undermines this reading. As for its contradicting the consonantal text, that is a very slight difference that does no harm; perhaps the accusative was written in the dialect of Rabi'a in pausal forms of the tanwin accusative without an alif, so there is no contradiction with the consonantal text. As for what is reported from Sibawayh, the understanding of Sibawayh's speech about "in" has differed. As for what he reported from al-Kisa'i, the report from al-Kisa'i is that he related its operation, and nothing followed it as an affirmative. What appears to me is that this interpretation they gave, that "in" is for negation, is not correct, because the reading of the majority indicates the affirmation that the idols are servants like those who worship them, and this interpretation indicates the negation of that, which leads to the non-correspondence of one of the two statements with the other. That is not permissible with respect to Allah the Exalted. This reading has been interpreted in al-Tashil in a way other than what they stated: that "in" is the lightened form of the heavy "inna," and it operates like the heavy form. It has been established that the lightened "in" may operate like the heavy form in non-pronominal contexts, by the mutawatir reading: ﴿And indeed, all of them (لَمّا) ...﴾ [Hud: 111], and by Sibawayh's transmission from the Arabs. However, in this reading he put its predicate in the accusative, like the accusative of Umar ibn Abi Rabi'a al-Makhzumi in his saying:

"When the darkness of night turns black, then come, and let your steps be light, for our guards are lions."

A group of grammarians went to permit the accusative for the predicates of "inna" and its sisters, and they cited evidences clearly showing the correctness of their position, which the opponents interpreted otherwise. So this irregular reading may be interpreted in accordance with this dialect, or be interpreted according to the opponents' interpretation of the proponents of this view, namely that they took the accusative as implying a suppressed verb, as they said in his saying:

"Oh, would that the days of youth were returning (rawaji'an)."

Its estimate is: "they came returning." Likewise, this reading is interpreted as implying a verb, estimated as: "Indeed, those whom you invoke besides Allah, you invoke servants like you." Thus the two readings agree on one meaning, which is the report that they are servants, and there is no difference between them or contradiction, which is not permissible with respect to Allah the Exalted. It was also read: "in" lightened, with "servants" in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the suppressed pronoun returning from the relative clause to "those whom," and "like you" in the nominative as the predicate. That is: indeed, those whom you invoke besides Allah, while they are servants like you in creation or in ownership. Therefore they cannot be gods. So call upon them, that is, test them by your invocation: does a response come from them or not? The command to "let them respond" is for the purpose of challenging, that is, it is impossible for them to respond, just as He said: ﴿And if they heard, they would not respond to you﴾. The meaning of "if you are truthful" is: in your claim of their divinity and their deservingness of worship, like the saying of Abraham, peace be upon him, to his father: ﴿Why do you worship what neither hears nor sees, nor avails you at all?﴾ [Maryam: 42].

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 189–194 (part 1 of 3):

﴿He is the One who created you from a single soul, and made from it its mate, so that he might find rest in her. Then when he covered her, she bore a light burden and went about with it. Then when she grew heavy, they called upon Allah, their Lord: "If You give us a righteous child, we will surely be among the thankful."﴾ ﴿Then when He gave them a righteous child, they assigned to Him partners in what He had given them. But exalted is Allah above what they associate with Him.﴾ ﴿Do they associate with Him what creates nothing, while they themselves are created?﴾ ﴿And they cannot give them help, nor can they help themselves.﴾ ﴿And if you call them to guidance, they will not follow you. It is all the same to you whether you call them or you remain silent.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those you call upon besides Allah are servants like you. So call upon them, and let them answer you, if you are truthful.﴾ ﴿Do they have feet to walk with? Or do they have hands to strike with? Or do they have eyes to see with? Or do they have ears to hear with? Say: "Call upon your partners, then plot against me, and give me no respite."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 195] ﴿Indeed, my Protector is Allah, who revealed the Book, and He protects the righteous.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 196] ﴿And those you call upon besides Him cannot help you, nor can they help themselves.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 197] ﴿And if you call them to guidance, they do not hear. You see them looking at you, but they do not see.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 198] ﴿Take what is easy, enjoin what is good, and turn away from the ignorant.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 199] ﴿And if a prompting from Satan touches you, seek refuge in Allah. Indeed, He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 200] ﴿Indeed, those who are mindful of Allah, when a passing thought from Satan touches them, remember, and then they see clearly.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 201] ﴿But their brothers (i.e., the devils) keep them in error, and they do not fall short.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 202] ﴿And when you do not bring them a sign, they say: "Why have you not chosen one?" Say: "I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord. This is insights from your Lord, and guidance and mercy for a people who believe."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 203] ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent, that you may receive mercy.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 204] ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and in fear, without loudness of speech, in the mornings and the evenings, and do not be among the heedless.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 205] ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord do not disdain His worship; they glorify Him and prostrate to Him.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 206]

Ṣamata yaṣmutu (صَمَتَ يَصْمُتُ) with a damma on the mim: ṣamtan wa ṣumātan, meaning he kept silent (سَكَتَ). As for Iṣmit (إصْمِتْ), it is a known desert (فَلاةَ مَعْرُوفَةٌ), and it is named by an imperative verb whose hamza has been cut off. This is the rule for naming with a verb that contains a hamzat al-wasl. The mim is kissed because change accompanies change, and so that it does not enter a pattern that does not occur among nouns.

Al-Batsh (البَطْشُ) is seizing with force. Batasha yabtishu (بَطَشَ يَبْطِشُ), with a damma or a kasra on the ta'. Al-Nazgh (النَّزْعُ) is the least movement, and "min al-Shaytan" (مِنَ الشَّيْطانِ) means the least whispering. This is what al-Zajjaj said. Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is a movement that involves corruption, and it is rarely used except for the act of Satan, because his movements are swift and corrupting. It is also said that it is the dialect term for a strike that occurs at the time of anger. Al-Farra' said: al-Ighra' (الإغْراءُ) and al-Ighdab (الإغْضابُ) is al-Inṣat (الإنْصاتُ). Al-Farra' said: it is silence for listening. One says naṣata, anṣata, and intaṣata with one meaning. The verb anṣata has also come transitively in the poetry of al-Kumayt, who said:

"Your father is the one through whose aid he was helped, so he silenced every speaker after him against me."

He said: he means "fa-askata 'annī" (he silenced me).

Al-Āṣāl (الآصالُ) is the plural of aṣl (أصْلٌ), which is al-'Ashiyy (the evening), like 'unuq and a'nāq. Or it is the plural of aṣīl, like yamīn and aymān. There is no need for the claim that it is a plural of a plural, as some have held, since it is established that aṣl is singular. Although the plural of aṣīl could be uṣul, making it a plural like kathīb and kuthub. Whoever holds that āṣāl is the plural of aṣl, and that the singular of aṣl is aṣīl, is al-Farra'. It is said: "We came to them muṣilīn," meaning at the time of aṣīl.

﴿He is the One who created you from a single soul, and made from it its mate, so that he might find rest in her﴾. The connection of this verse to what precedes it: when the question of the unbelievers about the Hour and its time was raised, and among them were those who did not believe in resurrection, He mentioned the beginning of the creation of man and his origination, as a reminder that re-creation is possible, just as origination was possible. Since bringing him from nonexistence into existence has occurred in fact, his re-creation is more fitting to occur in fact. It is also said that the connection is this: when He explained those who distort His names and derive from them names for their gods and idols, and commanded contemplation and reasoning that leads to His uniqueness in divinity and lordship, He explained here that the origin of shirk is from Iblis, to Adam and his wife, when they wished for a righteous child. Allah answered their supplication, and then Iblis introduced shirk to them by saying: "Name him 'Abd al-Harith, for he will not die." So they did that. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said, in summary: when He commanded contemplation of the dominion that indicates oneness, and divided His creation into believer and unbeliever, and negated the power of any of His creatures to benefit or harm themselves, He returned to establishing monotheism. End of quote.

The majority hold that what is meant by "from a single soul" (مِن نَفْسٍ واحِدَةٍ) is Adam (peace be upon him). So the address in "khalaqakum" is general, and the meaning is that you branched from Adam (peace be upon him). The meaning of "and made from it its mate" (وجَعَلَ مِنها زَوْجَها) is Eve. As for "from it" (مِنها), it is either from the body of Adam, from one of his ribs, or it may be from its kind, as He said: "He made for you mates from yourselves" [An-Nahl: 72]. These two opinions were discussed in the beginning of Surat al-Nisa' in more detail than this. The report after this sentence is about Adam and Eve, and its explanation will come, God willing. On this opinion al-Zamakhshari interpreted the verse. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi rejected this opinion and refuted it in several ways. First: "Exalted is Allah above what they associate with Him" indicates that those who committed this shirk were a group. Second: He said after it: "Do they associate with Him what creates nothing, while they themselves are created?" This is a rebuttal of those who made idols partners, and no mention of Iblis has occurred in this verse. Third: if the intended one were Iblis, He would have said: "Do they associate with one who does not create?" Al-Razi then mentioned three other aspects from the viewpoint of reasoning, which can be found in his book.

Al-Hasan and a group said: the address is to all creation, and the meaning of "He is the One who created you from a single soul" is: from one form and one shape. "And made from it its mate" means from its kind. Then he mentioned the condition of the male and female of the creatures. The meaning of "they made for Him partners" (جَعَلا لَهُ شُرَكاءَ) is that they distorted him from the natural disposition (الفِطْرَةِ) to shirk, as it has come: "Every child is born upon the fitrah; then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian." Al-Qaffal said something similar to this opinion. He said: He is the One who created each one of you from a single soul, and made from its kind its mate, and mentioned the condition of the husband and wife. "They made for Him partners," meaning the husband and wife made partners for Allah in what He gave them, because at times they attribute that child to natures, as the naturalists say; at times to the stars, as the astrologers say; and at times to idols and images, as the worshippers of idols say. End of quote. On this view, there is no mention of Adam and Eve in the verse.

It is also said: the address in "khalaqakum" is specific, and it is to the idolaters of the Arabs, as they bring the newborn near to al-Lat, al-'Uzza, and the idols seeking blessing in them at the beginning, and they turn their hope to Allah the Exalted at the beginning of the creation of the child until its separation, then they associate partners. Thus astonishment arose from them. It is also said: the address is also specific, and it is to the Quraysh contemporaries of the Messenger (ﷺ). "From a single soul" (مِن نَفْسٍ واحِدَةٍ) means "from it," i.e., from its kind, a female mate, an Arab Qurashi woman, "so that he might find rest in her." The "righteous" (الصّالِحُ) is the sound child. "They made for Him partners" since they named their four children: 'Abd Manaf, 'Abd al-'Uzza, 'Abd Qusayy, and 'Abd al-Dar. The pronoun in "yushrikūn" (يُشْرِكُونَ) refers to them both and to their descendants who followed them in shirk. End of quote.

﴿So that he might find rest in her﴾ means to be at ease and inclined, and not to flee, because a kind is more inclined to its own kind and more comfortable with it. If "from it" is taken literally, then the rest and love are more intense, just as a person rests in his child and loves him with the love of his own self or more, because he is a part of him. The feminine form appeared in "from it" (مِنها) by considering the word "soul" (النَّفْسِ). Then the masculine form appeared in "li-yaskun" (لِيَسْكُنَ) by considering the meaning of "soul," to clarify that what is meant is the male, Adam or another, according to the differing interpretations. The male is the one who rests with the female and covers her, so the masculine form is more fitting to the meaning.

﴿Then when he covered her, she bore a light burden and went about with it﴾. If the report is about Adam, then Eve's creation was in the Garden, but the covering and the bearing took place on earth. "Covering" (التَّغَشِّي), "ghashayan," and "ityan" are euphemisms for intercourse. The meaning of "lightness" is that she did not suffer from it the hardship that afflicts some pregnant women. It may be that "ḥamlan" is a verbal noun, or that it refers to what is in the womb. "Al-ḥamal" with a fatḥa on the ḥā' is what is in a belly or on the top of a tree, and with a kasra it is what is on a back or on the top of something other than a tree. Ya'qub related it in regard to the load of a palm tree, and Abu Sa'id related "khamala" and "hamala" regarding a woman's pregnancy. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the light burden is the seed (المَنِيُّ) that the woman carries in her womb. Hammad ibn Salamah related from Ibn Kathir a reading "ḥimlan" with a kasra on the ḥā'. The majority read "fa-marrat bihi." Al-Hasan said: that is, she continued with it. It was said that this is inverted, meaning "fa-marra bihā," i.e., he continued with her. Al-Zamakhshari said: she went on with it until the time of its birth without any delivery or slipping. It was also said: "ḥamalat ḥamlan khafīfan" means the drop, "fa-marrat bihi": she stood with it, sat, and continued with it. End of quote.

Ibn 'Abbas, as reported by al-Naqqash, and Abu al-'Aliyah, Yahya ibn Ya'mur, and Ayyub read "fa-maratʼ bihi" with a light rā' from al-miriyah (المِرْيَةِ), meaning she doubted what befell her, whether it was pregnancy or illness. It was also said: its meaning is that she continued with it, but they disliked the doubling and lightened it, like "waqarana" for those who read "qarar" with a fatḥa. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As and al-Jahdari read "fa-mārat bihi" with an alif and a light rā', meaning she came, went, and turned with it, as you say: "mārat al-rīḥ mawran" (the wind moved about). Its pattern is fa'ala. Al-Zamakhshari said: from al-miriyah, like His saying: "Will you dispute with him?" [An-Najm: 12]. Its meaning, and the meaning of the lightened form "fa-marat," is: the thought of pregnancy entered her mind and she doubted it. Its pattern is fa'ala. 'Abd Allah read "fa-istamarrat bi-ḥamlihā" (she continued with her load). Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Ibn 'Abbas also, and al-Dahhak read "fa-istamarrat bihi." Ubayy ibn Ka'b and al-Jirmi read "fa-istamarat bihi."
