The singular was used because He separated His saying ﴿and you see them looking at you﴾ from the conditional clause and resumed the report about their evil state in the negation of seeing, just as hearing is negated. It has also been said that the meaning of His saying ﴿looking at you﴾ is that they face you (*yuhadhuna-ka*), from the expression "the dwellings face one another" (*tatanadharu*) when they are opposite each other, one facing the other. Some of the Mu'tazila (a theological school that held that human reason can determine what is good and evil and that God's attributes are not eternal) argued from this verse that the servants will look upon their Lord but will not see Him. There is no proof for them in the verse, because looking at idols is purely figurative, and the pronoun refers to the idols. This was the view preferred by al-Tabari, who said: The meaning of the verse is to show their lifelessness and the insignificance of their status. He said: The matter was repeated and the verses about it recurred because the affair of the idols and their veneration was firmly rooted in the souls of the Arabs at that time and dominated their minds, as a kindness from God Most High toward them. Mujahid, al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: The object pronoun in ﴿you call them﴾ refers to the disbelievers, and He described them as not hearing and not seeing, since nothing of benefit came to them from listening and looking, and they gained nothing of worth from it. This is a good interpretation, and in it the affirmation of looking is literal, not figurative. The verse after this strengthens this interpretation, for at its end is: ﴿And turn away from the ignorant﴾ [al-A'raf: 199], meaning those who by their nature, when you call them, do not hear, and look at you while they do not see. Thus it is ordered upon the cause that necessitates this, which is ignorance. (p-448)

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 199:

﴿Take what comes easily, enjoin what is customary, and turn away from the ignorant.﴾ This is an address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it encompasses all of his community. It is a command to all the noble qualities of character (makarim al-akhlaq). 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, 'Urwa, and the majority said: that is, accept from people their characters, their wealth, and their companionship with whatever comes to you effortlessly, without strain or constraint. Al-'afw is the opposite of al-jahd (exertion), meaning do not demand from them what burdens them, lest they flee from you. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded this when he said: "Make things easy and do not make them difficult." Hatim said:

"Take the easy from me, and your affection for me will endure; and do not speak in my anger when I am enraged."

Another said: "If a modest provision comes to you effortlessly, take it, for wealth is pasture and drink. When the little agrees and there is peace in it, do not seek the much, for in it is war."

Al-Sha'bi said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked Jibril (peace be upon him) about the words of the Exalted: ﴿Take what comes easily﴾. He informed him from Allah, the Exalted, that He commands you to pardon those who wrong you, give to those who deprive you, and join those who sever ties with you. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, and al-Suddi said: it concerns wealth before the obligation of zakat; he was commanded to take what was easy from people's wealth, that is, what was surplus and in excess. Then zakat was made obligatory and this was abrogated, and it is taken willingly or unwillingly. Makki reported from Mujahid: al-'afw is the obligatory zakat. Ibn Zayd said: the whole verse concerns tolerance toward the disbelievers and not holding them to account, and that was then abrogated by fighting. End of quotation. What appears correct is the first view, that he was commanded with the noble qualities of character, and that this is a continuing ruling among people, not abrogated. This is indicated by the hadith of al-Hurr ibn Qays when he brought 'Uyayna ibn Hisn to 'Umar; he spoke to 'Umar with harshness, and 'Umar wanted to rebuke him, but al-Hurr recited this verse to 'Umar, and 'Umar settled and stopped at it.

Al-'urf: what is known and good of deeds and words. 'Isa ibn 'Umar read ﴿bil-'urf﴾ with a damma on the ra'. The command to turn away from the ignorant is an exhortation to adopt forbearance (hilm), to keep oneself free from disputing with fools, and to overlook what displeases, like the saying of one who said: "This is a division by which the face of Allah was not intended," and the words of the other: "He was your paternal cousin," and like the man who seized his cloak until it cut into his neck and said: "Give me from the wealth of Allah." Al-Bazzar in his Musnad transmitted from the hadith of Jabir ibn Sulaym what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) enjoined upon him: "Fear Allah, and do not belittle any good at all, and that you meet your brother with a cheerful face, and that you empty the surplus of your bucket into the vessel of one who seeks water. If a man reviles you with what he does not know of you, do not revile him with what you know of him, for Allah will make for you a reward and for him a burden. And do not revile anything that Allah has bestowed upon you." Ja'far al-Sadiq said: Allah the Exalted commanded His Prophet with the noble qualities of character, and there is no verse in the Qur'an more comprehensive of the noble qualities of character than this one.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verses 200–202:

﴿If a prompting from Satan should prompt you, then seek refuge in Allah; indeed He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ That is: he pricks you, by bringing you through his whispering to what is not fitting. So seek refuge in Allah from him. Al-'iyadha (seeking refuge) is al-liwadh (taking shelter) and al-istijara (seeking protection). It was said: when the verse ﴿Take what is easy in forgiveness﴾ [al-A'raf: 199] was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "How (can I do that) while there is anger?" Then this verse was revealed. Its connection with what precedes it is evident. The subject of yanza'annaka is nazgh (a prompting), in the manner of their saying "jadda jadduhu" (his fortune was fortunate), or it is an absolute use of the verbal noun, meaning nazgha (he prompted). He concluded with these two attributes because seeking refuge happens through forgetfulness, and it benefits only with the presence of its meaning. So the meaning is: All-Hearing of statements, All-Knowing of what is in hearts. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the verse is a charge from Allah the Exalted to His Prophet that encompasses his ummah man by man. The prompting of Satan is general, covering anger, making sins appear beautiful, acquiring calamities, and other things. In the Sunan of Abu 'Isa al-Tirmidhi, on the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "Indeed the angel has a whisper (lamma), and indeed Satan has a whisper." With this verse Ibn al-Qasim based his statement that seeking refuge at the time of recitation is: "I seek refuge in Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from Satan the accursed." End of quote. Deriving this from the verse is weak, because His saying "indeed He is All-Hearing, All-Knowing" came in the manner of a reason for seeking protection in Allah, meaning: do not seek refuge in other than Him, for He is the One who hears what you say, or who hears what the disbelievers say about you when they wish to anger you, the All-Knowing of your intention in seeking refuge, or the All-Knowing of what their hearts conceal of plotting against you. So He will support you against them and protect you from them.

﴿Indeed, those who were mindful of Allah, when a visitation from Satan touches them, remember, and then they are seeing clearly.﴾ The prompting from Satan is lighter than the touch of a visitation (ta'if) from Satan, because nazgh is the slightest movement, while mass is reaching and striking, and ta'if is what circles around a thing and revolves about it, so it is undoubtedly more intense. Thus the state of the mindful surpasses in this respect the state of the Messenger. Observe the excellence of this eloquence: where the address was to the Messenger, the condition was phrased with in (if), which allows both occurrence and non-occurrence, and where the address is to the mindful, it came with idha (when), which is set for certainty, or for likelihood. On this basis, the prompting may or may not happen, while the touching is certain, or its occurrence is more likely. Mass means contact of the skin, and here it is a metaphor. In that earlier sentence the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to seek refuge, while here the sentence is declarative, containing the condition within it. The predicate "they remember" indicates that the touch of the visitation has taken hold to the point that forgetfulness occurred, so they remember what they had forgotten. The meaning: they remember what Allah commanded and what He forbade. With the very act of remembering, their sight was gained; the sight of truth and rectitude came upon them suddenly, so they followed it and turned away from them the touch of the visiting Satan. As for "mindful" (ittaqa), it was said: it is general to everything one guards against; it was said: it means shirk and sins; it was said: it means Allah's punishment.

Ibn Kathir, al-Kisa'i and al-Nahwiyyan (the two grammarians of the Kufan school) recited ṭayf (with a yā'). This could be a verbal noun from ṭafa yaṭīfu ṭayfan. Abu 'Ubayda recited:

"When the phantom (al-khayal) comes to you visiting (yaṭīf), and its visit to you is a remembrance and passion."

It could also be a lightened form of ṭayyif, like mayt from mayyit, or layn from layyin, because ṭāfa with doubled fā' may be from ṭāfa yaṭīfu or from ṭāfa yaṭūfu. The rest of the Seven recited ṭā'if, an active participle from ṭāfa. Ibn Jubayr recited ṭayyif with shadda, which is fay'il. Al-Farisi inclined to the view that ṭayf is a verbal noun; he made ṭayf like a passing thought (khaṭira) and ṭā'if like a passing thought-bearer (khāṭir). Al-Kisa'i said: ṭayf is madness (lamam), and ṭā'if is what circles around the human being. Ibn 'Atiyya said: how can this be, when al-A'sha said:

"And she becomes in the morning, after the weariness of the journey, as if madness from a visiting jinn had seized her."

End of quote. There is no cause for wonder at al-Kisa'i's explanation of ṭā'if as what circles around the human being with this verse, because the meaning of what al-Kisa'i said is valid in it. If his astonishment and rejection were because the human was specified, then al-A'sha's words are a simile, since he said "as if" (ka'annaha). If his astonishment was because it was explained as what circles around the human being, then "a visiting jinn" can be said to circle around the human. He likened the she-camel, in her speed, vigour, and crossing of deserts with haste, to her state when madness from a visiting jinn seized her. Abu Zayd said: ṭāfa means to come and go, yaṭūfu ṭawfan and ṭawafan; and aṭāfa means to surround the people and come to them from their sides; and ṭāfa al-khayal means the phantom seized, yaṭīfu ṭayfan. Al-Suhayli claimed that one does not say the active participle of ṭāfa for a phantom, saying: because it is an imagining, not a reality. As for "then, when a visitation (ṭā'if) from your Lord visited her" [al-Qalam: 19], it is not said about it "ṭayf", because it is truly an active participle. End of quote. Hassan said:

"A jinn-woman whose phantom kept me awake, which departs at dawn and is seen in dreams."

Ibn 'Abbas said: hamm (a passing impulse) has the meaning of nazgh (prompting). al-Suddi said: al-ṭayf is madness, and al-ṭā'if is anger. Abu 'Amr said: both mean whisper (waswasa). It was said: both mean lamam (a passing touch) and khayal (phantom). It was said: al-ṭayf is palm trees, and al-ṭā'if is Satan. Mujahid said: al-ṭayf is anger; madness, anger and whispering are all called ṭayf, because it is a lamma from Satan. Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr and al-Suddi said: when they slip, they repent. Mujahid said: when they intend a sin, they remember Allah and abandon it. Ibn Jubayr said: when he is angry, he suppresses his rage. Muqatil said: when a prompting touches him, he remembers and knows that it is disobedience, so he withdraws from it out of fear of Allah the Exalted. Abu Rawq said: they supplicate. Ibn Bahr said: they take refuge in the remembrance of Allah. It was said: they reflect, and so they see. All these statements are close in meaning.

Isam ibn al-Mustaliq al-Shami insulted al-Husayn ibn 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) with excessive abuse, and his father as well, since he was hostile to his father. Al-Husayn ibn 'Ali said: "I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. ﴿Take what is easy in forgiveness and enjoin what is good﴾ [al-A'raf: 199], up to His saying ﴿then they are seeing clearly﴾." Then he said: "Be at ease with yourself. I ask Allah's forgiveness for me and for you." He supplicated for him in a lengthy narration, in which there appeared from his noble character, his breadth of chest, and his leaving matters to the decree (qadr) such that it made Isam the most loving of people toward him and his father. That was by his using this noble verse and acting upon it.

Here "mubṣirūn" (seeing clearly) is from insight (baṣīra), not from sight (baṣar). Ibn al-Zubayr recited: "from the Satan, reflect" (ta'ammalū). It could also be a lightened form of ṭayyif, like mayt from mayyit, or layn from layyin, because ṭāfa with doubled fā' may be from ṭāfa yaṭīfu or from ṭāfa yaṭūfu. Al-Jahdari recited "yumadduna-hum," from madda on the pattern fa'ala. The majority recited "la yuqsirun" from aqsara, meaning he refrained. The poet said:

"By your life, my heart is not inclined to her people, nor does it refrain one day so that it comes to me with a ... (qur)."

That is: nor is he withdrawing from what he is in. Ibn Abi Abla and 'Isa ibn 'Umar recited "thumma la yaqsurun" from qasara, meaning: then they do not diminish from their extension and their misguidance. Al-Zajjaj went far in his claim that His saying "wa-ikhwanuhum" (and their brothers), the verse, is connected to His saying ﴿and they cannot help them, nor can they help themselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 192]. There is no need to strain for that. Rather, it is a coherent speech, one part holding to another. When He explained the state of the mindful with the devils, He explained the state of the non-mindful with them. Those (the mindful) were, as soon as a touch from Satan touched them, quick to withdraw immediately; these (the non-mindful) are in continued extension from error, with no withdrawal from it.

Abu Hayyan's commentary (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 203:

﴿When you do not bring them a sign, they say, "Why have you not chosen it?"﴾ It is narrated that revelation would sometimes be delayed for the Prophet (ﷺ), so the disbelievers would say, "Why did you not choose it?" The meaning of the expression in Arabic speech is "you selected it and chose it." Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd and others said: what is meant is, "Why did you not invent it and fabricate it on your own account and from yourself?" The meaning is that all your speech is like this, as Quraysh claimed, just as they said: "This is nothing but a fabricated lie" (Q. 25:4). Al-Farra' said: the Arabs say, "I chose (ajtabaytu) the speech and fabricated it (ikhtalaqtuhu) and improvised it (irtajaltuhu)," when you compose it on your own account. Al-Zamakhshari said: ijtaba al-shay' means "he gathered it for himself," i.e., collected it, like the saying "ijtama'a" (he gathered), or "jaba ilayhi fa-ijtabahu," i.e., he took it, like your saying, "I displayed the bride to him, so he took her in (ijtalaha)." The meaning is: "Why did you not gather it, composing it on your own account?" Ibn 'Abbas also said, together with al-Dahhak: "Why did you not receive it (talaqqayta)?" Al-Zamakhshari said: "Why did you not take it sent down upon you as a demanded sign?" End of quote. This statement of theirs is one of the consequences of being left to persist in error; they would ask for specific signs out of obstinacy, such as turning al-Safa into gold, reviving the dead, and making rivers gush forth. How many signs came to them, which they denied, and then they demanded others.

﴿Say: I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord.﴾ He made clear that the coming of signs is not up to him; rather, he only follows what Allah the Exalted has revealed to him, and he does not invent it or propose it.

﴿This is insight from your Lord﴾, i.e., this which is revealed to me, which I follow and do not originate. It is the Qur'an, "insights" (basa'ir), i.e., proofs and clear evidences by which one sees and hidden matters become clear. It is the plural of basirah, like His saying: ﴿Upon insight I and whoever follows me﴾ (Q. 12:108), i.e., upon a clear and manifest matter. He described the singular with the plural because it contains surahs and verses. It was also said that it is by omission of a noun, i.e., "possessing insights."

﴿And guidance and mercy for a people who believe﴾, i.e., a guide to right conduct and a mercy in both abodes, in religion and in this world. He singled out the believers because they are the ones who gain insight, and they are the ones who benefit from the revelation: they follow what it commands, avoid what it forbids, and believe in what it contains. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Razi said: the origin of basirah is sight. Since the Qur'an is the cause of insights of the intellects in the indication of tawhid (divine oneness), prophethood and the afterlife, the name basirah was applied to it, calling the cause by the name of its effect. People in the knowledge of tawhid, prophethood and the afterlife are of three categories. The first are those who pushed these cognitions to the point where they became like witnesses to them; they are the people of the eye of certainty ('ayn al-yaqin, direct vision of the truth), so for them the Qur'an is insights. The second are those who reached the ranks of those who reason from evidence; they are the people of the knowledge of certainty ('ilm al-yaqin, certainty through demonstration), so for them it is guidance. The third are those who held that belief with firm conviction though they did not reach the rank of those who reason from evidence; they are the general body of believers, so for them it is mercy. Since these three groups are among the believers, He said: "for a people who believe." End of quote. In it there is completion, and some condensation.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 204:

﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent, that you may receive mercy.﴾ When he mentioned that the Qur'an is insights (basa'ir), guidance, and mercy, he commanded listening to it when its recitation begins, and silence (al-insat), which is keeping quiet while giving it attention. This is because that which possesses these attributes of insight, guidance, and mercy is worthy of being listened to, so that the listener may attain these great results and benefit from them: he gains insight out of blindness, is guided out of error, and is shown mercy by it. The apparent meaning is the call to listening and silence whenever the recitation of the Qur'an begins and whenever it is recited. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayrah, Jabir, 'Ata', Ibn al-Musayyib, al-Zuhri, and 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Umar said: it refers to the polytheists, who, when the Messenger (ﷺ) prayed, would say: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it﴾ [Fussilat: 26], so this verse was revealed as a reply to them. 'Ata' also, along with Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Amr ibn Dinar, Zayd ibn Aslam, al-Qasim ibn Mukhayrah, Muslim ibn Yasar, Shahr ibn Hawshab, and 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak said: it refers to the sermon on Friday. This view is considered weak, because the portion of the Qur'an recited in the sermon is small, and because the verse is Meccan, whereas the sermon was not instituted until after the Hijrah from Mecca. Ibn Jubayr said: it refers to silence on the Two Eids, on Friday, and during the parts of the prayer in which the imam recites aloud. Ibn Mas'ud also said: some of us would greet one another during the prayer and speak to one another about their needs, so we were commanded to be silent in the prayer by this verse. Ibn 'Abbas said: he recited in the obligatory prayer, and the Companions raised their voices, confusing him, so the verse was about them. It was also said: it is a command to listen and be silent, since he conveyed the revelation. A group, including al-Zajjaj, said: the intended meaning is neither the prayer nor anything else; rather, the intended meaning of His words "listen to it and be silent" is: act upon what is in it and do not transgress it, like your saying "God heard your supplication," meaning: He answered you. Al-Hasan said: it is general in its application, so wherever the Qur'an is recited, it becomes obligatory on every present person to listen to it and be silent. If the address in His words "listen" is to the disbelievers, then mercy for them is hoped for by listening to it and giving it attention, by it being a cause of their faith; if it is to the believers, then their mercy is their reward for listening, being silent, and acting in accordance with its requirements; and if it is to all, then the mercy of each is according to what befits him. The word "la'alla" remains on its original basis of expressing hope; and it was said: it denotes causation.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 7, verse 205:

﴿And remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and with fear, and without loudness in speech, in the mornings and the evenings, and do not be among the heedless.﴾ . When Allah, the Exalted, commanded them to listen and to be silent when the Qur'an is recited, He elevated from their command to the command of the Messenger (ﷺ) that he should remember his Lord within himself, that is, in a way that he watches over Him and remembers Him in a state that no one perceives, and this is the noble, exalted state. Then He commanded him to remember Him without loudness in speech, that is, to remember Him with a quiet utterance that does not show humility and submission by means of shouting or intense vocalization, just as kings are addressed in private and their favours are sought, and as he (ﷺ) said to the Companions when they raised their voices in supplication: "Indeed you do not call upon One who is deaf or absent; be gentle with yourselves." The speech of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) to the Messenger (ﷺ) was in a low voice, and as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the chambers, most of them do not understand﴾ [al-Hujurat: 4], and the Exalted said: ﴿Do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet, nor speak loudly to him in speech﴾ [al-Hujurat: 2], because loudness indicates indifference to the one addressed, and a display of superiority and a lack of humility. The remembrance includes each of glorification by tahlil (saying "La ilaha illa Allah"), tasbih (saying "Subhan Allah"), and other things. "Humbly and with fear" is in the accusative on the basis that they are objects of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), because remembrance results from them, namely humility in hope of reward and fear of punishment. It is also possible that they are in the accusative as two verbal nouns in the position of a state (hal), meaning: humbly and fearfully, or possessing humility and fear. It was also read as "wa-khifyah" (and in secrecy). The apparent meaning is that His saying "and remember" is addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ); it has been said that it is addressed to every person who remembers. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is addressed to him and includes all of his community. The apparent meaning is that the remembrance is connected to the Lord, the Exalted, because summoning the Sacred Essence is summoning all of its attributes. It has been said that it is by elision of a noun (mudaf), meaning: "and remember the blessings of your Lord within yourself by continuous reflection, so that you do not forget His blessings, which necessitate continuous gratitude." In the expression "your Lord" there is an honour of address and an indication of the kindness that proceeds from the Owner to the kings, which is not hidden. The phrase "wadhkur Allah" or any other of the names was not used; and the word "Rabb" also suits His saying "humbly and with fear," because it explicitly states the station of servanthood. The apparent meaning is that His saying "and without loudness in speech" is a state different from His saying "within yourself," since it is conjoined to it, and conjunction requires difference. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the majority hold that remembrance does not occur within the self and is not realised except by movement of the tongue. He said: this verse indicates it by His saying "and without loudness in speech," meaning this is the rank of secrecy and whispering with the utterance. End. There is no proof in that for what he claimed; rather the apparent meaning is the difference between the two states, and that they are two kinds of remembrance: an inward one and a spoken one. For this reason al-Zamakhshari said: "and speaking words below loudness," because concealment is more conducive to sincerity and closer to the kind of reflection. End. When He mentioned the two states of remembrance and their cause, namely humility and secrecy, He mentioned the times of remembrance. It was said: He intended the specific two times, because they used to pray at two times before the obligation of the five prayers. Qatadah said: al-Ghuduw is the dawn prayer, and al-Asal is the afternoon prayer. It was said: He specified these two for their merit. It was said: the meaning is all times, and He expressed it by the two extremes, which indicate the night and the day. As for al-ghuduw, it was said to be the plural of ghadwah; on this basis the contrast of a singular collective noun with a plural becomes apparent, and the intended meaning is the mornings and the evenings, even though it is the verbal noun of al-ghada'. So the intended meaning of the times of ghuduw is that a plural time is contrasted with a plural time. Abu Mijlaz Lahiq ibn Humayd al-Sadusi al-Basri read "al-iyṣal," taking it as a verbal noun from their saying: "aslatu," meaning I entered the time of asil, so it contrasts a verbal noun with a verbal noun, and it is like "a'sara," meaning he entered the time of 'asr, which is the evening, and "a'tama," meaning he entered the time of 'atamah. When He commanded him to remember, He emphasised that by prohibiting him from being among the heedless, i.e., "let remembrance be necessary for you and do not be heedless for the blink of an eye." It is known that he, peace be upon him, cannot be subject to heedlessness because of his infallibility, so this is a prohibition addressed to him (ﷺ), and what is meant is his community.

[p. 454]

**﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord do not scorn to worship Him, and they glorify Him, and to Him they prostrate.﴾** They are the angels, peace be upon them. The meaning of "with Him" (al-ʿindiyyah) is nearness and closeness to Him, exalted is He, in rank and not in place. This is because they devote themselves to His obedience and seek His pleasure. When God, exalted is He, commanded remembrance (dhikr) and encouraged persistence in it, He mentioned this trait of theirs, and so He informed about them with three reports.

[p. 454] The first: the negation of arrogance (istikbar) in worshipping Him. That is the manifestation of servitude, and the negation of arrogance is what necessitates acts of obedience, just as arrogance is what necessitates disobedience, because the arrogant person sees in himself superiority and distinction, and this prevents him from obedience. The second: the affirmation that they glorify Him (tasbih), which is declaring Him free of imperfection and purifying Him from everything that is unfitting for His holy essence. The third: prostration to Him. It has been said: the fronting of the prepositional phrase (al-majrur), *lahu* ("to Him"), indicates exclusivity, meaning they prostrate only to Him. But what appears to be the case is that he fronted the prepositional phrase so that the verb would fall at the end of the clause (as a *fasilah*, a closing rhyme), and so he placed it later for this reason, to harmonize with what precedes it of the endings of the verses (*ruʾus al-ayy*).

Since worship arises from the absence of arrogance, and worship is of two kinds, inward worship and outward worship, he mentioned both. The inward is glorifying God, exalted is He, above every evil, and the outward is prostration, which is the state in which the servant is nearest to God, exalted is He.

It is related in a hadith: "The heaven has creaked, and it has the right to creak; there is not a space the width of a palm in it where there is not an angel standing, bowing, or prostrating." ﴿And to Him they prostrate﴾ refers to the place of prostration (sajdah). It has been said that the prostrations of recitation (sujud al-tilawah) are four: in Alif Lam Mim Tanzil (al-Sajdah), Ha Mim Tanzil (Fussilat), al-Najm, and al-ʿAlaq. It is also mentioned from Ibn ʿAbbas that they are ten, dropping the last of al-Hajj and Sad, and three in al-Mufassal (the later short surahs of the Qur'an). It is narrated from Malik that they are eleven, dropping the last of al-Hajj and the three of al-Mufassal. From Ibn Wahb, fourteen, dropping the second of al-Hajj; this is the view of Abu Hanifah and al-Shafiʿi, but Abu Hanifah dropped the second of al-Hajj and affirmed Sad, while al-Shafiʿi reversed this. From Ibn Wahb also and Ibn Habib, fifteen, the last of which is the closing of al-ʿAlaq. From some scholars, sixteen, adding the prostration of al-Hijr.

The majority hold that it is not obligatory, while Abu Hanifah said it is obligatory. There is no disagreement that its conditions are the conditions of prayer: purity from impurity (khabath) and from minor ritual impurity (hadath), intention, facing the qiblah, and the proper time. Except what al-Bukhari related from Ibn ʿAmr, and from Ibn al-Munkadir, from al-Shaʿbi, that he would prostrate without purity. Al-Shafiʿi, Ahmad, and Ishaq held that one says the takbir and raises the hands. Malik said: one says the takbir for it in lowering and raising during prayer. As for outside of prayer, there is difference of report from him. And one gives the salam according to the majority, while a group of the early scholars and Ishaq said: one does not give the salam. Its time is all times without restriction, because it is a prayer with a cause; this is the view of al-Shafiʿi and a group. It has been said: as long as the sun has not brightened and has not yellowed. It has been said: one does not prostrate after Dawn prayer nor after ʿAsr prayer. It has been said: after Dawn prayer but not after ʿAsr. These three views are in the school of Malik.

In the Sunan of Ibn Majah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, that he (ﷺ) used to say in the prostration of recitation: "O God, remove from me through it a burden, write for me through it a reward, and make it for me a treasure with You." The well-known position of the school of Malik is that one does not prostrate in an obligatory prayer, whether silently or aloud. The school of Abu Hanifah holds that it is obligatory upon the listener, whether he intended to listen or not.

Praise be to God, first and last, and outwardly and inwardly.
